A pretty fun RTS that somewhat reminds me of Settlers of Catan. No bum rushes, just calculated moves to achieve a victory condition. I really enjoy the  winter mechanic, which adds a survival element. The games are quick, and you can usually beat in a sitting or two, which makes it a great for multiplayer matches.
I wish it was more like AoE in that you have more individual control over your villagers. The just run off on auto pilot a lot, and are generally pretty dumb. The computer AI is otherwise pretty decent, and the combat feels satisfying. Although it seems like they start to gang up on you at times.
Tech tree could use more options, as well as the more varied faction sprites.
All in all a pretty fun game! Can't wait to see the improvements to come. Love the throwback to a classic feeling RTS.

Sleeping Dogs shouldn't be confused with Watch_Dogs as Sleeping Dogs is the older of the two. Even so, if you were looking for Watch_Dogs you should most certainly have a look at this game too.
Sleeping Dogs is another one of those GTA clones, although it manages to stand out on its own with its own mechanics and style. The game is set in modern day Hong Kong where you as an undercover policeman attempt to infiltrate the dark underworld reciding there. It is seems like a cheesy story from a Hong Kong action movie, and that is exactly what it is too, in a good way.
While being a GTA clone there are exciting things to do like kung fu fighting! This mechanic works like the free flowing fighting in the recent Batman games and is quite fun to do. The atmosphere really makes you think Hong Kong as well with neon signs, english and chinese writing as well. The game also stays true to Hong Kong in that you drive on the left side of the road there too.
It was also recently announced the game is going to get a big visual upgrade in order for the game to launch on the new next gen consoles. This will also happen for PC users and will be a free of charge upgrade too.
If you're looking for a fun and differernt GTA clone then Sleeping Dogs would be a very good choice, and a very overlooked game in my opinion.

Northgard is a really good RTS type game that is visually very nice on the eye and plays like a mix of AoE/Settlers/Civilisation... with Vikings. Northgard has a style all of it's own though and is very enjoyable to play. Be prepared to invest a bit of time playing this as Northgard is a strategy game that makes you think where and what you build while you explore the island of Northgard with your Viking clan. It's not always easy to get the balance right on where and what task you allocate your Vikings, but that's the fun part right?
Even at the Early Access stage Northgard is a game that is fun and addictive to play and is constantly getting more polished with frequent updates from the developers ... so it is a game that can only get better as it grows and evolves on it's way to a full release in 2018.
Northgard is definitely a game I recommend.

This game has to be a new low for Bethesda, sh@t has more bugs than a dog living in the streets. The gameworld in itself is pretty nice and there is tons to explore but the rest..... almost looks like they were nearing the end of their deadline and said "f@k it.... people that play our games already know we are the champions of mediocrity, lets not upset them with a game that actually works"
First of all the story is bland, all the while I was playing I kept saying to myself "who the h@ll writes this cr@p ?!"
Quests are "go get this" and "go kill that" and that is about it, the only memorable quest was a murder mystery from a overpriced DLC and that was pretty much copied from a Fallout New Vegas mod. You have to wonder do these people even have imagination to write quests. Hell, every game mechanic seemed to be copied from a New Vegas mod and they did not even try to iron out the bugs. Ah, Kingdom Rush. I've played it since the Armorgames and Kongregate times. I have it on my phone (and its expansion as well!) and now I have it on my Steam account.
This is a tower defense games with quite a relatively small arsenal of towers compared to other tower defense games (4 basic tower types that eventually branch out into 8 different towers at maximum upgrade level). However, despite its simple mechanics, the variety of enemies as well as the level design actually contribute to a very fun game. The great cartoon art as well as a number of memorable voice acting lines don't hurt, as well. ("Reinforce!")
For those not in the know, there are free versions written in Flash that you can access at the above websites, and are available for very cheap (~$1) on mobile. This Steam game is a complete rewrite of the game using Unity. Why should you care about buying this when you can get it for cheaper elsewhere? There are a multitude of reasons, so read on and judge for yourself.
* No microtransactions. The most noticeable difference is that you can get all the heroes on Steam just by playing, whereas on mobile and the Flash versions, you will have to spend way more money than what the Steam version costs to get all of the heroes beyond the three that you unlock with game progression. Granted, the game is designed in such a way that you don't really need to buy heroes to win. (As a note, it appears that the last three heroes have not yet been released on Steam, but will appear in a future update.)
* High-def art and full-screen resolution. The overworld map is much more stylized and beautifully detailed than the other versions. If you don't like playing on a small Flash window or a small mobile screen, the Steam version might be for you.
* Steam Trading Cards and Steam Achievements. If you're into these, then this game is for you. The achievements are of particular note; it is actually not difficult to achieve them, only time-consuming (for a few of them, at least).
* Premium content in terms of maps. There are a bunch of levels and mini-campaigns in this version that you needed to purchase in the other versions. Also, an exclusive campaign will be released in a future update.
Once again, use your best judgment as to the choice between free and paid versions. My recommendation, however, is BUY this amazing game and support the developers.

Definitely a fun little tower defense game that's worth the asking price. The gameplay is fun, some maps are actually tricky, and overall it's pretty well balanced and fair (just ignore the usual forum grumbling of people that don't really pay attention to the enemies and then die to them).
It's a kind of mix between the more passive tower defenses (build everything, watch) and the active ones (build stuff to slow enemies, then mainly kill enemies yourself, such as Dungeon Defenders) and hits a pretty sweet spot there. Your main interaction with the game, aside from building towers, is summoning a pair of grunts that can hold enemies back with a short cooldown, summon a small rain of fire with a long cooldown, and finally command a single hero to move around.
There is no mazing, because your towers aren't built on the lane the enemies walk on, but you can also build a building which spawns soldiers, who will attempt to hold off the advancing orcs, wolves, et cetera.
And it's fun. If you want a pretty relaxed tower defense game that needs you to think some, pick this one. It sure has the gameplay to be worth it.

Summary:
Contains the fundamental goodness of the SF series. Ruined by careless optimization/porting, freemium content, and design direction.
Not worth $60 CAD. Only worth if <$20 CAD.
As a beginner who is entering into the fighting game genre, I would not recommend this particular version of Street Fighter. The delay from your attacks is only obvious after you have played a more responsive game like Skullgirls. IMO playing this version actually has a negative effect of making a noobie spam his attacks hoping the response will go through.
Gameplay:
[+]Combo System
Great if you can pull it off. I do enjoy the difficulty of having more strict inputs compared to skull girls and having to learn what moves can link together.
[+]V-Skills
The V-skill addition is enjoyable. It adds a uniqueness to each character. Particularly in my case I enjoyed Juri's dash and Ryu's counter.
[-]Input Delay
As you have probably read from everywhere, the input lag is very noticable and really inhibits the joy of this game. Imagine playing a MOBA game of around 60ms, you click and theres clearly something wrong, but you can't put your finger on it until you realize the timing of the game is clearly mismatching from what you expected.
[-]Story is subpar
For those who enjoy the singleplayer part. The story is not very interesting. It is alot of build up that gets nowhere and alot of repeated character match ups. Furthermore, there are no cutscenes but there is voice acting, instead you are treated to a story-board style, barely colored, 'cutscene'. If this was the style Capcom was aiming for it heavily falls short compared to SFIV. Otherwise, I would write it off as Capcom cutting the funding/focus on this portion of the game and simply doing only a below-satisfactory job. (C- at best.)
[-]Freemium
I am bias towards these type of marketing strategies. If the game is going to include DLC content that cost money, the base game better be cheap or full of content. SFV is neither.
I find it rediculous that the base game, with so many bugs for PC, is priced at around $60 CAD ($40 USD) (at the time of my purchase). Additionally, the new characters all cost additional money and the 'ingame cash' you can accumulate is hard to come by. You have get a few 'dailies' that reward around 100, and you get some for winning ranked matches, You need a whopping 4000000 or some huge amount to actually buy a character. (It is possible to get around 2 characters for free if you finish all the story possible, repeating the story DOES NOT reward the ingame cash again). If Capcom really wanted to charge for characters, the base game should've at least been priced at around $30 USD.
Technical:
[+]Netcode
In most games I've played, there is no noticable 'lag' if you wanna call it that. Of course, it is quite hard to tell anyways thanks to the input delay, but overall gameplay is consistent.
[-]Terrible Optimization for PC
The game itself on steam is quite terrible IMO. I run a triple monitor setup and I CANNOT alt-tab. If I do the game will eat up all my memory (Win10, GTX980, i5-3570K, 8GB RAM for those who are spec-obsessed). I believe I am well within range of running this game and this issue occurs on low-spec mode. So I can only conclude it is a coding issue on the developer's part.
[-]Fundamental Bugs
If I do a combo challenge, then exit to training mode and put in some inputs, this results in the game crashing from a memory violation. I figure its a coding issue as well since I can't see why this would be due to specs (still occurs when ran as admininistrator).

I am someone people pay, at times, to play games and give serious opinions about them.  With that being said, with my reputation being what it is, I cannot recommend this game in good faith.  As an amateur connoisseur of truly terrible games, however, this game is a treat.  It's cliché, but Rogue Warrior is so bad, it's good.
The premise is a microcosm of my feelings about this game.  You play as Richard Marcinko, best known as the first commanding officer of SEAL Team Six, as he rampages violently throughout Commieland -- namely, North Korea and Russia.  He does this while being voiced by Mickey Rourke, as he swears at enemies in the most juvenile way possible.  When Marcinko's not insulting communism to death, he's shooting or stabbing its followers to death through eight levels.
The graphics seem alright at first, until you realize that this was made in 2009, and that it pales in comparison to graphics in other first-person shooters in that year (MW2, Left 4 Dead 2, Borderlands, etc).  When one starts to play this game, they'll notice other things, too.  By far the worst thing about this game visually is its motion blur -- it is laughably nauseating.  However, when I turned it off, I found out that the motion blur hid some very consistenty blatant screen tearing.  So, it's a pick your poison scenario with this.  The animations are also laughably bad, from the lack of animation moving in and out of cover, to the various melee animations.
Gameplay is similar to Call of Duty.  Run and shoot (or stab) people until you get hurt, then you take cover until you regenerate to full health.  Rinse and repeat.  The objectives, gunplay, and level layout are all so bland and uninspired.  I've had this game crash a few times and encountered numerous bugs.  Multiplayer is predictably dead.  The cherry on top of the fecal cake is that while enduring all of this, I finished this game in less than two hours.  I would normally say that this is a major flaw, but this is no normal game, so I consider it a gameplay feature.
The audio deserves special mention.  I've had the audio cut out numerous times in numerous ways, either via the dialogue cutting out or the entire game audio being muted.  It's a shame this happens, because what puts this game over as a truly bad game you should play is its dialogue.  I cannot believe a AAA publisher (Bethesda) released a game with this dialogue.  I cannot believe Mickey Rourke got paid to say these lines.  I cannot believe I played a game like this.  The dialogue is so laughably bad, it truly does give the game that je ne sais quoi charm only found in these types of horrible games.  It all culminates in the end credits, which MUST be experienced.  It is one of the low points in gaming history, that I can think of anyways, and it is glorious.
If you're the type of gamer that considers games art and/or expects quality out of the industry, then you should pass on this game.  That being said, if you're on a Steam sale binge, and you're looking for one of the true mistakes in gaming history, play this game at your own risk.  It is that hilariously bad.

This is basically the closest it gets to Cube World, which some might remember as a voxel game with a lot of potential that just stopped getting updates.  Trove hasn't stopped getting updates, and while it's different in many ways it's a great alternative and is fun in its own way.
I only recently started playing it again.  I've had it since it was announced, jumped in early with a founder pack, but stopped playing a bit because at the time it didn't pull me in and just didn't seem to have a lot to do.  Now it has lots of worlds, enemies, activities, and loot, and a bunch of classes to play around with.  There's also a ton of collectibles, from gear to mounts and pets to decorations, and they're pretty much the main drive to play.
My favorite feature is actually pretty unique to Trove.  Every player gets their own personal living/building space, called a "cornerstone".  These are permanently saved, whether you're subbed or not, and you can bring them with you wherever you go as long as there's an unclaimed parcel (which are scattered throughout the various areas of the game).  Just find one, interact with the sign, and your home pops into existence.  For a larger, more permanent home, you can create a club, which is expensive but effectively gives you your own server to expand and build in.
I also appreciate the F2P model Trion uses.  The push for lootbox purchases isn't as strong as the push for packages of unique content.  If you don't pay anything you'll still receive a pretty regular flow of all kinds of loot, some of it just for collecting loot, with pretty decent login rewards on top of everything.
Sometimes in chat I see players complaining about the changes to Trove over time.  Maybe I'd appreciate that more if I had been playing more consistently, but it seems like most of the changes, in addition to all the content added over time, ended up being for the better.  New players in particular have a much better starting experience than anyone who was playing back when it was more of an early access game.

Great pixel art and what looked to be a touching story about the relationship between a dog and his boy initially drew me to Balthazar's Dream. It being an indie title with a lot of heart put into it by a small team also made me want to show support. The game as it is, unfortunately, is a clunky, average platformer lasting a brief 100 minutes; its touching story is ham-fisted and poorly-written; the level design and mechanics range from solid (bouncing around, general platforming) to nearly broken (throwing items, using 'instinct' to long jump).
I think the story was the biggest letdown. It starts off well enough, if a bit predictable a scenario -- you're playing this for easy tears, right? Your master, a young boy named Dustin, is hit by a car during a game of fetch. You -- Balthazar, his dog -- stay with him in the hospital as he slowly passes, keeping him company on his journey via a shared dream. For the most part, it's told in a barebones and surreal fashion, but then the ending just gets lost in itself as it pulls an Interstellar, using the -- **spoilers** -- 'Power of Love' to save Dustin's spirit from a monster literally called Guilt Incarnate. After having the Power of Love spelled out to the player repeatedly in a short timeframe, we get a closing text epilogue that smears in complete nonsense, each addition more absurd and poorly-written than the last:
"Not only was Dustin alive and kicking -- he woke up with an amazing ability to understand and talk to Balthazar. Needless to say both led happy lives and had loads of fun."
"Using Balthazar's oneiric superpower they woke 3182 coma patients. They retired after 30 years of therapeutic work (longevity miracle drug for dogs was invented)...To a serene farm in Oregon."
"...In fact, Balthazar's grandgrandgrandson Salazar was the first cyber dog on a Mars colony in 2343. He was instrumental in the famous search and rescue mission of the DSS Pupperprize."
None of this adds *anything* to the story, and each sentence is somehow more insane and poorly-written than the last.
The pixel art is Balthazar's Dream's best asset. The dog breeds you can play as have plenty of character and detail -- the Australian Shepard also looks spot-on like my dog! -- as do the world's forests and enemies.The music, while good, is primarily composed of short, 10-second loops that quickly grow tiring. The 10 levels range from unusually brief to painfully long (e.g.., the first level is something like 20 minutes, and the second or third only 2; levels 8 and 9 are two overlong, boring shmup levels that play the exact same and probably shouldn't be back-to-back), and the level design itself is all over the place. Bouncing off of mushrooms and beds makes for great platforming, but trying to make a floating table fall on top of your doggy for cover, or throw a stick at just the right spot on a wall to provide a platform almost comes down to random luck, making for tedious segments in an otherwise enjoyable game.
Balthazar's Dream is a forgettable platformer with occasional charm in its artstyle. It's not worth playing, but I feel like the devs are worth paying attention to if they continue to refine their skills over the next 150 years (human lifespans will evolve to 180+ years by 2038 and everyone will live happy lives and have lots of fun).

Sanctum 2 is a fantastic Tower Defense game. I've played a lot of TD games, and after a while they start to just get repetitive. Sanctum 2 keeps the gameplay fresh by upping the difficulty, offering huge amounts of customization, and by placing you directly in the path of your enemies. There are many weapons to equip and switch between, each offering their own strengths and weaknesses. The characters themselves are different, each focusing in different play styles. Some characters are good at crowd control, others excel at sniping enemies. You get many different types of towers to equip before you start playing the game, and these towers, in combination with others, can drastically help you on the battlefield or blow some enemies away. The game lets you play how you want, and I love it for that. Each map is different, and requires you to think before you place blocks and towers to alter the path enemies will take. The level-up system offers new perks and weapons with each level, and the levels come easily, depending on the difficulty you play at.
Overall, it's a great game that lets you be you and really brings out your inner gamer. Every time I lose I want to go back in with a new setup and see how I can make it work that time. I highly recommend this to fans of Tower Defenses or First Person Shooters in general.

Nearly everything about this game to me was enjoyable and fun. It looks good, runs well, and plays well. I found myself hooked after a very short amount of time and did not take long to purchase a copy for SO to play with as well.
I would recommend this game if you are a fan of CIV and tend to get bored by more in depth alternatives like EU5 or even Total War. This of course might be precisely a reason for some people to not purchase this game as well. It's easy to learn as the curve is short, the options for you to take might also become limited over time.
The replay value of this game is great but I imagine only in short bursts, otherwise you grow bored. It's the kind of game I'd imagine a friend or two can make a night of and not revisit for a while after that. It's a board game and even with a large map a fairly quick one at least compared to CIV or other options. This is what I would argue makes it so appealing to people who do not have the time to invest in a complex game but want some sort of strategy world dominating kind of game.
The balance and progression of this game I would argue is solid. It really gives the CIV 5 vibe as you balance hunger/growth and happiness with your people and prepare against invaders either AI, friends, or just random enemies like wolves or goblen like creatures (dragur? or something to that extent).
As for suggestions to make this game excellent I would only request steam workshop capabilities. I imagine people tweaking the aesthetics, the classes, the buildings and monsters. You could swap in Nordic creatures for Greek or Egyptian, A Song of Ice and Fire and Lord of the Rings. Augment the weapon types and companions and suddenly you have a very exciting and rich gaming experience at you fan-bases fingertips. The possiblities could be endless with a modding community.
This game even at this state deserves a great deal of praise and I hope the developers keep at it. No doubt worth the $20 for anyone who enjoys a less meticulous strategy game.

It is a great game for the price I paid, while the game was on sale, I don't remember how much it was, but it wasn't that much for me to pay that much attention...
However, nonetheless I tried the game before purchasing it, I completed the first two missions, the game has nine.
After laughing for about the 15 minutes or so it took to complete my "demo" I bough the game immediately.
And didn't complete it until now.
Probably the biggest complaints I have about it is two things:
1.- The game is locked at 58fps, without the ability to unlock it, nor can you alter the refresh rate at higher resolutions than 4:3, I tried to change this using "SpecialK" a program specifically design to fix this in plenty of games, but for this one, it didn't work, it kept crashing before I could even install it in this particular game.
2.- The game is incredibly short, about 40 minutes or so...
It is a shame, because the game has been "panned" by almost everyone that has played it, and their arguments against this game are reasonable.
The game has a terrible voice acting, terrible dialog, it is incredibly short (as I said), the gameplay generally is incredibly simplistic, and repetitive in the sense that it requires you to do the same things over and over again.
But for me personally, it ended up being a very wonderful, and enjoyable experience, a fantastic one at that.
I found the incredibly "foul mouthed" dialog to be hilarious, every time I heard Mickey Rourke voice say something worthy of one of those fanatical advertisements from the cold war era, I would laugh histerically, if not, internally.
Then there was the gameplay, the levels are diversive enough superficially, in terms of their aesthetic, but more importantly, they're simple to explore, and complete.
The game is incredibly linear, but I enjoyed because of it, it gives the game a certain amount of "flow".
Then the gunplay feels great, even if there's not more than around six weapons or so in the entirety of the game.
The game is quite violent, which is something I really like, you can, in some areas, play the game silently, and, or, stealthily, sneaking behind enemies and executing them in brutal ways, all of them limited, and repetitive, but equally as satisfying, I enjoyed them a lot, they're just the right amount of silly, as they are, "bloody".

Rogue Warrior could have been just a forgettable generic shooter amidst a tide of them back in 2009. Instead, the designers made the fatal mistake of trying to inject an over-the-top personality into their lead, wrote a story that made little sense, and made the shooting itself unimpressive and unsatisfying. Some people may be tempted to look up this game to hear the streams of cursing and obscenity that spews forth from Marcinko courtesy of Mickey Rourke, but the lines are repeated so often that you’re better off just thinking up a bunch for yourself and saying them out loud in an angry voice. Don’t worry, this game assured me that as long as you’re cursing people out loudly enough, they won’t hear you, and then you can sneak up on them and kill them in a way that will leave their corpse clean enough to put in the funeral casket immediately.

Everything Rogue Warrior tries to do it, it does it wrong. The cursing doesn’t make Marcinko seem hard, it makes him seem juvenile and pointlessly angry. The cover system is pointless compared to constantly crouching, and the machine gun is so good at what it does and ammo so common that weapon variety is meaningless. Stealth sections have no thrill since they’re set up perfectly for it with no challenge to pulling off the killing moves, and the killing moves themselves end up equally as repetitive as the voice lines. Coupled with a plot written about a guy with military experience by people who seem to have no understanding of the military, and you’ve got yourself a game that went from run-of-the-mill shooter to a game that stands out as awful in a genre that is full of generic and uninspired games.

McPixel is a point-and-click adventure game with a very simple premise: in each stage, prevent a bomb from exploding within 20 seconds. The gameplay usually consists of interacting with various things on the screen and figuring out what the solution is, usually by deduction (there aren't that many possbilities per stage). If you lose, no problem. The pace is pretty quick, so you'll be back in the action soon enough. It's definitely a refreshing take on the genre, sort of like Half-Minute Hero.
A major part of this game is the crude humor. There's a ton of it. This is the sort of game that a 13-year-old boy would love to play but probably shouldn't. That said, I enjoyed the humor quite a bit. When you interact with something, the character normally tries to be a huge jerk. The default interaction with people is to kick them in the groin (male or female). If you're holding something, you'll probably hit them in the face with it too. McPixel rarely does what you expect him to, and that's a lot of what's so funny about the game.
The graphics are bad, but still charming. The music is a little grating. The controls are simple and effective. Keep in mind that this is a short game. I finished it 100% in three hours. Overall, I'd recommend McPixel if you find it cheap, especially for adventure game fans. It's not a bad way to spend an afternoon.

TLDR: While it has the same classic gameplay as original Street Fighter titles, the lack of content is inexcusable.
I played Street Fighter IV back when it first came out quite a bit and while I was never very good I still had fun playing it. The stylized graphics and soundtrack were both high points and it had very solid gameplay. Now comes Street Fighter V which has almost identical features so one should reason that its at least as good, right? Wrong.
The game is a carbon copy of Street Fighter IV with a few exceptions. The storyline mode is a DLC which, if you have to wait to download instead of it just downloading with the rest of the game. This may not be that bad, generally just requiring some patience, but it is annoying. On the other hand, the lack of playable characters in the start is the heaviest weight attatched to this game. You get a few characters which come standard, but then there are a whole host of characters which you must purchase seperately. This wouldn't be too bad if it was a couple of special characters but this is used with almost half of the characters including some high-profile main characters like Guile, and Balrog. As if this wasn't bad enough there are also stages which must be purchased as well. There are a total of 22 stages and half of these are a DLC purchase.
If you have the disposable income to spend to unlock half of a game which you must pay a full $40.00 (USD) for at the beginning anway and are a massive Street Fighter fan, then go for it. Otherwise I would ignore this and just get the last version of Street Fighter IV.

This game was one of my most highly anticipated releases among the already massive list of gargantuan AAA games that we're getting this year and I can't say I'm disappointed in the slightest. I was a backer for Balthazar's Dream on Patreon as well as Kickstarter and I got to speak with the developers about their creative process and vision for what they desired from the final product and I'm glad they've achieved what they set out to do. This game is very short, only about three hours of gameplay and it lacks what you'd expect from your average indie platformer (not many hidden secrets and no collectibles).
However, what this game does possess that I haven't seen in an indie platformer in a very long time is a gripping and charming narrative that kept me intersted and wanting more until the very end, accompanied by a beautiful musical score that honestly sets the tone for this game so well that I can't even begin to think of words that might do justice to the soundtrack. The pixel art is absolutely breathtaking and believe it or not, was done by a single person and you can tell that they've poured their heart and soul into it. Environments are sort of contradictory in the sense that they're static but full of life at the same time and I think they've pulled that off extremely well.
This review is meant to be completely spoiler-free and all I choose to mention is that in Balthazar's Dream, you play as a dog journeying across ten levels, accompanied by the ghost(?) of his owner, who he's been faithful to since the day he was a young pup. The game kicks off with a beautifully animated and emotional cutscene that sets the general tone for the direction of the story and the dialogue between the man and his dog (if you'd consider barking in different tones to be properly structured dialogue, of course) really showcases the strength of the bond that the two have formed over the years and takes you on a journey as you find out more and more about the memories that they've made together.
The gameplay itself, I found to be extremely enjoyable but I would highly recommend a controller if you're going to play this game. My first playthrough was done with a controller and I did try playing through with a keyboard on my second but it wasn't nearly as enjoyable. One of the reasons I played through the game multiple times aside from my love for this gem is so that I could try and find any bugs that I might be able to notify the devs about and I was very happy to find out that across three playthroughs, I had only found one recurring minor bug involving text boxes and have spoken to the devs about what their plans are for the future of Balthazar's Dream.
Needless to say, any and all minor bugs are going to be removed from the game very soon and the devs have also stated that they're looking into implementing achievements and trading cards; both of which the game lacks at the time of this review but I personally don't have a problem with this because of the small time frames and lack of people and resources that they've had throughout their development process. Despite being a game packaged into three hours, it feels so complete and every component flows together so well that I can't bring myself to complain about the price tag on here. I wanted to show as much support to the developers as possible so I bought the game on Steam before asking them for my  keys and I honestly don't regret it at all. This game doesn't do anything groundbreaking from a gameplay standpoint but it's an experience like none other and I'd recommend that you pick it up if you've ever got nothing to spend money on and a few hours to kill. Personally, if there's anything more I'd want from this game aside from achievements and trading cards, it's that the soundtrack should be available for purchase on Steam. It's currently available on bandcamp but I feel that it would probably recieve more attention if it were available on the same platform as the game.

I always liked Doom 3 well enough, but the VR mod
REALLY brings the game alive in ways that make it a better VR game than most games designed with VR in the first place--the "spooky" funhouse horror stuff that was a bit cheesy on the 2D screen actually kind of plays in VR--huge spiders jumping at the screen becomes a huge spider JUMPING AT YOUR DAMN FACE, those kinda-fiddly-but-cool touchy interfaces that were always in the game are actually really fun with to mess around with in a virtual 3D space with motion controls--you just point at the buttons like you would if you were actually there. It even kind of retroactively justifies the initial decision to have a limited flashlight--dark corridors with demons in them are WAY cooler and sometimes genuinely scary in the VR environment, and even more so if you leave the flashlight off here and there. It's a shame so many games for VR aren't willing to let the player just fully move around in them--it might sound super uncomfortable, but I actually feel fine in this game with the 45-degree comfort turning and all other comfort settings off, and the result feels like exploring an actual mars base in a way that wouldn't be nearly as immersive if you were limited to static/teleport movement like so many other VR games tend to use. The game uses this weird partial Resident Evil-ish third person view by default, but you can (and should) turn it off to be just normal dual analog first person setup in terms of movement and camera, but with virtual/motion control gunplay and in-world interfaces that work just like you would hope. (Even the e-mail/audiolog stuff on the PDA, there's this Dead Space hologram setup there that is really cool to play with.) My only big complaints are occasional crashes (again, it's an unfinished mod), and that the "Fist" weapon still just works as a "push the attach button to active the fist attack" kind of setup, when I want to punch demons all GORN style. (The chainsaw works exactly like you'd hope, though. Yes, it is very cathartic and probably kind of unhealthy.) If you have arachnophobia, stay the HELL away from the VR mod, otherwise this is the best VR thing yet.

Remember Aliens? This is basically a video game adaptation of it. I wonder if they had the Aliens license and the deal fell through so they just made it a Doom game instead.
Either way, they aim for atmospheric alien base with creatures sneaking up behind you in this iteration. And by sneaking I mean that they always spawn behind you. Since you can kill creatures while they're spawning, whenever you hear the auditory cue just turn around and kill it as it spawns. The rooms are really small so you can't miss them, and enemies don't spawn simultaneously/there aren't more than 5 in a room so it's not too difficult.
The atmosphere consists of the same metallic sort of grey textures so by 'atmosphere' what I really mean is that everything is dark and you'll likely strain your eyes like I did. What hurts more is that everything is so cramped so that a little under half the time you're looking at walls...or at least trying to if there is no light source (there is no lightsource).
Adding to the atmosphere are audio logs strewn about that are updated into your PDA. You get emails and audio logs about employees bit*hing about their jobs and talking about their departments (we need to fix the gas leak; the energy capacitor is going well) but no actual world or lore building. It's all inconsequential stuff that does nothing for the world other than having you acknowledge that there were multiple people in this base that worked in various departments, but what actually occurs in this world isn't delved into as much as fixing the toilet in sector 3G. There were some funny logs but otherwise...meh.
We have established that there is a martianbuddy company that sends junk e-mail to people. Otherwise go through the messages and emails to listen to their locker combinations for supplies.
The plot is....oh who cares about plot its Doom. The funny thing is they sort of tried something here but it sorta of falls flat. A third of the game is "catch up with the marines" and you'll always see them in the distance every now and then running about. You never catch up to them and its almost comedic how close they are to you. The constant prompts about "catching up to bravo squad" or whatever are also funny. You've been telling me that for 5 hours now dude I get it, the devs needed to give me something so they have you chiming in every 20 minutes to remind me that there's an objectove.
I feel like I'm being harsh on the game, because I am. But I do wanna say it isn't a bad game, not necessarily. It's fine, there's nothing wrong with it. It's just very drab and uneventful, and I feel that the technological limitations of the time really brought it down. Its apparent when you actually see the models up close; clearly all the DARK was meant to hide the technological limitations of the time....and this version is actually improved on the graphical front. Additionally, all the corridors and small rooms are probably due to tech allotation placing more emphasis on environments and creature detail rather than enemy count and wider spaces.
If this game was released more recently odds are it would be better purely on tech allowing for more. This is the BFG edition so keep in mind that this is actually with the brightness increased.
It's not a bad game. It's just not a game I would recommend. You can play Doom 2016, Shadow Warrior 1 and 2, Sonic Mania, Nier or Metal Gear Rising, etc. With over 200 or so games released a year (I assume) there's a ton of sh*t to play and your time is better spent elsewhere.

It allows you to be creative and imagative in the fallout setting, while making you work to find all the materials needed to make that giant sniper tower or the  ♥♥♥♥♥♥  made out of Neon lights. In fallout 4, those random items that you'd find like brooms, steam gauge assemblies, scrap metal, etc, become incrediably usefull and no longer are just filler items that bother you while you look for ammo. Instead of being packed down with every weapon in the game taking all your weight, you instead become a hoarder of postwar junk , taking it home to turn it into whatever you desire (kinda , mods open up opportunitys however i havent tried any)
The Weapon customization is fantastic (to an extent) and allows you to make a lot of unique weapons with characteristics and mods that you would prefer, although if you just come from playing Fallout New Vegas you will be incrediably dissapointed at the lack of: options, durability, weapon variety, etc. you will also miss fallout NV's detailed and researched/thought-out reload animations , in that Fallout 4 has very dissapointing and annoying reloads (looking at you far harbor Lever action rifle, why is it that i need to reload all 5 rounds in a tube magazine when i only shot 1 round)
The Power armor system is brilliant, with a good amount of customization again available. Fallout 4 also makes Power armor feel like actual suits, with great animations and the requiring power supplies (fusion cores) to use it. Instead of just another armor/clothes option, power armor becomes a full on suit that requires you to enter, exit, power, and maintain it. (side note, after 200+ hours or less for some, a variety of methods to farm items at settlements youve built to make caps allows you to have plenty of fusion cores available allowing you to never not be in power armor if you desire. this however can get boring as you become almost invincible and makes the game less of a challenge and boring)
Even on a potato computer, the graphics are great and are an improvement over previous fallouts, and on a decent or amazing computer the graphics are stellar. On a potato computer you may experience crashes commonly though so unless you love the game as much as i do to deal with it, make sure you can afford decent/average hardware  as this isnt a 2010 fallout new vegas but a 2016 Fallout game.
For previous fallout fans the music is great, although those who played fallout 3 will become bored of it faster as they recycled a few songs from fallout 3 sadly. On the rare occasion that you turn off the radio, the environmental music is great and has great orchestral tracks.
The environmental setting is fantastic, with a real fealing of being in the massachusetts commonwealth area, and the inclusion of weather is an amazing addition that adds to the games feel.
The games varying companions are ok , with a few being much better as far as interaction and story goes [looking at you Nick valentine]
One VERY major dissapointment is the DLCs. compared to Fallout 3 and NV, Fallout 4s DLCs are a giagantic  letdown and are either very short, small, useless, or have dissapointing stories. Nuka world for example costricts your options to experience the DLC if you dont want to become a ******* Raider , and the Workshop DLCs include items that should have just been included in the main game from launch. Far Harbor is amazing and the only real amazing DLC that i wish was longer, as it has a great story,setting, weapons,etc. Automatrons robot building option is very useful, however the story is lackluster and is in the main map area instead of a new location.

Left 4 Dead is a zombie-themed cooperative (or competive) team FPS made by Valve and Turtle Rock Studios, released in 2008 for PC. You play as one of the four survivors who have to get from point A to point B, while defending themselves from hordes of 'fast' zombies and search corners for supplies. Or you can play as special infected too, in more competive mode. Don't mind "Game of the Year Edition" over the banner, it's just there for coolness, not some complete edition. It did have three "free DLC" / big updates that added survival mode, Crash Cource and Sacrifice campaign since it came out.
Multiplayer community is still quiet alive, even though most moved over to Left 4 Dead 2. You will not always find exactly what you want, but you will still find some people playing the game. Aside from Survival mode, that part is empty, everybody was overrun by zombies it seems.
And well, it's a pretty great game. It got great setting, with a great atmosphere of always being set at night. With four likable characters. Simple yet deep gameplay. It is simple compared to L4D2, you don't have much choice, variations, in weapons for example. Feels more refined too. Somehow I dig it more. It even has two grenade types, which are actually useful and tactical in this horde based game.
The best thing about it is AI Director. In other words, it's a system that keeps track of players "stress level" and then would change position of items, zombies and other small changes. It's quiet clever in that it both serves as randomizer and also follows general rules of pacing. No, it's quite predictable. Moment of rushing zombies and wandering zombies change around, when it gets quiet that it means that something heavy is coming or that you barely survived previous challenge. And that it doesn't spawn zombies so good, so in Versus modes people just rush forward.
And while it's predictable, the different pacing still makes it much more addictive. The question is not what, but how soon and when.
But there is one thing which would make it hard to decide if to recommend it or not. All the campaigns ended up being included in L4D2! Not only that, but they were expanded with all the new stuff that L4D2 added. Weapons, special infected types. Not only that, but if you want more original experience, then you can run the mutator that limits content back to L4D1. Though it's a bit uneven. But still.
The only different things would be nitpick, like some slight level alternation, or not being able to see your body when moving camera down, or if you hate watching flying gibs from explosion for some reason.
And well, most people should just purchase L4D2 instead, as it has all that L4D1 got. The first one still has it's own appeal, to be honest, in small changes. Very small differences. But eh, leave it to purists of sorts. Otherwise, if you are core gamer of sorts, then buy it, It's awesome game by itself.

A magnificant example of the genre. Easy to learn, tought to master, like chess. This game is polished to a shine, and balanced to perfection. Being a big fan of Tower Defense games, balance is always an issue for me. Not so here. Everything has been carefully weighed and priced (via gold to buy towers) to make it seem tough but fair. The early levels teach you everything, and it slowly escelates into an all-out rage-war that will leave you screaming and hitting the "try again" button because you were so close to winning that time. Its addictive, has a steady (though unforgiving near the end) learning curve, and the boss characters that show up are just amazing. Its packed with easter eggs (perhaps a few too many, each tower has recognizable lines and there are things hidden on EVERY map), good dialogue and excellent voice acting. You even unlock more levels when the campaign is over. Worth every penny of my mere $10 that I had to pay to get it. Two thumbs WAY way up, this is a buy!
EDIT (After Finishing the Game)
=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=
So, having finally finished 100% of the game, gotten all the achievements and such, I have to lean back and philosophize for a bit. So, what is the general thought when it comes to this game as a whole? I wonder why barracks just become useless over time. That's 1/4 of the game right there. I wonder how much work went into balancing such a wonderful game, and how many hours got devoted to making it just so, because it shows and I love it. I still like to gush over the Citedal, Fungal Forest and the Rotten woods-- those are my favorite levels by far.
My favorite hero is Thor, though to beat some of the harder levels you simply have to change heroes. Which makes sense, I think.
I got over 40hrs of solid entertainment out of this, and it is certainly worth ever penny I paid for it. A gold standard of the genre.

I do recommend the game for the great storyline, narration, and gameplay.  The only downfall I found was that after 9 hours, I'd completely beaten it AND gotten ALL of the "extras".  After beating it once through, you get to go through again, but keeping all of your XP and weaponry.  While it's nice to run through some of your favorite locations again, there's nothing *added* to the game by this.  If anything, then it just becomes that much easier to do a speed run through the game.  My general rule is that a game should provide enough entertainment for about 75 cents per hour.  (Thus, if I pay $60 for a game, I expect a minimum of 80 hours of good, enjoyable play time.) At the $15 price tag for Bastion, I would have expected 20 hours of gameplay, not 9.  So while I think it was overpriced for what you get, when the price drops to about half, it'll be worth every penny.
Still, I recommend it for the uniqueness of it, and overall enjoyable experience.  Just wait for it to go on sale.

A well-written RPG that pays hilarious homage to many iconic figures of the 80's. If you're familiar with G.I. Joe, Transformers, Care Bears, Back to the Future, Michael Jackson, Top Gun, or Jean Claude Van Damme, you will find many chuckles to be had throughout the course of the game.
You play as Marty, and the game is played through 5 episodes, each introducing unique locations and characters to the overall plot. Gameplay itself mostly consists of the standard RPG elements: Explore, level up, complete quests, and advance the storyline. Your party will always be a one-person affair, but this is acceptable due to the customization options available to Marty.
You will find stickers, 5 of which can be scratched prior to each battle to give Marty bonuses (or debuffs for enemies). In addition to this, there is a pretty big selection of items that Marty may also equip. Each of these items is an attack that Marty can perform in battle, and each item ranges in damage, speed, accuracy, and uses per battle. Many of these items also have unique QTEs that give the fighting a bit of flavor as well. Add this with a charging system that is required to make your attacks more lethal, and a timing system that puts emphasis on speed as well, and there's actually a little strategy required in some of the fights.
The music is also pretty good. It probably won't make many Top 10 lists, but it is quite fitting for the gameplay. I wish they would've gave the music more of an 80's hair-band vibe, but I was satisfied with the overall score.

But yeah in all seriousness this game is fantastic and the  version is of course hugely superior, I completed it first on PS3 and when I switched over to PC the graphical and frame rate difference was staggering, everything is super sharp.
Upon first playing this game I immediately noticed that even the most basic punching attack is represented on screen as incredibly brutal, and the violence only escalates as fights go on, character models show massive amounts of visual damage and the fatalities are sometimes hard to watch because they are just that gruesome.
Artistically this game revitalise the class MK character designs we all know and love, modernising old classics. The environments are also fantastic recreations of areas from MK 1-3, complete with stage fatalities. The only issue I have with the character designs this time around is that it is very clear that each humanoid male and female character all use the same underlying body model with the same normal map applied, some have variants like Johnny cages tattoos, but it is a shame we don’t see much variation in musculature and body proportion. This complaint it most apparent when looking at the female character models that show allot of their body, I understand that this may have been done to synergies the animation transitions and hit reactions with each characters rig but more body type variation would have gone a long way in hiding this minor gripe.
This edition contains all of the DLC characters that were released; the additional PS3 character Kratos is nowhere to be seen however due to that consoles exclusivity. The DLC characters themselves are great additions to the game, unique MK characters that may have been forgotten about are brought back in a great way here with unique move sets and fatalities. The only out of place character that falls short for me was the addition of Freddy Kruger, some say he fits in with the MK universe well but I don’t agree, his move set isn’t that interesting at all and for being a famous horror movie slasher villain his fatalities are quite rubbish.
Aside from having fantastic brutal combat and finishing moves, this game also gives you so much to do, various modes extend the lifespan of the game and the kyrpt contains hundreds of fantastic unlockables.
If you’re an MK fan like myself this is a must have, if you’re a fighting game fan I would also say it’s a must have.

Incredibly stupid gameplay mixed with incredible stupid puzzle solutions - you've got the best puzzle game of 2013!
McPixel is a fast paced humorous mini-puzzle game, where our main hero McPixel (an obvious reference to Macgyver) tries in 20 seconds to defuse a bomb and save the day. Everything is controlled with one mouse button and that's where it's charm lies. To use or pick up an item you just press it. And hope for the best. Sometimes pressing something (or someone) will pick that thing or even a person up to use with other items. In other cases, pressing will lead to McPixel kicking the said item or person. Usually that kick will result in everything blowing up.
Sometimes the solution is to press on the fire to take your pants off and take a♥♥♥♥♥♥ saving everyone's life. Pressing the fire in the next puzzle will make McPixel jump to the fire, combusting himself. In the third puzzle, pressing the bomb will make McPixel kick it, destroying half the city. The solutions range from simply press the fire extinguisher to extinguish bomb to kick a fat naked guy in the showers, so that he would slip on the soap and land on a bomb, defusing it.
Every single solutions is stupid, yet brilliant at the same time.
It also offers FREE DLC, a thing that you wouldn't get in a 60$ "realistic millitary shooter". And for a such a minimal price, you'd be an idiot not to try this game out.

I get what the creators are trying to do with this game, and I respect that. The first two episodes are the best part of the work, with some clever design and interesting ideas.
Sadly, the remainder of the game starts falling flat and doesn't really recover. The fifth episode is unfortunately both obtuse in the puzzles presented and pretty short, and the story they laid out just kind of takes a sharp left turn into "wut" territory.
The nostalgia factor is pretty strong, but the humor is a bit overly pun-dependent for my tastes. I picked it up on Steam sale, and I'd recommend giving it a shot in a sale if you have nostalgia for 80's pop culture, but other than that I can't really recommend this one.
A final note: if you have motor disabilities, steer clear of the game completely. A lot of the combat is based around either timed presses or button mashing/control stick shaking, and if you have trouble with fine motor movements, you will likely have a much harder time with this game. I did not see an accessibility option for getting around that requirement.

I can easily say this is the best Mortal Kombat game ever made and one of the best fighters of all time. Mortal Kombat Trilogy comes close but this is better. Mortal Kombat 9 has an amazing combat engine, everything feels very fluid, it has all the fan favourite characters and even new ones with the great DLC, the addition of online is great but it doesn't work very well. Mortal Kombat 9 takes everything that was great in the older games, puts them into this and removes everything that was bad in the older games.
Mortal Kombat Komplete Edition follows the events of Mortal Kombat 1 - 3. Raiden, a thunder god, is having visions of the future and he is trying to make sure that Earthrealm is safe from Outworld. If the future is safe, his broken amulet will recover and be fully repaired. You get to play as all the characters (Excluding some villians such as Quan-Chi, Ermac, Sheeva) and it is fun to play as all of them.
This game's combat is so amazing due to the fact that it has very good looking graphics, great sound, X-Ray moves, everything is very fluid, combos, special moves and of course the fatalities. There aren't only fatalities as well, there are babalities and stage fatalities. The babalities are hilarious and all of them are unique and different in their own way.
Mortal Kombat Komplete Edition has an amazing amount of content such as the challenge tower, concept art, alternate costumes, new characters with DLC, the story mode, online mode and the "Test your ___!" games. Anyone who enjoys fighting games, especially the Mortal Kombat series, should play this game. I guarantee that you will have a great time while playing. Even people who don't like fighting games could play this, it's an amazing game.

When you pick up the Stanley parrable, you are in an office. One of the most boring places on earth. Instead of being boring however, the narrarator plays off the absurdity at every moment.
When the narraration started for this game, I legitimately believed that the narrarator was going to be replaced very early on. As time went on that hope begin to fade. The office in the Stanley parable had nowhere to go but up. This on the other hand, promises a very serious background to complement the narrator, but it just goes nowhere.
It becomes clear early on that where the Stanley Parable was about the relationship between you and the narrarator, this is about the narrarator and his game. There is no broom closet scene where you do something pointless and it's a full on thing. Instead, you are told to do these things. and then the delivery is the same "woah you should have followed the arrows, oh uh this level isn't done yet. Look at some cool beta demos. What? You were actually having a good time exploring? Well thats a shame it doesnt go anywhere"
Finally, ICEY is the most interesting part of the game and as far as I am aware there is nothing there. There is no characterization or arc. The game appears to be on the same level as Hollow Knight, but the action serves as filler for the narraration.
This style of game can work. You can have Narraration styled in a way where the main character would berate you as your actions cost lives. Or where she would fight with the narrarator. Anything to avoid losing the charm that made the Stanley Parable so great
In Bastion, Rucks messes with you a few times and it's hilarious, yet he still manages to deliver a serious tale. That doesn't happen here. Do not play this game for the world. You will be dissatisfied.
I'll wrap this up. This game feels like someone made a game but realized they had no confidence in the story and couldn't get voice actors so they made it into a skinsuit and put it onto something else. The art of the game clashes with the little terminal sequences. The tone of the game clashes with the narrarator. The narrarator himself clashes with the genre.
It's certanly well made and well put together. If you are absolutely dying for the stanley parable, you will probably enjoy this game. If you want a humerous metroidvania or hack and slash with fun characters and an interesting world, you won't find it here.

Full disclosure, I bought this game more for the super cheap steam-link than  the game itself.
First the positives: This game is nothing like what I expected. That's a good thing, since like Pony Island or Stanley Parable, knowing what's going on ruins the experience. It's extremely enjoyable, and tells a very interesting (if confusing) story. It hits some similar notes to The Stanley Parable, and succeeds in being a meta-meta-game. The action is enjoyable, if easy. Also, the aesthetics are beautiful, every single background is wonderful.
Now, the down-side: It's short You'll see I've got about 5 hours into the game. As far as I can tell, that's the extent of the game. I have all achievements, and I believe I've seen all of the 'endings.' After 4 hours, I'd finished the 'story' mode of the game and gotten 28 of the achievements purely by accident. It only took another hour with a guide to finish off the achieves and final 'story' points.
Finally, my biggest pet peeve: This game is incredibly inconsistent. You unlock a power which allows you to pass through grates... except for about 70% of them, which you can't pass through.  There are segments where a passage is traversable, but an identical passage nearby is a hard wall. Fortunately, none of this is punishing in any way, so it rests as a pet peeve, rather than a fault in the game.
In short, I want to criticize it for being a 4 hour game that costs $10. That said, I pay $6 to see a 2-hour movie, so I guess I can't be too harsh. It's a worthwhile investment, just know what you're paying for.
If you're expecting a traditional game, you'll be disappointed. If you're expecting a unique narrative action experience, I think you'll be satisfied.
PS: Please make this into a full-length game. I want to play it.

The main storyline follows an emerging gang war that threatens to overrun the city of Hong Kong. You then follow a series of fairly redundant missions before beginning to shake down local vendors for money and beating up enemy gangs to bolster Winston's ego. Occasionally meeting up with your police handler, to hear the same lecture about not getting too emotionally involved to the monsters you’re working for.
I have to be blunt, aside from the really pretty graphics, the game takes a face dive into the floor for it's combat system being nearly non-existent. You can pretty much just sit there deflecting attacks till your enemy just spontaneously dies, since the actual combat is a bit meh by having it just be a combo of clicks. This wasn't suppose to be a point-and-click game, yet the combat system makes it feel like one. So with 80% of the game revolving around combat, it's a real let down there.
Another complaint I have to make is basically how terrible the handling of any vehicle was. There is virtually no chance of speeding and driving properly what-so-ever, as someone who has grown up playing various race games, this is another disappointing factor of the game.
The game’s second biggest issue is with its camera. It can often positions itself towards center even when you’re trying to maneuver whilst driving. This can significantly complicate navigating tight quarters or getting a look around your vehicle in open spaces. The camera can also be frustrating in some combat situations, though it doesn't happen quite as often or severely.
I also have to point out that in a gang game, it is virtually impossible to actually acquire a weapon. For memory you get a gun once during the entire game for approximately 5 minutes and nothing more. Knives are also irritatingly rare with maybe only one person in a random gang you attack to have one which you can sometimes have the option of picking up.
It redeems itself within it's story-line, but, character development, bar the ones in cut scenes seem so cut short and abnormal. You go from just meeting a person to seeming like you have been in a relationship for years. It just doesn't quite flow in my opinion.
All that aside, I did enjoy the random health shrines, deterring from the usual 'Pick up a health pot to gain more max health', within combat you can't just go to the side and chew on regenerative dirt, it takes a bit more time to actually gain it back. Another really redeeming quality is the animations to fight scenes, they are quite realistic. Also, the sounds of punching and slashing (when you finally acquire a knife) are brilliant.
Moving on.. People chattering away in the background, or random vendors trying to sell certain things to which you can also interact with a few odd ones here and there make it feel a lot more in-depth and was something I did enjoy. Also actually just having pedestrians is such a tiny detail that make a game feel so much more real. It pulls it off with flying colors. I also have to make a comment on the voice acting. It simply adds to this emphasis on realism. The game employs a unique mixture of Chinese and English that doesn't sound corny or ill-executed which can be pretty difficult to pull off.
In all, pretty good game, just a few frustrating little downfalls.

I try to review as if I'm giving developers feedback.
Pros:
A hybrid of Civilization and Warcraft, with elements of Endless Legends.  Micromanagement of resources and settlement growth strategy are meaningful.  The game pace is on-point in a way that few strategy games ever achieve.  If you're a developer reading this, and anyone has complained that your game is too slow or too fast, play this game to see an example of perfect pacing.
The AI does not come across as buffed in this game, despite the flaw described below.  If the AI is cheated, then this game does a great job of hiding the fact.  The AI seems to be constrained by the same rules as the player, with the catch being that there's n >= 1 of them, and only 1 of you.  Again, if you're a developer of strategy 4E/4X/Civ/colony games reading this, then you can't afford to not play this game.
Cons:
It suffers from zerg addiction.  Early in the mid game every other faction on the map will attack you, all at once.  It's not possible to have a military big enough to defend everywhere by that point, so it becomes a question of what territory you're willing to lose, unless you play strictly war-focused.
Like most strategy games in the style of civ games this generation, the AI is far too aggressive while your relationships, trading, and behavior are meaningless with regard to the other factions.  Everything you could possibly do results in the same outcome with the AI.
Conclusion:
It's early access.  They still have plenty of time to do something different.  Compared with this generation of civ-strategy games, A+.  Compared with past generations, this whole run of games gets a big F.  I guess we'll see what comes down the patch pipe in times to come.  If you like this over-aggressive, military-forced generation of strategy games, Civilization, Endless Legend, and Warcraft, you'll love this game.
If the aggressive AI is a deal-breaker for you, then you might try playing maps 1v1, with bigger maps to forestall war and make it more interesting.  But make no mistake: war is inevitable, and there is absolutely nothing you can do to change that.

Full disclosure, I bought this game more for the super cheap steam-link than  the game itself.
First the positives: This game is nothing like what I expected. That's a good thing, since like Pony Island or Stanley Parable, knowing what's going on ruins the experience. It's extremely enjoyable, and tells a very interesting (if confusing) story. It hits some similar notes to The Stanley Parable, and succeeds in being a meta-meta-game. The action is enjoyable, if easy. Also, the aesthetics are beautiful, every single background is wonderful.
Now, the down-side: It's short You'll see I've got about 5 hours into the game. As far as I can tell, that's the extent of the game. I have all achievements, and I believe I've seen all of the 'endings.' After 4 hours, I'd finished the 'story' mode of the game and gotten 28 of the achievements purely by accident. It only took another hour with a guide to finish off the achieves and final 'story' points.
Finally, my biggest pet peeve: This game is incredibly inconsistent. You unlock a power which allows you to pass through grates... except for about 70% of them, which you can't pass through.  There are segments where a passage is traversable, but an identical passage nearby is a hard wall. Fortunately, none of this is punishing in any way, so it rests as a pet peeve, rather than a fault in the game.
In short, I want to criticize it for being a 4 hour game that costs $10. That said, I pay $6 to see a 2-hour movie, so I guess I can't be too harsh. It's a worthwhile investment, just know what you're paying for.
If you're expecting a traditional game, you'll be disappointed. If you're expecting a unique narrative action experience, I think you'll be satisfied.
PS: Please make this into a full-length game. I want to play it.

If you are a fan of tower defense games I highly recommend this game.  If you're unsure about paying $10 ($9.99) for a game, try it free online in a web browser.  The money you spend on steam gives you access to a much better engine (rather than playing on flash).  The game runs smoother.  In addition, you have access to heroes and Ironhide Game Studio (the publisher/developer) has reported the expansion content will come at no additional costs once completed.
As others have said, I first played this game on a tablet.  I'm not a fan of microtransactions.  It upset me to see awesome content (like heroes) which I had to pay to use.  This has all been fixed in the steam version.  People might argue well what's the difference between micro transactions and buying a game?  Either way you are still paying money.  The difference is one group of people doesn't have an advantage over others (granted not an issue in a single player game) and I know how much I'm paying up front.  Microtransactions can add up real quick and before you know it, you've spent more than the $10 it costs to buy the game on steam.  Thank you Ironhide for listening to your fan base and bringing this to steam.

This is a really fun, lovingly crafted RPG. I delayed buying it because I was afraid it would botch the mid-80s setting or turn out to be an unimaginative parody. That was a mistake. This game is a genuinely creative love-song to the era. The NPC's have personalities, the setting and art is delightful, and the music is perfect. One quibble is that the soundtrack could have been longer. The combat system could be deeper, but it's adequate to make the battles exciting and often challenging.
I was particularly impressed with the writing. The authors managed to combine some of the best storytelling elements of early RPG's with mid-1980s' cartoon serials. Like it's inspirations, the game's stories are funny yet also morally sincere. The snarky irony of 1990-current storytelling is conspicuous by its absence.
Highly recommended. It's not necessary at all to have lived through the mid-1980s to enjoy this game. I hope to see more from this game's developers.

The "Definitive Collection" review:
I recommend this version of doom 3 because it allows you to easily play doom I and doom II in higher resolution along with achievements.
Just simply copy over the .WAD file from your "Ultimate Doom" installation and copy it over to your Doom 3 BFG installation and viola you're running the original doom at a higher resolution and with achievements without having to bother with editing any CFG files.
One thing to note is that since Doom 3 BFG has different menu options, when you run with the Ultimate Doom WAD file you can't change the settings and quitting the game results in Doom 3 BFG crashing rather than going to the game selection screen. If you want to change settings, simply run the BFG WAD file, adjust some settings, then run the normal Doom WAD file.
Main differences between normal Doom I and II WAD file and BFG version include:
1. Options are different, BFG version has more sensitivity options and has a fullscreen toggle
2. "Quit" menu is different, BFG has a menu where you can either cancel, go back to Doom 3 BFG game selection screen, or quit the game entirely. Normal Doom has a Y/N option, and running normal doom in BFG results in a crash as soon as you press "quit".
3. Censorship. Doom II BFG has quite a lot of textures that are changed to be more appropriate for a worldwide release. Doom I BFG has minor changes in this regard.
NOTE: To change controls, you have to go into Doom 3 and change the key bindings there which in turn change the keybindings of doom 1 and 2, changing WAD files does not affect any of the keybindings.
I recommend these keybindings:
Forward: W
Sprint: LSHIFT, RSHIFT
Attack: RCTRL, UPARROW, MOUSE1
Other settings can be kept as default.
The BFG collection does not include Final Doom and Master Levels for Doom 2, so you are not getting the "definitive collection" but it's close enough. For the ultimate doom experience you must buy both Doom 3 BFG and Doom Classic Complete.

Fallout 4 represents to me the culmination of a few trends in the gaming industry and the RPG genre that I've been around long enough to see, and I cannot recommend this game because of the direction they've taken during their growth. The RPG aspects are more streamlined and simplified than others in the series and the DLC is disappointing, it's nothing that really extends the game's lifetime and replayability. What actually does so is the modding scene, which has always made Bethesda RPGs much more interesting. Modding has, for the first real time, gone beyond developer endorsement and support through modding tools into integration and paid access.
This development in the history of modding comes as the cost of producing games has increased and developers find innovative ways to offset them, so they naturally capitalize on what's become an asset to Bethesda RPGs. It's yet another unfortunate trend in the industry that shouldn't be condoned, just like microtransactions and DLC, as not all changes during the maturation of a hobby are going to be positive, and they tend to have clear winners and losers. This change, like others, segments more content and the community beyond an array of pay walls, taking us away from the old formula: paying one price for full access and taking a hands-off approach to homebrew changes ('modding') that individuals would make for themselves and end up sharing to the community
The only thing about the game I truly enjoyed was the settlement system, managing a settlement in a post-apocalyptic setting and a first person shooter is pretty enjoyable. It does get stale after a while, and I found Fallout 4's story to be lacking compared to the previous two titles.

Let's get something straight here - I love this game! I really do. Plenty of people like to discard this game because of how far it differs from the classic run-and-gun formula of the original (and 2016) DOOM installments.
Yes, this is a vastly different installment into the franchize, but it is far from the "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Child" of the series.
Naturally, the game has it's flaws, such as moderately underpowered weapons (Chainsaw and BFG Need not apply), cheap jumpscares, etc.
But it makes up for these faults with a foreboding, spine-chilling, sadistic atmosphere, guaranteed to leave you on edge the whole time. Yes, there's the occasional predictable cheap scare, but the constant level of dread in the atmosphere leaves them in the dust.
Some say it's too different, I say it's different enough.
It isn't just riding on the identity of the classic DOOM games for popularity, but rather, it sets itself up in a totally different way - it has it's own identity! Sure, there are nods to classic DOOM here and there, but aside from that, without the DOOM label, this would be an exceptional survival/horror first person shooter.
The fact that this is bundled with DOOM 1 and 2 as well as RoE and the Lost Mission, really expands on the replay value of DOOM 3. Sure, I don't have the longest playtime on record, but I still come back and play this game when I feel the need to get my eyes sucked out through my o-ring.

It is time for an honest review...
In some aspects every early access game should learn from Northgard. The game is very polished, bugless and is being updated a lot, which is nice and shows that devs don't care only about a quick buck, which is kinda the trend in early access and kick starter games.
BUT, at this moment the game is too shallow in my opinion. It isn't a sim like Settlers, no, there are no supply lines, farms give you food as a finished product, woodcutters give you wood as a finished product etc. The "tech tree" is very small and doesn't give you much choice and the difference between each clan is too small.
The replayability is only based on random maps built of a few different tiles and you playing a different clan against a different clan that as I already said differ only a bit. The different types of victories are quite straight forward and simple too. I don't mind simplicity but I think that devs overdid it here a bit.
It is up to them to add some depth into the game and make sure it will be more replayable, because at this moment, there isn't enough possibility for the games to be different.
So for the verdict I would say I don't think the game is worth the price tag at this moment, but on the other hand I don't regret spending the money on it because it is the most promising early access strategy I have seen so far and devs deserve the motivation. If they released it now and said it was done, they would be liars. If they keep updating it for the next year, add more tiles, "tech tree" upgrades, buildings and other stuff for overall variability, then it will be worth it.
I am clicking recommend but I wouldn't rate the game more than 5/10 because of the replayability and depth, which are too important to me.

Sooo...  I can't lie.  This game's not perfect.  Though problems occasionally arising with the diagonal isometric view and aiming not being very accurate as such, the narrative makes up for any such heartbreak.  You have to actively be searching for everything, but if you look you WILL find it all, no obscure hidden tricks are here because the game wants you to find all its narrative.  A game that WANTS you to beat it is rare now-a-days but when designed properly like this one is, it's completely welcome.  With games like Nuclear Throne, Dark Souls, and Wings Of Vi becoming maybe too common and putting narrative second to gameplay, I keep finding all these well made experiences that are too hard to play, too boring to keep playing, or both, and its been getting me down lately.  This game has a spectacular soundtrack, decent gameplay, wonderful stylized visuals and clever design choices that make those attuned to them recognized their artistic genius.  The problems don't stop there, however.  This MUST be mentioned, but be warned of SPOILERS.  This game has no final boss.  This is a game that NEEDED one, but it did not get one.  This was a narrative choice, and I can respect that, but depending on how heartless you are the final encounter can make you feel a little emptier.  This is because, clearly, the game was made so most naturally fall to one path over the other, but for someone like me, worried about the path ahead during my blind playthrough, I almost couldn't decide what to do.  Oh, yeah, there's a choice system towards the end, be prepped for that because your choices will have immediate consequence.  Be careful Peacemakers, and enjoy this art that pretended to be a game.  OH WAIT, one more thing.  I got this while it was on sale for 4 dollars.  I'm not sure how much it may be worth full price, but whatevs, not mah problem!
