If you find a character you love to play with, you can get good with them. Takes a lot of played games and the understanding of basic concepts before you can play the game with a sense of competency. When I say basics I mean that you - as a player - should know what a frame trap is, should know what a meaty is, and understand what frame data is and how to use it to your advantage when learning about your character and matchups versus other characters. If you do not understand these three things, other players that do will use them against you and it will feel like you are in the dark (because you are) and can't get any better.
Once you have learned these concepts, you will begin to understand how it is a give and take relationship. If you can use this information and do these things to your opponent, they can do them right back. If you have a situation where only one person in a match has knowledge of one or multiple of these things, the player that lacks the knowledge is at a severe disadvantage and will hinder their progress.
Besides the technical stuff, there is also fundamental gameplay strategies and mechanical execution that need to be constantly trained during matches and/or in training mode. A combination of all of this stuff will lead you to the progress you seek. Most importantly of all though is the sheer amount of games you need to play in order to learn the matchups and be exposed to all types of gameplay styles and strategies.
The biggest issue with SFV is the netcode and matchmaking system. It's not crazy to expect "5" bar connections to be worse than 1 bar connections. Often you will get matched against people out of country or VERY far away from you and the game will claim that it is a "5" bar or "4" bar connection when it is obviously not. This is a problem with the matchmaking system and seems to have gotten worse since the NEW CFN was released. Also, the netcode could use some work. After watching a talk about GGPO and how they deal with rollback and "The Rift", it is clear SFV netcode does nothing about this Rift. This causes a lot of 1 sided rollback in most cases (where one player will have about 1-2 frames of rollback while the other has double or triple that amount). Capcom has even bought a license for GGPO in the past but is not using it or a similar structure for SFV's netcode at the moment. GGPO eliminates this one sidedness by evenly distributing the frames of rollback to each player.
TL;DR - Fun game if you find a character you really like playing. If you want to get good, then learn about frame traps, meaties, and frame data. On top of that make sure to practice fundamental strategies (like anti airs and footsies) and use training mode to practice your character's setups. Also # of games = improved ability over time due to experience with matchups and other people's strategies. Finally, Capcom needs to fix their matchmaking system and improve their netcode!

AVP (2010) has nice graphics, good sound design, solid atmosphere, and an interwoven story for Human, Xenomorph and Predator species spread across three campaigns.  The campaigns can all be beaten in about 10-15 hours of play total - give or take some hours based on your proficiency and desire for achievement hunting.  And it has difficulty settings, xp for rankings, and blah blah blah...
The story isn't bad, but it really only serves as an excuse to move you through each of the rather linear mission areas.  Every species receives communication from a leader that sends them from objective to objective until the mission area is complete and you can move onto the next one.  The story environs allow you to experience the inside of a hive, a colony base, and an ancient Predator pyramid amongst ruins in a tropical jungle.  You'll encounter several variations of Xenomorphs,  Predators, and Androids - SPOILER:  They all want to kill you.
As each of the species have different abilities - the playstyle for each is completely different.  Xenomorphs can climb on almost all surfaces, leap at enemies (also vents), claw at enemies, whip them with their tail, and bite into their heads.  They can also "harvest" enemies by grabbing them and allowing a facehugger to attach.  Xenomorphs specialize in stealth and speed and to that end they can hide in vents, crawl through tight spaces, destroy lights which helps them hide in the dark, and hiss to lure enemies to their (tasty) demise.
Xenomorphs can see fine in the dark and they can see the auras of enemies (even through walls), so long as they are not too far away.  They can regenerate health, provided they aren't taking damage.  The Xenomorphs have the shortest (or quickest) campaign, it seemed, but also the most fun.
The Predators specialize in gadgets.  They can cloak which is good for disguising their presence from a distance, but they can't sneak up on humans from behind like Xenomorphs can, and they can be seen even while cloaked by the Xenomorphs, or if they get too close to humans and androids.  Stepping into water also decloaks the pred, as does interacting with elements in the game.  As the Predator campaign progresses they unlock (find) new weapons and an extra view style.  Predators have two razor claws on each forearm to melee with.  They can also get the shoulder cannon, prox mines, disc, and combi stick.
The shoulder cannon produces some splash damage, but a direct hit can kill most humans and xenos.  Using it causes you to decloak though and also drains the limited energy you have, which can only be replenished by finding power sources.  The prox mines can be dropped and remotely detonated, but to be honest, I never used them.  The disc is good for range attacks - you guide the disc with a laser sight and it returns.  A careful aim can take a head off.  The combi stick is the most lethal weapon in your arsenal, provided you aim carefully.  A direct hit will kill humans, xenos, and androids.  The Predator can also leap pretty high/far using a mechanic called "focus", which also helps point out things in the environment you might not otherwise see.
The Predator has a "normal" human vision mode, a heat vision mode (only good for spotting humans and androids), and sometime midway through the campaign or so you gain a "gray" vision mode that allows you to spot Xenomorphs (to the exclusion of other enemies).  The Predator also can zoom in from afar using any mode of vision.  They heal using shards - they can carry 3 at a time.  You feel the most badass as the Predator.
Humans (Marines) have it the toughest.  They're an easy, doughy, more meltable target for the other species.  They have a motion tracker, sure, but it's really limited in it's usefulness.  They have a sidearm, but it's really not the weapon of choice when being swarmed by Xenos or charged by a Predator.  They can get the pulse rifle which fires bullets and has a limited capacity grenade launcher.  They can use a shotgun, which is very deadly at close range, and a sniper rifle that's deadly at long range.  I found the sniper rifle to be a pretty useless weapon - good for picking off still targets, but not the aliens.  The best part of the human arsenal is the smartgun, but you're limited on it's availability and ammo, and are forced to drop your main weapon when picking it up (humans can only carry two weapons aside from the sidearm).
For some reason the marines don't get the night vision they had in both the movie and the previous AVP games.  This to me is a sore spot.  They do get flares they can toss, but they are, at best, impractical.  While you can putter your way through the darker areas of the singleplayer campaign putting up with this limitation, it becomes a severe handicap in dark multiplayer games against the other two species.  The humans have 3 health bars.  They can regenerate health in a bar provided they aren't taking damage.  However, if a bar is completely emptied it doesn't regenerate.  In order to fully heal then they need to use a health stim - they can carry 3 at a time.  The human campaign felt the longest to me (probably had something to do with all the dying I did).
Control-wise I had issues with all three species.  The controls are at times stiff, clumsy, non-intuitive, and downright frustrating.  Part of the problem, I think, is that the game was clearly designed for controller fondling console gamers first and foremost.  It explains the wanky mechanics, the constant handholding you sense as you play, the strictly linear flow of the missions, and the god-awful item hunt to unlock masturbatory achievements.  The idea is these are 3 species fighting for survival against one another, so why am I expected to waste time snooping around for stupid hidden items that serve neither the plot or your survival?
The Marine feels like his boots are made of lead.  He's slow, not particularly responsive, he can barely jump - he can't even crouch behind cover for blueberry muffin's sake!!!  WTH?  He can climb onto waist high crates and stuff, but there are only one or two places in the entire campaign where that's necessary.
The Xenomorphs are faster and more agile, but you will often find yourself stuck on surfaces struggling to get off, disoriented by the unpredictability of it's movement mechanics when going from one surface to another, or fighting to get things squarely into view so you can leap into, use an interactive element, or bite into some jerks head.
The Predator may fall somewhere between.  He's faster than humans, but not xenos, but he also can't crouch *sigh*.  He can leap high and far, but the mechanics in doing so is more complicated than it needed to be.
Multiplayer is where this game should really shine and unfortunately it's a bust.  The game is heavily weighed against the Marines.  So, IF you can find a server to play on, all of the regulars will be either Aliens or Predators.  First off, the Predators and Xenomorphs can one-hit kill the Marines, and because both the Preds and the Xenos can leap long distances, move fast, and track you based on vision - you won't even know what happened half the time.  Remember, Marines don't get night vision, and the tracker is completely useless against opponents that can move so quick you're dead before you even register the blip.
If you're looking for an AVP universe game then this is decent, though I'd still recommend AVP Classic 2000 over this game.  To be honest, I'd recommend Alien Trilogy, Aliens:  Colonial Marines, and Alien: Isolation over this, but they don't have Predators *tear*.  The production values are all there, but the end result fell short of expectation.  Recommended if you are a fan of the franchise or are in desperate need of a decent singleplayer FPS game.

Review based on a PS3 playthrough; please use a gamepad or fight stick to play this game on PC.
Good Points: Amazing presentation, nostalgic game play, loads of gamer content, they gave MK fans exactly what they wanted (finish him!) and plenty of gaming modes to mess around in
Bad Points: Pacing and difficulty among A.I. is classically bad, MK purists may not completely agree with the story mode, definitely not the world’s best fighting mechanics, character endings are still 2D panel frames and not full cut-scene cinematics.
Unique Strengths: The best single-player storyline of any fighting game, possibly the best presentation I’ve ever seen in its genre and it carries the weight of a nearly fifteen year old franchise
Gamer Tastes: If you’re even the slightest fighting or MK fan and if you just enjoy watching blood and guts get thrown around your television screen.
Worth Buying? - The people at NetherRealm Studios made sure a purchase was a requirement to fully enjoy this title.
Theme: 9.5/10- Everything anybody loved about the older Mortal Kombat titles has returned in Mortal Kombat 9 but that doesn’t mean it’s all relevant in today’s world of gaming. The story is still unbelievably ridiculous; the characters are sexist renditions of classically bad Hollywood archetypes and the unnecessary amount of gore has returned. But that’s exactly what everyone asked for and many got it with copious amounts of satisfaction.
Story Structure: 7.8/10- This is the best story mode you’ll get out of any fighter but this is still a Mortal Kombat story. Not much makes sense but as long as you go with it it’s actually a fairly entertaining experience. Followers of all previous Mortal Kombat games will thoroughly enjoy this reboot disguised as a continuation of the last episode in the main story. And I congratulate NetherRealm studios for even including an actual story in the first place; considering that most fighters barely include one to begin with.
Game-play: 6.0/10- Everything I hated, and hopefully many would agree, from the older Mortal Kombat games have unfortunately returned in Mortal Kombat 9. The return to the side-scrolling method of fighting has already shown signs of Mortal Kombat’s potential as a tournament fighter but it is barely progressing to such a status. The strategy is greatly hindered by the exploits of the game’s major faults; an incredibly skewed balance between offensive and defensive fighter abilities with a myriad of cheap tactics ranging from every fighter. Luckily everything I liked (what little I did) from the original franchise’s game play returned with it.
Soundtrack and Acting: 8.0/10- The overall voice acting is as terrible as the dialogue that goes along with it but that’s a default association for the Mortal Kombat universe; it’s what everyone should expect. The sound effects are sharp, tight with their animations and will echo through your ears in all its high-definition glory. And don’t forget the old-school soundtracks that hardcore Mortal Kombat fans know and love. Although little has changed as far as overall sound goes, for most, that’s the way they wanted it to be.
Technical Quality: 10/10- Never have I seen a fighter so pretty, this is what a modern-day fighter should look like. It’s a nice change of pace from the comic and more cartoony looking fighters of today’s library meaning that such a visual tone is needed in today’s increasingly small line-up of triple A fighters. The developers also throw in queues from the original Mortal Kombat while evolving it with today’s technological capabilities. Do I enjoy watching a body dissolve in the background of the DeadPool level? Yes, very much so.
Replay Value: 9.0/10- NetherRealm studios threw in so much added content outside of multiplayer and arcade ladder it almost seems as if  they expected people would be dissatisfied with the core features of the game. But in case you actually are, this game is still worth the purchase; challenge tower, test your might, sight, luck, fatality tutorials, the krypt, story mode, King of the Hill, tag team battles and so on and so forth. Not every extra feature seems to fit or be as worthy as the next but it is more appropriate than Tetris or kart racing.
Conclusion: The presentation is amazing, the content, oh sorry I meant to say Kontent is overwhelming and the story mode is simply superb for any lover of the franchise. Although the title suffers from some of its previous outings (Shang Tsung borrows a fatality from Mortal Kombat vs. DC Universe) and not all characters are present at first (where’s Rain!) much of what we loved about the original Mortal Kombat games has returned with a modern day bang. Even if the game suffers from mediocre game-play mechanics and finicky online connectivity (but honestly when have console fighters ever had good internet connectivity?) there isn’t much more a fan of the series could ask for.
Overall Score (based on an average): 8.4/10

Single Player Review
This is a review specifically of the marine portion of the AVP single player campaign. I have to say I am not impressed. It looks right, but it doesn't feel right. The core gameplay is inherently flawed in several different annoying ways.
Firstly, the basic combat is just wonky. The weapons are not particularly well balanced. The pulse (assault) rifle for instance is good for pretty much nothing, yet the shotgun will kill basically anything that moves. In fact a sniper rifle-shotgun combo makes this game stupidly easy. This brings me to another particularly idiotic game design quirk: every time you start a new level, the game takes away your weapons and gives you a predetermined loadout. This is utterly inexcusable.
To my surprise the aliens did actually make decent use of wall climbing maneuvers, and generally being sneaky little buggers. Little buggers. They are not nearly imposing enough in my opinion. This is where it loses me. Not only can your hero marine character literally knock the seven foot tall monstrosities on their spiky arses, but it is an integral part of the combat that you will be doing over and over and over again. This is a complete misrepresentation of a formidable movie monster, and it should not be overlooked.
The predators rarely make an appearance in the marine campaign, and when they do they are portrayed as a vastly superior monster compared to the unfortunate alien which has been reduced to cannon fodder. The predator boss battle if you would call it that is bizarrely easy however. I didn't take any damage at all for the duration of the fight. The thing would just stand on rooftops, shine its massively visible laser at you and then shoot an impractically slow plasma ball at you. If you are imagining the imp fireball from doom, you wouldn't be far off.
As far as the actual level progression, and design goes, it is a lot of follow that nav point and the open this door/press this switch/secure this area/etc. It attempts to vary up the level design with some “jungle” exterior settings, and a cave system, to take the player away from the familiar steel corridors for a while. I say jungle in the loosest possible terms. It is about four trees and a bit of shrubbery.
The story isn't even worth mentioning, aside from the fact that they got Lance Henrickson to play Weyland Bishop.

Kingdom Rush is one of the most fun tower defense titles I've ever played. It has charming, cartoony graphics and the addictive gameplay we've come to know from games as Defense Grid and Pixeljunk Monsters. It isn't a big game, the main game exists of 'only' 12 levels, but there are several bonus levels to be unlocked for those that can't get enough of it. These bonus levels are actually quite tough, let me tell you. I had to retry them multiple times and still wasn't able to finish any of them.
Anyway, there are also heroes to be unlocked and, thankfully, these are all very different from each other. Switching between them makes the levels less repetitive and makes them more fresh, even though nothing has changed. The hero can make the difference between victory and defeat and is a must if you want to finish the levels without making any mistake.
Of course, using your buildings wisely and upgrading them as you go is just as important. The tower upgrades are done in a fun and exciting way; upgrading eventually allows you to make a choice between one of two towers. So, for example, an artillery tower can be upgraded to a tesla tower or a missile tower. After that you can start upgrading the skills of these towers, so you can upgrade it to have a bigger blast radius, things like that. Very well done.
Kingdom Rush wouldn't be a proper tower defense game if it didn't have boss fights and luckily for us, there are several bosses to be slain during the game. They're usually slow enough to kill them before they enter the base, except for maybe the last boss, which I won't spoil here.
Additionally, the game has a few fun easter eggs/achievements that can be found by clicking on random things like a fish in the sea. It has no use or anything, but it's cute nevertheless.
I think I've told you pretty much everything there is to tell about Kingdom Rush by now. Kingdom Rush is a brilliant game that needs all of our support. Like, right now. Go get it !

With no other objective other than moving a "shape-shifting" geometric figure (a circle while moving, a triangle while jumping and a square while standing still) through rhythm-based obstacles, it can still be quite a challenge. Although the game's learning curve is pretty smooth, it crosses a rather wide spectrum of difficulty: starting stages are pretty basic, but the "boss battles" border the
! Added to that is the special mode, unlocked after beating the main game, which requires you to beat the stages in a single take -- failing takes you back to the beginning, regardless of the checkpoints you may have reached during your run. To compensate for that, the soundtrack is a pretty driving mix of ambient electronic music and dubstep, getting you pumped up to not give up.
In fewer words,
is a clever side-scrolling platform puzzle with elements of rhythm-based games and even a hint of
-like gameplay; an odd combination that works impressively well.

A mind-expanding psychoaccoustic platforming experience akin to what I imagine an LSD trip to be. Somewhere between Fez, Thomas Was Alone, and Super Hexagon, this game strikes an excellent balance between visual effects, audial cues, and twitch gameplay. Taking up 1-2 hours of time, it's concise enough that it doesn't overstay its welcome, but you're not quite left wishing for more. Well worth the $5.
The visual effects are quite vivid, and may exacerbate any preexisting headaches or nausea. I had a minor migraine when I started and got along pretty well, but others may experience some more significant illness.
The gameplay was wonderful, intuitive yet challenging. I was never lost on where to go or what to do, yet continuously challenged to modify my reflexes to suit the ever-changing situations. The superb minimalism managed to convey exactly what needed to be done without any tutorial text or voiceover whatsoever, and stunningly subtle environmental cues.
Overall, I heartily enjoyed this game and recommend it to fans of indie games and retro-style games, and split-second timing wizards. Visual effects could be too much sometimes, but the length was perfect and the gameplay was wonderful. 9/10.

I must make a full disclaimer before I begin the rest of this review: my main impressions of this game are based upon single-player interactions, primarily with the Story Mode.
With that being said…wow! Until I had played Mortal Kombat, I had no idea that this is what a fighting game could have in regards to a story, providing hours of content. Equally impressive is the fact that the Mortal Kombat franchise incorporates a giant roster of colorful characters, most of which are properly represented through the long campaign. Seeing certain characters pop in and out, such as Kintaro and Shiva, honestly surprised me.
While the adventure may make sense to Mortal Kombat fans who have followed the lore from previous games, there is much to be appreciated to newer players, although the end of the game does clip events into a cliffnotes version, with several off-screen fights and deaths occurring. Mortal Kombat is essentially a re-telling of the first three games, only with a Star Trek-esque universe reboot providing a new spin that I found to be very fun and interesting. However, the game breaks the narrative into chapters, with each playable story character only taking up three or four battles each. By the time you really start to get hooks into how a character’s special moves and combos flow together, you are placed into another role. This was annoying on a few occasions, especially so when going from a character that I would just get and then being forced into a new toon that had a completely different move set and combo system. It just felt like hitting a brick wall.
That being said, while I do appreciate an epic story, I also like being able to pause or skip cutscenes altogether…which, for some reason, you cannot do in this game. This was particularly annoying when an inconvenience would occur right in the middle of a five-minute-long cutscene, and I could not stop for a moment. Or, if I had to exit the game for whatever reason, I would then have to re-watch the scene prior to the match that I had left from. It’s very odd that a modern game would not provide some type of cutscene control, or even patch it in later on.
Also, the AI cheats. Granted, this is nothing new to fighting games, but I think that if you manage to beat this game on “Hard” mode or greater, you’ve earned your stripes, as far as I’m concerned. Your opponents will be able to pull off combos and unblockable moves that you simply cannot achieve yourself, but that happens in most fighting games, in my experience.
The game flows well with a standard controller, and I imagine that using a fighting stick would be a better match for someone aiming to be more competitive with the game. Mortal Kombat has always seemed to have a “dial-a-combo” system in place, so busting out a chain doesn’t involve so much skill or timing, but rather ramming out a sequence as fast as possible and then watching the hits happen. Also, the block button plagued me – I would eat a ton of hits because I’m used to tapping backward and blocking, so I personally have just turned my offense into a defense by keeping constant pressure on my foes from all angles.
The Krypt, introduced way back in the Deadly Alliance days, is present once again, with a few hundred items to unlock using in-game currency earned from simply fighting matches. Typically, most of what is to be unearthed is gimmicky concept art and stage music, but every once in a while you can find a new secondary fatality for the characters hidden away. I think this feature could be trimmed down in future iterations of Mortal Kombat – it’s very bloated as it stands. There isn’t much to be found as far as extras are concerned, besides a model viewer and general backstories for each toon, but not much else is needed or missed, really.
From what I’ve heard from others, the net code of the game is buggy and unreliable, but that shouldn’t stop you from having a few friendly matches with buddies on the couch. Even if you don’t have an interest in playing against others, I would still recommend giving the game a play through, if only to experience the single-player functions. This is a great return for Mortal Kombat, providing plenty of new features mixed into nostalgia, and I’m very excited to see what else Netherealm Studios can offer with future releases.

Doom 3: BFG edition is a game that includes 3 games within it. These games are: "
", "
", and "
". Click on the titles to access my reviews of them. Notable differences from the original copies of the games are: In the Ultimate Doom the secret Wolfenstein level is heavily censored and removes all Nazi imagery and all Nazi soldiers from one particular level. Unless you live in Germany in which case both the original copy and this version of the game will be censored. In Doom II there is an additional campaign called "No Rest for the Living" which consists of nine levels. In Doom 3 there is an additional campaign called "The Lost Mission." The Ultimate Doom censor kind of sucks but only covers a small niche of the game. No Rest for the Living is very fun and honestly had some of my favourite levels for Doom 2. Lost mission sucks. It has nothing new about it like in ROE, it reuses a lot of the same sections, the story is practically identical
, there are no boss battles apart from the final boss who you can easily kill with three BFG blasts, the ending sucks, it doesnt last very long and the programming for where the enemies spawn is awful. At the start it is very easy but then you get bombarded with hoardes of enemies all of a sudden and sometimes they spawn around you and you get trapped in the enemies and can't escape and they attack you from all sides. This is not fair. Lost Mission was most likely implemented in this game so that Doom 3 fans would buy the BFG edition to play this exclusive content. However, as someone who has played it, it simply isn't worth it.
Although it isn't exclusive content "Ressurection of Evil", which was originally an expansion pack for the original Doom 3, is included in this game. ROE is fun because of the new artifact that upgrades with a magical new ability each time you defeat one of the three bosses. The artifact becomes usable when it comes into contact with a human corpse and when used activates the effects of all the upgrades you have achieved so far in the game. The first upgrade is the ability to freeze time, the second upgrade is the ability to use the berserk fists which completely obliterates even the toughest of enemies within a few punches, and the third and final upgrade which makes you invulnerable to damage. It's a shame that the campaign is so short and that between the third upgrade and the final boss is especially short because that means you won't have many oppurtunities to use the fully upgraded artifact, but it was still enjoyable nevertheless and I'm glad it was implemented. It's good to see an expansion pack that adds in something new instead of just making more levels for the sake of more levels. Another plus is that is fixes the scarcity of boss battles and includes five boss battles in a campaign that is approximately half the length of the Doom 3 campaign. It also includes the "grabber gun" that is an obvious rip-off of the gravity gun from Half-Life 2. It isn't that fun to use and the programming for this weapon is clearly inferior to the gravity gun in Half-Life 2 but it is an optional weapon to use so I can't really consider it to be a con.
If you loved Fallout 3 or New Vegas, you'll love 4. Definitive improvements from other titles in the franchise and did I mention you're probably a Synth?

Grand Theft Auto never really appealed to me, because I don't like playing the bad guy in games.  At the same time, I enjoy stories whose moral setups emphasize the practical, and Sleeping Dogs delivers big time.  Imagine an open-world action game where you're the cop, not the criminal.  At the same time, since you spend the game undercover, your duties for gangs and for your police advisors will make you question the line between good and evil more times than you can imagine.
Wei Shen's romp through the streets of Hong Kong is a viciously bloody one, but the game never substitutes style for substance--the story in general is tremendously well told from start to finish, the characters are distinct and memorable, the friendships will make you cheer, and the betrayals will make you angry.  Wei feels like a character with a difficult past and a complex personality, so his behavior seems plausible no matter how you play him, even if you go on a rampage.  Speaking of which, the game even has leaderboards where you can compete against your friends for doing a huge variety of tasks, such as how long you can hold a wheelie on a motorcycle--and, yes, how many kills of a certain fashion you can string together.
The integration of morality into the game mechanics is among the most interesting I've ever seen.  You don't pick your choices from a dialogue menu.  You have two morality meters in your missions, one for the cops and one for the triads.  The former starts as perfect and goes down if you hurt innocents or even if you're clumsy at jumping over things (I restarted checkpoints I don't know how many times because of this), and the latter starts at zero and goes up if you're particularly creative--and brutal--in terms of how you fight.  The game focuses primarily on melee combat, which plays out like in a Batman Arkham game.  You don't get the Dark Knight's mind-boggling array of gadgets, but you do get to spend your cop and triad levels on various new abilities, such as being able to break your opponents' legs by stomping sideways on them.  This makes other opponents (and possibly the player) wince, so this even has a useful purpose.
The game does also have guns, and while they're fairly typical, two things impress me more--
1) The scripting and writing for the story missions is excellently done, making each fight a blast, and
2) This game's implementation of bullet time feels like a reward and not like a cheap gimmick.  You have to jump over obstacles to be able to use it, as opposed to simply pressing a button, so the combat bonus feels like something you actually earned.  You can also disarm your enemies through a variety of means.
The setting of Hong Kong is absolutely gorgeous, especially with the free high-definition textures, and you'll find plenty to do there, even at the arguable expense of plausibility (drug busts I can see, but I'm glad Wei also has time for street racing).  Players who aren't comfortable with stealing cars usually won't be forced to--there are plenty of taxis in the city, and more importantly, you can drive around in your own private vehicles while listening to a nice variety of radio stations, including classical music.  Just remember to drive on the left!
The vehicles themselves are a joy, especially during the on-wheels combat segments.  Ramming cars sideways into walls a la F-Zero does not get old, and neither does jumping onto another car and hijacking it a la Pursuit Force.  Or you can just shoot out the fire and send a vehicle speeding into a light pole or another car.
There are a number of bugs in the game, including one in the first level (don't get too far ahead of the person you're running alongside, or you might have trouble continuing the mission), but don't let that get in the way of experiencing an incredibly well crafted adventure that really surpasses its genre in my view.  Oh, and I personally didn't care for the keyboard controls and vastly preferred my wired 360 pad, but your experience may vary.  The game works perfectly with a gamepad, though.  If you have any questions about the review, or if there is anything you'd like to know more about, please feel free to leave a comment!

This game makes me feel... at home. I don't know how else to describe it. Just comfortable, at peace, and makes me forget my worries. It's fun, engaging, and exciting. However, it is also serene, detatched from urgency, and simply relaxing.
I've played this game since it released in late 2013, and after playing over the past two and a half years, seeing the development really makes me happy with how far along this game has come.
Now, about the game and not my experience.
Exploration, creation, survival. These are my favorite aspects, in that order. Going to new star systems, in my own star ship, is my favorite thing about this game. While some planets feel similar to others, it's always a thrill to beam down to a planet not knowing exactly what lies ahead.
Creation is great as well. I'm not the most creative person, but I enjoy creating a home organically without planning ahead and expanding when I need more room. I've seen some amazing designs and admit I've used some of these designs as a homage to the people who are more artistically skilled than I am.
Survival is nice. I like the danger of wildlife, the environment, and other intelligent life that may or may not pose a threat.
All in all, I'd recommend this game to everyone, although I know this game isn't for everyone. No game is, but it is for me and I haven't personally met anyone who has played the game that didn't enjoy the experience.

This is my favourite Single Player game, ever.
Bastion is an isometric top-down action game developed by SuperGiant games.
It revolves around the story of a great calamity that claimed the lives of most people, and fractured the world into floating islands. The story is rich and moving, but delivered quite simply and effectively.
The narrator, who is actually one of the characters you meet in the game, is the highlight. The narrator dynamically comments on your actions as the game plays, as well as delivering information. Sometimes he might comment on your weapon choices, or your eagerness to dawdle around breaking crates. The narrator feels incredibly alive and human, and you really become attatched to him. Not to mention the outstanding voice work.
The art style is wonderfully charming and colourful, reminiscent of an oil painting. The music, one of my favourite parts, is beatifully composed, with mixes of emotional, intense vocal pieces among catchy Western-themed tracks.
Now to the gameplay. Bastion has action-packed top-down combat, that involves a lot of rolling, a lot of dodging, and a lot of good timing. There are a plethora of weapons to be unlocked throughout the game, each of which are completely different from each other in design, play style and effective uses. These weapons can be upgraded throughout the game with parts and currency you collect in the levels. Each upgrade also has 2 paths, often allowing different ways of play, such as fire rate/damage, or accuracy/spread. Enemies in the game are all unique and aptly named, and attack you with projectiles, charges, pickaxes and stink clouds, you name it. There is also a "counter attack" which you can perform by timing your shield blocks well.
Bastion has plenty of extra content to keep the game time going. You may just want to upgrade all the weapons to see what cool ultimate abilities you can use, in the "New Game Plus" mode which surprisingly fits with the story. There is also a shrine in which you can activate "idols" that add extra challenge in exchange for money and Exp. boosts. You might want to replay just for another ending. You can also play "score challenge" mode, racking up scores based on your performance in-level, or try the proving grounds, that test your skill with weapons to unlock upgrade parts and secret skills.
Some say the game is too short (6-8 hours to play the campaign normally) like the hours mean anything. Bastion did all it needed with the time it had, and I couldn't have asked for a better experience from a game of this genre. It immersed me, it made me emotional, and I'm on my 4th playthrough.
No sane person will go through their life and never play Bastion. It is a work of art, an interactive one, a FUN one.

AvP was one of those games that critics unfairly judged. Upon its release in 2010, critics largely gave it negative reviews, citing clunky controls, a thin plot, and a weak Alien campaign. However, as time has gone on, AvP seems to have grown on gamers, as evidenced by the shockingly high approval rating it has on Steam. I am one of those gamers, and I am confident in saying that AvP is the best Aliens experience available on PC, surpassing even Aliens: Colonial Marines in its sheer enjoyability and technical prowess.
PROS:
+ Strong Marine and Predator campaigns that deal with what is, in my opinion, an exceedingly immersive and interesting story on par with those from the comics. The Marine campaign in particular is by far the closest you will get to being a Colonial Marine, with your film-authentic pulse rifle constantly blaring as you see shadows shift across the walls and your infamous motion tracker pinging you over and over again as certain doom approaches.
+ An amazing Predator campaign that genuinely makes you feel like the notorious interstellar hunter. Stalking Marines or fending off hordes of Xenomorphs never gets tiresome. Additionally, this is the only big-budget, triple-A game offering the ability to play as the Predator, and I am thankful the experience does not disappoint.
+ Surprisingly impressive graphics, especially for 2010. The Aliens in particular are stellar, with light perfectly reflecting off their oily skin and saliva constantly seeping from their maws.
+ Excellent animations; again, the Aliens are the best example of these, moving perfectly across walls and ceilings with the same ferocity we witnesed in the Aliens film.
+ Enjoyable boss fights, particularly in the Marine campaign. The duel with the Queen about 3/4 of the way through it is possibly the best boss battle in an Aliens game.
+ Generally satisfactory voice acting, most notably  by Lance Henriksen, the actor who portrayed Bishop in Aliens. There are exceptions to this; without spoiling anything, you encounter a character halfway through the Marine campaign who nags at you incessantly and has voice acting you would expect from an English-dubbed Russian movie.
+ Gore, gore, and gore - the sheer violence and brutality of this game is on par with the likes of Gears of War. Cruelly executing hapless Marines as the Alien or snapping a Xenomorph's spine as the Predator never gets old.
CONS:
- The Alien campaign is surprisingly weak, forcing you into repetitive, cliched corridors and lacking the length of its two counterparts. Although the execution animations are enjoyable, they are limited and will become mundane by the last two stages.
- Multiplayer is DEAD. Do not trust the other reviews for this game claiming that you'll be able to find a multiplayer match; there are very, very few active players, and most of the matches that are miraculously full are often plagued with unbannable hackers. If you plan to play multiplayer, be sure you have a few friends who own the game; otherwise, disregard it entirely.
- Terrible AI exemplified by the stealth mechanics present in both the Predator and Alien campaigns. Are you seriously trying to convince me a Predator would be able to spam pre-recorded lines audible to every marine near it and somehow distract them every single time? How about an Alien hissing and separating marine units despite said marines knowing they're dealing with a Xenomorph, a creature renowned for its stealth? It's sheer stupidity and should have received much more attention during the game's development. This is partially redeemed by the enjoyability of said stealth sections, however.

Grand Theft Auto never really appealed to me, because I don't like playing the bad guy in games.  At the same time, I enjoy stories whose moral setups emphasize the practical, and Sleeping Dogs delivers big time.  Imagine an open-world action game where you're the cop, not the criminal.  At the same time, since you spend the game undercover, your duties for gangs and for your police advisors will make you question the line between good and evil more times than you can imagine.
Wei Shen's romp through the streets of Hong Kong is a viciously bloody one, but the game never substitutes style for substance--the story in general is tremendously well told from start to finish, the characters are distinct and memorable, the friendships will make you cheer, and the betrayals will make you angry.  Wei feels like a character with a difficult past and a complex personality, so his behavior seems plausible no matter how you play him, even if you go on a rampage.  Speaking of which, the game even has leaderboards where you can compete against your friends for doing a huge variety of tasks, such as how long you can hold a wheelie on a motorcycle--and, yes, how many kills of a certain fashion you can string together.
The integration of morality into the game mechanics is among the most interesting I've ever seen.  You don't pick your choices from a dialogue menu.  You have two morality meters in your missions, one for the cops and one for the triads.  The former starts as perfect and goes down if you hurt innocents or even if you're clumsy at jumping over things (I restarted checkpoints I don't know how many times because of this), and the latter starts at zero and goes up if you're particularly creative--and brutal--in terms of how you fight.  The game focuses primarily on melee combat, which plays out like in a Batman Arkham game.  You don't get the Dark Knight's mind-boggling array of gadgets, but you do get to spend your cop and triad levels on various new abilities, such as being able to break your opponents' legs by stomping sideways on them.  This makes other opponents (and possibly the player) wince, so this even has a useful purpose.
The game does also have guns, and while they're fairly typical, two things impress me more--
1) The scripting and writing for the story missions is excellently done, making each fight a blast, and
2) This game's implementation of bullet time feels like a reward and not like a cheap gimmick.  You have to jump over obstacles to be able to use it, as opposed to simply pressing a button, so the combat bonus feels like something you actually earned.  You can also disarm your enemies through a variety of means.
The setting of Hong Kong is absolutely gorgeous, especially with the free high-definition textures, and you'll find plenty to do there, even at the arguable expense of plausibility (drug busts I can see, but I'm glad Wei also has time for street racing).  Players who aren't comfortable with stealing cars usually won't be forced to--there are plenty of taxis in the city, and more importantly, you can drive around in your own private vehicles while listening to a nice variety of radio stations, including classical music.  Just remember to drive on the left!
The vehicles themselves are a joy, especially during the on-wheels combat segments.  Ramming cars sideways into walls a la F-Zero does not get old, and neither does jumping onto another car and hijacking it a la Pursuit Force.  Or you can just shoot out the fire and send a vehicle speeding into a light pole or another car.
There are a number of bugs in the game, including one in the first level (don't get too far ahead of the person you're running alongside, or you might have trouble continuing the mission), but don't let that get in the way of experiencing an incredibly well crafted adventure that really surpasses its genre in my view.  Oh, and I personally didn't care for the keyboard controls and vastly preferred my wired 360 pad, but your experience may vary.  The game works perfectly with a gamepad, though.  If you have any questions about the review, or if there is anything you'd like to know more about, please feel free to leave a comment!

- Some of the minigames seemed like an unnecessary shift in gameplay.
Overall:
Great game.  I don't mean to spoil anything since this genre is obviously bolstered by its story, but I will say that I thoroughly enjoyed this game.  It took some odd turns, and every one of them was weird and wonderful.  There were many times it felt like this game had reached into my nightmares and pulled out the most disturbing images it could find.  Somehow, it also managed to achieve so much charm and depth.  All of this was intensified by the effect of Fran's childish narration.
Fran Bow is a wonderful game.  I definitely recommend it to anyone in the mood for a great point and click.

MCPIXEL was shockingly enjoyable and entertaining. To break it down for you, its a point and click puzzle game set in brief different scenarios, such as in a falling elevator, you need to analyze how to save the day. You have  an emergency button, elevator buttons, an old man, a bell hop and an extinguisher. What do you do to save the day? These are wacky and weird situations, usually involving bombs or gasoline. None of which lasts no longer than 15 seconds. The game is broken up into 4 chapters, each chapter has 3 or so clusters of 6 scenarios / challenges. If you fail doing a challenge, you don't do it over and over until you get it right, you just go to the next uncompleted scenario.
I completed the entire first chapter in about 15 minutes, which is 18 challenges? There is free DLC, which is a series of selectable clusters made by fans or whomever. There is a lot of content here, but the real catch is the challenges just don't last a long time. They're pretty easy to figure out.
The cherry on top of this is that there are some laugh out loud results. Maybe the results are so LOL because they're so unexpectedly random. Again, I expected nothing from this game and got a lot of entertainment from it. I'll be returning to the game to see the other quirky scenarios with crude graphics.
Dont forget to rescue your son!

Finally a game showing how Richard 'Demo♥♥♥♥♥♥ Marcinko single-handedly stopped World War III (right after having almost caused it)! What, you've never heard of him or the mentioned scenario? Of course not! Covert Operations, you dummy! Then how would one even know about such a person or event? Because he wrote books about it, obviously! Duh!
You could probably best describe the game as a cover-based 3rd-person-shooter, except that it's played in 1st person most of the time. But it will remind you about it by frequently switching to 3rd-person-view whenever you take cover, climb ladders or perform instant kills (more on those later). There are also some stealth mechanics, you can shoot out lights, use night vision goggles, sneak up to enemies and perform instant stealth kills (more on those later). But why would you waste time doing that, when you can just directly run up to an enemy (they're bad shots) and quickly take them out with an instant kill (more on those later) instead?
OK, ok, I'll get to it. You can instantly kill enemies by pressing "e" when you're close to them. And you'll make use of this A LOT. In fact, you will hardly bother sneaking or shooting enemies as the instant kill attack is so overpowered and instant that you'll hardly want to use anything else at all. You can even skip reloading during a firefight and run directly in front of enemies instead. For whatever reason, they can hardly hit a moving target but are good at hitting you even when you're in cover. Go figure!
There are even a few different killing animations. However not nearly enough, so by the end of the game, the novelty will have worn off and you'll have seen each and every one of them about a dozen times. Whoever thought knife-stabbing and neck-breaking never gets old, was wrong. Horribly wrong. Watching any old Steven Seagal movie on repeat over and over again is more exciting and less repetitive, actually.
So why would you bother playing the game then? Because of Mickey Rourke's voicework for the main charakter, of course! There are lots and lots of different kinds of swearing and insulting, and contrary to the instant kills, they never get old. They even give insight in♥♥♥♥♥♥s personality. Like his balls are big and hairy... and he likes them wrapped around. Don't ask me why or how he would do that - it's from one of the game's more memorable lines of dialogue.
So basically you run around stabbing people and breaking their necks, listening to Mickey Rourke cursing for about 90 minutes until the credits roll. That's right! The game is that short! But it doesn't even need to be any longer to get its entire story accross. You'll start shooting Koreans and end up shooting Russians and once in a while, stuff explodes. Oh, and the music is good. It does a fantastic job at making things seem more important and urgent than they really are.
So why would I actually recommend the game nevertheless? Because it's some good old stupid guilty pleasure fun, especially because of the oneliners. And it's over before it starts getting (too) repetitive and boring as well.
It definitely isn't a good or memorable game, and it's probably also not even worth the full price of 5 bucks, but there's no harm in grabbing it when it goes on sale for 1-2 bucks. Some things - like the game's dialogue - just have to be expierienced to be believed!

I find it a shame and astonishing that a game as good as Saturday Morning RPG has not done better commercially. The game has some crazy achievements, such as fighitng 1,000 and even up to 5,000 battles, based on an initial idea of 20 episodes. Since it didn't do well, they had to limit their ambitions to six episodes, hopefully with a fine tuning of the achievements in the future.
But why is all this necessary? The game has everyone a gamer would be looking for. A series of episodes with a simple story, with tons of nostalgic references for one thing. I mean the main character is a guy named Marty, who rides a hoverboard, and gets his powers from a mysterious man known as The Wizard. The retro graphics are a joy to behold, the music is killer, and the gameplay is a very solid Paper Mario/Super Mario RPG type of thing, with button presses for better defense and better attacks.
Not to mention your magic spells use everyday objects, from cookies and paper airplanes, to swords and baseball bats, up to toy aircraft carriers and transformer-like figurines. Hell even your notebook plays a part in the game as depending on the cover and the stickers you can enact various bonuses before each battle.
As it stands at this time there are four episodes, with total time of about 10 hours to get through all of them. There is an arena mode against two semi-tough bosses, and endless battle challenges based around each chapter. You can get the grindy achievements I mentioned earlier legitimately, but my first run through the game got me less then even 100 battles, not counting everything else. Still if you want to, the game is a pleasure to play, and with the huge episode 5 coming early next year, there's no time like the present to get in and get ready for it.

First, while I admit this game isn't as close to being as good as the one developed in 2001 (AVP 2), it does have some perks, but I'd give this game a 7/10 for effort.
Perks:
1)  Great atmosphere, you will get some level of fear playing as the marine (which is where the main story is)
2)  Predator and Alien campaigns are pretty well done, while adding depth to the species
3)  Enjoy the limiting of the marine's weapons, requiring you to make valid and calculated choices.
4)  Lance Henrickson . . . enough said
5)  Fighting off an alien hive in an adult bar . . . epic and scary at the same time.
5)  Being able to attack the Preds with a cohort of Xenomorphs.
Flaws:
1)  The melee combat for humans?  WTF is a pistol whip going to do against a Xeno or Pred about to shaft you?
2)  Predalien that can hop through lava?  Come on, downing the queen early on was more plausible, as was the Praetorian.
3)  Voice-less main character?  In this age of story-telling, having a silent protagonist is kinda lackluster to the product.
4)  Doesn't seem to be enough fear and suspense in some areas for a game based on two classics of the same genre.
So, while I give the game props for decent level design and graphics, along with some interesting play options . . . it's kinda lackluster for the series compared to the two originals.  I recommend this game to those who truly love the series or like the potential in the multiplayer . . . other than than, it's kind of a meh level thumbs up.

Better animations, more intuitive puzzles and solutions, less needless areas, and a proper mystery story that promises even more to come… in short, Abandoned 2 managed to fix the biggest issues of the first game and improved upon its Myst-like 2D point ‘n’ click formula.
The first Abandoned game felt more like a prologue; as it turns out, it really was that, as the second game, Through Abandoned 2: The Forest, is the one where things are actually getting started. Things that mostly fall in the suspense mystery story category—Abandoned 2 is not a horror game, but it still manages to create a sense of dread, as we explore an abandoned world (yep, the title finally makes sense), following the trails of the protagonist’s brother.
Gameplay is similar to the first one, mostly in the veins of a mobile/Flash first-person adventure game: the player scrolls through a grid of static screens, looking for items, interactive spots, or doors that lead to some kind of a smaller sub-dimension that could contain some crucial element. There are also some puzzles, both mandatory an optional; the former are relatively straightforward, but the optional ones can put any adventure gamer to the test. This dual nature and the better variety in scenery result in a rather enjoyable adventure game, if you like these short indie types.

This game was better when it was free.  I don't say that because 'free is always better,'  no, I mean when the game was free it was engineered in subtle, but noticably different ways then this version for the PC.  I see all these glittering reviews, claiming this is the best TD evar.  Really?  Which version where these people playing?  The free version they've played to death, or the PC version that has a load of problems?
I've played the free version ( the one that had locked premium content ) on PC, and it's the superior version.  Why?
One : Hero units.  The game needed to be rebalanced for the hero units, and they added mechanics that honestly, weren't needed.  The free version was engineered in a way that you -didn't need hero units to play the game -AND- win-  I could beat the game without a hero in the orgininal, now I need to.  Got some issues there, because the enemies are buffed up to make up for the heroes simply existing.
Not only that, but the melee heroes are pointless.  Utterly, and completely, pointless.  If you didn't swap out to a ranged type hero when the flying units started showing up, then the exploding demon type enemies will have pointed out how useless they are.   And, on top of that, the ranged heroes have a plethora of abilities that are just synergize better with the towers : Abilities that slow, waylay, or simply stop an enemy for the towers to wittle down.
Two : Complete reliance on acing levels to have the necesary upgrades to succede later in the game.  Now, it's no big secret that beating level one means you can play level two.  Here, though, you -need- to ace level one, so that you can have the upgrades that will make the game 'easier' later on.  If you simply beat each level, say getting one or two stars a pop, the game is significantly ( and un-neccesarily ) more difficult later on.  Because that makes sense, right?   And in some cases, you need to do the challenges to get more stars to... you guessed it... have the neccesary upgrades to have a better chance of beating the game.  So what's the magic solution?  Repeatitive game play forcing the player to redo earlier missions over and over again in the hope of acing the level so that you get the upgrade points you -NEED- by the end of the game.
Three : Problems with upgrades.  Specifically, if I try to do a challenge level, it takes upgrades away.  Towers cost full price, or don't have the buffs you spent so much time earning.  Why is that?  Isn't the challenge hard enough already?  'No hero.'  Okay, get that.  'No barracks, no hero.'  Okay... I'd... kind  of like to have the buffs I earned.  And honestly, I don't know if the upgrades even matter in the long run.  Do the top tier upgrades even function?  It'd be nice if there was an indicator that the top tier 'chance for double damage' arrow talent was working, an exclamation point over an enemies head if they take double damage would be nice.  'Spiked Armor?'  Does it even work?  I can't even tell!
Four : What I'd like to call 'The Korean Problem.' Now, you all know the meme 'Koreans play video games better.'  This game falls prey to this, as a in the last third of the game ( and the bonus content ) are incredibly difficult, requiring precise tower placement, upgrade, and unit movement.  In fact, I have no clue how in the heck you beat the swamp level.  The boss wave is ludricrous!  How is swarming the lanes with enormous amounts of enemies supposed to be 'challenging?'  This just tells me there's -one- way to place and upgrade the towers in many of these levels.  -One-  How is that supposed to be 'fun?'    Any answer that revolves around 'look it up online'  means the game is an utter failure.  I've played far better TD's that offered challenging experiences -and- allowed for more freedom in tower placement.
Bottom line, this game isn't worth 10 dollars.  It isn't even worth 5 dollars.  I could play the game for free, and have far more fun, and not need the heroes or bonus content.  I feel ripped off.  And if you bought this game on Steam you've been ripped off too.
Oh.  And PS ~
For anyone that wants to leave a comment about the review, please spare me the subjective stand point of how much you loved the game.  Subjective means 'opinion' and everyone's got one.  Objective statements, on the other hand, are not opinionated in anyway.  If you want to leave a comment, then do so, but at least try to have a better leg to stand on then 'oh, poor you, you couldn't beat it?  you must have been stupid'  Because that's a great way to start a conversation right?

"FIGHT!"
The long-running Mortal Kombat series once again heads to PC, with a pared down fighting system and character roster that evoke the series' simpler days.  There's no 'run' button, though you can double-tap movement keys to dash back and forth.  You don't have Animalities, Brutalities, Aggression meters, fighting-style switches, in-stage weapons, or goofy puzzle minigames.  Combat takes place on a 2D plane, so you're not moving toward or away from the camera.
The game has three primary modes--the story, the traditionally structured Arcade ladder, and the challenge tower.  (I don't count the multiplayer since I have never ~once~ gotten it to work properly.)  Yes, the game does have a plot, and it's surprisingly well done.   Many of the older games' most iconic characters--Jax, Liu Kang, Sub-Zero, Sonya Blade, and so on--make their "return" in this retelling of the series' central narrative themes.  Johnny Cage and Sonya have their goofy interactions.  Liu Kang and Kung Lao do their thing.  Sub-Zero and Scorpion have their drama, and so on.  Instead of keeping the story in the background and limiting it to text epilogues--other than in the ladder mode (quick to finish, highly replayable) -- the story unfolds in a format that feels like a movie but is more entertaining than a great deal of actual movies I've seen.
The campaign is fairly lengthy without feeling drawn out, and one of its best decisions is to force the player to constantly switch up characters.  You start off as the movie star Johnny Cage, allowing you to get used to his mix of close-range and projectile-based battling before the game gives you a perspective shift.  You essentially have so many player characters that I'd have to stop to count them, and while some of the excuses for fights are silly contrivances, the game uses these misunderstandings as a really good excuse for exposing you to a wide variety of fight arrangements in a nicely diverse array of settings, some of which will look familiar to series veterans.  The actual story gets off to a rough start, as Cage is rather patronizing towards women, but even if his personality can be rather aggravating,
1) He has a personality at all, which is more than I can say for too many game characters, and
2) He eventually grows out of it and becomes more tolerable.  That, and this does lead to some welcome comic relief.
The voice acting throughout the campaign ranges from decent to laughable, but the capable writing actually manages to evoke legitimate emotion at times without becoming melodramatic.  You really feel like something has happened by the time you reach the end of the story, you won't be able to predict every little thing that happens just by playing the earlier games, and even though the ending is bittersweet, it's satisfying and nowhere near as much as a waste of time as the plot was in, say, Deception (no points for guessing why).  The story mode's difficulty can be changed from within the options menu, and the challenge scales up really nicely by the end of the campaign.  The final boss fight--and you will know it when it comes--is HARD but is extremely satisfying to finish.  The game is generous with its autosaves after fights and cutscenes, so you rarely have to repeat content if you want to take a break.  You can't perform fatalities during the campaign, though, because you will routinely see characters exit the story and come back in later on.  This being Mortal Kombat, people do die, and the opening of the game does a very good job of establishing a grim atmosphere.  There are also scenes that shift into some really, really well done albeit grisly animation, making for some of the best moments in a story that feels sincere without coming across as exploitative toward either extreme (whether inappropriate comedy--usually--or excessive tear-jerking).
That being stated, even as much as I really enjoyed the story mode, it pales in comparison to the Challenge Tower, which in my view is the single best reason to buy this game.  You have hundreds of ridiculously creative self-contained challenges that pit a wide variety of characters against one another under unpredictable circumstances.  The humor is scaled up a lot here from the story mode, and there's a much larger variety of things to do when compared to that mode, which has basic matches, handicap tag matches (which you will feel awesome after beating), and little else.  Try defeating your opponent when neither of you has arms.  Try doing it without the use of throws, or special moves, or the ability to block.  Sometimes you have to contend with a slot machine that randomizes the terms of your next fight.  At one point you play a cyborg whose internal systems are shutting down, making each of his attacks deal less damage with every one you launch.  Make them all count!  There's even a bizarre variant on H-O-R-S-E, where you try to mimic or exceed your opponent's percentage of damage dealt across a number of miniature rounds.
There's a lot of stuff to unlock, such as fatality design-concept sketches, alternate costumes, special codes to change the terms of multiplayer engagements (remember these?), and tons of concept art.  Having to buy things by walking up to headstones and torture devices in a really creepy graveyard, in first-person mode, can be a bit aggravating.  You do get a map, which is also good for auto-transporting you to locations you've overlooked, so you don't get lost.
The game's learning curve is very gentle.  You don't have ridiculously long combos to learn, and the tutorials (which love the use of a game controller but are doable with a keyboard) perform an adequate job of teaching you basic and advanced concepts, some of which have changed from what you may remember.  You do get a special meter that you can expend in whole or in part to enhance your attacks or to break your opponent's bones, which usually takes off about a third of their health but doesn't affect their fighting abilities.  You can even learn the basics of fatalities--per character, not just for one individual as a "demonstration"--which is a really nice touch.  You can also practice, but in my mind you might as well just play the arcade ladder and keep referring back to the move list.  The AI is patient enough to wait.
Even though the game does have its camera leer over women who are for the most part stuck in sexualized outfits (as are a number of the men, really), the girls can generally hold their own, and they're every bit as enjoyable to play as the guys are.  The game does pretty much everything it can not to show nips on the ladies, but if you want to see Liu Kang's or Quan Chi's, well, there you go.
Overall, I still would name Deadly Alliance my favorite of the series, but since that's not on Steam, this is still worth a buy.  You may as well wait until it's on sale for $5 like I did, because even though the multiplayer is ... shall we say, not up to the level of Skullgirls', the single-player game still has just enough content to let you experience its extremely gory thrills to the joy of your heart, if probably not your stomach.  (You may seriously want to check out YouTube videos of fatalities to make sure you can handle them before buying.)  Local multiplayer also works well and will probably not cause frame drops even if, like me, you game on a system with integrated graphics; the graphics and especially the character models still look really good even with the resolution and settings turned down.  There is no open world that the game has to render, so that probably helps.  This is worth a look!

tl;dr: atmospheric point'n'click with psychological horror and an open ending. Good story and fitting (if somewhat unimpressive) artstyle, but a little short for the money.
Fran Bow.
Now I'm not big on point'n'click, so I can't provide much intel on how good the game is from that angle - so I just don't. Fran Bow is a very calm and atmospheric game and doesn't really have jumpscares. It is more a psychological type of horror and with the open ending (If you don't like things to be left unclarified fran bow isn't for you, I guess) and the many little bits of information you get throughout the game it gives you a lot to think about and a whole lot of room for interpretation and although I think I have I pretty good idea of what really was the case there are still things left that don't quite add up. That may be a design-choice of the devs or something I'm missing here. From the perspective of the story overall and the implementation I can recommend the game.
Graphics are nothing special and "point'n'clicky" (?)
basically nothing impressive just what you would expect from such a game. The Artstyle used within there is fitting. From the gloomy elements to the colourful, outright childish, cute-sy elements... It just adds up and enforces the atmosphere.
The difficulty level is rather low. I dare say no puzzle is really gonna stomp ya.
The game however is rather short. You can play through in no more than a couple of hours, even in one go if you would want to do so - without missing out on anything I might add. The game feels plenty long enough to though and complete. The main critic I have on this game is that in being so short it feels a little pricey if you purchase on full price. All things considered probably worth the money anyways.

A work of art. Of dark and eerie kind, but still.
This is not a game for everyone. But if you enjoy deranged stories full of demons and gore, all kept in a distinctive, eye-catching visual style then this game is highly recommended.
And don’t be fooled by the fact that this game was developed by a small studio consisting of two (!) developers – both Fran Bow and its creators prove that a pair of heroes may challenge the entire world. And succeed.
To be clear: I am a fan of exceptional art design in games and I'm able to turn a blind eye to some flaws in mechanics or gameplay if the game keeps me entertained with its unique climate or artistic vision. And the climate is one of the best things in Fran Bow. Art style and dialogs written for 10 year old Fran are the strongest points of this game that maintain an impression of experiencing a really, really twisted fairytale. The music fits perfectly, scary and disturbing right when it needs to be.
Also the overall style of the game is really dark and combined with the pills mechanism creates an impressive duo. The backgrounds and animations are really well done and able to convey characters’ emotions pretty well. I enjoyed the level design and the creativity put to preserve diversity – you traverse both corridors and open spaces, some of them kept in gloomy tone, others drawn in a fairytale fashion. Not to mention most of them come in 2 (or even 4!) different variations you and Fran keep switching between.
Some of the devs’ ideas I’ve came across turned out to be really disturbing for me but having seen the trailer I knew what I was signing up for. In a nutshell – discretion advised.
Plot revolves around Fran facing a family tragedy and having to solve a mystery of a monstrous crime she is accused of committing. While the story may be predictable, it surely holds a handful of WTF moments only enhanced with the way a particular scene or character is drawn.
The story is not explained completely and personally I do not mind some space for your own interpretation. However, if you’re not into theories and speculations, you may find the story and its conclusion a bit disappointing.
As most point and click games, Fran Bow offers many puzzles that require you to search for items, combine them and use in an appropriate way. I find the riddles on a decent level with some requiring you to ponder a little longer. From time to time, the game offers some more interesting puzzles, like mechanisms or combination locks (though these are too easy to break in my opinion). There are also a couple of very simple mini-games here and there. One of them was boring, another one had irritating controls, but you can skip any of them – you just miss an achievement by doing so.
One of the key features of the game is switching between two (or more) realities to complete puzzles. This introduces many possibilities to combine actions made in different, complementary worlds to achieve your goal.
Yeah, a separate paragraph for cutscenes. They are just awesome.

As a total Obsidian/New Vegas ♥♥♥♥♥♥rider, I can 100% say that this game isn't as bad as it comes off. There are way way worse games in the series and way worse games in general. This game, at the very least, is generic and average. At the very most, it's an interesting departure from the series norm while bringing Fallout into a new generation with some old mechanics.
By the "interesting depature" I mean more of a focus on FPS mechanics with traditional fallout RPG elements supporting it. If that sounds like a turnoff for you, then you're probably not going to like this game. If you want your Fallout experiences to be PURELY APOCALYPTIC ADVENTURES WITH MUH CHOICES AND MUH RPG ELEMENTS then you won't like this too much either.
The game has a lot going for it while it loses some of its' old charm: Graphics, new mechanics (Settlement building is interesting), a new and vast location, as well as a decent storyline if you can get past some holes. Despite the damage Bethesda did to the fallout RPG elements, the game still stands slightly leaned toward tolerable despite the shell of it being taken away. The game in the end kept my attention and was a fun experience overall, even if it wasn't the MUH FALLOUT RPG everyone hoped it to be.

This game takes everything the "Grand Theft Auto" games do, and does it all better. The driving is less frustrating, the missions are more varied including a bunch of goofy side quests, the soundtrack is immense (even on fast-forward mode, the music section of the credits takes over 5 minutes to scroll through) and well-selected, the story is more engaging, the character building system is deeper, and the combat is more fun. It also has a great sense of place; aside from being nowhere near as crowded with people as the real thing, the game's Hong Kong does a great job of evoking the actual city.
Fighting and driving games are near the bottom of my list of preferred genres, so it's pretty remarkable that a game that's centered around those two things kept me glued to my screen.
Some of the DLC is worth getting too. Here's what I'd recommend getting and the order to play it: "Wheels of Fury" (wait until near the end of the main story; the reward is fun but a bit OP), "Zodiac Tournament" (okay to play any time, but again probably best near the end of the main story since that's when you'll be strong enough to win), "Nightmare in North Point" (play after the main story), and "Year of the Snake" (play this last). The other DLC is either cosmetic or, worse, ruins the game balance, so avoid it.

I actaully bought the game before I played it on browser (had no idea it was f2p), but I can say I don't regret it at all. I've played a lot more hours than steam states since I play it on university computers.
Anyways, the game is a whole lot of fun (I'll spare you a rundown of how to play since other reviews do that), it does a great job of creating distrust between players and there can be some really tense moments when you think you are about to die or you are an evil character and you think you've been found out. It's a perfect mix between tension and funny moments. There's also something for every mood your in. If you want something serious there's a ranked match system (and to an extent ranked practice is somewhat serious), if you want something casual there's ranked practice or classic, and if you just want to mess around in a game where no one is being serious go for AllAny.
I've seen some other reviews complaining about the toxic community, but in my experience (100+ hrs.) I can say the community is pretty decent, nothing special. Yeah, you sometimes get trolls and gamethrowers, but that happens in any online multiplayer game, and in the more serious modes, most of your games will have a decent quality of players.
All in all, try it online before you buy, but buying is seriously worth it to help the devs (plus you get some cool extras)

This is one of my most favorite games of all time that I feel it has so much more than Terarria (Sorry, had to be said.)
Even though I took a break off of it I do enjoy the idea of jumping into a random world, fully kitted out and fully upgraded, just to build some mega city for all forms of live to live in peace, then go off looting other planets of it's treasures and resources. Hell I feel like a crazed American/Eagle hybrid for draining a single planet of it's oil content and leaving it a dry crusty rock in space.
There is a lot to explore including portals, communities, hostile fortresses and even your friend's ship for a random space party. The variety of weapons and items are pretty unique and could very well expand more. The best day of my life when I can buy a space chocolate bar from the intergalactic space station.
I do get annoyed with hostiles slaughtering me over and over and knowing I am not equipped well enough, but that is still part of a challenge and it could be a great victory, even if the hostile bandits or robot knights have little loot.
So yeah, I love this game and I do hope there will be so much more to offer in the future. Play it with friends, play it for challenge, play it when you're bored, buy it for a friend even if you'd like. The most fun you'll ever have when you're flying around in some crazy space ship in a shape of a train whilst being an entity of living spark life dressed like a drifter of the old space west.
Oh yeah, I hope there will be hover bikes and crazy highways someday. Heh.

That process repeated seemingly endlessly with me able to get away from them maybe a little bit each time. I finally gave up and quit.
