When I started this game, I didn't know what to expect. I'd played countless legendary FPSs including
,
,
and even
(see last months review). Obviously I hadn't expected much out of this game at first, but as I got off that first helicopter and saw the grenades rolling, I was already ducking in my chair. The immersion was incredible, and that was just in the cut-scene. Even
didn't have me this engrossed at the get go. When you first take control of Marcinko, you feel like you can do anything, and this game doesn't hold you back.
The combat is spectacular, from the quiet yet lethal silenced pistol, to the untamable roar of the AK-74, you feel like a real American Army Marine. To the view-models, animations, and sounds, the guns are incredible. The innovative “Kill Move” also adds another layer of strategy to the combat. The enemy AI is rather stupid, which I initially assumed to be a fault of the games programmers, but I quickly realized it was intentional because after all, I was fighting communists.
Moving away from the combat, the plot was nothing less than genius. Much like a well written TV show, (see my review of
) it had me glued to the seat for the entire duration of the game. The consistent and unpredictable plot twists kept me thinking to myself “just one more chapter”. There were moments where I cried, but that only made the ending so much sweeter. I'll leave that one for you gamers to experience for yourselves. Trust me, it's worth it.
I noticed many of these reviews didn't mention the level design. This game stole the crown from
own
. Except
genius wasn't limited to just a single level. You see,
didn't just overshadow
, it—to quote Marcinko—made it “suck it's balls, it's hairy f*****g balls, wrap them around it's mouth”. Even now I find it difficult to compare the two.
One of the things that impressed me the most about this game was the sound and graphics. Both of these lent themselves to the total immersion I was experiencing. Even on my Apple Airpods™ and Compaq™ CRT monitor I still felt what can only be described as ecstasy. Even when zoomed in on Marcinko's magnificent beard, I could see every individual hair and pore. I could hear the brush of the trigger and the deafening crack of the sniper rifle. This is something that can only be experienced, not described by a mortal such as myself.
In conclusion, It would feel wrong to even give this game a 100/100 rating, because then I would be comparing it to other games with similar scores. You see, no game can be compared to this masterpiece, even on a point scale. In light of this, I have lowered all scores on all my other reviews to compensate. All past and future games will now be measured on a scale of .0 to 1.0.

Through Abandoned 2 is an interesting game. Classical point&click adventure, drawn by hand, in worlds where no people were left. There can be clearly seen a big inspiration from Mateusz Skutnik's Submachine. While the basic inspiration is good, I am afraid it went a bit too far in the second chapter as an opposite of the first one, which was better in some aspects. I want to mention specific problems of the game now mainly for the author to get better next time, so expect spoilers in the following parts of the review ;)
In the whole game, you tend to tell the whole plot you invented. Since your game is a type of art (do not say it is not - I know it is!), there should be some place for the player's own thoughts. The story is told through the fingerprint-displays, but most of the messages are just asking a question and then answering it on the next display. That's a method for kids, not for adult people :D When you look for example onto diaries in Submachine 2, they are very mystical and unspecific, which is a working way how to tell just a bit of the story. In the whole Submachine, there are facts you know and facts you can just wonder about. The second is somehow missing in this game.
It is a very hard challenge to create a point&click game in the right difficulty. Because, it has to not be both too easy and too hard. The last puzzle with cubes behind the door with 8 lights was very hard, not for the principle, but because there was no signal you are doing right. Every time I left the room, all cubes were reset except for when there was the correct  pattern or something like that, so I have set it right a few times on both sides, but since it did not respond, I thought it was wrong. Apart from that, it is a bit strange that some of the tools are keeped after using while others are not - the shovel disappeared after digging the hole, but I was left with the UV lamp all the time, so I tried it everywhere without effect. But that's not so important.
The UI was not good. It is a fullscreen game, what's the point of having a hidable toolbar? That means two additional clicks almost every time I want to use an item, or when I left it open all the time, it hides the most bottom clickable space, so I am not able to move down. The items could show up on mouse hover, or just use a permanent toolbar.
Due to these problems, Through Abandoned 2 is far from perfect, but that does not mean it's bad. It still fits to the classical point&click genre, which is quite falling nowadays, so this game can be a good pick. Dear Author, good luck to the next chapter! :)

So again, slight disclaimer at the start of this, I given this copy of the game.
Overall I like it.  It's a neat concept, and the world seems interesting and is fun to explore at this stage.  It's a little reminiscent of a few other things, but it seems to be going in its own direction.  I also found the puzzles to be for the most part fairly intuitive, with a few exceptions.
There's no internal monologue.  I think that's at least in part a stylistic choice, and for the most part it works.  instead of there being a distinct character the player occupies, the player can react entirely in their own way to what happens in the game.  The downside however, is that there's also no hints on what to do next.  For me this lead to some confusion in a couple points, one where I didn't realize that I could in fact use a certain item on doors, and other times I wasn't sure if I was missing a critical item to complete a puzzle or merely approaching the puzzle wrong.
My other main complaint is that the game is rather short.  It is definitely an episode, and while I would say it is priced appropriately, one should not get this game expecting a long adventure or lots of replay value.  Althought it is worth noting that there are secrets, which require some inventive thinking to find.  So someone might be able to spend some time hunting those.
Overall, I would say it is probably worth the price, if you enjoy point and click adventures.

The sound design is exemplary, the obstacles are challenging but not frustrating in the slightest, every mistake is very much my own. Even the one-hit KO versions later in the game are a wonderful experience. I could sit and play this all day if I didn't have to eat, sleep and work. Sublime.
And, much later after the game's release, a fourth stage was added out of absolutely nowhere. And it is every bit as stunning as the original three, as well as managing to step up the difficulty curve just the right amount. As with the game at large, it's challenging, but highly rewarding in its incremental synesthesia, beginning as a foreboding dark ambient theme and somehow reaching its crescendo with a sound reminiscent of oldskool 90s house.
If it wasn't apparent, I really, really enjoy this. And the emergence of a whole new stage 4 years down the line has only reignited that captivation. If this looks and sounds like your sort of thing, or if you enjoyed titles such as Rez, the BIT.TRIP series or other games with dynamic music, 140 will surely go down a treat.

This game takes everything the "Grand Theft Auto" games do, and does it all better. The driving is less frustrating, the missions are more varied including a bunch of goofy side quests, the soundtrack is immense (even on fast-forward mode, the music section of the credits takes over 5 minutes to scroll through) and well-selected, the story is more engaging, the character building system is deeper, and the combat is more fun. It also has a great sense of place; aside from being nowhere near as crowded with people as the real thing, the game's Hong Kong does a great job of evoking the actual city.
Fighting and driving games are near the bottom of my list of preferred genres, so it's pretty remarkable that a game that's centered around those two things kept me glued to my screen.
Some of the DLC is worth getting too. Here's what I'd recommend getting and the order to play it: "Wheels of Fury" (wait until near the end of the main story; the reward is fun but a bit OP), "Zodiac Tournament" (okay to play any time, but again probably best near the end of the main story since that's when you'll be strong enough to win), "Nightmare in North Point" (play after the main story), and "Year of the Snake" (play this last). The other DLC is either cosmetic or, worse, ruins the game balance, so avoid it.

It's admittedly not a bad game. It started out beautifully, but it starts to fall apart at the mid-way point. Then add in the confusing out of nowhere ending and it appears to be less a matter of ambiguity and more that the creators couldn't make up their minds and threw in a twist at the last minute a la M. Night Shyamalan. A twist may be unexpected and shocking, but that doesn't make it good.
This is a point and click game that is mainly story-based and driven by narrative, but that only works against it as the mood and narrative ended up all over the place to the point that I had to question what game I was supposed to be playing after a while. The story started out dark and creepy with a little girl whose parents died being stuck in an institution and wanting to escape to find her lost cat. It's a good starting point and the setting and tone of the chapter were perfectly eerie and unsettling enough to draw me in and make me question what Fran and by extension we as the players were seeing. Even with the pills being used as a way to transition between the "real world" and the darker world where you can see shadows haunting the other people in the institution and revealing their pasts and trauma. It was creepy and tragic and a wonderful theme, and overall implied that what Fran may have been seeing in this other reality had a major basis in truth. It was a good premise and would certainly have been interesting to see addressed. Even the second chapter was similar, and even brought up the question of whether it was the house or the well that was actually "real". It was intriguing and left me both guessing and wanting to play more to get these answers. And to find the cat, because he was adorable.
But it all starts to fall apart midway through when the story made a leap from dark and horror to magical fantasy in chapter 3 and just kept going from there. It ended up being a serious case of mood whiplash and lost the aspect of the game that had me interested in the first place. The multiple fetch quests within fetch quests didn't help. Plus with the scenes being just as quirky and over the top off the reality-switching pills as they were when on them, that threw the question of "is this real" out the window because there stopped being a difference. And with everyone being unhelpfully vague or close-lipped when it came to getting some actual answers while throwing in a conspiracy in the last chapter, the game appears to be trying too hard to be ambiguous without actually being ambiguous. We ended up going from trying to uncover the conspiracy behind the murder of Fran's parents to having a different conspiracy sprung on us at the last part of the final chapter about the truth behind some doctor we never met and his never before mentioned plans or why those plans involve removing Fran's brain. The doctor and the aunt literally come out of nowhere and nothing that followed made any sense. That's not ambiguity, that's just poor writing.
It strikes me as one of those games that's meant to invoke discussion and make the players ask questions that won't be answered. The problem comes in that the only question I have is: What was the point?

Wow. Where to begin? This game is anchored around an incredibly fascinating, emotionally intelligent narrative that bursts out of its genre-box and into the kind of interpreative transcendentalism that reverberates after you've finished the game. All the while, it's supplemented by strong symbolic codes, provocative aesthetic choices, and immersive storytelling mechanics (imagine Adam Sandler's 'Click' but if the remote allowed you to open the doors of perception). The story's structure would make Christopher Nolan grin from ear to ear, and its carefully crafted elements and subtleties would make Vince Gilligan proud.
The storytelling is high-wire. It doesn't fully reveal how well-crafted it is until the end. You'll want to go back and consider past chapters with a new-found sense of epiphany.
All of this is in spite of the fact that I was initially very skeptical of diving into a "mental illness as fodder for a horror game" type of game. They won me over with the care and reverence they so obviously poured into this project. Play this game.

Having a voiced protagonist and limited dialogue options takes that away. Your guns don't wear out (loved that feature in NV) and you can't craft more ammo. Just another exampled of dumbing down this game and taking away RPG elements. Because of this the replay value sucks, I must have made 3-4 different characters in 3 and NV each, one playthrough was enough for me in this game.
Settlements was a cool idea but they made it so you constantly have to babysit them otherwise they get wrecked. Not to mention when you finally do go to them, THE ENEMIES SPAWN INSIDE YOUR SETTLEMENT! I spent many hours walling off all of my settlements completely. Sanctuary alone took like 2 hours to wall off and was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥due to how placing walls next to other walls is. On the trailer it showed enemies crossing sanctuaries bridge and getting torched at the entrance. Well too bad this isn't how it works, the enemies spawn all over inside your settlements. That's not even to mention the limited amount of stuff you can place in settlements. I know you can mod or use console commands but why the ♥♥♥♥ does this even exist in the game.
I'll be honest there is much more I can write but I just don't feel like it, I just wanted to give an overview of some of the bigger gripes I had with the game. First, I'll address the problem everyone has and I have as well. Capcom, honestly the DLC being characters is absolutely terrible; like what the hell no one should ever have to pay $90 for a complete game. You could have atleast made them inexpense so people could enjoy the full game with new content. Either way; I hope someday SF6 will be better in that reguard.
That being said I bought this game months ago and never touched it; because it sucked. Just recently I have revisited it and I have to say this game is pretty great now. It was bare bones when I first bought it; no story mode, online was garbage and the roster was a joke. It was laughable but I'm glad I kept this game on my account now. The added story mode made this game very fun including the sections you can revisit and play through; it reall improved this game. The added roster helped as well; honestly 16 characters is too little in this day and age it was like you were trying to recreate SF3 all over again. Paying for characters suck as well but the Capcom Steam sale sold me a ticket to Season 1 DLC Town. The complexity of this game is a problem for most people because it's considered "Dumbed Down' but I enjoy that aspect making it easier for newcomers and continued play; not everyone wants to have the complexity of Guilty Gear. I've played  a lot of fighters from SNK, Arc, Capcom and more but the pick up and play aspect is inviting for my friends who don't go crazy for fighters. You can play thorugh Story Mode (Cinematic & Character), Survival, watch the Demonstration videos and complete the Tech/Combo missions for Fight Money. Said Fight Money can be used in the Shop to unlock costumes, stages and the most importat part characters. You can buy those characters with a Season Pass or for $5.99 USD if you don't want to unlock them but that's highway robery. As for controller use I haven't had an issue, I use fightsticks and the game has given me nothing but joy. everything is nice and responsive and acts like a hot knife going through butter. I'm not sure how a normal controller is but I would assume great (If you are using your keyboard for a fighting game please don't).
ADVICE FOR BUYING THIS GAME:
Get yourself a nice controller. Buy the Season 1 Pass when it is on sale (Don't waste your Fight Money on Season 1 Characters). Play through the features and Story Modes for that Fight Money, you'll have fun and enough FM for all of the Season 2 Characters. Play with friends and add people on Capcom's network; no one wants to play a fighter alone.
PROS:
+Everthing is unlockable for free if you want to sink time into it
+Story Mode is finally a thing now and it's fun
+Welcoming for beginners and non fighters
+Cross platform play with the PS4
Cons:
-FM is scarce, you need to save it for only characters
-Online fights don't reward you with much FM
-Online will lag and honestly mess a match or two up for you
-OG roster is small and makes instant couch/online play frustrating
Overall I'd rate this game : Heavy 7/Light 8 out of 10. Not a must have but honestly an enjoyable fighter.

The Aliens and Predator franchises have had there ups downs, and when combined into films it was the ladder. In gaming however they really worked! Starting back in the Arcade as a “Final Fight” style beat-em up, the Atari Jaguar in 1994, the PC version in 2000, and a sequel in 2004. All were fun games for their time. So how does the latest in the series hold up? Well it helps if your a fan of Alien, and The Predator movies, and I am so my review may be biased. The game is broken into three campaigns that tie in the main story. Players can choose a Colonial Marine, the Alien, or The Predator. Each class plays very unique with their own abilities. The Marine campaign was my favorite, it captures some of the Aliens feel. There is a great line-up of movie weapons, tense scenes, and a lot of action. My complaints for the Marine are minor. I really wish they added “Aim Down Sites”. Firing from the hip in gaming is just old school, I need my sites! Second complaint is the motion tracker, It's all but useless in the game. I know I'll get some heat for saying this, but Aliens Colonial Marines made far better use of the motion tracker.  My second favorite campaign was The Predator. With all of his tools at your disposal, you will feel like an unstoppable hunter. My only complaint on The Predator is the “pred jump”. At times it can be a pain to line up, but once you know the map its less frustrating. The Aliens campaign was my least favorite. The Alien can transition to walls, and run in 3D. It has some interesting fatalities, and is extremely fast. However This is extremely disorientating in first person view, and I can't tell you how many times I ran right by an enemy because of the speed the Alien runs at. This could have been easily fixed if the Alien had 3rd person perspective. The game offers a decent amount of multiplayer modes, and a decent number of maps. The only thing I wish is there was a little more variety in the scenery. Your either in a Jungle, or a pyramid, and that’s about it.  The game will run on almost any PC if you adjust the resolution, and graphics options (Not your Apple II, but anything from 2010 and up should be fine). Overall this game despite its flaws is a very fun play, and I recommend it. If you've been passing on this one, and your a fan of either franchise you should pick it up. You can typically find it during a Steam sale for $5

140, where to begin... This game is brilliant in just about every regard. It involves jumpy shapes and procedurally generated music.
Music - 25/10: Yes, it's that good. The entire game revolves around the music. All the puzzles in this game are based on the fluctuations the music is going through. Everything is really seamless; if you're just listening to the audio and you die somehow, it honestly sounds like part of the song even though it's very harsh static. The music also only progresses when you do, which in my opinion is one of the best things about the game - and it always sounds so seamless when it does. And besides, the "drop" that happens when you progress to the next sequence of a stage is one of the most amazing sounds I've heard so far.
Art - 6/10: The art style is a bit like Thomas Was Alone, but not quite as nice. It's basically just a bunch of rectangles and circles and triangles. Nothing much. However, there are some really tiny details, like the jump and the level progression sequence. It does have a sort of odd charm to it though, which is why I'm giving it a 6 and not something lower
Gameplay - 8/10: You're essentially just trying to navigate your way through a series of obstacles and static-y square things. Nothing too special when considered by itself, but when you add the music to the equation, it's phenomenal. Everything changes based on what's going on in the music, for example, platforms will start moving as a new sequence is added to the ever-changing song. Really, the only negative is that the boss battles are a bit more trial-and-error than actually puzzle based, but honestly that's not a bad thing.
Price - 10/10: At $5, this game is a steal. Hell, I wouldn't mind if I had to pay $15 for it; it's just that good. If you're still not convinced, get it on sale when it's somewhere hovering around the $3/$4 range. You'll be glad you did.
Overall Rating - 9.5/10: This isn't so much of a game as it is an experience. The music is so much more than brilliant, and the gameplay and art style works fantastically well with the concepts it's working towards. The only downside I would say would be the shortness of it all - it only has three "stages", but they're all intuitively designed and great fun to play.
BEST GAME

Just a bit of warning for readers of this review, this review is somewhat lengthy as I try to explain all the important details of this game in short, but descriptive paragraphs. This game just has so much content that it’s hard to sum it up in one or two paragraphs. If you’re still interested in reading my review, enjoy!
Mortal Kombat 9 is the great return to the very gory and satisfying fighting game series. This return to mortal kombat offers a lot to any fighter fans alike, great character roster and an excellent combat system that is not too difficult to learn but offers a good amount of challenge to master. Mortal Kombat 9 also introduces a new special move system called the x-ray attack, which showcases the bone breaking bits that you get to see with a press of two buttons.
Story:
The game offers a detailed story mode that allows players to know a little bit more of each of the characters in the roster. The developers also set up the story mode in a way that you don’t need to play all the other mortal kombat games to get a good understanding of the story for this game. For length, I got about seven to eight hours of gameplay from this mode, so it does offer a good amount of time for any story mode player. The only negative I have to say is that the ending to the story mode was kind of unsatisfying and a bit of a sequel bait in my opinion.
Arcade:
Arcade is just the traditional mode in any fighting game that lets you play as any of the characters from the roster freely, while others have to be unlocked form the story mode. It offers a good amount of opponents to fight and like every other mortal kombat game; you get to go against a very tough and somewhat unfair final battle. I won’t spoil the final boss of the arcade ladder, but the battle itself is a bit unfair as the final boss has a golden shield that can make him invincible for one second. This means that if you land a punch to stun him and the golden shield pops, he can just instantly hit or grab you while being close to him automatically, dealing tons of damage that can sometimes kill you instantly. Other than that arcade mode is a pretty fun time waster and practice mode to fight against bots or against a friend.
Extras: The game also offers a few extra modes that include challenge tower and the crypt. Challenge tower is pretty much what the title states, a set of about two to three hundred different mini games or fights that increase in difficulty as you move higher up the ladder. Once you’ve completed the tower you get a special item that is somewhat disappointing, but also cool at the same time. Krypt is the traditional and scary return of trading coins you get from fights and using it to buy extras like artworks and costumes that are defiantly worth the purchase of any collector of in-game items.
Summary: Mortal kombat 9 is an amazing fighting game that offers a lot to returning fans of the franchise, classic characters, new fighting combos, a new special move system and a solid story mode that fits into the mortal kombat universe very well. This is a fighting game that I can truly recommend to any fighting fan that also loves blood and gore…oh and did I forget to mention that fatalities are back?
Pros:
+ Komplete edition has everything, even all the DLC characters from the start.
+ Great selection of classic characters from the mortal kombat universe.
+ Solid storyline that can give about six-eight hours of total playtime.
+ Great arcade mode that allows players to test their abilities against a set of easy or difficult bot opponents.
+ Good amount of detailed and sometimes beautiful stage levels.
+ Introduction to the most badass fighting system yet, the x-ray system.
+ And of course, fatalities are back and bloodier than ever!
Negatives:
-Unsatisfying ending to the story mode.
-Very difficult final boss fight in arcade mode, even on easy difficulty.
-X-ray moves tend to get pretty boring and repetitive after you seen all of them from every character.
-Unsatisfying reward for completing the challenge tower.
Overall Score: 9/10 Amazing Fighting Game!

I bought this game with the recent steam link bundle. I made the purchase mostly with the intent to take advantage of the amazing deal for the link. I was also happy to look into this new game as the art and overall theme look appealing. The reason I am giving this game a negative review is that it left a rather terrible impression very early on. As you can see I haven't put much time into the game and I wont be putting any more time until given a good enough reason. I'll be doing most of this review in a pros and cons format to quickly explain what I think about it overall.
Pros:
1. The art is very well done. The backgrounds are detailed and the combat is flashy. This is the main selling point of the game and the reason why I think most people go about buying it.
2. The 4th wall breaking is cute. I enjoyed having the game react to whenever I refused to travel the directed path. It added a very human touch and I thought that was refreshing. Kind of like how I felt after playing " The Stanley Parable."
3. The music helps breath life into the setting. Sometimes it'll calm down and feel peaceful yet stay within the cyber ninja theme. While othertimes it will kick up for a fight and help make combat feel more exciting.
Cons:
1. The combat. I don't know if I'm missing something or if the combat is supposed to feel this unfinished early on, but I stopped playing specifically because of the combat. Your character has a massive hitbox while the enemies have very small ones. This wouldn't be too much of an issue for me if it wasn't coupled with the absolutely terrible enemy attack design. Most of the attacks give very little time for any sort of reasonable reaction rate. This is made worse by the complete lack of visual and audio cues to signify when an enemy is about to attack. Most attacks will also stagger you and toss you around the room after your shield depletes. This can often lead to stunlocking because there seems to be a lack of invincibility frames. To  which I understand not all games need, but ones focused around fast paced combat like this need a way to give the player some breathing room. You'd also think the dash parry (which allows you to attack the enemy with a critical strike if timed correctly) would work more consistently if it were to be seen as a main component of combat, but that just doesn't seem to be true. The enemies react and attack far too quickly for the parry to be used consistently if not being spammed in hopes that one will connect. The upgrade system is your typical hack and slash Devil May Cry style, where you gain new moves with the currency you gain from killing enemies. Nothing new or all that exciting. What bothers me is that some of the moves seem to not want to work together. There is a move that allows you to sacrifice some HP to deal a lot of damage at a pretty decent range for melee combat. This move is fairly good. If it wasn't mapped to the same button of another move that is....The Other ability mapped to the same button is more used for a reaction to something that happens in combat. If you press this button when an enemy is staggered it'll unleash a few extra attacks. The problem being that often when you press said button your character will choose to use the HP consuming attack. Which isn't always useful in situations where you just wanted to use the reactionary attack. I have plenty more gripes with the games combat like how the developer added these very tiny fly like enemies which can at a moments notice send a laser beam across half the screen all while being one of the hardest enemies to actually hit. But this segment is getting very long.
2. The story. I know I haven't played enough of the game to understand the full scope of where the story was headed but I honestly don't care. It was so poorly done and mundane that all I can remember is "Judas bad." If there is some massive shift in plot and narrative later in the game than I guess I'm missing out, but I shouldn't have to slog through a boring narrative just because there's a suggestion that it might get better.
3. The music. Yes I said that the music was good before but l can have multifaceted opinions that can have contradicting natures. The music does sound very well done, however it doesn't loop smoothly. Its very irritating to be running around just to suddenly have the song poorly fade out (Or simply stop) just to have it come back around to the beginning with a completely different pitch or tone from how it ended.
4. Checkpoints. This game is terrible at checkpoints. They are either far too close to eachother or too far away. They segment the game into odd little pockets. Like this one checkpoint before a new ability where if you die before reaching the next one you'll be forced to grab that ability and watch the tutorial video on how to use it. This also happens with boss battles. I don't know who decided it was a good idea to make you rewatch each bosses intro each time you enter the boss room after a death, but it gets very annoying very fast.
There's my review. I am in no way an avid reviewer. This is not a proffesional opinion as I have not played enough of the game to actually give a solid argument. This was just my insight as an individual who was not satisfied with a product. I am not trying to tell anyone who enjoys this game that their opinion is unjust. I am just trying to give my personal opinion as to what I got out of my expereince. If there are people who see some of my cons and consider my input a valid way to assess your purchasing habits I am happy to have added some insight.

This game is artwork. Interactive audiovisual platformer.
The soundtrack is electronic- house music/minimal techno, something like that. It's good, simple but classy.
The looks suit the music- simple and bold, minimalism.
The game itself is incredibly simple. No tutorial, no hints, no story, no text at all. It throws you right in and leaves it up to you to realize that the arrow keys are the only controls.
It's a straightforward platform game- jump on the platforms, don't fall, don't hit the TV static that kills you. Quickly you come to notice that the platforms and moving objects are all synced to the music, resulting in puzzles that require following the 4/4 beat of the music closely to predict the movement of objects.
The game is very simple, but just challenging enough to keep you going. It's a very short game. 3 levels, finished in 3 sessions of about 20-30 minutes each. Each level has a unique "boss" at the end with original gameplay. One has the feel of a Castlevania boss with your weapon only firing on a specific beat, another reminded me of SuperHexagon. The bosses were very fun to play given the gameplay is unique and unexpected.
Despite the game being so short, it is well worth the $5, especially if you like techno music and minimalist art. It may be 1.5 hours long, but it's an experience far more enjoyable and worthwhile than any $5 Mochafrappulatte.

Well, this is a challenging one. This game is quite fun due to the challenge it brings and the strategizing it requires. I love the way this company combined strategy and FPS, it being a first-person tower-defense game. Very cleverly designed. There are four playable classes, each w/ their own unique characteristics which assist them on a level (shotgun, sniper, rocket launcher, and assault rifle), along with there being an expandable variety of towers to choose from for each level, each excelling at killing certain aliens. The variety of aliens is even quite astounding, from there being a leeching alien which explodes on impact dealing massive damage and moving at insane speed, to a tanky light-bulb shaped alien called a soaker which has a ton of Hitpoints but also moves very slowly. To challenge the player even more, they even give powerups to the aliens called Feats of Strength, which rank the player up faster if they can sustain the fact that the enemy is stronger with them. All I can say is, thank God this game has Co-op available.
In summary...
Pros:
-Gameplay is very cleverly designed, combining two completely different genres (FPS and Tower Defense)
-Takes an immense amount of strategizing, making the gameplay more fun
-Feats of Strength add an annoying, but challenging enhancement to the gameplay
-More than one game mode (Campaign, Survival, Sandbox, etc.)
-Thank God it's Co-op :3
Cons:
-May be very laggy (in terms of framerate) on most computers
-Can get boring after awhile if you aren't into challenge or complete the campaign too quickly
-Very challenging (but that's a pro :)
Overall, would recommend 9/10

Fran Bow is an adorable horror adventure that takes you across both beautiful and eerie landscapes. The game plays as a point and click and would technically fall under the horror genre given the imagery in the game. I love 99% of this game, for any fan of horror aesthetic this is a must have. The story is very well done and is not cliche, in addition Fran is a different kind of horror protagonist considering she is 10. For some general pros and cons about this game
Pros:
-Level design is amazing, I can not stress this enough the first level alone makes the game worth it
-Characters, there are plenty of lovable and terrifying characters. There is a good balance between serious and quirky that gives this game great diversity in its cast
-Puzzles are not ridiculously easy, there are a couple of portions in this game that are challenging but not insane which is a breath of fresh air
Cons:
-Ithersta, this level is nice at first but the game wants you to learn everything here. Every single backstory for characters you were not even aware of until this point. This section for some odd reason is significantly longer than every other section of the game because you are tasked on about a 9 item fetch quest for a wizard who has the memory of Dory in Finding Nemo. In addition this section has minimal horror vibes, they are good when they happen but it's mostly running errands for the wizard
-For more casual players a skip option is added for the mini games, this is fine, however I have an issue with it since this skip is not offered on the one mini game/puzzle that could really use it which is a gear puzzle which I do not believe anyone has ever been a fan of
-Ithersta again, I cannot stress this enough how tedious this section of the game is
Overall the horror parts of this game are amazing and the horror imagery is very powerful, considering a major complaint of horror gamers is that too many games use jump scares, Fran Bow offers horror without the cookie cutter mold. Pick this up on sale unless you have some undying love for tedious nature sections, in that case grab this now as that is literally one of the only complaints I have about this game.

Bosses have also been added to the mix.  All and all, this is a must have game for any steam library.

This game is a classic, it does so much so well but has a few CRAPPO moments too. This was meant to be a retelling of the original Doom but simultaneously redefine its own genre. This is by far the definitive DOOM collection (at least up until the fourth title) and a must own for any fan, new or old.
Story: Its the 22nd century and the Union Aerospace Corporation has a huge cutting edge facility on Mars where they conduct various weapons and genetic research (including opening portals to hell apparently). One of the lead researchers on the site, Dr. Malcolm Betruger has been making preparations for a Demonic Invasion (without the consent of his fellow humans of course) and return for receiving the power to rule over them. The UAC sensing something is wrong due to the increasing amount of on work casualties sends an ambassador, his bodyguard, and an unrelated Marine transfer (you) to Mars. Shortly after arriving all hell breaks loose and your left alone. Now you must regroup with your fellow survivors and find a way to stop the hell portal. Meanwhile on another part of the station, the last surviving marine from Bravo Team (the protagonist of "The Lost Mission" Expansion) is fighting his way through the base in order to reach the Exis labs in order to decommission a teleporter that the forces of Hell can use to invade Earth. With the help of Dr. Richard Meyers, this marine will fight through various locations, both on Mars and Hell, and will fight a mixture of the original DOOM 3 enemies alongside the newer Resurrection of Evil enemies. A year after the events of the incident, a small team of scientists and marines return to Mars in order to research and survey the planet for any possible details as to what had previously occurred on the abandoned base. While on a scouting expedition, Betruger is accidentally reawakened and unleashed on the small band of UAC personal. The new protagonist must now fight his way back to the station to regroup with the expedition's commander, all the while mastering the power of a mysterious artifact that possesses the ability to manipulate time itself. Little does this battle scarred hero realize that he is being hunted by the three Helltime Hunters, all bent on returning the artifact to their master.
Overall Score for Story: 8/10
Gameplay: The gunplay in Doom 3 isn't anything unique or special. You get tons of guns, they all have the same crosshair, you can sprint, crouch, jump, all the basics are accounted for. However, the guns stand out from the rest of the series due to their weak performance. In most games, each gun has a standout strength, but in this game, each gun has a standout weakness. For example: the pistol has a really low fire rate, the shotgun has horrendous spread, the chain gun is woefully inaccurate etc. However, these attributes do help make Doom 3 feel more like a survival horror. Also the grenades bounce like silly putty when you throw them. One cool thing however was how the marine interacts with in-game screens, instead of merely pressing a button to activate something, your cursor will appear on any screen when you look at it which makes the world feel much more real. The Resurrection of Evil Expansion does however include a fun artifact that allows the player to slow down time which makes for some pretty awesome action moments.
Overall Score for Gameplay 9/10
Characters: There are only five important characters in Doom 3's base game. None have any real development, they leave the screen in the end pretty much the same way that they came in, some more alive than other though. The characters in the "Lost Mission" DLC are interesting enough, especially the Dr. who really has a lot to add to the story and fills some significant questions about the plot. The characters in "Resurrection of Evil" are interesting enough and add something as well though there is little closer as to what happens to them due to some confusing directing and writing choices.
Overall Score for Characters: 8/10
Graphics: The visuals are what people think of most when they think of Doom 3 and they do hold up well. The lighting is still pretty good. The textures are ugly when you get close up (just like my wife) but in the heat of action you won't notice.
Overall Score for Graphics: 9/10
Sound: The sound is alright in this game, the gun sounds really fake and weak but I guess that's sort of the point since the game wants you to feel vulnerable. Footsteps are ok, they don't have too much weight on them but they work. Monster screams and growls sound convincing enough.
Overall Score for Sound: 8/10
Soundtrack: The soundtrack is practically nonexistent except for the Title/Credits Theme and some ambient noises/chords throughout the game.
Overall Score for Soundtrack: 6/10

I originally bought this pack having never played a single doom game. Doom 3 BFG Edition is the definitive experience for playing the earlier Doom entries, and has been around long enough to be pretty cheap on sale - that’s probably why you’re here.
While the convenience that this pack offers rivals the level of quality you would receive through buying/downloading the games individually, there are mods out there that work for the first two Dooms. The mods are
, and
. They use a more updated engine, and they feel a bit more polished than the original experience.
These games that came out a year apart in the early 90s delivered a fast-paced shoot-em-up. You came for that, but stayed for intricate (and sometimes confusing) levels, loose story and tough enemy placement that made the most out of the graphical limitations of the time. It was a challenge - ammo and health were scarce (even if you came across the rare secret), enemies did significant damage at higher levels, and strafing was king. I could see this being a worthy challenge back in the day, and even seasoned FPS players who grew up in later times could struggle with a few levels. There is a lot of content, and most of it can feel like more of the same. However, there are conversion mods that can really stretch the longevity of the game without boring you. If you only made time for one, I’d suggest Doom 2 - there are more levels packed with new enemies and a super shotgun with a range that matches modern sniper rifles.
The biggest drawback for the bundle was Doom 3. Though the FPS made a lot of people’s top ten game lists for 2004 (along with Half Life 2, Halo 2, CS: Source, and Unreal Tournament 2004), the game’s story and combat system doesn’t hold a candle to an FPS that’s come out in the last decade. 90% of the game is on a Mars factory that closely resembles Black Mesa, with the rest of the environment being genuinely good representations of Hell. I will give credit to the game’s fairness in terms of ammo/med placement, and it does a great job in setting the ambience in terms of lighting and cryptic ways of disseminating story. Although weapons and enemies are polished remakes of its predecessors, it fell flat in the face of slower movement controls and poorer damage output from weapons. Though there were fewer enemies, they soaked up more bullets. It made for pretty easy fights that got boring fairly quickly.
TL;DR: Buy this for Doom 1&2 and their modding potential (honorable mod mentions: Total Chaos and Legacy of Suffering). Doom 3 leaves much to be desired - don’t go into it expecting too much. Play Doom 2016 instead.

What is Town of Salem?
Genre: best guess: Online Multiplayer Round Strategy Mind Game
Setting: Different factions trying to get the power/control over the town (town members, mafia, loners with own goals)
Difficulty: 3/10 - depends on given role - some are harder to play, some easier; also: easy to get into the game
Length: 10-30 Minutes for a single round; after addiction has spread: there is no known end ;)
Mode: multiplayer, different types and settings
Similar games: can't name any, sorry
I bought the game around Christmas and since then, I'm in for a round or two every day. Why?
- lots of different roles with different play styles
- casual gameplay for now and then
- easy to get into
- unpredictability in the course of the game - every round ends different
- collaboration and/or verbal disguise in text chat influences further decisions
- Still getting updates and improvements
- cosmetical items (for those who care)
- well balanced factions
The negative aspects:
- some roles are pretty passive and useless for a long time of a round (medium, retributionist, survivor)
- use of a lot of abbreviations you have to learn fast to not get lost in the text chat (f. e. RT, vfr, NE)
- frame drop issues --> delay in sending text
Result (and summary for those who have no time reading):
Town of Salem is addicting! For every round consists of up to 15 people with different roles, every round ends different. Whether you can win a game depends on how you fulfill your role's tasks and your ability to verbally disguise yourself to hide your true intentions. A round only takes 10 to 30 Minutes, so its a nice-to-play game for now and then. Also the developers are still pushing the game, and there are cosmetics to vary your avatar, character, and background house (if you're in for that).
Totally recommended!

Lately I've taken to playing shorter games, and I've found that games like Kane and Lynch 2 and Rogue Warrior, which were panned on release for their length, can take on a decent life as short one-in-done games that you don't have to commit to so long as the price is right.
Games like this are sort of the equivalent of direct-to-video Nicolas Cage movies, in the sense that they don't need to innovate or do anything particularly new, they just need to provide a competent take on something familiar, and Rogue Warrior fit the bill for me. Gameplay-wise, Rogue Warrior is a typical FPS, but it does what it sets out to do. It's not glitchy, the guns are satisfying to use, the cover system works, etc. There is not a single fresh or new idea here, but the gameplay is fun and it's over in about 110 minutes. I think this game launched as a $60 product, and at that price point, it would definitely be a bad choice compared to other games in that price range, but for $5 you get something familiar and playable in a shorter form, which makes it perfect for one of those rainy days where you want to play something, but don't really want to invest in something more demanding.
On a technical level, it's okay. The environments look surprisingly decent, the lighting is especially solid, and the animation is fine. The game lacks a lot of typical PC options, such as Antialiasing, VSYNC, or Ansiotropic filtering, which is disappointing, but being an older game it will probably run well on just about anything.
What really sets this game apart from other budget games though, is the increasingly silly story and presentation. I think this is probably the purest representation of the cheesy 80's action movie in gaming. There lots of games that try to recreate this feel, ranging from garbage like Duke Nukem Forever, to fun games like Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon, but those games never quite capture the feel as they're intentionally setting out to be cheesy. Rogue Warrior, on the other hand, is the perfect storm of unintentional funny that makes it feel so much truer to those movies than any of the more concerted efforts to capture this feel. This is based on a series of novels written by the Richard Marcinko (I haven't read them), a real life Navy SEAL who apparantly founded SEAL Team 6, but also writes military fiction books where he's the protagonist. Someone legitimately thought they were writing a cool military story here, the series of books the game derives from just happens to be set in the 80's, and the fictionalized Marcinko just happens to check every 80's action movie stereotype. I don't think the game really sets out to spoof these movies, but the circumstances around it's production make it reflect them in a way other games just can't. Marcinko himself is a hilarious protagonist, where guys like Stallone or Schwarzenegger have cool, relevant one liners, this guy mostly comes up with new, increasignly bizarre  permutations of the F-Word. Normally this could be grating and in other games it has been, but they're so astoundingly inneffective at being offensive, that it becomes endearingly funny to see just how much he wants you to see him as a tough guy. The end credits music is even a rap remix of the "best" of these. This is one of those rarest of games, a game where the gameplay is legitimately competent, but the storytelling is so silly as to be so-bad-it's-good. It's not even that overt at first, it starts out like a typical bland military story, but then he mentions Reagan and the Soviets show up and that's when it clicked for me that I was playing a Steven Seagal movie. This is where Rogue Warrior truly excels. It's the gaming equivalent of an MST3K movie, being entertaining enough to watch from start to finish, but absurd enough to laugh at it along the way.
Overall, Rogue Warrior isn't a
game, but I think it's worth having tucked away on your Steam account for one of those lazy days you just don't want to play something too demanding, but still want to beat a campaign. The game itself is fun enough and the story is so ridiculous you really have to see it through, which makes this an easy buy for $5.

Oh boy...I would start the review with a moderately long intro paragraph, but so many other reviewers have described the game so well that I'll do things a little differently, and let the pros and cons lists do most of the explaining.
In Rogue Warrior, you play as Richard Marcinko, a real U.S. war veteran, as he fights his way through hordes of Communists, while avenging his fallen comrades and disobeying orders along the way. Sounds fairly generic but fun, especially as you get to play as a real war hero right? Well, I'll explain where the real fun of this game lies...
- There's really no other game like it; almost every line of dialogue from Marcinko is loaded with ridiculous combinations of obscenities. I won't list them here for the sake of decency, but watch any playthrough on YouTube and you'll see it very quickly. This has the simultaneous effect of making Marcinko one of the funniest protagonists of all time, while also making him look like a big jerk. This is the only real reason to consider buying this game, because the laughs you might get will far outweigh the enjoyment you'll get out of the subpar actual gameplay.
-The (limited) soundtrack is decent.
- If you can get a group of people to play online with you (good luck with that one), then the game becomes legitimately possible to 100%, for those who like to get achievements.
-
The biggest issue is that the game does not run smoothly. I've played this game on two laptop PCs, and it doesn't run optimally on either of them without lowering both the graphics settings and possibly tinkering with computer settings that shouldn't need to be disabled to make the game run somewhat well. There is a guide addressing this issue on Steam. Even with this though, expect very likely frame drops at certain points. Doesn't help that there's only a few extremely basic graphics settings that can be modified.
-
In addition to the poor overall frame rate, the controls are
clunky. Some default key bindings are very strange for a first-person shooter game, your grenade toss is delayed and extremely unwieldy to use, the cover mechanic is stiff and almost unusuable, and you'll often have to mash your 'Kill Move' button to perform a stealth kill just because half the time, pressing it just makes the target jerk around. The controls are not completely broken, but they never feel smooth. Instead, the whole game feels clunky.
-
You get three difficulty settings to choose from at the start of the game. The harder ones seem to only make your enemies hit harder; the AI for most of those Commies is extremely foolish and they often fail to target you even when you're in range, and they almost never attempt to counter your attempts to take cover, and none of them take more than a few shots to dispatch. In fact, on the easy and normal difficulties, most of the game can be completed by simply rushing most of the opposition and performing your kill move before they even have a chance (you're also completely invincible while performing kill moves). There's no boss battles, less than 10 missions, and the few times where the game may actually pose a challenge come from fake difficulty, due to the controls and performance being such an issue.
-
All missions are short and are simply a series of you heading from waypoint to waypoint. Most of the weapons lack recoil and feel the same, so you'll only care about which ones have the highest ammo capacity. Your pistol sidearm even has infinite ammo. While the maps themselves are fairly large, there are no Easter eggs, alternate objectives or routes, or anything else to encourage you to explore. The game is extremely linear and that hurts its replayability a lot. In addition, the story is overall quite ridiculous and doesn't take itself seriously, which is a shame because it could have been legitimately funny yet serious at the same time. The graphics and textures are overall dreary, muddy and would be shameful to the eye on a PS2 or original Xbox, let alone at its 2009 release. The game can be completed in a mere hour or two.
Overall, I recommend Rogue Warrior ONLY if you're ready to put up with how badly it will handicap you. I had a lot of fun just laughing at the ludicrous dialogue, and it never gets old to me. That's the only reason to consider buying it, and if you have a group of friends around to watch you play, it could make for one hilarious day. Also, I would strongly recommend buying it only when it happens to be on a sale. If for any reason you were considering buying it for anything else, do yourself a favor and don't let these Commies take away your precious dollars. Maybe one day, Richard Marcinko will get the REAL game he deserves, not this shell of a game that's so bad, it's "good".

The game is really just a multiplayer game - there are a few hours of singleplayer content, but it's not especially interesting, so my review is based on the multiplayer. The gameplay itself is fun, and the game is well balanced. The netcode isn't bad, although there could be improvements (even just the ability to filter players by connection speed or region would help massivley). The big issue with the game though (and it's far worse than sf4), is it's set up as a cash grab. If you want to play this game and have access to all characters (ignoring costume, colours and other various cosmetic content) you have to pay, and pay a significant amount at that! Not just for new content either, but content Capcom (as has become usual for them) created and bundled with the game but locked out behind an additional paywall (after already paying a premium fee for the game). Capcom claim you don't, but the 'fight money' (in game currency) you earn isn't nearly enough to buy many of the characters, unless you want to spend hundreds of hours grinding in the (not at all fun) offline survival mode.
In short; good gameplay, but even when taking into account the fact that companies have to earn money and obviously aren't charities, this is a very cyncial attempt by Capcom to hold their fans by their ankles and shake them for every penny. For that reason alone, unless you like being taken for a ride, avoid.

First off let me say this: This is the first time I've played a game of this style besides maybe Castle Crashers (Years ago). Side scrolling with enemies thrown at you here and there. There are a whole list of things that set these two games apart. So I'm just gonna say what I think about this one. (All opinion)
1. The Combat: While infuriating at times, it is nice and responsive. I wish the keyboard could have a little more variety, maybe using the mouse. But I'm not that deep into the game (Idealon) so I wouldn't know if the mouse already has some use. Fighting enemies is... interesting. The attacks that ARE telegraphed usually get lost to me mainly because of the blinding blue light that is my sword. And the attacks that aren't telegraphed end up stunlocking me because I have to dodge at just the right moment for damage to be negated. (Mainly why I'm stuck on Idealon) Some of the hitboxes are also a little wonky but nothing you can't manage.
TL;DR: Not bad, could be better.
2. The Soundtrack: This is my favorite part of the game. Even if you don't plan on buying the game, I honestly recommend listening to the soundtrack. Fighting most enemies over and over and over again, began to get tiring, but the music was something I looked forward to just bob my head to. I can't say much else, I like it.
TL;DR: I like it.
3. Art Style: This one is probably my least favorite. Not because I think it's bad or anything, no. But mainly because I don't very much look into the art while playing a game. The bosses are cool looking. The fodder, are just that, fodder. One thing I can say is that the boss introduction, with the effect and their name, give some real... gusto? I guess? It adds 'oomph' to them.
TL;DR: It's nice I guess.
4. The Story: It's pretty funny, not gonna spoil anything, but I'd say it's kind of a 'Stanley Parable' if I had to make a comparison, centered around where the narrator tells you to go. The secrets make me chuckle when I find them, and it's refreshing, instead of trying to go all out with seriousness.
That's all I can really think of right now.
TL;DR: Pretty fun so far.

Well the game is fundementally underwhelming compared to others. First content is lacking. Buying base game alone will get you a versus mode with either against CPU or another player. There is a survival mode, which isn't really a good one and, 16 characters. Honestly I expected more characters on day one, expected a ARCADE MODE, or even more stuff to do that didn't require having online connection.
First fundementally flaw thing is content. Launch day priced this game at $60 and relies on updates or dlc for futher expanding the game. It has only 3 modes you can play alone, Story which is just a brief 15 minutes of the characters' history placed somewhere before the games actual featured story, while using only drawings and voice acting to tell it like a graphic novel with one round fights. The general story is a free download and does have unique fights against some unplayable characters like Bison's 12 dolls or officer peter, but is only worth playing for getting fight money to spend, rather than enjoying the story. If you never played street fighter game before this, you may enjoy the story and seeing the full use of the games character models and enviroments. The training mode has tutorial and also character use demonstrations, these are short in game automated fights with descriptions of the best way to play each character, detailing their strength and weakness, what moves they have, how they work, which best situations to use them in. Is very much the only improved thing with the game, but still falls shame to games like guilty gear xrd and Blazblue character tutorial. There is combo challenges to show the player how to perform some useful combo, but you will probably forget them during a real matach and never get the chance to use them most of the time.
I mentioned fight money, well let me tell you, fight money is the games "Reward" system. You earn fight money by doing things like completing charater story modes, completing their combo challenges, some weekly rewards, or even survival mode. Is enough to spend on things in the shop. The game allows you to unlock characters and stages this way. Each character is 100,000 fight money which is a lot if you want to get them all, or you can spend your Real life money on buying each character individually or even character season passes. My advice is to wait for discount on the character season pass for least %50 off if you really want them, You can also use the money to unlock new stages to fight on, each is 70,000. Though some was timed holiday exclusives and could potentially be available again in future but capcom has no word on it. Some are just altered stages of existing one while some are brand new stages. Some can only be gotten as a DLC purchase only, known as premium content, which brings me to my next thing, costumes.
In this game only one kind of costume is unlockable, the story costume. (Basically a costume the character uses in their personal story which shows what they would appear before the current time kinda like retro costumes in killer instinct) You unlock them by completing their story, but you STILL HAVE TO BUY IT! Those special costumes like the battle costume or pre-order bonus or even the holiday ones are all DLC only exclusive listed as premium content.
What is more is yo can unlock colors for characters too. Survival mode has 4 difficulties, a easy one with 10 fights, normal with 20, hard with 30 and expert with 50, each one not only increase the fights required to clear but also the difficulty. You only earn the unlockable and fight money for clearing all fights of each difficulty. (And no you can't complete the same character and difficulty for more fight money.) The survival mode is bad too. You win score points for fighting well and can use it for bonuses like restoring health, regain cricital art meter or v trigger, even sacrifice life for higher damage, put some handicaps on for more score multiplier. But the point of survival mode is to never lose, the problem is that each survival mode has fixed characters. I never seen any game with a survival mode that has you fight the specific characters EVERY SINGLE TIME. Usually survival mode is randomized fights. After you get bored with the 1 player content, you probably only will play this when someone ask you to play with them or looking to play with them online.
Suppose you did all that fight money gathering and spent it all on avoiding using Real money for DLC unlocks insteaad got 1,000,000 fight money, use it to buy the current 10 released dlc characters for 100,000 each and no more fight money to unlock, how do you get more? Got to play rank match. I'm honestly not a competitive player, I never play ranked match in my games. Couldn't they have a wager betting system or something? Bet 200,5000 on a match and earn money that way watching replays like super smash bros on wii u has? Maybe some random fight money bonus chances? No, you have to only win ranked matches which has some of the BEST PLAYERS, the ones who do care enough about the game to play more than you probably will to get good, instead of people your own skill level. While you can earn enough fight money to unlock enough stuff, what is the point when you can't get some things cause is premium only?
Games like street fighter alpha 3 had more content in it than this, and even when we had to unlock them, it was rewarding and not blocked by some restrictions that place them at too high a difficulty for people who just want a simple pick up and play game. If you looking for a fighting game to play with friends, I suppose is not bad, there some things that is fustrating about it others have said, but I still think street fighter 2 and Street fighter 3rd strike was okay before it got too far with balancing the game, adding combos and too execution heavy based gameplay. You may enjoy marvel vs capcom games more or some anime fighters, even Netherealm games more for single player content and multiplayer content.
If you read this far and think I didn't do a good job, that's fair, not used to writing steam reviews, but I do wish to share opinions and know others was helped in making decision on buying products. Compared to street figher 4, not much was change to make the game better than existing games. Replaced focus attack with V skill which is unique for each player, or just a move the legacy characters already had in a previous game. V trigger is something similar in concept of killer instinct's INSTINCT MODE, where characters gain extra special moves or powered up state. Again, something they had in previous street fighter game now restricted. Basic content now missing, how can you not have a arcade mode?

I picked this game up during the Halloween Sale going on this year, and am very happy that I did. I loved the art style and really enjoyed the game mechanics. This game is a combination of a visual novel, point and click adventure, and puzzle game.
Pros:
Most puzzles were very rewarding to solve, and a few were difficult enough for me to stop the game and sleep on them. (this is a pro for me, but may be a con for some)
I really enjoyed the game mechanic introduced by the medication.
The art is beautiful and the style is perfect for the story.
I enjoyed unraveling the story, and all of the extra dialogue available by speaking with characters.
This world feels very fleshed out and the lore is present, but not forced on you. I really enjoyed having the choice of reading/finding as much as I wanted to when it came to the background and the lore of the world.
Cons:
There were several "puzzles" that were very simple and ended up being more like fetch quests than a puzzle. However, they were all there to advance the story or help you get to an item you needed.
Little to no replay value unless you just want to get all the achievments. I want to play this game again because I enjoyed the story, but I would not enjoy playing it again until I have forgotten the solutions to all the puzzles so I can figure them out again.
Overall I would definitely recommend picking up this game if you enjoy casual puzzle games, gothic storytelling, and interesting stories dealing with the human experience. I got this game for $4.49 and am very happy with what I got at that price point. This is a game that has little replay value, though. I may play it again next year around Halloween, but it is something that I will need to play after a long period of time has passed so I forget how to solve the puzzles and can be engrossed in the story again.

Kingdom Rush is one of the better iOS ports on Steam. They've obliterated the microtransactions in the game and KR legitimately feels like a TD game for the PC.
After completing the game in a little under 18 hours, here's what I think..
Pro:
- battle system is refreshing all the way to the end of the campaign
- the various towers and specialties are introduced at a proper pace
- the bonus stages offer adequate challenges (although a difficulty selector would be great)
- game has absolutely no microtransaction gimmicks
- the art is vibrant (dem colors man)
Con:
- the new units introduced in the bonus stages are not too special (they were predictable to an extent)
- at one point, the units got stuck outside of the map and reduced frame rate by a lot (can be fixed with RoF)
- rain of fire spam and hero usage make the game much easier
Overall it's a good game. It needs more variety but that's a common issue with most TD games.
I'm definitely looking forward to playing the new content once it's available for PC!

I just have to say I'm speechless. Wow, like really wow.
This two-person made indie game is amazing. Artwork, story, music, atmosphere, philosophy, general point of view on life - all are just 100% amazing. I never imagined I'd play a horror game with 10 year old protagonist Fran Bow. And this game is very spooky... right from beginning you are sucked together with Fran into this horror realm. This "other world" will not let go of you, actually Fran's inquisitive mind needs to visit this scary place via drugs to solve puzzles on her way to find her cat Mr. Midnight. The puzzles in this game are quite logical, no random clicking needed, just patience with solving them.
The narrative of the game is well made, linear but beautiful and frightening at the same time. Mid-game you are introduced the same mechanic of horror realm trips yet another way - by switching seasons, again to solve puzzles and interacting with the world. Gameplay is really point and click, no keyboard needed. I'll have to agree, that save games would have been nice extra option for achievement hunters but actually not needed, game autosaves and due to linearity nothing can go wrong.
So I highly recommend this horror game, to explore authors point of view on human psyche.
edit:
TL;DR; A nice zen-quote from the game: "Death is nothing more, then absence of love." And Fran Bow, this game shines love.

Floating Point is an amazing relaxing game which can be played entirely using only the left and right mouse buttons.
The game has a very satisfying and fluid physics system and responsive controls. It's very easy to learn and master, but even inexperienced gamers will have no trouble playing the game, as there are no time limits, no restrictions, it's simply level after level with the only goal being to "collect" every "red bars" on the current level to move on to the next, which is pretty much the same thing over again.
The game is particularly relaxing and a nice "time waster". It's simple, fun, easy to pick up but hard to let go.
It's the kind of game you just launch and play for a few minutes while waiting or doing other tasks, or simply to relax and unwind for a bit. It features an excellent and equally relaxing soundtrack.
And finally, the strongest point for the game? It's absolutely free. No pay-to-win, no exclusive content, no DLCs, you just iniciate the very small download, launch the game, and enjoy it freely. To be honest, I consider this game better than most paid games on Steam. Turns out there are some hidden gems in the free-to-play section of Steam.
The only cons I can think of for this game is the fact that the gameplay can get rather repetitive; No real goal, not much challenge, and it most certainly won't give you much sense of achievement. After a while, just going level-to-level can get slightly boring.
Overall, I HIGHLY recommend this one. It's free, so you know you've got nothing to lose. Heck, I'd recommend it if it were a paid game either ways.

I'm still not sure what this game wants to be. The initial premise - the one people got excited for and bought thousands of copies for, anyway - was "Terraria but in space", but the developers have done nothing but undercut that premise that for the entire development process. Instead I guess they wanted it to be a difficult action platformer, like a 2d Dark Souls or a really hard SotN? Except a) they didn't seem able to implement that vision coherently and b) no one liked or wanted that. So after years of development, after years of making terrible changes in the name of 'balance' and enforced progression (in a largely-single-player sandbox game), after years of methodically removing the good and fun things (sand mining and the good grappling hook, just to name a few), after adding content which just straight-up ignores the basic premise of the game (the plot dungeons where you arbitrarily can't use the matter manipulator)... after ALL that, what we are left with is basically "Terraria, but much less good." I don't regret the $15 I paid for this game, but I do regret all the time I put into a game that was better during it's early-access launch YEARS AGO then it is now.

Have a nice and gently laugh at that 80s/90s aura you would otherwise find a little too kitchy. The game is so full of quotes and referencies you are bound to get -at least up to a certain extent- and to feel a bit old and nostalgic with some self-awarness of the time passing by. It's a melting pot of crossed pop referencies that blend up into a school canteen soup: lines and expressions are accurate enough to get you into the mood just by themselves (I'm not a native english speaker but somehow they bring me back to the ones I once was used to), the tools you'll use are a trip in a yardsale, the end battle screenshot are shiny as they should, the music is nothing short than a Journey, the "cinematics", the main and the side plots are a collection of action films memories. It's not a gem of crazy humor in itself but mostly in the eyes of the player who picture himself and his childhood through the eyeglass of an older person.
Moreover you can enjoy a pre-battle and in-battle tactical system that it's easy enough to get but gives you a decent rate of improvent and learning. Basically, you have to combine power-ups and buffers and the tools you use in battle, so the options are vary and not repetitive and suit the rpg concept of the game. To add more flavour (said by a very clumsy guy) the developers put into a certain number of minigames, mostly to trigger weapon and tools side effects and to charge up your attacks (I'm not using a mouse and I'm regretting it). Last but not least it's cheap. This is not a lifetime game experience but it actually gets, in a rather honest way, it's primal goal: to help you sail through a lazy saturday morning when you are in vein of a time back flip.

Coming from a long career with Age of Kings/Galactic Battlegrounds, and a fair amount of time with Civilization, and the Total War grand strategy games, I can say that Northgard provides me with what I feel is a fresh experience.
While civilization allows you to wage war or diplomacy on a global scale, and Age of Kings is a more local, regional scale, Northgard is a very small scale - county size or so. Some people have complained about the building limits and destroying a mine to move to the next plot, and while it is somewhat cumbersome to be on the lookout for more resouces - it seems more plausible to real life.
I am one to have also played a fair bit of Rimworld and Stonehearth, and those games also force you to be on the lookout for your next plots of resources. While you don't have the territorial boundries to deal with in those games, you still have to expand at some point.
I enjoy the experience, and I know it will get ironed out and expanded on. I'd get it on sale or if you really like Historical RTS games.

Kingdom Rush takes the increasingly stale tower defense genre and infuses it with some much-needed wit and good old-fashioned polish. The core experience is familiar – waves of enemies follow a pre-set path, and must be taken out by towers players purchase and place.
The twist is that players can place "Barracks" towers that send footmen onto the field that will battle and slow down enemy creeps. By placing enemy-blocking barracks next to high-powered towers, players can turn the tide in their favor.
Although Kingdom Rush only contains four base tower types, each can be upgraded down two separate paths, and can then be customized even further with special abilities. This gives players a surprising amount of versatility, and pays off for those that plan ahead. For example, the mage tower upgrades into the armor-weakening Sorcerer or the enemy-teleporting Arcane. The former is useful at the beginning of the enemy's path, the latter at the very end.
Kingdom Rush is one of the best tower defense experiences I've had. Each stage is perfectly balanced to present a very stiff challenge while never feeling unfair. Packs of smaller enemies slip by you? Use more artillery. Flying enemies trip you up? Next time try more archers. It's a game that teaches you how to win, one level at a time
It certainly helps that the entire thing looks and sounds fantastic. The detailed and stylish cartoony visuals set a distinct "fantasy-comedy" tone, reinforced by the game's sparse but spot-on voice acting. Every tower spouts one-liners when upgraded, leading to plenty of opportunities for sly pop-culture references.
Kingdom Rush is an instant classic and is guaranteed to turn up on “best of” lists. Anyone remotely interested in either tower defense or strategy should consider it a most-own. Gamers that think they don’t enjoy the genre should give Kingdom Rush a shot anyway – it might just win you over.

There's some really interesting ideas in here that are far more creative than the cliches one might expect from a horror game about a young girl trapped in an asylum, and the art was really well executed. I'm not easily disturbed but the art and storyline genuinely creeped me out at times, and worked very effectively together - there's clearly been thought put into how to make the horror elements drive the story forward. I gave up partway through chapter 3. In the first two chapters, Fran's ten-year-old perspective on the things happening around her ranged from charming to disturbing, in counterpoint with what I could piece together for myself as an adult interacting with the game world. In the third chapter, the mood changes significantly, and while at first the switch to a more hallucinatory, Neverending Story sort of vibe was refreshing, it quickly got tedious - frankly, I stopped feeling like the game was designed for adult players, because there was none of the same sense that I was seeing anything Fran wasn't. Also, prosaically, I read fast and was getting super bored continually clicking through the dialogue (and the minigames were totally pointless). Nice concept, but the execution just stopped working for me completely.
