From reading other reviews, I understand this game was imported to the PC from mobile platforms. The goofy graphics and simpler audio support this as well. That said, this is one of the best tower defense games that I have ever played. The mantra of "keep it simple, stupid" is extremely obvious here, and used to wonderful effect. There are only four tower types that I have discovered so far, each with a four-tier upgrade system, and the stars you unlock by completing levels actually go immediately toward your choice of upgrades. Despite being kept relatively simple, the tower abilities and upgrades allow quite a bit of customizable defense.
After completing each of the basic story playthroughs, missions have challenge modes that limit your ability to use certain towers, or prevent upgrades which have been unlocked past an established tier. The challenges are just that - not insane, but not necessarily easy. Each challenge CAN be completed. I also have yet to play a normal level that feels like an unnecessary, punishing grind.
For a mobile port, I'm very glad that it actually plays like PC game. Unlike others, notably the Fieldrunners series, this game does not require you to post to twitter or facebook to earn extra stars or to level yourself up more quickly.
I bought this game on a whim - and I'm definitely not disappointed in the slightest.

I'll keep this review mostly about BFG vs Vanilla Doom 3, if you're interested about my opinion on doom 3 you can check my profile for the review of that particular game, in short I freakin' love DOOM 3, to me it's a perfect game, love the atmosphere, the gunplay, the horror elements mixed with a lot of action, it's just so perfect.
Anyways, I do recommend this version of DOOM 3. It is a bit easier than the vanilla doom 3, there's more ammo and health packs scattered around the world and the shoulder-mounted flashlight makes the fights a lot easier and kinda takes away from the horror aspect of the game. Veteran is the difficulty I'd recommend in BFG edition most definitely, even Nightmare is manageable with all that health lying around.
Compared to the original DOOM 3 I gotta say, this DOOM 3 feels smoother, you can definitely feel it's modernized, it runs on a newer engine but the gameplay is the same. Actually, they might have increased the player movement speed slightly, maybe they haven't but it's just something I feel when playing this version. Sure DOOM 3 offers a lot of mods, which are visually better than the BFG edition, but the BFG edition feels... I dunno, really good when playing it, it's just very enjoyable. The performance and optimization is top notch.
It has a new mini-campaign called "the lost mission", which is a pretty cool campaign, well put together. There aren't any new additions when it comes to lost mission, like for example a new artifact or even enemies, but it's still pretty fun to play. Of course the BFG edition also contains the Resurrection of evil campaign which is classic.
It also has DOOM and DOOM II and an exclusive DOOM II expansion 'no rest for the living', which is pretty awesome.
All in all, I definitely recommend getting this, even if it's a bit casual when compared to the original DOOM 3. It's a great pack of great DOOM games and it feels great just having them all in one place and you can access them all with one click. Sure DOOM 3 has awesome mods, but BFG rivals it very well, it's just well put together.  And hunting those achievements is also very fun!

An isometric action RPG, Bastion is Supergiant Games excellent debut title in where you play as the Kid, with every action you make is narrated to you by Rucks, the sole voice in the game. In the wake of a catastrophic event known as the Calamity which destroys the city of Caelondia, you travel to the Bastion, the safe-haven for Caelondia's inhabitants. There you meet the games narrator Rucks, the other only apparent survivor of the Calamity who sets you off on the story.
Particular to note is the games fantastic art style, all of which is fantastically hand-drawn, with every environment/level you come across being unique and memorable in its own way. Bastion's soundtrack is also worth mentioning as being an excellent listen. Ruck's, being the only voice you hear in the game does a fantastic job of being the aged, badass survivor guiding you, the hero on his journey.
The combat is one of the games weak points, sometimes feeling inconsistent and clunky at times. The games length is also somewhat short, averaging at around 6-8 hours in length. However there is a New Game+ mode at its conclusion, giving some excellent replay ability. Never the less, Bastion's story, soundtrack, art-style and of course the narrator are enough to carry the game on its own. One of the first things I noticed about Rogue Warrior was how good the music is. In a lot of games I end up turning off the music because it’s too depressing or repetitive. The music in this game is awesome, its genuinely cool and adds to the fun.
Mickey Rourke did the voice acting, for the main character here, who’s name is Rourke. His dialogue and performance are hilarious. Even though he literally sounds, like he’s not bothered on some of the parts between levels. I really enjoy when games don’t take things too seriously and with Rogue Warrior this is definitely the case.
I had to tweak things a little bit, so that I could play it, at a smooth 60FPS with no stuttering. It’s easy to find some information on this with a quick search. Having made these basic changes the game runs really well for me (my specs are on my profile).
Rourke's 'ultimate badass' attitude is ridiculous in the most entertaining way. His dialogue is hilariously over the top and the violence is taken to a weird level. Even though it's poorly made, even for 2009 (it looks like a PS2 remaster), this somehow also adds to the 'so bad, it's good' charm of the game.
The only thing that’s a bit annoying is the poor hit detection but it works ‘okay’ enough to still be fun. I’m also assuming  that this game was not full price on consoles back in 2009 because it is crazy short. This is fine for a cheap silly game on Steam but just know that this game is basic in it’s gameplay mechanics and over very quickly. It’s a fairly challenging game though, for what it is, if you’re not careful you will die a lot (even on the standard difficulty).
In my opinion, some games try to be too dramatic and this can end up ruining the fun. Rogue Warrior doesn’t have that problem, at all. It's a blast and It captures something I love about videogames. Which is when the fantastically crap and ridiculous ends up being surreal and fun.
P.S: Rourke climbs ladders like a ♥♥♥♥ing machine!!

I got ICEY specifically for the Steam Link bundle, and I decided it would be a waste not to at least try it. Most of the time I can work through a mediocre game, but in this case it has seemed especailly painful.
tl;dr
Gameplay: meh
Story: meh
Art: decent
Music: meh
Voice Acting: UNBEARABLE
Okay hack'n'slash if $5 or less
Note: I have only played this game on Hard difficulty with and XBox 360 controller. This review is based soley upon the Hard mode experience.
The Gameplay:
Combat isn't something spectacular, just standard 2D hack'n'slash, with the controls seeming a little loose.
When I first started playing the timing of the damage dealt by ICEY's (or UCEY's) attacks felt just slightly off. within the first area I adjusted to that, but after taking a break and returning, I had to readjust myself to the rhythm of the game again.
Along with the timing of attacks, sometimes attempting a dash does nothing, even when you still have all 5 charges available. The first fight where I really noticed this was against the optional boss Jack in the Marionette Theater. During my first attempt at the fight, I noticed that some of my dashes didn't seem to be going through, so I stayed away from the boss and tried chaining dashes together. To my dismay one or two of my dashes on occasion would not activate. Thinking it may have been my controller, Ipaused the game and tried swapping to one of my others, only to find the same problem. Finally I grabbed a wired controller and was again disappointed.
This game allows the player to counter certain enemy attacks given they react in time when an exclamation mark appears above their head and dash through their attack area. This mechanic can be a bit annoying at times because it can be tough to tell exactly WHERE the enemy's attack area is.
This brings me to my next top, enemy attack areas. They suffer from being ill defined to players in some situations. The biggest example I have of this is among the first few few bosses of the game. There are two bosses who have mouths on their lower body and who have an attack where they move forward,  their chomping mouth on the ground, attempting to grab ICEY. The surprising part of this attack is that if you are in the air anywhere in front of the boss, even if you are well above the mouth, you are magically put into the monster's mouth and suffer the damage of the attack. There are a few less dramatic examples, but that seems to be the worst perpetrator.
Movement feels a little slippery, with ICEY sliding forward just a little when coming to a stop. There is no animation to indicate that the character is sliding to a stop. Holding forward while using light attacks causes you to move forward by increments based upon the stage of the attack chain. The problem is again that there is no stepping animation during or between any of the attack animations in the chain. Stuff like this makes ground movement feel a little slippery.
Progress in this game feels a tad bit meaningless. You begin the game with every skill available to you, with the option to spend collected currency to upgrade each to a maximum level of 3. The problem with this is that each upgrade doesn't feel like it changes gameplay. Each of the combat skills is ony upgraded with damage, and while your health, overshield, hp drop rate, and counter frequency, even those change virtually nothing.
The game path is essentially linear with the path indicated by arrows. There are optional side areas which, upon completion, give a small piece of text indirectly explaining a tiny bit of the lore of the game world. Some optional areas also have some in-game indications of world lore, though that is less common. In one of the side areas, there happens to be one level of a better game, albeit a more casual one.
Story:
The story of this game has is based in a world where a technological apocalypse was brought about by a follower of the "Yellow King". The man who caused the end-times is a cyborg named JUDAS, and your mission as ICEY is to put an end to his reign. The references and allusions the story makes are for the most part painfully obvious, but I can forgive this because this is a Chinese company, and what may be an obvious reference in the eyes of a halfway educated American may not have the same level of in-your-face in its native market. For the most part the story is revealed through the optional areas as described in the gameplay section and through an in-game narrator who directs the player and explains ICEY's thoughts and motives.
Art:
The style of art in this game is consistent throughout, though the backgrounds suffer at points from the developer attempting to illustrate 2.5D movement in a 2D game.
The animations are acceptable. For the most part, animations use tweening to cut back on cost and effort, though this does look a bit wonky to anyone who knows about animation. Any animation that doesn't use tweens suffers from an extremely low keyframe count, making them look choppy.
Music:
The Music of this game is for the most part forgettable aside from one track: the background music from the forest area and town at the beginning of the game. The fact that it has the SAME TWO BAR BASS LINE playing the whole time was infuriating.
Voice Acting:
The voice acting almost makes this game unplayable. The only voice actor is the narrator, who exists as a director of sorts for the player in an attempt to be meta, in the same fasion as the Stanley Parable. The lines are almost unbearable to hear in a game with an actual plot outside of a commentary on video games and the voice actor himself completely phones in his performance. The most aggregious example that comes to mind is in the hidden area where you obtain the Instant-Kill skill, and have to fight off waves of enemies without activating it. One of the lines of dialogue from the narrator is something along the lines of "Oh, oh, oh! Here it comes! You have to resist!" The utterance of the words by the narrator was so poor that I physically winced.
All in all, this game isn't terrible, but as a mediocre title with attrotious voice acting, I can only reccommend this game if it is on sale for $5 or less.

I was looking for a game to pry me away from Civ V, something that might not require so much time to play a single game, something more exciting yet less complicated.  Northgard nails it.  It's an early access game, but it's absolutely playable right now.  The action of the game is fast-paced enough to keep you moving, but it's not so crazy that you feel overwhelmed... that is, unless you find yourself being invaded on 4 different fronts by different factions while your food is low and winter is coming.
PROS!
-RTS that gets as crazy or stays pretty calm depending on your play style.
-A seasons cycle that affects the production and happiness of your people (as well as the game's aesthetics).
-Several clans (factions) that are balanced but truly unique.
-Environment variables that you will either adapt your strategy to or lose... or keep playing on Easy Mode, you sissy.
-Limits on warband (army) size that prevent the game from deteriorating into a race for the Domination Victory, but you can invest in upgrades to expand the warband size.
-Well thought-out and interesting Victory Conditions!  For once!  I LOVE this about Northgard.  The Map Victory Condition option is a great feature.  It's like a quest determined by the map, if that makes sense.
-A great setting and plot!  Friggin' Vikings!  With lots of different Viking-specific buildings, units, and bits of lore!  There's giants and wyverns too!  Both of which contribute to the game in interesting ways!
-Cheap for the countless hours I'm bound to spend on it.  Like I said, it's still an Early Access Game, but it's fully playable.
cons.
-I really wish it were easier to get the Jotnar involved.  By the time I've traded enough with them, someone's already achieved 98% of one of the Victory Conditions.
-Less utilization of naval units than I would have hoped.  It is cool that they can just raid, but...  Maybe it's just because my preconceived idea of the game included sending boat-loads of Vikings to attack across the seas.
-No way to break the warband into individual units to make holding multiple lines easier.  If I could have two warbands with one of each unit that I could select with a single button, that would make my fights so much more fun.
-The fact that any citizen who has a specific job has to run to a house to become a villager in order to change jobs, build or repair something is annoying.  Maybe it was done intentionally to add another challenge, but it doesn't make sense.  Maybe if they had to run to grab tools or something it would make more sense.

A great collection of the DOOM games.  The classic ones are updated with modern controls and don't have the issues that you may otherwise get with the DOSBox versions.  They run at a higher resolution as well.  DOOM II includes the No Rest for the Living episode that was exclusive to the XBox Live Arcade version, and it is a great mapset that feels on par with a very competent community WAD.
DOOM 3 is remastered slightly, some better, some compromises.  The graphics are a little "compressed," not sure how to describe it but it helps tremendously with the framerate.  The game loads extremely fast!  The change to allow the flashlight to be used with weapons I think helps with the gameplay, even if making a little easier.  The new Lost Missions are uninspired, since a lot of it is reused assets.  I was impressed with the hell levels however.  Note that BFG Edition does not support mods at all.  The multiplayer is matchmaking-based, and doesn't seem to have anybody online consistently.
The big question is whether it is preferrable to buy this edition or the original games seperately. I recommend the BFG Edition if you are looking for a great value and want to play through the trilogy with minor tweaks to make it more accessible.  For the classic games there's not much difference, but for Doom 3 it depends on whether you want to play mods and use the legacy server browser.  The new episodes for DOOM II and DOOM 3 make the BFG edition worth it in my opinion.

Doom 3: BFG Edition...
Hoo boy, here we go.
So this is a nice HD remaster of Doom 3 which, for all platforms, includes the unaltered levels for the original Doom 3 campaign, Resurection of Evil, and previously unseen Lost Levels (which I'm sure have been back ported).
On top of that, it comes with full copies of Doom and Doom 2. So what's not to love?
Well, let's go into detail about that.
The Ultimate Doom, the original mo-fo, remains unchanged as far as I can tell.
Same great gameplay, same great music.
Doom 2 however, has been changed in a small, but still very impactful way.
One of the most famous and most well-known easter-eggs of Doom 2 was that you could access Floors 1-1 and 1-9 from Doom's predecessor, Wolfenstein 3D through a secret exit in Map 15: The industrial Zone. These maps occupy slots 31 and 32 respectively.
Usually, you get to these levels and you get to drop Nazi soldiers left and right and eventually killing four Commander Keens dangling from nooses (in Map32).
You won't do such a thing in this version of Doom 2, though.
The even legendary Wolfenstein 3D levels have been violently disfigured and defaced in the most disgusting of ways.
In Doom 2: BFG Edition, there are no Nazis in Maps 31 or 32. No Nazi symbolism, no hitler portraits. Nothing.
Not even a single swastika. Even the names of the maps were changed.
(Doom 2 Classic)
Map31: Wolfenstein
Map32: Grosse
(Doom 2: BFG Edition)
Map31: IDKFA
Map32: Keen
Since it's release almost six years ago, I've been trying to wrap my head around why they [id/Bethesda] would go out of their way to censor these two levels.
The only possible explanation I've heard is that (apparently) Nazi symbolism is not okay to show anymore and that they didn't want to offend anyone.
But this explanation is rendered null and void by a few simple facts:
1) The original Doom 2 and Wolfenstein 3D are still on Steam.
2) Wolfenstein as a series is still alive and well today.
Only two facts, but they hold a lot of weight.
If they wanted to pander to those who are far too sensitive to such "evil" symbolism. Why didn't they [id/Bethesda] remove Wolfenstein 3D from Steam and censor the levels from the original Doom 2?
On the note of censorship, another explanation I heard was so it could be legal to sell in Germany.
If that was the case why didn't they simply make this censored version only available to Germans?
This is only strengthened by the fact that
1) The PC version of Doom and Doom 2 BFG Edition do not include the console version's multiplayer
2) The prior version of Doom 2 available exclusively on XBox 360 contained all of Doom 2's maps unaltered.
The tl;dr is: Don't bother buying this game. Go and buy the Doom games seperately, there are codes for em on♥♥♥♥♥for pretty cheap (that's where I got this game. I paid two dollars for it.). On top of that, there are HD graphics and textures mods for Doom 3 that look a thousand times better than Doom 3 BFG Ediiton.
Who needs brain cells anyway?

After playing this game for over a year via browser, me and a friend both picked up the Steam client, since this is basically what we do together most of the time. The bonus skin and town points were really more of an 'icing on the cake' incentive to what we thought would be a streamlined, browser-free version of the game, but there's been several noticable drawbacks.
The Steam version seems to be less stable, and so far it's varied between twenty-second input lag and being relatively okay (The browser version has never lagged for me, at all). It also seems like migrating my account has reset my ELO, which means that I'm being put into more games with spamming, abrasive, gamethrowing, and outright "I'm just here to trollolol" players. Normally I wouldn't much mind being reset, but the differences in ToS' community further up/down the ladder are staggering.
Pros/cons:
Five bucks gets you an exclusive skin and some currency to buy other skins.
The Steam version doesn't require you to launch your browser and includes a fullscreen option.
No more ads on the login page.
Lobbies draw from all accounts so you can still play with your browser friends.
Seemingly resets your ELO.
Steam client seems less stable.
The skins are purely cosmetic.
Lobbies draw from all accounts so there's no getting away from persistent FtP trolls.
If you've been playing the game for a while and made a niche for yourself where you enjoy the players you're matched with, stick with the browser version. You can always buy the cosmetics there as well, excluding the Steambot.
That being said, now that I have this version, I'm going to try and regain my ranking. Maybe in a few days I'll stop being paired with the same a♥♥holes that I was happy not to be paired with anymore.
::Edit:: Update: Additional review:
It took me about a week, but I've managed to climb back up the ladder far enough to stop being placed with the types of players who join ranked matches for no reason other than to troll/spam, which has vastly improved my continued enjoyment of the game.
I have gone back to playing exclusively on the browser, as it doesn't have any performance issues whatsoever and is a much more comfortable experience.
I don't regret my purchase, especially considering that merging my account (while still having had a temporary negative effect) has also granted me the X2 multiplier on merit points earned in games. It feels good to know that I supported the development team more than just providing ad revenue, and the Steam client does serve the additional function of providing an easier place to make purchases than doing it through the browser (using my steam wallet instead of a credit card).
All things considered though, unless you're exclusively interested in gaining that X2 multiplier and the SteamBot skin, I still don't recommend purchasing this client version,  since it has consistent performance issues the browser doesn't.

Floating Point is a game all about elegantly flying through the air while collecting red bars to complete each level. It's very relaxing, and guess what? It's FREE! Absolutely free!
-GAMEPLAY-
Each level is randomly generated. The levels are made of many floating blocks. Further down, there's water and more blocks under it. The water is harmless, but can be a burden. You can choose your preferences and adjust how it generates in the menu, which I think is a neat little feature. You are a very small red ball that glows. Your objective is simple: collect the red bars on the many floating bricks. How do we do that? Well, our small ball has a grapple that you can use to swing from block to block.
Aim and click the right mouse button to instantly attatch your grapple to the desired brick. Hold the right mouse button to pull yourself in, and press the left mouse button to remove your grapple. This is your only tool. You glow brighter and the red bars grow taller when you move around. You have an orange trail as well. I haven't really payed much attention to it, but I think it grows and shortens with your glow. The rate your glow brightens and the bars grow is judged by how fast you are moving. If you bump into a block, you lose some glow and the bars shorten. It's okay to make sharp turns, but you will usually slow down. When you slow down, your glow and red bars gradually shrink. Invisible walls surround each level, but bumping into them won't hinder you at all or even slow you down.
You win each level by collecting the needed amount of red bars. A message appears in the top left corner of your screen to let you know when you can advance. You don't have to get all of them. Usually, there's 3 to 4 left when you are allowed to move on Press ENTER to move to the next level. If you want to get the last bars, you can stay as long as you want (I usually get them all). When you collect every bar, you are rewarded with a complete drawing of all of the movements you made and you and your trail turn white. You continue to add to the drawing as you play on. You can stay longer if you want. It's entirely up to you when you want to move on.
Gameplay is fun and often challenging, but never tedius or frustrating. It's not something you'd want to play every day, but it's a nice game to play when you're bored or just feel up to it. When I do play, I spend about an hour or two on it. It may also help you calm down if you're stressed.
-GRAPHICS, UI, AND PERFORMANCE-
Well, graphically, you can't expect that much out of a game so simple. It's not a bad thing, though. The textures fit the game. The graphics are nice and crisp.
The UI in-game is neat and non-intrusive. In the bottom left is your score, and in the bottom right is the amount of bars left. When you collect enough bars to advance, a message appears in the top left of the screen that tells you to press ENTER when you're ready to go. My first complaint is that it's a little too small. The message that tells you when you can advance to the next level is small and may go unnoticed for a short time while playing. Fighting Games have long begun a slow-burn demise, but for fans of the neon lit, pulsing arcade halls of the 80’s and 90’s, the siren call of ‘Flawless Victory’ is hard to resist. ‘Mortal Kombat: The Komplete Edition’ is a polished, frenetic and gloriously bloody update to the venerable 2.5-D Fighting series, and a must-have for any Fight Game enthusiast.
Released by NetherRealm / Warner Bros. in 2013, ‘Mortal Kombat’ boasts the best example of a true ‘Campaign | Story’ mode ever constructed for a Fight Game. A true-to-form outrageous plot set in a war between Outworld and EarthRealm, narrated through well conceived animated cut-scenes and interspersed with 1-on-1 and Tag Team battles, allow gamers to control their favorite characters as well as try some others they might not have been so inclined to. The usual suspects are all here – from Scorpion, Sub-Zero, Sonya, Johnny Cage, Liu Kang, Sektor, Raiden and Shao Khan to a host of new faces like Smoke, Noob Cybot, Rain, Quan Chi, Scarlett and Cyber Sub-Zero. In addition, a variety of Single Player Arcade-style ‘Ladder’ Tournaments, Online Modes (to include Tournament’s, ‘King of the Hill’ events), and lots of unlockable Achievements, round out a robust content-rich title.
Gameplay is fast and savagely bloody - and PC controls are tight, responsive and well optimized for both M&K and Controller. Newcomers to the franchise (or fight games in general) will relish the fact that unlike other fighters (which can be notoriously difficult to master), ‘Mortal Kombat’ utilizes a manageable 4-5 buttons for even its more complex combos making elaborate ‘Take Downs’, ‘X-Ray Hits’, and ‘Fatalities’ executable even for non-veterans. Mastering this system however, is another challenge altogether. Another positive is that all playable characters come already un-locked, eliminating the usual grind. Graphics and Sound are great overall as well.
In considering its flaws – 1. Multiplayer Connectivity Issues, and 2. an un-even difficulty curve – the continuing issues with online connectivity are the biggest concern. Online matches are frequently laggy and result in too many dropped matches (Be warned, although your mileage may vary).
Overall, ‘Mortal Kombat: The Komplete Edition’ is a fantastic modern fighting game and a worthy re-boot of the legendary Arcade brawler - with a large collection of fighters (30+) to choose from, a lengthy well-crafted campaign, satisfying fight mechanics, all the brutality we would expect from the series, and lots of SP and MP modes to keep you busy through a sustained gaming session or a shorter pick-up-n-play distraction. Highly Recommended for both Fight fans and newcomers. “Get Over Here!” - Rated (8.8/10)

TLDR:  So it's situations like this that I wish there was a Mixed option of whether or not I'd recommend a game.  But given the time that I have now on ICEY, I just can't recommend it to most people.  I also want to put here that I've played the game primarily with an xbox controller.
Combat:
While fun and engaging at first, it begin to become a chore later in the game.  Animations and sound design are well done and give a large amount of meat to the game, however the overall inconsistency of what will work on what began to drag on me as I went further in.
I can understand not allowing the juggling of boss mobs or super sized enemies.  However, there came two particular enemies I came to hate, and those were the massive hand bots, and then the massive hand bot with legs.  These two variants felt horrible to try and combat as you'd go in to start a combo, and then get a no warning grab that breaks all your shields from full just to toss you.  You'd then be comboed by everything else on the screen at that point.
The "perfect" dodge also seemed to be rather inconsistent as to when the game recognized it as such.  There were times I'd get it just for randomly pressing the dash key and then there were times that given thought and timing it just decided "nope you didn't dodge that"
Combos also seem inconsistent and difficult to pull off just because.  It is as if the game doesn't fully recognize input from the controller resulting in you doing one combo instead of the one you were going for.  For instance, in one case I was trying to pull off the XXXYY combo on an enemy for the airiel dash attack, but the game took it as XXXXY instead.  I'm not sure how it registered the extra input of X.
Story:
I get where they were going with the story in this game and I do find it interesting really.  The diversions that create the intreresting narrative interactions are amusing to experience.  However, the narrative isn't anything to write home about, and the "meta" aspect of it is all that the game has going for it.  Well in cases like Bastion, the story was at least interesting to behold and were only enhanced by the narrator.  Well here, the narrator is really the only point of interest and he starts to ware on ya after a while.
Controls:
I stated most of this in combat section, but the controls in this game feel inconsistent and at times sluggish.  It's as if they didn't optimize them properly after initial development.  And for a game genre like this, if the controls are as close to pin point accuracy and responsive it will drag the whole experience down.
Art and Music:
The art style is nice and animations flow well.  Music is ok, but ultimately forgettable as it gets lost in the background with how unimpactful it is.  I do like the way that the menu looks in the game, gives the right vibe considering the story.
Overall:
I can't recommend it, even though I picked it up on sale I don't feel like it was worth it in the end.  Cool character and concept, but the gameplay wasn't optimized enough to put such a thing in this genre of games.

DOOM 3: BFG Edition is not really a game, but rather a pack that contains three games:
1. The Ultimate DOOM
2. DOOM II: Hell on Earth (Warning: The secret levels contained within this version are censored globally) + Bonus Map pack
3: Doom 3 + two expansions
The original DOOM games are classic First-Person Shooters. It might take some time to get used to the controls, but the music, the different enemy types and the level design (especially in the first DOOM) are amazing!
Lower difficulties are rather beginner-friendly, while the higher ones pose quite a challenge (especially the infamous "Nightmare!" mode).
There is pretty much no Story in the originals at all, as DOOM is mostly about the gameplay.
The player is unable to jump, but he can run at insane speeds and he can find quite a few different weapons, starting with nothing but a regular handgun, all the way up to the iconic BFG9000, which will eviscerate pretty much anything it's pointed at.
The sequel didn't really shine as much when it comes to level design, as most levels can be rather confusing for first time players, but the addition of a new weapon and new enemies still make the game quite enjoyable.
...dammit, do I have to talk about DOOM 3? Okay, fine, I'll do it.
The third game tried to go in a different direction and attempted to use horror elements, including very dark environments combined with an almost useless flashlight and excessive use of so called "monster closets", walls, that open (mostly when you're walking past them or picked up a specific item) to reveal enemies inside.
In addition, it has you pick up documents that contain codes that allow you to open lockers which contain equipment or possibly even important items and last but not least, you move at a more realistic (read: slow) pace.
So...is DOOM 3: BFG Edition any good? I say yes. The first two games are absolutely amazing for those who want a classic experience while DOOM 3 is quite an okay horror game for its age. I recommend picking this one up while it's on sale, chaps!

Fran Bow is the most moving game I've played in a long time. The gore is not what stuck with me; rather, the light this game shone on gruesome and inhumane eugenics practices that were actually historically performed on mentally ill kids--the lobotomies, in particular--hold a special place in my heart as some of the most heartwrenching scenes and stories. The otherworldliness in this game is fantastic, and atop that, so is its world building. The game doesn't force you to look into every single detail of the world, but you're given the tools to if you wish to, and I find that absolutely fantastic. Coupled with fantastic artwork, an interesting mechanic for "seeing things that are not seen," and a main character who is full of true Goodness, Fran Bow is topping my list for recommended games right now.
My only real complaint of the game is that Fran felt younger than she was actually portrayed, in dialogue and choices. She felt like what people "think" an eleven year old should be, instead of what one really is, and I pegged her more toward the five-seven age range. That said, this is not a huge detracting factor from the game, so while it bothered me a bit, I still highly recommend this.

For some like myself who has spent a considerable time on this game and has decades of gaming, this is not an easy thing to rate.
Do I recommend the genre?
Yes. They require a high degree of skill and have a good reward for your time.
Problem is this in an online game. I spent a considerable time practicing before playing online.
Single player wasn't available on launch. That was a detraction. The reward system to purchase items needs a lot of reconsideration as well, but for the most part, I was fine with paying for things.
Except, why would I pay for items to use in single player modes and not get a use online from them?
I wouldn't.
Can I play online?
I live in Australia. Not far from Sydney. I ping Sydney fine. I can't get a game right now. When I do, the connection quality is so poor, getting 60 frames per second is impossible. Try 5-10 max frame rate.
It's not my PC. It's not my friends either. He has a beast PC and we can't get a solid connection in the same location 7km apart.
This game relies strongly on you upgrading your skill level. Playing other players online does that. Finding players quickly and getting a good connection is vital.
Street Fighter V, at August 2017 fails at this.
So should you buy the game?
No, you should get a guarantee of a solid quality connection and THEN pay for the game. It's beyond pathetic. This is 2017 and this game should have stable net code. It doesn't. I can't even excecute a basic move online let alone try and get a combo. Not me that is stopping this...it's Capcom and their net code.
For all the industry advancements, this area of expertise, net coding and matchmaking quality, nothing seems to have improved across the industry. It's still 10 years ago. It's still absolutely shocking. I don't blame Capcom, but the game has very little extras to offer you IF you get a poor connection.
Got a great connection, because of random good luck ... yes, buy it. But beware how poor this can be. Honestly a full refund is warranted by Capcom and Steam. Not even close to being good enough.

While most of the issues with this game have been fixed with various patches, there are still a few glaring flaws that haven't been addressed that prevent me from recommending this game.
First, this game is still heavily skewed towards gunplay as opposed to tower usage. It's better than it used to be, but the low resources between rounds and the relatively low tower limit means you'll be killing a lot of enemies yourself, which some players may like, but it doesn't have the balance that the first game had. The levels are smaller in general as well, limiting your maze building options. Strangely, despite the focus on guns, you can't upgrade them like you could in the first game.
Second, you have to grind to unlock new weapons, towers and perks, and worst of all, perk slots. This makes portions of the game extremely frustrating where you don't really have the towers and guns you need yet to progress but the only way to get them is to grind or try to tough it out with what you have. A better approach would have been to have new things unlock with map completion, with the maps balanced so that you have the towers you need.
Lastly (and most disappointing to me) is that there is no true singleplayer mode. Single player is simply multiplayer mode where nobody can join. Which means you cannot pause the game. Any single player game that does not let you pause immediately gets a very low score from me, especially given how long some of the waves and maps are in this game.
Another point: I haven't played multiplayer, but I've heard that in multiplayer only one player gets to place towers, everyone else is just running around playing a FPS. Kind of defeats the purpose of playing a hybrid action tower defense if you can't even place towers.
Other than that, I like the game. The graphics are good, the levels have lots of fun little secret areas to find between waves, there's a nice selection of guns and towers, but I wish the devs had focused more on that balance between guns and towers that made the first game so great, and the extremely poor single player implementation (seriously, why can't I pause in single player) and the tedious grind to actually progress through the game means that I really can't recommend it.
It's a fun little game to play in your freetime and one I would certainly reccomend.

I bought this game on the last day of the holiday Steam sale on a whim, and it was one of my best purchases to date! Admittedly I am the exact target audience for this game - I grew up in the 80s and still remember sneaking downstairs waaaaaayyyy too early on Saturday mornings to watch Voltron, Dungeons & Dragons, Josie & the ♥♥♥♥♥cats, etc. and nearly dying of  excitement the year we finally got an original Nintendo. Everything from the music, to the quests, to the NPC dialog perfectly captures both my real and imaginary life from that time period - I love it.
Speaking somewhat less subjectively. The episodes are short - for me that's a bonus. Each one took me 45-80 minutes for the first run through, and that was fully exploring. But that is perfect if you don't have a lot of time and want to feel like you're accomplishing something in a gaming session. Also, there is some replay value, as you get to keep all your new shinies when you replay a level, so you can experience the satisfaction of instantly obliterating a baddie that gave you trouble the first time around. But I can see how a short game would be unsatisfying to some players. But don't say it's not worth the $$. It's like, $1.50 now, and even if you pay the full $6.99 that is around $1 per hour of fun at most. If you're willing to pay even $5 for a matinee movie, you can't complain this game isn't worth it.
Also the battles, turn based, can be a little repetative - especially in the beginning. But once I had a few more weapons/defensive options/buffs I had a lot of fun playing around with various combinations.
No the graphics aren't up to Witcher 3 standard. Or 2. or 1.  Or...   80s remember?
That said, if you've ever seen the Transformers cartoons and thought only "Ugg, this is unbearable" or can't stand music from before 1998 then maybe this game isn't for you. But anyone who had to sit through a D.A.R.E program, or rushed home aftrer school, hoping not to miss the Transformers OP please, please "risk" $1.50 (or whatever!) on this game. Maybe fun at a low level, but once you get to a mid level (I was at super platinum online) the game doesn't really feel very deep or interesting. It's much slower than every other street fighter and has more lag, so it's harder to play defensive/neutral. That, combined with skewed risk/reward on things like crush counters and certain VTriggers, means that you find yourself throwing out a lot of buttons that would be a bad idea in other games. It gets to the point where you can't really understand why you're winning or losing, other than "he got the crush counter and I didn't". Comebacks are too easy in this game, and that's coming from a Marvel 3 player. It's incredibly easy to turn a match around with a wakeup jab into VTrigger.
Street Fighter 5 rewards aggressive play and pressure too much. Defensive characters don't really exist in this game outside of Guile, but his VTrigger means that even he's going to be playing offense most of the time anyway. There's no balance between offensive and defensive playstyles. The roster is almost entirely viable, but that isn't saying much since they're all forced to play basically the same way. A good counterexample would be MvC2, where only like 8 characters were viable at the highest level, but you could play as offensively or defensively as you wanted. There's a lot wrong with this game, and I pity the players who became pros in SF4 that now have to play this trash for their livelihood. If you want a deep fighting game, play guilty gear. If you want a fast fighting game, play marvel. If you want a good balance between them, play Under Night. If it weren't for the Street Fighter name nobody would be playing this game, and neither should you.

Really good game...truly brings all your Alien/Predator nerd fantasies to life.
There are 3 campaigns, one for each of the alien species, and one for the marines. Each species has their own unique gameplay, which I think makes the devs worthy of some props. They basically had to make 3 entire games, in one. These days, we can't even get 1 complete game for our money, but I digress.
The Xenomorph gameplay is my personal favorite. You're fast, can run on any surface (which, I admit, can be pretty disorienting), and you have powerful melee attacks that utilize your claws, or tail. You have grab attacks that allow you to do some of the famous xeno tactics...using your "little mouth" to punch into an enemy's skull, shoving your tail through their back, etc.
Playing as the Predator, I think, was extremely true to the movies. You have your arm blades, shoulder-mounted plasma gun, thermal vision, stealth (yes, water does cause it to malfunction), and several other gadgets and tools. You also have finishing moves that do the character justice; ripping off your enemies head and spinal column, for example.
The marines are the least fun to play, though I believe it's mostly due to the contrast of playing 2 really cool alien species, and then hopping on to play a standard FPS style game. They have all the signature devices and weapons from the movies, like the pulse rifle and motion tracker.
There are a few areas where this game falls short.
It's pretty obvious that some corners had to get cut when making this 3 in 1 game, and the campaign is where this is most apparent. Every campaign starts with a cool introduction to the character, the xeno being the most creative. After this, it turns into a "go here, kill all these enemies, activate/destroy something to open up the next area" cliche. The good gameplay makes this FAR more tolerable than I'm making it sound. With the xeno and predator, pretty much every kill feels satisfying.
Another gripe I have, is how trivial the Xenomorphs are, as enemies. As in most games that feature them, they're a swarm enemy, that can be mowed down pretty easily. Anyone who's seen the movies, knows that this doesn't do them justice. Hell, even their acid blood is turned into a non-issue. Stand in, or get covered in, the xeno blood, and your screen goes a little blurry, and a sizzling sound plays. That's it; you don't even take damage. It just would have been nicer to see the xenos be more than just a minor inconvenience.
Beyond that stuff, this is a good game. Not amazing, but it's definitely worth every penny of the current price.

I don't usually write reviews for games, but seeing as how this one is early access and all, I'd figure I'd do my part in drumming up support for it.
While not the deepest city builder / RTS, there is a surprising amount of depth for how simple of a game this really is. Think of this as a relaxed RTS, but don't be fooled. There is a very real anxiety that begins to rise when your entire village begins to die from starvation from your lack of planning.
Artwork - 9/10
Very good feel and fits the laid back gameplay of the game. I especially love the art of the clan selection screen, though I would suggest they add a glow to the eyes of the goat clan. All of the other animals have glowing eyes, that bit just feels a little out of place.
Music / Sound - 9/10
Fits the vibe very well. The music is charming, clean, and fun to listen to. Think a quiet wardrum beat with some flutes over it. Very relaxed, but with a surprising amount of gusto for when you enter battles. The warning and alarm cues are also spot on. They give a sense of urgency and immediately you know what the game is warning you of.
Gameplay - 8.5/10
My only complaint here is depth. Every game could use more of it and this one is no exception. I wish buildings and tools could be upgraded more than once and a wider variety of lore upgrades, environments, weather conditions, random events, special territory resources, buildings, and units would really finish rounding this game out. Other than that, it is very satisfying to watch your small village grow into a bustling warcamp. I'd have to say my favorite aspect of this game is the very calm feel of it. It's been a long while since I played a game that didn't feel a bit like work just because of the stress it causes. While the game certainly has it's moments of intesity, they are perfectly paced between moments of seren simplicity.
Price - 9/10
I bought it on sale for $!5.00 and it's worth every penny even in it's current early access state of July 2017. I would happily spend $20.00 on it knowing what I know now, especially considering that the games depth and content will only grow from here.
The Little Things
A more specific request I can call to mind is the ability to queue multiple commands in a chain. I didn't really search very much to see if it was an option, but as an avid player of RTS games, such a command is usually fixed to the shift key, and I didn't find that to be the case. I'm unsure if it might just be a different key.
Summary and Final Score
8.87/10 (But considering it's in early access and is already as good as it is, I predict a solid rating of 9.5/10 in the near future.)

Kingdom Rush is a tower game.  It is fairly simplistic I used I think my mouse, and maybe 2 or 3 keyboard keys to play.  It was I think originally a tablet/flash game.  The campaign is the following: you are a leader who works for a king and you're taking back the kingdom from an evil wizard and fighting off evil hordes and “bad men.”
On the Steam version you get a variety of towers (like any tower game) and they do a variety of different things.  The animation is cute.  It appears to take a lot of processing power and the settings are apparently unable to be reduced by much.  There are also "reinforcements" like dropping down risk pieces to bolster your defenses or attack certain mobs. One spell exists that rains down meteors on the enemy.  The story is light.  There are a number of achievements which are relatively easy to find if you click around enough. Certain levels are amazingly more difficult than others.  Several heroes are OP and others are so weak that no one would choose them.  There are Iron and Heroic challenge options to give you more stars. These stars allow you to “purchase” upgrades to make gameplay easier. These challenges are pretty much optional as there is no need to get more than about 40 stars to achieve optimal tower consideration for any map.  Certain towers are more effective on certain maps.
The game is pretty inexpensive for roughly 10-15 hours of play you're basically paying 1 dollar per hour.  The replay value is relatively low.  Supposedly the developer is creating more DLC or an expansion.  That has yet to be seen and today is 1/12/14.
Would I recommend this game?  Yes.  It is cheap and for the entertainment value for what you will get out of it is worth it. I’d rather play this then watch a Hollywood movie.  I don't see much reason to complete the Iron or Heroic challenges as there is relatively no "added value" in doing so it is just something to waste time with to create an "optimal" strategy for the level.
I'd rate this 3.5/5 for what the game is compared to others.
Inexpensive, easy to put down, and simplistic method of game play are the positives. It is colorful and cute and the music is okay as are the sound effects. The "Easter eggs" and "jokes" aren't very funny or cool but it is a tower game.

I got this game back in 2011 or 2012 as part of a Humble Bundle. My computer at the time probably wouldn't have handled it, but I had a pretty good feeling about the game.
A few months ago I finally got a laptop that would be able to run my games and Bastion was the first thing on my mind. This game is simply beautiful, there's no other way to put it. The graphics may not be something amazing but I felt they fit the game perfectly. The story? I found myself wondering what happened to the world, what the Calamity was, how it happened. I was interested in these character's stories. What lives did they leave before the Calamity? (This lead to one of my disappointments. Rucks is an amazing narrator, and I would've loved to hear more about where he came from. Maybe I just need to dig a little deeper.) The narration is great. I kept switching my weapon loadouts, going back to places and doing things just a little differently to find out what Rucks had to say about it.
As for the soundtrack? Well, that was the best part of the game. The OST for Bastion is surreal. If you took Bastion and played something else over the levels it would probably feel like an entirely different game. The soundtrack blew me away. The three vocal tracks in this game are honestly my favorite tracks in any OST ever. The OST was about 30% of the reason I kept playing the game, even when it made me frustrated. But all of it, the world, the narration and the soundtrack, it's all a part of the experience, and the experience is unforgettable.
Would I recommend this game? A thousand times yes.

Bastion review:
Well, it's bin a while.
I played SuperGiant's more recent game transistor recently, and got the feeling Bastion had been the better of the two.
I was right.
Although Transistor's gameplay is more complex, and perhaps more nuanced than the simplistic platformer mechanics of Bastion, while Bastion has a heart, Transistor is somewhat emotionally and narrationally aenemic.
Bastion plays like a story, feels like a story, communicates important plot points through gameplay and using gameplay mechnics - a win-win.
Ultimately I think Bastion wins because it feels cohesive - everything is encompassed - simplistic gameplay allows for that.
The music is great - a middle-eastern/spaghetti-western crossover  that works quite astoundingly well.
The graphics are nice - colourful, great use of shaders in an ostensibly indie title (though distributed through Warner Brothers).
The gameplay, somehow I found much easier this time around - some areas were great challenges - and the in-game system of using the shrine room to increase challenge was quite inventive, even though some of the shrines just made the game more annoying rather than harder exactly.
They must've tweaked the title since I initially played it, because I both found it more fluid and can't remember there being a 'new game plus' mode (somehow that's all the rage these days - even in games that it really, really doesn't suit - like anything heavily story-oriented - like this.
The one thing that struck me by the end was how they Delivered the ending - without wanting to spoil anything, they took great pains to give you an option where neither is the 'best' solution - each decision has good points and bad points. Which is a far cry from what most titles of much higher budgets, absolutely fail to measure up to (*COUGH*MASSEFFECT3*COUGH*).
This time, I was missing the place within a week, and sad to leave it.
Overall, 8/10.

I have a few problems with this game, and I'll say them up front:
-The game is still pay-to-win, but DECA (the current devs) are trying to pick up the pieces of what KABAM did to milk as much money as possible out of the game.
-The extremely end-game dungeons, namely the shatters and the lair of draconis, are a lot less about being a bullet hell than they are about being kiting the enemies, or just dodging the enemies themselves.
-It can get tedious (like grinding in a game. Some can find it fun!)
-there are a decent amount of hackers and spambots who's only goals are to make your day worse, or make your wallet worse. DECA is also trying to fix this as well.
but the pros, in my opinion, really outweight the cons.
-The game is far from a standard MMO, with actual dodging, and skill based combat. You have to be good to be at the top!
-It's even better with friends, because you can both run dungeons making them easier, and you can both use equipment your other friend can't use.
-At the moment, there was a new dungeon released recently (the "Mountain Temple", for a time reference), and there are 3 more dated to release within 2 months.
-The feeling of getting something rare is SUPER good!
-It's a rogue-lite, meaning there IS permanent death. It greatly increases the risk/reward ratio. If you lose a character you've spend literal hours on maxing out, you'll probably get mad. But it's never the game's fault you died.
All-in-all, if you're looking for something to do with a friend, or you are looking for something different than regular MMOs, or just loking for a fun bullet hell, I reccomend this game for you.

I want to give this game a positive review in the worst way, but I can't. Two big reasons why:
the first crime is Saturday Morning RPG is obviously imitating 90's jRPGs. While it gets the walking around the world part right, the jRPG style battles are god awful. I get the designers' decision to make the process involved with timed button presses, but they went overboard. Almost every attack relies on button mashing or QTEs. Worse is your character is so freaking weak your basic and special attacks hardly do anything to enemies so the battles drag needlessly. To be fair, there is a charge move that multiplies the damage your next attack does. Unfortunately charge is so OP I find myself relying almost entirely on it just to effectively damage normal enemies. And, of course, the charge move that gives you the best bonus is the one that involves hammering on a single button. REALLY annoying. The combat is easily bad enough that it ruins the game.
the second crime is the soundtrack is not included with the game or offered as a download. The music was co-composed by Vince DiCola. If you don't know who that is, he composed the instrumental tracks for the Transformers The Movie (also the awesome montage medley in Rocky IV which undeservely won a razzie) so Saturday Morning RPG has the exact same super cheesy 80's synth sound and its a perfect fit for the game and its theme. The OST is wonderful. I'm actually really ticked I can't listen to it!
Aside from these 2 issues, Saturday Morning RPG does everything else correctly. It crams as many sly references to 80's and early 90's Americana (including a Fruit Stripe reference) into its cliched cartoony plots that seem heavily biased towards Transformers and GI Joe (not complaining). Nostalgia is a big part of the enjoyment if you're old enough to pick up on most of it. The writing is actually good. There's a lot of awfully odd and amusing flavor text sprinkled thorughout. In fact, most of the references in the game are amusingly cornball nonsense. If it weren't for the game's awful combat system, I'd fully endorse the $7 asking price, but that awful combat system is like 1/2 the game and sucks a lot of the enjoyment out of it.

I don't usually write reviews for games, but seeing as how this one is early access and all, I'd figure I'd do my part in drumming up support for it.
While not the deepest city builder / RTS, there is a surprising amount of depth for how simple of a game this really is. Think of this as a relaxed RTS, but don't be fooled. There is a very real anxiety that begins to rise when your entire village begins to die from starvation from your lack of planning.
Artwork - 9/10
Very good feel and fits the laid back gameplay of the game. I especially love the art of the clan selection screen, though I would suggest they add a glow to the eyes of the goat clan. All of the other animals have glowing eyes, that bit just feels a little out of place.
Music / Sound - 9/10
Fits the vibe very well. The music is charming, clean, and fun to listen to. Think a quiet wardrum beat with some flutes over it. Very relaxed, but with a surprising amount of gusto for when you enter battles. The warning and alarm cues are also spot on. They give a sense of urgency and immediately you know what the game is warning you of.
Gameplay - 8.5/10
My only complaint here is depth. Every game could use more of it and this one is no exception. I wish buildings and tools could be upgraded more than once and a wider variety of lore upgrades, environments, weather conditions, random events, special territory resources, buildings, and units would really finish rounding this game out. Other than that, it is very satisfying to watch your small village grow into a bustling warcamp. I'd have to say my favorite aspect of this game is the very calm feel of it. It's been a long while since I played a game that didn't feel a bit like work just because of the stress it causes. While the game certainly has it's moments of intesity, they are perfectly paced between moments of seren simplicity.
Price - 9/10
I bought it on sale for $!5.00 and it's worth every penny even in it's current early access state of July 2017. I would happily spend $20.00 on it knowing what I know now, especially considering that the games depth and content will only grow from here.
The Little Things
A more specific request I can call to mind is the ability to queue multiple commands in a chain. I didn't really search very much to see if it was an option, but as an avid player of RTS games, such a command is usually fixed to the shift key, and I didn't find that to be the case. I'm unsure if it might just be a different key.
Summary and Final Score
8.87/10 (But considering it's in early access and is already as good as it is, I predict a solid rating of 9.5/10 in the near future.)

This is a fun, campy 8-bit style bullet hell shooter made into a cooperative MMORPG. The game itself is built in Flash, playable on the Realm's official website, Kongregate, and on Steam; definitely easy to find people to play with and also to get friends to try as well, even if they don't have Steam! The Free-to-play model comes with the trade-off of micro-transactions, but this game is by no means pay-to-win. All possible paid benefits exist within the main hub called The Nexus; once you enter the battleground, the titular Realm of the Mad God, it's up to your quick reflexes and the cooperation of your fellow fighters to fend off the forces of the evil Oryx.
At the start of the game, five classes are available; Priest, Archer, Warrior, Rogue, and Wizard. Each has different stats, and a different ability. Once you reach Level 20 (the cap) on one or more classes, the remaining 9 other classes become unlocked, including the Paladin, Necromancer, and more. There are 14 classes in all, each of which can be unlocked through normal play or through micro-transactions, if you're impatient. As you play through the game, you earn Fame through the slaying of monsters, evil Gods, and during the assault on Oryx's castle (the culminating event on a single map that holds up to 85 players at once, cooperatively completing tasks). Steam achievements for gaining fame, helping other characters level up, and more exist. This game also has Trading Cards and Badges to show off your love for the game on your Steam profile.
Realm of the Mad God is a fantastic game, offering a frantic, fantasy-themed, bite-sized bullet hell experience that can suck you in from the moment you step foot. I highly recommend this game.

Full review:
I’ll admit it, 140 surprised me. I’ve played quite a few platformers in my time, but this… this was an experience. In a nutshell, 140 is a very minimalistic platformer set to the rhythm of upbeat electronic music. It is quite challenging at times and requires “rhythmic awareness” in order to pass the levels.
Gamepaly is where 140 shines. I had a lot of fun with the various platforming mechanics of this game, some of which I’ve never seen before. It’s interesting that your one enemy is this “static” and, upon touching it, your immediately reset to your last checkpoint. There was one segment where the static was forming into blocks that the player had to jump on, but, in coordination with the beat of the song playing, these blocks would shrink back to a smaller block. The catch here was that while the block was shrinking or enlarging, it would be static. This mechanic was used effectively in the third level, the last level. I did notice that the last level seemed to ramp up the difficulty quite a bit, compared to the pace that the first two levels were going at. The last boss “battle” was utterly brutal to complete and required quick acting, or you’d have to restart the fight. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but the difficult should have been panned out better over the three levels of the game, instead of throwing it all into the last level. The game also has another mode, which I was told is “hardcore” mode. I played a bit of this mode, not knowing what to expect. Upon death in hardcore mode, I was kicked to the main menu of the game. In order to beat hardcore mode, you’ll have to go through it all without dying. Yep, that sounds hardcore enough for me, a little too hardcore. I was unable to complete hardcore mode and quit after five or six tries. Overall, the gameplay was challenging, unique, and kept me entertained.
The graphics of 140 might turn a few people away, but I assure you, they fit very well with the gameplay. I’m glad the game was chosen to have this minimalistic style, its been my first exposure to an art style like this. The vibrant colors and the varying shapes of the player sparked my interest in the game to begin with, well, along with the fact that the music was awesome too. When idling, the player remains as a square, when moving, a circle, and, when jumping, a triangle. These shapes fit well with the task that they’re assigned to now that I think about it, square remains flat and is not easily moves, circle can roll, allowing movement, and the triangle allows for easy landing opon a surface. The background seen in the game appears to follow the beat of the music as well, which is quite nice. Overall, minimalistic graphics = win.
The sound and music in the game was very catchy, working very well with the other aspects of the game. The game even won an IGF award for excellence in audio, which was well-deserved. I believe that the title of the game is also derived from the BPM of the music playing, I found quite interesting. I’m probably going to go looking for the soundtrack after I write this, if it exists. Anyways, the audio was excellent! Nothing much to say about the controls here. I used an Xbox 360 controller during my playthrough. The game has only a few actions: move, jump, and exit. In my case, an analog stick, the A button, and the pause button. Very simple, nothing needing changing here, easy to understand controls.

Amatuer hour Bayonetta. Someone looked at the flashy combat and epic combos of Bayonetta and though "hmmm, lets make a 2D sidescrolling game that has fast paced combat like that." Except this person has no clue what makes Bayonetta a good game.
Now, I do not think the game is inherently a bad idea. A 2D sidescrolling action game like this could be really good if it is executed well. The thing is, ICEY is not executed well. It is a mash of poorly implemented features designed to make the game cool and fast paced, but it ends up being a mess.
I won't get into meticulous detail, but I will explain some big issues with the combat. First off, there is a shield mechanic, where you can take a certain amount of damage before you will be staggered. This is represented by a yellow bar under the health bar. Unfortunately, the only way I could see to refill the bar is to defeat enemies or do a dodge-counter (which I will get into in a moment). The thing is, EVERY attack after your shield is broken will stagger you. Some enemies have a laser beam attack that is near instantaneous, although it doesn't do much damage. But if you have no shield, the one laser beam will stagger you about 4-5 times in a row. And these enemies spawn abundantly. You can imagine how much of a nightmare the fights get to be when you're being staggered from across screen with no chance to avoid the attack.
The dodge and counter move. This, again, is not inherently a bad feature, as it is one of the key components of Bayonetta, and in that game makes fights a game of parry and riposte in between your large combo. In ICEY, if you dodge right before an attack hits, you can stun an enemy for a chance to do a flashy follow-up strike. Again, not a bad idea. The problem lays in the enemies' attack patterns. There are some enemies in the game that have seemingly no windup time for their strikes. In Bayonetta, enemies telegraph their strikes through a bright flash and a distictive sound effect, for almost every attack. The attacks that do not have a flash preceeding it are telegraphed through large enemy motions instead. ICEY's enemies have a telegraph in the form of a red exclaimation mark, but only for "counterattacks" that they perform when you break their guard. The rest of the time, they only telegraph through animation. Some enemies have proper animation for their strike. Others have almost no way of knowing when and where they will hit, as the attacks come out near instantaneously. On top of that, enemies (I noticed this on one boss in particular) can turn on a dime to hit you, so a long attack cannot even be avoided by jumping over. The dash is really finnicky as well; I lost count of how many times I thought I dodged at the right time only to be hit anyway.
On a slightly better note, I liked the way the game told its story through a meta-narrative not unlike The Stanley Parable. I wasn't expecting much, but it was surprising how much choice there was. I only wish there was a way to tell whether going in the opposite direction as the was the game wanted you to go was a path to a treasure chest or something that would change the narrative.
In conclusion, the game succeeds in giving the player flashy combat, but it doesn't exactly hold up mechanically. As a huge fan of Platinum Games' work, I couldn't help but be disappointed at the many missteps ICEY has in trying to provide a similar experience to games like Bayonetta or Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance. ICEY is too inconsistant in its gameplay: one fight might be a fantastic opportunity to fly across the screen slicing up enemies, but for each one of those, you have three more fights that are simply a frustrating excercise in patience. In my almost 2 hours of playing, I fought about 6 bosses and made my way through about as many zones, but I have no desire to slog through the rest. Maybe someday I can go back to this game to find everything just clicks, but for now, I have better games to play.

This is the ninth installment to the (in)famous Mortal Kombat fighting game series, and it's a modern reimagining of the first 3 games, bringing back the classic 2D-style Mortal Kombat gameplay, the characters from the first 3 MKs, and even the Babality finishing moves. The result is a brilliant success, and features a retooled fighting system that is arguably one of the best that's been used in the MK series. The fights are bloody, the new bone-crunching, X-ray super moves are over the top with violence, and the fatality finishers in this game are wonderfully brutal and gorey, just how fans of the series like 'em. There's also local and online gameplay, tons of unlockable content, and new mini-games.
Bottom line: if you're new to the series, this is definitely a great starting point. If you're already a fan of Mortal Kombat or if you like the games but haven't played it in a while, there's no reason why you shouldn't buy this game. You're almost guaranteed to love this!

I got this game back in 2011 or 2012 as part of a Humble Bundle. My computer at the time probably wouldn't have handled it, but I had a pretty good feeling about the game.
A few months ago I finally got a laptop that would be able to run my games and Bastion was the first thing on my mind. This game is simply beautiful, there's no other way to put it. The graphics may not be something amazing but I felt they fit the game perfectly. The story? I found myself wondering what happened to the world, what the Calamity was, how it happened. I was interested in these character's stories. What lives did they leave before the Calamity? (This lead to one of my disappointments. Rucks is an amazing narrator, and I would've loved to hear more about where he came from. Maybe I just need to dig a little deeper.) The narration is great. I kept switching my weapon loadouts, going back to places and doing things just a little differently to find out what Rucks had to say about it.
As for the soundtrack? Well, that was the best part of the game. The OST for Bastion is surreal. If you took Bastion and played something else over the levels it would probably feel like an entirely different game. The soundtrack blew me away. The three vocal tracks in this game are honestly my favorite tracks in any OST ever. The OST was about 30% of the reason I kept playing the game, even when it made me frustrated. But all of it, the world, the narration and the soundtrack, it's all a part of the experience, and the experience is unforgettable.
Would I recommend this game? A thousand times yes.

I'm still not sure what this game wants to be. The initial premise - the one people got excited for and bought thousands of copies for, anyway - was "Terraria but in space", but the developers have done nothing but undercut that premise that for the entire development process. Instead I guess they wanted it to be a difficult action platformer, like a 2d Dark Souls or a really hard SotN? Except a) they didn't seem able to implement that vision coherently and b) no one liked or wanted that. So after years of development, after years of making terrible changes in the name of 'balance' and enforced progression (in a largely-single-player sandbox game), after years of methodically removing the good and fun things (sand mining and the good grappling hook, just to name a few), after adding content which just straight-up ignores the basic premise of the game (the plot dungeons where you arbitrarily can't use the matter manipulator)... after ALL that, what we are left with is basically "Terraria, but much less good." I don't regret the $15 I paid for this game, but I do regret all the time I put into a game that was better during it's early-access launch YEARS AGO then it is now.

Bastion review:
Well, it's bin a while.
I played SuperGiant's more recent game transistor recently, and got the feeling Bastion had been the better of the two.
I was right.
Although Transistor's gameplay is more complex, and perhaps more nuanced than the simplistic platformer mechanics of Bastion, while Bastion has a heart, Transistor is somewhat emotionally and narrationally aenemic.
Bastion plays like a story, feels like a story, communicates important plot points through gameplay and using gameplay mechnics - a win-win.
Ultimately I think Bastion wins because it feels cohesive - everything is encompassed - simplistic gameplay allows for that.
The music is great - a middle-eastern/spaghetti-western crossover  that works quite astoundingly well.
The graphics are nice - colourful, great use of shaders in an ostensibly indie title (though distributed through Warner Brothers).
The gameplay, somehow I found much easier this time around - some areas were great challenges - and the in-game system of using the shrine room to increase challenge was quite inventive, even though some of the shrines just made the game more annoying rather than harder exactly.
They must've tweaked the title since I initially played it, because I both found it more fluid and can't remember there being a 'new game plus' mode (somehow that's all the rage these days - even in games that it really, really doesn't suit - like anything heavily story-oriented - like this.
The one thing that struck me by the end was how they Delivered the ending - without wanting to spoil anything, they took great pains to give you an option where neither is the 'best' solution - each decision has good points and bad points. Which is a far cry from what most titles of much higher budgets, absolutely fail to measure up to (*COUGH*MASSEFFECT3*COUGH*).
This time, I was missing the place within a week, and sad to leave it.
Overall, 8/10.

I recommend this to anyone with a slightly twisted sense of humour. If you squeal over dark Alice in Wonderland adaptations, this will fit you perfectly. It started very strong and carried my interest with some occasional variety in the gameplay; however, that feeling eventually turned into impatience as it began overstaying its welcome. After a few chapters I had already felt the game was longer than I expected, and was anticipating its end repeatedly, but it just kept going. Yet, when the end finally did arrive, it felt abrupt and incomplete. At least it wasn't ever confusing.
There were moments that felt very silly and unrealistic. But if you interpret what you experience in the game world as something NOT presented from a neutral point of view, but from, say, the point of view of the title character, Fran, then any obstructions should be removed. Still, there was that one moment... You'll see.
As for the mechanics, it's all mouse-based puzzle solving and clicking on things for flavour text. if you are familiar with the old point-n-click adventure games (King's Quest V+, Secret of Monkey Island, etc), you will find this game very easy. Additionally, any sections that require quick reflexes are skippable, so you can take the game at a leisurely pace if you prefer. There are a few Easter eggs to find, and it's not just a walking simulator with light gameplay elements, but overall this game is designed to be experienced—the art, the sound, the quirkiness really bring this title alive.

How many of us remember waking up early on Saturday morning when we were back in school, when the biggest question wasn't "how much sugar disguised as breakfast food can we down in a sitting", it was "what cartoons do we want to watch?"  Those were the good old days- when CBS, ABC, NBC and FOX all had Saturday Morning blocks of cartoons.
You get to play as Marty, a guy who watches too many of these old cartoons.  His goal is to stop the forces of evil from taking over the world- and to stop them by using as many 80s pop-culture references as he can cram in his Trapper Keeper.  You can attach scratch-and-sniff stickers to your binder to give you special powers and increased stats when you scratch them, but let's face it- Marty's no Lion-O when it comes to battle.  Relying on physical attacks just won't get you anywhere- instead, you can rely on those same pop-culture shoutouts, like giant plastic playsets (like G.I. Joe's old giant carriers) and rainbow-striped zebras, and obvious knockoffs of Care Bears to do damage.
If you remember the late 80s, you'll love all the shoutouts to cartoons that anyone born after the early 90s will never get the references to- if you were born later, you'll love the game for its playstyle- it's easy to pick up, fun to play, and it won't run you that much.  There are four episodes currently- if you count the overly short and played-up-for-cheesiness Christmas Special, and I'd like to see a fifth, if they ever decide to make one- or a sequel.
