This game is incredibly fun, hilarious game with plenty of references to old TV shows and movies like Star Wars and such, you can play with keyboard, Xbox controller or PS3 controller so all the in game button prompts are corresponding to how you are playing. (I played this game with a Xbox controller so for the sake of this review I will using the Xbox buttons).
The combat in this game is turn based like your average olden days RPG, however it has timing aspect to it. This includes pressing A at the right time to block enemies attack so they deal less damage to you, doing small mini games in some of your spells and starting every battle spinning your joystick to get buffs that you choose beforehand in your little notepad. Some of the powers include spawning rainbows out of you to attack your enemies, playing simon says to kill the enemies and I would go over all of them but I feel as if I would be spoiling it for you if I did.
The story is broken up into 4 episodes (soon to be 5) where our hero, marty is trying to save the world from Commander Hood while trying to gain the affection of his crush, now that may sound cliché but trust me, this story is anything but cliché, It is incredibly enjoyable to watch play out and obviously you have dem sweet sweet side missions during the episodes which I found myself laughing at on multiple occasions.
Oh you finished the game you say, well you can also replay old episodes with your now stronger character whom you can also take into arena mode to fight stronger versions of enemies, also an endless battle mode where you choose an episode and fight endless waves of enemies from that part of the game, and of course you have leaderboards so you can show all your friends just how much better than them you are.
The only thing I dislike is the length of each of the episodes if you were to ignore all the side missions you could finish the first 2 episodes in around an hour or two, however if you are playing an RPG and not doing side missions and exploring, Then you are doing RPGs wrong, oh and you also get XP for exploring which is great.

I recommend it, but I wouldn't go into this expecting the same experience that you had with previous FO games. FO4 isn't as good as any of the previous titles, if you ask me.  Its still enjoyable, but I didn't find myself wanting to replay it like I did the other games.
I think a lot of this has to do with:
- The main character now has a voice and as a result his/her conversations are seemingly far more limited in comparison to the wacky conversations you could have in the previous FO's.
- Power armor has been turned into a "vehicle" and requires (IMO) too much maintenance.
- The map feels smaller than either FO3 or FONV. I've read it is larger, but I swear it feels smaller.
- "Radient Quests": while a good idea in concept, these quests turn into nothing more than recycled "go here, kill a bunch of guys and come back" scenarios that get tiring unless you're just in the mood to go fight something.
- The games "villain" and a lot of its story is dull in comparison to the previous games.
- The DLC/Expansions are for the most part lackluster and don't feel nearly as up to the same quality that was presented in FO3 or FO:NV. That being said, I CAN recommend Far Harbour.
- The perk/leveling system was radically changed and it makes you feel like you're not playing a genuine Fallout title.
- Settlements are a cool idea, but they end up feeling like a waste of time. They almost seem like what Bethesda started with the Hearthfire add-on for Skyrim and taken up a notch. However, the result is still the same; they don't really provide much of anything beyond a superficial notion that you have a crop to tend or a home to mind. All that being said, I've noticed that some people really get into it, so if you like running around a small location and building things, then maybe you'll love it.
- There is a seeming amount of "emptiness" within the game that feels like it was meant to be filled with mods. Whether or not this was intentional on Bethesda's part is unclear, but I think they could have done more to make their base game more interesting.
I could probably go on, but I want to keep this short.  In any event, like I said, I still recommend it; just don't get your hopes up. There is potential to keep it interesting with mods (which was what I ended up doing), so keep that in mind.

If you are a child of the 80's like I am and you have the slightest interest in turn based RPG's you owe it to yourself to pick this game up.  However, even if you did not grow up in the 80's I think you will enjoy this game as long as you like a good old school RPGs.
Pros:
- great dialogue that will make you chuckle, even if you don't get all the references it is relatable enough for anyone to get a laugh out of the characters in this game.
-fun turn based combat- think super mario RPG, if you never played that shame on you, you really should, but basically it is turn based but with timed button presses.  Different moves you do bring up different mini games that require timing to inflict max damage.  Also when enemies attack you, timed button presses reduce the damage dealt, the better your timing the less damage they inflict.
- lots of cool items to collect, the weapons in this game are varied and funny and range from ordinary stuff like baseball bats to some bizzare things like simon says and fruit stripes gum.
-free DLC coming in the future, 4 episodes right now and the game will probably take you roughly 4-5 hours to finish if you do most of the side quests (you will want to, as they are generally worth a chuckle), the developer has confirmed episode 5 is coming soon which will be free, any future episodes will also be free.
-epsiodic layout gives the game a nice feel, each level is large enough on its own and riddled with secrets and side quests and the episodic nature of the game means you don't have to worry about doing any boring backtracking which is all too common in RPG's
cons
-linear character development, not a huge con but if your into branching paths and stuff like that you won't get it here, you quickly learn that magic is the best, you will pour your stats into that and wreak havoc with your flying laser discs and karate kid headbands.
Overall if you are into turn based rpg's with fun combat system and a funny story you will like this.  It is not an epic game, and it does not take itself seriously, but it is fun and you will laugh while you play it, and IMO that is what video games are all about.

Saturday Morning RPG is your classical turn based Role Playing Game with the feeling of the old 80s cartoons. The main character Marty has a vivid dream about the super villain Hood as he kidnaps the hero's love interest. Equipped with a magical notebook, he gets from a spontaneously appearing wizard, Marty makes his way into the enemy main base. And so begins the first episode of SMRPG.

Gameplay
SMRPG features the very classical RPG Systems. Top down view while travelling through the overworld, doing some quest and turn based battles when engaging an enemy in the overworld. If you don't know what a RPG is, well, you missed quite a lot of video game culture. If a battle get started you switchSaturday Morning RPG 01 to a battle screen. During the course of the game you only have Marty as playable character, so goodbye party formations. The enemy side can consist of up to three opponents with varying color scheme. Luckily the devs got every scheme unique looks and features. Your different actions in the battle consists of a normal punch, a power up move and the various tools and toys you collect in your adventure. You get stuff like a floppy disk, a transformer, or even the power of a share bear. All with varying stats and effects. For some of them you need to beat a little mini game to unlock ist full power, but nothing really difficult. The power up action is a neat little feature. You have a damage multiplier in the lower left corner, that you can increase with every action. You have three possible options for that, two of them are mini games where you either need to press the button multiple times, or in the right moment, and an option where it happens automatically. You lose a round by doing that, but you get a multiplier increase of three or four points each time, so the pay of is quite nice.
Story (Spoiler Warning)
This game is a living 80s reference. The main character Marty travels on
a hoverboard (Who can guess his last name?), transformers, Share Bears, and a villain who comes back every week with a new idea to take over the world. The game currently consists of four episodes. The first is a dream episode, Saturday Morning RPG 02where Marty gets ist power and rescues the girl of his dreams. Sadly it's only a dream and this girl is still together with the greatest jerk in school, bet, hey, at least he can keep his new powers and in the next episode he can use them against this giant death laser his arch-villain commander hood has hidden under his school and ruins the bake sale with it. With the third episode you see a little change in style, because this time you have nothing better to do than fighting giant evil transformers. And saving the city dam on that way. In episode four the devs proudly presents you the christmas special episode, where you need to save christmas and bring back all the stolen presents. (guess who did that) In the end of the episode you even see a nice surprise.
Future
Currently only four of once 20 planned episodes are in the game. The problem was that this game was first made for iOS and didn't really well there. But since it's on steam now the sales are much better and the good guy devs promised to bring out new episodes FOR FREE. Episode 5 and 6 are even in production right now. And that'S good, because there are some loose ends from a few side quests i really want to know how that's going to end.
Conclusion
Pro:
- Classical old school RPG
- many 80s references
- Entertaining story
Con:
- low content at the moment
You have a nice looking game on your hand here. If you take your time to do all side quest you can get around 5 to 10 hours of fun out of it, depending if replaying some episodes, which some side quests and the achievements encourage. The battle system works flawlessly, the story is good and there a lot stuff to collect to keep you occupied. But see for yourself, theres nothing that can go wrong with it. And if still have concerns wait for a steam sale. A 75% Off will definitely convince you to buy it.

My RTS experience is limited primarily to Civilization, so I'll compare this game to Civilization V & VI. Northgard is much faster than either Civilization, largely due to the smaller map, and with only 1-3 competitors the competition is limited. There are also various victory types to achieve like Civilization: Domination, Fame, Trade, Wisdom, and Helheim. Unlike Civiliation, Northgard is not turn-based nor is it rigidly tile-based. Thereby it feels like Age of Empires or other more traditional RTS games.
Assigning your little Vikings jobs gives a rewarding feeling, and the limited micromanagement (especially compared to titles such as Civilization V), makes the game very enjoyable to play. I haven't beaten the game on harder difficulties yet, but from my easy mode experience I can say the Northgard provides a quick, fun, casual RTS experience that can fill you with rage when your neighbors conquer one of your territories, but then fuel you with bloodthirst just a few minutes later when you go for your revenge!
All in all a good game, although I don't know if it has the depth necessary to log hundreds of hours into learning, exploring, and perfecting it; but for a quick fun RTS with a satisfying Viking atmosphere, Northgard hits the spot.

I have a hard time recommending this game. I am a fan of the Alien-license (not a hardcore one that would notice plot inconsistencies, mind you) and picked this up on a Steam sale, and I just don't feel like playing any more of it. For reference, I only beat the Marine campaign and some of the Predator campaign so far, and I don't think I'll go and beat both that and the Alien campaign any time soon. Each campaign seems like it'll last you about 2-3 hours, considering I beat the Marine one in about 2 hours and felt like I got halfway through the Predator one.
Its not that I feel that I didn't get my money's worth with Aliens vs Predator (I paid, like, five dollars for it), but I think its not something you should get excited about playing. It works, the environments can be pretty, and it does feel like an Alien game, but the scenarios are bland and not very exciting, and the weapons feel like toys and aren't very satisfying to kill enemies with.
A linear, story-driven FPS needs more than just enemies that you point and shoot at. This genre requires satisfying gunplay mechanics and scenarios that give you an adrenaline rush, or make you feel tense. There have to be challenging rooms filled with enemies that come out of every corner, and you should feel awesome once you overcome that challenge!
Aliens vs Predator is so unexciting that even dying on harder difficulties didn't get me frustrated or angry - I just didn't care enough. At first I thought it was because I was playing the Marine campaign, but the few minutes I played of the Predator campaign were even worse. Again, its not that the game is awful or unplayable, but there are so many other story-driven FPS games that play better. Not every game can be Half-Life, Bioshock or Wolfenstein: The New Order, but a game this mediocre just isn't fun to play nowadays.

Update: I've produced a video examining the world-changing feature described in my original review below:
This is wonderful. It's brief, and it's easy, but it is wonderful.
140 is a simple platformer that is almost entirely about executing basic rhythm puzzles.  The levels are alive around you, and as the elements of level design move they create sound, stereo positioned relative to you, that participates in the music.  That music in turn guides you through the game's obstacles which comprise it.
At the same time, it is an aesthetic delight that plays with color and shape just as much as with sound and rhythm.  There is some replay value in the traditional sense in the form of mirrored versions of the three levels that remove checkpoints, but I would play through the game again anyway just because I like it.
The entire structural idea of moving past half-spherical ports embedded within the ground, finding an orb, returning to a receptacle, watching the world become washed over by the colors contained in the orb, and seeing that new environmental mechanics have come to life and are contributing to the music is
to me. It just captures my imagination so vividly.
The fact that the orbs emit micro versions of the music that they will add before they have been integrated—and exhibit behavior similar to the level element that will come to life with that sound—makes it even better by providing thematic and logical consistency.
Just one of many things that I love about this gem of a game.
Inexpensive and well worth experiencing.  I hope you'll pick it up.

If you’re into games that require simultaneous focus on rhythm, time, patterns, direction, then this is for you. If you’re into deep medi or minimal dubstep, then 140 then definitely check this out. As someone who listens to and mixes a lot of minimal dubstep, I didn’t even have to try to figure out what 140 means. The music basically has a meditative, dark, bassy, and psychedelic feel to it at 140 beats per minute. I highly recommend **subwoofers, quality speakers with great bass**, or quality headphones during gameplay. I always cranked up the volume to really feel the music.
140 really forces you to exercise different parts of your brain simultaneously. That’s what made it tricky yet interesting for me. I had to focus on direction, shape, timing, and sometimes memorization all at once. You basically have to find equilibrium in concentrating on all of those aspects.  However, it is easy to accidentally focus on one thing just a little too much. You’ll see what I mean when you get there. That last segment of the third level almost drove me insane!!! I literally felt like I was going crazy with those rotating arrows. I probably was. I loved and hated it at the same time. It felt psychedelic!
140 was developed by the same designers of Limbo. I sort of had the feeling due to the similar simplicity of the visual design, which I really admire This balances well with the simplicity of sound. 140 is a two-dimensional design comprised of a circle, triangle, square, and rectangle. The developers kept color theory in mind, as different colors or lack of colors went well with the tone of the music. The colors are flat, but chosen in such a way to balance well with the music.
140 is more complex than it appears. The deeper you get into each level, the more rhythmic concentration is required to complete each level.  If you’re musically inclined and have appreciation for minimal dubstep, you’ll probably really enjoy this.
As you progress through the game, so do the rhythmic sounds. They begin with a simple low frequency samples, then get layered with more beats as you encounter different segments of the levels.  Within these segments, there are various obstacles that animate to the beat of the rhythm.  As the beats layer, so do the obstacles. This really kept me locked in.
However, this is also what made it tricky. As I was feeling the sounds, I had to stay focused. I’ll be playing and sometimes I wanna start dancing or nod my head to the beat. There were times when I had briefly memorize a beat or move in a rhythmic manner to overcome obstacles. This is why I think it’s helpful if you’re musically inclined and/or you pay close attention to the sound of music. The slightest wrong movement can throw you off. So it’s important to really listen and observe what the obstacles are doing and where you’re located. Also pay attention to patterns.
Also, as someone who gets distracted easily, I really had to force myself to stay concentrated. I actually think this is a great exercise for anyone who wants to improve their focus.
HOWEVER
Think twice before completely exiting the game in the middle of a level (holding ESC). You will only be able to start from the beginning of the level(s) once you completely escape. So if you’re playing Level 2 and you escape in the middle of Level 2, you will have to start at the beginning of Level 2 once you reopen 140. However, it the levels after you surpass each one (there's only 3 levels).
Luckily, you can continue after your last checkpoint if you didn’t completely escape.
You also cannot pause.
As annoying as that was, it kept me playing and forced me not to give up so easily. This has really sharpened my concentration and I hope they release more levels or some kind of addition.
Let me know how it goes if you guys start playing. It's a fair price too.

If you wanted a game where most enemies can stunlock you to death, oversized hitboxes that don't match animations, an unresponsive dash (or more specifically, iframes that don't instantly activate), and pathetically weak attacks where the beginning enemies take 20+ hits to defeat, this is it.
At least it's stylish, but as far as I can tell, that's all it has going for it. The comical narrator isn't as unique as it thinks. It's just a generic unreliable narrator.
It probably gets better going in since the game is so obviously balanced around the upgrade system, but for at least good hour the gameplay is dull largely because of enemy's obscene health, and ICEY's animations making it impossible to see the enemy animations on the standard enemies. The exclamation point shows on only very few enemies and very few of their attacks, so you'll get hit and stunned by massively damaging attacks, and then the stunlock continues by something off screen. I can only assume combat will only get faster and more hectic, so these are critical flaws.
I'll probably get around to it some more, but so far, the only thing that would drive a player forward would be the narrator, and he isn't as interesting as it's presented, or the combat, and it doesn't feel as responsive or as fluid as you'd expect.
It's not bad by any means but I feel like it's sacrificed some polish for the sake of its aesthetic. If it didn't take itself so seriously and just focused purely on the gameplay, it had the potential to be one of the best 2D action games.
And like others have said the English narrator isn't very good in this role, so probably turn on the Chinese. He mumbles a bit but it's an overall improvement.
Edit - Another complaint, the button prompts don't change to your rebound controls, which will be confusing in fights. And this cant be something extremely difficult to fix, so why hasn't it been addressed yet?
Edit 2 - It's still worth picking up for the massively discounted Steam Link, though.

So, I'm gonna just jump right the ♥♥♥♥ in.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Bastion is a game centered around the adventures of 'The Kid', one of very few people who survived the 'Calamity', a mass genocide, persay, leaving most people a sickly stone statue of whom they once were.
The Kid, who never speaks, nor gives us an official name, heads to the 'Bastion', a small sanctuary in which any survivor is welcomed, in the event of the 'Calamity.' Upon arrival at the Bastion, The Kid sees an elderly man, known to us as 'Rucks'. Now, this beautifully voiced man is the narrator for most of the game, and I argue, someone whom truly makes the game what we all know and love. Logan Cunningham, the voice of Rucks, has made an appearance in another SuperGiant Game that I will be writing a review for shortly.
So, after chatting Rucks up for awhile, they decide they need something known as 'Cores', in laymans terms, they are bits of immense power that they will use to power and upgrade the Bastion. From here, The Kid's journey is mostly centered around finding these Cores and using them to power the Bastion, to further one of two purposes..
So, the Bastion can offer it's survivors a choice. Do they continue to live as they are, happily in the air with one another, or do they give humanity a second chance, reversing the Calamity's effects.
I won't go into great detail involving the plot or my personal choices, as I've much more to cover.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The sound on BFG continues to be excellent and I give great credit for the sound assets.  The game breathes and is really entertaining walking around and taking in the ambient noises, waiting for a pinkie to pop-out.  This is bolstered with some truly amazing sounds, particularly the plasma gun reload; where it  cadences a musical scale that sounds really satisfying. Doom 3 Also has the best Title music I have ever heard also!
The sound design in Doom 3 in general are awe inspiring in my opinion - It really adds to the game and makes it something special.
All in all it is a decent remake;  Its not broken at all (not sarcastic at all!):
Possible issues:
The graphics are better of course which may be good for most people, however, I do think,  SOME of the flooring in the hell levels have issues where some textures are not as good as the original.  Previously, from what I remember, they were customised floors which had gaps in them, made up of blocks, those seem not to have scaled well in this one and there are only simpler floors instead.  All other floors are fine and look similar and nice.
The difficulty also seems VERY easy.  I played hard and it was quite a cake walk.  this goes for the comment above too, where some of the platforming sections(Computer Complex)seem to have been smothered and made so you can run over them.  This also extends to some creatures who have been 'nerfed'.  Take the 'Demon' or 'Pinkie' in Doom 4.  It was a nasty thing in the original which could do real damage if you were not prepared for it.... Here, its weaker(and less of a threat than an imp) I don't know why...
I also believe some 'unimportant' parts of the levels have been scaled down once or twice... One place was the Alpha complex where I felt it was less labyrinthine than my experience years ago... and it may be that I don't remember it well.  I thought it was the case at most twice.

Look, I'm not gonna sugar coat it: Doom 3: BFG Edition is not a good game. Now that we have that out of the way, let's begin.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Released in October of 2012 and working as a sort of "Doom Anthology", Doom 3: BFG Edition was released at a peak moment of worry for fans of id Software's seminal shooter; The last game in the series came out in 2005, with Doom 3: Resurrection of Evil, and Doom 4 (later simply titled DOOM) was extant only in rumors and hearsay, not physical content. Those who have played the original, both on its native PC and the Xbox console will know that it was a remarkably frightening game, with a slower pace, pitch black lighting and enemies that literally jumped out at you, with RoE adding to that. Despite that, BFG Edition feels... Bland. Blase, almost BORING in how it's presented - a simple application of id Tech 5's superior lighting model to the old, almost decrepit halls of the id Tech 4 tech demo. Don't get me wrong, however, I appreciate what this game did for Doom 3, though I feel they went a little too far. But what do I mean by that?
For starters, the opening hour or so of the vanilla Doom 3 campaign is FAR too easy compared to the original. I don't know the full reasoning behind this, but I'm sure it was to make Doom 3, which would strangle players who used ammo supplies too recklessly, a more welcoming game to start. At its core, this makes sense - the majority of people who would buy this game are going to do so on console, where they might not have lightning quick reaction times. Normally, I would't have a problem with this if NOT for the fact that Doom 3, albeit with minor alterations, was released on the Xbox with no changes to the difficulty. In addition, the campaign for RoE is neutered as well, for there is a section of that game where you must traverse a dank, wet sewer system wearing a gasmask using O2 bottles scavanged from your slain enemies. Later on, an entire segment of Hell was carved out of the game, a segment that WAS LEFT UNCHANGED in RoE Xbox, again for perceived difficulty, which I find mind boggling.
But enough about that. In addition to Doom 3 and Doom 3: Resurrection of Evil, BFG Edition includes a new campaign of seven levels titled "The lost Mission", which... Is nothing to write home about. Aside from a new story and new characters, it's nothing special. On top of that, the Xbox Live Arcade versions of Doom and Doom II are included, but even THEY have problems, such as a wonky soundfont for the music and weird audio balancing for the weapon SFX. In closing, Doom 3: BFG Edition is a nice gift from Bethesda, made with the intention to keep Doom alive, but in the end it was pointless, at most forgettable, which wasn't helped by the fact that the Doom modding and multiplayer scene was still alive and well at the time of release.
Doom 3: BFG Edition. An unecessary installment with the intent to revive a franchise that was never dead to begin with. While it's a good launching point for those new to Doom, I personally don't recommend it.

Fran Bow is a game that stuck with me, personally. It was like nothing I had ever played before. Don't get me wrong; I had played adventure games like this before, but from a thematic and general artistic point of view, it is truly a unique title that I cherish and relish playing every Autumn. You'll recognize a lot of tonal elements from fantastical fairy tales and psychological thrillers, but it somehow engineers the game mechanics, plot line, art style, and general sense of intrigue it evokes to create a game that stands out as the sum of its parts.
It contains a generous amount of disturbing gore almost guaranteed to make even the most apathetic among us wince. And yet, at the same time, the gore is not unneccessary and the scares (while admittedly a bit jumpy at times) are never cheap. Instead, the nightmarish dual-reality you are exposed to reveals not only the physically macabre, but lifts a veil on the ethereal and abstract components behind the horror of the human psyche; depression, shock, terror, death, love, hatred, knowledge, etc. The concepts introduced through the course of the game (if you pay close attention and keep an open mind) seem simple and child-like at first glance, but after a while you begin to see that there is something much more enlightening (and, in some respects, sinister) behind the story.
This becomes ever-prevalent about halfway through the game, where a dramatic tonal shift takes place - Ithersta. If you have not experienced the game for yourself, I suggest you play it, if only to reach this part of the adventure that leaves you in a melancholy longing for more. In such a short time, a multiverse of endless mystery and fascination is established, symbolizing the many internal facets of the human condition. I will admit that this game was released at a tumultuous time in my life, and the philosophies that it proposed - the thoughts it provoked - stuck with me, and, if I am to speak candidly, changed my life. That said, you may just think that the only "philosophies" posed through the course of the narrative are nothing more than moral platitudes and generic assertions of a bleeding heart, and that's perfectly fine.
Even without it, you still have a damn good game.

Loved this game, start to finish! As a man born in the 80s I loved many of the references to the cartoons of that era.
However, nostalgia is not the only thing this game has going for it. Nor is the fantastic soundtrack. The battle system itself proved to be surprisingly addictive, to the point where a considerable chunk of my time playing was spent in the Endless battle mode. The battle system reminded me of the likes of Paper Mario, with having only one character and emphasizing tactics over level-grinding, especially if the difficulty option is set to level the enemies to match the player.
You can generally tell if a game's retro-style sprites are a stylistic choice, or a sign of laziness on the part of the developer- the former being graphics like those of Mega Man 9 and 10, which have real effort behind them and would have been considered top-of-the-line during the period of gaming they imitate, while the latter often would be considered ugly even by early NES standards. For Saturday Morning RPG, I'd say it falls quite squarely in the stylistic choice category- I could easily imagine the sprites wouldn't look too out of place on a 16-bit era title. Your mileage may vary on how willing you are to have that merged with the 3D backgrounds, but for me it reminded me of how things worked with some PS1 classics like Star Ocean: Second Story, Breath of Fire III, and Tomba. (Yep, I got some 90s nostalgia out of it too, not just 80s.)
The buyer should be aware this game is short. Its four episodes are written to feel like episodes out of a Saturday Morning cartoon, and their length is set accordingly. The plotlines are very much self-contained, and emphasize nostalgia-related humor over deeper storytelling. I still considered it well worth the small price tag and then some (liked it enough to buy it twice, even- Ouya and PC versions!), but don't go expecting $7 to buy you a Final Fantasy-class epic. I read there's plans for two more episodes in the future, but I've no idea how far in the future.
Overall, Saturday Morning RPG is a surprisingly addictive title, well worth it for anyone with any fondness for the 80s, or who enjoys RPGs like Paper Mario that have unique battle systems that stand up well on their own.

A fun diversion, if nothing else.  Give it a try.

Short review: Buy this game.
Longer review: Buy this game, because it has a lot of elements coming together in the right ways. The gameplay has a classic JRPG feel, but still does its own thing. It's turn based, with timed attacks (and defenses). There's enough complexity to make strategy more than just selecting the same attack every time. You can select several stickers, that give combat buffs (or to your enemies, debuffs), as well as your special attacks in the form of items. These are balanced in terms of speed, power, accuracy, as well as price. One item might do massive damage, but be costly, or take a long time to be used once selected, or maybe not always hit. A big part of the strategy is selecting the best prefight equipment.
The episodes are decent length, about an hour or so, depending on how much you like to explore and do side quests. What I really appreciated was the lack of artificial extension. The game doesn't have you backtrack, or wander around to find where you need to go. Objectives are clear, and you can always tell where you need to go by arrows on screen. It keeps the game moving quickly if you want to rush, but you're also free to explore, talk to characters, and just enjoy the environments.
While it's fun enough as an RPG, the overall atmosphere is the main draw. It lives and breathes nostalgia for the 80s (and early 90s), and anyone who spent their childhood watching Transformers, or playing with GIJoe will have an extra appreciation for it. Though, even if you weren't a kid in the US during the 80s/early 90s, you can still appreciate it.
The nostalgia isn't forced, or bled dry. It's just there, so the game feels like it's of the era, rather than just looking back at it. It's challenging, but not frustrating, and the humor is subtle. In short, the game has charm.
My only complaint would be the lack of length. It doesn't have 100+ hours of gameplay... probably more like 10-20 until you get bored (I clocked in about 16 hours, when counting replaying the episodes, and trying out the arenas). Still, those will be pretty fun 10-20 hours.

This game is amazing. It is a complete recreation of the original binding of isaac, but the new engine allows for more capabilities, more items, more synergies, and actual bullet hells that don't depend on "if, then" calculations to work. The pixelated art style, while it isn't as interesting as the original, still holds its ground.  The gameplay is very smooth, and this game is the ultimate stress test. No other predicament has made my heart pound faster (this is actually true. During a crucial fight, I died at what should have been my winning point. I could literally hear my heart thrashing at the speed of a piston in a lambhourgini engine) than this game. This game, however, still manages to be a fun casual game. If there's one thing I must complain about though, it is the soundtrack. Like the graphics, it holds its ground, but the original soundtrack had emotion, fear, and had a dark feel to it. The music here is very much like ambient metal, mostly because it is. This is fine, because the metal gives the game a more "high octane" feel, but no more than the original. All in all, 10/10, would buy three times over again.

Fran Bow is a really solid point & click adventure game with a slight gimmick. You play a traumatized little girl trying to escape a mental asylum to reunite with her cat. Right off the bat, it hits you with dark themes like murder and child abuse, but: the very storybook-like art and especially Fran's childish/unhinged way of commenting on things add much-needed levity. Fran even takes shadowy demons and scenes of bloody gore in stride, which helps the player deal with them as well, not as frightening but more as absurd things.
The game's gimmick is a bottle of pills you acquire early on in the game. By taking a pill, Fran's perception of the room she's in flips to a different one where she is able to for instance see people's traumas manifested as shadow creatures, or straight up ghosts and other weird things (often extremely bloody), but also sometimes find items and doorways where there were none before. You can flip back to the 'regular' world by using the pills again (which is slightly odd), letting you flip back and forth to make your way.
The game takes many surprising twists and turns and gets far, FAR weirder as time goes on. Not to give too much away, where Fran initially only sees strange and inexplicable things when she takes the pills, pretty soon she'll see them even without the pills, and since the game doesn't strain itself to explain anything, you're left to wonder whether the designers just let the plot go wherever it wanted or if it's actually about Fran's dwindling sanity. Whichever, it really doesn't matter. Fran Bow is a good, challenging adventure game that'll keep you intrigued and entertained all the way through it.

In case you have a Rift VR, Doom3 has a really fancy VR mod which makes this game one of the most interesting VR titles out there which works great with the Rift and the touch controllers. It is easy to setup (next next next ok) and has one of the best settings out there. It even has roomscale support.
Now to consider a few things when it comes to the VR version.
The good
- It has support for a lot of different movement styles: teleport (like in Robo Recall) or moving with the stick (like Lucky's Tale), even in third person if you like. It has also a lot of support for different techniques reducing motion sickness. Great to test out how much VR you can take and which methods work well for you.
- The much hated lamp can now used with one hand, with the weapon in the other. This makes a very different and quite useable setup.
- I'm pretty sure performance won't be an issue
The bad
- The large amount of cutscenes places the view in weird positions. However this is mainly a problem in the beginning.
- There is some overused amount of jumpscare which doesn't work well with the VR and controller scheme.
- The game has in general some pacing issues.
- The graphics are considerably dated when it comes to the textures.
- Generally, the game mechanics aren't really designed with VR in mind, like strafing is a bit difficult and it is a bit hard....
The awesome
- .... but you get to click with your hands on the buttons.
- You get to fight with imps in a game.
- The ingame content is huge and the station is very detailed, resulting in a fun experience.
- Doom1 and Doom2 were the pioneers in introducing immersion to PC gaming and iD software was pushing immersion more and more. We came a long way.
- again, full touch controller and roomscale support.
Other thoughts:
- You get Doom1 and Doom2 as a bonus. I replayed them two years ago and they did age really well mechanically.
- You get Doom3 and the expansion.
- On sale, it is a steal. As a VR product, you get also a hell of a lot of game for your money.

The movement at times feels a little clunky, but overall the graphics, the gameplay, the mechanics, are much improved from previous games. It didn't feel forced at all, it was one of those stories that I wanted to continue the main questline so I could see what was going to happen, the end of the story was not entirely what I was expecting. I had a feeling, but I wasn't totally sure.
There's tons of side quests, which I've been going through now. I don't have any of the DLC and I hope to get it at some point, but as for the base game, there's a lot of quests to do. I like that, because I can continue to explore without getting bored. Some games that are open world are still a little linear, I think that this felt more of a 'choices matter' type game, as all the other Fallout games have been as well.
Overall, I gotta say, this is a great game and I'm very excited to continue to play it and see what the DLC is all about.

Vanilla Cons

There are more things, but I don't want to nitpick too much.
Despite the glaring flaws, I actually enjoy FO4 quite a bit, but again that is thanks to the mods. Granted, I don't think that the vanilla experience is unforgivably terrible, but mods really, REALLY help bolster the experience.
Not a fantastic entry for Fallout, but otherwise an enjoyable experience.

A hilarious setting comprised solely of 80’s nostalgia and references that saturated teenage life at that time. Everything from key guitars to 80’s cartoons and ad campaigns make up the entire world of this RPG. The story is nonsensical and funny, but it’s also a two-sided coin in regards to its audience.
It’s one thing to have a story take place in the 80’s and quite another to have the story entirely constructed out of 80’s Easter eggs. People who never grew up with the “friends don’t let friends do drugs” cartoon ad campaigns, never had to use a floppy disk, never watched “Back to the Future” or know what a scratch and sniff sticker is might get a little lost in the humor. That’s not to say younger audiences couldn’t enjoy it, but most if not all the jokes are intended for those who grew up in the 80’s.
Still the game is fun and solid. There weren’t any bugs, combat was interesting and there was some obvious thought put into its funky visuals. For the price it wasn’t to short on playtime ether, I spent roughly $3.00 on this at a steam sale and several hours later I am still playing it.

They really went crazy with it. I like an RPG that can force me into a bit of cardio for that bit of extra power. The story is simple, and still entertaining. I like all of the, 'I see what you did there,' moments as well. Anyway, the bottom line is t hat this game is a refreshing satire on all of the 80's era cartoons and games, with a little bit of 90's thrown in to boot, and it's well done. Well, i don't know why people say that this is like Age of Empires, nothing to do with it!!!. For me it's like Settlers II (or even Anno) mixed with Popoulus III. Anyway, I loved both games so I'm enjoying so much Northgard.
The micromanagement it's very basic, you build a woodcutter hut and you obtain wood ready to use (no need for a wood processing plant or something like that..) So you don't have chains of resources for creating others, like Anno. If you expected that, don't mind, I've too, but once you see the mechanics of the game you will forget this part.
It's very easy to play and the interface helps a lot, it's very  well thinked.
There are of course things that i don't like so much, like the fact that you have to have specfic places to build a farm, for example, and it's frustrating to see how your people die of hunger and you have a beautiful field empty. Another thing is that makes no sense for me to limit the number of buildings per zone, or at least i see the limit to low. For the tecnical pow, the graphics and animations are very good and even with my modest laptop (i5, 8gb ram, nvidia 940mx) runs decently at full detail. The weather effects are really nice. There is only one music tune, but is pretty :)
I recommend without doubt this title,

So, Northgard?
Northgard is a board game. A board game in video game format. And I don't mean the format of Civ which disguises itself as a board game but is far beyond recognizable as a board game; but a proper board game, realized as a video game. And it's wonderful.
It's good to sit around to play with some mates. A game can take about 1-3 hours. It's still fresh, has had some problems. But the devs are active, and are constantly bugfixing, tweaking, and adding. It's great support.
It's cheap too. It's the sort of game where you can get a lot of fun out of not too much money. You can complete a game in a sitting, there's a few different ways to win, and it's divided into sectors with resources in each. So, a small fun board game.
And when I say board game, I don't mean Monopoly, obviously. I mean Settlers of Cataan or something of the kind.
You can enjoy it even without having played any of those types of games, its video game format makes it much more accessible.
So, I rate it positively. Buy it, play it with your mates. Or solo even.

Street Fighter V is a very polarizing game. You will either love it or hate it. With that said, I think it succeeds where it matters most and that is delivering fun and deep gameplay that (if you are willing to invest time in) will reward your skill and exploration. All the stuff outside the core gameplay may be lackluster or average at best. Still, even as a more casual fighting game player, I find myself coming back to play people online, play friends locally, and practice my skills and strategies in training mode. Yes, the game favors an offensive playstyle. Yes, there is less depth in combos. Yes, characters feel more similar than they have in past Street Fighter entries. However, I do not feel any these things take away from the game's depth. If anything, it adds depth to the use of tactics and strategy which (in my opinion) is most important in fighting games. The game certainly felt incomplete and over priced when it first came out. I don't think that is the case anymore, and, while it follows the unpopular freeium model, it is possible to get almost all the game's content for free.
Overall, I recommend Street Fighter V to players who enjoy competitive fighting games and are not looking to do much more than play against other people. If you are looking for a fighter that offers a lot of single-player content, you probably want to look elsewhere and it shouldn't be difficult to find something you like as there are a ton of great fighters on Steam currently.

Your character's skills can alter what you can find in the game based on what the skills do.  The differences between the different dungeons are as different as night and day.  The random dungeon crawler has taken major leaps in the past few years, and this game has added a new chapter in its evolution.
If you like randomized dungeon crawlers, random spells, being able to choose between spells, different classes, a list of interesting aspects, and an easy to use style of gameplay, then you'll love this game.  If nothing else, you can play with the bodies of your enemies.  Kicking a dead rat down a hallway can be fun, especially if it bit you before you killed it.

As the multiplayer is pretty much dead you'd be paying £10 for the three in game campaigns, and having beaten all three atleast twice (including on nightmare) I can say its worth it.
This entry does a much better job at getting the feel of the marine (and how slow and sluggish he is), the predator (and his overpowering strength & impressive agility) and especially the alien, getting just how nimble and agile these creatures are. Xenomorphs can easily transition between walls and ceilings, harvest humans with facehuggers, pounce unsuspected enemies from the dark and even destroy lights to make your job easier. The alien also has regenerating health, which is something I missed in the other two games (because xenomorphs don't need to feed, they survive on their blood alone).
Though if bug hunting, facehugging and trophy collecting isnt your thing, I recommend Alien: Isolation, as it swaps out the action for horror.

If you like it, then play it, but I started playing again for the first time in ages, and it only just now occurred to me just how effing DULL this game can be. For the first I-don't-know-how-many-hours, be prepared for such exciting locales as "Dimly-Lit Hallway", "Darkly-Lit Science Experiment Room", and my personal favorite, Grim-Looking Room-full of Computer Servers That Serve No Apparent Purpose"! Thrill to the excitement of reading dead people's inter-departmental emails and hunting down corporate PR videos, and then WATCHING THEM!!
And oh yeah there's a lot of demons and zombies and other allegedly creepy stuff going down too, except that none of it actually feels creepy; seriously, for a game that's supposed to be ominous, it seems to have less atmosphere than Mars itself, maybe it's the lack of music, or the fact that every damn NPC looks like the same, one constipated dude; sometimes he's Asian and sometimes he's Black, but he's almost always bald and forgettable. The weapons are all the standard generic stuff we've been used to since the original DOOM; move along, nothing to see here. And I also have to say: enough with the monster closets already! It may work in a more action oriented game (like the originals or the 2016 game), but for a game that's trying so hard to have you take its narrative seriously it just feels contrived for random walls to open up and "oho! there was a monster there in that hidden panic-room which exists for no other apparent purpose than for someone to hide their monster stash!"
Look, I know we're talking about an old game here, and I shouldn't expect it to be BioShock or something, but I don't care which version you play, DOOM 3 has not aged well. But I'm not so sure that it really had that much going for it to begin with aside from the 1. awesome -for its time- graphics, 2. freaky enemy design, and 3. the name DOOM. Taking all this into account, it's not surprising that Rage was a disappointment; ID Software doesn't really make games so much as they design playable demos for their game and graphics engine tech. Granted, some of them do turn out to be great games (DOOM 2016), but all too often it seems like their heart just isn't in it - DOOM 3 is IMO a pretty good example of this, a symptom of a larger problem. Evidence of this engine-first mentality is the fact that if they're not showcasing a new engine, chances are the next game in a franchise will be developed by RavenSoft or some other dev. So to sum it up, DOOM 3 is a symptom of a much more fundamental problem, and should be taken with this in mind.

What can I say about this game other than its fantastic. The version created for steam trumps the iOS version by far, with no additional costs for heroes, premium content or microtransactions, if you're a TD type of person or ever thought you wanted to give it a try, the Steam version of Kingdom Rush is for you.
Let me begin on the first day I was introduced to the flash version of this game I ended up being hooked. It was so easy to get into, gave me hours of entertainment and laughs and even some aggrivation whilst trying to figure out how to complete each level with 3 stars. By the time I had finished the original campaign mode of the 12 levels, I couldn't believe that a game such as this one, with the graphics, gameplay, voice acting, music score and overall enjoyability, was free! I felt like it should've been worth something!
Which is what happened with the iOS version. However... I'm not a fan of purchasing a game only to have a ton of microtransactions needed for the full experience. Premium content wasn't included, no heroes etc. That wasn't a good way to go about it in my books at least. Left much to be desired...
That is why the day it released on steam I had no reservations or hesitation on buying it and diving right back into it. Now it included all the premuim content and all the heroes and has a promise of more to come ontop of that!
The Steam version's gameplay is smooth and enjoyable. I only had one hiccough on an Iron Challenge level with a certain enemy getting stuck on the edge of the map for a few attempts. The issue eventually resolved itself, but Iron Hide has been very good about providing bug fixes to this game in a timely matter so I expect that'll be fixed over soon.
The graphics for this game are fantastic! Each level has its own attention to detail, the NPC's and enemy's movements are smooth and while some might argue the cartoonish animation is childish and unappealing, I beg to differ! I absolutely love it!
The sound in this game is amazing! The music in this game is simply stellar. It brings the right amount of emotion to each level. When I hear the boss music que up, I always felt my pulse quicken and the sense of urgency rise as if I needed to pump up my offense and defense and quickly! Any game thats able to do that with a simple musical score is worth your time to look at. Not to mention the voice acting! I nearly died the first day I upgraded my Dwarven artillery to the Big Bertha, added a rocket only to hear "Yippie Kai-yay mother *BEEP"! I remember going out of my way to upgrade my dwarven towers just to be able to hear that one line over and over. And still to this day I get a giggle out of it.
I just finished this game 100% now on all levels and I couldn't be happier with my purchase. I had hours, hours of enjoyment! And I will definitely play it again and again, not just because I want to see how I could complete each level with different strategies, but because it is simply fun!
So granted there are some bugs with the game so far, the purchase price of 10 bucks is so worth it! I mean, there are so many people who are willing to throw 50 bucks or more out the window for games that are absolute garbage and here you have the chance to get a great game with high replay value for 10 bucks! It has great graphics, great music, great acting... you can't get much better than that!

Left 4 Dead is a 4-player co-op survival FPS set in a world full of infected that crave your flesh.
You play as either Zoey, Bill, Francis, or Louis (depending on who you choose to play as) and with your friends (online) or
NPCs (if being played offline) along with you on your side, plowing through hordes of the infected whilst trying to reach the safehouse. The final level of each chapter has you escaping in a vehicle of some sort. Each chapter usually contains 4 levels. The game contains 9 chapters.
This is how the main game mode is played.
But besides killing common, there exist other dreaded creatures....
The special infected! Unlike the common infected, these guys have their own unique abilities.
The Smoker, a tall slender infected with a long tongue that's ready to grab you!
The Boomer, a bloated ball of puss, ready to puke on you! Which attracts a horde of infected, so don't get too close!
The Hunter, a hooded covert that pounces and mercilessly claws through your flesh! You'll know when he's near, once you hear his dreaded growl.
The Witch, a sobbing woman that gets enraged when you get to close! Keep your distance, or else she'll shear you into pieces!
And the worst of all.... The Tank!
A giant mass of muscle and speed, ready to smack you to Timbuk2! Killing him usually requires a group effort!
But besides killing infected until you reach the safehouse, other fun modes exist!

Other game modes, such as Infected, has you either play on a team of survivors or special infected, all being controlled by live players, duking it out until one team has been completely wiped out.
Survival mode is a horde mode where you and others fight through countless waves of infected, the goal is to survive as long as you possibly can! This is an online game mode as well, but it's possible to play this one offline.
Even though this game was released 6 1/2 years ago, it holds up extremely well! This is a title that you shouldn't pass up on!

Bethesda markets Rogue Warrior as a “character-driven first person shooter”, which is stretching the definition of character slightly. The game takes place in 1986, where North Koreans and Russians are doing sinister weapons research. This calls for our hero called♥♥♥♥♥♥ who is ready to stop them, armed with an enormous amount of lovely one-liners like “Goddamn♥♥♥♥♥♥breath commie ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s”. It’s like poetry.
This game is only slightly better than the very worst a game can be. The music sounds like it’s from a free music library, but probably isn’t, while the graphics and audio also only meet the quality standard of free template assets. You know you’re in trouble when something as simple as “walking forward” feels bad.
To the game’s credit, it only took me 109 minutes to complete. I was in the mood to play something that was total♥♥♥♥♥♥ and it certainly delivered exactly what I was hoping for. If you’re going to make a garbage game, this is the level you should aspire to hit at a minimum. I wasn’t bored by it, and it had the decency to end early. It also didn’t feel like some crap thrown together at random.
They tried to make something coherent here, something that resembled a real game. But they didn’t have the means, talent or maybe even the will to make that happen. There’s a reason this game is consistently brought up as a legendary piece of crap 7 years after it came out, while thousands of other bad games are forgotten. It’s hard to put my finger on just what makes this memorable, but it’s the “right” kind of bad to leave an impression, which many mediocre games don’t. Maybe it’s simply the one-liners.

There have been a lot of nostalgia-related computer games lately, but this is one of the ones that speaks to me most.  It has a lot of references to 80s shows I watched like GI Joe and He-Man.  Plus it has nods to other things I did back then, like putting stickers on Trapper Keepers, and chewing Fruit Stripe gum.  On the downside, I didn't love the graphics.  The low-res sprites are a reference to older video games, and I appreciate that.  However, the characters are too detailed to realistically be called "8-bit", so they didn't actually push my nostalgia buttons.  Instead, they just look blocky.  Different characters and backgrounds have different levels of detail, making characters look out of place.  Again, the graphics are intenionally bad - it's not like the programmers just got lazy.  It's just I would have preferred they presented the 8-bit references in a different way.  I've played enough modern games with 8-bit graphics, and I think this particular game would have worked better using an art style that emulates 80s cartoons rather than 80s video games.  But that's just my opinion.
Getting past the art, the gameplay is just okay.  It's your basic turn-based RPG.  Some of your special moves require minigame-like button presses to do more damage, but if you don't like that sort of thing, you can always favor the more straightforward moves when customizing your character.  It's fun, but if you play a lot of RPGs, it's nothing you haven't seen before.  The bottom line is that you're playing this for all the 80s references.  If that doesn't describe your childhood, you probably won't get much out of this game.

If you're looking to get into fighting games, Street Fighter V is arguably the best game to pick up and learn.
Street Fighter V has many simple mechanics, allowing for newer players to be able to compete without being completely bulldozed by more experienced players. This can also harm the game, seeing as it allows less skillful players to come out as the victor in many matches, even at high level play. Core-A-Gaming offers an amazing analysis as to what this can mean for the game and it's health here:
Street Fighter V does offer some exhilarating gameplay, with many exciting moments coming from reads, reactions, and various combo strings. There's a stigma in fighting games saying that they aren't much fun until you have memorized long strings of combos, but that doesn't have to be the deal in this installment of the Street Fighter series. There are some easier imput characters like Zangief and Ed to allow newer players to enjoy the game without having to constantly perform the numerous motions required to pull of a long combo. You can even perform guranteed strings of damage without having to consistanly perform "1-frame-links" or "plinking" making regular controllers competetively viable.
There may be some rude individuals sprinkled here and there amoungst the Street Fighter V community, but that's a given with any online community nowadays. There are many places for new and experienced players to enjoy and discuss the game, my main recommendation being the
. They offer lots of insight on gameplay, new techniques for various characters, jokes, and fanart. There are also many insightful guides all throughout Youtube for every character.
While this game is, in my opinion, a great installment in the Street Fighter franchise, it does come with its own downsides. Capcom makes many mistakes when it comes to the balance to this game. For example, the fairly recent nerf to DPs (i.e.: Cammy's Cannon Spike, Ryu/Akuma/Ken's Shoryuken, etc.) made it so they no longer have initial invinsibility frames if you don't spend a EX meter on it. This came because newer players were having trouble countering this, thus Capcom nerfed it rather than have these players learn and adapt. The game also offers few defensive options, allowing for more aggressive "button-mashers" to win more games due to players being unable to defensively maneuver and weave through these attacks with V-reversals or specials. Street Fighter V can also drive away more competitive players. The lessened skill gap between top players and lower skill players takes away from the skill portion from the game and replaces it with some luck, giving some unfair advantages.
But all in all, I believe that Street Fighter V is an amazing game worth picking up if you are new to playing fighting games. It looks beautiful, plays well, and can open a gate for new players into the always improving FGC.

The worst problem is the transition (wall climbing) which used to be toggleable (i.e. press down a key to climb smoothly over the walls and ceilings, release it to drop). Here you have either to use the auto-transition, which means that once you get near a wall you will start climbing automatically, even if you wouldn't want to (easy to get disoriented and killed if this happens in a bad situation). Another option is to press mouse3 once for each transition, which in fact is really clumsy and can accidentally make you drop.
I also hate the fact that Alien view modes have been removed. The darkvision was really useful.
Another thing I didn't like was the Predator which also has somewhat clumsy controls and a really, really ugly HUD compared to the previous titles. Where in AvP 1 and 2 you instantly knew you were playing a Predator (the sounds, HUD etc. were loyal to the movies), here it just looks like a generic FPS.
Recommended if you want to play the Marine. Alien and Predator are much more interesting in the older AvP games.

Aight so last night my friend asked me to write a review for this game because of the steam link deal. Last night i was also drained and exhausted so i just put "i just didn't like it...". I woke up and it said "i just dont like you" and there was a "1 out of 16 people found this helpful". But I didnt mind since that friend i mentioned happens to be my roommate and they told me to write what i told him so it would actually be helpful. So here we go.
First of all I would like to say that I do not like this game.
Now that we've covered that and we're aware that I have a bias we can continue into why:
1. I just really dont like the narration. I realize that this game was ported over and i can't expect it to be perfect but i just really didn't like this guy's voice. To quote Borderlands 2 "Everytime he speaks I feel my brain cells committing suicide 1 by 1."
2. This game tried to balance certain things that I enjoy in games. High speed combat and "exploration" (the term im gonna use for finding the hidden♥♥♥♥♥♥i put it in quotes because my friend doesnt consider this exploration and therefore i must pander to him). For me it succeeds at neither.
I think i read in someone else's review before i bought this game "Within the first 10 minutes youll find one broken move or another that youll use for the rest of your time playing" and its true. Unless you really love watching those combo points rise then you might switch it up but if thats not your thing than this game might not be for you. I was like that and every fight felt tedious almost. The boss fights were a fresh change of pace and they weren't overwhelmingly difficult but their movesets swapped between "easy predictable dodge" and "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t". Thats probably my bias seeping through but hey thats what reviews are all about.
As for the exploration I begin with a note on what exploration SHOULD feel like. You see something, its off somehow or maybe its juuuuuuuuust right while everything else is slightly off. It piques your curiosity, it makes you wonder. Eventually you stray from whatever path you were on to go take a look. And off you go on your adventure. Ya know what exploration SHOULDNT feel like? A narrator telling you "DONT GO THAT WAY" and hoping his irritating voice drives you to disobey. Thats not all of the hidden things in the game but its a damn big chunk of em. Overall the "other paths" are eitherr blatantly obvious when you see them or dont feel genuine to the setting of the game.
3. i just dont like it.... Its not the graphics or anything. I played the game and i got a few of the endings and i just didnt really like it. I was fighting the big bad when i looked at the time played thing and saw 2 hours on there. I thought about it and decided i really didnt like the game so i returned it. And now here we are.
Overall, if you want a steam link for $8.69 plus shipping with a free game that you may or may not play, go for it.

I've now finished* the game, and I wanted to change my review from a negative to a positive one as it's since grown on me a bit. As of writing this, I've put 4.3 hours into ICEY. I have to iterate here that I still would NOT recommend buying this unless it's on discount or unless you get the bundle where it comes with a $1 Steam Link, like I did.
Bottom line: I had some fun with ICEY, but there are some serious problems with how this game is put together.
I need to talk about the big American/European elephant in the room: The narrator. This game was originally released in China, and the English narrator that we get detracts from the experience so much that if there was no way to turn him off I would not recommend this game to anybody. His acting ability is non-existant and it doesn't sound like he's putting any effort into his lines. It sounds like he's reading everything off the script for the first time, and a character that sounds like his just doesn't belong in the world that's trying to be set up here.
The dialogue is also pretty bland as well, with the narrator regularly saying "ICEY..." followed by an action, as if it adds something important to the game. It is literal first-grade level writing and I'm disappointed that other reviewers seem to think this is a good way to write a character like his into the game, although I admit part of the problems I have with dialogue might be due to problems with translating the game from Chinese to English.
The best part about ICEY is the gameplay, which is combo-driven combat, although comboes don't seem to be very important. There's nothing too innovative about it but it feels fun when you start getting into sequences of dodging things, looking around for the next option, and then executing. You can dodge attacks to quickly kill enemies and get heals, there are some move combos you can buy from a store, the enemy variety is different enough to be consistently interesting to fight, all in all it's a very "alright" experience. It'll get stale after a while but the game doesn't seem too long to begin with so it's a non-issue.
*Full disclosure: I don't actually know anything about how the game ends since I decided to play on hard mode. Hard mode just makes you take more damage from attacks, and the already difficult on normal-mode final boss becomes straight up impossible on hard unless I decide to grind for more health to beat him, which honestly sounds really boring to me and I'd rather just not bother at that point. There are multiple endings but I know nothing about them.
The story and the in-game world really isn't good at all. It's okay if you liked the story, I'm not attacking your opinion, but you have to know it's just a very simple story with basically nothing happening under the surface, and to me, that's boring. It's very shallow stuff without much to discover at all. The world is in chaos, you're a robot in a simulation, you fight other robots while a narrator guides you along a path, and there's a bad guy at the end. Maybe there's a twist at the end of something, but it doesn't really make up for how bland the story's been up until that point.
The game tries to make the story interesting by forcing a "meta" 4th wall-breaking theme. This "meta" theme has been done to death by other games (Metal Gear Solid, No More Heroes, Undertale, and Bravely Default to name a few) but the difference here and with those examples is that they're cleverly written and implemented so they actually work and feel appropriet. Here it just feels clumsy and forced, as if it was meant to be a substitute for an interesting story or interesting characters.
I also found myself getting disproportionately upset over very small things in the game that bothered me. For example, paralax scrolling in the backgrounds, or rather lack thereof. There are a few points where there's perspective in the background, like one part where you come across a road that goes off into the distance, but if you walk to the side and back...it doesn't paralax, or scroll in seperate parts like an environment in real life, at all. But then there are lots of places where trees in the background have nice paralax scrolling. It's really jarring when paralax scrolling just suddenly stops and it sort of ruins the entire point of trying to make the environment look presentable in the first place.
Even with all this, the game isn't awful. If it looks like something you'd enjoy, I say go for it. It looks fine, controls fine, music is actually pretty good for an indie game. If you like animu you might enjoy it more than the average dude. It's been a strange experience to say the least.

I've played a lot of point & click games in my time. Some good, some bad and many unmemorable. This game falls firmly into the first catagory.
In this story you play Fran Bow, an eleven year old girl who's family have been murdered in mysterious circumstances. Due to the trauma Fran has been taken into an asylum, which is where you start exploring a quite extraordinary world.
The game art is gorgeous and at times disturbing and creates the perfect atmosphere for the tale to unfold. The mechanics are simple to understand but manage to be, at times, challenging as the scenes change from reality to reality. I particularly liked that about this game, whether it be taking your medicine or changing the season, it left much more to uncover than the initial number of scenes suggest.
The one downside, for me at least, was that it was a real bugger to get working and keep working. I run Windows 10 and also have Norton antivirus. I'm not sure if it was this combination but the game wouldn't launch from Steam initially and Norton detected the game as a virus. In order to get it to work I had to uninstall and reinstall the game after adding an exception in Norton and then run the .exe file in Win 7 compatability mode as the Administrator - all quite a faff, but ultimately worth it. As an additional note, I had to repeat the above steps after rebooting.
Pros
Original concepts
Excellent Story
Beautiful artwork
Creepy enough to be interesting
Logical puzzles
Cons
Technical issues running it
A tad too short
Fran was way too nice for an eleven year old!
Overall a great indie game - 7/10

Doom 3: BFG Edition is a collection with Doom 1 & 2, along with a Remaster of Doom 3. Doom 1 & 2 are the old school shooters that surprised people back then on how violent it was. Both games don't really have a story. All you do in Doom 1 & 2 is shoot Demons, find secrets, complete the level, and repeat. It might sound repetitive, but they're fun to play (even though it's a bit dated.).
Doom 3: BFG Edition is what I'm mostly going to focus on for this review. Since Doom 3 was Remastered,
Doom 3 Remastered doesn't really have a story. Hell has broke loose on Mars, and it's your job to stop it. There are some moments in the game that explains the story some more, but that's mostly it.
The Gameplay has changed. Instead of Survival, it's now more focused on Action.
You remember in the original, the game was super dark? You remember in the original you can only hold your flashlight and guns separate? You remember the cool light effects in the original? Those were changed. The game is more brighter, you now have a shoulder-light (which means you can hold your gun and turn on the flashlight at the same time), and the light effects when shooting the guns are gone (that includes The Plasma Gun).
The Gunplay in Doom 3 Remaster, while it shows its age, is decent. Controls are really responsive, and aiming with a mouse feels great. The Gunplay is kind of like Doom 1 & 2, but it's a bit slower. When you first start the game, it isn't all that intense, but later on things start to pick up and the game feels a lot more like Doom. In the game, you have the Pistol, Shotgun, Chain Gun, Machine Gun, Plasma Gun, and much more. The enemies you face are the same enemies you face in Doom 1 & 2. Some do attack kind of differently, but that's mostly it. Heck, there is even some new enemies that are fun and interesting to fight.
You will get hit, so you better find armor and health so you don't die easily. Every level has Medkits, Healing Stations (You can only use the Healing Station gives you 10 health every time you interact with it, but you can only heal 10 times on a single Healing Station.), Armor Shards, Ammo, and much more. The healing and armor mechanics are the same, but feel different at the same time.
The Remaster looks cleaner than the original. While some icons are still blurry, the look of the game has improved. Even the game runs very smooth.
The game does have some issues that does make the collection less enjoyable:
-Doom 1 & 2 are censored. The Red + on the Medkits were replaced with a Red and White Pill, and the Secret Level (
) was strongly censored in Doom 2. They removed
.
-Since Doom 3 Remastered is brighter and you have a Shoulder-Light, it does make the game less scary.
-Some guns feel more weaker than they should (Like the Shotgun. Sometimes it takes 4 shots to kill an Imp.)
-The Storage Mechanic. You might disagree, but finding the Code for a Storage Unit is very tedious usually.
-Doom 1, 2, and 3 aren't moddable. While this doesn't effect me at all, it might turn some people off.
-Doom 3 doesn't have any Subtitles.
Over and all, Doom 3: BFG Edition is a good collection. Even though it has issues, Doom 3 Remastered is a really fun FPS. Doom 1 & 2, while censored, are great classics.

Now this was a treat!
Truly impressive considering the small amount of people involved with the creation of this, well I do not know really, fairytale-game-ish? It kind of had everything, it is disturbing, cozy, chill, intriguing and some serious depth to the writing. The graphics may not be on the level of AAA-games, but the writing sure is. Although the arts and animations got their unique style.
It is easy to see that a lot of effort went into this one, especially considering it is mostly a creation of two people, with some backup.
The story and writing is immensely deep, it delivers in so many ways. As a point-and-click you really want to explore it to get the full epicness of the story. The characters are alive, in the sense that you both know them and do not know them. This is more like reading a book or hearing a (somewhat disturbing) fairytale, although expressed in the medium of a game. And it all comes with a truckload of references and clever nods to more stuff than I recognized.
There are some (skipable) mini-games that comes with it, that act as a contrast from the regular game, in the sense that they are more like a challenge or game where you can fail. It feels like a flashback to the time where point-and-click had their prime time, so if you are a fan of those, you are in for a treat.
The only thing that really could make this better than it is, would be voice acting for the characters. But the text works, as it is quite a lot of it. The music is atmospheric and sound effects are both hilarious and sometimes disturbing.
If you have a fancy for the calm nature of point-and-click, where challenge is not really a thing but the gaming experience relies more on cleverness and creative thinking, then this is for you. In short it is kind of a mixture of Alice in wonderland, The neverending story, a whole shelf of horror movies and a course in theoretical physics.
Epic, to say the least!

Fantastic game! I play it since the early days from time to time and saw it being an intriguing construction site with great ideas, a laggy b*tch with cool new things, and now finally a polished product.
If you're coming from terraria like me with my 400+ hours, you'll notice that you have to adjust
heavily.
Combat feels very different. There is more weight behind everything. you can't change direction while in mid air,  many attacks have to be charged up or take a bit to execute, every attack uses energy, which regenerates but is quite limiting in long fights.
Crafting and building feels okay. It feels like you spend more time trying to navigate the menus while juggling with many different items than actually playing, but you get used to it.
The world is fantastic! So many animated objects! So much detail! Really feels alive, especially in the outpost and generated villages. Speaking of which, there are wonderfully designed auto generated villages, outposts, camps, caverns, temples and much more. And they all look wonderful!
And the music! It is so god damn good. Calming, emotional, sets the tone for the whole game.
In conclusion, you don't get a terraria-clone. Instead of a blank canvas for you to fill with life focused on fantastic combat, you get a beautiful, living world to explore and experience.
