After many hours, a great number of ranked matches and late night lobbies, and a couple local tournaments, I can finally say confidently that I do not recommend this game.
The singleplayer content is barebones and not at all worth playing. This is fine in a competitive fighting game, since the focus is more on competitive multiplayer. If you're not interested in that, take a hard pass on Street Fighter V and play a fighting game with worthwhile singleplayer content. Guilty Gear Xrd is a good one.
Mechanically, the game isn't bad at all. It's fairly simple, with a modest amount of easy to understand mechanics that lead to interesting gameplay. It's also popular, so you can always find people online to play with. It's not a difficult game to pick up, and it's more accessible and rewarding than most other fighting games. That said, I still have a few problems with the gameplay.
Namely:
* Defensive options are awful. This is why high level play is just watching people do meaty setups on eachother. It's also why throw loops are as prevalent as they are.
* Questionable design decisions, such as removing frame 1 invuln from all meterless DPs. This really skews the risk/reward of those moves, which is an odd choice from a game franchise that's so rooted in pure and simple fighting game fundamentals.
* Timing is sort of strange. It's a game with 3 frame normals, so things like blockstrings and meaty attacks need to be pretty airtight. If they're not (and it's hard for them to be with any sort of network stutter in the mix) then mashing light buttons will get you out of a lot of situations. This should be a bad habit, but it's rewarding in this game for some reason.
* The input delay/netcode makes it feel pretty unresponsive. If you're coming from other fighting games, expect to get hit by many fullscreen moves (Balrog's rush punches, Cammy's EX spiral arrow, Ken's EX tatsu) if you don't block preemptively.
In terms of everything aside from the gameplay, it's an inexcusable travesty. The netcode is terrible, and even on wired connections with people in my own hometown it feels jerky and frustrating. Other fighting games add input delay, or seem to run the game in slow motion. SFV just teleports you from one connected attack to the next so you can watch yourself die in a jerky mess of unreactable attacks. The netcode also seems to send all the lag to the person with better internet. I remember having a really good night on ranked with seemingly stable connections and slow witted opponents, only to later realize I had been torrenting and my sister had been watching Netflix, presumably sending all the lag to my opponents.
Unlocking characters, costumes, colors, and stages requires either making microtransactions with real world money, or spending ingame currency, which is extremely limited and for the most part non-renewable. You get 50 fight money for a win in a ranked match, zero for a loss. Characters cost 100,000 fight money each. You do the math. All the good cosmetics in this game are behind paywalls that you'd expect to see in free to play games. But it's a full price triple-A title, and the character season passes are also inexcusably expensive.
Capcom has been pretty terrible with supporting this game as well. Patches are frequently delayed by weeks if not months, and it's missing many quality of life changes that should have been included at time of release (eg. saving battle lounge settings when the game closes, or being able to skip the awful tutorial on a fresh install). They also straight up lied about a Linux release. That was supposed to happen concurrent with the Windows release, but there has been no word from Capcom on that front.
I could go on. There's been a very long train of disappointments with this game, and you shouldn't hop on it. Maybe they'll release Super Street Fighter V as the rumors say, and then I'll give this review another revision, but I don't see things changing for the better. The game is still going to be expensive, laggy, and unsatisfying. But it's got a lot of players, so it's got that going for it.
Crossplay is very nice though. I wish more fighting games had that.

I think I must've put over 200 hours into this game before it was released on steam.
The gameplay is very smooth and has a sensible learning curve which also introduces more challenges and strategy based gameplay around the 4th or 5th level. There are only 4 towers but this keeps you thinking about which towers to place, most enemies have their weaknesses and strengths. The 4 different towers can all be upgraded to different towers, you have to choose very carefully.
Your hero, soldiers and reinforcements are very stupid, they are short-sighted and would rather hit enemies with a bow and get beaten to death rather than stay away and shoot skin piercing arrows that can easily finish them off. I do not like this and think you should have more control over your heroes, soldiers and reinforcements.
The graphics are good, they are enjoyable, cartoony but simple at the same time. This means that you can play this game on something like a netbook. I don't really care about good graphics, I think high resolution and high framerate is good enough for me.
Unlike on the iPad, there are no ingame purchases available which I personally think is a good thing. You unlock heroes in by progressing through the game, the traditional way of playing.
On some levels you can repair buildings to access the ability to train warriors or you can break ice that is blocking a friendly sasquatch from fighting for you. You can also click on sheep several times for them to explode into a bloody mess. I like that. Infact there is even an achievement for making sheep explode into a bloody mess. I really like that.
If you beat a level succesfully, you will get 3 stars. If you loose a few lives, you get 2 stars. If you had a hard time completing it and lost a load of lives you only get 1 star. You can spend these stars to get bonuses for your towers or special abilities so you often find yourself visiting old levels trying to get stars to complete a level you're stuck on.
Great game, definitely worth $9.99. I'd give this 9/10.

SPOILERSS:
as the summarry states, the game features an unrealiable narrator narrating everything you do, stanley parable style (ex. Icey went to the left. Then they went to the right. Then they did this. Nevermind, Icey didnt listen, also Icey is DUMB FOR NOT LISTENING). But here is the deal, you can buy the Stanley Parable or the Beginners Guide right now. And you should. This game's unreliable narrator feels like a cheaper and less interesting version of the stanley parable narrator, and the consequences for not following the narrator are usually quite underwhelming. There was an interesting easter egg but the 'comedy'/social commentary just wasn't coherent enough to be entertaining or intriguing and didn't really make me want to play more to find out more easter eggs. So the game's story is kind of a swing and a miss. A respectable effort I wanted to like, but sadly poor execution.
As for the combat, it's ok. Its got some very evident flaws mainly with how the attack are designed and with what the game wants you to do. The game features dodging, quick attacks, heavy attacks, and a stamina bar. Soudns like a souls-like game mixed with a 2d fighter right? No. You see the game has systems in place that reward the player for staying away from strong enemies and instead focusing on killing smaller enemies. If you focus on a large enemy, its easy to get combod by whatever strong enemies are near you and your smaller enemies hanging around using ranged attacks. However, most larger enemies have a short range and smaller ones are often (not always, especially during the first stages) long range. You get health for performing finishers on enemies and you are invincible while doing a finisher, finishers are the easiest attack to land in the game as you can just stand near a weakend enemy and press one button, and finishers dispense these "damage tokens" or something which allow you to instantly do a screenwide attack that does good damage and renders you invincible for the duration. So the actual rewards for killing enemies clashes with the means you are given for dealing with them

After far too much time on steam and more than double my current hours on the normal flash version, I think I can finally come to a conclusion about RotMG.
I've seen it all. Since Amulets of Resurection were around to the dark days of Kabam. And finally, where we are now. The advent of DECA.
First, I'll talk about the game itself. The gameplay is fun and a ruch. Early game you roam around figuring out the mechanics and what classes you like best and trying to reach level 20. Once you can consistently do that and start earning enough to get some nice gear, you'll be done with your "noob phase" and enter the "midgame" Now, Permadeath starts to go from a small setback to a looming threat. The fear of death is always there, and once it hits, especially late game, it SUCKS. One con I have is the difficulty to rebuild, especially mid-game when you're trying to max your stats. Mid game is the biggest hurdle. You know the game, you get it, but you keep getting set back by deaths and wasting time and precious stat boosting potions. But as long as you save up enough and gain enough, you'll be able to build a good character. You'll have to play safe, as dying will ruin everything you've tried to build up, but once you've maxed a character on most of your stats and can build up a second (which you'll annoyingly have to play to get a second character slot) you'll be able to safely be secure in case you die. This is the late game. Once you do well enough in late game to stock up more and more stat potions (which also are currency! Realm has a functional and interesting economy), you start to hit a bit of a boredom block. You'll find most content becomes easy, and the more exciting content is few and far between. However, it'll take ages for this to happen. But as long as DECA is here, they'll hopefully be adding much more exciting content (such as what they're adding now).
Now, the current state of the game. Now, many reviews i've seen bash Kabam, the former game owners, for lack of updates and leaving RotMG to die. Which is true. They did that. But friends, we're in a new era now, the era of DECA, who overthrew Kabam as devs of Realm. As of now (April 2017) DECA has been adding frequent updates, many cosmetic, however 3 new dungeons have been added since their takeover, and 4 more are on the way. Hopefully DECA stays consistent with this, and it seems so so far. They even communicate with players on the game's subreddit (/r/RotMG).
Overall, i'm going to now go through a quick pro-con list which should serve as a nice informative TL;DR.
PROS:
-Fun, exciting gameplay that keeps you on your toes-
-Good rougelike feel
-Diverse classes
-Diverse dungeons
-Exciting loot
-Good progression system
-Good devs
-Spicy memes(?)
CONS:
-Hard to bounce back after deaths mid-late game
-Loot system favors damage over use to everyone (RIP Priest)
-Pets make things easy
-Bosses too easy in large groups
-Boring late-game: essentially just hoard loot
-Some items feel pointless (ray katana, leaf bow, etc.)

Truly impressive considering the small amount of people involved with the creation of this, well I do not know really, fairytale-game-ish? It kind of had everything, it is disturbing, cozy, chill, intriguing and some serious depth to the writing. The graphics may not be on the level of AAA-games, but the writing sure is. Although the arts and animations got their unique style.
It is easy to see that a lot of effort went into this one, especially considering it is mostly a creation of two people, with some backup.
The story and writing is immensely deep, it delivers in so many ways. As a point-and-click you really want to explore it to get the full epicness of the story. The characters are alive, in the sense that you both know them and do not know them. This is more like reading a book or hearing a (somewhat disturbing) fairytale, although expressed in the medium of a game. And it all comes with a truckload of references and clever nods to more stuff than I recognized.
There are some (skipable) mini-games that comes with it, that act as a contrast from the regular game, in the sense that they are more like a challenge or game where you can fail. It feels like a flashback to the time where point-and-click had their prime time, so if you are a fan of those, you are in for a treat.
The only thing that really could make this better than it is, would be voice acting for the characters. But the text works, as it is quite a lot of it. The music is atmospheric and sound effects are both hilarious and sometimes disturbing.
If you have a fancy for the calm nature of point-and-click, where challenge is not really a thing but the gaming experience relies more on cleverness and creative thinking, then this is for you. In short it is kind of a mixture of Alice in wonderland, The neverending story, a whole shelf of horror movies and a course in theoretical physics.
Epic, to say the least!

Kingdom Rush is a flash-style tower defense game that has been around for a while on sites such as
,
, or
. While it has high quality for a browser game, I think it should have stayed there.
Plot 5/10
You are a nameless general that is saving a kingdom from eeeeeviiil. It's not that bad, but not good, either. The purpose is served well enough. Won't rag on this.
Sound 9/10
The sounds are terrific, and fit everything very well. They also add to the game's visual style. The voices probably steal the show on this game, though. They're corny, over-acted sometimes, but always funny, distinct, and fun. KR also has comedic references to other media including Portal, Half-Life, Star Wars, Die Hard, the Bible, and many others. The sound is KR's pride with the exception of the music. While entertaining, there's about 3 tracks that last 30s long and are set to loop. It just could have been a bit better.
Graphics 10/10
The graphics too are wonderful, colorful, and stylish. Visually the game isn't too flashy, which is good because it clears up visual clutter. With so many things moving on screen at once, the visuals organize everything to give the player what they need to see. Enemies are fun and recognizable. KR's visuals are spot-on. Bull's-eye.
Gameplay 10/10
With the barrage of tower defense games out there, it's easy to get weary of the grind. KR however, brings much, much needed personality and freshness that this crowded genre so direly needed. You place towers that are immune to enemies, and auto-attack the enemies. Placing a barracks trains 3 infantry to stop up to 3 passing enemies allowing your damage towers to wittle them down. The infantry can die, though, and have a respawn time. Some enemies have armor and are weak to magic, while others have magic resistance and low armor. Towers can be upgraded for more damage, alternate attack styles, and different personalities from the crew. It all works wonderfully and the game gets REALLY challenging fast. It works so well, KR is a high standard on how tower defense games should be made. It's that good.
The Verdict
"Everything's so good, so why do you not recommend it?" Good question: the only con is the game is waaaay too short. Once you get half-decent at it, you will BLAST your way through the campaign (and most side missions) in about an hour. The game has high quality, but is far, far too short for recommending at $9.99. If it had an acceptable length, it'd be 10/10 but KR's final score is 7/10. It's a great game that you can beat in one afternoon. Just go to the above listed sites and play it for free. Or if you find that it's on sale for $5, you can go for it.

For a point-and-click game, this one is as cute as it's dark and gloomy, and I really, really liked it.
*Very cool artwork, especially the black/white scenes with details in red.
*The music is "meh", but it doesn't really bother.
*Interesting story, even though the "plot twist" was predictable from the second minute in the game and somewhat cliché.
*The story (except said plot twist) may give way to different interpretations, and I found it to be deeper -and darker- than it seems at first glance.
*There is a remarkable portrayal of certain aspects of mental illness and conditions, without being "pamphlet-y" or "on the nose".
*Most of the "puzzles" are rather logical, almost no "click everything until something works" (almost).
*Most of the "puzzles" are not really puzzles, but inventory based actions, not my favorite.
*There was a bit of the classic backtracking to 3 rooms behind for that one item you need now three rooms ahead, but it only felt draggy toward the end.
If you're into the point-and-click genre and enjoy dark stories, go for it.

Saturday Morning RPG is a nostalgia based RPG with turn based battles that use timing and button mashing attacks. It is a love letter to 80s cartoons, full of nostalgia.
It feels incredibly unique for a RPG with a style all its own. You get a trapper keeper that you can put stickers on it for buffs. Well a chance at buffs. You can put 5 stickers on the trapper keeper, but when a battle starts, you have a certain amount of time to scratch the stickers for buffs in battle. The battles are incredibly simple, yet take far too long. You have powers, none of which feels powerful. Each power has a limited amount of uses per battle, but it replenishes after each battle. The battle has a timeline. Depending on what attack you're going to use determines where you are on the timeline. Certain attacks are quicker, such as using the pencil put you first. When a battle starts, the enemy always goes first. No matter how many times the game bluntly tells you 'sneak attack,' they'll always attack first. It feels like a glitch. Most abilities have button timings to do more damage.
Because your abilities and attacks do little damage, you have the ability to 'charge your battery' which will become a damage multiplier for your next ability or attack. You can keep charging until its 9.9x. You have a variety of ways to charge the battery, either by spamming a button to charge it, being accurate on a slide bar or just picking a default 2.8x. I got tired of button mashing, so I just always selected the default 2.8x.
You can get more abilities by finding them or purchasing them in vending machines. You have to do something with the gold you collect. Like the stickers, you can only have 5 abilities equipped at once, but that's enough. I made it through the entire game without buying an extra ability. I would visit the vending machines, see everything laid out and there wouldn't be any descriptions. Sure I could buy the abilities and equip them to see what they did, but my first episode abilities were good enough to take me through the entirety of the game.
Most of the abilities and attacks all have a timing to them. I never really liked timing based attacks, because you quickly get the hang of it and exploit it. That's probably why other RPGs just use random chance. However, the powers can only be used X amount of times in battle. After each battle you're fully recharged. HP, MP, powers and everything. You never get any other characters, its just you against Cobra soldiers, He Man lizard men and Transformer robots.
You can block / dodge attacks by pushing a button at the right time, but even though it tells you that you defended, it sometimes damages you more than an undefended attack. I'm not sure if that's a bug. The timing with some things seems off where I know that I've missed a perfect time window, but it still counted as perfect. It is also odd hearing a boss laugh about how you fool energy attacks only make me stronger, right after I energy attack him, right before he dies after saying that. It is also odd that I can get a 'sneak attack' on an enemy where it bluntly tells me sneak attack, yet the enemies get to go first. You'll see the enemies on the map, so there are no random battles. Enemies don't respawn, so you can't really grind. The enemies and battlers aren't varied enough and eventually just feel like a chore. Another cluster of 3 soldiers, another pair of red transformers. Even moving into episode 3, you'll still find the same soldiers from episode 2.
If you die, then you just restart the battle or from the last checkpoint. That keeps you playing with no real consequence for losing. To top that off, there is an arrow that bluntly points you in the direction of your current quest. You will beat this game if you keep playing.
The overhead map uses 2D sprites on a 3D map... yep. You heart that right. The 2D 16 bit sprites on a 3D map with millions of colors. It just looks out of place. The sprites aren't that impressive, but the 3D has a good look to it. It makes me think this game was rushed or cheap. They could have done 3D modeled characters, because the entire world is 3D modeled, but nothing is animated outside of the 2D sprites.
The game has four 'episodes' and they're pretty quick within 40 - 50 minutes each. There is usually one puzzle per dungeon / episode. The puzzles show some interesting stuff and real thought put into them. If only there could have been more to keep me engaged. The final episode was a disappointment and just felt quick with no challenge, the final boss was a sad pushover.
The game takes a brief 3 hours or so to complete it. There are side quests, an endless battle mode and an arena mode. I just can't justify the $7 for this game when it wasn't fun. I've played other games that I really enjoyed that last only 3 hours, but this isn't one of them.
This game just seems rushed and shallow. More like a set of awful mini games disguised as a RPG. Battles are extremely repetitive and you feel very underpowered. You'll button mash far too much to buff yourself so you can actually damage enemies. Each attack takes way too long due to attack animations and killing animations. It also feels pretty linear even if episode 2 opens up into a less linear area, which is entirely inside of a school.
Avoid this game.

Rogue Warrior is an old-skool corridor shooter with limited cover mechanics and minor stealth elements.  Your objective is to one-man Rambo; an eight mission campaign, set in the Peoples Republic of North Korea.  Choose to kill by stealth but be seen and its time for gun-toting action.  The campaign is single-player but it has a multi-player arena style deathmatch with a few maps.
+ Simple gameplay. Other than picking up weapons/ammo, there is little to interact with.
+ Fast-paced action.
+ Cheesy voice-over from Mickey Rouke.  Some great one-liners.  Sounds like it was made while sitting on the crapper!
+ Who doesnt like taking on PRK enemies!? ^^
+ The music is old-skool tacky, gradually getting boom-tastic at the end.  Perfect for this game!
+ Nice range of achievements which are fairly fast to gain.
+ On sale its very cheap.
- Its very short.  Too short!
- Cliche backstory.  But who doesnt like them right!?
- Scripted levels are purely linear.
- Rudimentary graphics give it a minimalistic ambience.  Well its an old game.
- Mostly similar enemies that just carry different firearms.
- Enemies attack in waves but even on Elite difficulty numbers are very low.
- Some MP achievements require other players.  At least four.  This is a problem to get them even if there are a few die-hards on the discussion boards.
- Very limited replayability.  Everything is virtually the same the second time around.
- No matter what weapons you pick up in the previous chapter, they are reset at the start of the next one.
* Gameplay is fairly one-dimensional apart from minor stealth and cover mechanics.
* A.I is adequate but nothing to write home about.
* Short 8 mission campaign.
* 3 difficulty levels.  Just go to elite.  Its really not that difficult!
* Lite in-game story-driven cutscenes.
* Arena based PvP multiplayer. If youre into that sort of thing.  Unfortunately all but dead.
* Carry 2 weapons but can choose from 13 different weapons (pistols, shotguns, SMGs, assault rifle, sniper rifle, LMG and a grenade-launcer.  Unfortunately none are realistically modelled or very satisfying to use.
* Decent K/M controls.  Unbidden tendency for weapon-switching to occur with mouse-wheel.
* You will need to complete the game three times; once at each difficulty to get 100%.
Rogue Warrior is frankly terrible!  Its a mediocre FPS.  Ultimately limited by its age its levels are designed to be completely linear.  Gameplay decisions mostly fall as to whether to kill with silent takedowns or alert enemies and blast them with whatever weapons you have to hand.  However Its enjoyable in a minimalistic kind of way.  Just dont expect anything like a modern-day shooter or a AAA title and you may find enough to saite your appetite.  It will appeal to fans of brainless, easy to beat FPS.
Definitely one of the 'Its so bad, its good!'  One to miss unless you love old-skool beer and pretzel-style shooters or if you are a sucker for punishment!

Micromanagement the Viking video game. Compete with up to 5 other players to complete a victory condition, whilst balancing your resource income with the few villagers avaliable to you.
So this is a game I picked up early on, before Crow and Bear clans were added to the game. I actually think this makes my purchase the moment it entered EA. So my 52 hours as of this time writing has been spent pretty evenly between updates.
This game is best described as a micromanagement strategy game. Whilst working towards one of the five victory conditions to win a game, you will be constantly shuffling your workers about various tasks, as you try to keep yourself and your clan alive. You will often never have enough workers at any one time, so you will never often be idle whilst you're struggling to keep your clan alive. Between striving to have an excess of food and wood to survive the harshest winters, you'll also need to have enough workers studying ancient runes for technology, as well as collecting gold to cover your taxes as merchants. And of course, you also need just enough of a military presence to ward off the wild creatures of Northgard - or even a more aggressive player.
* Charming art style. Almost every building and worker is unique and easy to quickly identify.
* Simple UI streamlines things. Your resources are easy to keep track of, as is your population, without you being overwhelmed by any obtuse or complex menus. Anything that isn't readily avaliable on the game screen is reachable within one click.
* You will not often be sitting around waiting for something to do, at least until the very end game, when the game is actually drawing to a close.
* A lot of variety in win conditions giving the game a bit of depth in regards to how you play out a game, from begining to end.
* The combat is simplistic but varied enough that focused micro can often win you battles you would have lost. Though this is no Brood War, there is a little satisfaction in having been able to peel back weaker units to maximize your damage without suffering losses. It's worth saying that combat is really not the focus of the game, but the systems that are there are solid and bug free. However, bigger clashes are often decided by who has more, as there's no real depth in unit selection.
Overall, I would say if you want a game to occupy your time for two hours at a time, I would recommend this to you. It's easy to be sucked into a game with the constant fiddling and management you need to do, only to discover at the end of the game that you had just lost a couple of hours to it.

Finally, a rhythm platformer that's NOT an auto-runner. I've always wanted to play something like this after New Super Mario Bros. had the enemies dancing to the music. I thought for sure that an entire game could be built around this concept, and here's one at last.
So how is it? ... Well, it's a brilliant proof-of-concept, with interesting and satisfying puzzles and mechanics, but it's way too short. You can breeze through Normal mode in about 30 minutes, and the difficulty is smooth sailing all the way until the second half of level 3. If you like tension and frustration, you can give Hard mode a shot, which removes all checkpoints and gives you one life.
But still, this really needs to be a full-length game with dozens more levels and ideas. As it is, it's probably not worth the $5. So unless you're really into quirky innovative indie platformers, better to wait for a good sale or an Indie bundle.

Left 4 Dead is a first-person, cooperative shooter that takes place in a zombie apocalyptic Pennsylvania where you play as Bill, Francis, Louis, or Zoey and fight the hordes until you reach rescue. The game sounds very obvious and doesn't sound too special nowadays. However, does the game still appeal to gamers in today's standards?
Before I continue on to this review, I got Left 4 Dead in mid-June 2009. What is that previous sentence relevant or important? Well, let me tell you. If you had brought Left 4 Dead from November 2008 to December 2010, Left 4 Dead was a magnificant game. Heck, it was a great classic and a perfect gem. When Left 4 Dead was released back on November 2008, the game spawn a whole new genre: Multiplayer Cooperative. Sure, there were some games that had that genre, but Left 4 Dead won over the general gamer's perception of a true, cooperative game that you have to rely on your friends to help and assist you. Arguably, Left 4 Dead had also build a foundation of a new video game genre (which is now getting a bit overboard now): Zombie games.
Left 4 Dead is a multiplayer game that put you and your three other friends (or players) in various campaigns (which takes around 45 minutes or so, depending on difficulty level or pace) to reach rescue (or finale that is called).  What is interesting for Left 4 Dead is that you replay the campaigns over and over, but each replay feels "different" or new in some extent. This best feature is known as AI Director. AI Director is a system where items, zombie spawns, and various props are randomized in different locations, making the players not always assuming that the items are in that one, specific area. Thus, this increase replay value by a good margin. Left 4 Dead's atmosphere is actually very immersive and impressive for an aged game. In addition, Left 4 Dead's Survival Mode is worth playing and is very fun so it is encouraged for the potental buyer to try it out.
A summary of positive features...
+ Strong, cooperative multiplayer without a doubt
+ It is really fun playing with your friends, and a lot better when you make new friends on the game
+ AI Director increase its replay value
+ Very immersive and night atmosphere which is better than Left 4 Dead 2 (even when Left 4 Dead's maps are transferred over to the second game)
+ Survival Mode is really fun and really worth playing to get your personal best, breaking records, or achievement hunting. Either way, you might make new friends when you play Survival Mode
A summary of negative aspects about the game...
- Versus Mode is an interesting concept and can be fun, but it is ruined by arrogant players
- The game used to have over 30,000+ players when I played back in 2009 and 2010. Nowadays, it is around 500 players thanks to Left 4 Dead 2 and Valve's abandonment when the sequel was released.
- The game has aged and less than 500 players are around. Might be a bit discouraged for a potential buyer to get it
Left 4 Dead was a legendary classic that spawn two gameplay features that remains popular today and it is highly recommended.

The only reason to use the BFG Version is because of the exclusive new addon for Doom 2 which is actually quite good.
But now lets say something to Doom 3.
Doom 3 is a good horror game. A horror game. Not what you would expect from a Doom game. FPS wisely it is way too mainstream and doesnt even feel that great. However, all guns feel solid except the shotgun, which is a shame. The enemies are repetitive and are not the smartest. They usually blindly charge at you. Or jump at you quite often when you open a door. So often that it gets repetive as hell. Repetitiveness is a problem of the game anyway. After a hour you saw the whole game including all its different scares. Levels all look the same and its always the same procedure. You open a door. Demon jumps at you, more demons spawn behind you. Some utility shafts open and zombies run out, press button, insert code, light flickers like hell, demonic Betruger laughing and repeat. Congratulations. That is the game. Well, you have some small hell passages which at least change this a little bit but mostly its still the same. One word, BORING. The game didnt age well for todays standards but even back in 2004 I thought that Doom 3 is overrated. It really has a good (but repetitive) horror atmosphere but thats about it. I had more fun with shooters like F.E.A.R. or Far Cry which came out around the same time. The game just loses itself in repetitive averageness which is sad for a shooter like Doom 3. Didnt live up to the predecessors. I didn't finish the game completely ever. I often tried but just couldn't do it. I dont play videogames to be bored, sorry. The game also comes with its addon and some new unreleased story addon. Never played them though. You know, the fact that the original Doom 3 had the flashlight as a own weapon, made the game a bit more special. This was removed from the BFG edition. However, I can understand both factions who prefer it and which dont. I dont know if its just me but did they higher the amount of monsters in the BFG Edition? The game is not made for this. Often I had too many mobs around me and not enough space to shoot them. I got more hit by melee attacks than other attacks... Maybe they wanted to make it more like the original games. This doesn't work in this games concept. Make up your mind devs! Also weakens the horror atmoshphere a bit further since mostly you have to deal with enemies. There are definitely too many. Games like Dead Space had a perfect amount. Here its too much. Also I often died more often because of falling down the stairs then from getting killed. The checkpoints are also bad. Like really. Save yourself!
To say something to the technical aspects. Its a mess. The engine is really not that great. The BFG editions fixed at least many of its original games problems. This alone is a reason to buy it over the original. However, the graphics menu for the BFG edition is a joke on PC. Generally I feel like its a cheap console port. Another thing that is absolutely horrible, is the sound mixing of the game. Like really, it just sounds so weird. Doesnt even feel like proper surround to me. Often when I listen audiologs, I have to stand still for like 1-2 minutes because if I go to the next room tons of demons spawn and I cant understand ANYTHING from what they are saying. The fact that the game has NO SUBTITLES WHATSOEVER is a shame. Wtf was id thinking? I honestly couldnt understand like 50% of the spoken dialogue because of the abysmal sound mixing and no subtitles. The sound of the game is really weak in general.
Here is a quick overview of the pros and cons of the Doom 3:
Positive:
- Good horror atmosphere
- Amazing lighting effects
- Well made horror enemy models, CREEPY!
Negative:
- Repetitive
- Boring
- The engine sucks big time
- Horrible sound mixing
- No subtitles
The game is simply overrated in my eye and I don't see it as a official Doom game. Doesn't feel like that. It feels like any other corridor shooter nowadays. The only good thing about it is the atmosphere. The technical issues just weakens the game even further. The Doom 1 and 2 versions are pity too. In general the game feels more like a fast cash grab. I dont recommend the game to anyone. If you want Doom, buy the originals or even the new DOOM. If you want horror, get Dead Space or FEAR. Dont bother with Doom 3 BFG, really. Doom 3: Overrated Cash Grab Edition.
Fun Fact: The main enemy is named Betruger. Betrüger is a German word for something like impostor or cheater. Doom 3 is an imposter.

Micromanagement the Viking video game. Compete with up to 5 other players to complete a victory condition, whilst balancing your resource income with the few villagers avaliable to you.
So this is a game I picked up early on, before Crow and Bear clans were added to the game. I actually think this makes my purchase the moment it entered EA. So my 52 hours as of this time writing has been spent pretty evenly between updates.
This game is best described as a micromanagement strategy game. Whilst working towards one of the five victory conditions to win a game, you will be constantly shuffling your workers about various tasks, as you try to keep yourself and your clan alive. You will often never have enough workers at any one time, so you will never often be idle whilst you're struggling to keep your clan alive. Between striving to have an excess of food and wood to survive the harshest winters, you'll also need to have enough workers studying ancient runes for technology, as well as collecting gold to cover your taxes as merchants. And of course, you also need just enough of a military presence to ward off the wild creatures of Northgard - or even a more aggressive player.
* Charming art style. Almost every building and worker is unique and easy to quickly identify.
* Simple UI streamlines things. Your resources are easy to keep track of, as is your population, without you being overwhelmed by any obtuse or complex menus. Anything that isn't readily avaliable on the game screen is reachable within one click.
* You will not often be sitting around waiting for something to do, at least until the very end game, when the game is actually drawing to a close.
* A lot of variety in win conditions giving the game a bit of depth in regards to how you play out a game, from begining to end.
* The combat is simplistic but varied enough that focused micro can often win you battles you would have lost. Though this is no Brood War, there is a little satisfaction in having been able to peel back weaker units to maximize your damage without suffering losses. It's worth saying that combat is really not the focus of the game, but the systems that are there are solid and bug free. However, bigger clashes are often decided by who has more, as there's no real depth in unit selection.
Overall, I would say if you want a game to occupy your time for two hours at a time, I would recommend this to you. It's easy to be sucked into a game with the constant fiddling and management you need to do, only to discover at the end of the game that you had just lost a couple of hours to it.

Disassembly 3D: Ultimate Stereoscopic Destruction is a simple game where you have the ability to take apart dozens of different things.
That's it, there's no story, gimmick, or central theme, it's just you taking apart machines.
There are 15 packs of items and 48 items, each with their own unique features and secrets.
All you do is go piece by piece taking apart the objects until you disassemble the entire thing.
The priority of the game is to disassemble all of the pieces as fast as you possibly can.
You can't complete the level until disassemble
of the item.
Once completed, you unlock the Bomb for that item but you have to restart the level to use it.
The game is called "Disassembly 3D: Ultimate Stereoscopic
".
I expected to disassemble things by destroying them, not be the world's fastest mechanic.
Even the trailer itself only shows you the vehicle sections where you can crash them, but the majority of the items are household appliances like a speaker, toilet, lamp, etc...
The only ones that I did like were the Titanic, Submarine, Skyscraper, and Space Station because I love watching giant things fall apart.

Sleeping Dogs starts with gusto, with its sense of place and physicality on display.  The game opens with a foot chase through a dock area in Hong Kong as the protagonist, Wei Shen, flees uniformed police who have inadvertently interrupted an undercover operation.  You maneuver Shen as he bursts through windows, slides over fish-market stalls, pivots to clamber over walls and make leaps over black stretches of water.  Shen bashes someone’s head into a fish tank, kicks legs out from another attacker, and clambers onward.  There are shouts, sirens, screams, chatter.  I almost smell it. The scene feels fast and colourful and physical, representing the best parts of Sleeping Dogs.
[TL;DR? See bottom.]
Somewhere the experience falls apart. Shen is sent undercover to break up a local gang of Triads, and the story progresses as he moves up in the organization’s ranks and rediscovers a city he’s only recently returned to after years in the United States.  His motivations are purposefully ambiguous, but rather than successfully knitting the tensions between Shen’s various roles into a compelling tapestry that underscores the stress and desperation of living undercover in a city that’s not quite home, the character and his arc unravel into orthogonal knots of narrative and gameplay.  I stopped wanting to do anything with Shen besides makinging his stats go up and generally horse around about halfway into the game.  It’s not that he grows into some awful person, but rather that neither the gameplay or narrative significantly advance the premises of his character that are laid out at the outset. After a while, he simply fails to be very interesting, except as a kind of schizophrenic mannequin who bounces between disparate activities.
Shen’s mission start in the midst of his childhood neighborhood, and he is simultaneously presented as wanting to exact revenge for harm done to his family and to cut through police corruption and bring cold justice to the streets.  At some point, he becomes frustrated by his handlers’ unwillingness to take actions that result in more than superficial change and, moreover, seems seduced by the power accorded through the respect he’s given as he makes a name for himself amongst the Triads. Both speak to the isolation Shen experiences as an outsider and a person living a double-life. However, while cutscenes (and some trite auditory dream sequences) portray Shen as an essentially heroic, hard-nosed pragmatist, privately tormented by the consequences of others’ decisions, the general experience doesn’t bear this out.  Similar to the Grand Theft Auto series, there are a variety of activities to participate in, from street races (which are quite fun) to karaoke (which is not).  Sleeping Dogs, however, lacks GTA’s biting satirical aspirations and so fails to generate the kind of ironic distance that is needed to forgive or reconcile the weird, sometimes misanthropic hodgepodge of behaviors that the player can make Shen engage in.  For example, I wasn’t too bothered with the dissonance of a cop gleefully ignoring all sorts of civil and criminal laws in his spare time (‘cause, like, who wants to obey speed limits and not steal lots of cars in this kind of game?), except that Sleeping Dogs punishes you for breaking and ‘borrowing’ stuff when you are on a mission. For some reason, if Shen has a real hankering for a pork bun, he’s got no qualms about mowing down a few pedestrians with a stolen car enroute, but if he as much as nicks a lamp-post or taps a jay-walker while he’s chasing a serial killer for the HKPD (or taking out a snitch to gain favor with the Triads), XP for upgrading police abilities are successively deducted.  All of a sudden we are asked to pretend like these kinds of behaviors are important to his character progression - and without explanation.
Another example of this kind of disharmonious design is how Shen interacts with female NPCs.  In general, the characters of Sleeping Dogs are kind of static (Shen included), but with a couple exceptions, the game’s portrayal of women is outright abysmal.  Various consumables result in temporary boosts for Shen, but inexplicably, while both massages from men and women result in the same buff, getting a massage from a woman generally starts with a kind of thinly-veiled sexual innuendo and ends with the masseuse adulating Shen, sometimes offering future discounts if-his-friends-are-as-sexy-as-him-oh-big-boy-yeah. More notably, Shen has the opportunity to date a few different ladies in what amounts to short quest chains that end in some kind of exploration perk once he sufficiently impresses his date. These relationships amount to nothing, ending abruptly after the player made the ambivalent Shen do or say whatever thing will earn them some snippets of fawning, mildly titillating dialogue. It’s a kind of puerile power fantasy where the player gets to feel like women just want what they’ve got (even if they don’t know it yet).  Wag your♥♥♥♥♥♥ get the perk, move on to the next (con)quest.  Worse, if Shen has successfully wooed a particular perk-interest, you will get a side quest where Shen is tasked with stalking her until he catches her seeing another man.  Aside from being confused by the obvious hypocrisy of accepting this quest, I had sort of forgotten who this lady was by the time it was offered to me.  In the end, Shen finds them talking and intimidates them both in exchange for some XP.
Collectively, these kinds of decisions exemplify why Sleeping Dogs isn’t able to do something terribly interesting with its premises; as an experience, taken on its own word, it
.  Of course, this isn’t something particularly uncommon amongst big-budget games, but the amount of time I spent being frustrated by, for example, the most tedious lock-picking, camera-surveilling, and computer-hacking mini-games ever invented makes Sleeping Dogs a game I won’t recommend.  You can read about all the fun stuff that Sleeping Dogs does in terms of gameplay in a plethora of reviews. To mention some, I found the racing surprisingly fun and, as stated previously, the city itself an immersive, beautiful, and interesting place to explore (and looks really, really good on PC).  The game’s action moves quickly, in a satisfying way.  Leaping from vehicles, clambering over obstacles, although mechanically uninteresting, always feels really good and well-paced.  The melee combat sets it apart from other third-person games and, although simple, involves a fair amount of different moves.  After a while, though, even this loses its luster, as it overwhelmingly introduces moves without deepening the execution of the combat.  Even as the difficulty increased, I found that having Shen simply stand idle until an opportunity to counter appeared was a safe bet for tackling hairy situations.
Ultimately, I won’t recommend sinking the time in this game necessary to see it through.  If you can get it cheap and just want to♥♥♥♥♥♥around for a few hours, fine; it's got some fun things going on.  But if you’re hoping to see its various elements brought together and its premises developed, you’re in for an experience whose frustration and dissonance outweighs the many fun and immersive things you can do in Sleeping Dogs’ Hong Kong.

First of all I'd like to point out that I finished the game 3 times. (Twice on my console.)
Anyway, Sleeping Dogs is what people nowadays call a "GTA clone" when in fact it's more than what GTA can normally give in terms of a: Amazing and tense lore, the morale of a cop in Gangster's job, the act of having two separate story lines from either the Triad missions between the Police Case solving missions.
Sleeping Dogs as a game was amazingly enjoyable for me. The open world was fantastic, the humor was really satisfying here and there, Wei Shen as a main character is really likeable and the game really does make you feel emotion when a character dies at certein events.
The combat in Sleeping Dogs really does set itself to be the main glory point of it. Simillar to the Batman Arkham franchise, the combat consists of Melee attacks and counters between attacks, the controls are only somewhat unusual from the standart open world experience but it takes not too long to get used to it. The enviroment kills like shoving someone's face into a lobster rock or a ceeling fan or destroying their face with a car door or just for simplicity shove them into a public toilet till they suffocate. The combat is not very challenging however in Sleeping Dogs, though for new players it will take time to get used to the timing of the counters and of such but with little training they can take on rival Triads with no sweat.
Gun combat in Sleeping Dogs appears a bit later on in the game and eventually turns into something you often get used to. Wether it's a firefigth against rival Triads or a armed high speed chase around Hong Kong, the feel of the gun mechanics feel really satisfying, even when ammo tends to be something you'd scavange for since you can't buy weapons though you can stuff a pistol in your back pocket.. Again not really challenging but really satisfying.
The story of Sleeping Dogs really sets itself as an Undercover Cop which tries to cripple a gang from the inside while also having the gang be his childhood friends...and enemies. Destined to revenge his sister's death he accepts this mission to cripple and weaken the Sun On Ye Triads while also being one himself as part of one of the gangs. The story has dramatic moments and amazing plot twists that are always rememberable.
Graphichs are simply gorgeous on the PC. Having said that I can really only tell that I almost never had enough of looking at the amazing road textures and the neon signs on the streets at nigth!
Game has alot of side activities like Poker Majong, street races,♥♥♥♥♥♥figths to bet on (Yes♥♥♥♥♥♥figths..) and also a battle fight club and much more!
All due these amazing stuff said about this game, it does suffer from some glitches that can be frustrating at times, some of which just look really odd that to be honest I never experienced on a console. They're not horrible but they can bug you at times.
All in all, Sleeping Dogs is an amazing game! By far one of my faveorites of all time! I recommend this game to anyone that enjoys the standart Open World genre and also to those that are looking for a change from your typical GTA/Saints Row.

Sleeping Dogs is an open world action adventure game set in Hong Kong. You play as Wei Shen, an undercover cop with ties to the triads. Throughout the game you work your way up, gaining the trust of the triads while trying to help the HK police take them down. Similar to the Grand Theft Auto franchise with open world gameplay, side missions and activities this game takes a slightly different approach with on one-on-one combat as a main weapon with guns as a second. The city of Hong Kong is beautiful and filled with so much detail and is in my opinion one of the best looking cities I've seen in an open world action game. This game is full of content and plays out like a good action movie. As I got further into the story I found myself getting more and more addicted to the story line wanting to know how it would play out for Wei. I cannot reccommend this game enough for anyone who is into open world action games or even just action kung-fu movies! This game is definitely worth the full retail value and on sale it is a steal. I'm 20+ hours and still have lots of side missions and activities to complete.

Doom 3 is not Doom and I've made my peace with it. The first two games encouraged you to speed up, while Doom 3 urges you to slow down in so many ways. Very narrow and dark levels, characters you meet, PDAs with emails and audio logs, video disks, etc. In the original Doom 3, the flashlight, which was another thing to slow you down, wasn't mounted on the armor like it is here and I was certainly not enjoying myself back then. In the BFG Edition I was able to, for the first time, take in the scenery at my own pace. Not having to deal with the flashlight makes a big difference. Once I got to "relax" with Doom 3, I really noticed a cool looking game, sterile and metallic in its environments, soon covered in nightmares and blood. The lighting, shadows, smoke and sound design bringing it all to life. I even grew a new appreciation for the soundtrack, some of it very reminiscent of the soundtrack of Full Metal Jacket. It feels like a cold place and the demons you encounter look like the stuff of nightmares.
Resurrection of Evil steps even further away from the roots of Doom, introducing a gravity gun and rechargeable Helltime with The Artifact, making it a pointless experience of throwing/catching stuff in narrow quarters and slowing the game down on top everything else I mentioned, sans the flashlight. I opted to use Doom 3's main arsenal to get my kicks, but the grabber comes handy in some situations and is sometimes even necessary. When you upgrade your artifact with rechargeable Berserk, it enables you to punch or shoot all non-boss enemies back to hell in slow motion and once you upgrade it with Invulnerability, there's no stopping you. Makes perfect sense then to have the final boss be a dragon-like demon. Resurrection of Evil adds plenty of projectile enemies on top of the Imp and others seen in Doom 3 and once you get sick of using the grabber with its incredibly narrow operational area only limited to its crosshair, you'll be using The Artifact a lot since there are plenty of glowing bodies around to feed it. If the game wants to be Max Payne, you might as well roll with it.
Enemy AI is not Doom 3's best feature, to say the least. Jump scares only make you hate the game more, not offering a genuinely scary experience. Enemies will jump at you from every possible angle, behind corners, doors, panels, floors, ceiling, etc. They disorient you by beating the hell out of you, jumping in your face, scratching your face and technically it should be scary but I just find it incredibly annoying. Better to kill them before they get anywhere near you. Worst of all, some triggers enable Imps to do 180 degree jumps around corners or even through office cubicles. Enemies wait for you in dark corners until they can jump out like a clown or a sexual predator. A zombie walking out of darkness is way more effective.
Weirdly enough The Lost Mission is the most Doomy of the Doom 3 experience, released here in the BFG Edition, roughly 7 years after Resurrection of Evil. But since most enemies still announce their arrival well in advance, you can run up to their spawn animations and shoot them in the face at point blank. Doom 3 is a bizarre collection of design choices, that's for sure. One mistake I did was not using the double-barreled shotgun in Resurrection of Evil in this playthrough, yet it was my primary weapon in The Lost Mission. It's incredibly powerful at close range and very fun to use. You can take down a Hell Knight with 3 shots, for example.
This version is the only version to enjoy Doom 3, as far as I'm concerned, despite its many flaws. The pacing makes you appreciate the care put into the design of the environments, the monsters, the sounds and the lighting. It genuinely looks like a place you can't wait to leave, it is both a depressing and lethal work environment. The BFG Edition also includes Ultimate Doom and Doom II, along with achievements for every game included, making this the most comprehensive Doom experience for newcomers. Playing on Veteran gave me a good 30 hours across 3 games, I'll leave the classics and Nightmare for another time.

All crafting is much more expensive, Dyes have been forced into usefulness (you can't make some crafting surfaces without them), and there's a new crafting table that you have to craft and use to craft all other crafting tables.
The ramp up in difficulty is rather nuts, especially considering a new survival mechanic where you have to eat to heal or live is in play.  Missions have been added, but no level scaling is there at all, so a mission issued by a villager on the first world got me killed repeatedly because pancakes.  Your character is much less intelligent in that things you'd learn are much slower.
Campiness has been ramped up and slaughters any sense of immersion you could have with these largely leave-it-to-your-imagination graphics. Halfway toward the core, which I was digging toward out of habit more than any degree of purpose, I found gnome cities.  That's right.  Gnomes.  Little tiny hospitals and houses and windmills.  In Terraria this would make sense, but in Starbound, it's just stupid.  What's worse is that they serve as an early ranged weapon.
Yes, you read that right.  An early ranged weapon.
It's called "Ball of Gnomes" and does a pretty hefty amount of damage against weak targets.  Apparently, your character is comfortable with balling up a sentient species in his hand, smashing their houses as he goes, and throw the little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in a shotgun blast at your target. That's good, because it's going to be a long, long time before you find that un-mapped location that has a supposed energy source to leave the planet.
This is effectively a completely different game from the version we've seen evolve for 5 years, and not in a good way.   For a long time this release was anticipated, but it's honestly a disappointment with no way to go back to where we came from. I was going to get another copy of this for my son, but now he'd just make fun of the gift for how silly it becomes, and then quit because of the unbelievable difficulty spikes.  This plays like an overthought, overfeatured sequel to a game that I came to know and love for years before.  Unfortunately, it also completely destroys your saves and removes your copy of that original game, and replaces it with something that doesn't even come close to resembling the difference between an open beta and a final release.

Nostalgia is a powerful force and one look at what's currently on the market for gamers can attest to what a soft spot consumers have for it. The downloadable market is flooded with games that emulate everything from 16-bit RPGs to 2d platformers. Kickstarter has brought us updates and sequels to the games we grew up on and some of the key titles that defined the childhoods of 90's gamers have received HD re-releases. While some games simply play the nostalgia card to give us the warm fuzzy feelings that get us to open our wallets faster than an inebriated middle aged man at a strip joint, others use nostalgia as a vehicle for humor and personality. Saturday morning RPG falls into the latter category.

Following an interesting episodic structure, Saturday Morning RPG places players in the role of Marty, an average teenager who is given a magic trapper keeper by a power glove clad figure called The Wizard in order to face off with Commander Hood. It waste's no time conjuring images of Fred Savage and a certain band of real American Heroes. Each episode plays out like an episode of your favorite 1980's cartoon with some sort of malicious force attempting to carry out a destructive plan and your Hero's journey to thwart their efforts. The episodic structure is actually quite interesting, your level and inventory carries over between episodes and players can go back to previous episodes to uncover missed items and sidequests. Also there are a couple minor cases where something that your character does in one episode carries over in another. The narrative elements are minimalistic but some characters carry over between episodes creating a bit of continuity. The problem is that characters have very little personality, they instead lean too heavily on what they are supposed to reference. Players who are unfamiliar with the source material used to create these characters will find little interest in them and some of the jokes centered around some of these characters read like overused memes.

Unlike most RPGs, Saturday Morning RPG doesn't dwell too much on it's narrative and in instead a bit more focused on combat and it managed to offer a surprisingly robust system for a small budget title. Aside from sharing an acronym with Super Mario RPG, Saturday Morning RPG borrows heavily from the timing based combat system in Mario's first role playing outing. Timing button presses during attacks yields greater damage and timing a button press at the last second can help players avoid major damage. Almost every special attack has some sort of mini game that requires a bit of skill and dexterity to make the most of. In addition, turns can be sacrificed in order to charge Marty up, giving him a damage multiplier. The charge function can be used in one of three ways, the first and most effective requires players to rapidly press buttons to build the multiplier, another requires timed button presses to make the most of the multiplier's potential and finally there is a charge function that requires no interaction but yields the smallest multiplier. Being able to dish out five times the damage in a single turn makes it well worth foregoing an action. Additionally, there are dozens of items and up to five can be equipped--each giving Marty a new special attack. Their abilities recall the abilities that Final Fantasy's Blue Mages are capable of learning and provide a mix of offensive and defensive skills.

The final piece of the combat puzzle comes in the form of stickers and covers for Marty's magic trapper keeper. The cover can be swapped out for a stat buff and up to five scratch and sniff stickers can adorn the front. At the onset of each battle, a fixed period of time is allotted for players to scratch each one of these stickers. Doing so can further buff Marty's stats or debuff your foes. The catch is that the more rewarding the buff or debuff, the more time it takes to scratch the sticker so finding the most beneficial combination of stickers that you can feasibly and consistently activate before each battle adds an appreciable degree of strategy.

The problem with this whole system is two fold, the first of which is that fact that it can make the game exhausting to play. Starting each and every battle furiously smashing our analog stick back and forth to scratch stickers then mashing the A button like a coked out woodpecker in order to gain the highest multiplier become taxing. It should be noted that Saturday Morning RPG was originally designed with phones and tablets in mind so some control input issues are not surprising. The other, more serious problem however is that the game is simply too easy. Anyone who is reasonably quick and has respectable timing will breeze through the game largely unopposed. It is completely feasible to build a multiplier in one turn and knock a boss out with your second action. There is one fight however that is an appreciable test of your skills and ability to strategize to be uncovered.

Rounding out the trip down memory lane, Saturday Morning RPG features a hodgepodge of graphical elements to recall games of the past. Characters are composed of 16 bit style sprites but inhabit a 3d world recalling the look of Paper Mario. The environments are rendered in simple 3D with a cartoonish aesthetic. Unfortunately the environments can appear too simplistic at times with blocky geometry and flat textures. Being a mobile device port, it's not surprising that the tech isn't up to scratch but a little more spit and polish for the PC release could have really given Saturday Morning RPG an invigorating style. Audio is generally strong however with a soundtrack composed by Vince DiCola of Rocky IV fame and Kenny Meriedeth.

Saturday Morning RPG a solid and enjoyable game for those familiar with the pop culture of the 1980's and early 1990's but gamers unfamiliar with the bag from which it pulls it's gags are less likely to be tickled by it's appeal to nostalgia. Even so, the robust combat system and episodic gameplay make it really enjoyable to play and if you feel so inclined, replay. It's just unfortunate that players who want a bit of a challenge have to dig for secret boss fights to find it and that your favorite input device may fall victim to the harsh stick waggleing and button mashing required to play. Even still with a budget price, four complete episodes to enjoy and a fifth and sixth on the way, the good exceeds the bad and if you are of the right temperament, you may even find the experience totally righteous.

First impressions:
Saturday Morning RPG is an episodic turn-based RPG (self-classified as a JRPG) heavily influence by the 1980s, with a great soundtrack to match.
The game heavily emphasizes the combat aspect of the gameplay, with new fights just around the corner (literally). I was drawn into a fight very frequently and could barely navigate my way around with so many enemies. It is a great way to grind for XP, if you're wanting that kind of action. Although I didn't happen to be in existence during the 80's, I did understand most of the references made throughout my experience in Saturday Morning RPG. If you frequent the Internet and know just a little bit about pop culture, you should be fine.
The references, packaged with the game's humor and absurd writing, is where Saturday Morning RPG really shines. I thoroughly enjoyed that aspect the game and that alone could serve as the basis for my recommendation of the game. The game's combat does get repetitive, very quickly in my case, but I still managed to enjoy myself despite this. There are plenty of side quests available, adding a great deal of content to the game. The game wouldn't take that long to beat by itself, so the side quests really add value to the game as a whole.
The game's graphics were nothing too fantastic. In fact, it looks like the graphics originated from a mobile game. Most of the graphics are sprite-based, so can't really complain there. The graphics blended both 2D and 3D objects into one, large 3D environment. It took a little getting used to, haven't played a game with this style in a while, but it wasn't anything to complain about.
Saturday Morning RPG is a great effort, I really enjoyed my time with it and look forward to completing it in the near future. And for $7 too!

First of all I'd like to point out that I finished the game 3 times. (Twice on my console.)
Anyway, Sleeping Dogs is what people nowadays call a "GTA clone" when in fact it's more than what GTA can normally give in terms of a: Amazing and tense lore, the morale of a cop in Gangster's job, the act of having two separate story lines from either the Triad missions between the Police Case solving missions.
Sleeping Dogs as a game was amazingly enjoyable for me. The open world was fantastic, the humor was really satisfying here and there, Wei Shen as a main character is really likeable and the game really does make you feel emotion when a character dies at certein events.
The combat in Sleeping Dogs really does set itself to be the main glory point of it. Simillar to the Batman Arkham franchise, the combat consists of Melee attacks and counters between attacks, the controls are only somewhat unusual from the standart open world experience but it takes not too long to get used to it. The enviroment kills like shoving someone's face into a lobster rock or a ceeling fan or destroying their face with a car door or just for simplicity shove them into a public toilet till they suffocate. The combat is not very challenging however in Sleeping Dogs, though for new players it will take time to get used to the timing of the counters and of such but with little training they can take on rival Triads with no sweat.
Gun combat in Sleeping Dogs appears a bit later on in the game and eventually turns into something you often get used to. Wether it's a firefigth against rival Triads or a armed high speed chase around Hong Kong, the feel of the gun mechanics feel really satisfying, even when ammo tends to be something you'd scavange for since you can't buy weapons though you can stuff a pistol in your back pocket.. Again not really challenging but really satisfying.
The story of Sleeping Dogs really sets itself as an Undercover Cop which tries to cripple a gang from the inside while also having the gang be his childhood friends...and enemies. Destined to revenge his sister's death he accepts this mission to cripple and weaken the Sun On Ye Triads while also being one himself as part of one of the gangs. The story has dramatic moments and amazing plot twists that are always rememberable.
Graphichs are simply gorgeous on the PC. Having said that I can really only tell that I almost never had enough of looking at the amazing road textures and the neon signs on the streets at nigth!
Game has alot of side activities like Poker Majong, street races,♥♥♥♥♥♥figths to bet on (Yes♥♥♥♥♥♥figths..) and also a battle fight club and much more!
All due these amazing stuff said about this game, it does suffer from some glitches that can be frustrating at times, some of which just look really odd that to be honest I never experienced on a console. They're not horrible but they can bug you at times.
All in all, Sleeping Dogs is an amazing game! By far one of my faveorites of all time! I recommend this game to anyone that enjoys the standart Open World genre and also to those that are looking for a change from your typical GTA/Saints Row.

I'm already an established and satisfied owner of MK PS3, so let's start with it as a game: Thoroughly recommended. This is a reinvention and celebration of all that was and is good about the glory days of ye olde Mortal Kombat. The goofy kung-fu-movie camp vibe is still there in full force, and now the gameplay is good. The combat is weighty, visceral and satsifying, and the control is well-behaved. Very little AI ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to be had here, either. Losing to a computer opponent usually leaves me feeling like I lost to something a particularly competent human could have done, not to HAL9000 reading a human button input cheat sheet. This is especially true of the bosses, who are actually now a fun and well-designed challenge instead of an under-the-table deal to make people break their controllers and buy new ones. Yeah, they still do cheap stuff now and again, but overall I've had very little anger towards this game. The presentation is completely outstanding, and everything about the game shows that the creators really wanted to make it as good as it could be, like they owed it to the fans and the characters. _Even Stryker is kind of cool_.
Challenge Tower mode and Story Mode are somewhat less satisfying than regular old Arcade Ladder mode, admittedly. The story's worth doing, but the fights are  less fun and the cutscenes can't be skipped. Challenge Tower at least frequently mixes up the action with wacky circumstances found nowhere else in the game, so that's something, but usually I'm just content to do Arcade. Also there's a tag team ladder mode where your partner, assuming he's conscious and alive, can hop onscreen and do a special move, or even tag in with one. It's pretty well thought out. In any case, even if I'm not doing well, I always have a good time with it, which puts it way, way ahead of a certain other street fightery franchise whose name eludes me.
Now, to examine as a PC port: It looks like you're given plenty of freedom to tinker with graphics options so you can throttle it down, which I guess is all you really need to know. But the game is pretty 'puter heavy, as I expected. I'm running it at 1280x800 with pretty much all of the optional settings turned off, and I've got disappointingly muddy textures (which were gorgeous on the PS3, like you can even see the realistic brushed-metal texture on the cyborgs) and considerable frame rate jank, which surprisingly doesn't really affect my gameplay though.
That's about the worst thing I have to say. It's attractive and violent and exciting and just a good old time. Do it.

Sleeping Dogs is an open world action adventure game set in Hong Kong. You play as Wei Shen, an undercover cop with ties to the triads. Throughout the game you work your way up, gaining the trust of the triads while trying to help the HK police take them down. Similar to the Grand Theft Auto franchise with open world gameplay, side missions and activities this game takes a slightly different approach with on one-on-one combat as a main weapon with guns as a second. The city of Hong Kong is beautiful and filled with so much detail and is in my opinion one of the best looking cities I've seen in an open world action game. This game is full of content and plays out like a good action movie. As I got further into the story I found myself getting more and more addicted to the story line wanting to know how it would play out for Wei. I cannot reccommend this game enough for anyone who is into open world action games or even just action kung-fu movies! This game is definitely worth the full retail value and on sale it is a steal. I'm 20+ hours and still have lots of side missions and activities to complete.

Considering that it's Mental Health Awareness Week at the time of this review, I feel like there's something that needs to be said about this game which I really haven't seen in other reviews.  While this game was clearly made with immense dedication and creativity, it seems the creators didn't put nearly as much effort into researching what mental illness is actually like.  Honestly, the lack of attention to that chunk of the story is enough to sour my opinion of what is otherwise, an extremely well-made game.
The artwork and soundtrack are gorgeous, the minigames offer a shift away from standard point-and-click gameplay (but are thankfully skippable if you'd rather move the story along), and the worldbuilding involved in a few of the later chapters goes above and beyond what I'd typically expect for a $15 game.  They managed to hit a perfect sweet spot with the level of gore- it's enough to make you uneasy, but not so much that it becomes bland and cheesy.  There's a lot of parts that really were enjoyable about this game, even downright whimsical and lighthearted, and I was hopeful that maybe, just maybe, the resolutions to the many mysterious aspects of the story would provide a satisfying conclusion that showcased Fran's development as a character and how she was more than just a diagnosis or a set of symptoms.
However, the game essentially just leaves you, the player, to decide whether she's "dangerous crazy" or "quirky crazy", and neither option gives an accurate, nuanced picture of mental illness.  Advice for writers: people with mental illnesses are actually more likely to be the victims of violence than the perpetrators, and hallucinations are not indicators of being deeply in tune with the true structure of the cosmos.
Given the setting is in 1944, it's sadly, fairly accurate to show the asylum as oppressive, full of heavy sedatives, freudian psychoanalysis, and non-consensual psychosurgery.  But this setting is so overused that people really don't have a good idea of what 21st century mental health facilities look like.  This might sound like a dumb argument, but attitude surveys have shown that a lot of people are afraid of seeking mental healthcare because they're afraid of being labeled as "crazy".  We really don't need yet another piece of media reinforcing the idea that mental health patients are delusional and incapable of leading normal lives, or that mental healthcare providers are all drug-pushing lobotomizers who look down on their patients with distain.
If the creators had just cut out all the references to mental illness, this would have been a really nice story.  They definitely could have come up with a coherent storyline about Fran facing the challenges of horror and fantasy worlds, without all the
vibes.  If it's on sale, I'd say check it out for the artwork and puzzles, but the problems with the story aren't worth full price.  I am cautiously optimistic about the developers' next projects.

You are not going to believe what you're going to find in this game.
IF you are into storylines that can hook you into the game
IF you are NOT faint of the heart
IF you like an emotional plot
Then this game is for you.
About the graphics and sound:
1. It's a simple 2d based game that mimics a 3d effect. Nothing really fancy with special 3d or enviromental effects, BUT that leaves room for it's incredible artistic and appealing to the eye animations, with a great and colorful contrast of the characters and scenes.
2. It doesn't have voice for the characters BUT that make us imagine how their voices would be in our perspective, just like a book that when you read a dialogue and a voice pops up in our heads to make the character's personality come to life.
3. As mentioned above, the scenes are composed by 2d artistic ambiance. From beautiful spring-like sunny lands to dark creepy twisted worlds.
About the gamelay:
1. It's a puzzle solving game BUT with a twist. Sometimes the main character have to do things that wasn't supposed to (for a little girl) in order to continue the story.
2. The mechanics about combining items are good. SOmetimes characters give you clues or items that you have to combine and figure out.
About the Story (my personal notes):
The story is "the main juice" of the whole game, makes you keep going to find out more and leaves little "gaps" in it for the player's interpretation. It's based in the idea of a little girl fighting a mental disorder, but in a few minutes of the game you are able to see other patients with other mental disorders as well wich makes us stay at least "a little" connected to reality.
Overall it's one of the best games i've ever played wich is the main reason that i took some time to write a descent and honest review of this game.
If you are in doubt, BUY IT! It's worth it!
