Left 4 Dead is a CO-OP first person shooter game. The game uses Valve's well known Source engine, released in 2008.
The game is set during the aftermath of an apocalyptic pandemic, you take control of one of four protagonists, which will be known as the "Survivors". They will be pitted against hordes of infected zombies in four different game modes, a single player mode which the three other characters are controlled by the AI. A co-op campaign mode, an online versus mode and a four player survival mode.
the game play focuses mainly on cooperation and working as a team. You will see all the regular features included in other FPS games, such as outlined teammates throughout the world, so you know where they are all the time. A cool feature which I found to be a nice surprise was if a member of your team were to fall off a ledge, they won't automatically plunge to their death, they will manage to hold onto the ledge and the other team members may go and "Help them up" much like you would do if you were healing them.
The campaign mode has six levels, each containing anywhere between three and five individual chapters in them. Each of the chapters takes place in a set environment which allows the player to explore around to find little Easter eggs, pick ups - such as medi-packs, pain pills, weapons and ammo. These points are supposedly randomly generated so each time you play, they will be scattered around in different spots. There are tons of rooms, tunnels and buildings to explore on every level, and there is no time limit either so you can roam around to your hearts content, provided you don't mind the odd zombie jumping out of the closet to try and eat your brains every now and again.
Each of the Survivors are individually voice acted very well; and you can communicate with your team using quick menus. Some voice commands will sound off automatically such as when you are reloading, you'll let the rest of your team know so they can cover you. This to me was a small addition but added to the realism of the game.
Throughout the game you will encounter a number of different zombies which have their own special attack or mutation, such as The Boomer, which is a bloated zombie that will spit bile onto the Survivors which attracts other zombies to your location. This again adds a lot of variety to the game so you don't feel as if you are just mowing through hoards of regular zombies all the time.
The graphics, while are running on an engine which is a number of years old now, still look awesome, and games today sometimes struggle to present them selves as well as Left 4 Dead. Even with settings right the way down on low, it still looks impressive - meaning any rig or potato will be able to run this.
I played the single player campaign on normal mode; while I had no real issues finishing the game, apart from the last level, I still was satisfied with the level of challenge which was on offer, I can imagine the hard and advanced levels will be completely mind fumblingly hard though. I tried to play the campaign mode online, but sadly there weren't many games available at the time, but it is something I really want to try just to experience the co-op side of things on this game.
Pretty much every one owns Left 4 Dead already, and most will have probably already played it; but I really suggest people that haven't played it or at least purchased it but not tried it to play. You will not be disappointed and this is one of the classics of our generation that you need to experience.
P.S - if anyone would like to have a play through the campaign with me, please add me or hit me up as I would welcome any opportunity to give it ago!

This game is loaded with references and throwbacks to pretty much everything from my childhood. It triggers a lot of nostalgia, and I am really enjoying it. The controls are really not well explained and you have to figure out how to use each new attack all on your own through trial and error. I still recommend this game because in spite of the gameplay issues, I'm enjoying it. And that's really all that matters.

I like Dust AET and The Stanley Parable, so I thought this game might be enjoyable. It held promise, but I can't get into it.
"...a META game in disguise" as your description on the store page is not the best introduction. You can be honest about a game being meta, but
The combat is okay and it might actually be a bit deeper than Dust's system with more attack combos. However, there isn't much that's remarkable about it. Quite flashy, but that's about all I remember.
The main rub, though? The voice acting.
Bastion would have been a very irritating game to play if it did not feature Logan Cunningham's talent. His high quality contribution made that game. The Stanley Parable flourished with Kevan Brighting.
The voice acting for ICEY was originally just Chinese. He was okay, but having to constantly read subtitles is not helpful in a game. Lee Hand sounds like he doesn't really want to be the VA. He either tried too hard to make the game sound more epic than it really is, or was forced to do so and was determined to undermine the game. Roles like this are very demanding for a VA. Hand was either not up to it, or didn't really want to do it. Considering how crass the game is with being meta, I wouldn't blame him for the latter.
Games can be good and have meta elements, but ICEY's gameplay isn't good enough to draw me in and have the meta as another layer. That in itself is okay. A game like that can be run on the voices acting and good meta. However, ICEY doesn't have those, either.

Sanctum 2 has much more limited maze design opportunities but adds Borderlands-style class mechanics with perks, different loadouts, etc.   This changed the game a lot which seems to have upset a lot of Sanctum 1 purists.  However, the changes actually justify the sequel since they amount to a huge overhaul of the game and not simply a slight modification of the original.
The game is designed well, controls well, and runs pretty well.  I've had very occasional glitches but it's better than par for the most part.
Sanctum 2 ends up being much more fun in multiplayer than singleplayer - so much so that I'd really only recommend getting it if you have a friend or two to play with.  That said, it is REALLY fun in mutliplayer and since you can often pick it up for $5 per copy, it's great value.

Sleeping Dogs (and the True Crime series, of which this is a spiritual successor) often gets written off as another sub-standard GTA clone. It was this established view that stopped me from bothering with it for a long time. As such, when I finally got around to playing it, I was pleasantly surprised to find an intelligently written, well-designed game which improves upon GTA in many areas, while still excelling in most others.

Its brutal and tactile melee combat, fun (if basic) free-running, solid gun-play and overall world-design combine to create a more measured experience than GTA, exchanging that title's humour and wacky, surreal characters with a more serious plot and grounded, realistic cast. That's not to say SD is without a sense of humour entirely, but it's not out to provide constant lolz; it exists to provide a genuinely intriguing undercover-cop story in which you're connected and engaged with your protagonist like few other games released in the last decade.

It succeeds on every level, and is well worth a few dozen hours of your time.

I realize it's just another tower defense game but this one has some charm.
Not quite sure what it is about this game, probably the art style... It looks like something cooked up by Dan Paladin from The Behemoth, the genius' behind games such as Alien Hominid, Castle Crashers and Battle Block Theater. If Dan didn't  have anything to do with the art for this game, then he should be getting some royalties.
Great game, easy enough campaign with some added challenge modes to each map to cater to the hard core TD players. It's really not just your average TD, it has soul.
It's a lot of fun watching things happen in this game where as most TD games are boring but the variety of animation is astouding... There's lots of things happening and lots of tricks the enemy units can pull on you, sometimes there's more to them than meets the eye... like transformers, except not as Robosexual.
It has some MOBA / Warcraft III elements in it with the way hero's work, they're essentially on auto mode but you can move them around the map like a mobile tower. They all have strengths and weaknesses and some are better for certain maps than others so it's fun to experiment.

The music is great, the campaign is a decent size and will keep you busy for a while... there are also extra missions and hero's that unlock after the campaign is over so the fun doesn't stop there.

Funny thing about this particular incarnation of Doom 3 is that, at large, it is played by people who already played the original. Either lured by expansions or original Doom and Doom 2 to give this one a chance.
With this in mind. What's in it for you fellow doomguys?
Most alluring part of BFG edition is simple fact that it includes all that Doom franchise had to offer up to BFG's release date. Meaning original Doom (Ultimate), Doom 2 with expansion "No Rest for the Living" and Doom 3 with "Ressurection of Evil" (which is not standalone, so buying them together is required) and earlier unreleased "Lost Mission" - campaign based off cut content from original Doom 3.
Hillarious as it may be I completed Doom and Doom 2 for the first time in 2017 with this edition. I can highly reccomend that once you have beaten the Doom 3 or any modern high-end shooter. Experience brings things into perspective.
Still the meat of it all is Doom 3. And the things have changed. I don't mean that now game runs in high resolutions and has improved lighting effects. BFG's Doom 3 has  a slightly different gameplay. Doom 3 was meant to be something else to begin with - a survival horror game. Moving stress from "run and gun" to "thread carefully, it's right behind you and that wall". Game slowed its pace and required far more methodic approach. Scarce munitions combined with jumpscare theatre and dark claustrophobic corners kept you on your toes.
They don't anymore, at least not quite. Moving flashlight to your shoulder rather than requiring you to carry it instead of a weapon seems mighty convenient and it is. Too convenient in fact since with wise battery usage there are no dark corners anymore making most zombie sequences entirely harmless. Probably being the reason why some encounters were scrapped althogheter. BFG also revises the ammount of supplies avialable and ammo capacity for some guns (f.e. 600 cap instead of 540 for Machine Gun). You don't have to count bullets anymore or search for hidden stashes as primary means of survival. The amount of armour avialable is simply ridiculous and there is now way to use it all while progressing the game normally.
Lost Mission is the only completely new content and being rather short it is fun to play and let's you see some of the designes that haven't made it into the final cut of Doom 3 (f.e. hell was originally meant to be an entire "zone" like Alpha labs not a big level).
Summing it up BFG Edition makes the game simply easier. I can't help the feeling that they tried to put a little of "run and gun" into the Doom 3 with this revision but should they really do that? I leave judgement up to you. For survival experience I recommend playing original Doom 3. If you are up for having a blast then BFG's Doom 3 is simply more convenient to play.

"Polished" is the word I would use to characterize Bastion. It's a compact, well thought out, beautiful looking game with interesting story telling.
Even thought the mechanics aren't complex, they work very well. You have a melee weapon, a ranged weapon, shield, special ability and you can dodge. In tough fights you should use the combination of all of those things, especially if you don't wont to get hit. You of course can play with just button smashing and that could very well be sufficient for most parts, but it doesn't look and feel good.
As the story progresses you build and upgrade the Bastion. There are six buildings and upgrades for all of them. You can switch weapon sets here, level up your character, upgrade weapons, "change difficulty", buy items and such.
The leveling is very slow and very basic. Every level up gives you boost in maximum HP and you can choose one passive bonus. There are multiple melee and ranged weapons which you'll find through out the whole game. Each of them presents a little bit different play style so everyone can find his match. But I'm not sure if some of them are really necessary, if there really are people who will prefer them. Each weapon can be upgraded five times. On every level there are two options to choose from, and you can switch between them freely, when you are in Bastion. Usage of special ability is limited to the number of special drinks you have on you.
The world is beautiful, especially the way it's build right before your eyes. The sound track is quite nice. The story is very interesting and the narrator did an amazing job. They predicted some actions that player will probably do, so if you do them narrator will comment that also. That's a really nice feature.
There are some small problems here and there. Some assets weren't distinguished enough, I thought they were horizontal, plane that I can walk on and they were vertical so I fell down. The aiming was weird in some cases. You aim at a creature and you miss, because the collision model was set weirdly. You had to shoot at the shadow to hit it. At the end of the game the physics change a bit, instead of dodge you jump, quite hight. It was a nice change but there were instances where you had to jump from one small plain to another and due to controls it was hard and I fell a lot. Also, the defence auto lock system is terrible if there is multiple opponents shooting at you. It was a little bit infuriating.
But those are just minor issues in otherwise really strong game experience. The game will take around 7 hours to beat. You can play new game plus and there are multiple challenges you can try to beat. You can also change difficulty by giving different bonuses to enemies, in the shrine. There are 10 bonuses to choose from in the basic game, 15 in new game plus. You can active all at the same time, if you are crazy enough.
(When I first tried to play it I was bored and stoped after two hours. I don't know why but I'm glad I gave it another chance after few years)

Imagine that a writer and a composer watched
and were so inspired by Michael Bay's brilliant explosions and Hans Zimmer's catchy riffs that they decided to make a game inspired by that hit 90's movie. Except this time the protagonists are fighting foreign communists instead of domestic terrorists. They nail the superficial aspects of the style while forgetting to include any substance. That's Rogue Warrior.
It's a brash, simple, and pointedly racist FPS with little that's notable about it other than the repetitive and profane one-liners voiced by Mickey Rourke. He is by far the best choice possible to pull this off, but how they convinced him to take the job I have no idea. Maybe he didn't see the script ahead of time. Or maybe that's where all the budget went.
The strangest thing to me is that the game claims to be "character-driven" in its description while actually being the farthest thing from it. There's more character development in an alphabet book.
You've only got a couple of tired weapons to choose from and a couple of dumb enemies to fight. So gameplay-wise it's even below par for standard FPS fare. Throw in an awkward cover system that forces you into third-person mode and that's all you need to know about the mechanics.
The game is also terribly short. My first playthrough on the highest difficulty was just north of three hours. My second run on normal was just about an hour and a half. And my final go on easy was under an hour. There's just not much to this game in any dimension.
And yet...there might be a place for it in your library. A fast, not-challenging run through of an FPS you've never played before can be a fun experience. It can scratch a certain kind of itch. If you've already beaten every Call of Duty and Battlefield there is then there might not be many other places you could look than Rogue Warrior. But it's not fundamentally
. It's just
.

Playing more than ten minutes of this game (and you can "beat" the game in less than two hours), requires a strong stomach.
The only bright spot is that I can use this game in my Game Design class as a bad example of how not to do an FPS game.

As for the Predator campaign, weak melee controls let it down and with the combi stick as only a ranged javelin and your claws as the only melee weapon, it feels as if something is missing. The wall crawling suffers in first person and from rather glitchy controls and getting stuck on lights and wall/ceiling (or floor) edges. This is, however, easily mastered with a bit of practise.
I have tried the multiplayer rarely, and that was mostly early on in the game's history. It has always been underpopulated, even then. It was not especially brilliant, and lacks any structure which saves the singleplayer from utter dull chaos!
For the Alien campaign I give it 8/10.
For the Predator campaign I give it 6.5/10.
For the Marine campaign I give it 4/10.
Overall I give it only a sad 6/10.

Aliens vs. Predator has a very short and sweet intertwining story between Aliens, Predators and Marines. So with that said, you play as all 3. If you've seen the Aliens VS. Predator movie, you're stepping into the same idea. There really isn't anything special about the story in any of the 3 campaigns but the best one is Marines in terms of this.
Each character you play as has their own unique set of skills and weapons. Marines are able to use an assault rifle, shotgun, grenades and pistols. Predators have their scanners, claws, stealth mode, distraction (this obviously won't be in multiplayer), plasma cannon, discs, polearms and mines. Aliens just use their claws and tail and rely on the shadows and speed to gain their kills. Aliens are easily the hardest as they have very little defense and health, but this makes them very fun.
Multiplayer in Aliens VS. Predator is among the most broken if not the most broken multiplayer system I have ever seen. I went into multiplayer expecting maybe a little bias towards predators and aliens and thinking maybe it would feel slightly unfair until you got the hang of things.....but there is clearly very little if any skill involved being a Predator. You have to rely on your set of skills as each class like in the campaigns, only Predators have no limit to their gadgets. They don't have to wait for a recharge or take their time to aim their charged shots and so all you will see is them camping up on buildings and using their auto aimed plasma cannons. In the event that they do come and fight you face to face, marines cannot knock them back or stun them making them virtually impossible to kill unless you aren't spotted. As an Alien, it's best to work in numbers like they naturally do. Aliens are fun to play and you can defend against them as a predator or marine making the battles with them even. And you already know that predators can just use their plasma cannons to home in on you nearly instantaneously. Basically, if you want to enjoy multiplayer do not play as the marines unless you're a masochist as they're slow and easy targets. Stick to Predator and Alien for the multiplayer experience and you will have fun.
This isn't a new game but the graphics and sound are very well done. The only thing that will annoy you is hearing the marines say the same few lines over and over again. But this can be overlooked as the game is fun to play.
Singleplayer will take you about 6-7 hours getting through the 3 small campaigns. Apart from the ridiculous balance issues and frustration that followed realizing this, the game is solid and is fun as an alien or predator in multiplayer, and all 3 are equally fun in the campaign. I just wish singleplayer could've been a lot longer. Recommended on sale.

So the premise of this game is that humans have established colonies in the skies over an alien planet. They use magical blue balls of light (cores) to convert the gasses present into oxygen and kill the native spores. The problem is that the planet is already occupied by an alien race of highly evolved mushrooms. The mushroom people under the direction of unknown telepathic boss entity whom you never fight create giant organic shafts to the colonies to try to murder them dead.
In the game you will create a maze of towers in an attempt to halt the advance of the mushroom people before they destroy you're magical blue ball as is typical of a Tower Defense game. you will spend 5, 10 or 15 minutes per level depositing towers that will ultimately only do about thirty percent of the damage necessary to kill the enemy waves. The rest is up to you. You can choose two of a plethora of weapons to aid you in the struggle. The game does not address why a gun held by a five foot two to six foot tall human out damages half dozen tool shed sized tower mounted guns you drop and arguably that means this game isn't really a TD. There are "perks" you can select to improve you're characters/towers performance but there’s really nothing that will turn this game into an actual Tower Defense, which is unfortunate.
The longer you play the game the more powerful guns, perks and towers you can unlock, particularly if you buy the DLC. I'm sure we all know the DLC drill by now. For an extra five dollars you will get access to all the content that was cut from the game during the alpha and beta tests for quality control and balance reasons. Ideally that content has since been fixed/balanced/polished but we never know until we shell out the cash. To their credit the DLC for Sanctum 2 does provide a lot of interesting content. The towers, perks and maps it adds do a great deal to increase replayability of the game and it rounds out the base games story that ends on a cliffhanger.
The real strength of this game is the level design. Like every other piece of science fiction made in the past twelve years almost everything looks like an Ipod that said this game does it particularly well. The integration of organic vines and spores growing over the utopian surfaces/structures in this game are very imaginative and well done. A lot of games (Doom 3/Dead Space) place a strong aesthetic emphasis in a human environment being reverse terraformed by some perverse alien influence but truthfully Sanctum 2 does it better. The levels are distinct from each other in groups as you proceed from an idealistic lived in colony under attack to the deteriorating front lines to an industrial themed colony abandoned some years or generations earlier. The theme is that the further into the game you go the closer to the planet you get until ultimately you are beneath its surface in a giant cavern with mushroom Jesus. In the tradition of classic FPS games there are many many secret areas and players are rewarded for their diligent exploration. Ironically the maps are far bigger in scope then the developers were prepared to work with and you’ll shudder when you realize that you can’t incorporate some of the games incredibly ideal choke points into you’re defense as they are simply too far away from where the action will be…. If they allowed you to place your own cores the quality of the game would quadruple immediately but thats something they will have to consider for a sequel.
The biggest issue with the game is the many many clipping errors. This game will kill you or force you to consul command suicide many times as you fall through solid objects or get stuck between them. In the basic game it doesn’t matter very much as you can wait out the 9 second respawn time once or twice and it isn’t likely to lose the game for you. Tragically the developers compounded this issue by encouraging the players to play with “five feats of strength” on to create a more challenging experience… One of these “feats” is a no respawn mode… So basically each time you die to a developer error, which will be once or twice a game, you’ll also lose the level. is a 2D point and click horror adventure game. It's about Fran, a mentally ill 10 year old little girl who is treated in a mental hospital after witnessing the brutal assassination of her parents.
Given a new experimental drug, named Duotine she is eventually uncovering Osvald Asylums horrible truths, while trying to find out who and why killed her relatives slowly sinking deeper in to insanity to a point where she can't tell the difference between reality and imagination.
The base story and the atmosphere is already things i would have gladly given my money for, but what comes next is something every one should play through at least once. To witness the world of a tormented little girls subconscious thoughts, the way she sees, looks, and treats things that aren't real, and  understanding the meaning of the little references hidden in front of your eyes, are the things a point and click horror game rearly does to a player.
In the 10 hours of playing the game had me hooked up, always thinking, always trying to put the pieces of the puzzle together, learning to think like a 10 year old girl, while at times playing 2D ingame-minigames, hanging on to the grip of what's real, and what is not, while seeing realitys converge together, leading to a startling and confusing conclusion.
The game lacks voice acting, dialogs only exist in a textual way, but it's not a bad thing, for this game, it's the best mechanics they could come up with. Puzzles are what i would say medium-difficulty, there are not always instantly obvious, sometimes you have to think more, or look up a walkthrough, realising afterwards the answer was in front of you all along. It was just a matter of the right perspective.

I played Doom 3, including all the expansions and most mods literally countless times (Last Man Standing Coop and OpenCoop, both of which I highly recommend if you have vanilla Doom 3). Therefore, I believe it's safe for me to give a very valid review.
Let me say first of all, that I only paid $4.99 for it. My main purpose was to play the Lost Missions campaign. I saw this as basically $.62 per map, since there are 8 maps. This review will focus on that.
Things that I immediately liked, was the settings option to change the resolution to 1080p. Keep in mind that you can also do this in the original Doom 3 as well, via the console with the correct command. It's simply more convenient now. I also like that you could change the FOV without having to access the console. Though, it doesn't go any higher than 100 unless you change it manually in the console, thus preventing the awarding of achievments (which I could care less about). Their is the added option of Motion Blurr, but I personally don't care for that feature in most games. Others will feel diffferent.
For the game itself, I enjoyed playing the Lost Missions (on veteran). It put me back to the early days of playing the original game. It starts off quick, and for me, I was instantly drawn into the game. There could be more action IMO, but I consider myself an advanced player. Most who aren't as familiar with the game, will likely enjoy the action a little more. But in all, I though it was simply a little too easy. Despite the easiness, I did enjoy it for the 6.2 hours it took to complete.
Most of the weapons sound different, which I don't feel as positive or negative. It's just different. The footsteps sound is slightly too loud. In the old game, when you didn't run, it didn't make a footstep sound. Now it does. Once again, I didn't see this as a positive or a negative in the end. It just could have been turned down a little.
The graphics aren't as good as the original game, and you don't have the graphical options that you do in the original game. As others have said, it looks blurry and hazy. It's missing certain shadows, and an overall crispness. After a while, I didn't notice it that much because I was focused on playing the game. I'm not implying that the graphics are bad, it just isn't as good as it once was.
A big negative for me personally, is the overall sound quality. There is only the option to adjust the volume, nothing else. I suppose this is to be expected from a game that's been ported to the pc. Things simply sound muddy, and lack any articulation. The option for EAX is no longer there. For any user, as myself, who has a Creative X-FI (Titanium HD in my case), you will miss this feature. Every room in BFG Edition sounds mostly the same. In the original game, the environmental audio changed depending on the room size. It lacks good positional audio as well, something once again that users of the original game running EAX will miss. I used to be able to pinpoint enemy location easily, not so much with this version. I miss hearing the bullets fly pass my head. Keep in mind, none of this will probably matter to users who didn't play the original game with an EAX 4.0 capable soundcard.
All in all, I still recommend it, but only for the price that I paid or less. I had fun, but I would not recommend it for full price, or even for $9.99 for that matter.
I hope this review is useful.

It takes some giant balls to switch up the formula for the DOOM games like ID Software has done following 3's release.  But I must say, after having playing the remastered version, much praise is deserved for this installment.  In contrast to previous games in the franchise, Doom 3 threw us with a curveball by not only retaining the already established and loved fast paced  action, except this time with a horror twist which has you holding onto your seat until you know every demon in the room has been vaporized.
Doom 3 certainly is not AS speedy as the classic games because 3 is much more linear and in almost every room you're in there is not a lot of open space to run, dodge enemies, comfortably take shots with the rocket launcher knowing you won't hurt yourself from the blast, and so on - combat is certainly more confined and this works in 3's favor because from the moment you encounter your first zombie guy you are on edge.  Enemies can instantly appear from random corridors and spawn behind you when you least expect it which forces you to be on guard.  Want to pick up some armor in a room? Well, if you do, enemies can instantly spawn as a result.  I lost track of how many times I was caught off guard and actually jumped while playing this.
There is a good variety of enemies here and many have been brought back from the classics such as the zombie and shotgun guys, imps, hell knights, lost souls, bull demons, cacodemons, mancubi, and a few new demons too. Enemy variety is well-rounded which is necessary.
Weapons stay true to the classics also.  You still have the regular pistol, super shotgun, chaingun, rocket launcher, plasma rifle, chainsaw, and of course the BFG 9000.  Added to the game are a few other new weapons/gadgets that fit perfectly during combat, those I won't reveal.
A different route was chosen for 3's soundtrack, going for a more brooding and atmospheric sound instead of metal fans have been accustomed to hearing in classic Doom.  This was an appropriate change because the metal music without a doubt fits classic Doom's much faster gameplay, while the new music here fits 3's gameplay perfectly.
I suppose my only complaint is the levels - most of them feel too similar to one another but I guess that's to be expected since you are a marine trapped in a facility on Mars.
One more thing to note is the performance - it's excellent.  A few frame drops here and there but with a solid setup you can easily get 100 fps or more.  What I didn't expect from this remaster was ultrawide support; and what a pleasant surprise it was to play this in 2560x1080 resolution.
The base game is about 12 hours long on the second difficulty, not short but not dragged out either.  This particular edition comes with two expansions: Resurrection of Evil and the Lost Mission, both of which I have yet to play.  From what I heard they both will last about 6 to 8 hours combined.  Moreover, the BFG edition includes Doom 1 and Doom 2 so you will have all 3 in one place.  Very convenient and appealing package here.  I couldn't recommend this more.

If you are like me and born in the late 70s-early 80s and 'Merkin (I say that because I dont know how well 80s american pop culture references are going to translate to other cultures. If you live in a county that imported a lot of american stuff back then, you might like it too), this is pretty much a must have.
You find yourself grinning at 80s stuff you totally forgot existed, and a lot more you remember. Just off the top of my head (and Ive only been playing for 20 mins) Lisa Frank style trapper-keeper with scratch and sniff stickers on the cover, rainbow brite-like belt, michael jackson's glove, people saying radical and bogus, fruit stripe zebras, care bears, the battle summary page looks like those strange bar graphs that were on the back of Transformer's/GI Joe boxes (or a card inside)...I could go on.
But underneath of all the stuff that will make someone in the vicinity of 30 years old remember their childhood is a well made RPG.
The controls are fluid and intuitive and although you are given a brief tutorial, anyone who has played video games will know how it works.
Theres a lot of button press/joystick wobble quicktime events in battle to keep you from just mindlessly selecting fight or a special skill over and over, simple things any gamer recognizes. Hit the button at the correct point, tap the button repeatedly, wobble the joystick and so forth. T
heres also plenty of awesome stuff you can get to have different attacks in battle, all of them amusing (IE chewing fruity gum causes a heard of rainbow zebras to run out and trample your enemy, a sword you hold over your head ala He Man causes a beam of light to hit someone). Also you can collect scratch and sniff stickers that you have to wobble the joystick before battle to "scratch" that provide powerups, the more you scratch in the alloted time, the more powerups.
The graphics are bright and colorful, and remind me of Paper Mario. And to top it all off, the soundtrack is really really good. Or should I say "radical", har har.
The game is episodic like a cartoon show, with 4 episodes included and a fifth to be released for free soon. If you fondly remember your 80s childhood, grab this game. You wont regret it.

My video impressions on the game:
Every now and again a game pops up and surprises you. This was one for me. It is a very casual JRPG game oozing with 80's nostalgia. It features very unique abilities such as a 3 1/2 inch disk slap to the face or a care bear stare. Pair that with active defending and a couple other surprises during combat makes it quite enjoyable.
The game is broken up in to 4 current (5th to be released later TBD free of charge) episodes. Each features a different story line and location. The first episode was about 30-40 minutes and the second was about 2 hours taking my time.
The gem with this game is best equated to the book, "Ready Player One" where the nostalgia drives the story. For someone my age (31) or older, you will love the references from times past (ie: stay off the adult BBS's or The Wizard with a Power Glove).
Do yourself a favor and pick up this game. It's the price of a value meal and will provide you with quite a bit of entertainment, just don't take it as a hardcore JRPG, because that would be doing it all wrong.

Don't. Just Don't. Don't let your children near this game. It's designed solely for the purpose of extorting money from you. Absolutely every aspect of the game is behind a cash wall. The grind is real here. Seriously, without spending money on this product it will take you a literal century to achieve any kind of progress. This is what should be a light hearted, relaxed and fun adventure with your friends/family however, it's just not. This is essentially a monetized predatory product that plays on the exclusivity of the imagination and the minds of vulnerable and young people. Imagine for a second those penny slot machines with the coins moving back and forward at the fun fair. This is like that but a lot worse.
Long term players tell me the game used to be much more fun and family friendly and that over time the developers seem to have gone on a man hunt with sucking every aspect of what could be called 'fun' out of this game and have put everything behind a huge cash wall. So much of the stuff you find, unlock or use is untradable, the economy in the game is absolutely destroyed, without buying the premium pay monthly service it could take you between 1-2 months of solely investing in trade slots (before inventory slots, personal stash slots) to actually generate some coherent level of flux or hitting the jackpot and finding a valuable tradable item.
The gem upgrade system in the game is essentially locked behind RNG mechanics that again, without investing money will take you centuries to level up. The entire dungeon system in the game is essentially the same thing, items quickly become valueless and often require incredibly large amounts of flux to upgrade and improve later. You go into a small procedurally generated dungeon, kill a boss for a portion of XP (which doesn't improve with any change in zone or difficulty as everything scales to your character) Thats it. It's a giant slot machine, the whole game world is a giant slot machine.
The servers are beyond terrible. Their is almost constant lag, even on a 220MB internet connection. You find your character dropping out of the sky, getting stuck between walls/spaces, losing gear due to connection drops (lost an entire weeks worth of shapers stars because of a server disconnection)
The conclusion is this, what starts as very friendly, inviting and colourful quickly becomes a complete mess of corporate greed, marketting tactics and financial extortion to the highest of levels. The only excuse developers have for this is well, the product is free. So why does it matter? This is precisely the point.
This game needs to have a serious injection of 'fun' put back into it, I think the developers could profit seriously for providing a more subscription based service that gives players essentially the full game experience without all the other stuff. Though it does have a premium service like this, it doesn't stop the developers from still wanting more and more from you.
If you want a game like this for your children or a younger audience, I highly recommend Minecraft or Blockworld.

I am not an avid player of games like Floating Point, but I was surprised by how much I enjoyed playing this game. It’s a great physics based game that’s only 24mb, and it’s free. Even though the game has simple mechanics, there are endless amounts of enjoyment that can come from this game.
The objective is simple, and learning the game is very easy. Even though the objective is straight forward, how you complete that objective is up to you. You can try and score as many points as possible, or just go to the next level. The movement in this game is all inertia based, and the grapple system looks and feels perfect. Watching that orange arc trail behind you as you play gives you a sense of awe.
The only thing you need to play is a mouse, and the simplicity of the controls makes the game fun for anyone. I enjoyed the single player aspect of the game, but I would like to see multiplayer implemented somehow because I think that this game could be improved with one or more extra players. The fact that the game is easy to play makes the aesthetics and music even more beautiful, on more than one occasion I found myself letting the mouse go and listening to the music. The change in music depending on where you are in the level and how well you are swinging is a great way to get players to engage with the game.
As you swing around the levels, it is enjoyable to see the pillars growing and shrinking depending on how you swing. This is one of my favourite parts of the game because it not only gives players a visual queue on how well they are doing, but it is another great aesthetic addition. The game runs very smoothly, and when you reach top speed and let go, it looks amazing seeing the graceful arcs through the air.
My main concern with the game is that it gets very repetitive. Swinging around is fun, but after a while, you long for more. Apart from that, I really enjoyed this game. The visuals and music were my favourite parts, but the progression of the levels was also good. Having a snapshot of what’s coming next is one of the things that gives this game its flare.
Overall I personally find Floating Point less of a game, and more of an experience, and the experience always takes your breath away. Floating Point is perfect for relaxing, and it always manages to bring a smile to my face.
This game is a great experience, and I have no doubt that others have had the same experience as me. The game is also free, so what do you have to lose. I would recommend this game to anyone who wants to relax, and have some fun.

Man this game looks good considering it's age. I'm guessing this was one of those system-killer games back when it came out. The lighting looks amazing. Environment models and character models look good and are quite detailed. The only thing that actually looks like it's from 2010 is the foliage.
The story for all three campaigns(alien, marine and predator all have separate campaigns that take place simultaneously) is passable at best. But I don't think anyone would expect this game to have a super interesting and detailed story with amazing characters.
The quality of the gameplay varies from one campaign to campaign.
Marine get's a pretty standard fps campaign. You walk around and shoot stuff. What makes it noteworthy is the fact that xenemorphs in this game are super well made. So you are a slow and clunky human being that has to fight fast, agile aliens that can walk on walls and attack from any direction. What is also cool is that you can hear them before you see them. The radar beeps that notify you about the presence of an enemy combined with how fast xeneomorphs make the first few levels really tense. Unfortunately I got used to it after a while, but it was nice while it lasted.
The alien definitely has the weakest levels. The story is simplistic even for a game like this. Gameplay gets repetitive and boring super fast. The only positive thing I can say about it is that's it's short... so there's that.
And the predators campaign. Is just awesome. It's exactly what a predator should feel like. You are fast, powerful and stealthy at the same time. You systematically work your way through groups of humans leaving gore and carnage behind you, and decimate swarms of aliens with your blades and gadgets. All for the glory of the hunt.
It's a grate game if you can catch it on a sale.

Every mount seems to be either chaos chest related (that is to say, rare boxes that you get daily or rarely from high-level dungeons) or Dragons. Dragons are VERY expencive in terms of resources and money, as they used to come from daily reward chests as progressable rewards, but now come from crafting using an egg found through specific conditions. The lag. THE LAG! This has been addressed by several people in the past, though the lag on this game is unbearable at times and slows the gameplay down a lot when it comes right out of nowhere. Seriously Trion, up your game!

Yeah, Trove has gone down a downward spiral that it probably won't be able to get back out of. As for the devs, bless them I know they are trying but they are not doing it right. Not even close.

Sleeping Dogs is a realistic look at the undercover life in the Hong Kong Triads (organized crime) played as a third person open world game. I guess you can compare it to the Grand Theft Auto games or Saints Row games in terms of actual gameplay.
In Sleeping Dogs you’ll find yourself driving in cars for large portions of the game since the game world is actually very large. There’s a fast travel option that I didn’t even know existed until I replayed the game a couple of months ago. The combat in the game is very similar to the Batman Arkham games (strike & counter), but with no gadgets. There are also sections where you’ll use guns, but it’s about 90% hand to hand fighting.
Where the game really shines is in story. You’re an undercover cop trying to worm your way into the Triad and slowly get pulled in more and more into the life. It’s how I imagine real undercover cops experience their jobs.
Overall I give the game a thumbs up. It seems like every game I review gets a thumbs up, but that’s because if I don’t like a game, I stop playing. Steam offers a free HD textures DLC so everything looks good with the graphics turned way up.

ICEY resembles a flash game a college student would submit as a final project for his Game Design class.
The Good:
-The art is right up my alley for the most part. The cyberpunk themes and vivid contrast of colors are pleasant to look at and in some cases are just absolutely stunning (Ideon's fight, for example).
-The soundtrack isn't amazing, but it's passably good and pairs well with the visuals.
The Bad:
-The combat system is poorly balanced on multiple fronts. Enemies have disproportionately large hitboxes on their attacks that don't match the attack's visuals. ICEY's numerous combos are flashy and fun until you realize you could just spam the X button endlessly for the same effect... Which is to say, very little effect at all. Against bosses like Ideon and Dahal, your attacks are pathetically weak and are easily interrupted by the boss' specials which can break your shield AND slash half of your health bar if you aren't able to dash away in time.
-The difficulty settings are complete nonsense. At first, I played on Normal, then quickly grew frustrated with how quickly I was dying (I figured I might just not be good at fast-paced combo hack-and-slashes like this) and switched to Easy in order to focus on the story. This hardly changed anything. Most fights were either brainlessly easy or ridiculously hard, boss battles included. Gorger and Puck were laughably simple fights compared to Ideon and Dahal.
-The narrator is painful to listen to. It's very obvious that you're listening to an unpracticed 20-something male who is so busy trying to maintain his "Narrator Voice" that he doesn't ever change his tone, even when something "unexpected" happens.
-People are comparing and contrasting this to The Stanley Parable... let me put it this way: The Stanley Parable is set up to encourage the player to think about philosophical concepts the game presents through its various endings. ICEY, on the other hand, takes the narration element of TSP, beats it senseless, drives it into the ground, and engraves the words "Follow the Arrow" onto its tombstone.
TL;DR: 3/10. Good art, good music, bad gameplay, awful narration. You can find comparable games on Newgrounds. It's not worth $11, so if you're still curious, get it on sale.

TLDR: bug-free, strategically deep without resorting to complex mechanics, with interesting departures from RTS norms. Buy if you like games like civ or age of empires, but also roguelikes such as FTL or binding of isaac. Stands on its own already, but with great promise for new features also.
I've never played any of the Civilisation games, due to being put off by the extremely long match times, and the vast amount of managing required; I have played and enjoyed Age of Empires 1 and Age of Mythology, but was never particularly good at either due to the frantic pace required to expand as fast as possible. Northgard then strikes a neat balance between the two; matches tend to last around an hour, villager micro is unnecessary, and combat, while important, is not the focus of the game. Most importantly, there are several features that turn the usual dogma of RTS games on its head:
Winters are harsh in Northgard, and if you don't manage to build up a stockpile of food to see you through, your clansmen will go hungry, first reducing their productivity and happiness, and ultimately killing them if the shortage is severe enough. However, claiming new territory costs food, and new territory is required to access different resources, and to build more buildings. This leads to the most immediate of the many tough decisions Northgard presents you with: how much expansion can you get away with before the winter, and what areas should you expand into? Taking advantage of new resources requires diversion of clansmen away from food production; safe for a time, especially in spring with the whole year ahead of you, but eventually saving food for winter will become the main priority once again. Everyone has to eat, and so without enough gatherers, farmers, hunters etc. your clan will be unable to feed itself. Furthermore, colonising land you can't immediately spare the manpower to use is a dangerous move as claiming new territory costs a good chunk of food that increases with each new area; if this land isn't being put to good use, you have just thrown away your winter food for nothing.
The ultimate choice Northgard offers, and one that is influenced by the randomly generated map, as well which of the four very different clans you choose to play as; is how to win. Northgard offers 4 central win conditions, these being victory through wealth, as you exploit your territory in the name of profit; victory through fame, as you accrue a glorious reputation for slaying wild beasts and mythical monsters, as well as raiding lands both near and far; victory through wisdom, as you study the strange carvings throughout the island to advance your technology; and victory through simple annihilation, murdering your opponents' citizens and razing their town centres to the ground. Furthermore, every game will feature one 'unique' area; some of these feed into existing win conditions, such as the den of the great Wyvern, a terrifyingly powerful foe that grants an unsurpassed fame bonus to whoever manages to slay it. Some, however, provide a win condition in their own right, such as the Gate of Helheim, which grants victory to whoever can maintain control of it, (and repel the otherworldly creatures that flood out of it) for an ingame year. As will become clear, which of these methods of winning the game you choose to aim for is a decision that must be made each game; while some clans favour certain playstyles, the map layout, and scouting of your opponents' strategies, will ultimately dictate the final decision.
Overall I would say this is a fascinating game, in which the relative lack of mechanical complexity belies an impressive strategic depth. As for its early access status, the game has just enough features to provide a fulfilling experience already, and I've not encountered any bugs (although there are a couple of behaviours that aren't very well explained in-game, but don't appear buggy or exploitable). Strongly recommend.

For all two of you reading the reviews for this older game, I promise AVP is worth the $3.50 I paid for it. Players control the marines, Predators, or aliens in separate but interwoven campaigns. Each race behaves differently and requires a unique strategy to master. The marines follow a pretty standard (but enjoyable) first-person shooter model. The Predators use a combination of hand-to-hand and stealth, but also employ a number of high-tech gadgets, like laser cannons, proximity mines, and cloaking fields. The aliens are the most mobile of the three and use speed, stealth, and their ability to climb on any surface to get the drop on their foes. All three races battle each other in a storyline that basically doesn't exist but doesn't need to. Aliens bite through human skulls and Predators get mowed down by the pulse rifle, and it's awesome for any fans of the franchise. The campaigns also offer a nice variety in the enemy department. Unfortunately, a few blemishes mar this otherwise great game. Firstly, the multiplayer is dead. That's a shame, because the game was designed with a great balance between the three races that would have made for fast and furious team death matches. Secondly, while it's great to play as the aliens, I found a lot of faults with their campaign. I don't personally get motion sickness from games, but anyone who does will want to avoid playing as the Xenomorphs. Their ability to speed across any surface can be dizzying at times. I found myself having trouble adjusting to fully three-dimensional thinking, and some players might dislike the fact that the ceiling and walls can also be the floor. The aliens' full-spectrum vision made the world look a little cartoonish, and their campaign was simply too limited. It's much shorter than the other two, probably intentionally. The aliens can only slash with their claws and tails, so combat becomes repetitive. Allowing the player to control a spitting Xenomorph or a Queen for a few levels might have added some variety. Too bad the developers neglected to do that. Lastly, the Predator acquires a spear later in his campaign that's REALLY over-powered. I had to actually force myself to use other weapons to make the fights more fair. Overall, though, the game is fantastic for any AVP fans. All the sounds from the movies are in full use here, and it's great to play with human and Predator technology. It's definitely worth the bargain price. 8/10.

Saturday Morning RPG is a love letter to 80s nostalgia while at the same time playing homage to the timed-hits style battle system that has shown up before in RPGs. While I wasn't an 80s kid so I was never the biggest G.I. Joe or Transformer fan, I do know a lot about the pop culture of the time and I'm a huge fan of films from the decade.The real draw here was the game's battle system to me. I'm a huge Super Mario RPG fan, and this game draws inspiration from the series that follow it up: Paper Mario. It's also been used in Costume Quest (which the game is more similar to in design), and will even be in the upcoming South Park: The Stick of Truth. So as a fan of the genre, I felt it was nesscary to toss down the cash on it.
And I enjoyed it. The game isn't the best RPG I've ever played (of all time...ever), but it's the writing, humor, and references that made me want to keep playing. Now, I've heard people saying this is a short game. Well, not really. You aren't going to beat this game quickly unless you skip all the side-quests and head straight from point A to point B. I don't suggest this. You'll miss out on a lot of a fun events, like when you find a Mogwai-esque creature and have the choice to feed it and get it wet before giving it back to Phoebe Cates herself. There IS a point around the third episode where the battles started to feel repetitive, but that soon went away as I found myself smashing Transformers with a freakin' axe. Not everyone is going to like it, but there are enough options in battle to keep situations fresh if need be. Better healing options (I didn't find a single GREAT healing item in my run) and more PCs (or a Paper Mario-esque helper) would have spiced up the battles, but if you're a fan of this type of battle system then you'll enjoy it.

You'll spend almost 5 hours with the first four episodes of Saturday Morning RPG. Another five more if you go back for achievements or try a hand at the other game modes. And for $7, it's in a good price range where a blind buy isn't risky if you're a fan of the genre and have just a little knowledge of the 80s. It's not the best RPG of all time, but it's a great indie effort and I'm always happy to see more of these.

I was very excited to finally play this game. Although I had a fun time with it, I'd give it about a 50/50.
The player takes on the role of Fran Bow, a young girl who experienced a tragic incident and was sent to the mental hospital. I really enjoyed the mechanic of taking your pills, that allows you to see another world which is gruesome and psychologically twisted. Switching and interacting between the two worlds allows you to affect things you otherwise wouldn't be able to, for example you could open a door unnoticed in the "bloody world" and pass through on the normal world.
Fran Bow is a pretty standard point and click game, the player may move around and interact with the environment. The inventory system is easy and smooth to use. As mentioned before, there is a mechanic of switching between "worlds" or how Fran can see different layer(s) of reality when she takes her pills, which I really enjoyed.
The art style is one of the best parts of Fran Bow. Everything is unique and detailed, which really brought the gloomy and dark atmosphere of Fran Bow's worlds to life. The environments especially stood out, and made entering every new area a pleasure to explore.
I have mixed feelings about the story. Not going to spoil anything, but it started out strong in the beginning and kind of went all over the place near the end, finally just petering out. I wouldn't say I got very emotionally invested in the end. My favorite part was an area where you're stuck in a house of two strangers, and it was the art and atmosphere it created that made it memorable. The art style definitely made a longer lasting impression and carried the story, almost.
I did enjoy this game, and have nothing but praise for the art style and atmosphere. However the plot didn't feel tight, and at times it felt like as a player my motivation was slipping away. It was like one of those movies that you'd watch once and never again, nor really remember after a couple of weeks.
I'd say play it if you have it in your library anyway (Steam hoarders rejoice), or if you feel like playing a point and click game to kill time. Having played it, I personally wouldn't go out of my way to purchase it.

Left 4 Dead is a throwback to the arcades of the 1980's, giving the gamer a taste of the frantic action of the original Street Fighter and Mortal Kombat insanity that arguably started it all.
The gameplay itself is nothing like these old games of course, but the spirit is very much the same. Fast action interspersed with moments to allow the players to collect themselves before the coming onslaught that is not unlike the round based mechanics of those earlier games.
They also have great simplicity in common; nothing is wasted and there is little to no attempt to create characters (though surprisingly character is something that oozes from the game). Instead the developers rely on sparse dialogue and good character design to convey each of the four characters unique flavours.
Unusually this game, though designed for up to four players, is just as much fun to play alone. The AI of the computer controlled characters seems fluid and they help out when needed with a logic that can easily be taken for another human player. In truth of course it is best to play with several friends, especially when chat is enabled, but single player functionality is wonderfully realised.
If you want a game that plays well as a single player, but is an unbeatable experience in multiplayer this game is a hard one to beat. Regardless of whether you are a seasoned gamer or casual player the controls are intuitive (allowing for both keyboard and controller support) and the learning curve is only dictated by the level of insanity you require.
Left 4 Dead is highly recommended.

Icey as a game...does not work. It tries to mimic innovations and ideas of recent games, but without any real understanding of what makes those games work. The combat itself is pretty standard 2d action gameplay You get a list of comboes to use, but you really only need a few basic ones to coast through every battle. There is a dodge mechanic which works well enough, and functions as an exploration tool. All of this works well enough, though the dodge at times felt unresponsive even when testing outside of combat. The combat really fails in the "fun" factor. Getting hit applies a long window of flying through the air, where you can get hit again, and then lying on the ground. At times this means your character will be out of your control for seconds at a time, which I promise is much more aggrevating than it sounds. Not as much a threat as a constant nuisance, especially with enemies who can juggle you in the air with a little laser as you sit there waiting to play again.
Where the game really fails though is in exploration, story, and its "meta" commentary. This is another game jumping on the meta bandwagon, giving a story wrapped in a story. There are plenty of games that do this better and with more thought. You can hunt for secrets and at times find little tidbits of more info, usually in the most cryptic fashion. Mostly though it will be the game holding your hand saying "yes follow the arrows, DON'T go down that clearly marked path we want you to go down". The meta story itself (which I have read up on rather than spend another few hours completing everything) is partially just ruined by narration from what is quite obviously an amateur voice actor who can't sell the lines. But beyond that just surface level observations about your actions and who really makes decisions, and blah blah blah. It has been covered.
I guess I will speak to the visuals, which are likewise uninspiring. You'll go through the standard city, sewer, cyberpunk office, forest, etc. The game will repeat all of these exact visuals so have fun with that. When the game gets "creepy" through screens with eyes staring at you and "glitches" (once again, a technique used a thousand times over already), the game does little to make you actually connected to the area you are in. So instead the eyes just become another layer on the wall. And ultimately this is because the game never even attempts to give you a connection to the world, characters or events. Things happen, you move on. From what I read they will give you the secret of Icey and all that, but if they haven't done any legwork 2 hours in, then it will not work.
Overall, just don't buy this game. There are so so many games that attempt similar things in an interesting way. The 2d action genre is alive and well, find it elsewhere.

ICEY is a very short, action packed game that takes you through a roller coaster adventure of ICEY, an android built to destroy another anroid, Judas. Through the adventure, ICEY has to fight Judas' minions, consisting of minion robots and more advanced boss characters.
As much as it pains me to say, I can't recommend this game.
- The game leans way too heavily on the "unreliable narrator" trope. Multiple times throughout the game, the narrator will comment how you
follow the arrows, which basically eggs the player to go off on their own. As soon as they do, they are berated by an indignant and exasperated voice that hurls insults. It's not charming and the voice actor puts the same emotion on every line. Stanley Parable this is not.
- The plot seems to be all over the place, with most characters and events being explained and justified through vague paragraphs that you have to seek out. Even then, the method of telling the story is only told through the Narrator (although very poorly), and only through text. It doesn't seem like this game takes advantage of its medium, even though it tries.
- The story tries to justify the vagueness of it by including the Cthulhu mythos into an android story. Unfortunately, this seems to have given the authors the excuse to be lazy, because none of the mythos mentioned has a lasting impact on the game, its characters, or its story. It's a real shame to introduce such an amazing set of fiction only to do absolutely nothing with it.
- When exploring and discovering secret rooms, too often are you stuck in a room with nothing to do while you wait for the narrator to speak to you. In my 3.8 hours plays, I'm sad to say that the .8 was standing there waiting for something to trigger.
- ICEY can't decide if it wants to poke fun and break the fourth wall or take itself seriously. It fails on both accounts.
- The graphics and music seem uninspired and generic save for a few "glitchy" moments.
It's clear I have some issues with the game, but ICEY is far from the worst game on Steam. The things they get right, they get very right.
- ICEY is fun to play. You are agile, you have launchers, an instant dodge, and a full screen attack, plus other moves you unlock very early on. Enemies are tough but have their pattern and you are usually swarmed by half a dozen robots to mow down. I legitimately enjoyed my time playing and wish it didn't end so soon.
- It's short. At 3.8 hours, I've gotten every achievement and I only want to play it more. I know that had it been longer, my issues would've outweighed the enjoyement I was getting out of it, so I'm glad ICEY didn't overstay it's welcome.
Whatever the devs did to suck me in worked, and all in all, I'm glad I played ICEY, but it is very forgettable and does not fulfill the potential it had. I can't recommend it unless it's on a deep discount.

Sleeping Dogs is one of those games that while hardly mentioned regularly, most of the times ends in a circle jerk, and rightfully so. While hyped a good bit before release and achieving midly successful sales figures, it still seems to be put on the back-burner when in the midst of contemporary, and decidly lower quality titles.
Originally to be published by Activision under the title True Crime: Hong Kong, Sleeping Dogs seemed like nothing more than a disater waiting to happen, though the perseverance of its development team is truly laudable. Developed by little known United Front games, the end result would've been a tossup with their lack of lack track record.
Story: The Story of Sleeping Dogs is truly one of its shining aspects, settings a strong progression of events and plot twists. The player takes control of Wei Shen, a skilled but troubled police officer, in his assignment to infiltrate one of the many 'Triad' gangs, the 'Sun on Yee', and dismantle it from within. Lines get increasingly blurred as his loyalties waver throughout the plot, added greatly to by the games surpisingly deep back story for our protagonist.
Atmosphere: The setting and feel of Sleeping Dogs are yet more of its strong points, painting a vivid and believable interpretation of Hong Kong. The intricacies of different city districts, the clash between the criminal underground, the old world shops, and modern business all contribute to an enriching and deep experience in the city.
Gameplay: Gameplay is new and exciting, taking the best of other titles, and grinding them down into a polished system. Borrowing from the Arkham series, melee combat takes a free-flow styled system, with a large and varied set of strikes, counters, and combos, allowing fights to stay fresh without becoming stale and repetitive. Parkour is also a highly rewarding feature, letting you slide over cars, mantle buildings, and move around the city in the way you want to. Driving is very well done, even rivaling games where driving is its sole purpose.
Ratings:
Graphics: 9/10
Story: 9.5/10
Gameplay: 9.5/10
Audio: 9/10
Atmosphere: 9.5/10
Overall: 9.3/10

ICEY is a short indie platformer with a Megaman Zero and Metroidvania vibe.
Pros:
+Highly meta narrative that is both memorable and witty.
+Consistently detailed art, from ICEY herself to enemies and backgrounds.
+Catchy techno-like soundtrack
+Fast and fluid combat
+Responsive controls
+Many unlockable combo attacks
+Multiple paths to explore in the levels
Cons
-Can be beaten in less than 2 hours without doing any exploring, and 4 hours if you do explore.
-The combat is too simple to need to use anything but your favorite combo for the entire game, rendering the many attack options you have rather pointless.
-The "narrator" will sometimes teleport you once you've finished exploring an optional path, which forces you to backtrack to there if you were interested in exploring more in that area.
-The "narrator" will force you to sit through his dialogue on occasion (this really doesn't happen that often) which needlessly slows down the game's pace.
-The DLC is a dull, neigh-endless battle against hordes of enemies. It has no storyline and adds nothing to the game.
If you enjoy Metroidvania games, Megaman Zero, or Azure Striker Gunvolt, you will enjoy ICEY greatly. However, it is rather expensive at full price considering the amount of content. Pick it up during the summer or winter sale.

To those of you who are looking for a review in comparison to my thoughts on Terraria: you're not going to get it here, so look elsewhere. Starbound is a league of its own, and I'm tired of people expecting to come into this game thinking they can play it like Terraria, then realizing its not anything like what they were expecting. When they do that, they immediately ragequit the game and refund it without a second thought. That is not how you play games, and that is simply childish of people to do so. They miss out on several tens of hours of great content and fun, but that's their loss. It is rude and inconsiderate of people to ask a refund out of a game that someone put their time, heart, and effort into, only for people to hate it for what its not. If this is you, you do not deserve the wonderful games that people make for us.
Anyway, on with the review!
Starbound is about exploring worlds, trading with other lifeforms in the form of NPC shopkeepers, and completing quests at your leisure. The game has many things to do in it, mainly in the form of the hundreds of sidequests you can do. Some progress your tech, others simply require you to be a good person. Progressing your tech is a surefire way to increase your ablility to gather better materials, because as your ship upgrades, it unlocks the ablilty to reach said better materials.
I love the building in Starbound, simply because there are so many materials you can build with. The lighting is also very appealing in Starbound; it makes windows much more interesting and worthwhile. Because there are so many materials to build with, many styles can be made and built, and some of them are truly amazing. I have spent many hours simply building and experimenting with different materials, and gained much satisfaction from it. Furniture is also very immersive; there are so many furniture items you can craft and find, it can actually confuse me sometimes looking for specific ones in my inventory. That being said, Starbound is a wonderful game for building.
The crafting menu is also very appealing, because of how intuitive and simple it is. You can expect to need something specific when you go to craft, and you'd most likely guess it exactly. It has hardly every shocked me with something I've never heard of (besides when I first started playing it). Not only that, but it's click and go: no waiting times or specific processes. All you need is the right crafting station.
All in all, I really like Starbound, and give it a solid 9/10. The only con, I would say, is that after one of the updates, the worlds changed a bit. Everything was generally more repetitive after a while, similar to how No Man's Sky turned out. It used to be you could go somewhere and see a new monster and new world every time you landed, but then they narrowed it down on what you could find on planets. Anyway, the only thing, in my opinion, that kept me from playing this game longer. Still worth $10 (current sale) for 80 hours of awesome fun.

UPDATE 2:  A good friend insisted I give Starbound another try, so I did.  I can honestly say that I'm glad I did.  My dissapointment about the seperate races' stories still stands.  I still believe the loss of that element didn't improve the game.  That said, the overall content is strong, vast, and extremely playable.  Whether you want to build colonies, starbases, explore the galaxy, or pursue a story with a big nasty enemy and huge stakes...it's all there for you.
UPDATE:  I have no idea why, but so much of what made this game unique and fun has been stripped away in favor of a single story for go-live.  I understand the desire to want to tell a story, but there used to be one story for every race...now it's just one story.  This dissapointed me more than I can say and has resulted in the game feeling far more generic than it ever did.  Thus, I'm rescinding my reccomendation for this game at this time.  As it is, the game is essentially Terraria in space with some interesting variations.  I honestly don't understand the thinking behind the changes and am dissapointed.
Starbound is a Terraria-like game with a strong science-fiction element that revolves around a character who has been cast apart from his people for some reason and must now make a life for herself.  You start aboard your spaceship, make your way down to the planet below, and begin your adventure by trying to reassemble your ship so you can get access to the rest of the galaxy where your adventure will begin in earnest.  There is a story to pursue, items to craft, treasures to discover, and planets to explore. Video Review:
Saturday Morning RPG is an episodic turn based RPG with an art style modeled after an 80's or 90's cartoon/comic.  The game takes place in a boys dream where he explores the world on his skate board and fights off enemies to save the girl.  The script is deliberately cliche and has lots of vague references from the era.  For me the big let down was the combat, it just wasn't fun.  The attacks consist of either quicktime events with on screen button prompts or timing a button press with a cursor moving along a meter.  The player can also charge up for bigger attacks but this mechanic is another event requiring a button press timed against a meter.  With the style of combat, despite 5+ hours of gameplay, I can't recommend Saturday Morning RPG.
EDIT (2/4/14): Updated the gameplay time to 5+ hours.

Bastion is by far one of my favorite games I have ever played.  I do not say something like this lightly, as the amount of games I've played in my time attests.  The story is solid, the gameplay is fun as hell, and the narration is so good that I almost don't have words.  Not only all that, the soundtrack is one of the only video game soundtracks I find myself listening to on a regular basis; it's that good!
The game takes place in a world that has just had an apocalyptic event called the 'Calamity' that has resulted in a fractured and empty world.  This Calamity has snuffed out the majority of human life, and has driven the remaining indigenous species berserk.  You play a silent protagonist named simply, 'the Kid'.
Even though the game has the cliche silent protagonist, that doesn't make the game devoid of a voice.  As you make your way through the story, the narrator both entertains and enlightens you slowly about the world and what exactly has happened.  At times, the protagonist is funny with well timed comments; however, at other times, he is morose, lamenting a time before the Calamity.  You quickly start craving for every morsel he has to share as you make your way through Bastion's world.
Speaking of Bastion's world, the art style is colorful and vibrant and even works into the story.  The Calamity has upset the very balance of this world, and the gameplay consists of you traversing floating landmasses that appear from below as you walk across.  The smooth transition and animations make this mechanic enjoyable to play and watch.
The gameplay can be described as an isometric, top-down, beat 'em up.  There's also some RPG mixed in, including a leveling mechanic and weapon upgrades that you can mix and match.  The action is very fun and you'll find yourself grinning to yourself as you listen to the immersive musical score that blends perfectly with the setting and action.
Bastion is definitely a game that every gamer should play.

Northgard is an empire-building game where you compete with other clans.
Ultimately it’s reminiscent of the Age of Empires series, but with the incorporation of Norse mythology. At the time of writing, you can only choose single player – multiplayer and campaign modes are not yet available.
Playing the game is straightforward, but learning and mastering the strategy is a challenge of its own, and requires planning, trial and error, and preparing for the worst.
Moreover, there are currently only three different clans (with more to come), but each has two starting bonuses and two fame bonuses, and each clan caters to a different play style
(for instance, one buffs attack, while another will provide extra starting resources).
Particularly with random events, such as earthquakes that damage various buildings and set them aflame, or rats that threaten to devour your food supply.
You must also account for the seasonal progression, changes in weather, and unhappiness,
which prevents new villagers from joining, stagnating your otherwise budding clan.
As would be expected in real life, resource production decreases during the winter:
You must always stock wood before winter to stave off the cold harshness and looming devastation that could befall your clan.
For what Northgard sets out to do, it does well, and with the content that is soon to come,
the title is promising and worth getting at its price point, especially for those who enjoy
empire-building titles.
For those who love the tension, suspense, and the struggle to develop the perfect strategy
for a fierce and resilient empire that can dominate the world – this may be your game.

I have a slight case of motion sickness whenever I play FPS, so I haven't been able to play this game long enough to give a meaningful review. But having gotten past the first "world", here's my two cents.
First of all, this game was never meant to run on a Mac. The mouse movement in the menu is very slow, with no way to change it in the settings, and the lines in the graphics are jagged. Signs of poor porting. Everyone's heard the trope of Macs not having any games, but if you're going to try porting a game, you better do a good job of it.
Onto the gameplay: It's as good as you think it is. No better, no worse. A fun little exercise with tower defense, then the ability to jump around the map, shooting monsters that often try to ignore their target and run straight for you. Which is a plus, because at least the AI isn't so dumb as to completely ignore such a huge source of damage. Though the boss in the first level being able to trample the turrets is terrible to play against. (You can tell it's only gonna get worse.)
The game also includes a flexible perk system that rewards you well, though for some maps, after putting down a certain number of blocks/turrets, there's honestly nothing you can do with any resources left over. It just sits in your inventory, and with the 15-turret limit in every level, things can get a little hectic. Found myself chasing enemies to the core several times, which can be annoying.
Overall, good game. Excellent and flashy graphics ruined by poor porting. Really nice audio, suitable voice acting. Gameplay is as good as it gets with regards to tower defense games. Maybe not worth 15 bucks, but definitely worth a try. 7.5/10.
