As you can tell from my hours played, I have enjoyed SOME of my time in trove. I've never had a lot of fun on mmo's as they seemed to lack a certain something be it story, or imaginative quests, overly repetitive missions. Trove fails in all of these aspects, but the unique ability to build/destroy in the over worlds and club worlds and the creativity shown on the part of the designers always something that kept me around and playing. Recently however the developers have seemingly stopped caring about the game. The recent patches have added content that can only be described as pay-to-win. The three largest problems are: they're introduction of the gem system, they're completely lackluster server performance, and their almost hostile refusal to accept criticism.
It first started with the introduction of the gem system. In which you must grind for gems to equip to a character. Finding a decent gem to equip can take upwards of 3 hours of constant grinding or longer depending on your luck, as each gem is given by a randomized loot box that is in itself is a random drop from dungeons. Each character can hold up to a maximum of 9 gems. Then these gems must be leveled which takes gem fragments that are given for destroying unwanted gems. The leveling gems again introduces an RNG system in which you can pay in-game currency and dust to have a random chance at leveling up the gem or possibly breaking the gem, which in turn then takes a separate time-gated currency to repair. As an added bonus, you cannot remove these gems from characters once socketed unless of course you pay the time-gated currency to unsocket them. Overall your looking at hundreds of hours of grinding and months of waiting for the time-gated currency to fully level one characters gems. Not to mention that recent patches have added mounts that grant stats increases to all of your character that can take, literally over 600 HOURS of grinding to unlock, or, of course, you can buy loot boxes with cash for an extremely low chance at one of them.
The other problem is their servers. Upon opening this game you can tell within minutes that they do not have the capability to run this large of an mmo. Lag is a constant concern in the game, so much so that certain characters whose abilities are based on skill-shots/ fast fire rates are near unplayable at times because of the inability to hit the enemy from server lag. The developers are well aware of this problem so much so that they seemingly have started to develop around these issues. In game you are capable of using potions to restore health, however, due to unbelievable server lag the chances of you actually being capable of using a potion before you die is next to none. Therefore they have introduced a potion that auto-consumes on low health, of course they have also made this potion the most expensive one in the game by nearly doubling the price. The largest concern happened when they released their latest content patch during which they have stated they are being DDoS attacked. They servers have been disconnecting everyone every 20 minutes for the past 6 DAYS. Now during this event the developers commented that this attack was not directed at them and would be fixed soon. All of which is seems massively unbelievable as if they were not the target its amazing that it coincided with their latest patch, and if it is a DDoS attack, this is an exceptionally long one, during which they have done nothing to try to circumvent the issue.
This brings me to their inability to take any criticism at all. As you can imagine a lot of the long term community is aggravated about the recent patches that introduced time-gating, overly excessive RNG, poor server performance, etc. However if you look at their official forums they seem to have only overly positive responses and forum posts. This obviously is because they ban anyone who makes any sort of criticism to the games current problems. Recently I was banned for posting this response to their DDoS attack post
for “trolling other players”.
TLDR: The game is rife with RNG, loot boxes, and uncaring developers. Which is a shame because there is an absolutely amazing MMO with real creativity under the layer of all of this crap that has recently been added. Shame, but I think I'm finally done with this game.
PS. I would love a developer to comment the state of their servers since apparently asking a developer to on their forums is ban-worthy. After all I've given over 2 thousands hours into this game, and more than enough money to by a new AAA game, the least I think I deserve is answer.

An underrated classic.
Sleeping Dogs is one of those games that while hardly mentioned regularly, most of the times ends in a circle jerk, and rightfully so. While hyped a good bit before release and achieving midly successful sales figures, it still seems to be put on the back-burner when in the midst of contemporary, and decidly lower quality titles.
Originally to be published by Activision under the title True Crime: Hong Kong, Sleeping Dogs seemed like nothing more than a disater waiting to happen, though the perseverance of its development team is truly laudable. Developed by little known United Front games, the end result would've been a tossup with their lack of lack track record.
Story: The Story of Sleeping Dogs is truly one of its shining aspects, settings a strong progression of events and plot twists. The player takes control of Wei Shen, a skilled but troubled police officer, in his assignment to infiltrate one of the many 'Triad' gangs, the 'Sun on Yee', and dismantle it from within. Lines get increasingly blurred as his loyalties waver throughout the plot, added greatly to by the games surpisingly deep back story for our protagonist.
Atmosphere: The setting and feel of Sleeping Dogs are yet more of its strong points, painting a vivid and believable interpretation of Hong Kong. The intricacies of different city districts, the clash between the criminal underground, the old world shops, and modern business all contribute to an enriching and deep experience in the city.
Gameplay: Gameplay is new and exciting, taking the best of other titles, and grinding them down into a polished system. Borrowing from the Arkham series, melee combat takes a free-flow styled system, with a large and varied set of strikes, counters, and combos, allowing fights to stay fresh without becoming stale and repetitive. Parkour is also a highly rewarding feature, letting you slide over cars, mantle buildings, and move around the city in the way you want to. Driving is very well done, even rivaling games where driving is its sole purpose.
Ratings:
Graphics: 9/10
Story: 9.5/10
Gameplay: 9.5/10
Audio: 9/10
Atmosphere: 9.5/10
Overall: 9.3/10

I have played this game on Kongregate, iOS (both iPad and iPhone versions), and now this Steam version as well.
First of all, if you haven't played Kingdom Rush before, why not? This is a great Tower Defense style game that has all the usual elements you'd expect, such as upgradable "towers." Sure, there's only four different kinds, but they all serve the traditional TD roles, and you have some choices in how to upgrade them as well through the gold you earn in battle and the stars you earn from beating levels. The gameplay itself can be a bit difficult, especially as you progress to later levels, but it is never unfairly challenging in my opinion. The cartoony art style may or may not be likeable, depending on personal tastes, but the graphics are certainly done well. Plenty of content here for people to enjoy given the cost of the game.
Now that we've established that the game is a good tower defense game, there's ultimately the question of which platform to buy it on. There's always the free version that (I think) is still available on Kongregate, but it is a simpler, older version of this game that most likely will not be updated anymore. There's also the iOS/Android(?) versions that cost $1.99/$3.99 or something around there for the base game. If you just want to just play the game, both of those versions are probably "good enough" versions for the casual gamer.
However, this Steam version does have some goodies that, personally, made it a buy for me. There are the promised extra levels and heroes, which are coming soon, and that's certainly nice, especially since they won't be available on other platforms. All the heroes that cost money in the mobile versions are also available for "free" (well, you have to buy the game obviously) here, which saves quite a bit of money (buying all the heroes on iOS costs well over $20, for example). Even though the graphics are technically not any different, they do run at 60 fps, as long as you have a decent enough computer.
What if you already own the mobile versions? Is this new version worth getting? Again, the promised extra content might be nice, though its obviously not completely clear how good it will be. I would personally suggest that you try the Kongregate version first or the iOS version when on sale so that you get an idea of how much you like the game. If you like those versions, I would suggest getting it on Steam, as it will eventually have new content that you might enjoy as long as you like the rest of the game.
To bring this long review to an end, Kingdom Rush is a fantastic game. The only decision you really have to make is which platform to get it for. If you are short on money or just want to dip your toes in casually, so to speak, the Kongregate and iOS versions offer a good enough experience for you. If however, you want the complete (eventually) experience or just want to support the developers, get the Steam version. Either way, play the game!

I bought Bastion back when it first showed up on Steam and I played a while but I never got the chance to finish. Recently I was looking for something different to play so I thought I'd fire Bastion up again and give it a play through. I love this game.
Bastion is about a boy who "wakes up" in the middle of what the game calls the Calamity. Your story is narrated as you (this boy) progress through levels that build themselves around you. This should not be confused with procedurally generated levels, rather there's a hint of where a path should be and as you move, tiles form up around you. This is a pretty cool effect even if it's totally linnear.
As you progress the story deepens, you find new weapons, upgrades, secrets etc. to battle your way through the game's enemies with a goal of restoring the Bastion, the game's home point.
I never found the combat to be particularly challenging, with enemies brodacatsting attacks well before they happen and picking up fairly predictable patterns to counter. Your weapons and skills are more than strong enough to handle everything the game throws at you. You will have the opportunity to make things harder on yourself as you complete more peices of the Bastion if you wish. Weapons can be upgraded at the Bastion's forge, adding extra damage, or critical chance etc. You'll also be able to switch out skills and buy power up type items to help you along. And at the end you'll get to unlock a new game plus mode which adds a little replayability.
Level design is pretty cool, as I mentioned above the world forms around you as you move along. Sometimes leading to dead ends, sometimes leading to secret areas containing upgrade materials, or new story items, even companion type characters. It's worth exploring every corner you can in these well built, beautifully rendered, but often very small areas.
The story itself is at first just a narration of what you do as the game's hero character, but soon enough you'll start to feel it coalescing into something bigger. As you play, the game's narrator continues to tell the stories of the boy and various survivors of the calamity. This takes place in the game itself along with aquiring items to learn about and that help tell the history of the Bastion and it's home world and the people who inhabit it. Once things begin to move the story progresses quickly and in my opinion is told pretty masterfully.
Now, Ive heard of people complaining about the narration of the game. Saying that he's too involved, or too in your face. That he never shuts up and they just want to play the game. I'm sorry to say that you can't shut the narrator off for those of you who may find him annoying. But on the other hand, he's the one telling the story, and Bastion is a story driven game so you need the narrator. I personally loved listening to him, the voice is pleasant, smooth and to me at least was nothing close to invasive. The narrator is integral to the game's story being told so you'll just have to deal with it and even if you don't like listeing to him I'm sure as things go on you'll at least be interested in what he has to say. The story itself is emotial, fairly deep and told really really well.
As is usual these days the game is short, around 6 hours I think total with potential of a couple more if you complete the optional mini games. But the fact is the story is fully told in this time, so you get a feeling of completion even though you it's a short play through, and with new game plus you can double the play value and still have fun.
Bastion, also has an epic sound track. "Zia's song", and the end theme "Coming Home" are two that stick out in my head. I believe the game even comes with a copy of the sound track if I remember corrctly.
In conclusion, Bastion, is a beautiful, short, story driven game with an excellent story and great original music. It's inexpensive and worth a play through. Give it shot I'm sure you'll dig it.

To those of you who are looking for a review in comparison to my thoughts on Terraria: you're not going to get it here, so look elsewhere. Starbound is a league of its own, and I'm tired of people expecting to come into this game thinking they can play it like Terraria, then realizing its not anything like what they were expecting. When they do that, they immediately ragequit the game and refund it without a second thought. That is not how you play games, and that is simply childish of people to do so. They miss out on several tens of hours of great content and fun, but that's their loss. It is rude and inconsiderate of people to ask a refund out of a game that someone put their time, heart, and effort into, only for people to hate it for what its not. If this is you, you do not deserve the wonderful games that people make for us.
Anyway, on with the review!
Starbound is about exploring worlds, trading with other lifeforms in the form of NPC shopkeepers, and completing quests at your leisure. The game has many things to do in it, mainly in the form of the hundreds of sidequests you can do. Some progress your tech, others simply require you to be a good person. Progressing your tech is a surefire way to increase your ablility to gather better materials, because as your ship upgrades, it unlocks the ablilty to reach said better materials.
I love the building in Starbound, simply because there are so many materials you can build with. The lighting is also very appealing in Starbound; it makes windows much more interesting and worthwhile. Because there are so many materials to build with, many styles can be made and built, and some of them are truly amazing. I have spent many hours simply building and experimenting with different materials, and gained much satisfaction from it. Furniture is also very immersive; there are so many furniture items you can craft and find, it can actually confuse me sometimes looking for specific ones in my inventory. That being said, Starbound is a wonderful game for building.
The crafting menu is also very appealing, because of how intuitive and simple it is. You can expect to need something specific when you go to craft, and you'd most likely guess it exactly. It has hardly every shocked me with something I've never heard of (besides when I first started playing it). Not only that, but it's click and go: no waiting times or specific processes. All you need is the right crafting station.
All in all, I really like Starbound, and give it a solid 9/10. The only con, I would say, is that after one of the updates, the worlds changed a bit. Everything was generally more repetitive after a while, similar to how No Man's Sky turned out. It used to be you could go somewhere and see a new monster and new world every time you landed, but then they narrowed it down on what you could find on planets. Anyway, the only thing, in my opinion, that kept me from playing this game longer. Still worth $10 (current sale) for 80 hours of awesome fun.

Bastion is a polarizing game. Basically, I feel confident in saying you will either love this game to bits and find yourself writing essays about how brilliant and deep and awesome this game really is, or find it one of the most obscenely, dangerously overrated, yet pretty good-looking and fine-sounding, piece of pretentious indie [you know that word] you'll ever play.
Luckily for you, Oh Revered Prospective Buyer, you don't need to rely on the confusing cacophony of opinions of other people to figure out which camp you'll find yourself in in. Like, don't like, and wait... why? For, you see, O Might One, this game is endowed with the Mystical Power of The Demo.
Demos are strange beasts and too often misleading ones as well, willfully tricking the Player. But this will not be the case for Bastion: you will either think this game has the most boring minute-to-minute gameplay experience of the isometric action RPGs you ever had the terrible misfortune to play, or that it'll be to you about as good an invention as The Revered Sliced Bread, maybe even a slice better.
It doesn't matter which button I'm going to press when I am done writing, because obviously the majority thinks I'm the minority and thus this one single vote is simply a drop in the ocean and won't matter one single bit. That is fine and dandy as it gives me a chance to be completely honest without incurring in any unwarranted backlash, isn't that true Almighty Community?
You won't downvote this <cough>review, because while I almost dread every single hour I spent on it (, I'm still encouraging people to be open minded instead of trusting my judgment blindly, as it were The Word, and try the demo for themselves. Which you should really do: you have very little to lose and much to gain.

Sanctum 2 has given me hours and hours of fun. There’s nothing else I even want to lead with on this one. Let’s get going.
I – Story [10/10]
Sanctum 2 is a first-person shooter, tower defense game from Coffee Stain Studios. I’m assuming that the story of Sanctum 2 is following the events of the original Sanctum and we will proceed as such. The game starts off and wastes no time launching the player into the action. The Core Guardians (a specialized military group) are alerted to a major Lume attack on the Facility (part research center, part city). After fending off the attack, the Guardians head over to a nearby hotel park where the Lumes have also showed up.
The Guardians are ordered to travel to three other outposts, following the initial attack, to defend their cores. Upon reaching the last outpost, they learn the true purpose of their mission. The Guardians are to reach the ruins of Brightholme and find an abandoned lab containing details on the origin of the attacks.
Due to the high volume of poisonous spores in the area, the Guardians must travel from core to core, activating them to sterilize spores and defending them against ensuing Lume attacks. Once they reach the lab, the Guardians discover that using the cores caused a massive increase in spore production, thereby leading to an increase in the Lumes numbers. Skye and Haigen (two of the playable Guardian characters) decide to keep the data from Britech and instead send it to Tsygan (a group of revolutionaries) whom they believe would put the data to better use.
Staying under the radar, the Guardians follow fault lines of recent earthquakes which travel in an arc through areas they have previously defended. Using the information they recovered from the lab, the Guardians also discover a large cavern beneath the original Facility. Though it seems to be man-made, it has no apparent link with the surface. After fighting their way through the swamp, the Guardians find another underground cavern with a colossal Lume that releases a torrential wave of Lumes. The giant Lume, which is hypothesized to be the source of the Lume attacks, earthquakes, and caverns fails to destroy the core.
The Guardians manage to escape the Lume and reach the surface. The giant Lume is travelling towards Elysion 1 (the largest human settlement on Loek III) with a vast army of Lumes. At this point, the credits roll and the game leaves you on a cliff hanger (leading into the DLC).
I, personally, really liked the story in this game. Not only that, but the world of Sanctum 2 is probably one of my most favorite science fiction universes I’ve ever had the privilege of exploring. I found myself feeling pretty down when I finished all of the DLC. Hopefully, it makes a glorious return and we’re all graced with a Sanctum 3.
II – UI [10/10]
The user interface in Sanctum 2 is a big part of the reason I came around to the TD genre. I’m not much of a strategist (I’m more of the charge in guns blazing type) but Sanctum 2 made it easy to learn strategy. Easy to learn, but hard to master. During the build phase, the game clearly highlights where towers and walls can be placed and what route the enemy wave will take as they enter the map. The minimap (and the ability to zoom in on said minimap) is wonderfully implemented and crucial to victory. As far as being in combat goes, I was always able to quickly locate my ammo count, health bar, and everything else I needed to know before getting eviscerated by fungus monsters.
III – Gameplay [10/10]
While the user interface was a big part of the reason I came around to the TD genre, the gameplay of Sanctum 2 is what really won me over in the end. The fact that once I had placed my towers on the map I could directly support them with my personal weapons was a hugely attractive feature. I felt much more involved with the game than just watching from above to see if my tower placement was going to work or not. Combat itself is very smooth and the controls are perfect. Everything we’ve grown to love in games is there: sprint, double jump, gibbing enemies, etc. It will seriously keep you entertained for hours on end.
The other major selling factor for me on Sanctum 2 was the co-op. The majority of my 49+ hours in Sanctum 2 was played cooperatively. The game is fun to play by yourself, but as soon as you link up with a friend or two, it gets so much better.
IV – Content [10/10]
The core game of Sanctum 2 gives you a lot of content right off. You have four playable characters to choose from (each with their own innate abilities), eight weapons, twelve towers, seventeen enemies, and a smattering of perks to upgrade your character with. Not to mention the arcade games you can play in-game that are hidden around certain maps. Oh and the maps are fully explorable; you’re not just stuck in the area of play.
There are several DLCs for Sanctum 2 and they all add a significant amount of content (one even includes a melee weapon that reminded me a lot of the Quake series).
V – Visual [10/10]
If you don’t fall in love with the art of Sanctum 2 you must be crazy. The environments are incredible, right down to the smallest detail. The enemy and character models are unique, the weapon animations are beautiful, and the towers are great fun to watch do what they do best. In between maps you get several pages of hand-drawn comics that help tell the story. After beating the map, the comic pages can all be viewed in a gallery from the main menu.
VI – Audio [10/10]
The only thing better than the sights of Sanctum 2 were it’s sounds. The music was absolutely perfect for the game and no two sound effects sounded even remotely similar. Even if you don’t get the game, do yourself a favor and get the soundtrack because I cannot stress just how worth it that would be.
VII – Overall [10/10]
Overall, Sanctum 2 is an amazing game. I got it during the Steam Holiday Sale, but I would buy it again at full price in a heartbeat.

Review of Rogue Warrior:
Brief History:
Rogue warriow is based off a novel (or novel series) about Richard ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Marcinco, a US Navy SEAL. The books, including an autobiography, and several spinoff fiction books. The autobiography calls him a "death defying" soldier, who was in the United States's SEAL Team Six, an incredibly impressive feat.
Game Summary:
In this game, you control a profanity-spewing♥♥♥♥♥♥(as the game wants him to be called) Marcinko, murder hordes of communists in hilarious and over-the-top ways. You have to blow a lot of stuff up, including submarines and missles (yes, that is the entire plot). This game takes itself too seriously (like most modern shooters, Battlefield and Call of Duty to name a few), and seems like it tries too hard to earn it's M rating. Many times per mission, Marcinko spouts profanity; including every couple of hallways, every time he is hit, or just every like he says in general. The takedown cutscenes try to be brutal, but fail. The game has glitches, such as all enemies knowing where you are and enemies being able to shoot through cover, and all glitches work against you. There is one glitch where, sometimes, your guns will have no recoil while in cover, but that was all I could find. This game is incredibly short, with two hours of main campaign time. This game has lots of achievments, but sadly you cannot get them all due to some needing multiplayer (which no one plays). This game is actually tremendously funny, mostly because of lines like, "The wind was so cold, it could freeze the balls off a f**king polar bear" and "F**k! F**k you, you f**king ametuer peices of s**t" and most of all, "Suck my balls, my giant, hairy, big f**king balls, wrap 'em around your neck you c**k-sucking motherf**kers!"
I apologize for that.
Upsides:
This game is one of the funniest you will play in a long time.
Marcinko's dialouge keeps the "flow of gameplay" consistant.
This game has a good soundtrack.
The game is surprisingly fun.
Average shooter.
Stealth kind of works a bit.
Has a cover system that would be fantastic if improved on.
Good mix of FPS and TPS (First Person and Third Person)
Has the best end credits theme of all time, no joke.
Downsides:
Game is incredibly glitchy.
Game has ways of killing you out of nowhere.
Some of Marcinko's lines make you cringe. (Such as, "Fondle my hairy nuts")
Game is WAY too short, it feels like a Call of duty: Modern Warfare DLC.
Cover system breaks a bit.
Random difficulty spikes. (One minute you kill twenty enemies, no problem. Then one guy pins/kills you a bunch)
Difficulty levels have almost no difference.
Game takes itself too seriously.
Multiplayer mode.
Nobody plays multiplayer mode.
Most guns feel the same.
No jumping.
No melee attack, you get a cutscene.
Cutscenes usually make no sense.
Reload animation doesn't match up with actual reload.
OVERALL:
3/10 (Very bad)
Last comments:
This is one of those games that is so bad, it's good. It is a bad game, but it makes for two-three hours of intense laughter. I reccomend this game to those who want a more casual shooter that supplies fun in short bursts.

One the most conflicting positive reviews I've ever had for a game.
First let's get the elephant in the room out of the way...
I understand fighting games have a hard time making bank, but this is not the way to treat the consumer. Additional characters, stages, skins, etc can either be bought with money or the in-game currency, Fight Money. For the average day working person you will not realistically purchase everything with Fight Money so you either deal with that or cave.... However, with that out of the way...
To slam the gameplay is completely unfair based on displeasure of how they deal with content unlocks. I understand it, but it doesn't change the fact that this is one of the most solid, fun, fighters out there. I will not compare it to Tekken 7 because they are very different, and both great in there own right. SF5 is much more welcome to newcomers but very difficult to master. Matches play out like high-speed chess matches, and while the learning curve can be frustrating when starting, I can easily say it is also one of the most satisfying feelings to get better in this game. Put the time into it, and you will be rewarded in ways not a lot of other games can replicate. Wait for a sale, pick a fighter, master them, enjoy.

Very fun game. Granted, it is 5 years old now, it has pretty impressive graphics. Now, I've had this game for a while and never really downloaded it because I expected it to not work on my computer. I recently decided "I might as well try it" so I downloaded it, and played it. It ran perfectly.
But I'm not here to talk about the Graphics, I'm here to talk about why it's fun.
Well, first thing I thought of when I loaded the game up was Metroid Prime. Why? Well the Main Menu, as well as the gameplay just kinda reminded me of it. Especially the Predator's playthrough. I still can't shake the Metroid Prime vibe it gives me, but I like it x3
Now, onto the campaigns:
So. The ultimate bounty hunter (next to Samus Aran of course) in your control. I didn't really know what to expect at first, but I went through the tutorial and was like "hey this game's pretty neat!" I liked how the predator could jump to areas (it's a bit weird that it didn't let me sometimes, but then I realized you have to be at a certain distance). The Predator has a variety of weapons at his disposal (who doesn't know that though) and has an interesting playstyle. I kept uncloaking accidently when I mean to use the Predator vision, but that's my own fault xD I eventually stopped the confusion, and managed to play the Predator alright.
Now this was the second campaign I decided to try out, because I wanted to get a feel of all the playstyles before I go through the entire Predator campaign. This was a drastic change from the Predator, mainly because you can't exactly jump around or use special vision to see your enemies. I didn't mind it though, I actually liked the "helpess" feel it kinda gave. It gave a more serious, and spooky, playstyle because you only have a flare and a flashlight to see in the dark, and although you do have a gun, and a radar, you still need to be on your toes. If you want a good "scare" (and I mean that lightly, more so creepy if anything), I'd say play as Marines.
You know the saying "Last but not least", or, "Save the best for last"? Well, I didn't intend to play the Aliens last, but the Predator just caught my eye first. When I played as The Alien, I actually got a very strong "I'm a pet dog" feel. I dunno, I found it entertaining to act as if I were the humans' Alien pet. But aside from that, the gameplay of the Alien was AWESOME. I don't know about you, but the mobility of the Alien, and knowing you're a huge threat to humans (and maybe Predators) gives me the
most excitement when I play as it. Why, you ask? Well, my reason is that the Alien is the coolest freakin' thing in the game (next to the Predator) to play as. I just love being able to climb on walls, hiss whenever I want, and crawl SUPER FREAKIN' FAST, as well as have a huge tail. I love the tail. I can't even explain anymore why I love the Alien so much, it's just my favorite one to play as. He's so fast, and so sneaky. Gotta love it.
I know this game is 5 years old, but hey, I decided why not try the multiplayer? I searched for a lobby, and managed to find 2 other people. Yes, the multiplayer is unfortunately very very dead, BUT I do believe that if you get a bunch of friends to play with (which I have yet to do, but I
want to), you'll most likely have a great time.
Anywho, I really do recommend this game, and it's actually on sale now for like $3.74, so get it while it's still cheap!! It's worth it, trust me.
So yeah. That's my review of Aliens vs. Predator. Try it for yourself, see which playstyle is your favorite. :)

Fran Bow is a strange and surreal game, and I don't mean that as a criticism. In fact the sheer weirdness of it is one of the reasons it is so compelling to play.
Fran begins her adventure locked in a mental institution. She wants to escape and find her best fried, her cat Mr Midnight. That will be your first order of business and I'm not really going to say any more about the plot as it its best experienced yourself.
The gameplay is a traditional point and click adventure game that will involve you collecting and using items from your inventory to solve puzzles, exploring the environment, and talking to various characters to further the plot. There are also some logic puzzles and a few mini games thrown in for good measure. I did get stuck a couple of times, but for the most part things are fairly reasonable so long as you examine each scene carefully and pay attention to what the characters you meet tell you.
The graphics have a very distinct style that I really liked and I found it grew on me the further the game went on. The scenes are vivid and the characters are well animated and that helps bring them to life. It should be pointed out that the game can be quite gory at times, which suits the morbid nature of the tale, but don't be misled by the fact that the main character is a little girl, the game has some pretty gruesome bits, so be warned. This is all balanced out by the whimsical world view of Fran herself who tends to take an innocent childlike view of proceedings, which helps lighten some of the dark moments.
There is no speech but the sound effects and music are all very well done, helping to frame and add atmosphere to each scene and location. All in all it really helps to bring the world of Fran Bow to life.
Overall this is an excellent adventure that kept me interested right til the end. It did leave me with a few questions that I would love to see answered in a future adventure, but honestly the fact that I want to see future adventures shows that these lingering questions are more on the side of curiosity than frustration.
If you like graphic adventures and don't mind a bit of a darker twist to your tales, you are sure to enjoy Fran Bow.

One of the best TD games out there! Great, colorful graphics and animation, high polish!
Lets see about those towers! 4 towers, 3 upgrades each and 2 "Ultimate" upgrade choices for each tower. And every Ultimate tower has at least 2 abilities that you can purchase! To give an example: the Archer tower shoots rapidly at land or air targets and has a good range. Every upgrade increases range and damage and upon reaching Ultimate level you can choose to turn it into a Ranger tower or a Sharpshooter tower! The Ranger tower has Roots  that can AoE stun and damage many enemies around it and Poison Arrows that deal a potent DoT to whatever they hit. The Sharpshooter tower has the longest range in the game and gets Headshot that deals massive damage or outright 1-hit KOs an enemy and Shrapnel Blast that deals massive AoE damage.
Thats just the Archer tower! The other 3 tower types all have their upgrades and 2 Ultimate tower choices!
Now, we also have to talk about the Barracks towers. Kingdom Rush was pretty much the pioneer of the barracks type towers in which actual squads of soldiers will come out of them and stand on the creep paths. These soldiers will then block/stop enemies from moving while they do battle! You can, in an area, choose where the squads will gather to protect certain parts of the path! The soldiers have their own hitpoints, damage and once upgarded to their Ultimate forms they can gain all sorts of special attacks and defensive abilities!
The enemies are also increadibly varied and Kingdrom Rush sports some of the most interesting enemy types out there. Seriously, they send a new type of enemy at you on almost EVERY single level. Every 5 or so levels you'll get a boss battle and ooooh boy some of them are pretty intense.
You also get special Heroes that you unlock as you progress through the campaign and they each have at least 2 special abilites. For example Alera Windrunner summons a tanky sabrecat and has a multishot ability that fires 4-5 arrows at groups of enemies. Heroes can level up to 10 in every battle and will do more damage and power up their abilites. You can freely move them about the battlefield to help out where its most needed!
Whew, well, don't want to make this much longer so I'll just say that if you like TD games you really can't go wrong with Kingdom Rush unless you absolutely have to have tower mazing - of which their is none in Kingdom Rush. The Steam version comes with all DLC unlocked and will be strongly supported by the devs with new content and goodies!

UPDATE 2:  A good friend insisted I give Starbound another try, so I did.  I can honestly say that I'm glad I did.  My dissapointment about the seperate races' stories still stands.  I still believe the loss of that element didn't improve the game.  That said, the overall content is strong, vast, and extremely playable.  Whether you want to build colonies, starbases, explore the galaxy, or pursue a story with a big nasty enemy and huge stakes...it's all there for you.
UPDATE:  I have no idea why, but so much of what made this game unique and fun has been stripped away in favor of a single story for go-live.  I understand the desire to want to tell a story, but there used to be one story for every race...now it's just one story.  This dissapointed me more than I can say and has resulted in the game feeling far more generic than it ever did.  Thus, I'm rescinding my reccomendation for this game at this time.  As it is, the game is essentially Terraria in space with some interesting variations.  I honestly don't understand the thinking behind the changes and am dissapointed.
Starbound is a Terraria-like game with a strong science-fiction element that revolves around a character who has been cast apart from his people for some reason and must now make a life for herself.  You start aboard your spaceship, make your way down to the planet below, and begin your adventure by trying to reassemble your ship so you can get access to the rest of the galaxy where your adventure will begin in earnest.  There is a story to pursue, items to craft, treasures to discover, and planets to explore.  It's possible to meet up with friends across the vast distances of space and hang out with them while you kill monsters and build colonies.  I've had a blast playing this game (as one can probably tell from the number of hours I've invested) and can't reccomend it highly enough.

Bastion is one of the best game's I've played in recent years. The narration and gameplay is top notch, the art style is beautiful, and the soundtrack is even more so. What sets this game aside for me is its amazing art style and soundtrack.
The story follows 'The Kid' through a post apocalyptic world, as he travels the now shattered world. As he travels the twisted streets with his lifelong friend, his hammer, he meets a stranger. This stranger tells him to collect crystal Cores to restore the bastion and hopefully they can find a solution to the calamity. The game itself can vary in difficulty. If you find the game too easy, one can activate 'God shrines' which upon activation, buff the enemies, in turn buffing the amount of xp/money the player earns. The weapons are varied, and can be upgraded and respecced to suit the player's playstyle. My only gripe is that it can be easy to miss the narration during some fights.
Final Verdict; 10/10. A masterpiece. This is the best Indie game I've ever played, also the best ending i've seen in a game. Worth every penny. A must pick up, more so during a sale.

Well, I have owned this game for years, seen it's good times and bad times. I have waited to post a review of the game due to the fact that it's simply so far from finished.
I find myself no long able to wait. When I first bought VOX the devs were very active with the community...positive and upbeat, always answering their critics with fair answers.  Slowly however, as game sales started to drop and the patches became fewer and farther in-between the dev(s) simply disappeared from the forums.  A year went by without a word from the dev, and also without any updates to the game...then 2 years.
All of a sudden a big update hits, great news right? When the community asked for patch notes the dev responded with sarcasm, saying: "everyting has changed", and he was not kidding. He did not even want to take the time to release a changelist after not updating the game for 2 years.
Well, it's been about a year since the last patch...the engine is now open source but the game is still for sale here on Steam.  The dev still refuses to interact with his supporters on Steam, but you can find him screwing around on Twitter all of the time.
I had high hopes for VOX, I really did; as of now though I have uninstalled it. No doubt the dev is upset that the game has not gone as planned...but when you ignore your paying customers for years at a time it only compounds the problem.

Honestly I tried my best liking this game. I TRIED and because I was very excited about it, I did enjoy it. But fun can only last so much when there is so little to the game.
OVERALL
DO NOT buy this game. Wait until it is completely done (and on discount) if you really like 2D fighting games. This game feels like an early access game, all the content is still being created and some characters need rebalancing.
PROS
+Very cool character design
+Online matches are somewhat good
+It has nice graphics
+It has a roster that is currently still expanding and planned to be bigger
+Very good soundtrack
+Good for beginners but not people who are just getting into fighting games (i'll explain why)
CONS
-Very simple game mechanics. Too simplistic.
-The game mostly relies on wake up situations.
-A lot of the game is left to 50/50 situations
-MP shoryuken is useless. It was supposed not to trade with air attacks but it still does.
-Anti-air jabs are still in game and lead to 50/50 situations
-Too many comeback factors
-Urien has massive amounts of mixups when he has v trigger and has a neutral button that leads to +300 damage
-Balrog is really powerful and has a strong comeback factor as well.
-Ryu is used by basically nobody in tournaments and hasn't won a single one since season 2
-Little to no reward for skills when doing combos.
-Terrible release date game*
-CAPCOM is a money milking machine*
-It has free to play elements in it
-STILL in development
-Subpar when compared to other fighting games
RELEASE DATE
On its release date this game was completely subpar. Incomplete and very wonky, very inadequate for release in my opinion.
But I gave it a chance because I love fighting games. I really enjoy them and they are the games I spent the most time in, because they are challenging to learn and have cool combos, and interesting mechanics. However, this is NOT the case for SFV. The combos are VERY easy, the game mechanics are very superficial and the online play is not rewarding.
BAD INTRODUCTION TO FIGHTING GAMES
This game is kind of good for amateur players in fighting games, the mechanics are simple, there are cool combos. But once you get to a certain level, the core mechanics of the game offer so little depth to the game, ANYONE can win in a tournament if they get lucky. The comeback factor is so strong in this game that watching a comeback is really not impressive, specially if you are Urien or Balrog, for example.
IT PLAYS LIKE A FREE TO PLAY GAME
How come a game with AAA pricing plays like a free to play game? HELL, even free to play games are more rewarding to play than SFV; the amount of fight money that you get per fight is abysmally low.
Compared to ANY fighting game, SFV is the least rewarding in all aspects. Less money per play, no arcade game, short cinematic story mode. But the least acceptable thing is definitely the survival AI. The survival mode is EXTREMELY grindy. Hard and hell mode are EXTREMELY difficult because the AI does incredible reactions to the fireballs, it knows when you pressed a button on wake up, does appropiate combos almost almost all the time and it gets to a point where the AI techs around 8 out of 10 throws in a row. This is one way to obtain all the colors of the characters that you have. Even worse, you have to play each difficulty to get the colors. Or you could just buy them, which brings me to my next point.
OBSESSIVE MONEY MILKING
CAPCOM is a company that has shown that above all the interests of the player, they want money. Make no mistake, all companies want money, but CAPCOM goes to the next level when it comes to money grinding.
Proof that CAPCOM cares more about the money than its consumers:
-Season Pass does NOT include all the character colors
-There are items that you can only get through money and not fight money
-Season Pass does NOT refund the fight money you may have spent on characters
-Online fighting only gives you money if it's not in a lobby
-Fight money is REALLY hard to get once you complete all the things the base game has to offer
-Temporarily available content that you can only pay with real money

Got this in a bundle.
There's about 7 hours of gameplay, depending on how fast you do the puzzles. It seems to be aimed towards children and has the vibe of playing a children's game throughout.. however the puzzles are definitely not aimed towards children. It also uses a large vocabulary which makes me wonder whether the game was supposed to be aimed towards children or not. I don't think that a young child would be able to complete a lot of the puzzles in the game.
The Good:
-The aesthetics, graphics, character design etc are all pretty good. I like the way the town is designed.
- The game has a lot of narration and is occasionally funny.
- It has local multiplayer. Not sure if it's any good though because i haven't tried it.
The Bad:
- The puzzles start off very easy but quickly get to be pretty difficult by the start of the second act. A lot of them i found to be not very well explained which made me end up skipping through a lot of the puzzles.
-There's a feature where you can replay a cutscene from the beginning by clicking the mouse towards the end of the cutscene. I found myself accidentally clicking just before the cutscene was over and that caused me to end up replaying entire cutscenes quite a lot.
- The game starts to become boring about halfway through, and it doesn't help that there's not much variation in the puzzles. There's 90 puzzles but there's only about 10 or so puzzles with different mechanics. You'll see a lot of the puzzles being repeated over and over but getting more different and with a different theme each time.
-You don't even need to "play" the game, because you don't actually have to complete any of the puzzles to progress- you can just fail at them and then skip them. It doesn't help that there's no achievements either which makes it have no replayability.

Sanctum 2 is a tower defence game where player has to partisipate in the defence akin to FSP-game. This combanitanation brings to the player variating challenges and intriguing gameplay. Players position lies in both desing and upkeeping the defencive maze which the looms will try their hardest to breach. The dificulty scales from easy maps at the start to excingly difflcult maps at the end.
After playing the game through once i expericed both the peerless joy of succes and and furustation of loss. The game requires that player is able to adapt to the situation  and act accordingly. On the topic of theme the graphics and soundtrack at least to me created a feeling of ambiance relevan to the situation. There is also a multiplayer option which i personally recomend since the game is to my mind designed to be cleared with 2 or more players.

The game itself is nowhere near as bad as people are making it out to be. The core mechanics are tight, and the online works as well as a modern fighting game should. Crossplay is a great feature and solves a huge issue that PC fighting games usually have.
THE BIG BUT HERE: The business model is awful, and it can cost upwards of 100$ to get the full package, and it is lacking in single player content, which some players prioritize.
That being said, the game is great for those who enjoy online play, and continues to provide a great SF experience.

I cannot believe how this game can get a negative review, this is by far the best Fallout game since they redid the series with Fallout 3 and anyone who likes open-world, sandbox exploration will love this game.
Seems most of the negative reviews focus on the storyline or have some problem with modding and price.  All I have to say about the modding is that there are tons of high quality mods and I haven't seen any that require money, mostly because I use Nexus mods which are free.  Mod authors should have the right to charge if they want, I have a right not to purchase, as with anything in real life.  Giving a negative recommendation just because a few people would like to be paid for their hard work is puzzling.  Just pretend they didn't make a mod in the first place and you have no problems.
Secondly, all the DLCs add new functionality and new assets to the game and are worth the price.  Three also add new quests and locations, you should definitely buy the GotY Edition because you'll need all the DLCs.  Mod authors use the assets and functionality to make their awesome mods for this game.  That's something the negative reviewers don't seem to understand.  They might not have the ability or work ethic to use the assets or functionality, but there are others who do and you must have the DLC in order to play mods that depend on the DLC.
Finally, the storyline.  Yes it's not the best storyline, but Fallout was never known for the great storyline.  If you're buying for a story that will get old with each and every replay, then Fallout 4 and the entire Fallout series is not for you.
To me, Fallout is all about the open world exploration and sandbox aspects.  The world is more detailed than ever and is vertical too.  For example, there's virtually another "city" up on the rooftops of Boston, complete with paths and places of interest connected by walkways from roof to roof.  The elevated highways also are explorable and have interesting "things to see".  In all, you'll find an attention to detail that is UNMATCHED in any other game I've played.  I've never seen another game with tens of thousands of handplaced items that you can remove, or move around, along with notes and stuff that will tell a mini-story (like on a dead person you find in a home).  The way the objects are placed do tell a story and add to the detail and ambiance of the location.
Then there is the settlement crafting system that lets you build incredible fortifications/structures/cities only really limited by your imagination thanks to mods.  If you don't like to build and create, then this aspect of the game will be useless to you, but I've had hundreds of hours of fun just building and making my settlements.  I've built bar lounges elevated over a swimming pool with waterfalls and multiple layers.  Yes all that can be done with mods.
Finally that brings us to the mods which are numerous and add potentially unlimited gameplay.  There are tens of thousands of mods that are free and great.  Again, I have no issue with anyone wanting to charge money for their mod, I'm just informing everyone that it's optional and any negative review based on that is ridiculous.  In all, this game should be purchased if you like open world sandbox exploration.  It's not a perfect game, but I've yet to play a perfect game without flaws.  The positives are so huge, I frankly don't understand why someone would give this game a negative review.

Aliens vs. Predator is a great modern remake of a classic PC game. Having played Aliens vs. Predator and Aliens vs. Predator 2 in the early 2000's, I had high expectations for this game and it did not disappoint. Graphically speaking the game is sleek, detailed, and surprisingly good for a 2010 release. There are several games in the series before this remake, and one sequel Alien: Isolation, released in 2014.

I really enjoy this game, but I can see some of its shortcomings. I'm just gonna go into the Pros and Cons.
Pros:
Excellent Graphics
Fast and fun combat
Surprisingly spot on meta humor (at points)
Pretty good soundtrack, not the best, but really amazing.
Cons:
Somewhat of a button-masher when it comes to combat. I enjoyed it, but I did find myself mashing buttons randomly at times, particularly during bosses.
The Narrator at times could get annoying. I played with the English narrator, maybe the Chinese narrator is better.
Low variety of enemies
Confusing story
Overall, I like this game. The meta humor is hit or miss, but when it hits, it knocks it out of the park. I can't figure out its story for the life of me. I would say it's unimportant, but it keeps being referenced. If you wanna figure it out, go ahead. At times ICEY, the protagonist, is appears to be a bad guy, at other points, a good guy.
I found myself asking the question, "is the narrator talking to me or ICEY?" which is the point to be fair.
It's obvious that the developers took inspiration from the Stanley Parable in terms of its meta humor, I read that in a QnA. However, even though I like this game better than Stanley Parable, the meta humor in the Stanley Parable was better than this game's humor. In the Stanley Parable, your choices on following the narrator or not impacted the course of the game and the ending you received; in Icey, even if you find a secret, you sooner or later must follow the arrow, there doesn't seem to be a way to continue the game after ignoring the narrator, without having to follow his instructions.
The main reason I like this game better is because of its combat, which can be a little repetitive but is still fun, and its graphics, which are amazing. I got this game during the Summer Sale, and I think it's worth its pricetag.
I give it a 7.5/10. It certainly is an obscure, overlooked game that deserves love.

Allow me to describe my first L4D experience to you...
Opens the game at 11PM on the day I got it, excited, thinking "Finally, a new zombie game, I needed one",
(Mind you, the only zombie games I've played before this were the TellTale Walking Deads and TWD: Survival Tactics)
Suddenly, the Valve logo pops up and scares the crap out of me because I had my TV volume jacked up and the lights were off and the remote was gone.
Limping to the main menu, I decide to play Survival mode to adjust myself t the controls.
The Hospital level loads, I grab the shotgun and a medkit, bust the glass door and grab a molotov, then read the prompt to "Call the elevator".
As I make my way to the elevator, I say  "Gee, I wonder where the zombies will come from", I hit the button, the continue "I hope they don't come out of the elevator! I would never survive that!" My shotgun pointed at the elevstor, I begin to hear the zombies, and I resume my sarcastic rant.
Out of nowhere, a hunter bursts out of the wall and kills me instantly.
This game took me by surpise (and made me scream like a tiny baby man).
Essentially, it's a game based on survival through teamwork. Fast-paced, this game requires you to react and keep your eyes on the prize, which is... survival. Easy to learn controls, great level design, and more than just a horde of zombies running at you. The various zombie types is reminiscent of The Last of Us and the combat is similar to that of TWD: Survival Tactics, yet refined. To put it simply, it is what TWD: Survival Tactics should have been without the stealth facors (except the Witch).
8 out of 10, well worth $20
Recommended to anyone who likes fast-paced, teamwork, zombie, or FPS games.

Fran Bow is a point-and-click adventure-horror game exploring the dark world of dementia and schizophrenia (from my interpretation), the tragedy of murder and experimentation on humans, as well as the splendour of friendship, trust and love. Few games have managed to captivate me the way Fran Bow has, and the journey through it was absolutely amazing. With that being said, next I'll outline the pros and cons of the game:
Pros:
-Unique and beautiful art style to it, different from any game I've seen before
-Amazing soundtrack, blends perfectly to the story and overall atmosphere of the game
-A meaningful and creative, albeit dark and disturbing, story. One of the best stories I have ever experienced in a game
-It is (or was) an indie game
-The ability to shift between different realities is an amazing concept, and draws you more into the game and story
-The fact that the game is point-and-click actually adds to the uniqueness and atmosphere of the game
-The length of the game is just perfect, it does not take too long to complete, neither is it too short
-The puzzles are challenging, yet not impossible. They take some thinking, but won't have you clicking for hours pointlessly
-The fact that there is no voiced dialogue adds to way the game manages to draw you into the story, although I know a few people will disagree with me on this point
Cons:
-Being able to notice what items are available for use in the game is not too clear
-There is some translation errors throughout the game

Overall, this is a work of art, a surreal, life-changing experience and I would recommend it a hundred times over.

One of the worst things you can possibly do for a narrative game wherein the player is a participant is to tell the player that they are a participant. And in that respect, ICEY commits to itself a great disservice.
From a bare bones standpoint, ICEY is a great action game. The gameplay is like a 2D adaptation of the original "Devil May Cry," with the same fast pace and relentless enemies that each offer different dangers. The enemy variety is a little small, but considering the game's relatively short span, it doesn't have quite long enough for repetition to set in and begin to annoy. The boss fights are exciting, the visual design is nice, and the levels are very secret heavy. All in all, great action game.
However, ICEY bills itself very plainly as a "META experience in disguise." And as I may have slightly mentioned in my opening paragraph, this is absolutely the worst thing it could possibly do.
I realized that I went into the game with a completely different mindset than I would have if I hadn't been bald-facedly told to defy the narrator at every turn. I like the hidden plot and its reveals, the way that the game world is designed as being sort of a giant scavenger hunt. But selling the game in the opening pitch as being similar to The Stanley Parable means that, no matter what might happen, there are no real good, meaty surprises. Because the player's mind is already tuned up to expect that he or she will be participating in a story that's going to get weird.
This doesn't mean that I disliked ICEY, I'd still reccomend it. But in truth, I'm simultaneously disappointed; even the best twists and turns the game has on offer are undercut by the sales pitch. If only the developers/publishers hadn't been so enthusiastic as to spoil the nature of the game, it could have been that much more.

To those of you who are looking for a review in comparison to my thoughts on Terraria: you're not going to get it here, so look elsewhere. Starbound is a league of its own, and I'm tired of people expecting to come into this game thinking they can play it like Terraria, then realizing its not anything like what they were expecting. When they do that, they immediately ragequit the game and refund it without a second thought. That is not how you play games, and that is simply childish of people to do so. They miss out on several tens of hours of great content and fun, but that's their loss. It is rude and inconsiderate of people to ask a refund out of a game that someone put their time, heart, and effort into, only for people to hate it for what its not. If this is you, you do not deserve the wonderful games that people make for us.
Anyway, on with the review!
Starbound is about exploring worlds, trading with other lifeforms in the form of NPC shopkeepers, and completing quests at your leisure. The game has many things to do in it, mainly in the form of the hundreds of sidequests you can do. Some progress your tech, others simply require you to be a good person. Progressing your tech is a surefire way to increase your ablility to gather better materials, because as your ship upgrades, it unlocks the ablilty to reach said better materials.
I love the building in Starbound, simply because there are so many materials you can build with. The lighting is also very appealing in Starbound; it makes windows much more interesting and worthwhile. Because there are so many materials to build with, many styles can be made and built, and some of them are truly amazing. I have spent many hours simply building and experimenting with different materials, and gained much satisfaction from it. Furniture is also very immersive; there are so many furniture items you can craft and find, it can actually confuse me sometimes looking for specific ones in my inventory. That being said, Starbound is a wonderful game for building.
The crafting menu is also very appealing, because of how intuitive and simple it is. You can expect to need something specific when you go to craft, and you'd most likely guess it exactly. It has hardly every shocked me with something I've never heard of (besides when I first started playing it). Not only that, but it's click and go: no waiting times or specific processes. All you need is the right crafting station.
All in all, I really like Starbound, and give it a solid 9/10. The only con, I would say, is that after one of the updates, the worlds changed a bit. Everything was generally more repetitive after a while, similar to how No Man's Sky turned out. It used to be you could go somewhere and see a new monster and new world every time you landed, but then they narrowed it down on what you could find on planets. Anyway, the only thing, in my opinion, that kept me from playing this game longer. Still worth $10 (current sale) for 80 hours of awesome fun.

Sadly, this game caught a lot of hate from the community because of the fact that this game is linear and story-based unlike the originals.

Is it different from the original though? Yes.
Is it fun though? HELL YES and that is all that matters.
When this game came out in 2004 it was years ahead of its time. The lighting and shadows used to enhance the mainly dark hallways and corridors of the game helped Doom 3 to whip the competition and that wasn't an easy thing to do in 2004 which was a monumental year for video game greatness (Far Cry and Half-Life 2 came out that year folks...)
This BFG Edition of the game also caught a lot of flak since people who love to complain never fail to stop complaining. The community claimed they could get the same if not better experience with mods and didn't want to pay for another version of the same game...well then DON'T pay for it dummies, if you already own the game then why complain at all? It doesn't even pertain to you.
For those that DIDN'T own this game then this is clearly the version to get since there was no need to waste time modding it...it already looks and plays great as it is. The sound effects are slightly improved (especially that weak pistol) and the game now supports modern resolutions.
The environment is so immersive and the sounds are so amazing that this was pretty much the only game that ever creaped me out the first time I played it. The original version forced you to switch to the flashlight meaning your weapon was put away...this made the game a bit more terrifying than it otherwise is now. However, that was by far the biggest complaint from the community so when they remastered it they fixed that by making the flashlight attach to the chest armor so you can have it on while shooting.
This helps alleviate some complaints that the game was too slow moving because now you can run through more like a proper Doom title and not like an "Aliens vs Predator" type of game.
I played this game for countless hours on disc but really wanted to convert my library to digital copies and since Steam released this right around the time I was ready to leave the disc world behind I picked it up and never looked back.
There are a few complaints that are indeed warranted. This version of Doom 3 comes with the original titles as well. HOWEVER...Doom 2's secret levels were modified to get rid of the swastikas and I believe the original music is also different in those levels which is not cool since those levels had some of the coolest music. That is easily rectified by just buying the originals which are still the greatest FPS titles out there.

Nothing really special compared with many other RTS out here. You start with a "sector" in a map and must expand to other sectors killing foes and creatures that inhabit them. Every territory can host a limited number of buildings - that can be expanded a little once - and time after time some enemies \ monsters tries to assault and conquer perimetral regions. Resources are essentially wood, stone, money, food, happiness, lore and fame - earn wood by woodcutters or trade, money by treasuers or trading, food with gathering or hunting, happiness with brewery and house of skalds (that generate lore too), lore with scholar-like vikings and house of skalds and longboat raiding (that also can provide fame) and fame with conquering and expanding territories and with prizes and raidings.
One can use lore to acquire new useful technologies and fame to recruit higher level units and do some nice things.
I appreciate the survival aspect: you must provide food, wood and warm clothes (for your soldiers too) for winter, because even if there isn't a day\night cycle, there are seasons.
So... a nice game but reminds me the last chapters of the Settlers series with a nibble or two by Cultures \ Northland \ 8th wonders of the world and winter survival management that recall Banished and its sequel. Of course Northgard has better graphics than the other titles above, but the gameplay isn't so different.
The very bad thing here is the price: about 20$ for a game that, also when out of Early Access (but especially now, lacking a campaign and maybe some more contents) can be selled with an honest range 5,99 - 9,99 bucks per unit.
I'm going to refund this game, thinking about buying again when price drops or when some really original and important content has been added.

Wow. Just wow. This game ought to serve as a crash course on how not to design and execute a game. A literal crash course because I beat it in less than two hours. I would've beaten it faster if I didn't die because of so much random♥♥♥♥♥♥exploding all over the place.
Let me go over all the key points that every game developer should take note of in this game, and look not to do:
- It took me less than two hours to beat it. Seriously.
- There was no option to adjust resolution or lighting quality. In fact, there's exactly four options on the video menu.
- Thank god they allowed me to turn off the motion blur, because it's so ♥♥♥♥ing intense that it makes me nauseous just thinking about it, and I'm usually a fan of motion blur in games.
- There's no vsync whatsoever, and the game has screen tears like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
- The lighting quality is so inconsistent that it makes my head hurt. Some areas are completely unlit and others are really well lit.
- The fire effects look pretty similar to a 90's FPS. They look atrocious.
- There's grenade indicators in this game, but you're the only person that can throw grenades (WTF)
- There's no subtitles. Which as I point out later, is both a good thing and a bad thing.
- There's no other option besides English to play this game in.
- Let's talk about controls...for starters, you can't even access half the controls without using a controller, as the scroll menu can't be scrolled down using either the mouse or the keyboard..you'll need a controller to even do that.
- During the game, I was told to "pull back on the left stick in order to move away from cover" when I was using mouse and keyboard.
- The horizontal and vertical sensitivity for the mouse aren't consistent. The vertical sensitivity is about half as sensitive as the horizontal sensitivity, if not less.
- The horizontal and forward/backward movement isn't consistent either. Once again, you move almost 2x as fast when moving sideways or backwards (?!) than you do moving forwards. Wat.
- Iron sights are bound to the space bar by default, and the grenade key is bound to the right mouse button. Did anyone bother to play this game on PC? Seriously..
- There's only two weapons in the game, yet there's three different binds to switch weapons, all of which do the same thing. The hell?
- Speaking of weapons, there's a grand total of 8 of them in the actual game, and NPCs only ever use and drop 3 of them. Every weapon is obtainable in every mission.
- There's a huge amount of ammo in the game, so don't worry about running out of it.
- Can one-hit-kill everything by walking up to it and pressing F.
- NPCs are completely bugged, their AI is totally ♥♥♥♥ed up beyond belief.
- Voice acting quality is legitimately terrible, everyone sounds like they're talking through a cardboard tube. I had to turn voice volume all the way up because I couldn't hear a damn thing that anyone was saying.
- Lip sync is really really off
- The volume and sensitivity options are annoying to use. Instead of being like circles or vertical bars, they're slanted boxes which makes it easy to confuse two options as being the same thing. However, if you count the number of bars filled/empty, you'll quickly realize that this isn't they aren't the same at all.
- The main character is ♥♥♥♥ing irritating with all his god damn mother♥♥♥♥ing swearing about stupid ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t because he's a ♥♥♥♥ing American, bro, and that's how ♥♥♥♥ing Americans ought to speak, you ♥♥♥♥♥♥. I had one hell of a ♥♥♥♥ing time shooting at fire extinguishers and having the main character ♥♥♥♥ing yell "YOU MOTHER♥♥♥♥ING COMMIE SON OF A ♥♥♥♥♥". Who do those ♥♥♥♥ing Red fire extinguishers think they are?
- No buildup at all to the last mission, just feels like you're doing yet another mission. THE END.
- There's three types of enemies in this game: Asian Commies, Russian Commies, and Russian Commies wearing helmets
- Each mission: kill a few guys stealthily, suddenly you can't kill everyone stealthily so you have to go loud, and then you plant bombs on things and win. That's every single mission in a nutshell.
- In the opening segment of the game, the player character rants about his team being complete badasses/hardasses. After the next loading screen, they all die in the stupidest way possible.
- There's only one or two music tracks used in the entire game. You will quickly get irritated by listening to it.
- There's so much random♥♥♥♥♥♥that blows up, you'll never have any clue how you actually die. There will usually be an explosion offscreen and then "DED."
- There's no health or damage indicators, only a very very minor change in screen color when you're about to die. You'll have to squint often to see how much health you have.
Seriously. Nobody wanted this game, nobody asked for this game, and I can't imagine what the hell was going on at Rebellion when this game was being made. Did people just smoke a joint, play Duke Nukem and say "yeah, let's do this!" That's seriously what it looks like.
PS: Bethesda, stop shoveling♥♥♥♥♥♥games like these into Quakecon bundles. Thanks.

This game is wonderful for anyone who enjoys FPS- and TD-games. It has some RPG-elements in it, allowing you to level up in order to unlock new weapons and towers. Unlike the first game there are enemies  designed to hunt down players, adding to the action.
Originally this game was riddled with game-breaking bugs but they have since been hammered out. Be warned though. This game is not like most TD-games where the difficulty slowly scales. It jumps around alot, most levels are easy-med, then SUDDENLY a murder-level. There are many towers but as you learn more about the game and start playing at higher difficulties, and survival, you will notice that only a few are worth your while, meaning that the game is fundamentally unbalanced.
However, it is still highly enjoyable both alone and with friends. The levels are absolutely stunning and exploring them is encouraged by many easter eggs, achievements, and AR-Mines that are hidden throughout the game. Take a while on every level and look up and around and enjoy the beautiful artwork. Experience an interesting story with unexpected twists and have a great time.

To start off, I've 100% completed this game and all of its achievments in 4 hours of gameplay.
I'm honestly not sure what to make of this game or the very positive reviews.
The actual gameplay is.. repetitive at best, tedious at worst. It's your standard "go into a room, room locks, leave room when enemies are dead" type game with a very basic hack and slash combat mechanic and a very small array of enemy types.
The story is.. very minimal. There is this whole side meta story thing going on but it just makes the game more tedious with its inclusion. The triggering event for all of it is always the same. Defy the narrator. Defy the Narrator, come to a room where something happens or your told something, and then the game forces you to restart the level. Forcing a restart in this game only makes it more tedious and you have to do this several times per level should you want to unlock all the side bits. Granted I ended up doing it all in under 4 hours but those were not 4 hours spent having fun, it was mostly 4 hours grinding through combat to get to the next branch and then reset. The ultimate payoff for all of this.. Is very underwhelming. Honestly the meta doesn't even really make sense, it's just kinda supposed to seem neat because it tries to link itself into a Mythos of someone elses creation.
Soundtrack is alright. But nothing special either.

Sleeping Dogs is a great game and has a lot going for it.
First of is the graphics. The game looks amazing on pc if you download the free HD texture pack. All the settings you would expect to bee in a pc game is there, and im glad to see a publisher that actually give us the full experience thats possible with a pc.
The gameplay is no less then amazing. With the focus being on hand to hand combat, and using the environment to your advantage in spectacularly violent finishing moves, makes the fighting exciting and action packed. The guns are nothing special, the fun is found in the martial art style moves you can pull off. The combos aren't hard to pull off, but still give you that satisfying feeling when you do them. you learn more advanced and damaging moves as you progress through the game, and the pacing feels right.
The story of this game is actually really solid. When i bought this game I expected a mediocre story at best, but when I got when i started playing, i found my self sucked in. I played the whole main story doing every mission back to back, which is really rare for me. The characters are well developed and the missions where really varied, and there was no feeling of doing repetitive tasks.
The world it self looks gorgeous. I love the setting, and the city feels vibrant and alive. You can pretty much go anywhere you like, and there is a lot of little minigames, like participate in illegal fighting tournaments to win cash, collecting the jade-statues for new combos, hacking securety cameras and much more.
The only downside to this game is that the best experience requires a controller. If you have one, this game is a no-brainer.
The overall experience is great. I would reccomend this game at full price to pople who enjoy openworld ''GTA-Like'' games, and at a discount this is a must have for pretty much anyone.

Normally, I don't write Steam reviews, but this case deserves an exception. To be perfectly honest, I'm not sure what to think about ICEY. I came in expecting a decent hack and slash title with a simple and effective storyline as well as competent action; what I found instead was a convoluted, frustrating experience. Granted, the game had plenty of good things going for it; for starters, the graphics, aesthetics, and animations are clear strong points, and the music and sound design is effective, but that's where all the really strong points end.
The gameplay, while simple and fun at some times, wildly varies from fairly challenging to outright sadistic; the game will throw in fair enemies one minute to giving you lots of absurdly powerful foes the next. And these enemies will frequently stun lock you, quickly draining most of your health in a single combo. This effectively forces you to play on Easy Mode and/or grind for upgrades, and even in the latter case some instances of combat will still be absurdly frustrating. And the story just makes absolutely no sense whatsoever, and that dang narrator needs to hush. I won't spoil anything here, but in order to unlock the true ending of the game, you have to find all of the achievements and trigger all of the other alternative endings; while it attempts to encourage exploration and experimentation, I feel that the way it's executed is too cumbersome and offered little satisfaction if any. Didn't help that the controls were horrid, the keyboard control layout was absolutely terrible; I found myself frequently mashing buttons and hitting wrong keys in the middle of the action.
Overall, while I appreciate the unique presentation ICEY is trying to accomplish, the experience in my opinion falls flat and well short of reasonable expectations. At one point, I even seriously considered refunding the game, something that I rarely ever do. While it has some good points, the gameplay and story clearly miss the mark; my experience with the game was completely frustrating and at no point did I feel satisfied with the game. My advice, if you play games for fun, stay away from ICEY
