Fun and challenging game which has a wide range of procedural variation that allows it to stay fresh and enjouable hundreds of hours in. No Man's Sky could have learnt quite a lot from its approach.
There's also quite a dirty satisfaction gained from getting a grossly overpowered set of items and wrecking the most powerful bosses in the game in a matter of seconds.
It has a well balanced difficulty curve that eases you into the action, and many layers that just kinda keep unfolding the more time you sink into the game. If you're a perfectionist there are a few hurdles that may make you want to cry tears of blood, some made artificially frustrating through the many grindy and unlikely attempts that have to be made.
Personally a big fan of the stylized aesthetic and themes. The story is told in a very sideways manner that you piece together, and fits with the design of the environments, enemies, items, and playable characters to comment on quite a few topics (including religion, neglect and escapism (and dead cats)).
Well worth your money if it sounds even remotely interesting. As a person who wasn't previously very much into dungeon crawlers/rouge-lite style games, this was a great introduction to the genre. Maybe hold off on the Afterbirth DLC on initial purchase, and see if the game really gells with you. It's definitely good value, but is much more of the same and isn't at all necessary for new players.

I've been looking on Starbound's development since the release of the Koala version, and I was a backer with 20$ put into it. I didn't play for that long, because It didn't have that much content that you would expect from a AAA title. Since then, the game has developed quite a lot, first with no story whatsoever, and not a lot of things to explore, although the gear/armor sets were almost complete (but they changed it slightly, to more diverse armor skins for different races.) Even then the game felt complete in terms of the kind of experience its supposed to give you, the thrilling experience, feeling scared when you're in the dark on a higher level planet, or even starting on your first night (Now the game is much much much softer for your first planet hehehe)
But that is irrelevant if you aren't a veteran, so hello new crashlanders! or Starbounders, whatever. Lets talk about the 1.0 FEATURES and CONTENT. There is a complete storyline for you to enjoy (I haven't played the Unstable version, I wanted to save the experience for 1.0 -currently playing it), a brief tutorial of what the hell you should be doing - There isn't much else for the tutorial though, you might have to use the Starbound Wiki or Forums in end-game parts. One advice, explore your first world. Really, like seriously, EXPLORE IT. You'll see the beauty of this game, and you'll have enjoyment of the content of a AAA title in just 15 minutes (fun fact: thats a complete day and night cycle for small planets). Speaking of content, this game has a lot of it. Like, A LOT. Its not just because of the ''Sandbox'' style of the game, its more because of the actual content inside that the developers and designers have made, you'll see dungeons, missions and storyline quests throughout the whole game. You'll be even playing an Atari in the future! Yes, Im not kidding, thats an actual mission - you have to beat an Atari game. Its not that ''fun'', but you'll sure have a giggle If you're above the age of 25. Im 15, even I had a laugh because It reminded me of the older ''console'' games.
After you finish the storyline quests in about a good 1,000 hours (Im being sarcastic, you might beat it in like 200 hours if you're a casual. A filthy one, you're all fil- I mean, you might be able to beat in 200 hours if you know what you're up to.) Just a side note, throwing it out there; If you get stuck on a certain Tier (you'll know what Im talking about when you're playing the game), don't worry. I had that a good couple of times, thats the nature of the game. But DO NOT cheat your way through it, It ruins the whole experience. You might find it just a tad bit grindy when you try to get out of that Tier that you're stuck in. In Koala etc. It felt really boring mining, with the occasion of epic underground caves, but now most planets are FILLED with randomly generated structures underground, and huge♥♥♥♥♥caves. After I played this game for the first time, I could not believe what great reviews it had gotten.  Let me start by saying the obvious: this is not a role-playing game.  This is an action-adventure game.  I have a very simple rule: if my character's performance depends on my reflexes, it is not a role-playing game.  If it depends on the character's reflexes, that's a role-playing game.  This is emphatically not a role-playing game.  If you are looking for an action-adventure game where your ability to do well will depend on your reflexes and your hand-eye coordination, you may enjoy this game.  You will not otherwise.  Related to that, there is the additional problem that the default controls are horrible.  The game uses w, a, s, and d for movement, but uses q for special moves.  I lost track of the number of times I burned a black potion by accidentally hitting q when all I wanted to do was move.  The game also makes it way too much of a pain in the neck just to switch one weapon for another.  All in all, I found myself fighting the interface more than the enemies.  Things got much better once I reset the controls, but they ought not to have been that lousy in the first place.
My key complaint, though, was that I bought this game because it was sold as an RPG.  It is not.
Press F to get my money back!

This game is wonderful for anyone who enjoys FPS- and TD-games. It has some RPG-elements in it, allowing you to level up in order to unlock new weapons and towers. Unlike the first game there are enemies  designed to hunt down players, adding to the action.
Originally this game was riddled with game-breaking bugs but they have since been hammered out. Be warned though. This game is not like most TD-games where the difficulty slowly scales. It jumps around alot, most levels are easy-med, then SUDDENLY a murder-level. There are many towers but as you learn more about the game and start playing at higher difficulties, and survival, you will notice that only a few are worth your while, meaning that the game is fundamentally unbalanced.
However, it is still highly enjoyable both alone and with friends. The levels are absolutely stunning and exploring them is encouraged by many easter eggs, achievements, and AR-Mines that are hidden throughout the game. Take a while on every level and look up and around and enjoy the beautiful artwork. Experience an interesting story with unexpected twists and have a great time.

This is the easiest classic 2D fighter to get into, and I highly reccomend it for people who wanna get good, but every other game scares you. The input windows for combos are larger, the concepts aren't crazy complicated, and there's tons of information out there to learn the game. It's not as shallow as most easy to get into "fighters", but the game is just far more accessable.
However, this game ain't perfect, but it's getting better (at the time of this writing). There's almost no offline modes to occupy yourself, most of your learning will be getting your rear handed to you online. Survival mode is garbage, there's no arcade mode, and the character's stories are way too short and easy. However, the general story that's been added is a pretty good challenge for a newcomer, and has a way harder difficulty. The trials that teach you combos are also fantastic, and will teach you great tech.
This game at launch was awful, but it's progressively getting better. It's still a good game, but it's not where it should be yet. I've had a ton of fun with this game for over a year now, I've met friends through the community, and each update is very exciting to see all the new potential each time. Give it a chance, just, it's really not worth $60 because of how much of the game is DLC now. Grab it on sale or somethin', dude. Or better yet, wait for the upcoming arcade edition to get all the DLC in one big bundle.

Left 4 Dead is one of my favorite games of all time. Considering as I write this review, I have played the game 793 hours, I believe it is time to write my first review on Steam :)
I first started playing Left 4 Dead in high school, in 2010. I remember at first it was scary to me (most zombie games were scary to me back then) and I jumped at the first few zombies that came out of closets etc. The graphics of the game are not bad at all, considering the year it was released, and even though the game can feel repetitive, I still had so much fun playing it.
There are three game types for Left 4 Dead. Campaign, Survival, and Versus. You can also play single player, but thats boring ;) Once you play each campaign at least once, you may think the game gets boring, but it doesn't at all. I myself had the luck of being around when an old server was up, that could hold up to 16 or so players. I began playing this server every day. Another player was in the server as well, and he was developing his own set of servers. He asked me to test his 8 player server out, and I did. In the end he had a whole set of servers, an 8 player server, 16 player server etc. We became really good friends, and the HERO clan was created.
Now you may be wondering, what does this have to do with the review? Well if I hadn't joined these servers, and this clan, I would not have half as many hours played as I do. The mods in the servers made the game much harder. 16 players would get annihilated easily by burning tanks, invisible tanks, 10 witches in one room, that sort of thing. I became one of the best players, and loved every second of it.
Now, I really detest Versus. I've never been good at being an infected. I'm not sure why, but I'd rather be the survivor, killing the infected than the infected killing the survivor. That being said, survival is pretty fun, but really challenging as well. Getting gold is really challenging, and sometimes you need a perfect team of your best friends to beat it.
Overall this game is amazing. I would recommend it to anyone who likes first person shooters, and who enjoy zombie games.

Doom 3 is a vastly different experience when compared with classic Dooms. Whereas the older games focused more on fast-paced combat, Doom 3 is more about atmosphere and story. The original Doom game engine had a lot of emphasis on lighting and darkness, so it is no surprise that ID Software opted to make that one of the focal points of the game.
Some environments, including that of Hell (which really only makes up 1 and a bit levels), look awesome, as well as some of the moments when you're able to traverse out onto the Martian surface. However this is one of the negative points I would raise; interiors such as the tech base stuff and caverns in the later part of the game can make for some pretty boring environments.
While there are some hell influences on the environment increasingly as you progress through the game, unfortunately this at times can be only subtle or to a limited extent. The original Doom often included hellish themes quite extensively, particularly during the Shores of Hell (which incorporated a mixture of themes and environements as well as whole rooms etc), this game uses the hellish theme in a more sparing manner: flesh oozing out of doors, satanic offerings and other decorations.
This difference can perhaps be explained away by story; the original had you working your way through Deimos which had been transported to hell, and so not only were there hellish decor, but large parts of the base had become completely altered into hellish enviroments (which in my opinion created more room for variety and opportunity) given its placement within hell itself. In Doom 3 on the other hand, you spend most of your time on the Mars base, thus limiting the actual amount of hellish elements that can reasonably be shown.
A couple of final notes. The weapons are mostly disappointing (especially the Shotgun), and it's a shame mods cannot be used to address this (unlike the original Doom 3 release). Another note is that the included Doom versions are altered versions. For anyone curious enough to want to check out the older games, then this is still a convenient way to do so. However, for anyone who wants the full classic experience, I recommend purchasing the originals seperately from this, and using a sourceport such as GZDoom instead of DOSBox. Otherwise, a decent re-release.

This game changed Doom from a pure FPS to a survival horror game but after a while it ceases to be scary and delves more into a blend of horror and action with a greater emphasis on the action aspect. I give the game props for trying to be different but I couldn't help but feel that it tried to do too many things halfway instead of doing one thing really well.

When you first start the game you'll notice an impressive amount of polish right away. The movement is fluid and free like you would expect from a Doom game and the graphics are very impressive. It's obvious from the start that this is a pure AAA game with a lot of heart and soul poured into it. The atmosphere is on point right away and pretty much everything is inter actable. You can even shoot friendlies right away with no consequence and I love that. There's no "failure" screen or anything like that, the game just continues like nothing happened. This first impression is very positive and even purists who might feel like this isn't a true Doom game can't help but be impressed by it. You can even interact with computer monitors and push buttons that have no purpose. This is the type of polish that impresses me in a game.

The game is slow to start but as you play there is no question: this is a Doom game. It plays almost as some sort of survival horror fps rpg. The lore never gets in the way of the action and I think they did a tremendous job of balancing the two. It almost feels like two separate games at times, scary and atmospheric in the beginning but you become so powerful later on that it becomes hard to scare you anymore except for the occasional jump scare. This blend is refreshing and interesting and I feel this was the right direction to go for the modern version of the series even though it would have been interesting to see what it could have been had they gone full survival horror.

The lore is interesting and awe inspiring at times since it involves things that would have great ramifications on the origin of humanity itself. This is a universe where hell is real after all but not necessarily God or an afterlife. The hell in the game's lore may not be the hell as we know it in the theological sense but the origin of that story which turned into our religions on earth. The story of hell was told by the Ancients in the beginning of humanity on earth and it turned into a religion. This is a fascinating point of view and take on the concept of religion and only strengthens the horror element of the game. The hell as it is portrayed in the game is entirely alien to us when looked at from a scientific point of view and you always fear that which you don't understand. Sadly this is only touched on briefly in one section towards the end and I would have loved some more exploration into this theme.

This game almost became my own personal story entitled «The Quest For The BFG». It's teased twice before you get it, once when you read it's in a room but I didn't find the room, even though I was diligent in searching, and another time you see it behind a locked door but I couldn't find the code even though I looked. I was super thrilled when I actually got it very late in the game.

The use of codes to open doors is great because you find the codes in notes scattered around the levels and you only find the doors and lockers they open later on, some times not at all if you don't search hard enough. And when you do find it there's no hand holding popup telling you what the code is or an automatic unlock. If you don't remember the code from before you have to search your notes for it and this takes time and effort. This encourages you to memorize the codes as you read them, forcing the player to use his brain. Using your brain to remember numbers in this way is very rare in games that are often just thought of as mindless shooters and it brings this game's honor up to even higher levels. It's to the game's credit that it doesn't pander to the player in that way.

Reload is slow and you can't switch weapons in the middle of a reload which makes the survival horror part of the game just that more intense, especially in the beginning of the game. I didn't think this brought it down later on however, but added another layer of strategy to combat that you have to consider. For instance, at one point I found myself in a shooting gallery up against waves of though enemies with only 7 HP and a rocket launcher with no medkit in sight. I managed to get through it because each of their attacks can be countered and it takes skill to master it. It was exhilarating and fun and I felt accomplished when I got through it. It speaks to the game's great blend of survival and shoot 'em up gameplay.

If I had to pick one thing I didn't particularly like about the game it would have to be the sentries. They often block your way making it hard to move around freely and they end up shooting you very often as well. You can destroy them though so its not the biggest deal in the world but they could get annoying at times.

One thing I found particularly funny was the Cacademons and their altered appearance in this game. They look like Fire Piranha Plants from Super Mario Brothers. They spit fireballs as well so I don't think this was pure coincidence. The Lost Souls look a little weird as well since they're basically just disembodied heads floating in mid-air but they changed their appearance in The Resurrection of Evil and The Lost Mission expansion packs along with its name to Forgotten One. These bear a closer resemblance to the classic Lost Soul, hence the name "Forgotten One", cause they had been forgotten since the classic Doom games.

As far as I know this is the only place you can play the Doom II episode No Rest For The Living on PC since it was made for xBox 360 so its inclusion was very welcome in the BFG edition of Doom 3. It plays very much like the classic doom games except the levels aren't very labyrinthian but rather made to seem like they are. They're a lot more linear than the original games with colored doors leading to the same place even though there are several doors in the same color that leads to the same room. This is done to create an illusion of a maze when it's actually just one pretty straightforward corridor. I thought these levels were a lot of fun and with the increased amount of enemies on screen and a lot more ammo readily available than previous entries it turned into a visceral shooting gallery that I found to be very enjoyable to play.

Resurrection of evil introduced a way for you to move as fast as the original games but this isn't perfect because it just makes everyone else move slowly so if you used it before all enemies are spawned in you won't be able to use it for much more than a couple of enemies. It was a nice gimmick though and not necessary to use in order to complete the levels but more of a way to avoid taking damage from human enemies.

The Resurrection of Evil and The Lost Mission DLC is great because the super shotgun, that wasn't in the main game for some reason, makes it possible to one-shot enemies, giving the game a faster pace and enabling you to do the so-called ballet of destruction that Doom is known for. This was one of the biggest things I missed from the main game.

When you first start the main game you'll notice it takes heavily from Half-Life as the beginning level of both games are nearly identical. You walk around looking at the environment, taking in the setting and talking to people and then things go terribly wrong. I believe the shift from fast to slow paced shooters in the early 2000s was a symptom of higher performance graphics, dynamic lighting and shadows and the developers needed the game's mechanics to show off this new graphical fidelity. In that way Doom 3 is a product of its time and personally I didn't have too many problems with that when the game as a whole was as good as this.

First let me say that I wanted to love this game, I saw numerous reviews hailing this as a new version of Settlers 7 / Banished and a great base builder and economy management game.
I am here to tell you that is NOT the case, not even a little bit unfortunately.
The positive aspects of the game can be summerized in basically one sentance and its all superficial stuff, the graphics are good looking, sound and music are fine and the interfaces arent bad either. Controls seem fine if at times there feels like there should be more hotkeys but its all little things (in my opinion).
The down side here is that there really isnt any strategy or logistics involved here. You start on a plot of land which can support 4 buildings total, upgradable to 5 with some gold. The ability to build certain buildings in areas is limited to requiring resource plots, so if you want a farm, you need to capture a little chunk of dirt with a farm plot available. While i understand that this helps prevent turtling in multiplayer (just dumping all your buildings into a single viking megafortress) it ulitmately creates a slow plodding and overall unsatisfying base building experience. The victory conditions are laughable (think of Civilization VI if you've played it) with things like science, fame, trade (literally just hoarde a bunch of gold) as some of the conditions. And while you can change these conditions or continue playing after they're met, the feeling you get is that they exist to end the games because once you've built one of each of the 20 different buildings, there really isnt anything else left to do... The costs of expansion continue to scale making total domitnation  nearly impossible unless you go out of your way not to accidently kill off the AI or other players. Many of the bonuses for other buildings dont work and the upgrades to harvesters also fail to function (i.e. if you upgrade tools for miners to harvest 15% more, it doesnt do anything since they just harvest 1 unit of stone/iron per trip and the total gained never increases from the base 25 units in a node) so there really isnt any satisfying reason to upgrade things or to build an empire considering the only 2 resources that matter are food and wood (dont starve and dont freeze) since stone and iron are just used for some upgrades.
So to summerize if you want a game that has logistics like Anno or base layout design items like Settlers or Banished then move along as you will be disappointed. This game feels like something that could have been a mobile game but overall the combat is far too simple (this is actually the closest things it has in common with Settlers 7, which imo was the worst part) and the other facets of the game simply arent detailed enough to be interesting.

It's not been updated for 2 years and is very much incomplete, I have no clue where the devs went, but they don't seem to care anymore. Just get blockland or something, this isn't worth any amount of money to those forsaking devs.

The graphics in Bastion look beautiful. Everything is hand drawn, colorful, sharp and shiny. The levels are detailed, the characters even more so, and the enemies look unique and interesting. Everything is also very well animated, with plenty of frames for each movement. Nothing looks choppy or half-made. There’s also plenty of variation in the art for each level, so it doesn’t get boring, even for a second.
The music is where the game really shines, though. The soundtrack has that Firefly/Western/Country atmosphere, with a bit of an eastern touch in some of the songs. Honestly, this is the first game where I’m actually considering getting the soundtrack. The sound effects are not that notable, but with the amazing soundtrack, they don’t need to be.
The story is the unique thing that Bastion brings to the table. Every minute of gameplay is narrated by an old man with a great voice. I’m not talking just about cut scenes here. Every notable thing you do is described by the narrator. This improves on the atmosphere even more than the music. It makes you connect to the protagonist and really think hard about his your actions, while also keeping you interested in how it will all fold out. There’s also an ending changing choice you make right before the end of the game which adds to the replay value a bit, unless you are like me and go to YouTube to see the alternative ending.
Totaly recommend it, 10/10

Morgan Freeman narrating anything makes it infinitely so much better. Unfortunately, not too many games feature Morgan Freeman. A rookie mistake. I mean, why would you specifically decide not to? Game design 101 here.
But worry not. Some people still know how to make a game. I mean, it's not technically Morgan Freeman. But it's close enough.
Bastion, a nifty fully-narrated action-RPG, is one of those games. It's one of those indie games. From India. They sure know how to make stuff down there.
The world has broken into a million little pieces. And it's up to you to raise them all back up, by hitting things and walking around.
An especially story-driven game, Bastion has an immersive, almost seductive atmosphere. The world is painted colorfully and vividly, the story told through short narrated clips. Like listening to your grandpa tell a story.
"Eeyup. And then he walked over here, and hit the bad guy with a hammer. Mmmhmm. 'Course, back in my day we called 'em grizzly beaters. Those bears were always trying to climb through our windows, cause back then they were made of bubble-wrap. Eeyup, I remember the first time I fought a grizzly. My old hammer, we always called 'em Ol' Sledgie, we done fought a lot of bears together. But that was during the war, and President Truman said that there were tiny Japs piloting the bears. Aim for the back of the neck, they'd say. If you caught one, they'd take you to their pot of gold. Sweet, sweet gold. Just a few bars and you could afford real windows. But they had to have bumps on them to look like bubble-wrap, otherwise the bears would get smart and come through the chimney. Mmmhmm."
That's my interpretation of the game.
So much of the story's power and emotion comes from the voice-acting. It's really quite phenomenal. The sound design in general is fantastic, and the soundtrack is a joy to listen to. There's something about listening to an old guy ramble on to the sound of acoustic strings that just works. It melds perfectly together, and gives the game a sort of western frontier vibe. In addition to grandpa's stories, there are quite a few powerful gameplay sequences that convey emotion perfectly. Bastion doesn't rely on holding your hand through cutscenes or long walls of text. The most tense and emotional scenes will be directly controlled by you, the player.
Of course, the almost hypnotic narration and sort of old-timey western vibe aren't the only things this game has in common with some of grandpa's stories.
Because this game is empty as ♥♥♥♥.
The story might go on and on, but there's no real substance to it.
As far as action-RPG's are concerned, Bastion is really not all that special. You'll discover a multitude of weapons throughout your quest, a mix of melee and projectile. There's quite a few of them. And you can equip two at a time.
But each weapon is just what it is. The knife cuts. The hammer smashes. The gun shoots. There's no real depth to any of the weapons, and the battle system is just dull because of that. You can collect special skills too, but those require using up "skill tonics" and don't generally do much more than kill things faster and flashier.
You'll enter a level, spot a monster, run over to it and mash the attack button until it's dead. Repeat until you beat the level.
There's no depth, no substance, no hook to the gameplay. It's like your mom made broccoli and cheese, but you just licked the cheese off and left the broccoli. No one wants to eat the broccoli, because it tastes like♥♥♥♥♥ They just want the cheese. The outer part of the game is perfect, and you'll savor every moment licking it clean. But when you get down to its core, it's just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥broccoli. Or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥broccoli. That hyphen makes all the difference. Gross.
As I progressed through the game, unlocking new weapons and skills, the game started to drag on quite a bit. I'd found a few weapons that I liked using, and generally gravitated towards and stuck to those weapons. Certain levels all but required using specific weapons, leaving you at a severe disadvantage if you didn't.
But some weapons were just genuinely not fun to use or felt poorly balanced compared to other weapons. I just found a play-style I liked and tended to stick with it. Whenever I'd try other combinations of weapons, they didn't always work the way I'd wanted them to.
There are mild customization options to each weapon, allowing you to do things like make your gun more of a sniping gun or more of a rapid-fire gun. Things like that. A nice touch that adds a bit more RPG to an otherwise bland button-masher. But it doesn't help too much in alleviating the repetitive gameplay.
But not only did I play through the rest of the game after it started dragging on, I enjoyed it all. The atmosphere is really that good. Of course, when presented with the option to play the game all over again in New Game+ I did certainly hesitate.
It's a fantastic gem of a game, and the design is definitely aesthetically pleasing. The gameplay might be a bit hollow, but it's still tolerable. It's definitely worth at least one playthrough. The world it paints is truly beautiful and touching, and really captures a specific essence in its story-telling. It's different, it's unique, and it's incredibly well-executed. I enjoyed my time with the game quite well.

Left 4 Dead is a CO-OP first person shooter game. The game uses Valve's well known Source engine, released in 2008.
The game is set during the aftermath of an apocalyptic pandemic, you take control of one of four protagonists, which will be known as the "Survivors". They will be pitted against hordes of infected zombies in four different game modes, a single player mode which the three other characters are controlled by the AI. A co-op campaign mode,  an online versus mode and a four player survival mode.
the game play focuses mainly on cooperation and working as a team. You will see all the regular features included in other FPS games, such as outlined teammates throughout the world, so you know where they are all the time. A cool feature which I found to be a nice surprise was if a member of your team were to fall off a ledge, they won't automatically plunge to their death, they will manage to hold onto the ledge and the other team members may go and "Help them up" much like you would do if you were healing them.
The campaign mode has six levels, each containing anywhere between three and five individual chapters in them. Each of the chapters takes place in a set environment which allows the player to explore around to find little Easter eggs, pick ups - such as medi-packs, pain pills,  weapons and ammo. These points are supposedly randomly generated so each time you play, they will be scattered around in different spots. There are tons of rooms, tunnels and buildings to explore on every level, and there is no time limit either so you can roam around to your hearts content, provided you don't mind the odd zombie jumping out of the closet to try and eat your brains every now and again.
Each of the Survivors are individually voice acted very well; and you can communicate with your team using quick menus. Some voice commands will sound off automatically such as when you are reloading, you'll let the rest of your team know so they can cover you. This to me was a small addition but added to the realism of the game.
Throughout the game you will encounter a number of different zombies which have their own special attack or mutation, such as The Boomer, which is a bloated zombie that will spit bile onto the Survivors which attracts other zombies to your location. This again adds a lot of variety to the game so you don't feel as if you are just mowing through hoards of regular zombies all the time.
The graphics, while are running on an engine which is a number of years old now, still look awesome, and games today sometimes struggle to present them selves as well as Left 4 Dead. Even with settings right the way down on low, it still looks impressive - meaning any rig or potato will be able to run this.
I played the single player campaign on normal mode; while I had no real issues finishing the game, apart from the last level, I still was satisfied with the level of challenge which was on offer, I can imagine the hard and advanced levels will be completely mind fumblingly hard though. I tried to play the campaign mode online, but sadly there weren't many games available at the time, but it is something I really want to try just to experience the co-op side of things on this game.
Pretty much every one owns Left 4 Dead already, and most will have probably already played it; but I really suggest people that haven't played it or at least purchased it but not tried it to play. You will not be disappointed and this is one of the classics of our generation that you need to experience.
P.S - if anyone would like to have a play through the campaign with me, please add me or hit me up as I would welcome any opportunity to give it ago!

Sleeping Dogs is most similar to Grand Theft Auto IV, but with better graphics and some Saints Row elements like the vehicle handling.  In game you will level up three separate meters; Triad, Cop, and Face. There is also a money system which you can use to buy clothes (part of an achievement), food to regen health (part of an achievement), and cars (part of an achievement). As explained by a cop named Pendrew, there are not many guns in Hong Kong, and thus no stores to buy them at. However, through DLC you can have the most powerful gun in the game, Assault Rifle with the Grenade Launcher, respawn in your apartment every day.
The actual time to complete all the favors, triad missions, and cop missions in the Vanilla game is about 25 hours. There are also plenty of annoying mini-games that are required for an achievement. Mini-games range from karaoke to going on dates, taking photos and street racing. Four types of collectibles will keep you busy, as they are essential to several achievements.
Repetitive ground chases that last too long just to show off the game's "parkour" and shooting chases that spawn infinite cars are this game's downfall. That, coupled with the extreme restrictiveness in missions for a game that is supposed to be open-world. Want to regen health after being stabbed or shot? No! If you walk those three steps to get a Pork bun, the city will be destroyed! What a load. Even as a bona fide police officer in the Year of the Snake DLC, you still can't even carry a gun without other cops shooting at you and arresting you.

While the game keeps getting better with each major update, it's hard to recommend Street Fighter 5 as a whole.
As a fighting game, it's fine, with a great selection of really diverse characters, interesting mechanics, really good character balance and more depth than people give it credit for.
The problem is the overall package that said fighting game mechanics come in. While the combo trials and character tutorials are well above average for the genre, Street Fighter 5 on PC is laughably poorly optimized and still lacks many key of the key features that you would find in literally every other game in the genre - the complete lack of an arcade mode being the most noteable. The game also comes with disturbingly long load times, heavy emphasis on DLC-schemes  and it won't work well with a surprising amount of controllers.
The story mode is shallow, the survival mode manages to be both exceptionally repetitive and almost entirely luck-based,
and once you're done with them, all the game really has to offer is a variety of training modes and playing others online.
If you have a high-end computer, are primarily interested in playing online and you're fine with things like regular balance overhauls that can completely change the meta, using vanilla Xbox controllers or sticks and a heavy focus on DLC - this game might be for you.
But don't be surprised if you lose interest after a few hours when you run out of things to do.

First rule of ICEY is (or should be):   Don't talk about ICEY (with people who haven't played yet).
Honestly, the less you know before you play, the better.  If someone you know and/or respect likes it and recommends it, let that suffice.  If you hate the narrator, fine.  Really... FINE.  Or not fine.  If you get angry at it or think it is too short and too linear (judging by reviews) - I urge you to try a different approach.  A different approach to what?! you might ask.  Just do something different.  Or don't do something different.  Or do something different while not doing something different (welcome to enigmaville).
If you are tempted to look at the achievements... try not to.  They can be a bit of a spoiler.  The game is all about it's surprises.  It reminds me of something I did when I was little, that I really regretted.  Did you ever open the presents under the Christmas tree (or birthday etc) early and then retape them closed?  Well, I did once.  And actiing surprised on Christmas morning wasn't fun.  I went in to ICEY blind.  And I am so glad I was.  All the surprises and twists were fabulous to be part of.
I love this game.  And I absolutely recommend it.

Right from the beginning, this is not a complimentary review. Right the otherwise.
Buy vanilla (original Doom 3) instead.
As a loving fan of the original Doom 3, I wanted to finally play RoE datadisc, plus Lost Missions pack and the original game in one bundle, so I decided to shoot several targets with one bullet by purchasing BFG edition. Instead, I shot myself in the leg.
There are few new pleasant features, bunch of eye-rolling changes and a load of NO-GOs which will make you regret not buying the vanilla Doom instead of BFG.
The pluses:
+ Support for high resolutions
+ motion blur effect looks nice (except cutscenes)
now the drawbacks:
- textures are lot worse in comparison to vanilla. Even though remastered textures provide some additional details, compression artifacts kill it all. Like playing 2001 game. Normalmap textures seem compressed too. Surfaces are no longer believable due to bumpmap posterization.
- some fire effects do not provide any air shimmer effect any more
- scenes are too bright - it certainly kills the original atmosphere
- flashlight can be turned on while holding the weapon, which, again, kills the atmosphere
- player could smash zombies with flashlight, saving some rounds. Now they must be shot since flashlight does not serve as a weapon.
- vanilla menu was IMO more appealing, with Mars rendered in shadow. BFG menu plays bright video (!!!) of rotating Mars
- maybe it was just a matter of RoE, but missing volume options made important speech inaudible in the ambient sound
- BFG edition is not directly moddable
- there is no "previous weapon" key, so I cannot conveniently switch from shotgun to sth. else mostly used
The list will be further extended.

First let me say that I wanted to love this game, I saw numerous reviews hailing this as a new version of Settlers 7 / Banished and a great base builder and economy management game.
I am here to tell you that is NOT the case, not even a little bit unfortunately.
The positive aspects of the game can be summerized in basically one sentance and its all superficial stuff, the graphics are good looking, sound and music are fine and the interfaces arent bad either. Controls seem fine if at times there feels like there should be more hotkeys but its all little things (in my opinion).
The down side here is that there really isnt any strategy or logistics involved here. You start on a plot of land which can support 4 buildings total, upgradable to 5 with some gold. The ability to build certain buildings in areas is limited to requiring resource plots, so if you want a farm, you need to capture a little chunk of dirt with a farm plot available. While i understand that this helps prevent turtling in multiplayer (just dumping all your buildings into a single viking megafortress) it ulitmately creates a slow plodding and overall unsatisfying base building experience. The victory conditions are laughable (think of Civilization VI if you've played it) with things like science, fame, trade (literally just hoarde a bunch of gold) as some of the conditions. And while you can change these conditions or continue playing after they're met, the feeling you get is that they exist to end the games because once you've built one of each of the 20 different buildings, there really isnt anything else left to do... The costs of expansion continue to scale making total domitnation  nearly impossible unless you go out of your way not to accidently kill off the AI or other players. Many of the bonuses for other buildings dont work and the upgrades to harvesters also fail to function (i.e. if you upgrade tools for miners to harvest 15% more, it doesnt do anything since they just harvest 1 unit of stone/iron per trip and the total gained never increases from the base 25 units in a node) so there really isnt any satisfying reason to upgrade things or to build an empire considering the only 2 resources that matter are food and wood (dont starve and dont freeze) since stone and iron are just used for some upgrades.
So to summerize if you want a game that has logistics like Anno or base layout design items like Settlers or Banished then move along as you will be disappointed. This game feels like something that could have been a mobile game but overall the combat is far too simple (this is actually the closest things it has in common with Settlers 7, which imo was the worst part) and the other facets of the game simply arent detailed enough to be interesting.

I've been looking on Starbound's development since the release of the Koala version, and I was a backer with 20$ put into it. I didn't play for that long, because It didn't have that much content that you would expect from a AAA title. Since then, the game has developed quite a lot, first with no story whatsoever, and not a lot of things to explore, although the gear/armor sets were almost complete (but they changed it slightly, to more diverse armor skins for different races.) Even then the game felt complete in terms of the kind of experience its supposed to give you, the thrilling experience, feeling scared when you're in the dark on a higher level planet, or even starting on your first night (Now the game is much much much softer for your first planet hehehe)
But that is irrelevant if you aren't a veteran, so hello new crashlanders! or Starbounders, whatever. Lets talk about the 1.0 FEATURES and CONTENT. There is a complete storyline for you to enjoy (I haven't played the Unstable version, I wanted to save the experience for 1.0 -currently playing it), a brief tutorial of what the hell you should be doing - There isn't much else for the tutorial though, you might have to use the Starbound Wiki or Forums in end-game parts. One advice, explore your first world. Really, like seriously, EXPLORE IT. You'll see the beauty of this game, and you'll have enjoyment of the content of a AAA title in just 15 minutes (fun fact: thats a complete day and night cycle for small planets). Speaking of content, this game has a lot of it. Like, A LOT. Its not just because of the ''Sandbox'' style of the game, its more because of the actual content inside that the developers and designers have made, you'll see dungeons, missions and storyline quests throughout the whole game. You'll be even playing an Atari in the future! Yes, Im not kidding, thats an actual mission - you have to beat an Atari game. Its not that ''fun'', but you'll sure have a giggle If you're above the age of 25. Im 15, even I had a laugh because It reminded me of the older ''console'' games.
After you finish the storyline quests in about a good 1,000 hours (Im being sarcastic, you might beat it in like 200 hours if you're a casual. A filthy one, you're all fil- I mean, you might be able to beat in 200 hours if you know what you're up to.) Just a side note, throwing it out there; If you get stuck on a certain Tier (you'll know what Im talking about when you're playing the game), don't worry. I had that a good couple of times, thats the nature of the game. But DO NOT cheat your way through it, It ruins the whole experience. You might find it just a tad bit grindy when you try to get out of that Tier that you're stuck in. In Koala etc. It felt really boring mining, with the occasion of epic underground caves, but now most planets are FILLED with randomly generated structures underground, and huge♥♥♥♥♥caves. So you might not find it that boring either. Mining has definetly improved throughout the development cycle of the game.
I'm not going to talk to you about the game that you're probably going to play in 5 minutes because Its only 8$ dollars, so be sure to add me as a friend and message me when you've explored your first ''Extreme'' world. Tell me about it! Seriously, Im not kidding. Be sure to do so! Goodbye 'till then!

Great game! This game was actually the first game I bought on steam. But that aside, this is a nice game! The best part about it in my opinion is the fact is has 3 campaigns: Marine, Alien (Xenomorph) and Predator. Let's start off with the marine campaign:
In the Marine campaign you play as Rookie (what a surprise) who's squad is killed in a Xenomorph ambush. Basicly, you're on your own for the biggest part of the campaign. You will find other marines from time to time, but they usually don't last very long. It is a funny campaign since you have 3 'boss fights' in it: The Xenomorph Queen (ironicly the first and easiest one), the battle with the Predator and the battle with Wayland. There are some different weapons you can choose but for the most part it's a general FPS with the addition of aliens and the motion tracker.
In the Alien campaign you play as Specimen 6, one of the colony's guinea pig Xenomorphs. Unlike the 2001 version of this game, you start immediately as a fully grown Xenomorph. Your goal is to break out and kill humans, and eventually predators. Very cool campaign, unfortunately it's the smallest one. The fact you can walk on any surface is also nice, and the stealth kills and finishing moves are both amazing and gory. Be aware of the androids btw, they're very dangerous...
Finally in the Predator campaign you have to hunt down the Abomination (it's basicly a Predalien). To do this, the Predator has an awesome variaty of weapons at it's disposal. The plasma rifle is overpowered, the mines are too, the smart disk can be difficult to handle with fast moving targets and the spear as well. The cloacking, stealth and the different visions really add to the feeling of the predator campaign. Once again the stealth kills and finishing moves are both amazing and gory.
There's also a multiplayer in the game with many gamemodes that barely anyone plays. Seriously, 95% of the games are Team Deathmatch or Mixed Team Deathmatch. They are fun, don't get me wrong, but it can be repetative to do the whole time. Also by playing matches you can level up and unlock new skins for your Marine, Alien or Predator.
All in all, very good game, nice graphics and lovely 3 different campaigns. Get this game if you enjoy the different play styles it offers or if you just love the Alien and Predator universe! :)
P.S. I haven't really seen anyone play the DLC maps, so I don't know why they're there :P

I set it to easy because i wanted to experice the story more than the combat, jokes on me the combat was better.
In conclusion, this game is as disappointing to me as i am to my parents. Want story go somehwere else, want repetive but flashy combat then think long and hard about how much you want to spend.

Kingdom Rush is fantastic. I've played a lot of tower defense games over the years because it's one of my favorite genres (ever since it was invented on Starcraft/Warcraft custom maps), and this is right up there in the top 5 of all time. I first played it a couple months back on Android after it was featured in one of the Humble Bundles, and it is the only game out of that bunch I played for more than an hour or so. I literally would step away from my gaming PC once or twice a day to go lounge around with my phone and play this... It's that good.
A lot of people are concerned about microtransactions in this game because that was the main way they made money from the mobile app, but the new PC version is completely different. You don't have to buy heroes, and the gem store -- which was still intact in the premium version I played on Android despite having all heroes included -- has been removed. So in addition to rebuilding the game with the Unity engine instead of porting the Flash version, they've re-balanced the difficulty of certain levels or challenges that used to be really difficult to complete without consumable power-ups.
Don't be fooled by those complaining about the $10 price tag (or $7.50 currently, at launch). A free, outdated browser version or cheaper mobile app with microtransactions is not in anyway equivalent to the brand new PC version. You could play them as sort of a demo to try out the game and see if you like it, but then you should come back to Steam and buy the best and most complete version there is or will ever be. Ironhide Games has put a lot of work into making the game look good at high resolutions and of course the interface and controls have been updated to support the keyboard & mouse. New content updates are on the way (for free), and they're dedicated to quickly fixing bugs and refining features. I'm happy to support them for their efforts in bringing a great game to the greatest platform, and once you get a taste of this TD, I think you will be, too.

Street Fighter V was a massive disappointment on launch, and sadly has done very little to fix the still lingering problems that plagued its debut.
Street Fighter V is a very underwhelming package at its price. Included is your standard versus and training modes, an incredibly underwhelming and trivially easy cinematic story mode, a single-player "survival" mode, and online multiplayer.
If you are not a competitive player, there is nothing here for you. Survival is a boring distraction, and the cinematic story mode, in addition to being terribly written and absolutely no fun to experience, is trivivally easy (there is a video of an actual infant winning a match from the story mode by mashing buttons on a stick. No, that's not a joke.)
For those more like myself, for whom single player is a secondary concern, the multiplayer aspect, both online and off, leaves much to be desired. The online matchmaking is incredibly slow, and the netcode incredibly unstable, with frequent rollbacks which anecdotal evidence has suggested typcally only affects one player at a time, leaving for some incredibly frustrating matches. Local versus mode is functional (kind of hard to screw up), but has some baffling UI decisions, like the inability for player 2 to return to the character select screen, requiring player one to initiate it. This has been a problem for a year now, and there have been no attempts to fix it.
Now, the game itself. Be warned, a lot of this is going to be largely subjective, but I don't think I'm being too rash in saying some of my opinions are widely shared by the community at large.
Street Fighter V is a game that is focused on offense to a fault. For those fans of more aggressive fighting games like Guilty Gear, Marvel vs. Capcom. or older ground-based fighters like Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike and The King of Fighters, this might sound like a very good thing, indeed. The important thing to note, however, is all of the aforementioned games balance the offense-heavy meta with very potent defensive mechanics (I won't list them all lest this review become a senior thesis).
Street Fighter V has very few defensive mechanics, and those that are there are very underpowered, making many of the higher-tier characters extremely frustrating to deal with, as you have no recourse other than eat their pressure and mixups, and with normals being extremely short, stubby, and slow, footsies feel neutered and fighting to keep yourself out of those dangerous mixup situations is harder than it reasonably should be.
There is always the possibility that this could be fixed in the future, but the updates that have been released thus far suggest Capcom will make these problems worse, rather than better. The temporary damage received from blocking medium and heavy normals has been increased, invincible reversals have lost their invincibility, and V-reversals (a strike-invincible attack done out of block stun to escape pressure) have been slowed down, making them easier to bait with a throw. Not to mention, the individual character balance changes are simply baffling. The first balance update nerfed many low-tier characters, and nerfed others to the point of uselessness, while leaving the more problematic characters unchanged when further updates were released.
I'm honestly amazed how badly Capcom screwed up with this game. I used to talk trash on the problems SFIV had, with its numerous option-selects, vortex mixups, and other goofy parts of the meta, but Street Fighter V makes those all appear incredibly minor in comparison.

tl;dr Icey is a solid 2D action game. Mechanically, it’s fighting is fantastic and feels wonderful to play. Its plot may be somewhat weak, but the meta elements are deeply appreciated despite not being as deep or engaging as it could be. However, its gameplay length is short and may not be worth the full price for the experience. Having only taken 6 plus hours to finish the achievements and many of the secrets, I recommend buying it on sale. The experience doesn’t quite justify its price, though I happily support more intelligent games like this, on top of being an excellent action game.
As an action game, Icey feels amazing to play. Its attack combos feel good to execute and are a treat to see. The enemies are varied and interesting, with a decent collection of movesets and attacks. The bosses too feel good to play against and pose a good challenge. However, there is some room for improvement; while challenging, the last few bosses felt like a sudden spike in difficulty that compared to the previous gradual rise in challenge. Also, its system to counter enemy attacks feels more luck rather than skill-based, though I accept the possibility that the fault lies with me and not the system.
As for its story plot, meta and otherwise, I go with the full recommendation of going in blind, and then a guide for the final few achievements you missed, if you’re like me and go after such things but don’t have time to crawl through every nook and cranny wondering what you missed. Its main story plot is a slightly different take on a relatively well-known world/story that I showed appreciation for its interpretation, though not necessarily its execution. In terms of its world building, Icey falls short in several levels. Without giving away any spoilers, I can say that I wished the game had given more time and thought to building its main story plot on top of its meta elements.
Speaking about its meta aspects, these secrets and dialogue are best experienced first-hand as it is nice to try to break the game only to realise it’s already been accounted for. While accurate, its comparison to the Stanley Parable unfortunately raised my expectations of the game too high. It is not as intelligent and “deep” as the Stanley Parable, though I do not believe the game has ever compared itself to it. In spite of that disappointment, it was still an enjoyable experience to outsmart and be outsmarted by the game. If you are experienced in game-breaking attempts and general disobedience in conventional games, you’ll probably be able to get most of the secrets on your first playthrough. Its commentary on certain aspects of game development and the industry were amusing, as were its 4th wall breaking.
As for its voice acting, I will say YMMV (Your Mileage May Vary), as is typical of such things. I’ve always had a better appreciation of content in its original audio form, so I decided to stick with the Mandarin voice over with English subtitles. I felt the narrator was fantastic and gave quite the inspired performance. When you are in the middle of fighting however, it can be difficult to pay attention to the subtitles, which is a minor complaint. As for the English voice over, I only tried it for the first few seconds of the game and it didn’t sit right with me. Whether it was personal bias or a weak performance I could not say.
Icey’s music is acceptable and a good accompaniment to the game. It was not terrible, but it did not have any particularly noteworthy tracks or tunes. Given that it did add to the atmosphere, it performed its role adequately.
My biggest issue with the game is its length. As mentioned previously, the game would likely have benefited from a longer length to really flesh out the world, its characters (even if it’s just Icey, the narrator and the villain) and its unique interpretation more. More than anything however, I would have liked more reason to play the game. Due to its excellent mechanics, I would love for an excuse to play more of the game, beating more bosses, exploring more levels and slaughtering more mobs. Its DLC while providing some reason to do so, and free for that matter, didn’t feel convincing enough to continue. That being said, 6 hours of solid fighting is better than 12 hours of filler.
I hope that the developers of Icey will make a sequel, or build on its brilliant game foundation. It would be nice to have another well-executed action game of this calibre and to see more about the world and/or Icey. While somewhat lacking in its depth and quantity of its content, its mechanics and unique experience give me sufficient reason to not suffer from buyer’s remorse or bemoan its lower value to money ratio. I would recommend to buy on sale to relax for a day of solid action gameplay with a meta narrator.

I find this game extremely overrated (but I would still buy it again on discount thought, it was good enough). The story feels weak, mediocre at most. It had nice moments, but mostly was really straightforward, without any plot twists whatsoever. The side missions were insanely repetitive and the races were just easy. Fights are button mashings mostly (yes, it's a brawler in open world with missions rather than sneaking or going full loud with bazookas), only collecting jade statues (12 in total, but around half of them obtainable during main missions) can upgrade your moves. You had a weapon during mission? Too bad, it won't be any more after you finish it. You have a knife to butcher through your enemies? Too bad, it will last only a couple if hits. I wonder if it was made of wood or glass it would last longer... When you get accustomed to the notion of brawling with LMB-LMB-hold LMB-LMB and catching enemy from time to time there are guns introduced, but only for a couple of missions (remember above where I said about weapon lasting only until the end of the mission?) and it feels like a really forced addon. Most of the times you would crouch behind something and then vault in from of it, the game would put a huge slo-mo and you'd headshot everyone in the room. Booooring.
What's great is the port of the game itself. The game looks beautifully, uses DX10/11, has a free HD textures pack (additional 4GB to download), the steering/controlling is responsible and I haven't find any problems with camera as well.
Like I said, I would still buy it again, I just wanted to point out the most of the things that were downgrading my experience while playing the game. Of course, there would be achievement-♥♥♥♥♥s, who would play the game until 100% (which includes lots of golden in-game awards), but I play only for the story, and everything else which isn't good enough for me is just distracting me.

A slice and dice review of such a memorable game...
Realm of the Mad God or ROTMG combines a bullet hell experience with loot galore, infused with an retro 8 bit art style with a memorable theme tune, like a opening to your favourite TV show.
The game jumpstarts after a stress free tutorial. Free to roam the realm you have been spawned into.You survey the beach type enviroment being attacked by your first encounters, as a wizard you strike back.Once finished with such one either treks inland or finds the function of teleport on the map and clicks towards the center of the map. Then the first grey screen hits you. You have been killed by "insert reason here". Then one is probably gripped onto the fully realised experience of perma-death mechanics within the game and perhaps either hooked to the progression that one can achieve-the mighty challenge. Or straight out "I quit moment". Although the idea of returning might come apparent and the idea of a new class to choose.
After a few hours one will aqcuire the knowledge of peer to peer trading, the meeting of the varied community presented, "beggers" who play the game to ask for items, the meeting of the grim reaper ;) while barely exploring pixel surface of the ROTMG experience. Digging below that surface will come the many dungeouns,events and of course facing Oryx-the mad god.  Or throw your wallet at the screen and buy the gold purchasable items for real money...But the satisfaction of such would be nill. Pets also fit under the pay to win section in some essence as you realise  how a well brought up pet can be a massive game changer. Vaults and character slots will need to be purchased with gold as well. So non-buyers may struggle.
The game is frustrating, annoying and depressing after each and every death. Yet dancing in the "Realms of the Mad Gods" is seen super fun, especially in those naive stages where the world can so vast. I think many past and present players will be able to relate and agree.
Who knew death could be so gripping?

This is my early access review so this will change in the future.
That being said, playing hours into this game has made me really love it (and sort of hate it but in a good way). On first impression, the look is really simple and gorgeous (this is my game artist side saying that). The theme, norse era, really is an interesting choice to focus on, giving a different aspect of colonization compared to other popular rts games like Civilization 6.
Gameplay, it's pretty balanced to me. You do have to think of what's the best course of action for your village - do you wanna go fast to build an army, do you want to establish trade, etc and there are different ways you can achieve to win. With hiccups, this game does not hold your hand except for the basics and I do like that. Nature, monsters and even other clans are out to get you that you can't even take a minute of break. And you are limited, so it's relevant to be careful with your citybuilding.
For first time players, this would be overwhelming. I admit, I didn't realize I was on normal and lost 6 times till I went through easy to understand the game mechanics (so a goof on me!). The AI is incredibly smart on normal and of course smarter on hard but surprisingly, I don't feel angry with every loss. I am more motivated to try again and figure out how I can do better (something I am shocked I feel this way with this genre). A game can last about 5 hours give or take, which to me is reasonable and fun. Moreover, you have different clans to try with their own different perks.
There are a few nitpicks such as weird glitches but the whole game is a gem that covers over them. I do expect some game balance in the future since resources are your stronger tools and depending on the luck of your map, you can lose easily (one example of my losses was I had absolute no land to farm/hunt that I had to depend on gatherers and sadly they died from starvation just as my scout found one land...four tiles away. :'> ).
I'm defintely gonna play more even for the achievement and mulitplayer. I'm even looking forward to what else they will add when the game is finished. Of course, this is my opinion and on single player atm. If you guys would like more opinions, check out the Yogscast's vids on Northgard, it was theirs that got me liking this game too.

I highly recommend this game! Despite being a casual game, one that you might find on a tablet or smartphone, it is incredibly fun to mess around with the physics in a desperate attempt to grab the red bars at their highest, when they generate a huge score. Oveall, this game was purely fun to play, but after about 10 minutes it gets boring, as all casual games do. So, it's enjoyable in small stints, but not suited for gaming marathons. As for the gameplay, the physics are the spotlight. They never jerk around, and the game is incredibly smooth. And it's incredibly fun when you learn how to whip your dot into the air and send it soaring across the level. Easy to learn, but hard to master, Floating Point is a perfect example of how physics in games can be incredibly fun to exploit. Although the looping music gets a little annoying after the 3rd loop, it's incredibly fun to play for a game this simple.

Imagine this scenario: you found a phone sitting there, not locked. What would you do with it? What will the phone tell you about its owner? Obviously, it's an invasion of privacy, but aren't you curious? This is a "simulation" of such a phone. You will have to piece together the clues, "hack" your way into the phone by accessing the relevant info... and figure out what happened to Laura...
The interface is clever, as it simulates the interface of a smartphone, but there are a LOT of inane conversations that you will have to scroll through. And through the exploration, you will learn how to read between the lines... Who is Laura? Who are her friends? Her co-workers? Her aspirations and dreams? Her nightmares? Does she have enemies? Does her boyfriend treat her right?
And it is an interesting story that is also a warning... The story is not real, but it is REALISTIC. Without spoilers, let's just say, consider seeking help if you see some of which happen to you or your friends.
This is an exploration / narrative game and it's interesting enough that you can go through this in 30 minutes if you go really fast. At this low price, it's about as expected.  If you are tired of high res graphics and want a bit of a narrative puzzle in the vein of "Gone Home", this is a good way to spend a little time.

Another Lost Phone: Laura’s Story is just as brilliant as its predecessor, A Normal Lost Phone. The game is a little short, even if you take your time to read everything, but the story is compelling: just like a book you can’t put down until you’ve finished reading it. Once again, the conversations are very realistic and the attention to detail is impressive. The music app has nice and relaxing tracks which won’t distract you from your reading and exploring.
The phone interface is more aesthetic and realistic than the one in the first game, and the riddles a bit more complex. Nothing too crazy though, after a bit of digging into the different apps you’ll have them solved in no time. This game had more of a progression to it, since there were more passwords to find to unlock access to new apps, it felt more like a game and less like a book unlike A Normal Lost Phone.
What truly makes it different from its predecessor is the story, which is entirely new. Once more, the game starts out just like any low-cost detective game, with the owner of the phone missing, but it ends up being so much more than that. I actually had trouble determining the truth between what all the different characters were saying and felt like I was leading my own investigation. It’s great to see a story like this get such a nice ending.
I thoroughly enjoyed this game, and I recommend it without hesitation.

I've played more of Kingdom Rush on my iPad than any other Tower Defense game I've ever played - It's absolutely fantastic.
The one problem with the iOS version was that  (as is sadly standard for the platform) it had microtransactions - there was a store that let you buy consumables (for gold you earned in-game or purchased) to use in levels, as well as one-time purchases to unlock Hero characters. The Steam version fixes this, and has no DLC or microtransactions at all - all the heroes are included in the game, and it doesn't even have the consumables store anymore.
The Steam version also includes a bunch of the bonus maps/mini-campaigns added in updates to the iOS version after launch, with the promise that the rest are coming soon in a free post-launch update that will also add a new bonus campaign exclusive to the steam version.
My only small disappointment with the steam version so far is that there's no way (that I can tell) to add a keybind to call the next wave early. There does seem to be some sort of nonfunctional keybind-manager in the game launcher, so hopefully that's something they'll add soon. (UPDATE: This is no longer true - there's now a keybind for this!)
Kingdom Rush is, in my opinion, the best TD game out there, and this Steam release is the definitive version. At $7.50 it's a steal (I can't tell you how many hours I've sunk into this game), and I strongly recommend it to anyone who even remotely enjoys TD games.

Both this and the previous-- ah, volume, I guess is the word, since they're not a deliberate sequence: no carry over characters from "A Normal..." to "Another..."-- discuss some difficult and frank topics that NEED to be discussed. I'm really looking forward to the third volume. Against habit, I might actually join the fan community for this series.

While many would consider this a rip-off of the GTA franchise, and in a sense it might be considered one, but I don't believe so. While it borrows notes from GTA, and appears to be inspired by it, it is quite a unique beast all it's own with an original storyline and a different take on the mechanics. While GTA focuses on having guns everywhere, Sleeping Dogs is more heavily emphasized on martial-arts combat and more tactical choices. The storyline is very unique, featuring Wei Shen in Hong Kong, dealing with the Triad gangs in an unusual way that was a nice twist. The actual gameplay works well, and features a 'bullet time' type of effect when jumping out of cars with a weapon, or vaulting with a weapon as well. While the graphics are a little dated, the game still plays well and is fully enjoyable. The DLC can break some of the effort you would put into it, with bonus money and experience which gives you a big head boost from the beginning. But, if you prefer to, you can turn the DLC off in the steam properties window for the game. I found the game enjoyable from start to finish, and have played it several times since then. The DLC adds some nice features like outfits with special effects. The Drunken Master outfit being one of my favorites as I enjoy watching Wei Shen fight with the style of the Jackie Chan films, and the Cop Jobs are helpful for making some exrta money. Other goodies include the Agent 47 outfit, with a silenced pistol (Guns are hard to come by!), and the Sarif Industries armor, with a bonus rifle, and reduction for incoming gunfire damage. This game is a very good investment, and the DLC makes some very nice extensions to the main storyline, with two extra episodes, and a bunch of extra opportunities. (Dr. Tang's car IS AWESOME!)

First let me just say that i'm an avid Street Fighter fan, ever since SFII on the SNES as a child through to SFIV
(and it's expansions)
But now fast-forwarding to SFV, like most i really did try to like this game, but it's impossible to simply glance over the glaring issues with this game, It has possibly the worst tact on story mode within a game i have ever witnessed, for example the character story mode lasts no more than 3 fights where you will take on an AI opponent that will pretty much just stand there like a mannequin waiting to be destroyed, it's just embarassingly bad
Then onto the simplicity of the game,
Previous Street Fighter games ( and 90% of other Fighters )  rely on you putting in the practice to be able to pull off the combos you have been working on for hours, managing your meter and just generally building up your own style of play, In SFV there is absolutely NONE of that. you will see everyone playing X character the same exact way because the game has been SO over simplified that that's the only way you can play that character, you will see the same combos and the same setups, there is just no personality. also a lot of randomness takes place within SFV, If you make 1 mistake in this game that mistake can cost you half of your life without your opponent even having to think. Randomness like this happens at the highest levels of play too, I've seen seasoned Pros who put 100s of hours of practice into the game lose to Ameteurs at high ranking tournaments regularly which despite being possible, should never happen this often, but does due to the reward of randomness.
A few other things -
V System - at 1st sounds interesting then you realise it's very unbalanced, some characters have an amazing VTrigger while others get pretty much nothing out of it in comparison ( F.A.N.G )
Same can be said for V Skills and V Reverasals.

The UI
This is purely personal preference but i just find it looks messy and unappealing, i always liked the character art when at the character select screen in previous titles but in SFV you just get the 3d ingame model posing ( some characters also have pretty noticeable clipping issues.
Looks very sloppy IMO.
Online
Overall the online is pretty stable but again not without it's issues.
Sometimes the game will display a match as a 5 bar connection (5 bar is really good) but then you get into the match and it's stuttering and teleporting all over the place. This even happens whilst i'm playing people from the same Region as me.
You're also not able to search for a list of matches, instead the game will choose your match for you, this i really dislike, for example in USFIV i could search through a list of ranked matches and see a player i recognise and know is better than me or maybe around the same skill as me or  i just generally have a rivalry with and il go ahead and join said player, but in SFV i am given a player at random.
Also SFV makes it very hard to interact with other players and build friendships within the game, even just being able to say GGs is an absolute chore,
Finding a match can take anywhere up to 15 seconds to 3/4 minutes.
Load times are really slow.
i could go on but this review has already gone on for too long,
Just a heads up, the game has had a number of updates/patches with more characters/stages being added and a more in depth story, so maybe give it a try if you see it on sale, but for me the ship has sailed.

Creepy, beautiful, with a dash of whimsy. Fran Bow deserves a spot in your library if you are a fan of horror point and click adventures.
Fran Bow's world reminds me a little of American McGee's Alice which I also enjoyed. If you prefer jump-scares, this isn't the game for you. Instead, Fran Bow is a slow, bubbling, potion concoction. Decipher what you need from a rare witch's spell book, gather exotic ingredients from far and wide, then mix them all up together in a pot of pixie blood. The smell is exquisite as you stir gently, until finally, the potion is finished after 10 hours! Your tongue trembles in anticipation as the spoon reaches closer and as the colorful liquid begins to flow all over your tastebuds, you realize something. The potion didn't work. Plus it tastes like rose water with a hint
But maybe it doesn't matter because you still had fun preparing it.
Fran Bow is a very pretty psychological(or maybe not) horror point and click adventure which has a key mechanic that revolves around the protagonist switching between normal vision and Lovecraft vision to solve puzzles. The drastic environmental change adds beautiful layers to the atmosphere and lures the player in by presenting them with the choice to go down the rabbit hole and view the horrors that lie beyond.
The story is imaginative and entertaining if a bit messy and linear. Dialogue is mostly well written and conveys the right amount of innocence and curiosity from a child's perspective while remaining clever. The puzzles are logical and tricky enough but not overwhelmingly ridiculous (I'm looking at you, King's Quest).
That said, Fran Bow isn't without flaws. The build up is fantastic and you quickly get sucked into this wonderfully creepy world filled with compelling creatures and fully immerses and engages you. However, as the chapters progress, it gets more underwhelming in terms of presentation as compared to the earlier chapters right up to the ending which was abrupt and left you wanting more but not in a good way. Instead of "Aww...that was the end? I wish there was more...", it felt like "Uh...that was the end? I wish there was more..." but Fran Bow is more about the journey and not the outcome. I highly recommend it.

Bastion is simply one of the top 3 games I have ever played. Everything about it - aesthetics, soundtrack, storyline, gameplay... everything Bastion offered, I loved.
As an adventure/beat'em up game, with RPG elements, I think Bastion poses itself in a comfortable spot where there isn't that much mechanical complexity so character creation/enhancement becomes dull nor the core game becomes so simple that things get repetitive quickly. Instead, gameplay is always evolving (mostly due to enemies and weapons), and from time to time you start to re-evaluate your combat strategies. This is particularly true if the player follows a completionist route, in which this kind of strategic evaluation applies even on the proving grounds.
Story is really emotional and satisfying - the Stranger's narration does a great job (along with the soundtrack) at bringing a great immersive experience, in which I often pictured myself as an avid listener to a story that I was actually helping to write. These feelings, among with soundtrack fluctuations and the ongoing plot, amplified most of the experience for me, to a point where all the themes the game approaches - loneliness, hope, fear of uncertainty, etc - were instantly relatable to my personal life experiences.
