When I sit down to write a review, even for a game I actively despised, I try to stay away from overly abrasive sentences and opt for something a little more elegant with my criticism. Slip doesn't deserve this. While people often wave around hyperbolic remarks with little thought as to whether they really mean them, it's with no lack of deliberation that I say Slip is complete and utter garbage on a scale I haven't had the displeasure of since grinding my teeth through Rush Bros. Simultaneously taking the best ideas from numerous games and reworking them into an intensely unpleasant mess, there's little here that could inspire even a halfhearted compliment, yet alone any reason you should waste your time playing it.
The basic mechanics behind Slip are straightforward, partly from simplicity and because we've seen them quite a few times before. You take control of a little running jumping voxel man with the power to swap his color, and sent out into deathtrap obstacle courses with a big♥♥♥♥♥laser chasing you from behind. Each obstacle in the game itself also corresponds to one of your two colors, and thus requires you to swap your polarity to make it through alive.
To put it in relative terms, it's Ikaruga and Giana Sisters with a touch of Bit.Trip Runner and Super Meat Boy thrown in for good effect. All excellent games in their own right, but when mashed together in as disorganized a way as Slip show no resemblance of the quality of what they once were.
The polarity mechanic is among the first to falter, with no consistency as to whether the same or opposing color is what kills you, and requiring you to switch at a speed that requires copious amounts of luck to pull off consistently. The level designs are routine and poorly paced, as if you took a dozen different levels, handpicked the most frustrating segments from each, and then placed them end to end for the player to suffer through. It's difficult without being enjoyable, failing to recreate either the tightly designed torture of Super Meat Boy or the meticulously structured trial-and-error of Bit.Trip Runner. As a self professed masochistic gamer I love a good challenge more than most, but making failure entertaining is a lot harder than simply making the game hard, and Slip is entirely inept at knowing how to manage this.
It also liberally misuses what I like to call 'artificial content'; something that keeps you playing the game but doesn't actually show you anything new. Slip does this by making you repeat large segments of the game through its absurd difficulty, but should you actually manage to clear the levels the severe lack of content becomes readily apparent. I can only assume the developer intended for each level to be replayed multiple times for better scores and on higher difficulties, but this means nothing if those levels were not fun the first time through.
I can understand not every indie developer can be a great artist, but if nothing else I expect the art design in their games to be consistent. Mixing voxel backdrops with neon obstacles and pseudo realistic bosses, Slip is all over the place and it's all ugly. The lackluster performance is inexcusable (I even had it crash on me at one point), and the lack of any sound effects save the underwhelming death "fuzz" simply strikes me as lazy. I can't comment on the music because it doesn't even feel like part of the game, just something playing over it as if the in game sound was disabled.
Slip was something that immediately caught my eye when I first saw it, but after getting the chance to try it first hand I'm severely disappointed. I'm honestly scratching my head to come up with something nice to say about it, but it really does botch every single thing it tries. If you've read this far and for some reason are still considering purchasing it yourself, please, do yourself a favor and play any of the other games I've mentioned first (or replay them if you already have). There's a world of outstanding games doing what Handsome Games was going for, but Slip isn't one of them and you should rest easy knowing you won't have to play it yourself.

I didn't really know what to expect from Neon Drive. I figured it'd be 80's Audiosurf, but it turned out to be a little different, and a little more.
As soon as I launched it, I was greeted with a pretty picture and some very nice synth-y music. I love this kind of 80's theme, and I was already interested to see where the devs took it.
The first two levels aren't much to speak of gameplay-wise, it's a typical Temple Run-esque type affair. Dodge the things, keep moving. The music doesn't help too much at the lower difficulty levels, but once you get to insane difficulty, it helps you do the levels with your eyes closed (and yes, I tried).
The third one is where the dev's creativity starts to show. The camera rotates to in front of the car, and a spaceship fires lasers at you to the time of the music. It immediately put a smile on my face, It still kept the same kind of gameplay, but mixed it up with some artistic design that made it feel fresh.
From then on, the game kept surprising me by choosing to go down different types of gameplay, while still keeping the same two buttons. It was difficult to get used to occasionally, but very engaging, and the art style blew me away in some levels, particularly level 5.
It's short and sweet, but definitely worth your time. I'd love to see more games with this amount of creativity and art.

Slip is one tough run and jumpish platformer. It's somewhat like a mix between Super Meat Boy and BIT TRIP. Runner. What makes this game unique though is the use of the color switch gimmick. It starts of quite easy (even at "sassy" difficulty) but gets much harder pretty fast.
You need to collect as much cubes as you can in each level and try not to lose too many lives in hopes of a score bonus, there is also a multiplier for going really fast and passing through a number of checkpoints without dying. Every level ends with a mini boss battle, which is usually even more tough than the level itself.
On top of the 12 levels that are included in the main game (don't worry, the game isn't as short as you'd think, it takes some mastering before you can reach the final boss), there are also 20 challenge maps which focus on platforming skills (those resemble Super Meat Boy the most).  It would probably also be a good idea to mention the leaderboards (which work really nicely) and the handful of unlocks for different achievements like beating a level without dying.
When it comes to the downsides - I didn't quite enjoy the music. The soundtrack consists of slow electronical tunes which I found to be quite unfitting with the fast pace of the game. I'm sure a lot of people think differently (maybe even rightfully so) but I think a drum'n'bass soundtrack would be much better if done well. I also believe that not everyone may like memorising the boss patterns for example, but I think it's great myself to be honest.
All in all, I believe this is a great indie title and I'm hoping it gets the critical acclaim it deserves. I'd recommend it to all the tough as nails platformer lovers. I'd give it an 8/10.

Wow, this game is incredible. I have been a big RTS buff since Warcraft 1, and Command and Conquer back in the day. It's one of the best RTSs I have ever played and maybe the best game I have played in the last year (not including Zelda: BOTW).  Before I get into points about what I love about Northgard let me start with some things I would love the creators to work on!
Things to work on (imo):
1.Procedural map generation while amazing, the RNG of the tiles you get can win or lose you a game. I had a game where my teammates townhall was touching the tile my town hall was on and I had nowhere to expand because I had rock above me (needless to say I lost big time). Other times I get the perfect base, which is nice but I think there should be a requirement that you have more space between players on your team, and at least 2 nearby food sources. I've also seen very large portions of expandable land generate near one player and almost none near another- sometimes looks like a piece of the island was removed.
2. This one is obvious: balance. While the clans seem fairly well balanced there are a couple of things that could use tweaking, namely: the Mercenary raiding for raven seems very powerful with how low the cooldown is, maybe a very slightly longer cooldown. Wolf seems like it could benefit from some better survival talents, while making its military prowess slightly less powerful. One berserker early, fully upgraded, has immense power. Goat seems like it could benefit from a little more synergy from its early game talents.
3. Multiplayer: maybe a chat lobby for multiplayer?
4.Music: While I love the music, I would like more, and more unique music or It would be cool if the music took breaks and during the breaks there would be some more ambient subtle music that builds back up to the regular music (for an example: the Protoss music in SC2 does this)
Reasons why the game is great:
1.precise timing and building placement don't matter as much as strategy and villager allocation.
Games like Starcraft require more precision and micro skills rather than mostly strategy, whereas Northgard requires you to take risks, and manage your resources well to win games.
2.Multiple victory conditions: you can win by trade, fame, domination, Wisdom, or even map specials.
3.The game is more about survival than attacking. Sure you can try to build up and attack, but the tile system prevents early rushing domination type situations.
4. The game is gorgeous, stunning visuals and animation, the game looks really really good and feels pretty polished.

Windscape is developed by Magic Sandbox and published by Headup Games. With no surprise, the publisher entrusted another promising developer, since I found this game to be a perfect break from the “traditional” looks and feel of many RPGs played by yours truly for quite some time.

The initiatory journey in Windscape is partaken by a brave female protagonist which quickly turns from errand girl for her family into a fully fledged warrior for an entire fantasy kingdom. The first few objectives seem simple enough, but the difficulty is appropriately ramped up as combat becomes unavoidable. Speaking of which, both the shield defense and the attack (from several melee option as well as a bow) will require some grinding for the resources required to craft the aforementioned weaponry. I still consider it a far more suiting alternative to simply buying better equipment as you progress. You will need to purchase some tools necessary for gathering/harvesting some materials, but it’s not a problem since coins are also easy to come by. The presence of different potions found in one particular in-game store, does hint most likely to a magical combat option, which remains to be implemented. Indeed many parts of the map are currently locked in Windscape’s Early Access stage. But I do like what I’ve seen so far and the story along with its heroine show enough potential.

I really like the minimal style adopted by this game. It reminded me dearly of a tougue-in-cheek mod for Skyrim in which you can play in a similar visual mode with the textures being “below the lowest initial setting”. In reality, it offered the game a new identity and as I like to quote the remarkable catchphrase, “less is more”. Vivid colors and a relaxing soundtrack smoothen the experience even further. While the visual assets (from locations and down to the enemies themselves) are diversified enough, the same cannot be said of the sounds. I really missed even a slight form of voice acting but perhaps there’s still hope for that, in the final published stage of this title. It would breathe further life into an already intriguing RPG.

+ Beautiful minimalist graphics
+ Interesting story and setting
+ Crafting system
+ Steam Achievements
- Still in Early Access
- Needs more sound variation (and voice acting)
- No Steam Trading Cards
I would have played the game for much longer if it had any levels left outside of Early Access. It was fairly gripping and with so few issues, it’s a strong contender for this year’s best indie role playing game.

This game is honestly wonderful. I recommend buying it because a) it's free, so you won't waste any money if you don't like it, but also because b) it's incredibly relaxing and smooth. Often times when you buy a game like this it tries to be artsy or 'different', but floating point is just a fun, casual experience where you try to collect as many points by moving smoothly through a randomly generated level as possible. The introduction of water can be confusing at first, but overall the game runs well, the physics are on point, and the little touches (just as the beautiful red trail creating some really cool shapes, or the water affecting the soundtrack) make it an experience. Don't expect this game to last you hours upon hours of time, but it's a great 20 minute time-waster or break game. 9/10 for what it is.

I'm not a Street Fighter veteran, so I speak from the perspective of a newcomer to the series (I know, I know, 140+ hours since launch doesn't make me exactly a newcomer anymore) even though I played tons of Street Fighter IV (and it's Super Ultra whatever variations). But I never got as invested in SFIV as I did into V.
Coming into SFV I knew exactly what I wanted: good online fun against other players. See, Street Fighter 4 did not offer me that. The online matches were always not easy to find and most of them had a lot of lag and rubberbanding in them. I hoped  SFV would offer me a better experience and for that reason I bought SFV on day 1.
And since that day 1, I haven't uninstalled it once. Because SFV gave me exactly what I had wanted: for me, the online worked exceptionally well and it never took me over couple of minutes to find a match. Not to mention I could play other game modes against CPU while waiting for the matches.
The game looks crisp and colorful, the animations are sharp and fun, the gameplay is intuitive and I haven't found any character to be bad. My favorite character of all is the newcomer Laura but I don't mind having fun with Ryu or Cammy with a bit of Akuma in between. Every now and then I learn to play another character to see if I may like them. Lesson is that I do very badly with charge characters. I admire people who master them. And speaking of mastering characters, the community help around that is great! There's tons of guides out there and thanks to the clarity of instructions, learning new combos is never a chore.
And then the storymode dropped in summer of 2016. Playing through it, I didn't find to be exactly great. As usual with fighting games, the story is so often plainly nonsensical. However, the cutscenes are all rendered in-engine which is a huge plus and they are greatly animated. The overall story is also pretty clear and satisfying enough to beat. And difficulty wise it doesn't beat around the bush, there are a few quite difficult ones, including M. Bison as the last boss which I found difficult but fair. Quite unusual for fighting games which usually throw a special boss at you with cheap moves and inhuman reaction speed. Overall, I'd say the storymode is good but it could be so much better. It's also quite short. So I'm kinda hoping more story will be added in the future.
What people most complain about is the lack of arcade mode but I personally don't mind it's absence. Survival serves a similar purpose but it also has it's issues. If you lose you start all over and it becomes an obnoxious problem on harder difficulties that make you go through 50 and 100 matches which can take a lot of time and you can't quit in the middle as you'll lose all the progress again. There's of course a possibility of Capcom listening to the pleads of the fans and a proper arcade mode may be added in the future.
Now what sets Street Fighter V apart from the rest of fighting games? Tactics. SFV is not about long combos. And button smashing gets you nowhere. SFV is a very tactical fighter that allows some serious outsmarting of your opponent. Which is why I love playing it online. Of my 140+ hours with the game, I have spent about 120 alone just fighting online against other people. I started out mashing buttons, grew into flowchart Ken (it worked for a while but it's a dangerous habit to learn, which is why I haven't touched Ken since) and finallly graduated into a tactical thinker. That took me several hours of practicing whiff punishes, counter grabs and how to beat up a turtle. But I made it. There's quite no feeling like being able to figure out your opponent and then reading them like a book. The only dangerous opponents for me are people who never use the same tactic often. I still have long ways to go in mastering the game but the journey has been fun and there's a sense of accoplishment when defeating a strong opponent with your wits.
I also really appreciate the ability to rewatch the matches. Whenever I meet a player online that plays my character better than I do, I rewatch the matches to see what I did wrong and he did better. It's quite a powerful tool that even allows you to look up professional players and watch their matches with even inputs visible so you can exactly see how they play.
So to conclude, Street Fighter V's strenghts are:
*great online
*crisp visuals
*smooth gameplay
*tactical combat
*good tools to practice
*easy to learn, hard to master
*great characters, that share similarities but also are very much different
It's weaknesses are:
*lack of arcade mode
*no tournament mode online
*slow rate of updates
*Capcom doesn't always listen to it's players
But your mileage may vary on all of those.
I'd recommend this game to people who appreciate easy to learn but hard to master games and to people who appreciate mind games. I wouldn't recommend this game to people who want to just mash some buttons.

I was going to write a good review and recommend this game for being decent and worth buying during a sale, but then I reached the Abandoned Lab level.
This level shows how very flawed the game is:
You have the ability to jump, but I would not recommend you use it. Especially if you are using a weapon with any sort of knockback. Half the time you are going to get stuck in textures, fall off the map or just fall directly through it. This is not apparent in the early levels which are simple and flat, but as soon as you reach a map with multiple props or walls... Good luck, just good luck there, buddy.
Impossible to play Sweet without getting stuck, unless you're high enough to change primary weapons.
Also, bouncing pads? Bugged as hell. Rather than shooting you to their determined destination, they just bounce you up a tiny bit and then either cause you to drop down into enemies and get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by enemies OR keep you bouncing for a good 10 secs, letting the enemies destroy your core before you can intercept them.
There's little weapon variety and useful perks in vanilla Sanctum 2. Soloing the hardest maps (even without any Feats of Strength) is going to be extremely frustrating without DLC weapons and perks... and even if you do have those... have fun grinding for hours on end to unlock them!
Multiplayer is a joke. I understand that it's a great thing if you play with a friend - and some levels are extremely difficult without co-op, but playing with 4 people quickly becomes a cluster♥♥♥♥, especially since enemies seem to get 10x hp. The 15 tower limit stays the same, so you will cap it very early unless you just pump all your resources into overcharging maxed towers - and believe me, you will be doing this most of the time in multiplayer.
If you do play Multiplayer, do not play with random people. It will be horrible.
Another annoying thing is that you will be stuck with only 4 towers to take into your game. Really doesn't give much variety. The standard cookie-cutter build is Amp + Lightning + Scatter + Kairos.  Incidentally, some of the best towers outside this selection are DLC-only.
ALSO, you will usually get the same amount of resources every wave, regardless of whether it's the first or the last. With the lower max level for towers, this is understandable, but it sometimes feels like you could have done a lot better if you had 50 more for an extra tower or upgrade.
EDIT:
Not to mention the computer resource drains if you alt-tab this game. First time I ever experienced that every single program would lock up and an on-going voice chat would lag in sync with the game's dropped framerate.

Left 4 Dead is one of my favourite kick back and kill zombie games.
The campaigns are:
No Mercy
Death Toll
Dead Air
Blood Harvest
DLC Campaigns: Crash Course. The Sacrifice.
The campaigns are fun but rather limited, though with a shadow AI the zombies aren't always in the same place.
The enemies vary each time. You have special infected such as;
Tank: Big guy (on steroids at least) is the hardest one to down. Take him down before he takes you down.
Boomer: Big ugly pus filled infected. Pukes on you which covers your vision. His boomer bile also attracts the horde.
Smoker: Long range enemy. Will grab you with his tongue and choke you.
Hunter: Close range, jumps on you, leaving you helpless until a team mate shoves him off.
Witch: The witch will be sat on the floor crying, if you get near her she will stand up and growl. Annoy her and she will come after you. She will knock you down in one hit so it is best to avoid her or just shoot the living crap out of her before she can hit you.
The campaigns are basically short movies. You hit a safe room between each chapter. Make sure you pick up a med kit, heal and grab ammo. Guns are limited. You have a machine gun, shot gun and pistols. You can also pick up molotovs and pipe bombs. There are four or five chapters in each campaign, with the last chapter classed as a finale. You cannot avoid the masses of infected that come to get you whilst you wait for the rescue to arrive. Usually after the second tank appears and is killed, the rescue vehicle arrives. Always make sure you are near where the vehicle will stop as literally hundreds of enemies will appear making it difficult to get to the vehicle. Pistols are handy to carry as they have infinite ammo.
Achievements on this game are pretty easy to pick up aside from a few. If you have three awesome friends who will have your back then you should 100% this game easily, if not then good luck to you!!

This game finds a certain type of beauty in the macabre. I am not one for point and click games but Fran Bow really found a way to tie you into the story and constaly guess what reality is for the main character. Beyond the story, it holds itself well as an atmospheric horror game. Being someone who is not easily scared there were times while I was playing where I felt that little need to look over my shoulder as I began to feel uneasy. Fran Bow does an incredible job to make you feel safe and happy when the mood and atmosphere call for it and drastically takes it away in an instant with shock and confusion. I think that ultimate duality of the game is what made me continually want to boot up the game the second I turned on the PC.
The only true con of the games, which probably truly comes to my own ability to problem solve, are the puzzles and solutions to problems. For the most part the game makes it easy to move forward without the problem solving being to daunting. But once or twice I did find myself in frustration trying to solve certain problems, this issue was very few and far between and ultimately didn't ruin my experience, but felt it just to share for those who struggle with the problem solving aspect of games!
TL;DR
-Beautiful
-Amazing Atmosphere
-Unique Duality
-Highly Recommend

My relationship with fighting games is more of a nostalgia than actual interest. As a youngster i played of course all those editions of Street Fighter 2, lots of Mortal Kombat. But these games sequels lacked something to keep me playing. After years and years I only ventured once into the genre for a few days with Soul Calibur IV... it was nice... than came Street Fighter 4... of course I waited for the SUPER Edition... and guess what... played the "ladder" and... well what shall I do now? The online modes weren't very interesting for me... the game is indeed far more advanced... and somehow... well... I won't resell it... but it is on the shelf for some time now...
It is so easy to start playing, using special attacks and combos... of course the learning curve isn't that way up to the top... which I probably will never reach... but I see a lot o potential for new comers, as well as veterans. I will not talk about fatalities and gore... because it is simply awesome... as is written in every review on this planet.
What I consider a major update to the fighting genre is the
story-mode,which retells the events of the first 3 MK games. It is done
beautifully... B-movie style... it is so corny and over the top... a guilty
pleasure! And I don't know how Legacy will be reviewed once it is done (so far I am not a fan), but
this story-mode is the best motion picture experience of all times,
regarding the MK franchise of course!
I don't see the need to write about the insane amount of unlockables,
modes, tag-team specific combos, challenge towers, and all this stuff that
amounts to an unbelievable amount of content... You may argue which is the best fighter out there... but no doubt, MK9 is
the biggest (content-wise) fighter... and for me - not being a
tournament-profi-gamer - this accounts for far more than the supposed
little bit better fighting system in SSF4...

Update: I played the game again on normal difficulty. I saw the great reviews that this game has and thought, well there must be something here so maybe I'll play at least a little further in. No, it just made me dislike this game ever so more. The narrator's voice and voicelines are so bad. "Icey jumped over [insert what she jumped over]", "Icey fell down [insert what she fell down]". It just starts to make you go crazy. I understand that the creator did that, so that when you get to the Stanley Parable parts, where you can go off course, it feels more like you are denying something strict and obvious, but it ends up being just annoying because there was no choice there, there was no plot there, you were just going through the level. And the voice acting, plain and simple, was bad.
But what irritated me the most and probably makes this one of my most disliked games of all time, is that when you deny the narrator, go to this warehouse area, and go through a door, there is a loosely drawn level, and the creator of the game with the annoying voice actor cries to you about how he spent ten years getting to this point in the game development, how he is just a small indie developer who is strapped for cash, and how he put so much time and effort into developing this game. AND THEN HE HAS THE NERVE TO TELL YOU TO GIVE HIS GAME A 5 STAR RATING, because he says, glitches and a lack of content are to be expected of a low budget game like this, you spend all your money on games made on big developers that you won't even finish SO WHY NOT 5 STAR THIS AND BUY ANOTHER COPY! I probably sound a jerk here. Indie developers do have a hard time getting cash and they have to work epecially long and hard at making their games, but let me tell you. This is not the only Indie game on Steam by far. This is not the best Indie game on Steam by far. So don't try to make people impressed with you / pity you and then make them feel bad about buying too many games and then TELL THEM TO GIVE YOU A FULL 5 STAR RATING when the game does not deserve it. And people on Steam have bought into this and reviewed this game extremely positively, increasing sales (just look at some of them simply say they rated it positively because of the narrator). If you liked the game, great, but the reviews should not be skewed because of this kind of overly unhumble entreaty.
... I also want to note that the combat is not bad but not great. The dodge counter system for larger enemies is good. Combat is not as smooth as Dust: An Elysian Tale, though, by far, because of unpolished enemy attacks (and their attack ranges) and the fact that there isn't any actual way to dodge (the dash, unless in the counter movement, will just make you or the shield get hit).
The voice acting for Dust was much better as well as it actually had emotion and feeling in it.
The story after the beginning just sounds ridiculous, talking about how the evil cyborg Judas wants to "create a child of god". I don't know if this is a bad mistranslation, but this is the type of theme that I have seen poorly adapted by a lot of chinese media like Manhua and novels (there are good Chinese media out there like ISSTH, though). The narrator also talks about how Icey feels like the sewer level didn't used to be a sewer, but you look at the design for the level and how the walkway and sewer walls are and I'm pretty sure that it is a typical large sewer but with evil robots and raised platforms. I guess it could be a train tunnel but train tunnels don't have sheer drop offs.
The game is very hard (because of the enemy design) on hard mode, but is much easier on normal mode.
I'm doing this review in the hopes that you, the reader, are more informed than I was before buying this game. I'd give this game 2.5 stars or a 5/10. I'd give it a 6.5/10 if it didn't have the begging scene and narrator with some feeling.

I saw this game on sale for a pretty good price. Good thing that it was for a good price because I'm not going to be able to finish it. It seemed okay at first. You play a Hatsune Miku like character and go through interesting levels with interesting art. There is a hint toward a complex storyline with unexpected twists. However, after getting past the tutorial a narrator comes out and starts narrating everything that you do. I know that there are some popular games out there that do this, but, for myself, it just really annoys me unless I really like the voice of the voice actor or it is the type of game where a narrator's voice acting gives a nice comedic effect to the story (this is only viable in certian kinds of storylines in my opinion). Thus, the average voice acting and uninteresting lines just drove me away from this game.
The other reason that I couldn't play this game to the end is that they introduce these extremely annoying fly things that shoot instant laser beams at you. This would be fine normally (I find these annoying but not game breaking in most games), however, 1. the laser beams stun you, 2. the rate of fire is about two seconds, 3. multiple flies start showing up, 4. there are other enemies that are designed to punish you when you jump to destroy the flies, and 5. the beams cover a lot of the level and if you dash through them you get hit. So, you just keep constantly dying, because you can't kill the flies without taking massive damage and neither can you defeat the enemies because the flies will inevitably stun block you and you'll get hit for massive damage by the horde around you.
The art is good for a low budget game but I didn't especially like it enough to overlook its flaws. I really don't like the design of the villain.
The music cut out often and I didn't especially like it.
I confess that I started the game and ended up choosing hard difficulty. I could go back, reset the game, and choose easy mode, but I don't find it worth it at this moment. The story might be worth it, but everything else isn't.
I've never had a game that keeps getting better every time I play it. Infinite replayability and an all around great game. Perfect 5/7.

I'd hardly say this is a bad game. Just a bad port.
1st, BFG edition performs far worse for me than the original. As a matter of fact the original DooM3 runs like a charm in 1080p + widescreen hacks even with Sikkmod and Wulfen textures. However here my system struggles just to run it even without AA and Motion Blur. Furthermore, i can't lower the resolution to get any performance increase because the game is forced into borderless! Everytime i try to lower the resolution it just ends up as a borderless window in the corner of my screen.The game also has a bad habit of stuttering. My bloody assualt rifle sounds like some nitwit put the sounds through a swing filter and other times the game freezes for a few seconds whenever an imp throughs a fireball at me. To make matterd worse, at completely random the game just decides to slow down to the point it feels like it's running on a 486.
Something about the gameplay that bothers me is the flashlight. Originally in DooM3 you would have to switch away from whatever weapon you were using to use the flashlight. It sucked but that's how it was. Here however you can use the flashlight whenever you want. To be honest i appreciate the change but alot of areas feel far too easy with it and the game loses it's atmoshphere because everything is just lit up so brightly.
The lack of options is what really bothers me the most. The only graphical options availiable is Resolution, Anti-Aliasing, FOV and Flashlight shadows. No texutre options nor Anistopery. I had to force it in my GPU control panel because there wasn't a single option in the options. It also sucks that you can't change the type of AA or even know what kind of AA you're using. Is it FXAA? SMAA? MSAA?
If you were hoping for multiplayer then guess what? You have it! But good luck finding another player. Most players are probably playing the original. And do you hate people who use open mics in online games? Wel; guess what? You're stuck using Open Mic with whatever multiplayer games you find! There's no option for press to talk either!
I can really only reccomend this if you're looking for a good DooM3 port on console. I haven't played it on console because i'm farly content with both my PC copies but it feels like it was designed for console so i'm sure it's good there.
TL;DR: Get the original DooM3. It's probably cheaper most of the time, it runs better and if the visuals bother you, have a whole community out there full of all sorts of mods to improve it.

Windscape:
~~~~~~~~~

What scenery! Sitting against a stack of hay, looking at the beautiful blue sky with floating islands all around - it’s magic! It’s times like this that make living on a farm truly blissful. Well, your five minutes of rest are up! There are plenty of responsibilities on and around the farm. Hop up my friends, let’s explore the world of Windscape.
Windscape is a first person/adventure/RPG game where you play Ida, a young girl who lives on her parents’ farm.  At the start of the game, Ida will have to do a couple of farm quests so she can make a meat stew for dinner. After successfully cooking your first meal, your father will give you a quest to complete, along with a club and shield to defend yourself for your upcoming encounters during your travel.
What would you encounter within each quest? Angry wolfs, giant bees, spiders and nasty bandits, of which some will be armed with weapons and others will shoot fire balls. As this game is currently on early access, they are only a few quests at this stage. One aspect of the game I really enjoy is the crafting experience, it is great and simple. It will tell you how many items and quantities to collect to craft either a weapon, a potion or a meal, which restore some of your health. Also, each time you reach a totem, your game will be saved automatically and your health will be restored.
The fighting scene can be a bit awkward at times, but you will get used to it fairly quickly. As you eliminate an enemy, you might receive a bag of gold which you can use to purchase useful items at the general or alchemist stores, as well as hearts which will restore your health or other items. When you visit one of the general stores, make sure to purchase an axe to cut trees and a pick axe to brake stones.
This early access is full of potential in my opinion; I like the artwork and the feel of the game. For the controls, I would use the mouse and keyboard but this is a personal preference. In regards to music, it blends really well with the game.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great artwork
-	Easy crafting
-	Nice gameplay
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Need more content
-	No achievements or trading cards
Windscape is definitely a game to keep an eye on. I am looking forward to new updates! Great potential!
7/10

Slip is one heck of a hardcore precision-platformer. Here, it's not all about timing your jumps right only though...you also have a colour swapping mechanic, and there are bullet-hell shooter elements as well.
Mind you, the colour swapping mechanic makes the game really tough, at least initially until you get used to it. It kind of messes with your mind, since your mind has to process two things accurately at the same time - jumping and swapping the colours. I presume as you play more, you'd master the color swapping mechanic better, and get less confused.
Even from the first level itself, the game is difficult. As of the time of writing this review, I have played till the first boss (spent over 30 minutes trying to beat him, then said "**** it"). The game will definitely frustrate even seasoned precision platform gamers, and I wouldn't recommend it if dying over and over again is not your cup of tea.
However, I must make it clear that the deaths don't feel cheap...you just need to get your hand-to-eye calibration right, and at times, memorize the patterns and obstacles. Also, you need to be very alert and your mind needs to stay sharp while you're playing or else you'll get caught out and die needlessly, frustrating yourself even more in the process.
I readjusted the default controls to fully keyboard from a KB+M combo. You just have left/right, jump and color swap. Simple enough on paper, but wait till you play the game!
The levels are medium length. Not as short as Super Meat Boy, and not as long as Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams. But depending on your competence, a certain section might get you to keep on retying that part again and again. Good thing there are checkpoints after every few sequence of obstacles, or not you can wager on quite a few broken keyboards and monitors. On top of that, there are 20 shorter levels which focus on the platforming aspect of the game.
Visuals are simple for me. I'm not really a fan of the Minecraft-esque blocky graphics, but it does the job well enough. Soundtrack though is superb. It consists mainly of electronic music, but unlike Electronic Super Joy which had pumping quick tracks, here they are a tad slower. The tracks are relaxing and are something that you can space out to. Would get the soundtrack separately if I find it, that's for sure.
So yeah, that's Slip. Gameplay wise, it reminds me to a certain extent of Polara, one of the best games I played on my Android tablet. It also bears similarities to Outland and Ikaruga to some degree. It's well made, super challenging (and confusing, with the color swap mechanic) and has a great soundtrack.

I realize that this is an "Early Access Game", so bugs are to be expected.
That said, In the last few days my attempts at play have been met with crashes on loading, crashes at the main menu, and a horribly unresponsive game.  A gaming system that can handle many AAA titles seems to have trouble keeping up with Vox, leading to an less than enjoyable experience.  Even in an "alpha" state, I would have assumed that the game would be
.  As I obviously don't have access to the source, I can't say if the problem is due to naïve data structures,  brute-force coding techniques, the choice of paradigms/libraries, or just the trying to avoid premature optimization, but something is causing it to feel very laggy, both in response to input as well as in animation.
Now, bugs and what I will refer to as poor optimization aside, on to the gameplay itself.  I managed to create a character, customize the appearance somewhat, and get into the default world (biome?  It's a world.)  Right away I could see quest givers in front of me.  When I went to gather up a quest or three, I discovered that you can only accept one a time.  Alright, no multitasking it is- time to explore and complete a quest!
Except exploring the world is at best tedious.  It is easy for your character to get stuck on block edges, which happens often enough that I end up jumping everywhere.  The only things in the starting area outside of "town" seem to be hills and the occasional tree, There weren't any arches or caves that I could fine, although there is a screenshot of one so I assume they are somewhere.
Okay, okay, alpha state- I get it.
Combat felt...awkward.  It was difficult to have a sense of perspective concerning the monsters I needed to kill due to how "close" the character is to the camera, and the right-click "targetting" system felt awkward when combined with a left-click-and-hold attack, especially if you come from the 3rd-person gaming background where right click activates mouse look or run.  I kill my required number of bees (more annoying than I would have hoped, it was difficult to get them to "aggro" on you without some form of ranged attack to reach them first, approaching them was not enough), and realize that I have no idea which direction town is.  The limited landmarks mean that the simply colored terrain tends to look the same in all directions, and the quasi-random assortment of snow, concrete, grass, and what I assume is desert lead me down a few wrong paths for a bit.  Again, my own fault, but a mini-map of some form, or at the very least a larger draw distance might have helped smooth this out.
Turn in the quest, and decide to go check on the Steam sale. When I next opened the game, there was no recollection of me having completed the previous quest, so the same NPC has the exclamation point.  No, I don't want to kill bees again.  Somewhere in this process I leveled up, but I have no idea what that actually did.
I don't doubt that Vox
be an enjoyable, fun game, in a similar style to Minecraft or Terraria, but I do feel that the early access release was perhaps
early.  Reading through the notes from the developer, I am concerned that the focus on more content may be somewhat misplaced, especially in a one or two person shop.  I know throwing more people at a late project (or in this case, a project very much in need of more work) only makes it later (slower), so I won't say that more developers are necessary- but I don't see Vox leaving this current alpha/Early Access state for quite some time.  It does appear that the developer is active in the forums, responding to users comments and critiques, which is a good thing, but the desire to add new functionality seems to be overpowering the real need to improve the base game that is in place.
Overall, I wasn't expecting perfection, or even anything close, but the feel of the game in its current state is one that I can't recommend.  There is some potential here for fun, and the customization options are definitely a good start, but it feels like it will be a long time before this game is ready for the public.

Steet Fighter 5 is not a perfect game, and it's certainly not without it's flaws. It provides poor service towards casual players and there are plenty of questionable balance decisions made by the developers, but its merits most certainly outweigh its faults.
If you've played a street fighter game in the past such as 3rd Strike or USFIV, you'll understand that every game has its own system that mixes up the gameplay a bit. Street fighter 3 had parries which were a deep and interesting mechanic at the cost of centralizing the game around the mechanic, with tiers being decided almost solely on who benefits from parrying the most (Q=Bad because he can't capitalize on a parry or really anything, Makoto=Good because she can stun combo you off of a parry confirm) and Street Fighter 4 has Focus attacks and Ultras, both of which are such ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mechanics that it would take an entirely different review to cover all of the things wrong with both of these mechanics
Street Fighter 5 introduces the V-System, a deceptively simple system of another meter that allows you to pull off character-specific reversals, character=specific skills, and characte-specific V-Triggers, all of which set out to diversify the cast more than it is by default.
Now I'm going to speak from a competitive perspective rather than a casual one, so if you're not a competitive player then my review might not help you, but if you're a casual then why are you bothering playing this game? Don't you kids still stick to the numerous rehashed versions of street fighter 2 because you can't actually tell how horribly they've aged?
Anyways, Street Fighter 5 is arguably the most balanced roster to date in street fighter history. Virtually every character can be played well enough to be viable at a competitive level, so there's no shortage of diverse, viable cast members. It's a fairly easy game to learn, but like all fighting games still difficult to master all of its mechanics, and the difficulty is most often decided by how good your opponent is rather than any real difficulty mechanics you'd find in a singleplayer game.
The game doesn't provide you a tremendous amount of learning materials, but it does give you trials which give the player an opportunity to refine their execution skills and learn their BnB combos. And as for learning, there are plenty of materials online worth checking out if you want to take the game seriously, as is the case for all fighting games.
Capcom's DLC formula seems expensive at first but in practice it's surprisingly generous. all game-changing DLC can be accquired with in-game fight money unlocked through playing matches and completing missions (which are generally very easy and can give up to 5000 FM). This gives the player the option to grind out the game and collect fight money, or shell out a few bucks from their wallet to get one of the DLC characters. Another important thing to note about fight money is that you get an extremely generous sum of FM from completing things like the character prologue stories and the "Shadow Falls" cinematic story and survival on every difficulty. Completing enough of these would give you enough FM for a new character and you can do that in an afternoon easily.
This formula is wildly opposed to the Street Fighter tradition of releasing numerous standalone versions of the game every year or two, each time costing 30 bucks with all its changes exclusive to that version, and tacking additional things like DLC costumes on top (which is not necessary of course), Street Fighter 5 lets you collect content at your own pace inviting you to spend money fro myour wallet but giving you the completely viable option of just scrounging up the fight money for it. Season Passes arent even dissimilar from additional versions excepting the fact that you can still play online with people who have the passes and you dont need to own one pass to purchase another, meaning you could have all the season 2 characters without the season 1 characters and there's no issue
And for everyone still whining over the rootkit fiasco; grow up. It was a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ circumstance but it's long since been over, it was a mistake on Capcom's part and it's been gone for almost a year now, it's a nonissue and anyone still acting like it's some major scandal still thinks that GamerGate is relevant and important in media.
Anyways, SFV is a good game and you should seriously check it out if you want a fighting game that's fun and rewards you for learning its mechanics. Peace.

Ah, Aliens versus Predator, probably one of my favourite crossover universes ever created. While I’m not much of a comic fan, the games worked for me pretty well so far, with AvP2 especially well done in my opinion. The first one from Rebellion was pretty good in its time and the gameplay still holds up pretty well, so I decided that it’s time to give the second game from them a spin.
For starters – the story seems completely unimportant here. It merely sets the stage for the three species (humans, xenomorphs and yautja) to murder each other in a number of gory and spectacular ways. This is quite similar to the previous Rebellion-made game, and also quite different from the second outing from Monolith. While there is a plot here, with frequent dialogue and audio logs to flesh it out a bit, it never feels important one bit. Cross-species combat is the meat here, and the game does not try to hide it.
And fighting, while not without its flaws, generally feels good. Marine represents your standard FPS experience, with an assortment of various guns and a dislike for close quarter combat. Weapons feel good, though some of them lack the “touch” – you never feel you are hitting your target with them until it actually falls to the ground. Xenomorph is a bit trickier, relying solely on melee combat, stealth and gravity-independent navigation to hunt its prey. It is easy to die as an alien, and it forces quite different approach than the other two races. It is also worth noting that vent mechanics, requiring you to manually enter and exit them instead of doing so automatically can be frustrating at times. Finally, the Predator is a mixture of above two, with ranged and melee weaponry at his disposal. He’s quite fragile, which requires utilisation of his distraction abilities, cloaking and vertical movement – I must say that the snappy jumping mechanic quickly became second nature to me and I enjoy it a lot.
The game’s design is nothing special – environments are diverse enough, but there is nothing to gasp at here. The same areas are used with slight modifications in each campaign, but I didn’t get the feeling of repeating same thing over again. It’s all built very similarly to previous Rebellion game and I think it works pretty well in a game like this. All missions are very linear though, with few areas that allow different approaches.
I am, as is usual in my reviews, not going to talk about multiplayer, simply because I never played it and was never interested in it. Now, so long after the games release I doubt there would be any populated servers, but if the mood strikes me and I have time to spare, I’ll update this review with online play impressions. So keep in mind that for the time being, this is a singleplayer-only review.
Visually AvP is OK, with Direct3D 11 effects adding a little bit of flair into otherwise correctly looking game (the standard D3D9 mode does not look much worse though and might be a better choice for slower systems). Texturework is nice throughout, and characters are nicely detailed, but there is occasionally a jarring drop in geometric complexity. Vegetation is very simple while vision effects for Predator are interesting and replicate what we’ve seen in the movie quite well. Audio it OK too, with a couple of oddly sounding weapons and unmemorable background music.
Overall, Aliens versus Predator 2010 is an correct game, much like the previous from the same studio. It offers solid human vs xenomorph vs predator combat experience and nothing above that. Some floaty shooting and melee mechanics prevent it from shining in that aspect, though, but unless you can hunt down a physical copy of AvP2, this is the game of choice for the fans of the franchise.

If you came here for an honest, truthful, realistic game review than you came to the wrong place. This is an outstanding recipe for perfect pancakes!
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Left 4 Dead is a co-op, first-person shooter video game, with survival horror elements thrown into the mix. Just like Castle Crashers, this game is for that special friendship group, composed of four friends. With this game, you will find a bounty of endless fun, especially when setting the game's difficulty to an all-time high, as it really gives you that experience of being an endangered species, with the more stronger zombies wanting you dead, thus extinct. From my point of view, you can already tell I hold this game in high regard. Probably due to the fact it
developed by Valve.
The story takes place in an unamed location, within Pennsylvania. A highly contagious virus known as th ''Green Flu'' swarms the state, causing heavy mutation to human body cells and brain functions, resulting in the loss of humanity, meaning yes, the birth of zombies.
Two weeks after the infectious outbreak, four survivors, William ''Bill'' Overbeck, a bold, Vietnam veteran; Zoey, a sassy college student; Louis, an optimistic IT technician, and Francis, an aggressive outlaw biker, the four heroes of this game make their way through perilous cities, discovering along the way that the virus is causing more dangerous mutations. On a side note, the story of this game is split into campaigns, going in chronological order from top to bottom and progressively, the story is carried out on to the games sequel.
The player takes control of one of the four survivors; only if human players are not involved, thus the survivors are controlled by the CPU. The main objection of the game is to reach the safehouse after each level of the campaign.
Beware to watch out for the special infected. These types of zombies are the strongest of the common infected and if you get incapitated by one, you won't be able to shake them off, but unless one of your fellow survivors lends a helping hand and kills the attacking zombie. So, this just goes to show that teamwork in this game is the key of getting farther and staying progressively stable to continue playing.
Guns and other types of defense and weaponry, (in the shapes of molotovs and first-aid kits) are scattered among the map, usually on different occasions. This mainly happens after holding off an entire zombie horde, where they break through from left, right and centre. All of these weapons that you find are frequently random, but you can stick to the weapon you like the most. Just make sure to search for ammo at a seldom pace, especially if you're playing on a much higher difficulty. When outnumbered, just remember to always keep your health up, along with your teammates, as every chip of HP is precious into reaching the end of your goals.
This game is simply fantastic, but is usually overshadowed by its sequel, Left 4 Dead 2; possibly due to the inclusion of all campaigns found in this one and carried out in its said sequel. The one thing I personally prefer from this game is the feel of the slightly tighter controls it has when compared to Left 4 Dead 2. I would say this one is for the competitive players and the sequel is for the casual players. Considering you could just mess around, with the Shrek mod and all, and don't tell me you bloody haven't. It's a lot of fun and of course, the modding community adds to Left 4 Dead 2's advantage, much to this games' disadvantage.
In closing, I definitely recommend this game to all who are fans of survival horror video games and those itching to test their own determination and teamwork with one another. If you have have the sequel, I would still recommend getting this first game, just for its originality and or the fact you can add it to your godly Valve collection.

I really don't get why people rip on this so much. It has some flaws, but they're not NEARLY as "game-breaking" and whatnot as people make them out to be. I'm also going to actually review the WHOLE PACKAGE, not just whine about DOOM 3 and "hurr durr flashlight is for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥herp derp*.
The original games (Ultimate DOOM and DOOM II + expansions):
Let's go with cons first, shall we?
- They do support high resolutions but no widescreen. No up-down mouselook. And boo-hoo they censored the Wolfenstein 3D secret levels.
First off, I for one welcome the lack of up-down mouselook. This is where I don't get DOOM purists - first they whine about two little censored SECRET levels, and then they play with vertical mouselook and a crosshair? Get that weak crap outta here! Either go big or go home and take your ZDOOMs with ya! (although you can use ZDOOM and other mods with a bit of work, to be fair).
The pros, then!
+ Ultimate DOOM and DOOM II play, look and feel exactly like the games I used to play back in the 90s. Get over it. The BFG edition got this part of the equation right. It's old DOOM plain and simple, with all it's glory and slight shortcomings as the granpa of all things FPS. And just BTW, this edition is the only way to (legally) play No Rest for the Living (which is pretty good) right now. So far so good. TBH I really got the BFG edition for these games more than DOOM 3, and I was not dissapointed, the Steam version of UD and DII isn't that great (yay, more DosBox).
And now to the part that actually warrants some criticism, DOOM 3 (haven't gone through RoE and LM yet but I assume the same applies)
EDIT:
I have spent quite a good chunk of time playing Ultimate DOOM and DOOM II using proper, modern source ports. I tried the BFG Edition versions of UD and DII again to see how well they hold up after spending 40+hours in GZDoom. Fact is... it's still pretty good. Let's be clear: if you want 1080p/16:9, mouselook, crosshair, jumping and crounching (heavens me), this is not what you're looking for. If you just want to play the damn games the way they were intended to be played back in the 90s, this more than does the trick. If the source ports are a 10/10, this is like a 7/10. Like I said, gets the job done.
Now that I've revisited DOOM 3 properly, I get a bit more why people were disappointed.
Cons first, again.
- The ammo abundance is the biggest issue by far. It makes the game just a little bit too easy, even on Veteran.
I can't remember what the original was like (I remember I *still* had my combat rifle ammo maxed almost the entire time even in vanilla DOOM3 ), but I can't remember having my shotgun past 300 all the time and certainly not my chaingun or plasma rifle having upwards of 200 bullets/cells respectively (...before even entering Delta Labs 1). What this means is that tougher enemies like Revenants aren't that big of a deal anymore, I used to♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants everytime I saw one (or god forbid two), carefully popping shots to conserve precious rockets and cells. Now, I just unload and bam, gone.
Health also seems to be pretty generously distributed. It's not that big a deal if you get hit plenty, there's usually at least a small medkit nearby to get you back to 50+HP. Not as severe a problem as the ammo, but still a bit of "babyfication".
- the lighting, or rather, it's inconsistency. You can read my flashlight rant below, this is not (completely) about that. It's about how sometimes, I want to cry tears of joy because in some situations, you don't actually *need* a flashlight at all! The perfect combination of ambient lighting and enemy light sources (imp fireballs etc.) create this wonderful ballet of darkness, light and shooting action that a flashlight beam ruins completely. Other times, there's oh-so-obviously-booby-trapped armor on the ground, you pick it up, the room turns pitch black and fills up with monsters and at that point, mounted flashlight or not, I just want to snap my keyboard in half. The flashlight is not the problem - the real problem is cheap, cheap, cheap level design! Bleuch! But these moments are not THAT annoyingly common, thank god.
On to the pros.
+ 1080p like a boss. I have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop, but even this old pile of junk can run it well enough at 1920x1080 no problem (maybe lay off the AA, it didn't do anything other than clog the GRAM even back in '03. Literally no visual improvement).
+ the flashlight. Oh yeah. That's a pro. Seriously. I still don't get why you'd whine over that one. When DOOM 3 was released, the game reviewers cried "fresh, original gameplay mechanic" and we, the gamers, replied with "you crazy idiots, this is the worst thing ever". What's this? Duct tape mod! Hell YEAH! I remember how much this sucked back then and HO-LY crud am I glad they pulled it out in the BFG edition.
I actually tried playing it the "old way", like deliberately not using it while shooting, and it sucks every bit as much♥♥♥♥♥as it did back in '03. "Atmosphere", yeah, right. Nothing more atmospheric than spraying bullets into a black screen until your reticle turns red to show that you're actually hitting something.
+ it's still DOOM3, it runs well and it has the same vibe, at least to me.
All in all, it's a good package, not perfect, but decent, and definitely worth the money on sale. People make this edition look like it's a 1/10 deal, it's more like a 7.5/10, not perfect, but still good. I just wish they'd put three separate entries in the Steam library instead of one, but hey, you can't have everything I guess.
Anyway, flashlight rants aside, I would recommend this to any DOOM fan. Ignore the purists, seriously, it's a good buy, especially if you get it for dirt cheap during a sale.

Quick Summary: Doom 3 came out around the same time as Half Life 2, and while Doom’s story isn’t as good as Half Life 2, the graphics really hold up. Don’t be fooled by the crappy opening cut scene graphics, because Doom 3 is one of those games where gameplay visuals are superior to its rendered cutscenes (like Just Cause 2 or Injustice). If you’ve played the Bethesda game RAGE, you should have a decent idea what to expect in terms of graphics. The BFG edition contains not only Doom 3 and both its expansions (Resurrection of Evil and The Lost Mission), but also Doom 1 and Doom 2. Each time you start up the game it asks which Doom you want to play, and all three have Steam achievements associated with them. Keep this in mind if you care about your achievement % and don’t like playing “old” games. You also won’t find too many people playing the Doom 3 multiplayer.
Doom 1 and 2 are straight up shooters and don’t really have much story other than a screen of text that you only see after you beat the game, so Doom 3 is basically a reboot. Contrary to popular belief, Doom is not based on the time Satan borrowed money from Chuck Norris and then wouldn’t pay him back. You play an unnamed marine, newly arrived on the Mars research base when all hell breaks loose, literally. The scientists in the base have uncovered artifacts from an ancient alien civilization that when combined with teleportation technology, open a portal between our universe and a hell dimension. Despite the fact that the Mars base is packed with marines armed with an insane amount of firepower, the demons have quickly overrun the place (along with about half the base being possessed by evil spirits) and it’s up to you to quash the source of the invasion.
Like its predecessors, Doom 3 is a First Person Shooter with a horror atmosphere. You’re trapped in the darkness most of the time, and it seems like monsters are around every corner, as well as occasionally teleporting in behind you. There’s no regenerating health, and some levels require a fair amount of backtracking, so don’t automatically pick up every health and armor you see unless you know you’re about to finish the level. You might come back through the area and need it later. Doom 3’s difficulty setting only affects how damaging the enemy attacks are, not enemy HP or intelligence. This means if you get the timing right for avoiding enemy projectiles, the game won’t be too hard on Veteran mode (especially after you get an artifact later on that makes healing a whole lot easier).
You should get Doom 3 BFG edition if:
+You have no intention of modding the game. Most mods were made for the base Doom 3 game, and since BFG edition made changes to the game engine, most of these mods don’t work anymore.
+You want to spend as little money as possible in order to play Doom, Doom II, Doom 3, Doom 3: Resurrection of Evil, and Doom 3: The Lost Mission. The BFG edition includes all of these and adds Steam Achievements (which aren’t available in the base Doom 3 steam game). The Lost Mission cannot be purchased alone from Steam as a DLC for regular Doom 3.
+You enjoy horror games, with zombies, demons, big creepy spiders, and tortured souls. You should quick save constantly because those demons really, really love teleporting in behind you or hiding behind false walls.
+You enjoy moderate paced shooting games (slower paced than Serious Sam). You cannot run through commando style unless you really know what you’re doing. There are a lot of health packs lying around, but even the lower tier enemies can tear you apart in seconds.
You should NOT get Doom 3 BFG edition if:
-You don’t care to play the older Doom games (or the Doom 3 expansion packs) and are planning to apply game mods, like improved graphics, higher difficulty, new campaigns, etc.
-You hate jump scares or dark game environments. In the original Doom 3, the flashlight was sort of a standalone weapon that you could club people with. You couldn’t have it out along with a gun at the same time. This meant that when engaging an enemy, you would often be fighting in the dark. This has been modified in Doom 3 BFG, and the flashlight is now automatically attached to whatever weapon you have equipped. It drains battery when in use, so you can’t have it on all the time.
-You are getting the game mainly to play multiplayer. The game doesn’t have co-op campaign gameplay, and there don’t seem to be any games going on when I look for online servers. You pretty much have to create a game lobby and invite friends to it.

This is wonderful, jank retro-graphics and all.
It takes a solid concept (grim Egyptian space-future of the 1980's) and triples down on it, using pixel art and brief blurbs to create a setting that feels more alive than some AAA stuff that's currently on the market. On top of that, the design is simple, but very effective. Battles are one or two-hit affairs, you progress by buying stats, you have combat and out-of-combat stats, with after-combat rewards increasing the lower your combat stats are...it's smooth, it's simple, and it feels good.
Despite being a concept that could easily have been executed with some stock rpgmaker hackery, everything in this game is custom. It feels like a love-letter to the old DOS days. If it had come out back then, it would have been a fondly remembered classic.
Although it's not really what you're there for, Void Pyramid has a central plot, and it's pretty solid. However, the writing shines in the small details. Practically every other tile is examinable, and the descriptions are good enough that they're all worth examining. Add into that ten or so different variables that make up your ending, and this is a really, really excellent piece of freeware.

Neon Drive is my favorite rhythm-based action game as well as one of the most addictive indie arcade games I’ve ever played. It is deceptively simple; you use two buttons to move your vehicle left & right or up & down to evade various obstacles, both stationary and moving, which will send you back to the previous checkpoint (or, on harder modes, to the beginning of the entire level). That’s essentially it. The premise is simple and the learning curve mild, but even on the lowest difficulty (normal), you will die a lot. You will curse a lot. You will get so frustrated you’ll want to throw your keyboard or controller across the room a lot. But, when you finally finish a level, the sense of satisfaction & accomplishment washes over you in a way I haven’t experienced in this type of game before. The fulfillment in beating a Neon Drive level is akin to mastering an extremely difficult level in a platformer and finally beating it after dozens of attempts - it's part skill, part finesse, part memorization, and just a tiny bit of luck. The gameplay here is frenzied and cacophonous, yet it requires precise timing above all else. Once you’ve familiarized yourself with a level’s layout (and you will die a lot, often in the back half or final run of a level, so familiarized you will become), it’s all a matter of making very fast, precise movement.
Neon Drive has a vibrant ‘80s-style presentation with retro-futuristic psychedelia and synth-based soundtrack, 8 levels (one of which was added recently, so it’s clear that developer Fraoula likes this game and support for it is ongoing), and top-notch optimization including high resolution & refresh rate support. In addition to three difficulty tiers, each level has free-play and endurance modes (with an additional endurance mode that runs through all levels back-to-back). I applaud the style and sheer amount of fun Fraoula has squeezed out of such a simple idea, and considering the amount of content on tap (with the possibility of future content in the works), I’d say Neon Drive’s $10 retail price is well-deserved. On sale or in a bundle, it’s a no-brainer – if you like music-based games with frenetic action & psychedelic audio/visuals, this is among the best.

Hello,
I have completely explored everything this game has to offer so far, and let me say this game has ALOT of potential. I loved what I did play, I experienced very minor glitches, riveting battle, a beatuifully crafted soundtrack, secrets arcoss the land, and a decent storyline. I will go over the Pros and Cons of this game and give my general opinion.
Pros:
Beautiful Graphics - Everything looked great for cel shading and it ran very smooth at 60fps. I loved the way leaves fell from trees, the effects when mining rocks or chopping trees, the poofs of smoke monsters disappear into. Visually stunning land scapes and trees are most of the game so far, however there are some caves and mines that looked great as well. Crystal glowing effects looked good and really added to the depth of exploring. The only bad part about the graphics is the water. No sound effects when you're walking in it, it is static and never moves, and it seems shoed in.
Soundtrack - This game has the music. Evergreen island has a beautiful overworld theme, however it becomes repetitive after awhile. I wish it would change depending on what section of the world you were in. Sky Harbor's theme has to be my favorite. It sounds like a lively town and I enjoyed exploring it with NPCs walking around, even if there wasn't much to do.
Sound Effects - They were good, but could have been better. I wish that when you harvested purple herbs it didn't sound like a hachet going to town on the leaves. It feels out of place, some of the sword hits on Rat Bandits as well felt a little weaker. The web slinging spiders sounded great, and I was disgusted fighting them. The honey pots were awesome, a lively hive awaits perfect honey!
Rewarding Exploration - There were times where I set off in a direction just to see what something was. I found a cave hidden in the far corner of the map with it's own story to tell, a man living in a tree fearful of his angry wife, and a mysterious shrine shrouded in magic. I felt like the areas didn't feel reused or tacked in with a couple different rooms, each felt unique with it's own story to tell. I would add more things around the world, a quick 15 minute swoop of the 2nd area in the game and I had completely gathered all the crafting materials.
Cons:
Weapons - There is a lack of weaponry, and after you get the bow the game becomes very easy. I would recommend not making a bow to have a real challenge. The one boss fight in the game is a breeze with the bow, halfway through I adjusted to the sword to have a real challenge. It was easy, but better than the bow. I wish there were more weapons for crafting, and that iron was easier to get as the iron sword and bow are really over powered.
AI - This needs work. Enemies would rush towards me if I was miles away. It felt as if their detection rating was too far, and that they would charge you from across the map. Sometimes I would be off exploring and the spider I saw across the hill far away from me would come to tussle. Most of the time they would miss their attacks as well if I slowly strafed to the right or left. Combat felt dull at times.
Crafting Materials - After you start exploring, you'll notice that it's just the same 5 or 6 things scarcely scattered across the land. The worst part is once you gather all of these items, you never really use them. Dry Wood, Ore (which is just copper and a rare ore Pallas that only has 3 on the map), and logs. Cutting down trees takes forever, and it only rewards you with four logs no matter the size of the tree. 4 logs is 1 charcoal bag, and the conversion rate is slow and grindy to get. There are only two tools, a picaxe and an axe. Most of the materials either sat in my inventory or were sold to buy more arrows. I never felt the need for potions as the game never challenged me enough to make them useful. There is only one cooking recipe in the game and it feels way too overpowered. I could eat a soup at 50 hp and go full, whilst still taking combat damage during the healing process.
Collision/Detection - Finally, the last piece of the review before my rating. If you take a sharp turn around a wall or NPC, you will start to move very slowly and occasionally freeze wherever you are standing. This happended very frequently. If you turn a corner too sharp, try to pass grey rocks, or go around NPCs, you will encounter this bug. This happens as well if you try to jump up something you're not suppose to or if you go near any water. It really took away from the games otherwise polished movement. It was very frustarting going through the mineshaft at the end as every corner felt like a trap. The hidden secret inside the mine as well that requires a bit of jumping/platforming was much more difficult than it needed to be. There was a puzzle in the mine as well that I almost got stuck in. During the three color step puzzle, I was walking inbetween one of the steps and my character froze in between steps, I broke free after multiple jumps and walking backwards slowly.
Sometimes I would charge a power attack with the copper sword to strike at the bees with, but the attack would not register. I would point blank hit the bee, but no damage would be applied. It was frustrating charging an attack several times for it to miss. I know, just use normal attacks, but that would not help the developer polish this game more. It is not all bad, the bow and arrows really felt dynamic as the arrow has drop off the farther it flies, phyics in how much power it took to draw the bow and how far it was going, and damage at certain ranges. The arrow never missed no matter what part of the hurtbox I shot at.
Overall Rating - As I stated at the start of this review, this game has ALOT of potential. I really did enjoy what I played, and I really have high hopes for this game. For the 90 minutes that I played I find it is obvious that the developer has put care into this game and has created something I believe a lot of people are going to enjoy. When this product is finished I think it will be one of the better indie games for your buck on Steam. Despite a few problems during play, the game ran very smoothly. For an early access game, Windscape was an enjoyable experience that I would recommend to anyone reading this review.

When the creator of this game says that he was a fan of Zelda, Golden Axe Warrior, Secret of Mana... this is something that grabs my attention. The Zelda series was one of my favorite to get lost in growing up. Secret of Mana was an entire summer of my childhood... from when I'd wake, until it was time for bed. I think that Dennis and Magic Sandbox have done a great job at showing this influence in their early access game, Windscape.
Pros
-
1. Story in place is a great start! Looking forward to more content patches that allow for exploration of more areas, continuation of the story.
2. Gathering doesn't feel burdensome - you naturally come across what you need.
3. Combat is a great start with a selection of 7-8 different weapons you can craft so far.
4. Art style is great - it's going to be something people either enjoy or don't. There won't be people that are "ok" with it.
5. Music isn't heavy or intrusive to the experience. Ambience is great as well. Music fits where you are, sound effects reflect your surroundings.
6. Non-linear - You can explore. Love this <3
Cons
-
1. Mouse sensitivity is VERY low when initially launched. Easy fix - Options menu is easy enough to traverse.
2. Crafting could get boring over time - Click, click, and done. Maybe add some possibilities for additional interaction for improved/better crafts?
3. I know it's early access. This will get fixed.. but there are spelling errors in 4-5 different places that I saw.
4. Listing this as people will inevitably say it: Too short for the price. I was able to finish what was available (from what I could tell) within an hour livestream. I'm happy to pay the $17 price tag to invest in a future game. Some won't be.
I'm clicking that I recommend this game as I do think that, based off what is currently present, this game will be a fun one! However, if you don't want to pay to invest in the future.. and support the developer.. I'd recommend waiting until there is a bit more than 60 minutes worth of gameplay (unless I missed something!)
