Parts of the game were pretty enjoyable, but overall, I can't recommend because it had some pretty fatal flaws that frustrated me in the end.
This game had a lot of potential, including screwing with the narrator, the initial intrigue and metaness of the story, and the varied combat system. But in the end, the repetitive and unforgiving combat ends up being pretty anti-fun when you have to sit through 20 seconds of dialogue just to get stun-locked again. And many of your combat upgrades are useless, since the only things that matter are your counter-dash and maybe your specials (you have about a dozen combos which don't really matter because you will get knocked out of all of them). If you get hit (the tells are very short, and attack patterns are fairly random), then you can get stun locked for basically up to 75% of your hp.
Also, the story gets pretty confusing as you do all the side endings.  There's lots of cryptic messages sprinkled throughout, which are interesting at first, but it never really feels like it comes together, even in the true ending.
This game has potential like Terraria, just needs more attention. More updates and quicker, otherwise Chucklefish will miss the opportunity to grow.

Doom 1 and 2 are classics that everyone should probably play.
I'm here to talk about Doom 3. I heard alot about it before I started playing it. I heard "Everyone would love it if it wasn't named Doom". I heard "The original is so much better" (doesn't matter, already bought this one). I heard "It was revolutionary for its time". I heard "The new Doom should be a horror game too".
In my opinion, all of that is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. This game is terrible.
I'll start with the visuals. I spent almost my entire playtime looking at either drab grey walls or pitch black areas while my flashlight recharged. Aside from the Hell Knights and the baby-bug ♥♥♥♥s, all of the enemy designs are boring- all either grey or tan with models that fail to inspire anything except mild annoyance.
The gunplay is similarly bad.  First off, try scaring someone after giving them enough guns, ammunition, health, and armor to take over a country. This is probably the games biggest failure- horror games rely on frightening visuals and either very limited resources, or none whatsoever. They make you vulnerable- taking away the toys that other games hand out freely. This game does the opposite. On top of that, the guns feel extremely weak (poor sound design, lack of enemy response, etc.), so I can't even enjoy shooting at the grey blobs the game insists are nightmarish demons!
The level design consists almost entirely of tight corridors- even when I'm wandering the surface of Mars or in the depths of Hell, I'm in a ♥♥♥♥ing corridor. It feels like I'm not actually going anywhere, and the overuse of monster closets and teleporting enemies only reinforces that feeling.
The sound design is both good and bad, and might be what kept me playing as long as I did. The enemies do sound frightening, and the ambience is very good, as is the voice acting. The guns, however, sound extremely weak, and the teleporting sounds seem out of place.
I honestly have a hard time believing that anyone considers this a great horror game. To me it's a boring slog through some tight, dark corridors. There are just so many far, far better ones

I want to recommend this game, I truly do. But that thumbs down is for a reason.
Neon Drive has amazing potential. It could have been something great, a true recreation of the 80's OutRun aesthetic. But it falls short in numerous ways. It is clear that the developers of this game created something with the intention of simply milking it. Not to create a great game or an art piece.
Firstly, I will admit that visually it is pretty awesome. The maps, although there are only a measly eight of them, look beautiful. The cars, of which there are very few too, look pretty cool and very 80's. Think Countach, Testerossa, DeLorean...
But that's where it pretty much ends. The game is insanely difficult and checkpoints are too far between to really be fair or enjoyable. Sure, I'm not the best gamer out there and I'm sure there is a kid somewhere in Asia sitting behind his Alienware going through every level like its nothing. But that's him.
The cars aren't real but rather the generic knock-off designs like you see in Burnout and Grand Theft Auto. What really sucks is that you can do absolutely nothing with them. They didn't even bother letting you change the color of the cars, nevermind giving them body kits or perhaps special abilities.
The endless mode is especially ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Its not even procedural generation or some sort of special map, its just you going through levels 1 to 8 without stopping. I'd also like to add that the levels do at least have some variety. There is always the first stage where you dodge oncoming platforms in a five-lane road. Then, your car turns into a boat, ship, airplane, robot, whatever and a new game mode appears.
The music isn't that great to be honest and what really gets me is that it resets the song for each level when you die, completely ruining it. For most levels the closest you'll get to the "rhythm-based" gameplay is the simple bass sound hitting when you dodge the platforms. Otherwise, there's practically no correlation between the music and the gameplay.
Great idea, inadequate execution. Wait for it to go on sale if you really like it. The cards, backgrounds, badges and achievements at least look pretty awesome.

I would highly recommend this very, very good game.
This game has a good intriging story, engaging gameplay and a beautiful soundtrack.
There is a wide range of weapons, both melee and range. Use anything from a hammer to a cannon rocket launcher. You can only equip two weapons at a time, but in combonation you want, so you could use two range weapons if you wanted. The levels are linear with a geometric style. There is a huge variety of enemies each with their own unique ways to cause you grief. The hub world, the bastion, looks beautiful and you can decide where you want to place particular buildings that you unlock in the game. There are replayable arenas where you can fight waves of enemies for rewards. This game also has a very interesting difficulty mechanics. You can choose which parts of the game are harder, for example you can make it so that enemies can reflect damge, or you can make it so that they cause damge to you on touch, or, if you're really daring, both. There are 10 of these aspects which you can activate and deactivate.
Do not let this game fool you though it can get very, very difficult.
The story is post-apcolyptic and has you explore the fallen world. There are very few characters in the game, but they all have very rich and engaging identities. It is a story that must be experienced. There is also dynamic narration, the omniscient narrator comments on your actions in the game as they are telling the story. It is a good short game of about 3-4 hours with lots of replayability.
One problem I have with this game was that the levels are not replayable. Some argue that it would not fit with the story, but I feel it would have been a nice touch rather than having to replay the whole game to play a level again as I enjoyed some more than others. You also couldn't go back for collectables if you miss them they appear in the in-game shop and I would have prefered to revisit areas and search for them.
Overall this is a fantastic game and well-done to the developers. The game play is excellent, the story is simple but interesting and the soundtrack alone is amazing. I recommend this game to people who, like myself, loves a good story. It has a wide range of enemies, weapons and customisable difficulty which creates some very interesting gameplay.
The single player is good, unique but not amazing. The multiplayer is where this game realy shines.

Short: It's fun, pretty, and pretty varied. Gamers who like really long, deep games might be turned off, but if you want reasonably short sessions and a fun mix of caring for your village while expanding and conquering other clans, this is worht getting even in early access form.
I'd definitely recommend this. I really liked Banished and taking care of my little village through harsh winters, famines, and the growing pains of my village. This is similar, but with added combat and research/tech-tree mechanics. I find that I enjoy the game a lot in its present state, and I'm impatient (excited) for the developers to flesh it out. (Since I got it they have indeed been adding features at a reasonable pace.) It's a lot shallower than something like Civilizaiton or Total War, but I actually prefer a game where I can have a 1-2 hour session where I go from growing my vilage's little nucleus to conquering the map. (Or getting a different victory. Or having everyone starve before another clan smashes me.)
I really like the visual style of the game. (Though I think I'd enjoy it even more if the different clans had more distinctive looks.) I also really like the music. I like that there are many different victory conditions to choose from. I kind of wish there were a way to turn the speed up a bit or play some even shorter sessions, but as-is, the little 1-hour-ish sessions are still reasonable. The various clans differ enough to be worth switching between, and I feel recent updates have made them more distinctive from one another in terms of the playing experience.

NOTICE: This game is a work in progress. In buying it you are investing in further development, which you will benefit from as the game is updated as certain development milestones are reached. Being an Early Access title expect random crashes and bugs. Ignore all neagative reviews complaining about the bugs, apparently some people don't understand what Early Access means.
Vox as its title suggests, is a voxel-based sandbox game in the same category as Infiniminer and Minecraft. The game uses a more rastarized art style as apposed to the more blocky style of Minecraft. The game engine uses modern shader effects and lighting in ways Minecraft doesn't without a GLSL Mod. Where Vox differentiates itself from Minecraft is its focus on adventure and role-playing. Instead of starting the game as one character which you cutomize with skins, you create a new character the way you would in most other RPGs and give that character a name. You then create the world you want to enter and you're given some control over the biomes and overall size of the worlds you create.
Each new game starts you out in a town populated by named NPCs. Chests with loot litter the nearby countryside, whcih gives you some nice starting gear. Some of the chests are monsters, so be aware of this when looting them. Combat uses a Zelda-style lockon which helps in aiming your attacks, especially when using the bow and arrow. Sound effects at the moment during combat are minimal, though this may change throughout the development cycle of the game.
Vox has a fairly detailed crafting system which has some similarities to Minecraft, but goes a few steps further and also allows you to make improvements to certain times like tools and weapons. Like Minecraft you smelt ores you've harvested into bars which you then use to craft items. You can also harvest plants and harvest wood. You can also edit any item in your inventory at virtually any time.
Sound wise, Vox is baren with just a single repeating upbeat tune that drones on during the day, and a more melodic and slow tune that plays at night. Day and night cycles go by rather quickly, hopefully this will be fixed, and nighttime doesn't seem to change the game much. Its not like Minecraft where nightime becomes hazardous for the player if you haven't built shelter. This may also change in the future. I'm hoping for more variety in the music rather than the SNES-esque tune that plays now. Over time it can become annoying and you'll find yourself turning the music volume down most times.
Overall, Vox holds immense promise so I recoomend that anyone who likes Minecraft please spend some pocket to get this game and help contribute its further development. Additionally, I much give the developer kudos for making the engine for this game open-source. We need to see more of this.

So Tekken 7 just came out and I am now really having to think about how I feel about this game. I enjoyed Ultra Street Fighter 4 for a very long time. However, Street Figher V released and it's what we got so here goes
Street Fighter is a game that needs really no introduction. It's a fast paced fighting game with nuances and it's pretty great. It's been successful for a very long time, bringing together talented kids with tape mended glasses for years. However, this fifth entry is a bit divisive. The combat is pretty wonderful this time around. It feels just as responsive and fun as it ever did but with the port being poorly executed and the roster being much, much shorter this time around, it felt like Capcom had released an unfinished game. Down the line, we've gotten more characters but I think this game lost me.
This was not helped by the, at times, attrocious netcode. Fighting games need a clear, balanced playing field for competitive play. What they don't need is 1 full second of delay on competitive when said person is paying for high quality Fiber internet. This happened too often and it very much made me no longer want to even try.
This game did do one thing that I certainly commend it for, however, even if it was still a little smarmy. Streetfighter V has a good bit of "dlc" but these dlc's are the characters they didn't put in the game to start with and new arenas. The arenas don't bother me but my main, Juri, was locked behind a "paywall." This idea was obviously seen as trash by someone in the boardroom when they were finalizing the game because you /can/ earn currency in the game by winning online matches and you can use that currency to purchase characters and arenas. This is kind of cool, or would be if the other aspects of the game made me want to continue playing online.

To wrap this probably unfair fan review up, I wanted to like this game. But the glaring issues it had upon release and the glaring issues it has now and can't really fix just make me want to keep playing Tekken 7. I grew up a Tekken guy anyway. Unfortunately, I think that game has garnered enough good will for me to turn my back on SFV maybe for good.

Don't get me wrong I love this game. It's combat is one of the best in any indie game I've played because it's so fast-paced and combo heavy. The only other similar game I can compare this too in terms of speed and fun is Furi and I loved that and beat it on it's Furier difficulty as well. So I love these kinds of games, and am no stranger to really difficult and fast games. The combos are great, the animations are great, the soundtrack when you're in the middle of chaining together combo after combo and you're hack'n'slashing against multiple enemies at once - especially in the air is so awesome and incredibly satisfying. What I can't stand however and the reason I can't give a good review is because there are some bosses in this game
as well as some enemies that have instantaneous attacks. Some of these attacks also lock you in place as the enemy continues to just wail on you. In a game where dodging at the exact instant an attack is going to hit you, have an attack that has no indication it's coming is unfair.
I know sometimes there's an ! when an attack is coming, but often times it doesn't help. What I found myself doing for the few bosses that would just instantly attack and chunk my health is I wouldn't attack at all and I would avoid every single attack that wasn't a telegraphed one, and I had to rely on dodge-counters on those. Any time I get close to them, and I KNEW they were going to do their instant attack, I still couldn't dodge it. This is just bad design. Everything else is great, including the mobility but that's another issue.
If you're going to put in attacks that have no tell and come out 1-frame instantenous, don't put a cooldown on my dashes which is the ONLY way to deal with these attacks. I often didn't have a dash in the exact instant I got attacked so even if I had mind powers and knew he was going to attack and I tried to predict it (because this game is NOT reaction based, but prediction based) I'd be ♥♥♥♥ed cause no dashes.
All in all great game, and pretty hilarious too if you find all the little hidden bits the developer put in, but the constant and instant attacks that are so punishing just makes whatever fun the trash mobs inbetween bosses give, not worth the headache of dealing with unfair boss mechanics. For what it's worth, 7/10.

Fran's parents have been killed and she is kept in a hospital/asylum type place. However, Fran keeps seeing disturbing visions. She needs to get out of the hospital, and also wants to find the one who has killed her parents.
One of the most interesting fascets of Fran Bow is how the world changes, usually depending on if you have had your pills or not. It nicely spins the effects of perscriptions as one that just changes someone's perception of the same world. The puzzles also play off this quite often.
Fran Bow is briliantly written. The dialogue makes Fran seem so sweet and innocent because of the strange but true observations she makes about everything. The story delves into deep themes of conciousness and reality, or the lack thereof. There isn't too much that I can compare to Fran Bow, but Alice in Wonderland is the closest I can get. Fran Bow, like Alice in Wonderland, can be deceptively childish one moment, and then very gruesome the next, all while addressing deeper themes and morals. Also, the imagination used in this game is second to none. The world building is incredible.

If you enjoyed the 'games about making games' meta-ness of The Stanley Parable or The Beginners Guide, but found yourself wishing 'I wish this had more ANIME' then, my friend, ICEY is the game for you.

Oh boy, this sure is a Adventure game from the 90's, MAN, LOOK AT THOSE SEQUELS! Yes, I am going to review a couple of sequels from the Broken Sword franchise, I'll mostly focus of the differences with the first one though, as I explained how I felt about that game with detail, so I left a link up there, for you to read it, but you probably already saw that, unless you're reading it upside-down, then, good for you!
Broken Sword 2 picks up 6 months after the original left off, George and Nico started dating, but George had to go back to the States because of his father's health problems, which caused them to break up. Now, most of the game you will be playing as George, and one thing that bugged me is that he never really talks to Nicole about his sudden departure, and I think they needed to get deeper into it . I really want to see them happily together, it's kind of like the Mulder-Scully problem.
After a while though, George returned to Paris, only to find that Nico had an appointment with an archaeologist because of an odd stone she'd found, only for them to discover they've been set up, and they knock them both out, kidnap Nicole and leave George to die, at the hands of a terrible, evil, and psychotic… spider? Well, they've set the house on fire, but I didn't find a point to the spider, but I digress.
George then goes to the rescue of Nico, and after finding her, she explains that the man who kidnapped her was thought to be in a drug ring and that Nico was tracing him, but now she suspects there might be a connection with an even deeper conspiracy.
I can't really go into the story, I might've even spoiled the fact that George rescues her, but still, there's really not much to go into without spoiling, but the story is really interesting and worthwhile, an overall improvement over the first one.
The gameplay is pretty much the same, ya think, ya point, and ya click. But the UI and several tweaks to the engine and some mechanics makes the small differences good, for example, now you can cancel an action by selecting another one, which you couldn't in the first one, smalls changes like that that really improves the game in my opinion.
Now, the puzzles on the other hand are harder, there's really nothing obvious, and you have to do some serious thinking to get out of some situations, but still, most of it makes sense, you've just got to do some exploring and talking to people to get somewhere. There is one or other puzzle that is somewhat insane, but nothing too bad.
There are also some comedic situations that are really worth while and quite funny, just remember to get that coal.
The graphics and voice acting though, now that's what I call an improvement, the game looks much better than it's antecessor, and the voice acting is top-notch, the in-game animations are much better, the music is too an improvement over the first one, the music theme also complements really well this game's theme.
The game really looks and sounds great.
Overall, this game is an improvement over the original, mostly little things, but improvement nonetheless, I recommend it, but for starters, the original one should be played first, for a better introduction and building of the characters.

This game left me speechless and with very, very mixed feelings.
A fair review must be made from different point of views to help others decide if they want to give this game a shot:
The game does stand out for its very unique style and character design. A mixture of sweet, childish figures and creepy monsters are all over the Fran Bow universe, and it's a real pleasure to click each and every detail and listen to Fran's opinion on it.

This is what the developer did best: from a talking cat to a pair of witchy evil siamese twins to a skeleton with a top hat, the characters were made with very close attention to the details and were what made the game worth playing, at least for me.
Fran herself is a cute little kid of 10 who surprises you with incredible bravery and at the same time reminds you in more than one occasion that she is a child after all.
The minimal but very atmospheric soundtrack and sound effects of this game were extremely well done. Some tunes were recycled over and over but were not less enjoyable.
If you are lucky and nerdy enough to know something about Fibonacci sequences, then no worries, you won't need to look for any walkthrough. Otherwise, there will be 2 moments in the game in which you really will not be able to go any further.
Combination and utilization of objects in the inventory will be pretty self explenatory. Since the game has lots of tiny details you may find yourself searching for something specific a little longer than necessary, but overall, the logic of the solutions needed was pretty easy.
......and now we talk. I ended this game with more questions that I could answer, and even searching for meaning within my own interpretation  and that of those who played and enjoyed the game, I am still not satisfied by the different theories on what ACTUALLY happened.
The Fran Bow universe is built on 5 different realities from which different creatures (and, so it seems, feelings) arise, and Fran seems to go through each and one of them in her attempt to finally find her way home.
I will not go into every point of the story to which I could not get the answer, it requires a discussion on its own.
But, at least for me, the end of the game left a bitter taste in my mouth and the frustration of not really knowing what the developers really wanted to achieve with a not really straight-forward plot.
If you tend to play every point and click adventure  on the planet because you like the genre - go for it.
If you enjoy creepypasta just for the creepiness sake - go for it.
If you, like me, enjoy intricated stories that develop further during a game and then unravel themselves in the end - leave it be. You will spare yourself some anger and frustration in trying to make sense of a puzzle made of pieces that do not fit into one another.

ICEY is a very interesting game, I enjoy how it interacts with the player using the narrative, creating a fairly dynamic story. The combat is actually really quite fun once you get a hold of it, and it is so satisfying once you master it.

Movie and game industries with million dollar budgets that try to paint a picture of what a dystopian future would look like, with all the highly paid artists, designers, and marketing research, continue to give us a world of bratty teenagers and adults that don't know how to impose their yoke upon their domain with an unflinching hand. One would have to imagine that to survive in such a world you would occasionally need to let go of any ego you have, grovel and beg for your life to those in authority, or end up with your brains splattered against a wall, whether or not you have committed any crime. This is certainly a game that will make you wake up every day and be thankful you live in 21st century Earth, and not this world. If this is the type of game you're looking for, you will find it here, despite older-looking graphics and a simple combat model, and I would highly recommend this.

- Gets boring rather quickly

I would highly recommend this very, very good game.
This game has a good intriging story, engaging gameplay and a beautiful soundtrack.
There is a wide range of weapons, both melee and range. Use anything from a hammer to a cannon rocket launcher. You can only equip two weapons at a time, but in combonation you want, so you could use two range weapons if you wanted. The levels are linear with a geometric style. There is a huge variety of enemies each with their own unique ways to cause you grief. The hub world, the bastion, looks beautiful and you can decide where you want to place particular buildings that you unlock in the game. There are replayable arenas where you can fight waves of enemies for rewards. This game also has a very interesting difficulty mechanics. You can choose which parts of the game are harder, for example you can make it so that enemies can reflect damge, or you can make it so that they cause damge to you on touch, or, if you're really daring, both. There are 10 of these aspects which you can activate and deactivate.
Do not let this game fool you though it can get very, very difficult.
The story is post-apcolyptic and has you explore the fallen world. There are very few characters in the game, but they all have very rich and engaging identities. It is a story that must be experienced. There is also dynamic narration, the omniscient narrator comments on your actions in the game as they are telling the story. It is a good short game of about 3-4 hours with lots of replayability.
One problem I have with this game was that the levels are not replayable. Some argue that it would not fit with the story, but I feel it would have been a nice touch rather than having to replay the whole game to play a level again as I enjoyed some more than others. You also couldn't go back for collectables if you miss them they appear in the in-game shop and I would have prefered to revisit areas and search for them.
Overall this is a fantastic game and well-done to the developers. The game play is excellent, the story is simple but interesting and the soundtrack alone is amazing. I recommend this game to people who, like myself, loves a good story. It has a wide range of enemies, weapons and customisable difficulty which creates some very interesting gameplay.

The city itself is well recreated and fun to drive around, if you have a controller of course because keyboard controls are sadly horrible. A dissapointment when other 3ps have done better.
Content wise, the game feels a bit hollow. The side missions - outside a handful of enjoyable ones - get very repetitive very fast. The races are too easy, and the drug busts are too repetitive to be any fun. There is also a very gimmical and quite dreadful Karaoke mini-game, but all in all the side missions cruelly lack variety.
There are loads of collectables and items and vehicles to buy, but unless you're a very hardcover undercover pork bun ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you will probably pass once you've completed the game.
That said, it is still well worth playing for the main story.

I would love to recommend this game. I like what the devs were trying to make. I really do.
But I can't. There are just some flaws you can't overlook.
The checkpoint placement is "OK" at bst. Several times there was no checkpoint in front of a clearly seperate segment with a lot of enemys, forcing you upon failure to replay some screens, be it just RB-Spamming through them or even killing some enemys that could be counted as mid-bosses.
The best example has to be a boss battle that requires you, after respawning at the checkpint, to
- RB-Spam up a Tower
- Watch a 10 second cutscene
- Press X
- Wait another 10 seconds for the door to open
Until you can try to beat the Boss another time.
The other big issue is the fighting system.
Sometimes enemies are able to stack damage without the ability to escape. (~75 of the ~100 HP Bar in 3 hits in a row)
Other enemies seem to temporaily ignore their post motion delay, allowing them to Spam Attacks without any way to get through.
Also the dash-invincibility-frames feel really inconsistent, or at least are not he same as the animation.
Some simple fixes could easily make this game far more enjoyable
For some really small complaints:
The music doesnt loop correctly (at least for me)
Some Background Textures seem a little washed out at 1080p
Some of the narrator and fourth wall additions are a little forced.
A Cutscene at the beginning of the game depicts your Character basicly waiting to get shot. It feels really unpolisehd.

While being critisized by some for not being a classic Doom game, Doom 3 has certainly passed the test of time from my point of view. ID´s reimagination of Doom as a survival shooter with horror elements has certainly worked well on me. Since the original Doom 3 was launched in 2004, this technical piece of art and graphics advancement has aged very well. Not too many FPS games have managed to keep up as well as Doom 3 did. Every few years, I keep coming back to this title. The dense atmosphere, the sound effects and the setting keep drawing me in. Few games have ever managed to give me so many hours of full attention and involvement, being on alert and getting goosebumps over and over again. Doom 3 is one of them. Although some may (rightfully) argue that the BFG edition has toned down some of the orginal´s horror aspects (different shadow effects and the redesigned flashlight in particular), I can certainly recommend the BFG edition. The original Doom 3 comes very close to what the BFG edition has to offer, when being properly configured and modded with additional texture packs. But the BFG edition brings all of that right out of the box and provides two additional addons, making it a convenient revisit for fans of the original and a great value pack for newcomers.
While all of the Doom PC games are truly great titles and form a legacy that has shaped the way of modern PC gaming in so many differnt ways, I will always have a soft spot for Doom 3 for being different from the rest of the pack. The BFG edition provides the most simple way to experience this outstandig game.

Very disappointed with the AI in this game. I mainly wanted to play this as a singleplayer game but it is simply more frustrating than enjoyable to face the AI in this game. I cannot recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a fun singleplayer experience. If you want to purchase the game simply for the multiplayer experience then this review should be irrelevant to you (I suggest you look at some of the other reviews instead).
(1) The AI cheats massively. We are talking big bada boom dimensions here.
They pay no upkeep. They get resources for free. They are immune to disaster effects. They can recruit military units without having to pay crowns (gold) for them and so on. This leads to an AI which no matter how often you demolish them, does not give a single ****. Destroying half their base feels like nothing to them. Losing an army doesn't hurt them either. They can simply recruit a new one out of thin air. If you take a zone from them it doesn't have any effect at all. They just immediately retake the zone for free (taking a zone is very costly for human players). Do it once. Do it twice. Do it thrice. It doesn't matter how often you take it. They always immediately recapture it. They are not even trying to hide the fact that they have infinite food. They blatantly slap you in the face with it.
(2) The AI behaves completely illogical. This is closely related to (1) because why should they do anything that makes sense if there is no reward or punishment for them in anything they do? They will sacrifice an entire army to take a meaningless zone from you with no resources on it and once they capture it they won't even bother building anything on it until the end of the game. Because that is how bad they wanted that wasteland of a zone apparently?! Not like it really matters that they just lost their entire army taking it because a few seconds later they have already recruited a new one.
(3) The AI gangs up on you. You will often find 3 or more AI attacking you from several sides at the exact same time although they are not part of a team (this will happen whether you currently ahead in the scoreboard or not). What a fabulous "coincidence". I guess the 10 min timer for the "attack human now" subroutine just fired in the AI's code. Gotta make the game challenging for the human player eh? Nope, it is just annoying and totally breaks immersion if you have 3 AI attacking you at the exact same time for no apparent reason in a FFA.
(4) You are forced to stay in your base and pretend that this is an economic simulation game (which it is not unless you think that is what vikings were renowned for). Attacking the AI is pointless because you cannot harass or damage the AI's economy. The AI has no economy to speak of in the first place. Cheating is the AI's economy. This leads to only one viable playstyle against the AI. "Ignore" them, bunker up, never attack them and try to go for an economic victory. A very boring playstyle which you are forced into playing because of very poor design choices made during the development of the AI.
TLDR:
Decent multiplayer game with certain (-) but overall fun to play
(-) Bad netcode
(-) No matchmaker
(-) No dedicated servers
TERRIBLE singeplayer game due to horribly designed AI
(-) AI cheats
(-) AI behaves absolutely irrational
(-) AI gangs up on you in FFA
(-) You are forced into a certain playstyle

If the DOS game "PHAROAH'S TOMB" had a baby with the French indie RPG "OFF!" and then made game developer Porpentine the godmother and sent it off to be raised with her, you'd get something like VOID PYRAMID.
It was wonderful. I sucked all the content out of it (after 7 hours! And I *hate* playing D-pad games on a tablet!) and had a ball. There was a little grinding near the end, but could have been me just wanting to level up to get all the content. That's life!
Still recommended! And the sound effects are just as good as the music, if you ask me!
* * *
I've played VOID PYRAMID on my tablet for an hour now. I *hate* playing D-pad games on tablets, so that alone should tell you something.
I am in love with this game. It's a simple-looking, highly atmospheric 2D RPG/metroidvania? whose text descriptions have my imagination by the lapels. I open it up and am instantly transported. If you enjoy Porpentine's Twine/interactive fiction games, you'll probably get a kick out of VOID PYRAMID, for it feels like a Porpentine work translated to a more visual medium.
I also enjoy the design--I don't need a game to be hard like Dark Souls, but I appreciate the penalty for dying in this game--it doesn't cripple you, but it makes me more thoughtful about the way I play, and I like that. And I enjoy leveling up.
Want a surreal experience that's still a satisfying game? Enter the VOID PYRAMID.

The exploration of the pyramid is interesting and motivating and brings some new approaches to old concepts. While the mechanics are not very complex, most attributes and every of the few items is well-thought and has its use, like a warp item which shortens backtracking or a radar item that allows you to sneak through passages which are heavily populated with enemies.
The bizarre lore is made with passion and contributes to the unique atmosphere of the game.
The only downside is  the combat system, which encourages you to go for a simplistic one-hit kill approach. But most combats can be avoided, even grinding is possible without actual fighting: One "dungeon attribute" offers a chance to win an engagement automatically, another one allows you too flee otherwise. This way you'll get money and stats passively and without even having investested lots of attributes in the "combat" category.
The single rooms are full of details and keep you motivated. At the same time the game does not overstay its welcome. With a playtime of ~8 hours it gives you all the time to dive into the gameplay and the atmosphere before it gets tedious or shallow.

Tl,dr:
Is this a good game? Yes.
Is this what you would expect a 97% positive reviews game to be? Probably not.
So why the hype? Because the game's absolutely gorgeous. The music, the visual style, the narrator are ravishing each on their own, and combined they can hit like a truck, straight in the feels. The overall effect is just massive. By the way, I think buying the OST DLC is totally worth it.
Why don't I think it's a perfect game then? Well, it's somewhat boring at a low level. Fighting is pretty much what you do most of the time and it's quite repetitive. Sure, there are different kinds of enemies and different combinations of them, but for each kind of enemy you just repeat the same trick over and over again to defeat them and it doesn't really matter what combination is thrown at you.
So why do I recommend it? Because I think it's good anyway. Just don't expect it to be so good that you'll play it for ten hours straight until you finish it, completely disregarding the real world in the process. Expect to completely disregard the real world only for about an hour or two at a time.
PS I cried a little at the end.

Played this game on Android, and I really want to weigh in on it. As the hottest of takes, it's like System Shock 2 by way of Dragon Quest crammed into a Zelda 1 dungeon map.
This game is pretty excellent! The combat seems initially too simple, but as the game progresses, the simple math and the small numbers mean you know EXACTLY how screwed you are at any given moment. The map design can't be overstated, either. Every room is crammed with stuff to find and interact with, and the constant threat of (lightning-fast) random encounters draining your health adds tension to your exploration. The game has a very simple stat system, but the resource that upgrades your combat performance also upgrades your exploration skills, so deciding between one more point of Defense to survive a little longer and one more point of Agility to slide past those deadly lasers is very immediately meaningful.
Void Pyramid is just a fantastic, tightly woven experience that always offers more danger, more to explore, and a setting you definitely have not seen before, completely free of magic forests and military bases.

SFV is definitely a mixed bag.
The pure gameplay is great, it's tactile, easy to understand, visually pleasing, the sound design is good and the entire package is probably the most accessible fighting game I've ever played. It's been the only one that I've bothered to actually play seriously and see if I could get decent at it -- I actually had the confidence and desire to play other people in this, where SF4, BlazBlue, KoF13, MvC3 and others didn't spark any of that drive in me. The lack of a strong skill barrier-to-entry goes very far in making it approachable, as well as the relative transparency of the mechanics, and I don't think they really sacrificed any nuance of the combat in the process. This is probably a hotly contested topic since there seems to be a lot of people out there that think USF4(and/or maybe 3rd Strike?) was the holy grail of Street Fighter, and 5 doesn't play much like it.
Unfortunately, Capcom has really not done a great job representing the gameplay that they've put in this accessible state. The netcode and matchmaking are both below par, lag in matches is fairly common and ranges from annoying delays and stutter to straight up time-warping and constant rollbacks where you can't even tell what the hell is going on. People generally overstate how bad it is I'd say, at least from my experience in Canada (thus, your region mileage may vary), but it's definitely there and is definitely an occasional damper on things. It's apparently poorly optimized as well since I get a lot of inexplicable slowdown no matter what my settings are, using the built-in low-spec mode or not.
The FM system is... alright. You can get a decent amount of stuff unlocked just clearing story modes and trials, but it is still kind of a chore in the long term and the prices for things are a little high, considering you paid a decent chunk of cash for the game already, which in its base state is pretty bare-bones. 100k for a character, sure, but 70k for a new stage? You can't get -everything- with FM either, some things are real-money only. Still, it could be worse, for sure.
I will say that while the characters are distinct and do play differently, there's less gimmicky characters than one would be used to in other games. Fireball zoning is all but gone, which cuts out an entire playstyle in favor of the guessing games and wakeup pressure that things have evolved into. On that note, the balancing could also use work. The (currently) smaller character roster means there's less extremes between low tier and high tier, but the differences are still there. Any character that has a strong, varied offense tends to excel, while the characters with weaker offense or fewer tools to deal with offensive pressure tend to be weak. They're not free games like a bad matchup would be in a game with even poorer balance, but there's clear advantage/disadvantage.
Unless you favored another particular brand, this would probably be the game to start with in getting into fighting games.  It establishes and communicates the basics in an easy-to-play format (though you'd still have to look up guides and watch professional matches to really get an idea of how to play your character properly, which is the norm). But, like I read in another review and want to restate here, it's important to realize there's a social aspect to it. Relying completely on the online matchmaking will only get you so far; you'll get the most out of the game playing it with others, in lobbies with strangers with good connections, friends, or even physically at a meetup or gathering. The netcode and matchmaking are lackluster, and the general playerbase is a little small and spread a little thin among the rankings to make the online aspect an ideal experience, though it would suffice if you just wanted to play very casually.
It's a good game, even if Capcom isn't really a good company for it and brings it down with their practices just as much as they bring it up with their design.

SUMMARY: ICEY, from front to back, is a tragically short game with minimal replay value once you unlock every achievement, somewhat improved thanks to a free DLC with a sort of wave-based arena level that really challenges your skills. It might put off a lot of potential buyers to know how short it is, even to get everything. But what it hides underneath the exciting combat is a Stanley Parable-type meta story absolutely worth the admission price to experience.
GAMEPLAY: ICEY is a 2D sidescrolling brawler beat-em-up, at least on the surface. Gameplay is simple, and whether or not you've played similar games such as Dust, the controls are very easy to learn, and it more becomes a matter of learning enemy attack patterns and how to manage multiple foes at once. As someone who seldom plays these kinds of games, I found it less challenging than I expected, but it's certainly a tricky game to master. Minimal controls means that combat is a matter of applying basic attack combos in the most effective way possible while controlling crowds of mobs around larger enemies and keeping out of danger with coordinated maneuvers (the dodge move does not contain any invincibility frames from what I see, so it's not always so simple.)
New skills and modifiers can be acquired and combos can be enhanced through a basic menu at checkpoints, at the expense of cash acquired either through finding secrets or dispatching foes.
Level exploration is generally pretty basic. There's very few screens that have more than a left-to-right range of movement, but some screens have multiple exits that can lead to secret rewards or new story alternatives (more on that in a bit). Overall, level complexity is not as deep as some of the more prominent games in the genre, such as Dust, but this simplicity can mislead the player into missing a lot of important secrets.
A free DLC lets you unlock an area with an arena-style mode where you square off against numerous waves of stronger versions of all the game's enemies. I've heard there's an extra story bit that comes after surviving the entire onslaught, but I've yet to manage that achievement.
STORY: The main story is about as basic as it comes. You control ICEY, a cyborg of sorts who is tasked by the narrator to kill the character Judas, declared the bringer of the apocalypse and master of the robotic soldiers who impede your progress. If you play the story straight and do what you're guided to do, the story never develops. You're just the hero who kills the baddie, huzzah.
It is encouraged almost from the beginning to ignore every instruction from the narrator and try to disobey him as much as possible. This leads to a lot of fourth-wall breaking humor between the player, ICEY (who effectively never speaks) and the narrator, who acts as a peculiar combination of master, story-teller and a personification of the developer's frustrations towards the player. It's hard to speak much about it without spoiling things, but suffice to say, his aggressive hand-holding is meant as a clear indication that you should not take his word on anything.
Beneath even this bizarre second layer of plot is one that gets very grim, as each ending results in a humorous scene followed by a bizarre text scrawl that slowly reveals the motivations of the in-game bosses, none of whom speak throughout the entire game. The unlockable "true" ending is a truly Deus Ex kind of moment that really needs to be experienced before one finally puts down this game.
Each ending can be completed in a fairly short amount of time, but after each ending the game allows you to pick a checkpoint to start over from if you know where you want to start again. This level list is not available from any other menu in the game, unfortunately, but it's also possible to skip back to later-game areas in short order once you know how.
Overall, a short but sweet game with a lot of depth for the eager explorer, and satisfying brawler combat to boot.

Not as intriguing and well-arranged as the first instalment of the series,
still is a nice adventure and a decent sequel to a wondrous game. First and foremost, I am happy to announce that there has been no content cut in this remastered version compared to '97 original. Everything there was in the first place, is still there contrary to Director's Cut version of the first game. Also, it might be significant to mention that this is the only game in the series that wouldn't center around a mystery concerning Knight Templars.
It is a couple months after the first game's end. George has been back to America for some time to attend personal businesses - no spoilers - and Nico has been left alone in Paris. Without supervision from George and already having a knack for getting into trouble, Nico starts to investigate a party of drug smugglers that would import cocaine from South America in the guise of importing historical artifacts for a gallery. Nico gets her hands on a small Mayan tablet and André arranges a meeting with Professor Oubier, an expert on the Mayan culture and artifacts for consultation. Just coming back to Paris in time for the said meeting, George meets Nico as they arrive at Oubier's house together, only to be apprehended and left in a burning house! As Nico gets abducted by a South American Indian alongside the mysterious tablet, George starts yet another adventure after a criminal mystery which will soon turn very much esoteric.
Well, let's take a look upon this lovely setting. I have to declare that the story and power dynamics behind the scenes aren't as elaborate as the first game. It is pretty much black and white, good vs. evil this time, which is slightly disappointing. George and Nico are as witty and as able as ever though, with a notch of sexual innuendo building in between. Humor is slightly crueler and highly sarcastic too. Nico is a highly influential character in this game compared to the previous one though, not only a pretty side-kick waiting for George to save the day. As another side point, the ending wasn't that much of a satisfaction, considering the game cuts player involvement just before the actual ending sequence, leaving us with a cartoon cinematic. Oh, well... you can't always get what you want.
Display is nearly identical to the previous game. Hand-drawn art with engaging atmospheres and animated cartoon cinematics with classic scenes. Music is lovely as always too. Sadly, we are presented portrait close-ups of characters up on the screen in this remastered version, very much like the Director's Cut. Facial expressions of characters are a bit limited with those, and they mostly end up presenting characters unsympathetic, contrary to the original tone of the game. In those portraits, George was practically pouting half the time, and Nico always had an expression as if she just stepped onto something unpleasant.
As for the gameplay, it is slightly lesser compared to the first instalment. Some combination actions cannot be achieved before proper dialogue is triggered, even though the action would be quite obvious. You gotta step through everything in proper order to proceed. Fast transportation between scenes aren't there anymore either, so you keep walking on a somewhat prolonged pace. Puzzles are okay, yet not challenging much. You figure out everything at the first glance. They just mostly take time to get through, rather than actually thinking how to deal with. On a note, there is a truck load of funny easter eggs in this game, winking to some pop culture references or other games from the developer team, such as
. Wanna see a goat in existential crisis? Intriguing.

Ah yes, the little bag of secrets that is ICEY. I cannot sing more praise to this game purely because it caught me so off guard as it did, why? I bought it on a whim expecting close to nothing. What I got? I got a big smile and a bunch of surprises.
So, ICEY is nothing too unique regarding gameplay, its a fancy sidescrolling platform-fighter. Where you as ICEY beat and slice up big baddies and small minions of mechanical (or not) into tiny bits with your katana. The fighting feels very on point, combo's are plenty and the dodges and shield/hp seem all fair. It feels nice and balanced yet flashy enough to make you feel like you're actually doing something. Rather than just moving a little blade a bit fast.
The atmosphere, fantastic. I cannot say it any better than that. The music, the narrator, the enemies, ICEY herself. Everything brings the entire atmosphere in the game to a very good point of where you quite feel like doing things for ICEY.
The one note I do have, is that the game is a bit short as-is and while its true that some things are a little bit used more than once, I personally feel its not by choice. As its a little experience that will at least grant you a laugh or reward for being patient for once.
From the simple bit to where you then ask, why should I get ICEY if its not that special? Well, thats where ICEY is different from the usual sidescrolling fighter/platformer. Its secrets and little.. I suppose I'll call them agitations for a better lack of words. Is what makes ICEY great. It draws power from the narrator which tells you what to do but.
Then what?
That question right there, is what ICEY answers. The little "Then what?" for following the instructions and instead do as You want.
Its rare that a game like ICEY caught me so off guard as it did, I was for once bent on finishing it 100%, just to see what surprise was in store for me, and I can say.
I'm not disappointed a single bit.
If you're looking for a little fancy game to catch you off guard by being patient and thinking you're ahead of the game? ICEY will make you think twice on that.
(I know it did for me at least, every time.)

So that's ICEY finished. I really recommend it. I've said too much already in other posts to give the game away, but there are certain people who I know are reading this who would really enjoy... some of the places meta game element goes. I can't even give a hint without giving the game away.
Instead I'm going to focus on the core 'traditional' gameplay, rather the whole meta game aspect. You'll still need to play this even if you are in it for the wacky (and wonderful) meta plot.
In essence it's a 2d side scrolling brawler in the vein of Streets of Rage, or Golden Axe. Similarities end there however as the game's combat is very different, and plays more like a fighting game than a brawler.
Button spam is not actively punished (in a way that games like One Finger Death Punch do), but will limit your performance compared to considering every input. This is done by rewarding the player for pulling off Devil May Cry style combos. When you upgrade your attack ability, you upgrade specific combos rather than generic attack power. Combos also do a lot more damage and allow you to build up your hit meter, which goes up by one with each successful hit. The higher it goes, the more damage ICEY does.
ICEY has a shield that can take a small quantity damage and let's her 'no sell' any hits. Once it's down though your hit meter is reset and any hit will knock ICEY down and leave her vulnerable to attack.
What all this adds up into is a game that rewards you for getting into the thick of the action and pulling off flashy moves. Your shield will protect you from some damage, but you still need to be careful not to bite off more than you can chew unless you want to risk losing your damage multiplier (the hit meter).
The final extra is a dash mechanic. While it's not a blink (meaning ICEY physically moves from one point to the other and so is not invincible as she moves), executing it just as you are hit allows you to counter attack the enemy for high damage and some crystals that power your ultimate screen effect attack.
You can chain long sequences of dashes together and coupled with the fact gravity forgets that ICEY exists while she is attacking, savy players can (and should) stay airborne.
While ICEY requires a degree of precision and skill to play well, the basic difficulty isn't that high. Completing the 'core' gameplay (following the narrators instructions) wasn't that difficult- a couple of bosses were real ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s though. Even unlocking everything (which is pretty much how you REALLY complete the game) requires patience and canny thinking more than moment perfect combo executions.
All in all, it's fun, not too challenging, rewards observation and patience, and unwrapping the meta plot is...
Well it starts with fairly normal stuff. Backgrounds on bosses and their motivations. Hints at events that led up to the story. The sort of thing less creative teams stick in audio logs.
Then there are stranger, almost dadist moments of outright weirdness (typically involving you giving the game an existential crisis).
But then deeper than that you learn the eve[REDACTED]e smiling like an analogy joke in season 7 of Red Dwarf.
Either way, if you like the idea of a side scrolling brawler set in a post apocalyptic cyberpunk hell hole, coupled with hunting for and piecing together fragments of forgotten lore to reveal... deeper, mysteries, there are worse ways to spend 8 or so hours.

Games of Glory is a top down shooter. The story of the game is a glorious tournament that is held on the planets of Svandia and Arkashan. You play a team of heroes who are out to gain glory on the stage of battle. Every round each team will have a random player become the Superstar for their team. Your objective is to do the following 5 times.
a. Kill your opponent's Superstar before they kill yours
b. bring your Superstar as close to the centre ring after a period of time.
The gameplay is relatively dull and involves using the WASD keys to move your Clone around the battlefield trying to shoot an enemy. You are given 15 seconds to navigate and find your way among a confusing shop menu which is coded in such a complex design that one wonders what the developers were thinking. The in-game shop menu is absolutely atrocious.
Conclusion, there is really no point trying this game now. It needs to improve by leaps and bounds starting with massive improvements in the user interface. It's very early access quality. You can forget any major updates to the game since it's PS4, so I would suggest just having a look but that's it.
Note: Games of Glory is done in Unity. The developer and publisher is Lightbulb Crew, a Franco-Swedish game developer based in Paris and Stockholm. It is a 17 man team.
1. Multi-platform support
You can play on the PS4 and the PC and both systems can play with each other.
2. Advertising Video
Not bad. Quite well done.
1. Pay to Win
59.99 Euro for 8700 Credits.
2. Confusing Shop Menu Design
Drop downs within drop downs, sub menus within submenus. Want to buy something?
a. Open the shop menu with P
b. Choose range or melee
c. Choose one of the many generic weapons available
d. Choose to buy it
e. Press Yes/No
f. Buy an Upgrade
g. Press Yes/No
Repeat the same process for the other weapon you need. Do you see how many steps it takes? Who designed the user interface? It sucks. Once the game starts, the shop immediately closes.
2. Tiny Clickbox size
Want to upgrade the damage of your weapon? Find the tiny + boxes nestled right in between the other upgrades.
2. Yes/No Approval instead of One Click
If you wish to upgrade the damage of a weapon, you have to search for the
3. Latency Issues
Since this game requires fast reflexes, latency is a major issue ie Lag
4. Boring Story
Did you just copy Unreal Tournament's story? Clones and more clones?
5. Generic Weapons
a. Assault Rifle
b. Shotgun
c. Rocket Launcher
d. Pistol
e. Flamthrower
f. Sniper
6. Generic Heroes
There are currently 16 heroes (supposedly goes up to 25) but they all function in approximately the same way. 1st skill is for combat, 2nd skill for evasion and last skill is an ultimate. Every single hero has access to all the weapons.
1. Simplify your system
Don't make players choose a weapon. Make each hero start off with a unique set of weapons immediately. E.g. Melee Assassin starts off with Pistal and Double Sword.
2. Give some Flavour

I've owned this game since launch, bought the Afterbirth DLC, put ~500 hours total in to it, and just today finished it in its totality. Hence, I'm now fit to review this fantastic game.
The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth was the highly anticipated following the success of the original. It successfully built upon the item base by doubling it, along with solid 60fps gameplay, increased synergies, more bosses, mobs, floors, floor layouts, endings, characters. The whole kit-and-kaboodle. Your money's worth is right there.
Bosses must be beaten with each character to unlock new items, forcing you to adapt to different playstyles and challenges, keeping the gameplay fresh.
Afterbirth adds even more items, trinkets, modes, challenges, and characters, and I would go as far as recommending purchase of it to fully experience what The Binding of Isaac has to offer. An Alternate Reality Game to unlock a hidden character highlighted how fun and awesome the developers of this game are, and how they love community interaction.
I've had no end of memorable runs and experiences that I've screenshot, streamed, and talked about with friends. After obtaining 1001% (total completion of challenges, post-it notes, and picking up every item) I only now consider the game to truly have started, as I now have the breadth of items and trinkets at my disposal every run to make my time truly interesting. 1001% is one of my crowding achievements in gaming: the fact 2-3% of players have it is a testament to the dedication the fan-base has for this game and how much people enjoy playing it.
I can't recommend this game highly enough. Another DLC, Afterbirth +, is on the horizon which will round off this chapter of gaming. Thank you, Edmund and co., for some of the most rewarding, frustrating, and entertaining 500 hours of my life. Not being Greed-y or anything, but I certainly got my money's worth.

Excellent minimalist RPG set within a very weird universe, somewhere between Final Fantasy Legend and Space Funeral. The Ancient Egyptian / Sci-Fi atmosphere mix works very well, and manages to be both creepy and hilarious. The writing is particularly good, and is kinda reminiscent of these weird 80s PnP RPG manuals or Fighting Fantasy gamebooks, with MONSTER NAMES IN CAPS and an extremely serious tone applied to the most ridiculous subjects.
Your character has three "dungeon stats" (corresponding to the classic fighter / mage / rogue archetypes) which are used extensively through skillchecks, allowing you to explore rooms in different ways. There are optional treasures to find (which are described in detail and are a great contribution towards world-building, in a Dark Souls kind of way), and multiple endings (most of which being bad ends). Sadly, the combat is pretty barebones and usually amounts to spamming attack (or, when facing bosses, the item which allows you to attack twice), although the "dungeon stats" can alter the fights in a variety of ways (by allowing you to run away, killing the enemy instantly, or increasing the chances of a reward).
Although it's not really innovative gameplay-wise, it has that sense of wonder early 8/16-bit RPGs had, which is kind of lost nowadays.
+ Bizarre and fun setting
+ Excellent writing
+ Rewards exploration
- Kinda grindy
- Combat has very little tactical depth
7/10 It's free, it's not very long, it's fun and original. Give it a go if you like old-schools RPGs and weird settings.

Bastion's main attraction is the interactive narrator. With a beautiful raspy voice, one character directly comments what the player does. But the other parts of the game are great too.
Bastion is set in a place that was just struck by a disaster, and the game is a melancholic resource gathering journey through the destroyed region. On the way you get to learn much about the setting, its society and the calamity, and there's some interesting plot twists.
The visuals and music are superb, the world is filled with vibrant colour, you see parts of it regenerate and then crumble under your feet again, and all the now useless remnants of civilization can be broken.
The combat is really good as well, with tight controls and level design that's well-adjusted to enemy placement. You get to pair different weapons and customize them to suit your playstyle, and it's fun to experiment with different loadouts.
For an extra challenge there's modifiers that make enemies stronger, and optional survival levels where you get to hear some characters' stories in detail.
A fun viking settlement resource management game that sorta feels like an old school RTS game.

Sanctum, a tower defense crossed with an FPS, was the first game I bought when I had first gotta Steam, back in the Summer Sale of 2012. My awful laptop could barely play it, but that game, along with TF2, inspired me to put together my own PC so I could enjoy Sanctum to the fullest.
And then Sanctum 2 happened.
This game is amazing, and has TONS of replay value. Firstly, you have access to four different characters who have different skills and primary weapons, and access to a plethora of secondary weapons (which can even be other classes' primary weapons later on), tons of different tower types, and an overwhelming number of different perks, and every single one has a purpose. You can play by yourself, with friends, or with random people and try to go for a high score in a map or simply go throught he campaign. The story is good enough, and won't take you more than a day or two of playing to get through it. There's 16 levels, but through DLC you can DOUBLE that, and it's at a pretty good value during sales which this game has quite often. I would seriously reccomend this game.
Here's the pros/cons:
-=-Pros-=-
-Tons of replay value
-Fun in both single/multiplayer
-Great amount of content
-=-Cons-=-
-A little glitchy
-No level creator

Void Pyramid's design philosophy is almost paradoxical. It strips the dungeon crawler RPG elements to a minimalist, barebones approach that resembles mechanics you might find in an early to mid 80s CRPG for IBM or Apple II, with a relatively tiny game world to explore. And yet the game world is full of a densely packed and highly detailed variety of novel situations and features, NPC and narrator flavor text is taken to a high art, and the hazy history and ecology of a dismal, far-future posthuman society is yours to discover and piece together as you go along. And of course there are a lot of ways to die horribly.
The tone of the narration is simultaneously dire, morbid, flippant and occasionally hilarious. It's rare to see descriptive text that's done this well in an RPG. If you enjoy games where the graphics are chiefly symbolic and the real details are to be found in word form, this is a must try.
The combat is frequent, yet mercifully brief - both you and your foes are liable to die in 2 or 3 blows, or even 1. Only health, attack and defense stats come into play during battles, and there are no spells or special abilities, only a few consumable items at your disposal. But each fight is tense, as the damage dealt by enemies needs to be gauged closely. Misjudging a single turn in combat even if you're at mostly full health can quickly get you immediately slain by a critical hit, randomly losing some or all of your gold or items, and sent back to respawn. Even with such simple mechanics at play, the combat is very strategic; players of tough single-hero RPGs like Dragon Warrior 1 will feel right at home. (There's no autosave on death, so save scumming is totally viable if that's how you want to handle the death setbacks.)
The music and sounds together have a trippy, somewhat psychedelic feeling and add to the atmosphere of the game without being obtrusive. The graphics are minimalist but done with style and originality, with a lot of bright pastels contrasting with brown and yellow neutral tones. The monster designs are generally pretty fantastic.
The lack of gameplay depth in some areas may be a turn off for some players, as well as the retro style and rough graphical edges, but if you enjoy exploring a finely detailed game world and overcoming challenges at every turn, you need to give Void Pyramid a try. It's a role playing game.

If you are willing to try this game, you have to consider that is a permanent death game, thus meaning that upon defeat you will lose all your inventory and equipped items. This perma death system sometimes will bring you in a position of rage quitting but again its almost 100% safe to say that you will come back to the game. Definitely give it a shot if you are a fantasy genre fan and consider yourself warned : you and your friends won't be able to log out from this one...

My second time purchasing this game; I originally owned in on PS4 but after a lapse in my Playstation Plus account, I felt it was more cost efficient to simply purchase the only online game I would be playing for that console in a space that features free online multiplayer. Let's be honest though-- this is the only free part of this game.
This game is bleeding with microtransactions as you already know and I really shouldn't have supported Capcom by purchasing this game twice. If the fighting game scene wasn't dominated by SFV, there wouldn't have been a need to purchase this, but of course this game is still the gold standard of the genre.
I hate these pay walls, tantalized by the allure of spending 'fight money', a currency that comes quickly at first and slows to a trickle as the game goes on. Simply put, it takes a long time to unlock all of the characters, let alone the stages or alternate costumes as you progress through the game and that's a real shame. Street Fighter used to be based on the pull of having a massive selection of fun and varied characters, now we have a small pool that is even smaller with a good handful of the them hidden behind potential pay walls that will never be seen by many players as they leave the game after lack of a decent story mode or single player offerings. This is a bare bones multiplayer game that has a refined fight system that I love, but am ashamed of the roadblocks that Capcom is putting in place that will, undesirably I'm sure, but ultimately deter new players from staying with the game for series of time.
Oh, and if you think that there will be a collection soon that features all of this content in one nice package, I'd say think again, they've said this will be the delivery method of new content until 2020...
God dammit Capcom, you had a chance to bust open the fighting game scene with an amazing game; I come back to it one year later expecting better and it looks nearly the same as it did when I left!!!

Honestly i want to write a good review but i think there are many factors that stops this game being what i feel it could have been, As a forward i apologise for the essay i an about to write but i have been thinking about this for quite some time and would like to inform potential buyers of some things that i feel should be known before purchase.
To begin as you can see my hour count on the steam version of SFV is very low, but i do own and have played many hours on the PS4 version of the game. I had purchased the pc version as my ps4 and location did not allow for a great online connection. I do feel the steam and pc version in general is an improvement but its kind of a double edged sword as i will elaborate on my key problems with the game.
my main problem with five and capcom at this point is i feel that they are too concerned with making it a game that anyone can play. Fighting games are not really like others, the average gamer may pick it up play it lets say 10 to 15 hours like other genre's of games and then put it down. which is fine i am not saying thats bad or anything. i just feel that capcom failed at even that not really adding many modes or options for instance. no arcade mode,the story mode was added after launch and honestly compared to MK and other fighting games its....really bad. and the CFN that honestly doesent work amazingly, with bad connections, not really a viable punishment for rage quiting and an overabundance of DLC.
That is my next gripe, the constant microtransactions for new stages and costumes is ludicous, they are so overpriced for what they are and the season passes are way too overpriced. the characters are released one at a time over the space of months, the dates got pushed and pushed, at least when MKX and Guilty gear released there characters they were in groups and etc. because 6 over a year is really weird. capcom also has a backlog of so many cool characters from years gone but decide to make the entire second season brand new characters which bothers me personally.
but honestly my biggest problem is the underlaying mechanics and gameplay. they feel so barebones compared to other fighting games and even previous SF games, i feel that making linking and combos so limited doesent really allow a player to use a character in their own unique way. i feel that i see the same laura and balrog play in the same optimized fashion. the v trigger system that at first i really enjoyed now leaves a bitter taste in my mouth because i feel like its really subjective to each character where some for instance Balrog is really key, but fang just kinda sucks. there is no shared mechanice that the cast shares outside of the critical art system. as even v reversal's are specifc to each character really making the cast divided between good and terrible.
The pure lack of defence options really makes the game feel too attack orientated, now obviously its a fighting game... you attack you need to depleate your opponants life bar but that is just one area, what about neutral play, spacing and zoning and clutcing timing. they feel so dead in V. In my opinon it really just comes down to 2 things, either 50/50 play or mix ups if you guess incorrectly you get stuffed and in 3 trades your dead, and even if you are the one overwhelming your opponent a stray hit into a v trigger can lead you to get blown up.
My main problem with the mechanics is the crush counter system, its hard to have neutral and spacing when punished so harshly for pushing a button. and the reason i feel this is bad is because i dont think it teaches good habits, yes you should not always push buttons but the assigned button for a crush counter is Feirce. doesent this teach you to always try to hit your opponant with a heavy punch or kick. so dont push buttons but do push the ones that have the most recovery. and the game feels like such a scramble that i dont think this mechanic adds to the flow of the game it just comes out of no where.
as i close i would like to say that its not entirely without merit, its nicly polished in many places the steam version has some nice effects that come with it. and the graphcis are quite nice. exept for the hair on a few characters it moves quite nicely. thanks for reading and honestly i hope with time they can add a few mechanics and maybe some of the old cast to make it feel more complete.

Honestly, I don't go out of my way to write reviews for games very often, however this game is incredible, think "The Stanley Parable" crossed with "Castlevania" you are an android that has a 2.5D environment to explore while a narrator and on screen arrows keep trying to tell you where you *should* go. There is freedom during the playthrough in this game, and there are tons of endings and "Dead Ends" where you will get kicked back to the level select to pick another path. One advantage to this mechanic is that you only have to jump back a few screens from wherever you reached your last ending before going back to try the other path or in some cases, one of the other paths. The narrator usually has some awareness of what you're doing and tries to seem genuinely helpful
but it kinda sticks it to games where it feels like you're just playing the hero because someone told you you're the hero, and instead makes you question the person telling you that those guys over there are bad because I said so.
tl;dr: If you liked The Stanley Parable and you can play decent at sidescrolling action games, you'll probably get a good bit of enjoyment out of this title, worth checking out.

I have played about an hour of this game so far, maybe less. Already it has me enraptured. It's stunningly beautiful, meticulously fluid, intriguingly dense, and brilliantly colorful while retaining a dismal atmosphere on the environment. And that's just the graphics. When it comes to gameplay, as a hack-and-slash alone this game would have been great. The 2D fighting style is well-flushed out and the combat feels like both a power trip and a challenge at the same time. I simply love slicing through enemy after enemy, utterly obliterating them as I fly in the sky with my dashes. Then I reach a boss and still feel invincible while also being terrified at the sheer power and inconquerable nature of the enemy. The combat encourages you to be as aggressive as possible since you get health back by killing enemies, but you must also be observant as every enemy has at least two attack patterns, not to mention the enemies that can also grab you and break your shield immediately. But is it just a hack-and-slash? Oh no. No, this game decides to incorporate engaging narration that breaks the fourth wall when you refuse to follow what it tells you. Hell, I JUST got the scene where the developer chews you out because you go to the empty trophy room, and I unintentionally skipped portions of the game just by exploring, inviting some interesting commentary from the narrator. If I had to some up this game, it's a futuristic hack-and-slash that's also The Stanley Parable. Fantablade, excellent work.

This is not a bad game by any stretch, but ultimately the mechanics seemed to me to be so shallow as to make it not really worth anyone's time.
The art style is fairly charming, the music is pleasant and setting appropriate, but the core mechanics themselves just aren't sufficient to support the game.
In essence the game basically comes down to assigning villagers to different plots to produce different resources to produce more villagers to assign them to new plots, there's a combat system included as you assign villagers to become one of three different kinds of warriors and you can recruit a hero to lead them.
If you want an RTS, the combat is too shallow to really reward any time - what little micro is extremely minor and the unit variety is very limited.
If you're someone who likes to design nice looking settlements it won't satisfy as the sector design of the map prevents this - the map is divided into sectors each of which has a strict and very small building limit.  As expanding quickly becomes expensive and what you build where depends on whatever random objects are in the next sector you uncover this won't satisfy.
If you want a management game, there's little to do here - placement and assignment don't really matter at all, each worker assigned to a building just generates a set level of income.
Get this game if you want a simple and easy mix of the three, but if you're looking for something with more depth to it, Northgard is likely to disappoint you.
