This is a really solid indie gem for people that like games to test their reflexes. It also has a completely satisfying and nostalgic aesthetic that sucks me in every time I play it. I don't think I will devote dozens of hours to this game, but it's a stunningly simple, yet increasingly creative, production that I totally recommend for old school gamers especially.
The hard mode is no joke in this game. Insane will in fact test your sanity. Normal should be enough difficulty for most people and even experienced gamers. Since you can use just about anything to press the two buttons in this game, there should not be too much lag. For what it is this game is about perfect.
It also runs at 4K with 2xSS and looks nearly perfect on my 1070. A couple drops in level 5, but nothing too harsh for what I am running it at. And man, the Blade Runner and Fifth Element throwbacks in Level 5 will have you shedding a tear, that is if they were not so difficult the first time through. This game will change up its mechanics quite a bit, so after the first side to side segments you have to be ready for completely different types of gameplay.
The synth soundtrack brings me back to the 80s in a wonderful way, and it is worth owning by itself for sure. Gotta spread the love here. They did a great job on this one. I think the negative reviews are mostly coming from people with slow hands and anger issues. I'm definitely not the best at this game, and I am still having a blast. It's a great game.

Fallout 4 has a surprising amount of negative reviews. A lot of them blaming the stats systems being dumbed down or saying the story is worse than New Vegas. This is weird since Skyrim got praised for doing similar streamlining of stats. And I personally found NV to have a really boring plot. Anyway the main selling point of Fallout 4 is it's much more of a sandbox than previous titles. In addition to most of the same mechanics returning from previous titles(except ammo crafting). You also get power armor as a vehicle than can be modded, and customized. Weapon building with extensive customization. And biggest of all you can now take certain areas of the game world as settlements where you can build structures, and recruit settler npc's to live there. This can add a lot of replay value if you enjoy this type of sandbox gameplay. If your just in it to run through preset storylines then that's still here too, and it's descent. They even took inspiration from NV branching faction based endings, and your ending is dependant on who you side with again which is neat.
All in all I enjoyed the game, and don't see what the fuss is about. However it's dissappointing Bethesda didn't provide workshop support, and then tried to launch a paid mods service instead.

Verdict:
----------

It's one of my favorite games.  The good thing about Sanctum 2 is it 's good blend of tower defense and First Person Shooter genres.  If you like tower defense games you will enjoy.  If you like first person shooters you will enjoy.
One thing to keep in mind is the clear line of thought that cut straight through the center of this experience.  You must use both sides of your brain to play effectively.
1) You place blocks on the ground to build a maze.  Not just any maze.  Use your best creative efforts to create a maze that will make the Lumes (enemies) talk longer to get to the Core (objective).
2) Place towers in a STRATEGICALLY adavantagous location.  Set up choke points where the maze becomes it's most complex and give those lumes one for!
3) Suppliment the towers that you place acting like police and clean-up crew. FIGHT!
Half the time you MUST think like a chess player the other half think like a soldier.  Remember that there's no such thing as the best tower.  Being a good player is as a result of  thinking defensively; Look ahead and think ahead.
No, it's not all about the pew pew pew.  It's about using your brain and working for the TEAM.  Some people are good at mazes, some people are good at blowing s**t up and yet some people are good at both.
My point, what makes this game exceptionally goo is the players that play for the team.  You must always remember that. I see too many people that level up yet lack basic strategy that ruins the experience.  I'll put it this way.  Why would you spend 1 hour playing 10 rounds of this game without intent to be sucessful.  I play to win and most people play video games to, you guessed it, WIN.
If you can't think like a chess player then DON'T play this game.  Only half the game is fighting the other half is planning.  Really, of you 've taken a few IQ tests then some of it will look awfully familiar.
Usually a review would talk about game mechanics and I'm perhaps being remiss not going thta route but this game is unique.   I large portion of that experience comes from the synergy created between the players.  Remeber friendship is magic ;)

My Experience:
I saw my brother playing it, tried it out, liked it, downloaded it on my own computer, and I'm glad I did.
At first, when screwing around and trying to figure out how to build momentum, it was a tad frustrating for me. However, after a few rounds of play, I felt less klutzy, and the moments when I managed to produce a spike of insane speed gave me a nice sense of achievement. Not over-the-top achievement, but as good as it gets for a game like this one.
After a while, though, I found myself in a rut, unable to break my high-score, and the pleasant progression turned to boredom. I lost the little thrill of the game. Then I realized I was playing safely, just doing a giant round-about with very little skill involved. That was fortunate because the game then had more to offer me, and I continued, figuring out how to time grapples and weave through the blocks instead of just going around the longer, duller way.
In Summary:
It's not entirely stress-free, but there is a fair amount of skill required, especially when split-second decisions (Do I grapple now? Do I let go?) have to be made faster and faster as you gain more speed (you can go really fast). The music itself is great too, but it could use some more variety.
Advice:
Play it, it's free, it's relaxing (just watching the ball fall if fun), and if you ever get bored, be more aggressive.

It's actually worse than I thought it was. I'm not exaggerating. The input lag, specially on singleplayer, is unreasonable and ENDORSED by Capcom to "make the users adapt to online situations". A Season 1 character is 100,000 credits and you get 1000 for leveling up a character via grinding and roughly 100 creds for winning fights. I spent the first couple of hours trying to learn combos, and do hit confirms on training mode.  After I felt somewhat comfy with my training, I felt I could put up some sort of fight, and I tried joining casual and ranked games.  I could not find any game, casual or otherwise -- maybe it's because I could only wait 20 minutes at a time, didn't have a lot of time to waste.
So I tried going into the lounge, and looking into the games there -- for virtually all the games I saw all the players were teleporting all over the place.  I realized while watching those games SF5 has some serious low latency requirements.
At last, I was able to get an invite from a player who is in the same country as I am.  I thought I was going to get into a decent game -- I was sorely mistaken.  There was so much lag in the game that at one point, all I did was just to stand there, take hits, just so the game would end.
This is a big disappointment for me.  I had high hopes since this is my first fighting game, I watched so many videos prior to playing the game, and even read Daigo's book, which was very inspirational.  Based on my experiences, I think the implementation of the Capcom FIght Network (CFN) in my country, the Philippines, really stinks.
Hell, if this game had a decent single-player experience, I would've kept the game.  However, since story-mode is stupid and actually has no story to speak of, I cannot recommend this game to anyone in my country for either its singleplayer or multiplayer modes.
P.S. Even though I don't like SF5, I still highly recommend "The Will to Keep Winning" by Daigo.  It is an interesting look at the life of a professional fighting game player and the fighting game community he belongs to.  If you are in a country where the CFN implementation is decent, you might enjoy playing this game and belonging to that community.

This game is similar to Battlerite, another team brawler type game. The problem with Games of Glory is it's lacking execution. The Concept overall is fairly good, there are two game types that I know of, a point capture game, and a target elimination, both modes are team vs team. Point capture is fairly self explanatory, you work together with your team to capture and protect points for a score. In target elimination one person on each team is the "Star", to win the round you must eliminate to opposing team's star. Before the game and after each round you're given a short amount of time to either buy weapons and/ or upgrade your weapons, as well as level up skills. The upgrade system is so so, as it does give you a chance to ramp up through the match; however, unless you have a good grasp for the menu, the weapon you're using, and exactly the upgrades you want the time allotted isn't enough to wade through the clunky ui. Balance is also a problem with the weapons, especially the distinction between melee and ranged weapons, melee being quite a bit more powerful. A bigger problem is the game play itself. Controls feel delayed and almost unresponsive making it difficult to feel as if your character is doing what you want. Along with this the fighting is very colorful and there are a lot of particles making it very difficult to catch all that's going in in a fight. The last big problem I saw was matchmaking, which takes a lot longer than most games. Negatives aside this game did have quite a few good qualities. There are over 20 characters all of which are fairly unique. There are also a good amount of variety in weapon and weapon upgrade choices. Game modes are fun, but could use a little tuning.
Overall the game needs work, but it has potential. Also, as this game is only a couple months old it can't be criticized too harshly for parts of the game that will most likely improve as the developers continue to work on the game. Because I believe it will improve I could recommend giving this game a try and giving the developers feedback

Even though my guess is that most of the people who'll buy this game are familiar with the version that came out 19 years ago, I'd just assume there are new gamers who want to know whether it's worth checking out. So, here we go!
Broken Sword 2 - the Smoking Mirror is an adventure game that has its fair share of flaws. But oh boy, is it fun!
The game was released in 1997, back in the golden era of point and click adventure games (after the huge success of the first game), and I'm so happy to say it's aged quite well. In fact, I found the character portraits/facial expressions which are exclusive to the remastered edition completely unnecessary. Most of them are plain bad (starting with George's and Nico's) while others bear no resemblance to the actual characters they represent.
The Smoking Mirror is incredibly slow paced. You can't make your heroes run nor can you double-click on a location to be instantly transferred there. If you're striving for fast gameplay, you can rest assured there's none here.
One more thing - the game is very linear. Even though you get to travel the globe with George and Nico and visit so many places - most of them really colorful and interesting (bar London) - you are actually "stuck" in one place until you solve all the puzzles which are required to advance the story. Gone is the map from the first game that allows you to choose where you want to go and gives you the freedom of exploring the game the way you want it.
This also makes The Smoking Mirror shorter than many other games from the time (and more recent ones) - the game can be finished in 5-6 hours and there's not much to come back to once the main story is over (there are only a few easter eggs throughout the game).
Flaws aside, Broken Sword: The Smoking Mirror is still a must for every (true) fan of adventure games. The story will get you hooked from the start and you'll want to get to the bottom of the mystery revolving around a stone of Mayan origin and a (missing) professor. Of course, being a classic adventure game, TSM will make you face all kinds of obstacles and puzzles that have to be solved using your brain. Most of them (I'd say 85%) are based on pure logic so you shouldn't have too many problems if you've played other adventure games (or you can always go with the popular method of using all your inventory items with world objects/characters until you get a winning combination). Also, the remastered version includes a progressive hint system, so you can find your way around even the most complex puzzles in no time.
Most of the characters have been voiced really well, while the music is nice and never gets in the way. There's just enough music to make for a relaxed atmosphere or a tense moment. The ambient sounds are also up to par.
One final thing to note is that there are a few places where making the wrong decision will get your hero(es) killed. If you haven't played classic adventure games from the 90s, you may find this strange, but it was considered perfectly normal back then. So, save often and you won't have to restart the game from a much earlier point.
All in all, Broken Sword - The Smoking Mirror is the sequel to a fantastic adventure game that tries to keep the winning formula (more or less) intact and make some things even simpler, resulting in a casual-player-friendly title. The remastered version goes one step further in this regard and throws a hint system (and a nice diary) in the mix, making sure that you never get stuck and that you finish what could've definitely been a longer story (with a rushed final chapter) even faster. Still, it's more than deserving of your attention, especially if you get it on sale.

I would recommend this game to Vetran Broken Sword fans to replay through this great game again. I would also strongly recommend this game to any other 2D adventure game fans (Grim Fandango, Monkey Island etc.) who may have missed the Broken Sword series.

Sleeping Dogs was a game with a lot of promise in the first few missions.  Fun, Arkham Asylum style combat with a suitable open world and some of the more fun game mechanics that follow. (i.e. stealing cars, buying clothes, side missions to pass time, etc.)  Where it falls short, shockingly, is it's desire to make itself stand out.  It wanted to focus so much on melee combat that it made play styles go out the window.
Anyone can enjoy this combat, but what really caught me off gaurd was the gunplay.  For a game based off fist fighting, the gun combat was actually pretty amazing.  Simple, yes, and only with 3 or 4 guns to offer, but satisfying.  You can take cover, take hostages, the guns have a heavy, stomping power to them, and the 3rd person over the shoulder camera angle is actually better placed than some games that focus solely on it.  But then...
You can't use guns.  There are scripted moments where you can, sure.  But only scripted moments.  You find or get a gun in the open world, don't expect any ammo.  Fine, guns are rare and strong.  That's fair.  But there is more.  There are mission checks at the start and end of every mission that take away your guns!  WHAT?  It makes logic go right out the window!  Not just because you lose your gun, but because it punishes the player who is smart enough to try and save ammo for later.  I raided a drug lab and got a machine gun and handgun.  Was SOOOO happy.  Messed around a bit, started the next mission, and to my surprise, Harry Potter and friends decided it would be fun to make my guns disappear in to thin air.  Oh, okay.  Yeah, that's fair.  I risk my life to get a gun, succeed, try to save the ammo to make the next boss fight or level easier on me, then get punished by having my gun stolen.  That defeats the entire purpose of having ammo rare.  When something good is hard to get, you want to save it.  The world and all other games have taught us that.  Make it last.  This is the only game I've ever played that actually smacks you in the head for trying to play smart.
On top of that, anyone who has played saints row 2 or gta will laugh at this games attempt at cops.  When you go and cause some trouble, even if a cop doesn't see you or isn't there, one will spawn within 10 feet of you.  I'm not joking at all.  Then let's say you decide to run and take a car...  another cop will spawn 20 feet behind you in a car of their very own.  AND, no matter what car you are in, even cop vans can keep up with you.  Want that shiny sports car that costs so much?  No point in bothering, trust me.  If they were in a damn paddy-wagon they would still catch up to you.
Now, the game isn't all bad.  It really isn't.  It does some things really great and the combat is fun enough to warrent giving it a shot if you like kung-fu movies.  But, do not come here looking for your ultimate open world game, even if it tries to pretend like it is.  There isn't much to find in the world itself, and like I said before, there are some very intentional game design choices that prevent this game from being as good as it could have been.

A story of tragedy, friendship, strength and kindness.  I loved the dark visual style of the game; it was beautiful and imaginative!  I wouldn't say it was scary at all, but there are some amazing suprises and mildly startling jump-scares.  The story was not only compelling but also as touching as it was dark, and the characters were surprisingly detailed and relateable.  The story begins as what could be reality-fiction with a touch of the paranormal and later takes you to fantastical and imaginative realms and scenarios with a unique universe theory that adds extra intrigue.  Plot twists keep getting thrown out you throughout the game, which can be slightly annoying, but it ultimately gives you reason to keep going to get to the end.  The soundtrack is also lovely.
The game offers a combination of a linear storyline, puzzles that involve interaction with surroundings and individuals, and mini-games.  Because of this, you won't get bored with the puzzles themselves or with the story.  The puzzles are difficult enough that you won't be able to cruise through them but not impossible to figure out.
While many games only have a few strengths (such as a good storyline, good pacing, creativity, imaginative settings, good puzzles and fun mini-games), Fran Bow has all those great selling points and more.  I can see myself playing it again once the puzzles aren't as fresh in my mind.  Watching the story unfold again will be great.
All in all, I highly recommend this game!

A Scribe can read archaic hieroglyphs, a Slave gets help from their fellows and enter irradiated zones, and the Soldier can repair weapons.  Death has a random cost.  You might lose money, a stat point, or all your limited use items.  Finding the hidden treasure items will change the ending.
You have nothing to lose in trying this out.  It's a wonderful weird game.  Go for it!

1. So someone played
and decided that making a rhythm game w/ a similar aesthetic would be cool. They were probably right about that but they ♥♥♥♥ed it up bad enough that I don't want anything to do w/ it.
2. Essentially what you have here is some really good 80s inspired techno blamming away while you have to beat a tough-as-nails memory-based runner. You drive down a corridor and obstacles fly at you fast as hell and you have to avoid them. It looks pretty, it sounds great and it's not fun at all.
3. Theoretically, the moves you make are tied to the music. In practice.. yeah, kinda... The beat is relevant to how you time things but nothing else really is. Sometimes there will be three notes ascending in the melody and you will move right three times. Sometimes three ascending notes means you move left three times. Sometimes, you go left once and right twice. Sometimes the same music phrase is linked to a different set of moves. It's inconsistent and becoming familiar w/ the songs does not help you at all.
4. In fact, I felt many times, trying to follow the flow of the music actually hindered me. As I got drawn into the game, I actually found myself tuning the music out. I don't think that was intended by the developers.
5. The difficulty level is also a problem here. This is straight-out unforgiving in terms of timing. You have to make tons of very precise split second moves and the relentlessness of it feels oppressive. When you should be getting into the grove of things, you all of a sudden have to make like five really fast adjustments and it doesn't take long before it feels punishing rather than fun.
6. The game even seems to acknowledge how ridiculously tight this timing is by allowing you to adjust the sync w/ the music. I found I didn't need to for my setup but if you are playing on a TV or something else w/ higher latency this might be helpful--not that the game will feel fair even after getting it just right or anything.
7.  And I should point out that this is on the easiest difficulty setting. I appreciate the inclusion of a masochistic difficulty setting but there should be other ones too. Even the so-called training mode has just as difficult of timing, just more check points.
8. If I have one small complaint about the music it's that there is not much diversity to it. The tracks are all good but none of them stand out.
9. I quite like the art style and presentation to this. It's a hyper-80s kind of feel, Miami Vice meets
. The polygon counts aren't going to leave your graphics card screaming or anything but it's very clean and modern feeling, by which I mean it doesn't look like a PS2 game or anything.
10. Even the level select is pretty cool. It's like choosing an arcade cabinet in the mother♥♥♥♥ing future!
11. You can play the levels in any order you feel like. The last level is definitely way tougher than the first but in the middle the difficulty curve is a bit mixed.
12. It is really apparent from the design of this game, that the developers wanted to draw you into this music that they love by building a game around it. That's a great idea and I applaud them for trying. At the end of the day though, the game just feels too disconnected from the music for the concept to really work and you wind up w/ sort of a brutal mess that's neither fun to play in short bursts nor draws you in for longer playing sessions.
13. I admit a solid rebuttal of this whole review would be to tell me to just get good but, really, why would I do that if I'm not having fun?

Neon Drive fit right in with Synthwave and Vaporwave. Its got the 80's sci-fi futuristc stylings. It feels and looks like a tribute to arcade gaming. Not to mention has some arcade-like bits in it as well. Also, the game can be quite a resoruce hog to appear generations old in terms of the visuals. The game I what I would consider a causal game. In the case of this game it's a bad thing because of the difficulty it seems to have. It seems to require more skill and timing than one would expect one a title of this nature. Its rhythum based in a sense some come rhythimic parts seem a little too fast for the music. The game typically features three check points per level. Sadly, they aren't spaced out in expected percentages of the level such as 25%, 50%, and 75%. In fact level 5 lives up to this by not featuring a check point at 25% of the level where it has a transition. Level three seemed to feature this minor grime as well. The title may seem to say drive however, I didn't have that feeling while playing the game. Sure there is a boxy car that reminds us of a 80's Camaro or dare I say fox body mustang. However, a player would expect something of the nature of outrun or any other 2D arcade style racing game. That is endless and requires the player to be quite effiecent at getting to the next checkpoint. Also the off part is that the allows you to hit things twice. I would have pefered a thrid time. I now see why the game is so cost effective on game key reselling sites. I'd have a hard time recommending this game on soundtrack and astetics. Its just not the game I would share with other vaporwave and syntwave enthusaists. If you like rhythm based games then it might be worth the time.

Broken Sword: The Smoking Mirror is the sequel to the excellent Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars. Once again our protagonist duo, George Stobbart and Nicole Collard, are thrust into a story filled with mystery, danger, suspense, and have to use their skills to make it out alive.
Just like in the previous game, the story is pretty straightforward, with no shocking plot twists or anything. But still, it is very enjoyable, as the writers once again took a relativle simple plot and made it great with clever and witty writing and an interesting diverse cast. George and Nico are an excelent duo, retaining their incredible chemistry from the first game, and are stll backed up by great voice acting and dialogue. Some of the memorable side characters from the previous game make their appearance again, adding to the ensemble of colorful side characters who still have crazy and memorable lines.
In terms of graphics, the remastered version offers a full screen options, and slightly more detailed sprites, although this isn't a field I pay much attention to. However, I did enjoy the fully-animated drawn cutscenes.
Also, the game features one of the most insane easter eggs ever. Towards the end of the game, there is puzzle which, although not very difficult, does require a fair amount of time to complete, and multiple iterations of the same actions, which can be tedious. Well, in case you want to skip it... the developers put in an amazing way to get past it. Spoiling it in a review would be a shame, so I leave it up to you to search it on youtube. Seeing it is far more entertaining.
This is an excellent p'n'c adventure game with an excellent story, characters and fun puzzles. I recommend it to any fan of the genre, definitely worth your purchase.

: This was the main issue with the game for me. Sleeping Dogs isn't a game that does one thing perfect, but it's a game that does a lot of things incredibly well. The amount of effort that United Front Games put into development is shown from start to finish and the overall charm outshines that of any other sandbox game currently on the market. To help explain, the team spent weeks in Hong Kong taking pictures (20,000+) and recording audio to help their efforts in recreating the city. The world feels realistic and everything you encounter has personality. There was also extra work put into making it fully optimized for PC, fluid keyboard and mouse controls, specialized hardware support, and a day one high resolution texture pack to accommodate players with better machines are some of the few.
The game offers a nice mix of cop and Triad missions that help the pace of the overarching story, but there are plenty of things to keep you busy for the collector and completionist mind. Featuring a surprisingly well-driven narrative (... for a video game) centered around melee combat and parkour, there are also racing events, random jobs, fighting rings, hidden lockboxes, car deliveries, cockfights, gambling dens, dates (lol), and enough cars and clothes to collect to feel satisfied. Every character is fleshed out and feels real, the city is beautiful, and the soundtrack complements the themes and overall immersion very well.
After having owned the game since launch, it remains of one of the few that I still like to revisit every now and again. It's fun, it's cheap, and it deserves a spot in everyone's Steam library. Give it a shot if it's still sitting there with zero hours played and get hyped for Triad Wars.
Word of caution: You might be better off without the DLC for the first playthrough, as it gives you in-game experience that will unlock upgrades early on. It takes away most progression and is something to be wary of.

The good:

+ Great sense of control.
The bad:
- Rock, paper, scissors melee combat. (Humans shouldn't be able to beat an alien by punching their face, wtf!)
- Poor design, both for controls schemes and mechanics. Where the earlier AvP game was epic this one lacks depth and feels like 1 step back.

- Close-to-zero graphics support, e.g. no FOV settings.
- Poor story, lackluster overall.
- No balance or appeal.
Overall rating for me, 3/10.
I'd like to elaborate on mechanics. In the earlier versions of the game we were set with 3 different races: Humans, aliens and predators, and each of them had several advantages and disadvantages. On top of that, each class had variations, e.g. predators could be standard ones (beefy guys with blades, a combi-stick, a plasma cannon and a disk), also a heavy variation (plasma pistol, combi-stick, slower movement, more health, spear rifle...) and so on, here we are set with the same versions for everyone, where some stuff outshines the rest.
On top of that, mechanics have changed since the last installment.
- Humans could gain the upper hand using the heat radar, clump up in a choke point and mow enemies down with a shotgun, a minigun, whatever.
- Aliens could sprint across walls, stun and feast on unsuspecting enemies, leaping across the map and capitalizing on mobility and dodging attacks.
- Predators had average speed and could jump a little higher than humans, but they had their cloak to stalk enemies and kill them from stealth. They had worse weapons than humans' and worse mobility than aliens', but they made up with free healing and energy replenishment on demand, and were capable fighters both in melee and at range.
In this game:
- Humans can beat both predators and aliens (who have metal-shredding claws, acid, melee weapons...) using their bare fists. On top of that they have the range advantage since most of their weapons hit instantly and deal a lot of damage, and they still keep their heartbeat sensors. This makes them one of the preferred classes by most players.
- Aliens are the rant class. All they have that others don't is wall-crawling, and they are easily beaten in melee by anyone in the game, which makes them useless.
- Predators have autoaim plasma cannons, cloak, stealthy weapons and much better mobility (probably the best in the game, even better than aliens). They no longer have on-demand healing and their energy has been severely nerfed (very low reserves and needs power sources to recharge) and that's a pity. Also their weapon arsenal has been reduced greatly and some weapons are useless (like the combi-stick, which is now a throwing spear) since they are heavily affected by lag, which happens in any online match.
In short, the mechanics have been turned into garbage, thrown into the trash can, recycled and taken a♥♥♥♥♥♥on afterwards, because there's barely any fun outside the campaign.
Final verdict, buy it at a super discount (like 3-5€) if you want to play the campaign, which isn't the worst experience ever but it's more about hunting for collectibles than paying attention at the lackluster story.

A brawler first, a Hong Kong action flick second, an open world toybox third. Truckloads of character all round.
Let down by both shooting mechanics and too much bloody money in the second half. The scope could disappoint those looking for a "grand" experience. A bit too relaxed about endless murder for the good cop / rogue cop act. Many other minor complaints, but only when searched for.
It's easy to be intimidated by the amount of content in an open game. It's a balancing act. Will it be like Just Cause, and require a gruelling amount of bullets, bombs and explosions to complete? Will it be like Saint's Row and turn you into an invincible god of war, making the end game a cake walk? These games (JC2, SR3) are both excellent in their own rights, but illustrate some of the pitfalls of the modern open world game.
Sleeping Dogs performs this act well. It has it's flaws, but it is a top notch open world action RPG. I could rave about this game. I could rant about it's mechanics. So I will.
It's the right size, with plenty of hours on offer. Solid side activites. There are many vehicles (it does fall short of JC2, though) plus a good taxi system to get from A to B. An incredible level of world density and detail, with limited pop in (thank god). Great cutscenes and voice acting - extending to side missions and world NPCs.
Experience and progression system is very well implemented (unlocks plenty of interesting gameplay and combat mechnanics). Slow motion shooting is good, as is 'Matrix flipping' cars by shooting out tyres. Good wardrobe with gameplay effects. Nifty buff system with food and drink.
The brawling rivals Batman: Arkham Asylum. Possibly the best I have ever played. Described by Yahztee (from Zero Punctuation) as
"...what is known as FLIPPING OUT THE BUTTERED F*** CRUMPETS..." (being very angry)
I will close The Good on that note.
Major complaints include a lack of penalisation - the undercover cope tightrope should feel tense in gameplay, not just in cutscenes. The missions are generally a linear series of checkpoints (and thus rather linear/scripted). Not a great deal of "organic" gameplay to be had (i.e. just messing around isn't as much fun as it perhaps could be). The girlfriend system mission line is a bit silly and arbitrary - missed potential to build up a single female lead? The game fails to
differentiate it self from
- except simply by having a more limited scope.
The same restraint that builds atmosphere can destroy freedom. No planes, helicopters, jetpacks or the like. A limited selection of guns. No sniping (a curious omission). The karaoke, while cute, feels crowbarred into the game. The radio is hit and miss.
The amount of DLC for this game is a little extortionate, Square Enix and Co. Nearly $40 of DLC isn't The Sims (by an order of magnitude), but a bit much. The free high resolution texture pack should be applauded though.
The final complaint is the score - rather lacking (compare with Arkham City for a memorable score).
You will have fun with this game. You will get your money's worth. It's interesting and well executed, but a far cry from perfect. May not live up to to the scope of its GTA heritage, but an interesting blend. A
, still recommended if not. Your call on the DLC.
-Skiff

It is very simple:
In general, it is very difficult to describe VR to people that have never tried a HMD yet. You might say, it’s like you are in the game, it’s like you are surrounded by the game, fully immersed. This description might be sufficient for people that never tried VR yet, in order to understand that VR changes how we experience games, how real-life movement mixes up with virtual reality. For VR veterans, I like to point out the following – notwithstanding, if you have a Vive, there is no way around to not purchase Doom 3 BFG and simply download the mod for free and try yourself.
Don't take it seriously, and go on it with friend for max fun.

I just recently started playing Resurrection of Evil to continue the campaign, but I made a huge mistake. I played Doom 1 and Doom 2 recently, including Final doom and a bunch of other WADs for both titles. This had a profound impact on my experience of RoE that I didn't experience with my initial playthrough of Doom 3.
The Doomguy runs like hes an obese person on the brink of a heart disease related death. If you accidentally touch the side of a railing while strafing or any other sharp pointed object, you immediately stop moving, thus making you vulnerable to enemy fire.
In the original games movement was like butter. you could move around freely and engage enemies. Now its a chore. The new grabber gun is a gimmick. Whenever you have to use it further detracts from what you want to do (shoot enemies with a comfortable control pattern)
The original Doom 3 campaign has its share of flaws, but the addition of different gameplay elements like the artifact and grabber gun, both of which have no place within a doom game and were there to compete with Half Life 2, serve to make the expansion a tedious, horrid affair. The irony is, after all of this time, Quake 4 is the better throwback title.

Despite all the negative reviews out there, I will recommend this game.
The good and "meh":
It is, overall, a nice, immersive, thematic, and well rendered FPS game. It even is a commendable member of the Fallout franquise, don't let those "in my times" whiners tell you otherwise. The world is full of small endearing stories, some written in terminals or narrated in holotapes, but a few others are silent dioramas of a broken world. The main storyline is very much like in the previous games (i.e. quite simplistic, bland, straight-forward hardly-relatable motivation, everyone-but-you-dies faction endings, and "We did it Patrick, we saved the city!" general feeling), and there are memorable characters you'll end up liking, as well as very forgettable extras that would add nothing but a face to a plot device, even when they are pivotal in the main story. And of course, your plot-twist that everyone saw coming.
The world is very compact, but choke-full of things. You'll find the generic wasted office building, factory full of things to grab, a school with a suspicious food, police precint with confiscated goodies, military base with your standard doomsday stockpile of weapons, museum of magic, really creepy deity-looking metallic statue embedded in stone with complementary sacrificial knife, supermarket, a wasteland in a wasteland, a cave with an alien, etc. All of it also populated by (including but not limited to) your generic junky with access to guns, supermutants and their dogs, giant mosquitoes and flies, zombies (friendly and otherwise), clawed horrors, two-headed deers, and crabs.
Also interesting is the new crafting and settlement mechanics, which justify all your hoarding impulses to pack everything that is not nailed to the floor. You want a bat? A bat with nails? A BAT WITH ELECTRIFIED NAILS ON FIRE?! You can make it (probably)! Or you could mod your sad short rifle, into a sniper of death with military-grade performace. Or your fatman to rain apocalypse on your foes (and yourself). You wanted to keep using that Ratslayer forever? Now you can! "Legendary" weapons and gear can be improved upon by modding. All you need is a few tin cans, glue, tape, standard-issue radiactive isotope from your favorite tabletop game, and voilà! As for settlements, you can build small towns for your dirty commoners to live their miserable lives so Preston would shut up for a moment, or create dignified living conditions for the poor souls of this horrible world you have woken up to, or stablish an adhesive factory with free labor!
The disappointing:
Even though you can prance around the wasteland being a saviour to all those generic settlers and making the world a better place, one tin can at a time, the game itself doesn't really recognize your efforts; that annoying sentence from Preston "Another settlement needs your help!" will sooner than later become tiring. They are not "settlers", more like cattle, that would not do anything on their own and will inevitably die in an attack by filthy raiders with rusty weapons made with pipes, despite the Troy walls with laser and missile shooting turrets you have installed for their safety.
The RPG dimension of the game is much less prominent than in past titles. Very limited choices in dialogue but similar to what you see in other popular games like Mass Effect.
Aside from speech and intimidate, skill checks are much rarer than other Fallouts, and the consequences of such checks are often extra caps, freebies or just avoid an otherwise easy confrontation.
The ending, whichever you chose, is quite anticlimatic, and lack that wonderful slideshow closure where the consequences of your actions are displayed for your pride or shame. It's more like a "Now what?", which is arguably realistic, but game-wise disappointing.
The redeemable:
Also, as in all these recent Bethesda games, modding is a thing, so even if you find a few things annoying or quite lacking (COUGHPRESTONCOUGH) there is a community behind it that will offer their love and own support to correct from what should've been common sense, to small (kudos to the artists!) details like eye textures and hair styles.
As for DLCs, it's up to you. Far Harbor is neat IMO, and I liked the music. But others... generally just have that one thing that would make your game-life more enjoyable.
TL;DR: Despite its copious flaws, it's a good game by itself, specially of you like FPS games. Modding adds that extra spice to correct (most) of the criminal oversights by the original developers and more. And of course, Nick Valentine.

5 out of 5. Simply put an amazing game that has everything you want in a video game and does so at bargain basement prices.
Artstyle is literally like the pictures shown above. Gorgeous colors that cover the entire palette with detailed maps and smooth animations. Maps are varied and "grow" as the player progresses. Really helps set the feel of exploring a ruins floating in the sky.
Sound FX are generally good, but the soundtrack is amazing. I remember stopping play and just zoning out the first time I realized the utterly beautiful sounds I was hearing was an in game character singing the refrain of the soundtrack song of that level. Be warned...you may want to buy the soundtrack seperately after playing this game.
Gameplay is a multi-button hack-n-slash at its heart but seamlessly intertwines advanced combat mechanics if the players desires to use them. This is good because the difficulty can be set to a very fine degree through player controlled options...pray to a god and he (she/it) will give you more XP/whatever, but at a price (higher monster HP, damage, etc)...pray to numerous gods and you get an exponentially harder game should you so desire. There's a "Game+" mode for multiple replay and at 5-10 hours of single playthrough you'll actually want to do so to get those higher level skills (but won't feel bogged down / bored by doing so) .
Finally, the story is a fairly simple affair, but small affects given to it make it very impactful. The narrator is an integral part of your playthrough (and a character in the game) detailing your every move through the world as you explore it. The other chacters backstories are slowly developed, but rapidly you're put into a storyline decision where you honestly don't know which way you should go. In the end, the story was perfect for what this game is trying to do.
Can't recommend this enough...buy x2 if its on sale!

Neon Drive has just a hand of levels but boy are they difficult to master. At least when you want to complete them on the hardest setting. All you do is steering a car with A or D or the arrow keys while dodging obstacles. But every level throws another gimmick into the mix at the end. In one level suddenly appears oncoming traffic or suddenly an alien spaceship shoots purple lasers at you. All this is more or less synced with the fantastic 80s soundtrack that kinda reminds of Hotline Miami. I've heard that some players had problems with the music beeing not in sync with the level but for me it was perfect and helped a lot when I was navigating through narrow openings between the obstacles. Every level has 3 difficulty settings and everyone of them "just" makes the music and with it the speed of your car faster. On the fastest get ready to use that sweet sweet eye-hand coordination or for some ear-hand coordination because it gets insanely fast but not impossible. If you mastered all 7 levels you can prove your ultimate skill in an endless mode which loops all the levels so far and compete with others in raising your highscore.
If the developers would implement a level editor with the option to use music from your hard drive to Neon Drive then it would be more than perfect. Because if you are not interested in the endless mode you will get through it in 3-4 hours depending on your skill and experience with this kinda games.

Please take your time to read this. I read many reviews here and I think this game is mostly misunderstood.
1) ITS A COMPETETIVE E-SPORTS GAME!
The whole purpose of this game is E-Sports. Its strategically challenging and very hard to master. There are frequent tournaments so you can watch and learn from pros. And its very popular in circles of pro fighting game gamers. Everyone who is whining about stuff they dont get in the game that are not E-Sports related are looking for the wrong things or a different kind of game. You dont pay for a story its not even included in the game from start (its a free dlc).
2) ITS NOT PAY2WIN! - it just isnt. You cant buy anything for real money or ingame money that lets you win games more easy.
3) I admit its grindy to get ALL characters but if you play the storyline of every single character (takes you 2h) you get 160,000 points so you can atleast buy one char. So you can immediately start to learn/master your favourite character! Also if you were to learn all characters (which is a good idea if you want to get in higher ranked games) it would take you that much time that you could buy the rest of the characters too. Where is this a contra? There is plenty of hours in this game to explore!
4) I frequently read about ♥♥♥♥♥♥ netcode or cfn in general. Most of the problems with lags can be fixed. Capcom isnt silent about it, you can look it up and read solutions like port forwarding etc..
Conclusion: If you are looking for a competetive e-sports fighting game, go for sfv. If not, dont. Thats all

Life Beetle is a title that randomly floated (or scuttled as it were) across the ethereal wooden surface of my existential desk recently, so I figured I would give it a go. Since I jumped in without really knowing anything about it, I will take that approach here and jump right into the review.
The story in Life Beetle seems fairly obvious, although I imagine each player can derive their own meaning from it. For me, it seemed like you are in a mental institute and are a suicidal patient. The patient is actually you the player, and the beetle, in its anthropomorphic state is a representation of you being trapped in your mind. The beetle as an actual beetle is trying to find escape from this existence. The final message seems to be that there is no escape except through suicide or simple acceptance. Possibly both. So, this is obviously not a light hearted game. That said, for as short as Life Beetle was, and as poor a job of translating from Cyrillic to English as was done, I would still say the story was effective.
6.5 out of 10
For the anthropomorphic stages of Life Beetle, gameplay is as simple as watching cut scenes and simple interaction with a trigger point on the screen. The actual screen moves like you are on a ship when you walk back and forth. These sections of the game are 2-D side view.
For the straight beetle stages of the Life Beetle, the game is a little more complex. For one, the beetle always moves forward, although you can direct it to prevent it from crashing into objects and dying, by turning the room to accommodate its forward motion. At a certain point, you get the ability to dash, which will help you to avoid some of the moving obstacles (and evade bullets in a certain bullet hell section). You later get the ability to hold the beetle in place before launching him forward again. This will help you to line up your shot, so to speak, and further avoid obstacles. Each room (level) has a key you must pick up to unlock the exit.
That is pretty much all there is to the gameplay in Life Beetle. Simple and yet definitely handles well enough. I did use a gamepad for my playthrough, which worked just fine. Some of the key mapping needs to be fixed however, and specifically the ability to use F12 for screenshots (currently, it is set to min/max the screen instead for some reason).
7.5 out of 10
I thought Life Beetle looked really cool. I would have taken screenshots, but F12 seems to have programmed to minimize/maximize the screen instead of taking screenshots (as mentioned in the gameplay section). Although somewhat minimalist, I liked the two different distinct looks between the anthropomorphic sections and the beetle sections. The 2-D anthropomorphic sections reminded me a bit of Lone Survivor, whereas the beetle sections were isometric and had a really raw and basic,almost Hotline Miami type design (it looks nothing like HM, but the isometric presentation is similar).
6 out of 10
The music playing consistently in the background was nice. There really isn't much to the audio in Life Beetle, but what is there is pleasant enough and seems to fit nicely.
6 out of 10
Life Beetle isn't going to change your life or your perspective on gaming, but it was a nice 10-15 minute jaunt into the mind of a suicidal person via a more Kafka type approach. It's like a buck on the Steam store, and worth a try in my opinion.

So, I've been on a "play ALL the little games I get coupons" bender for the last few days, and I've played through some pretty good games and some pretty awful ones as well.
I'm happy to say that Life Beetle is pretty awesome.
FIRST THINGS FIRST: This story has themes of mental illness, abuse, and unreality/sureallism. If that stuff bothers you, you might wanna skip this. I would NOT call this a scary game, but I would call it a bit uneasy/weird. I thought the theme was pretty interesting.
The game's (english) writing isn't its strong point. The developer(s?) is Russian, so some of the verbs aren't where they are supposed to go and there's a lot of articles missing. It's endearing as all getout and kind of a bonus for me, but I'm willing to bet the writing in Russian itself is decent.
The gameplay is tricky, but not hard. I've seen a few other folks say that the game is unplayable because the controls are bad. Here's a quick pro-tip: Use the arrow keys instead of the mouse. I honestly do not feel like the game was developed for the mouse, as it's very clunky and hard to control. With the arrow keys, the game becomes an interesting mix of fast reflexes and basic problem solving.
Also, the beetle doesn't move forward indefinitely. If you press the down arrow, he'll stop, and everything freezes. If you press up, he chargerolls forward to manuver around enemies to safer areas. It's tricky, but not hard. I completed the game and got all the achievements in about 25 minutes.
Yes, the game is short. I paid $0.25USD for it with a cupon, but I would say that the game is worth the $0.99 the developer is asking for. You DO get trading cards and achievements for this game, which is a huge bonus.
TO THE DEVELOPER:
I loved your game, and I sincerely hope that you expand on it in the future. You may want to hire an English writer to help you. I would love to see some additional levels. Thank you for bringing this to steam!

I was kind of so-so on Broken Sword 1, but I approached Broken Sword 2 with an open mind, hoping that some of the things I didn't like in the first one would be fixed. In fact, it's the good things that were chipped away; the bad things were only amplified.
Pros:
+Idea for the story is interesting
+Same main characters and art style as Broken Sword 1 (assuming you liked them)
Cons:
- Lots of puzzles with annoying, nonsensical solutions that frustrated me to no end
- Story is not well fleshed out and is very poorly paced. After an interesting intro, the story stagnates and barely anything happens until the end. I remember repeatedly thinking "What am I doing here? Why am I talking to these people? What does this have to do with the story?" Finally in the end, the whole story is wrapped up in a single (non-interactive) cutscene.
- Shorter, less mysterious, less suspenseful, more linear, less intricate version of the first game.

The short version review is this: if you like the Point & Click genre, you will most likely enjoy this.
What are pros for some people may be cons for another, so here are some general points to consider:
*Puzzles are the usual P&C fare, meaning not always intuitive in terms of solution.  If you already enjoy the genre, you already know this and it won't bother you much.  If you are newer to the genre, you just have to remember the all-purpose "click on everything" rule and "combine your inventory with anything you can no matter how strange it seems" rule.  There's nothing too farfetched.
*Voice acting is quite good for the most part and the interactions are fully voiced, which I appreciate.  Sound and music in general is nicely done.
*Art is very cartoon-ish.  That could be a selling point for somel; it certainly isn't for me.  However, despite being sort of a snob about art style, I will say that it is very well done even though it's not a style I love.  It in no way detracted from the overall game for me, and some people might absolutely love it.
*The story was good, taking our heroes into Mayan Central America this time.  The end was a bit abrupt but did tie up the story nicely.  The addition of some optional graphic novel content helps flesh out the gap between this game and its predecessor.
*There is a built-in help system for when you get stuck, which you can choose to use if you like (or can ignore, if you like!).  The help is "progressive hint" style, giving you the option to start with a very vague hint and work your way up to a detailed solution if you're still stuck.  While some people consider this absolute heresy, others will appreciate not having to track down a detailed walkthrough for help on one small point.
*Play time is shorter than some comparable games.  I clocked in at around six hours, plowing straight through and not getting too hung up on anything (I'm too impatient to wait too long before checking to see what I missed!).  For someone not using any hints, it could probably take a couple hours longer.
So, I would recommend not only this game, but picking up the trilogy in a package if you don't have any of the games already.  It's a great deal and definitely worth it.

Sleeping Dogs was both a fun game, and a fulfilling open world experience. The story was interesting and had depth, gameplay never felt repetitive as the game progressed. Graphics were good minus a few texture glitches/lighting errors. Combat was complex and diverse while retaining simplicity. Player animations were great in number, and allowed for great mobility while parkouring around the map. The world was detailed and immersive. It's easy to get enveloped in the this digital replication of Hong Kong, as the details allowed it to feel very authentic. Voice acting was mostly in English with a little Chinese added, making it both intelligible and authentic.
As for negatives, they are few, but they will annoy the sh!t out of you. Bugs were not uncommon, glitchy textures/animations, AI wasn't the best, and map pathing was awful at times. Customizability for vehicles left plenty to be desired. Despite any negatives, this was a good game and definitely recommended. 8/10

5 out of 5. Simply put an amazing game that has everything you want in a video game and does so at bargain basement prices.
Artstyle is literally like the pictures shown above. Gorgeous colors that cover the entire palette with detailed maps and smooth animations. Maps are varied and "grow" as the player progresses. Really helps set the feel of exploring a ruins floating in the sky.
Sound FX are generally good, but the soundtrack is amazing. I remember stopping play and just zoning out the first time I realized the utterly beautiful sounds I was hearing was an in game character singing the refrain of the soundtrack song of that level. Be warned...you may want to buy the soundtrack seperately after playing this game.
Gameplay is a multi-button hack-n-slash at its heart but seamlessly intertwines advanced combat mechanics if the players desires to use them. This is good because the difficulty can be set to a very fine degree through player controlled options...pray to a god and he (she/it) will give you more XP/whatever, but at a price (higher monster HP, damage, etc)...pray to numerous gods and you get an exponentially harder game should you so desire. There's a "Game+" mode for multiple replay and at 5-10 hours of single playthrough you'll actually want to do so to get those higher level skills (but won't feel bogged down / bored by doing so) .
Finally, the story is a fairly simple affair, but small affects given to it make it very impactful. The narrator is an integral part of your playthrough (and a character in the game) detailing your every move through the world as you explore it. The other chacters backstories are slowly developed, but rapidly you're put into a storyline decision where you honestly don't know which way you should go. In the end, the story was perfect for what this game is trying to do.
Can't recommend this enough...buy x2 if its on sale!

Hello there! I have to say, this game is an amazing early access gem that is worth anyone's while. Before I bought the game, I had played some RTS games, but I wasn't a die hard fan or something like that. But looking at the previews and screenshots of the game, I decided to buy it. And BOY OH BOY did it not disapoint. I am playing this game non-stop currently.
This game does a wonderful job of inviting new players to the RTS genre with it's simple and clean UI and HUD giving it a lovely charm in comparison to many of the deep and complex games of the RTS genre.
Not only that, but it's appealing cartoonish style has quite a charm to it and makes the game much more loveable. The simple yet eye pleasing graphics not only helps players immerse themselves into a viking based strategic game but has countlessly helped me personally in managing each of my citizens easily and quickly.
The gameplay is not only fun but also challenging at times. This game tests your skills to think fast and smart in order to get through its various natural disasters such as wolf attacks, tremors, blizzards and many more. Although it hits you pretty hard after the first year or so, this game does a wonderful job of keeping the game relaxed and easy at times for any casual players but still leaving in the heart wrenching occurences that appeal to serious players that crave a challenge.
The game also does a nice job at giving players some time to prepare a foundation before kicking into winter where most players suffer from food and wood shortages. This may be little to many, but this simple feature has helped many including me slowly appreciate the game even more in the first few sessions playing the game.
Lastly, the game offers four different clans that players can play as. Each of these clans offers a unique unit or building to their clan that can help benefit the player in ways other clans cannot. This variety in uniqueness helps players to mold their territories based on their clan's benefits.
I recommend this game to anyone who has never played an RTS before and current fans of the genre. This game will make you indulge yourself in countless hours of conquering tiles, battles, dilemmas and of course fun.

Tl;dr frustrating, but nice to look at, short so 5€ at most
There is good and bad in here. Let's start with the good
the combat feels pretty good, you move fast, there are enough combos to keep you entertained for the playtime and finishing moves are satisfying
the art and animations are gorgeous to look at
it controls pretty well albeit a few combos refused to trigger for me every now and then but maybe I'm just bad at brawlers
there are a few nice fourth wall breaking moments
the soundtrack is pretty good
Now I come to the bad and a bunch of this could have been avoided pretty easily
it's pretty short, I was looking for secrets and checking out alternative ways when I could and played on hard (if there is a hardmode, I don't really know, maybe the game was just trolling me there but it certainly felt hard)
even being so short the second half of the game was almost completely recycled backgrounds from the first but in a different order or grey factory hallways
in fights with a lot of enemies it's possible to get stunlocked to death, which is always a shame
some of the checkpoints are pretty far apart
either some of the hitboxes are pretty dodgy or the animations for your attacks are much more generous than the actual attack area, either way a lot of my hits didn't connect when I was sure they should have
a few hard difficulty spikes that felt frustrating
the main of those difficulty spikes being the second to last boss, Dahal, when attacking him directly he would always just turn into a spinning shuriken with no time to react that immediately stunlocked about 1/5 of my health away (note: I only upgraded my health and shield once because up to that point I never had any major problems with it) the obvious solution is to bait him into a combo and then attack him from behind. The annoying problem with that is that with half of his moves he can turn around midcombo and start hitting you and he can also interrupt most of his attacks halfway through and turn into a shuriken and as I said stunlock you, with most of these things he gives next to no time to react or animations to anticipate what he is going to do.
Adding to that they were nice enough to place a checkpoint almost directly in front of his arena so when you die you can try again fast. What I mean with almost is that every time you have to walk through another room on the way to him, listen to some uninterruptable dialoge and kill an enemy that dies after one hit, costing you 20 pointless seconds every time.
Said enemy is seemingly part of the story that, at least to me, most of the time didn't make much sense, I can't remember having ever heard of the person before or after in the game and it's never elaborated on why she is stealing my time. As to the story, some guy called Judas apparently caused the apocalypse,♥♥♥♥♥♥hit the fan and now he is trying to upload himself into the interwebs or something. I am told by the narrator that that is a bad thing and he needs stopping, so after the really frustrating second to last boss I complained about earlier I walk straight into the final boss arena and kill Judas on the first try by just spamming the spin attack in his face until he's dead to which the sun rises over the city, a black hole opens in the sky, I disappear and the credits roll. Did you understand that? Me neither.
If you can put up with at times very frustrating combat it's alright but still not worth 12€ in my opinion, if you can pick it up for 5€ you're probably alright but all in all it feels a bit like a missed opportunity.

Okay so you control a character and smack some robots while listening to a meta narrative or whatever its called. So at first it looks like a pretty cool and visually slick 2D action game. One of the big cons with this game would be that it is very short. You can beat it blind under 2 hours unless you stop by to mess with the narrator. Now sure game having a short story mode doesnt necessarily mean that the whole game is bad... But with a combat system this braindead I cant see any replay value in it.
You spam X (on Xbox360 controller) and when enemies drop low you press B. You can also press Y for heavy attacks but the animation is so much slower that you might aswell never do that. Theres some combos but its mostly just X, X, Y or X, X, X, X that will result in slightly different animations and damage I suppose. You can launch some enemies into the air and juggle them but its so basic that it cant give the player a "git gud" itch and thus really hurting the logevity of the game.
Oh and dash doesnt give you any(?) invul frames which is really weird considering that majority of action games do that and actually even when you get hit you get no invul frames. So with some bad luck enemies can bounce you around for quite a while. The amount of dashes you can perform is also ridiculous. And you can dash upwards so you will be just flying most of the fight because uh bad design choices.
Each enemy has very samey approach and it just feels like "yea this one has more hp and damage". But hey some enemies are ranged so they surely will change your combat approach somehow right!? Well not really.. Because you can just go and dash right next to them and start spamming X just like you would do to any enemy. Enemies will also often attack without giving you an time to react mainly because theyre either missing appropriate visual and/or sound cues or theyre just blending with the other enemies/objects in the 2D space. Also you cannot cancel your attacks into dash so yea.. But taking random chip damage doesnt matter because they have this feature in the game that is shield.
Shield. Shield is like extra armor. Passive thing. It absorbs the incoming damage and doesnt break your combo as long as you have it. To replenish your shield you finish an enemy with B when they get weak. Now what this does it pretty much drives the combat even more into the X, X, X, X spam where you just kill the enemy before it can break your shield and then finish it with B restoring your shield. Now I'm no game designer but I would like to think that a 2D action game would benefit greatly from having a combat system that emphasizes on evasion and enemy variety that will force the player to approach fights differently but now you just zip zap everywhere effortlessly and then spam everything down.
Oh and the meta narrative... I mean I knew it was a thing in the game but I didnt think that it would play this big role in it. Not only that again: it hurts the replayability. But the dialogue is so stupid that I cant believe anyone enjoying it unless they're 12 (mentally). Its goes like "And then ICEY jumped over the pits" but if you fall into the pit (like really super easy "platforming") he will say stuff like "But ICEY slipped" and if you repeat it he will change his tone and be like "Are you doing this in purpose just to toy with me" and then the game gives you achievement. And no theres parts like that all over the game. I have nothing against the partial meta stuff in games but it uses it so much that its just UGHHH...
Yea I'm just really disappointed that this wasnt a good 2D platformer/hack and slash.
Like if youre looking for some short casual metafun I guess it could do but I mean theres a lot better options for that kind of games right?

In 2010 I got this game: Joined the game as Alien, kept thinking there was an alien running after me, realized it was my own tail.  Spent 1 hour chasing my own tail 10/10.
___________________________
An incredibly underrated game which did not deserve the hate it got because it was not the clone of a 10+ years old game that played like Doom on speed or because of a few graphical glitches which were quickly patched after the game came out. And let's not forget people whining about the lack of crouch for the Marine or Predator (seems fair to rate a game 1/10 if it doesn't have the one feature you want).
As many of the people here, I was really into AvP since the first comics were published and I played pretty much every single game ever made for it (from the capcom arcades up to the transition to PC and consoles) and now even own the AvP boardgame. So you can trust me when I say "I know what AvP is about, and I have seen what games can do for it".
Each game brings its own unique ideas to the franchise, just as AvP2010 did, so rather than listing all the things you can do in this game (which you can easily read from other reviews), I am going to post what new ideas and moods the game brings.
Unlike its predecessors, you do not feel like your character is an helium balloon sliding on oil, they finally feel like they have WEIGHT and a real presence within the world (with being able to look at your own body).
Running around mindlessly and shooting is not how you play it, with predator is all about being Stealthy and knowing your surroundings, finding the right spots and switch, with the Marine is about aim and paying attention to details studying your opponents behaviours, with the Alien is about hiding, testing the waters, waiting for opportunities and taking chances. The fact that a few environments are interactive, forces you to change your strategy with interesting results.
I often find that people who get annoyed at the multiplayer of this game are those who expect it to play like a game of Team Fortress, I for one am happy it plays NOTHING like it, and I wouldn't if it was as frantic, chaotic and "floaty" as that game. I like that I have a sense of understanding of what is happening around me.
To this day, it is a shame this game does not have a sequel because AvP2010 is the game who came closest to understanding what the AvP franchise are all about.
Highly Recommended

AvP2010 is garbage with a pretty veneer over it. The graphics are the only positive thing about it. Combat is abysmal, story is non-existent. Hell, there are only like 5 levels; I know Rebellion recycled levels in AvP99 but in 2010 it was like they didn't even try.
In terms of the story, what can I say? It's so predictable that you already know the lines the characters are going to say before they say them. And surprise plot twist: the obviously big bad evil guy is...dun dun DUN! Big, bad, and evil! As with the message of pretty much every work of fiction in the Aliens series being "don't ♥♥♥♥ with nature," this one is probably the most ham-fisted since AvP2. Not to mention that now Weyland wants to use predator technology for his military division; seriously what is it with this guy wanting to use aliens and predators as weapons? What war is so goddamn important to him that he'll sacrifice anything to be able to harness their abilities?
The controls are bizarre. There are way too many excessive buttons and way too few necessary ones. For instance, there's no crouch function at all. Each species can all technically jump but it's so puny that you'll never realistically use it. The alien has a sprint button you have to hold down (why would you ever NOT want to sprint?), you have to press a button every time you want to transition, and you have to hold a button for some weird sense ability that should've always been on. The way the predator switches weapons feels unnatural to me because he always keeps his blades out and "switching weapons" means using a different button to fire entirely (since all switched weapons are secondary weapons). The point of this was to keep the blades out to emphasize the melee "combat," if you can even call it combat.
Melee attacks and E-grabs form the meat and potatoes of this game's combat. You get two melee attacks, a light and heavy one (well, except for the marine, whose strong attack is just shooting), as well as a block, and this forms an entirely out of place rock-paper-scissors element to the game. Blocking protects against light attacks, a light attack breaks heavy attacks, and a heavy attack breaks blocking. Believe me, it's much less fun and much more repetitive and annoying in-game than it looks written down. Additionally, the alien and pred get E-grabs, which is nothing but pressing E next to an enemy to perform an instant-kill attack whose only vulnerability is that it takes a few seconds to perform.
In terms of gameplay, it doesn't push any FPS boundaries but many things just feel off. The marine can die for inexplicable reasons like acid when you're clearly not in acid, or falling from too great a height. I found it inappropriate how suddenly marines can melee xenos and push off facehuggers. A lot fewer marines would've died in Aliens if that were the case. Predators are indisputably OP with their super-jump ability that allows them to outrun aliens and marines alike, their cloaking device, and the homing and instant-killing plasmacaster. Not to mention that enemy marines are so stupid that you can throw your clearly predator voice to lead them right where you want them. But by far the biggest letdown for me was the control over the alien. I dare say that AvP2 was better in this regard (and I'm not fond of how AvP2 handled the alien at all), if only because you could actually transition between surfaces without having to stop and press a button to tell the game "Yes, this is really what I want to do." The alien felt like you were on rails the whole time and I honestly cannot play as the xeno, my favorite species, because of it.
The game is quite obviously catered toward a coddled generation of players. Compare the beginning of the alien campaigns in AvP99 and AvP2010, only 11 years apart. In AvP99, there was no hand-holding. You had to figure your way out through that temple on your own. No tutorial, no tips, nothing but you and your intuition. In AvP2010, you start out with, "Alright player, look to the right. Now look to the left. Verrrrrrry good! Now move around. You can move in any direction you want. Woooow
you're so good at this!" I don't know what it is about every modern game patronizing its players right from the start, but nowadays it seems developers go out of their way to immediately insult the intelligence of anyone with a functioning brain. Not to mention:
Tequila: "Hey Rookie! Glad you made it out of there alive. Looks like you're not the waste of oxygen we all thought!"
Olde: "Nice. I paid money for this piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥and it insults me. ♥♥♥♥ you."
On top of that, the game is basically a glorified tech demo. The animations are front and center and Rebellion must've been really proud of them because so much of the game revolves around these finishing moves. I'll admit I thought most of them were pretty cool the first few times I saw them, but it didn't take long before I started looking at my watch and counting the seconds before they're over.
Not to mention the game is glitched and bugged out the♥♥♥♥♥ Not quite as bad as A:CM but it's still inexcusable. The game has been out for five years now and you can STILL fall through the map when you respawn in multiplayer. And on top of that there are glitches you can exploit as the predator to make yourself even more OP. And then there's E-grabs. E-grabs are not only IMO the dumbest invention in any AvP game, but downright offensive since you ALWAYS see "Press E" when it's possible to perform one; the game is basically telling you to be a♥♥♥♥♥♥player. The melee rock-paper-scissors thing is out of place and was just an excuse to make the game seem like it has depth but still not give you the flexibility or mobility for it to actually be about skill (again compare a melee fight in AvP99 with AvP2010). When I did play, I was exclusively marine because he had no E-grabs and was at a disadvantage when not using the smartgun (I can't hit for♥♥♥♥♥♥with the sniper rifle anyway so I never used it). Experienced players have told me it's ridiculously easy to cheese the game as an alien or predator so I can't take it seriously as a competitive game. And multiplayer support is so bad as to basically be non-existent; this was a problem even in 2010 when it was released.
This game is clearly aimed at kids who just want to reach the highest experience level, unlock all the skins, get every "achievement," find every audiolog/bracelet/jar of jelly (wtf?), and then act all elitist when they brag to everybody else about how much they've "accomplished." I have literally had AvP2010 players ask me if they can farm off me for levels. That's the kind of game this is. It's not skill when the only thing challenging about the game is suffering through the intolerable gameplay and story, abusing glitches and exploits, and trying not to die of boredom as you farm for achievements/levels. Aliens vs. Predator is a first-person shooter, released in early 2010 and has almost one million owners on the PC alone. There are three campaigns in this game, one for each character/creature - the Predators, Aliens and Marines. All three of the campaigns have their own individual story line, but all link together in the main story plot.
Each campaign puts you in control of a different race. The Predator is a stealthy, agile race, allowing you to stalk your prey from the tree tops and sneaking around the back of enemies. You also have different vision modes, which will seek out the other races very easily. Each different vision mode however will make the other class invisible. Aliens are able to see through the predators cloaking device while the marines are able to gun down a predator with ease.
Aliens, which was by far my favorite race to play as, pushes you to fight in close-quarters with claws, teeth and tails. You have the ability to climb on walls and jump long distances. You can stalk in the shadows and pounce on an unsuspecting enemy.
The Marine campaign is that far more standard to a first-person shooter. You are able to carry your pistol along with two other firearms, ranging from shotguns to pulse rifles.  To help you work your way around, you are equipped with a torch, flares and motion trackers.
The graphics are nice; even though this game is a couple of years old now, it still stands the test of time. There are the odd time when you can tell its five years old, but you can't really complain that much as this is easily one of the better looking games from that year. The swamps and forest are lush of greenery, while the alien hives are also very pleasing to look at.
As with all horror games, the audio in Aliens vs Predator is top notch. Any sudden change in music will get your heart racing, but like all jump scare games, once you start to get used to them and the way they happen, they soon don't effect you at all and are able to just take them in your stride. Once you hit about three quarters of the way through, any horror aspect is lost sadly. Voice acting is very well done here too - all of the main characters are voiced, granted the only campaign with much voice acting is the marines, but you still get bits here and there in the other missions.
I played this on Normal difficulty; and didn't really have any problems - the only one which stands out for me is on the Alien mission when you have to climb through an air tunnel; this took me a while to work out how to progress and had to result to Youtube in the end. Other than that, there are no real hard points to be found, all objectives are clearly marked along with a way-point system arrow that points you in the right direction all of the time.
Playing all three campaigns on a normal difficulty; I was able to finish Aliens Vs Predator in just under six hours. You can replay the missions on a higher difficulty for an achievement if that is your thing; but once you play it through once, there isn't really any other reason to play it again. The multiplayer scene here is also pretty barren too; so you are really paying just for the single player story.  For me, I am happy with the regular price of £9,99 for this title.
This is really well put together game, all of the gameplay and story elements are very well presented. It does the franchise justice and fans of the series will love it. I wholeheartedly recommend Aliens vs Predator.
