I'm really kind of middling on my opinion of this game after playing it. So let's dive right in.
The story: You play as Fran Bow, a girl stuck in a mental institution after the gruesome deaths of her parents. After getting her hands on some meds, you gain the ability to jump back and forth at will between the "real" world and another reality, filled with creepy messages, shadowy creatures, and lots and lots of rotting flesh and blood. It's a point and click adventure game, and it takes really good advantage of this back-and-forth between realities. Later, you also get to skip between time periods, which is cool.
The tone: It's a "horror" game, in that there are some jump scares and lots of gore, but there is a huge section of the game that just takes place in a fantsy realm that may as well be in any normal fantasy adventure game. There's also an increasing sense as you play the game that reality and fantasy are merging, and you can't tell what's real. That's when, for me, the game starts to derail. You get no concrete answers as to whether anything is real, but there's really no point to asking the question of "real or not real?" Things get so outrageously unreal that there's no way you can even rationalize it as anything but the ravings of a mentally ill child. Sure, you can always have theories, but "This is actually happening just as you see it" isn't one of the possibilities.
The puzzles: There are some really good ones, and some kind of dumb ones. (There were a couple "gather a bunch of stuff from a list even though there's no clear reason those items are necessary" puzzles that made no sense except checking things off the list. There was also ones where items appeared in the area only AFTER the quest for them was activated, which meant all the exploring you did was rendered meaningless.) The good puzzles depended on information or items from the alternate reality or time frames, or were things that just made sense in the context of the story.
The aesthetic: Creepy and disturbing at times, definitely helped fit the mood. Tim Burton-esque characters, spooky monsters, creepy music. Again, there's a section where you're in a magical land of senient tree creatures, a Falkor-like furry flying creature, and talking plants, and it's magical and well done but breaks the mood of the story.
So, overall, I don't know whether or not you should play this game. I'm recommending it only because there isn't a neutral option. I don't regret playing it, I just wish the story wasn't so off the wall as to be incomprehensible at times.

The original Doom 1 and 2 are great. Really fun and can get fairly challenging at times. Definitly nothing scary because of the graphics, however I do still enjoy them and the retro feel; maybe you'll get caught off guard a few times when you don't realize there's still an enemy at your back. I may have had problems from time to time finding out how to open the exit or finding secrets in a few levels, but it doesn't take from the overall experience. Took me about 10 to 15 hours to get through the entirity of them, and you can get many more hours out of these games thanks to mod community (Brutal Doom is definitely reccomended). I feel like Doom 1 may have been more fun, but both will certainly be worth playing for years to come.
Now for the main game, Doom 3. I've played through once so far on Marine difficulty (normal), not RoE or Lost Mission expansions. I got the Speed Run achievement (finish in 10 hours or less) without really trying to, so it's not too long. However it does end up feeling a bit longer due to repetitiveness. Can't honestly say it's a whole lot of fun playing.
There may be a few times where the ambience gets a little creepy, but never scary. You'll get plenty of cheap jumpscares, such as a few occasions where enemies will leap at you through a doorway as it's opening. None of the bosses really felt awesome and powerful. By halfway through, the game was starting to get a bit repetitive; find out where to go, it's locked, go find the key, come back and progress.
One thing that gets annoying is the shotgun; it's crazy inaccurate with a massive spread, you need to more or less run right into enemies for it to be effective. All of the weapons feel pretty mediocre too, though this may be because I'm more accustomed to weapons which are more realistic thanks to the modern shooters.
Overall I'd say Doom 3 pretty average. Don't really feel like it was worth playing, but it certainly wasn't bad.
If anything, get this on sale if you haven't experienced the original Doom games.

I took to Steam in search for a 4X or light-RTS to pass the time. What choices I had were badly reviewed, unfinished or released broken. A few AAA titles remained but I had played them already. After mashing a specific queue I made a few times, Northgard appears. I liked the art style, smoothness of the videos, and aesthetic pleased me. So I downloaded it at full price and gave it a whirl.
While nothing here astonishes you or will compell you to discover new heights in the genre, what we have instead is a pleasant and enjoyable tiny sandbox upon which the developers will hopefully add the breadth of content it badly needs.
EA Score: 3.5/5, Recommended at asking price, but bored buyers beware, it does not have a lot of content.
Pros:
*Excellent visual and audio design framework across the board. Great sprites, environments, weather effects, map design, art style. I left the music on (rare for me) and it looped right into the background.
*Each faction has an interesting hook, even if they all take forks that lead back into the same road.
*Varied objectives that recently got rebalanced (but need it again) like cutural, tech, economy or killing victories.
*Has a stable multiplayer client, but is best with coop. PvP is... janky, because of the combat. More on that.
Cons:
*Not really, but for the purpose of full disclosure, the EA is skirmish mode only. No campaign.
*Combat system is pretty forgettable. R/P/S system of three units who fight over very finnicky systems. Lacking waypoints, multiple command allocation, or even decently sized armies. The issues come into play when you fight in hostile territory, where the game will often disallow you from retreating or staying depending on the circumstances of who owns that tile and tiles adjacent. It's weird.
*The meta world has a decent amount of stuff to explore, but not enough yet. Most are just resource points for scouts.
---
In Northgard you pick from a faction and set to work on building a few houses, a scout hall, and then exploring tiles around you in a 4x style. Explored tiles are 'meta' to the resources you need (gold/food/wood) and you can only build a limited amount of buildings on each one. For example I had a Forest tile, so I put a woodcutters hut and a few extra houses for popcap in there. To my East I had a Fertile Fields so I made a Farm, Grain Silo, and Brewery. Following? You can only build as you expand.
Over a set amount of time you can population, one at a time, and can assign jobs (Like Banished) from these Villagers. So if you have six villagers you could do 2x fighters, 2x farmers, 2x woodcutters and then wait for your town hall to spawn more villagers for new roles.
Exploring the 4x world will reveal gold events (crashed ships, abandoned mines, etc.) that scouts can bring in cash from. Big Bads to fight later on for prestige bonuses, and some other flavor events I won't spoil. The game runs about 85% summer and 15% winter, and during winter, all your guys stay outdoors but food income is crippled and wood usage to burn for firewood is doubled. Stock up. Every calender year 1-3 events can happen like earthquakes, draygr invasions, lightning, etc. These are moslty cosmetic and kind of underwhelming events but they help to plod along the experience.
When you're done exploring and fine tuning your simplistic economy, you will encounter other AI players. You can trade with each other using a relatively... odd trading system, or just attack. Attacking involves sending your warband into their tiles, killing stuff in them, neutralizing the ownership and then either claiming that new land (which blows up their buildings) or leaving it to rot if you don't feel like you can defend it. Since the AI tends to receive plentiful handicap buffs on Hard mode, your 4 or 5 dudes will often fight a dozen and infinite angry villagers. Very good first impression after playing a few hours of a multiplayer match. It certainly has that Age of Empires RTS feel where you're assigning villagers to different jobs for resources and building up your empire. But instead, you're using vikings. Even though I went in totally blind, having looked at no tutorials beforehand, I was able to figure out the game mechanics pretty easy. Anyone with RTS experience is going to pick it up relatively easy.
Instead of doing pros and cons, I'll just quickly say what it did right or wrong. The viking theme works really well for this game and it's my understanding that each of the 5 clans have a unique ability (the Wolf Clan has Berserkers and the Raven Clan can hire mercenaries, for example). I hope they work hard to differentiate the 5 clans in the future so that each one is truly unique to the game. There's also a surprising amount of constructable buildings for an early access and I found myself utilizing each building during my playthrough; I wasn't just building stuff for the hell of it. My friend made the mistake of not using healers during the winter time and all of his villagers straight up died. Not only do you need to keep track of the season so you can save precious resources, but you have to prepare for random disasters: earthquakes, rat infestations, and blizzards. I'd like to see more of these in the future to amp up the difficulty but so far, I'm pleased with that survival aspect of the game. You're not just competing against players, you're competing against the elements.
Now let's talk about some of its lower points. There are a very small number of military units and enemies. This can be forgiven because it's still in early access but I hope they put their money to good use and implement a lot more. The dock, where you can launch raids for fame or lore, doesn't seem to do much either other than passively gain resources. And as far as I can tell, there's no way to travel the sea or launch real coastal raids on other factions. I hope they introduce more complex mechanics with the dock, possibly with controllable ships that can carry units by sea to attack other players. Also, the exploration seems kind of empty. You stumble across ancient ruins and shipwrecks only to find a 100 gold and some lore. Perhaps that's something that could be expanded on in the future. Speaking of which, the lore system isn't very compelling. Options seem limited at the moment but I'm sure it will be expanded. The only other thing I can think of is the building placement, which seems to mimic AoE in that you can't rotate buildings. I wish RTS games would stop putting those limitations in and allow more diverse building placement. The city building has always been a focal point for me and the more freedom, the better.
All in all, it's definitely worth a buy (especially during the Steam Summer Sale). It's a fun little game with a lot of potential.   I hope they realize just how much potential it has because the foundations are there. Depending on how far they take this game, it could be something truly special. Only time will tell.

While fallout 4's map may not be a large and previous Bethesda titles, you will have no problem finding things to do within the game.  What makes this game great isn't the main story, but the side stories and hidden stories.  Bethesda did an amazing job at object placement within this game.  Some areas may seem to have nothing going on, however when examining what is around, the objects tell a story that the player has to piece together and draw their own conclusions from.  In addition, character development was particularly well done.  Almost every named NPC has some kind of backstory that can be found out.  Companion NPCs respond to the player's actions, making them feel more real than companion in previous Bethesda games.  All this makes the player feel more immersed in the universe of Fallout 4.
All that been said, the game does have its drawbacks.  Choices made in the main story progression have a direct impact on how the player will experience the world after the main story is over.  Non-faction specific side quests, while very good and well written, are fewer in number making the post game feel more empty without the addition of DLC.
At the end of the day Fallout 4 delivers well over $60 worth of content and enjoyment and all the DLCs are worth every penny as well.  Those that are returning from Fallout 3 or New Vegas will appreciate the bits of lore added that reference the earlier games, but there is plenty of exposition within the game for those that are new to the franchise.  4.5/5

I realize there are a few things about this game that did not sit well with most people. For example, the Fallout series has always been more of an RPG, and less of a FPS. Fallout 4 definitely falls over the boundary into FPS territory. That's just one flaw. I'm not even going to go into bugs left by the developers, or the mod scandal. However, there's still some life to this seemingly Frankenstien'd game. Without the mod community, I would not have played it as long as I have. Does over 1000 hours, at the time of this review, count as a long time? I remember RPG or RPG-like games taking 40 to 60 hours in my childhood, 80-100 if you milked the sidequests and other content. Then you just tossed them aside for the next one. I've been playing this game for almost two years, and playing games for as long as I have, in my life, I'd like to think I'm a good judge of video game character.
Fallout 4 manages to hold on for dear life under the scrunity of a seldom forgiving gaming community. We hold our developers responsibile for breaking the spirit of a game. Our voices have been heard, so I'll just mention two things that I like/dislike about the game. These two things matter to me. There are countless other reviews that touch on all the aspects that I have encountered, but these two things really stood out.
Like - I've always been a fan of the Brotherhood of Steel, since Fallout Tactics. I think their role in this game is overwhelming compared to he other factions, but there's just something about putting on a suit or Power Armor, and laying waste to everything that isnt human and friendly.
Dislike - The lack of more obscure approaches to choosing a path. Paths that require Charisma, or Intelligence to unlock. Sure it's great that using Charisma to get more cash and exp is great, but the SPECIAL categories just weren't that special this time around.
Hopefully the developers realize where things went wrong and make amends.

TLDR; Fun, albeit short. True to its prequels - although it doesn't quite live up to their caliber, it's still worth getting if you enjoyed the earlier titles. Gimped by "consolized" controls, but not too badly.
A decent & fun game overall (albeit short). True to its predecessors (The 2001 "Aliens vs Predator 2" by Monolith Productions, and the 1999 "Aliens vs Predator" by Rebellion) but just barely. It feels like a PC port of a console game, especially when playing as Alien.
In jumping especially, you don't have complete freedom of movement as it always tries to "snap" you to predetermined spots. For example, if you try to run forward and jump, you'll rarely end up where you would expect to be - in some places, even behind where you started.
Similarly, there's a "power kill" option you sometimes get (if you sneak up on someone, the game sometimes gives you the option to rip their head off before they get a chance to fight back). However, the animation for this takes ridiculously long and can't be cancelled - I can't imagine a Predator allowing himself to get shot / slashed / etc... just to take the time to admire a new "trophy".
Regardless, these are just minor annoyances. They only get in the way in about two or three places in the whole game, and even then are easy to work around.
You'll have a good number of epic boss fights with this game and the levels are well designed. For those reasons it's worth getting (but wait for a sale - its too short, IMO, to pay full price for).

I love the Predator and Aliens genre, and have played different games featuring them before like the old Predator vs Aliens game which was great.  However, I did not like this new Predator vs Aliens game.  It was too hard, the controls were clunky, and the nature of the characters were different from the movies.
Take the Predator for example...... there were lots of different buttons and controls to remember and use, and during the heat of battle, I often found myself hitting the wrong keys or forgetting what keys to press in which order.  The Predator was also different than in the movies - the cloaking device would automatically turn off as soon as I attacked someone, allowing other enemies to see me, and the shoulder canon could only fire a couple of shots before needing to be recharged, plus there were only 2 vision modes which were human sight and infra-red despite the movie Predators having numerous vision modes.  It seemed as though they made the Predator weaker in the game to balance out the alien and marine.  And with the tasks to be completed to progress through the game, all too often they were not clearly marked or apparent.
The earlier Predator vs Aliens was better with an easier control system, and smoother fighting system.  Plus I missed the ability to make the Predator roar to scare the enemy!  Not a good game in my opinion.

I decided to pick this game up when I saw the English voiceover announcement and decided to sit on it until that patch released. I'm glad I did, reading subtitles during high speed action gameplay isn't exactly my forte.

While the voice actor isn't perfect, he still did a wonderful job of setting the mood and managed to make me laugh out loud several times. The voice actor for ICEY (Stefanie Joosten) did an amazing job with her small role. Unfortunately, ICEY only speaks one time and it's during the "True Ending".
I see people giving this game tons of hate because of the English voice action but I was pleased with it. It was added for free, at no cost to the buyers, yet people still complain. I just don't get it.
The action combat is fairly repetative and there's only a handful of enemies in the game, which is to be expected in such a short game. The "platforming" is basically non-existent as ICEY can infinitely air dash. Yet, this game still managed to be an absolute blast and a joy to play.
I will be recommending this game to all my friends.

Broken Sword 2 is a typical sequel: it offers more exotic places (mostly Central America) and a greater number of complicated puzzles. Although it isn’t as polished as the original, and has a good chunk of mandatory going around in circles, it is still a fun adventure game.
Broken Sword 2: The Smoking Mirror wasn’t exactly on par with the acclaimed original: initially it was regarded as a disappointment, but the low quality of the third and fourth games elevated its status in the following years. It is really not bad though, just not as good as the first one.
The plot tries to up the ante by changing the Templar mythos to Mayan gods, legends, and doomsday predictions, but the new enemies are nowhere near as organised or threatening as the Neo-Templars were, and the low variety of scenery (mostly jungles) make it feel more of a step backwards. There are also several parts where progression is tied to lots of talking and running around in circles, unnecessarily halting progression.
There is much larger focus on dialogues, which undoubtedly have improved a lot since the first game, along with the voice acting and the audio quality. Thank heavens these conversations are rarely plot dumps, but unless you like slow-paced adventure games, they will feel like just padding added there to prolong game time.
The puzzles themselves followed the Monkey Island formula: even more complicated, even less logical. Their main focus is to disguise the slightly shorter run time of about 8-10 hours. (If you don’t get lost. If you try the jungle maze without help, you can wander there for days.) Don’t worry though; it’s not King’s Quest of Gabriel Knight 3 levels, just old-school adventure game difficulty, perfect for anyone who wants some old-school point ‘n’ click adventure.

A fun, modern take on the Age of Empires style of RTS & a fantastic example of when "Early Access" is done just right.
On the surface, Northgard might look like a modern take of the classic AOE formula but dive a little deeper and there's so much more. The biggest change is instead of having free reign to build as much as your recources allow - the map is split up into
(or areas) a bit like a board game -you start out with 1 tile and can slowly expand as you capture more areas, this is particularly imporant as a single tile will only allow you to constrcut up to 3 buildings so planning ahead is important!
Each tile offers a new challege or reward, one may be full of monsters & require clearing out. One might be rich in ore, or farmland & so on. It's this blend of resource management, but simple pick up and play gameplay that makes it worth your while, especially at the sale price of 12 bucks.
As for the early access part, don't let that bother you - from the full game I played for 4 hours I noticed nothing that would indicate the standard steam 'Early Access' pitfalls. The game felt polished, ran perfectly at 2560*1080 (a welcome addition!) & unlike some other reviews I didn't experience a single hitch or crash.

Buying Doom 3: BFG Edition was a huge mistake. It, in a way, was my fault for not doing enough research. However, that does not change the fact that the game is overall inferior to the original games and is not even close to being worth what you pay for it.
First of all, I'll start with Doom 3, since that is the main attraction here. You are promised a remastered edition of Doom 3. What you get is a terrible console port with limited options in every category. Because the graphics options are so limited, you can actually make the original Doom 3 look better without even modding it. Another problem for me is that there are no subtitles. A lot of people won't really by turned away by this, but I prefer to play games with subtitles for spoken dialogue. Now, for the game itself. The original Doom 3 was designed to be a survival-horror FPS. It was very dark, had the flashlight as a weapon, and had limited ammo. It was quite challenging, and was very different from the previous games. Doom 3 BFG completely changes this. The game is much brighter, the flashlight is no longer used as a weapon, and the amounts of ammo are increased drastically. Not only that, but the game is littered with bugs (for example, an elevator bug which causes you to start the entire game over). The only pro here is that it includes the Lost Mission, and that even that isn't worth it, considering that it is much shorter than the base game and resuses many areas from the base game.
Now, let's look at the classics. Both "Final Doom" and "Master Levels for Doom 2" are absent in this collection, however there is a Doom 2 expansion "No Rest For The Living," previously only available on consoles. The versions in this run in 4:3 resolution and are limited to 35 frames per second, which implies that it is trying to stay true to the originals. However, these versions are butchered and censored in many ways. The nazi symbolizm in the secret levels of Doom 2 were completely removed, the crosses on the health packs are removed, and the music sounds horrible.
And another thing that has been noticed by many people. The Steam default screenshot button (F12) is actually a console command in Doom 3 BFG Edition that disables the ability to gain achievements. Absolutely stupid.
In conclusion, though this package may seem promising, all of its games are inferior to the originals. Get Doom Classic Complete and the Doom 3 pack. While it may be slightly more expensive, you get much more quality content.

This copy of Doom I and II includes a free copy of Doom 3, should you ever be bored enough to plod around that for an hour or so before turning it off. More importantly, this is the most accessible version of Doom I and II for new players who don't want to emulate DOS and don't know how to run a source port yet. Speaking of which, the realy fun begins once you're running the Doom I and II WADs included with this version in the source port of your choice. I recommend GZDoom if you like pretty lights, or Chocolate Doom if you want to retain the vanilla experience.
BFG edition offers smoother controls over DOS, and that makes the game "easier" in a sense, but the rendering of dark sections, I feel is more important to a vanilla playthrough, and while DOS version caps at 35fps, I am not able to get a smooth 35fps through emulation, even on a pretty decent PC. I really wish had an option to raise or disable the frame-limit, but you can do that in source ports.
What BFG Edition offers over a source port is configuration-free rendering authenticity. Though the resolution is higher, and the scaling is better, you will notice the dark sections are as dark as they need to be. While source ports have many more options, they usually aren't preconfigured in such a way that these dark areas won't be too bright--and a new player may not realize it's supposed to be almost pitch black in this one area, and the difficulty suffers. If this is your first playthrough you won't know how things are *supposed* to look, and that's basically why I think newcomers should play the first time in the BFG engine. It's a consistent experience for all users that doesn't require prior knowledge of the game, DOS, or PC game modding, and you can't unintentionally break the near-vanilla experience.
No matter which version of Doom you buy, you will suffer a couple annoyances ar antiquities on the way to configuring and running the source port of your choice. BFG Edition wins over DOSbox versions in my book, especially for newcomers, because If I suggest the DOSbox versions to a friend I may then have to explain the archaic concept of Mouse Scooping and how to disable it. It's really too bad Final Doom wasn't included in this release so it could be run in the BFG client and have Achievements.
By the way, in the BFG client you can't use any cheats, which I guess would mess up the achievements or something. You also can't use AlwaysRun, indeed the caps lock key does nothing. You also don't really get any setup options. What you do get is An easy to run port of the games running in the Doom 3 client, and copies of the WAD files for Ultimate Doom, Doom II, and the latest "expansion" to Doom II made by Nerve Software which was I guess included in the X360/PS3 ports of Doom II.
I don't often use the BFG client unless I'm going for an Achievement. I primarily use GZDoom as it is my port of choice. The gresatest value in this or any official classic Doom release is the WAD files themselves, so you can run them in any port you want and check out some cool mods. But Doom I and II are great games in their own right. It's annoying that there is so much fragmentation between the current official releases of all these games.

Hmm... where do I start with this game? Well for starters, this overlooked title is frequently compared to the GTA franchise. So what does this game have to offer?
What I like about this game:
- The setting of Hong Kong, loosely based off of the real Hong Kong that is...
- The hand-to-hand combat with interactivity of the environment to even the odds a bit (and because it looks fancy).
- The story following an undercover police officer.
- The protagonist Wei Shen and the characters he interacts with.
- The colorful environment making Hong Kong feel active (especially the night market)
Stuff that gave me mixed feelings or have no opinion on:
- The AI: sometimes their behavior get pretty wonky at times, but nothing majorly broken with them
- The side activities: they're okay if not a little underwhelming since there isn't a lot of stuff to do aside from side quests. For me, the two gambling activities are kind of a waste of your time unless you want a method to toss your money away more quickly.
- Environmental glitches: I encountered about one or two bugs, with one of them involving a wire attached to a security camera floating in the middle of a parking lot, but nothing major.
- The protagonist Wei Shen never speaking a single word in Cantonese (he said one word in Cantonese in the wheels of fury dlc, much to my suprise). Honestly it confuses me a little bit, but that's just a minor complaint. I'm just going to assume he just has a preference to strictly speaking english anyway.
- Guns: yes, yes, nothing's fun without gunplay, but obtaining guns is a little different than what you would expect from GTA. While gunplay is pretty fun, there is no way of purchasing firearms or ammunition so the only way you can get them outside of story missions (and occasionally DLC) is to do it the hard way: steal them from the HKPD. Completing the story will get you a golden Desert Eagle for you to use.
- The map size: a bit small for an open world game, but it's tolerable.
- The mini map: most of the time, directions for way points work, but there was one area that partially breaks the GPS and tells you to go around in circles until you disobey it.
What I didn't like:
- The ending: It didn't bother me too much, but I kinda wish you could become a member of the Triads full-time or stay loyal to the Hong Kong Police Department.
- The DLC: personally I think most of them don't really offer much, but I think a few of them are probably worth purchasing, especially if they're on sale.
- The second to last story mission: specifically it is the quick-time event on the scaffolding where button mashing is required. The reason why I hate that sequence is because there is a programing error that if you rapidly button mash, you will fail regardless of how fast you press the spacebar. How to get past it is to find a steady rhythm and keep the rhythm for about 20 - 30 seconds. (Note that it took me 10 minutes to figure out what was going on and go to the forums to look for help. I know, it's really sad to admit that it took me that long for me to figure it out)
- Animation quality: they didn't put a lot of effort into animation outside of the official cutscenes. They put effort into lip-syncing and movement in the cutscenes, but didn't even try to put any effort outside of that, althought when it comes to movement like walking and running, they are just fine. (I should note that they "semi-locked" the camera to make sure you don't see Wei's face, and when you do see it, it's very obvious they didn't even bother)
- Camera angles: my main pet peev comes from driving when you want to go reverse, the camera automatically rotates around the car and I'd rather do it manually because it feels really disorienting to have the game do it for me.
What will kick most people in the teeth:
- The lack of a multiplayer: the game has a social hub for you to compare scores with your friends, but some people like me will not care about numbers and might be upset that there is no physical multiplayer to play with your friends.
Despite my complaints, this game has plenty to offer and is definitely worth the current price tag and deserves more attention that it currently has.

First things first: This is by far one of the best Early Access Games I've bought on steam for a long time. It hooked me completely and I'm loving every single minute I've played it.
Northgard is a strategy game in which you control one of four clans: Wolves, Stags, Sheep or Raven. Each clan has a "perk" and with increasing fame, you unlock 2 additional perks helping you out. For example, the sheepclan starts with 2 sheep and can construct the sheepyard, increasing your food output, while the wolfclan gets food from each wild wolf or bear you slay. This gives each clan an individual playstyle. Sheepclan usually gets nicely through the first winter (which is usually really rough) while the ravenclan can expand rapidly by using gold (kröwn) instead of food.
Unlike games like Age of Empires, you can't build anywhere. The area is seperated into zones, each zone can have space for 2 to 4 buildings. This makes building a lot more strategic since sometimes, you don't have the food for expanding into another area, but you really need a new building. Sadly, this makes the placement of the buildings rather futile, but I'll get to that point later on in the review.
You have a lot of ways to win a game:
- Win by Domination: Classic "Wipe everyone off the map" gamemode.
- Win by Fame: You get fame for feasts, destroying monster nests, research lore and a few other ways. At 1200 Fame + a special building, you win.
- Win by Lore: Discover all Lore. Rather simple to achive.
- Win by Trade: Earn Gold. Rather simple to understand, but not that easy to pull off.
- Win by crafting Odins Sword: There is a volcano area on each map. Claim it, build a blacksmith, and recreate odins sword. Probably the easiest win when you are rather close to the volcano area.
I usually disable the Odin's Sword, Lore and Fame win conditions since games end too early with those.
The combat system is pretty nice, but thin. You have common warriors, axe thrower which are stronger, but more fragile and shield bearer, who are weak, but strong, also those are the strongest units against enemy defense towers. Additionally, you can recruit a warchief who is rather expensive, but insanely powerful. A single warchief can demolish multiple enemy units, making it crucial to rush him if you have an enemy nearby, no matter if you want a domination victory or not. Combat is also rather simple. You send your areas into an enemy territory and kill everyone in it, no matter if warrior, settler or tower. As soon as the area is empty, a timer will start, after it ran out, the territory will be free to claim for everyone. This makes the choice WHERE to attack so much more important since destroying the enemies economy can lead to a fairly easy win against that clan.
One of the hardest parts of the game is the summer/winter system. While you can easiely survive during summer, your food gather rate is drastically reduced, so you can't just throw out your resources, you have to gather during summer to survive the winter which can proof more difficult the bigger your clan is. Certain events like rat plague, gates to helheim or snowstorm add an additional difficulty since you have a major problem if you don't react to those.
All in all, this game is absolutly wonderful and I really hope we get some additional content and the development won't just stop at some point. I also hope that it will support mods officially at some point since I have a few ideas which would really help the game.
But even in it's current state, it's worth being picked up, it's insanely fun to play and I didn#t even check out online yet.

I bought this during Summer Sale 2017, had not heard about it or discovered it previously. When i saw all the details on the store page i knew i had to have it.
So what's the deal with this? well if you couldn't tell by the information already given it's got a very vibrant and wonderful 80s inspired visual art style. Game length depends on how good or bad you are and whether you're interested in playing the other difficulties to get achievements and what not. It took me 3 hours or so to pass through it's 7 levels on the lowest difficulty setting. There is a free run mode which is nice and chill, no obstacles or hazards in your way, you can just cruise and feel the rhythym as you hit the music notes sprinkled along the track. Finally there is an endless/endurance mode where you can see how long it will take before you inevitably mess up.
You will crash and you will either start from a checkpoint or no checkpoints at all depending on the settings. You might find yourself playing the same sections over and over again but you will love it because you're a masochist.

And also Capcom... making combos easier isn't going to get more people into your game...You want to know what does? Content... having a lot of single player content with replay value will bring more people into your game and if they like the game enough to go online then that's even better. Having solid tutorials to help players learn the basics of the game. The crappy one they have already barely teaches you anything to be ready for online. What about Spacing? pokes? frame advantage and disadvantages? frame traps? meaties?... I could go on and on. Heck evem Skullgirls has a better tutorial than this game...
In conclusion. If you were looking into buying this game try to get it at a significant price drop. The game is really over priced for what you get even as a Street Fighter fan. If you've never played a fighting game and want to start at Street Fighter 5... well.. this really pains me to say this as a long time fan of the series but buy another fighter instead. This game does a poor job teaching its players and going online is where most of the meat is. You may have some enjoyment from the story mode and some of the other single player content for like a week (if that). Here's my quick review of ICEY
This game I stumbled upon on a daily deal on steam. Watching a quick review of this game I knew I had to play it. Comparing this game to Stanley Parable in the best of ways I had to make this part of my life.
First off the Graphics although not earth shattering or system breaking are very clean stylized and polished. The animations are very well done and I can tell this was a passion project. It also runs at a smooth 60fps which only dipped into the 40s during one scene which just had you watching and listening anyway so I didn't mind.
Secondly the story, This is a bit of a mixed bag. The STORY part of the story has you as ICEY traveling to defeat the evil bad guy named Judas. No context other than that. No idea what he did or why ICEY a robot (android?) awakened when she did to kill him. Where the story shines in the the literal LOL moments you get when you disobey the narrator. The things he said sometimes were just too good and spot on. The humor is much much better than I initially expected. I won't say much more I don't want to spoil this game which  is a measly 3-4 hours of play time but this is one of those games that you can get lost in because its so good even if its as short as it is.
This game is really worth playing if the thought of a hack and slash 2d game got frisky with the Stanley Parable one drunken night appeals to you. Well worth the money even at full price.
9/10

This game is very much a mixed bag. There's much to like about it and, equally, much to dislike about it. It's tough to explain.
The core of the game, it's gameplay, is very good. It's a 2D combo beat em up type game with a great amount of emphisis placed on movement and knowing your enemy. ICEY has a fair amount of combos to work with, each one giving you a kind of edge depending on how you use em. She also has a small selection of special attacks, such as a full combo with damage immunity in exchange for a chunk of health, or a shadow attack you can use to further damage foes you've stuck sometimes. And to top it off you have finishers, where when an enemy has taken enough damage you can chunck them for some health and get some healing, or straight up finish them if they're at that point. All of these are avalable in an upgrade menu you can access at checkpoints, with the only restriction being how much "Money" you collect from foes and explorations.
ICEY controls fluidly, never leaving you locked into something with her one and only defensive ability, dashing. You will be relient on this move, being her quickest movement option. It works in 8 directions, and is always avalibe in all of them for as long as you have a charge in her dash meter. If you manage to evade an attack at, as far as I can tell, frame perfect timing, you'll also negate that hit of the attack and be given a prompt to counter, dealing massive damage to the target.
Your only other defensive... anything is your sheild, an overbarrier of health that prevents knock back and recharges when it empties or when you kill something.
ICEY is a joy to control, with her nimbleness allowing for out menuvering foes and, with some skill, leading into chain kills that are aboslutly amazing to pull off. In terms of fighting a good fight, it all boils down to you skill. However...
The enemy roster is another matter. With the power they've invested into ICEY at hand, there is just as much if not even more power invested into your foes. Many mid to large tier enemies have super armor that only sometimes breaks, meaning it's up to you to outmenuver them. However, alot of them are relentless and attack very quickly. It's not hard to get overwhelmed in a pack and even comboed. Of the common rabble, the worst of them have to be the leg robots and the lazer bats. The leg robots attack very quickly and have pretty large attack boxes, and have a flip kick move that is near impossible to avoid when in striking distance. The lazer bats will shoot a straight lazer across the screen at you from their position. It's instantanious and have a very long if thin attack box. These are the turds that'll get you comboed. They even have a 3 shot rapid fire move and a sweeping lazer attack. They're not hard to deal with, but they will get you at the worst of times, what's worse being that some bosses infinitly spawn them along with other mooks.
There's enough veriety to keep from becoming stale, but ultimately I feel as though there is much to be desired from avarage enemies.
Bosses are an entirly different matter. Most of the time they serve as a larger threat to your progress that genuinly test your skill at handling ICEY. However, there are a few hangups about a selection of them.  Ideon can very easily be stuck into infinently using his lazer attacks. Carlos has one attack that has a huge hit box, hits multiple times, and has him move across the screen very quickly. It's super had to avoid if you happen to be in striking distance. And Dahal,
has one attack where he dashes to you from wherever it is to you super quickly and does an instantanious spinning uppercut that breaks your sheild, multihits, and can leave you exposed to aditional hard hitting moves that come after the attack. It makes attacking after any one of its attacks a gamble, and makes the fight overall not fun. I was once insantly true comboed from full health to death when it decided to spam it over an over.
I will stress this again. You will have to be on your game to win fights. Unless you pick easy mode.
The art is... quite simply, amazing. While there is a slight disconnect between ICEY and her surroundings, both she and the background are simply stunning to look at. Just like her control, ICEY moves very eggerly at the press of a button, the animations being inate and clean for her and everyone else. The background is a full scale art book on it's own, with such precise detail that, while stadic, are alive. This game is simply beautiful.
I wish I could say the same for it's storytelling. This game is
The whole game is narrated by a voice that prompts you to do things to progress the story and explains what's going on. However,
It doesn't help that the english voice was acted poorly. Every single line feels like a first read without much modivation, and the writing is bland. There are many instances that probably make more sense in the games native Chinese, but when translated over to english are simply tactless and dull. And the english actor needed much better direction. He comes off more as an older guy trying to seriously be a nagging teen who tells you how to play the game the whole time, and he lacked emotion at what should have been emotional moments.
The underlying story collected from text is very take it or leave it. It can add charactier or just be some edgy teen writting pulled from
The game is chocked full of little secrets that can be fun to find.
Ultimatly, I think this game is a great 12 dollar title that has a lot to offer that, despite best efforts, could have benifited from better writting and voice acting. It's all very worth it to complete the game  [spoilers] and finally see ICEY grow into her own right at the end.[/spoiler] It was a very emotional moment for me. I recomend this game, but only if you're willing to invest the time into it.
TLDR: Super fun, needed better writing and acting.

Fran Bow is a point-and-click adventure game. It starts out with all the psychological horror you'd expect from the promotional material, but it quickly heads in the direction of story, lore, and worldbuilding.
The gameplay is pretty straightforward and easy for a point-and-click. There are no tear-out-your-hair puzzles, and the real purpose of the game are the story, characters, and world.
Fran is the best video game protagonist I've played in a long time. Although she's a child embarked on on a perilous odyssey, she doesn't feel like a victim. She greets eldritch abominations with friendship and curiosity, and overcomes fear and adversity with firey indignation. Fran is well-written. Her naive-yet-perceptive dialogue and observations bring to mind Calvin and Hobbes.
The story is a little rushed at the end, but the journey is worthwhile. Fran Bow is a hand-crafted labor of love. It's a little creepy, a little cute, and an overall off-the-beaten-path gem.

The hate for the game isn't justified, at least not what most reviews state.
I have a total of 160 hours so far between PC and PS4 and the main gripes with the game aren't even functional such as netcode, input lag, and dlc barriers.
The main issue to be aware of is that SFV gameplay is not focused around neutral game, where on wake-up you're now always at a disadvantage. In SFIV getting knocked down is a reset into neutral. There are simply too many 50/50 mixup characters top tier at the moment, and they have the clear advantage over the original footsy based gameplay characters the game is known for.
Karin, R.Mika, Laura, and Balrog to name of few are at massive advantage over footsies characters like Ryu, Ken, Necalli, to the point that they modified charge input moves and characters such as Bison and Chun-Li to keep up with the faster gameplay.
3 good reads against an opponent's recovery will clear their health gauge, it just doesn't allow for a lot of gameplay variety.
Don't NOT buy the game because of netcode and dlc, because games nowadays are increasingly difficult to make. If you want a perfect experience play SFII local or something, because right now SFV offers more features than any other SF game to date. There is no fighting game that has no netplay issues, and game developers are not going to release free characters, that costs resources. Buying DLC keeps the game alive, or you can choose to grind your way to dlc content, that's fine.
I DO recommend this game because it is the clear cut best way to get into this impossibly difficult game, and SFV grew the community in ways SFIV could never have done.
While it's not perfect, SFV is fast paced, fun, and constantly rewards players who put in time to learn and adapt, so long as you're not one to throw your fightstick for getting crush countered on recovery.

I really like the point&click genre, just like Syberia, my favourite one from the childhood years. Fran Bow is, let's say, an ordinary point&click with an extremely unordinary plot and characters.
Let's start with the characters, shall we? The game isn't long, but we've got some worth mentioning. First of all, the mc, Fran. 10 yo girl who has just lost her parents. She's being kept in the child asylum and her cat, her best friend (I can kinda relate to this, I've got a cat myself) is missing. On top of that, she's being chased by a horrible monstrosity that wants her dead.
She's really cute throughout the game. Just a brave, sometimes silly, little girl who has found herself in the madness of the adult reality (when you're alone and don't know what to do) or, well, quite a lot of new worlds full of bizarre, sometimes hostile creatures.
I won't tell much about the lore but I must say that it is pretty complex for a short game like Fran Bow. I think that it would need at least twice as much time to fully touch the subject of all the realities Fran is visiting and all the characters that are worth knowing. Most of the mysteries remain unsolved for now and all we can do is hope for the second part. Of course, after the studio would finish Different Galaxy.
The rest of the characters are lovable (at least most of them). Mr Midnight, Palontras and Itward became a good example of friends that are going to help you go through even the worst moments. [Especially Itward. Really, when you meet him, you're so tired of all the unfriendliness around you, that you're starting to think he would hurt you too. And all he does is bring you home.] Some would use a better explained backstory but, again, the game's too short for that.
The ending remains open, which is good for the authors but not really satisfying, considering it explains nothing and can be used for many theories and stuff. I've come with the two strong ones myself, so people who love theories - the game's made for you!
I strongly recommend this to these people that want to have their mind blown or just to enjoy a good story.
It is indeed a good story.

I just finished my own playthrough of this game, six or so months after watching somebody's playthrough on YouTube. What a phenomenal game. It's my favorite type, just simple, point-and-click adventure puzzle game-- rich in story and perfect in art direction. It hits all the right buttons for someone like me. Something psychologically dark, yet remaining truly whimsical. The writing is spot-on, I truly feel like I'm living the game's story through a ten year old girl's pragmatic and curious point of view.
Now, naturally there are less than shining aspects to the game. The puzzles aren't the most challenging, but in a game like this it's more about the story for me. Sometimes the adventure involves clicking and pointing one too many times to get from point A to point B to point C... I know where I want to go, it shouldn't take me five screens to get where I'm going!
But all of the duller parts of this game are completely outshone by such an amazing story. Please take the time to read everything, click everything at least three times to see the details in the descriptions, try combining everything. It's worth it. It's worth your time, and so much effort was poured into this game to make it what a spectacular game it is.
But truth be told, this game is worth your time, even if you're speeding through it. The art, the music, and the atmosphere perfectly crafts a world (or five) where one small human girl must face so so many monsters...with only one small black cat on her side.
Take the time, spend the money on this game, it's worth more than both put together. Such a gem, I look forward to anything else these developers make.

Apparently the game wants to stay faithful to the original era, which is both good and bad. While the style can be kept retro, some improvements could have been made to make it a bit more enjoyable experience.
The bad:
- starts full screen (the pixelated text is almost unreadable in this size!)
- no tutorial in the game, you need to read the external manual to figure out how the game works
- the scripture text is written sloooooww... you lose the start of the sentence from your mind before you can read the full text, so either wait until the text is written and read it then, or suffer by the slow reading. Unfortunately as the text moves to next page, the page is changed immediately, so you really aren't given the choice of waiting for text to be done to read it afterwards
- character movement is slow
- controls are a bit weird at start (they do make sense for the rest of game mechanics, though), and anyway work a bit wonky as the game tries to help you from getting stuck next to doorway and automatically changes your walking direction, but if you try to manually fix the direction at the same time, you may end up walking totally wrong way
- changing camera angles at each map tile gets very confusing, especially at the start when you have no idea of the layout (intentional to disorient you?)
- some bugs in AI behavior (the abbot may get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at you for no reason)
- night time sneaking... why does the abbot wake up whenever you get closer to the church?
- final puzzle with mirror... never could I have thought that I would need to use keyboard out of the normal movement controls
But then... despite all those flaws, the game is playable and the story does capture you. More and more is revealed throughout the game and while William is making his deductions of the murder case, the player is also allowed to come up with other explanations and possible scenarios of the big picture. And the suspect keeps changing as more details are uncovered. If you can get past the 80s graphics and game mechanics, the price tag of "Free" is totally worth paying for the story.

One of my favourite games that I think I will never stop playing. The hidden lore is pretty interesting. The amount of items and synergies will blow your mind. Fran Bow does as the description says. You are getting exactly what is being sold, and it is a beautiful, imperfect product. You travel with Fran Bow, a little girl who has lost her parents in a horrific way and is trying to figure out how to cope. What is reality? You'll be asking yourself that question a lot along the way.
The puzzles are a good blend of initiative thinking and difficulty. The horror from the game comes from the distortion of reality with few jump scares. A warning, though; If you do not like gore, then you will have difficulties with this game. There is a lot of body horror that comes along with the psychological horror. It has some fun mini-games that are not puzzle based, and you'll need to play through some of the chapters at least twice to get all of the achievements.
The store itself has a lot of twists and turns that'll leave you trying to find out what has happened even after the credits end. While the ending is meant to be ambiguous, part of your questions will come from loose ends. There aren't necessarily plot holes, but there are some plot lines that are brought to the story and then shortly forgotten about. Just allow the story to push you along where it goes.
I'd definitely recommend this game to those that like a story with their point-and-click games, though it is not for the faint of heart due to the amount of gore in the game. I really hope that they'll create a sequel.

Hmm... where do I start with this game? Well for starters, this overlooked title is frequently compared to the GTA franchise. So what does this game have to offer?
What I like about this game:
- The setting of Hong Kong, loosely based off of the real Hong Kong that is...
- The hand-to-hand combat with interactivity of the environment to even the odds a bit (and because it looks fancy).
- The story following an undercover police officer.
- The protagonist Wei Shen and the characters he interacts with.
- The colorful environment making Hong Kong feel active (especially the night market)
Stuff that gave me mixed feelings or have no opinion on:
- The AI: sometimes their behavior get pretty wonky at times, but nothing majorly broken with them
- The side activities: they're okay if not a little underwhelming since there isn't a lot of stuff to do aside from side quests. For me, the two gambling activities are kind of a waste of your time unless you want a method to toss your money away more quickly.
- Environmental glitches: I encountered about one or two bugs, with one of them involving a wire attached to a security camera floating in the middle of a parking lot, but nothing major.
- The protagonist Wei Shen never speaking a single word in Cantonese (he said one word in Cantonese in the wheels of fury dlc, much to my suprise). Honestly it confuses me a little bit, but that's just a minor complaint. I'm just going to assume he just has a preference to strictly speaking english anyway.
- Guns: yes, yes, nothing's fun without gunplay, but obtaining guns is a little different than what you would expect from GTA. While gunplay is pretty fun, there is no way of purchasing firearms or ammunition so the only way you can get them outside of story missions (and occasionally DLC) is to do it the hard way: steal them from the HKPD. Completing the story will get you a golden Desert Eagle for you to use.
- The map size: a bit small for an open world game, but it's tolerable.
- The mini map: most of the time, directions for way points work, but there was one area that partially breaks the GPS and tells you to go around in circles until you disobey it.
What I didn't like:
- The ending: It didn't bother me too much, but I kinda wish you could become a member of the Triads full-time or stay loyal to the Hong Kong Police Department.
- The DLC: personally I think most of them don't really offer much, but I think a few of them are probably worth purchasing, especially if they're on sale.
- The second to last story mission: specifically it is the quick-time event on the scaffolding where button mashing is required. The reason why I hate that sequence is because there is a programing error that if you rapidly button mash, you will fail regardless of how fast you press the spacebar. How to get past it is to find a steady rhythm and keep the rhythm for about 20 - 30 seconds. (Note that it took me 10 minutes to figure out what was going on and go to the forums to look for help. I know, it's really sad to admit that it took me that long for me to figure it out)
- Animation quality: they didn't put a lot of effort into animation outside of the official cutscenes. They put effort into lip-syncing and movement in the cutscenes, but didn't even try to put any effort outside of that, althought when it comes to movement like walking and running, they are just fine. (I should note that they "semi-locked" the camera to make sure you don't see Wei's face, and when you do see it, it's very obvious they didn't even bother)
- Camera angles: my main pet peev comes from driving when you want to go reverse, the camera automatically rotates around the car and I'd rather do it manually because it feels really disorienting to have the game do it for me.
What will kick most people in the teeth:
- The lack of a multiplayer: the game has a social hub for you to compare scores with your friends, but some people like me will not care about numbers and might be upset that there is no physical multiplayer to play with your friends.
Despite my complaints, this game has plenty to offer and is definitely worth the current price tag and deserves more attention that it currently has.

First things first: This is by far one of the best Early Access Games I've bought on steam for a long time. It hooked me completely and I'm loving every single minute I've played it.
Northgard is a strategy game in which you control one of four clans: Wolves, Stags, Sheep or Raven. Each clan has a "perk" and with increasing fame, you unlock 2 additional perks helping you out. For example, the sheepclan starts with 2 sheep and can construct the sheepyard, increasing your food output, while the wolfclan gets food from each wild wolf or bear you slay. This gives each clan an individual playstyle. Sheepclan usually gets nicely through the first winter (which is usually really rough) while the ravenclan can expand rapidly by using gold (kröwn) instead of food.
Unlike games like Age of Empires, you can't build anywhere. The area is seperated into zones, each zone can have space for 2 to 4 buildings. This makes building a lot more strategic since sometimes, you don't have the food for expanding into another area, but you really need a new building. Sadly, this makes the placement of the buildings rather futile, but I'll get to that point later on in the review.
You have a lot of ways to win a game:
- Win by Domination: Classic "Wipe everyone off the map" gamemode.
- Win by Fame: You get fame for feasts, destroying monster nests, research lore and a few other ways. At 1200 Fame + a special building, you win.
- Win by Lore: Discover all Lore. Rather simple to achive.
- Win by Trade: Earn Gold. Rather simple to understand, but not that easy to pull off.
- Win by crafting Odins Sword: There is a volcano area on each map. Claim it, build a blacksmith, and recreate odins sword. Probably the easiest win when you are rather close to the volcano area.
I usually disable the Odin's Sword, Lore and Fame win conditions since games end too early with those.
The combat system is pretty nice, but thin. You have common warriors, axe thrower which are stronger, but more fragile and shield bearer, who are weak, but strong, also those are the strongest units against enemy defense towers. Additionally, you can recruit a warchief who is rather expensive, but insanely powerful. A single warchief can demolish multiple enemy units, making it crucial to rush him if you have an enemy nearby, no matter if you want a domination victory or not. Combat is also rather simple. You send your areas into an enemy territory and kill everyone in it, no matter if warrior, settler or tower. As soon as the area is empty, a timer will start, after it ran out, the territory will be free to claim for everyone. This makes the choice WHERE to attack so much more important since destroying the enemies economy can lead to a fairly easy win against that clan.
One of the hardest parts of the game is the summer/winter system. While you can easiely survive during summer, your food gather rate is drastically reduced, so you can't just throw out your resources, you have to gather during summer to survive the winter which can proof more difficult the bigger your clan is. Certain events like rat plague, gates to helheim or snowstorm add an additional difficulty since you have a major problem if you don't react to those.
All in all, this game is absolutly wonderful and I really hope we get some additional content and the development won't just stop at some point. I also hope that it will support mods officially at some point since I have a few ideas which would really help the game.
But even in it's current state, it's worth being picked up, it's insanely fun to play and I didn#t even check out online yet.

Bastion pairs an emotionally impactful and technically well-constructed and -told story with simple, time-proven hack-and-slash combat mechanics and a few basic but charming upgrade systems. The story is luxuriously unfolded by the narrator over time, and a surprisingly complicated and fleshed-out world is revealed without any in-game character interaction. Civilizations, wars, rebel-organizations, old friends, 4th-dimensional travel, religions, and mega-fauna are all engendered with little more than their in-game representations and descriptions by the narrator.
Bastion can be considered an experiment with narrative in video games; an homage, emulation, and new installation in the world of hack-and-slash and upgrade RPGs; and a genre-defining piece on its own.
By the same team is the newer game Transistor, which plays with many of the same ideas, expands them in clever ways that must be seen to be understood, and blooms around them a new story, a new world, and new characters. Any serious fan of Bastion should give it a try, even if only for the re-contextualization of the first game.

Simply put? Doom 3: BFG Edition is one hell of a game.
The main attraction here, as the title suggests, Doom 3. Even 12 years after it's release, the original Doom 3 looks sharp. It looks way ahead of anything else the same year. Simply put, it's a gorgeous game, and it's HD re-master is no different. Textures are sharp, and crisp: the only lacking part of Doom 3's graphical prowess of old. Character models were, well, not the best in terms of texturing. Now everything has been given a hi-res paint job and the game looks great.
Doom 3 plays excellently. Nothing was lost in the trasition. The slew of guns all feel unique. However the main problem of the game is the shotguns. They're, well, too powerful: almost rendering other weapons completely obsolete. But that doesn't subtract from the superb horror-themed shooting. Everything controls so well, and the addition of a flash-light mounted to your marines shoulder instead of a flashlight you're stuck having to pull out every time you're in the dark was a smart move unless you're one of those brain-dead players who forgets how the controls of every game they're playing works.
As for horror, Doom 3 isn't really scary. It was, once upon a time, for me. But 12 years and exposure to games like Amnesia have dulled any chances of being frightened here - plus, I first played it when I was a kid.
Doom 3: BFG Edition doesn't stop there, though. It includes the Lost Missions: approximately an hour of unreleased missions that use content from both the Resurrection of Evil expansion (which is also included) and the base expansion.
Thought that was it? Doom 1 and 2 are included: as well as all their expansions.
My only real complaint is Doom 2. I never really liked the game. It feels like clever level design went out the window, and exploration took a backseat to the developers cramming hundreds of enemies on screen at a time.
Recommend? Hell yes. Whether you're buying it for console or PC, Doom 3: BFG edition is one hell of a bargain.

The hate for the game isn't justified, at least not what most reviews state.
I have a total of 160 hours so far between PC and PS4 and the main gripes with the game aren't even functional such as netcode, input lag, and dlc barriers.
The main issue to be aware of is that SFV gameplay is not focused around neutral game, where on wake-up you're now always at a disadvantage. In SFIV getting knocked down is a reset into neutral. There are simply too many 50/50 mixup characters top tier at the moment, and they have the clear advantage over the original footsy based gameplay characters the game is known for.
Karin, R.Mika, Laura, and Balrog to name of few are at massive advantage over footsies characters like Ryu, Ken, Necalli, to the point that they modified charge input moves and characters such as Bison and Chun-Li to keep up with the faster gameplay.
3 good reads against an opponent's recovery will clear their health gauge, it just doesn't allow for a lot of gameplay variety.
Don't NOT buy the game because of netcode and dlc, because games nowadays are increasingly difficult to make. If you want a perfect experience play SFII local or something, because right now SFV offers more features than any other SF game to date. There is no fighting game that has no netplay issues, and game developers are not going to release free characters, that costs resources. Buying DLC keeps the game alive, or you can choose to grind your way to dlc content, that's fine.
I DO recommend this game because it is the clear cut best way to get into this impossibly difficult game, and SFV grew the community in ways SFIV could never have done.
While it's not perfect, SFV is fast paced, fun, and constantly rewards players who put in time to learn and adapt, so long as you're not one to throw your fightstick for getting crush countered on recovery.

I'm a sucker for atmosphere, so I was immediately all in when I saw screenshots of Fran Bow. The art and presentation for this game are the exact sort of thing I'm into, so despite any other issues, it was a solid experience. The protagonist, Fran, forms some genuinely touching connections to the other characters over the course of the story, which makes the tragedies all that more biting. And the fact that the surrealism never gets collapsed into a full version of the truth really showed me that the creators didn't buckle under fan expectations. There's almost no way this isn't the game they intended to make.
Some minor fussing points:
- The translation is a little awkward in spots. Not really a deal-breaker in a game more oriented towards visual storytelling, but still noticeable.
- Every adventure game should have some way to highlight interactive points on the screen. If your environments are well designed, it shouldn't come up often, but it's a nice concession to avoid pixel hunting.
- There are a few tasks that send you back through several screens without really presenting a puzzle or a valuable plot point. It's not offensive, by adventure game standards, but one of the values of low priced indie games is that they have no incentive to waste your time.
Most of this is excusable for a development team of two people. It's still a marvelous accomplishment and well worth the time spent.

I am only reccomending this because I got it on sale for $3.99. I have some gripes with this game, but I do think it's really solid overall.
Neon Drive is a fun rythem based game set with some amazing visuals and music inspired by the 80's. What I like most is the way the courses are laid out. Each level has a basic phase 1 where you dodge some walls to the beat of the music. About half way though, a phase 2 begins where the mechanics of the game are altered. One has your car turn into a jet fighter and gives the player room to do barrel rolls for example. These phase 2 parts are really well executed as it adds variety to the levels, But my personal favorite thing about this game is the music. Up beat, fitting perfectly with the setting.
Now for the issues I have with the game. For one, it's short. There are only 7 levels and although there are different modes you can play in these levels, I would have really liked to see more. More music and level designs are desperately needed. But the biggest problem with this game is its price. Now to let potential buyers know, this apparently was an iOS game, and on iOS the price is $3.99, which I find reasonable. However, the price of the Steam version is $9.99. At $10, I can't really justify purchasing this game. The quality of the game is great, but the quantity is severly lacking.
Neon Drive earns my reccomendation (just) for it's stunning visuals, soundtrack, and challenge. But I urge you that if you are planning to get this game, wait till it is on sale or it drops in price as it struggles with the lack of levels.

As someone who is essentially new to fighting games and looking for something to get into the genre I couldn't think of a better game. I've tried MKX online and played through the campaign of MK9. I've also been trying to get into games like Guilty Gear. While they're all good in their own ways I feel like SFV is the best out of what I've played so far to get into the fighting genre. Combos aren't as complicated and execution heavy as in MKX for example where I've ran into people who remove 60% of your bar if you make one wrong high/low guess. In that sense MKX was a rough start as a beginner. Much in the same way Guilty Gear felt quite execution heavy and very fast paced.
SFV on the other hand provides a less steep learning curve allowing the player to get into basic concepts of the genre such as spacing, punishing and mixing up your offense. The game has issues as many people are pointing out in these reviews such as having the occasional laggy game. I still don't think this ruins the experience, and in my opinion the way SFV works a lot around the fighting game fundamentals makes it a preferable game for a beginner compared to the options available at the moment. Being able to finally have a decent way into the genre and finally getting the chance to learn fighting game fundamentals has got me hooked on this game as well, I love it. In conclusion as someone who was looking for a way into fighting games I highly recommend SFV for anyone else interested in picking up competitive fighting games.

Now Capcom have added the features that should have been present at launch (for free) it now has a story mode, it has daily challenges, and combo trials. There's plenty to keep the casual gamer busy - and I should know; I'm a casual gamer that wishes I was more competitive.
The combo system is much easy than other fighting games, and every character feels fair and balanced with respect to the others.
The online netcode is still abit rubbish as such you're going to have a bad time playing online matches with poor wifi or with others with poor wifi. A good way to help cut out lag is to grab a LAN cable and directly plug your laptop/PC into your router.
The game is costantly getting updates, new stages, characters, and costumes with support from Capcom until at least 2020. And if you dislike what Capcom are dishing out the game is also modable with a good community out there to give you your nostalgia costumes and (god forbid) undress your waifus.

Here we go again George....
Once again George is thrown into another epic adventure along with Nico, but is it as capturing as his first?
While the sequel is a great game, and trust me it really is, it couldn't quite hit the high marks of it's predecessor.
The gameplay is virtually identicle, as in you will talk to people and pick up everythign you can to try and figure out how to proceed over your current obstacle. The graphics have been done in the same way and they still look great.
Instead of dealing with a conspiracy this time the story deals with drug trafficing and ancient gods, its a good tale, but I missed the not knowing what was really going on the original had, this time it's advancing much more quickly.
George visits Nico in Paris, they visit a professor together, and Nico is abducted while George is tied to a chair in a burning house, with a venomous spider slowly approaching him. Once he escapes its up to George to find Nico and uncover the dangerous work she had begun, which ultimatley once again leads them both all over the world, including France, Mexico, London and the carribean.
The remastered version isn't much special really, mainly it is just portraits of faces when people speak, it adds nothing to the main game.
In this game Nico is playable too (she wasn't playable in the original version of shadow of the templars) and you will visit different places and uncover different clues. The voicework and art is once again done very well, and has aged the same as the original, which was great.
A great sequel to a great game, but cannot really surpass it.

Neon Drive is not a rhythm game.
The visuals are very pretty, the music is nice to listen to and not overbearing, and it feels like the 1980s. But this game is not a rhythm game. It feels way more like a "Dodge the obstacles coming towards you" game. Unlike any other rhythm game out there, where the goal is to hit a specific coloration of blocks to the beat of music, Neon Drive does the total opposite. Instead, one has to dodge the borders and obstacles to the beat of the music. Not only does this completely throw off the beat, especially in the first level, but it doesn't feel rhythmic at all. Therefore, flawing the entire concept of the game.
As I said, the game looks and runs amazing, and the music is catchy, along with some challenge to it. But it most certainly isn't a rhythm game.

Fallout 4 in my opinion was a victim of its own hype. I was excited for this game, as a fan of the fallout franchise and bethesda in general. However I was gravely disappointed come release as it felt like more of the same. The game is well written, which is standard among bethesda games, and was not surprising at all. What surprised me is that a game released 4 years later was running in the same engine as skyrim! Graphically and mechanically it felt very similar to skyrim save the addition of guns and power armor. The branching dialogue and in depth voice acting was pleasant, but the picky building mechanic was more frustrating than it was worth. The DLC offered for the game add more well written stories, but I did not enjoy the game after the first few days of playing, as it started to feel more and more like a well made skyrim mod (that I payed 60 dollars for). Sadly I do not recommend this game.

Decent game in the GTA genre, although the cars are nigh indestructible here (which admittedly can be a lot of fun). The story is a little disjointed in parts but overall very good. The game has more melee/kung fu fighting than gunfighting, although there is a fair share of the latter. You play an undercover cop infiltrating one of the strongest Triads in Hong Kong, and the story is about family, loyalty, betrayal, and where your own loyalties lie.
I would rate this game a 6/10; there are a few things that keep it from really shining. As I mentioned above, the story seems disjointed in parts. You will meet a girl, call her once to hang out, and then she is never seen or heard from again. This happens on multiple occasions, with no explanation as to what happened to her. A few of the main storyline missions also thrust you into situations that don't make sense or haven't been properly explained, as well. It's not enough to ruin the game, and you figure out what's going on quickly enough, but it just feels unpolished, almost like there were supposed to be missions in between or a linking storyline to tie it together better, that got left out for some reason.
My two biggest gripes about the game are that your character Wei Shen, is basically Superman, able to take on up to 12+ guys at once with his Kung Fu that would put Bruce Lee to shame. He is also able to absorb an apparently infinite amount of bullets, as long as you let him rest for a few seconds in between getting shot. The second big complaint is the wardrobe/clothing system in the game. Different outfits give different bonuses, like extra melee damage or increased xp gain. You can mix and match different things like shirts, pants, shoes, sunglasses, and other accessories to gain various set bonuses. The problem is that it is extremely tedious trying to put together a set with a good bonus that also looks halfway decent. I spent most of the game wearing a pair of sunglasses that made me look like I belonged on the set of Jersey Shore, which made cutscenes where I'm talking to the Triad leader about loyalty and other Deep Sh*t™ just laughable. It didn't ruin my enjoyment of the game, it just made certain parts seem pretty silly. Imagine taking down a group of 8 or 10 rival Triads while wearing a straw sombrero, purple shoes, a giant neon green watch, idiotic sunglasses (at night), beach shorts, and a puffy jacket.
Overall, I would recommend this game if you like the GTA genre, but I got this game on sale ($4) and got about 24 hours of enjoyment out of it. A very good value if you ask me; YMMV.
