Burnout Paradise
by Criterion Games/Electronic Arts
Genre: Racing
Released: February 3, 2009
-----
“Take me down to the Paradise City, where the grass is green and the girls are pretty! Oh, won’t you please take me home! Yeah yeah!” – Guns ‘n Roses
So begins this ultimate driving/racing sandbox (EVERY SINGLE STARTUP!) from the geniuses at Criterion Games. It really says something that a game originally released in 2009, almost nine years old, still holds a place as one of the best car games on the market.
So what’s great about it! Well, it takes place in a massive open-world city, known as, well, Paradise City! There’s surprisingly a great variety of terrain to drive on here, from sandy construction sites to miles of black top and unfinished roads, all suitable to take a spin in any of around a hundred vehicles, all told. That includes more than 70 cars, eight motorcycles, five specialty cars and a few mini-racers just for the heck of it.
Another thing is that at every intersection out of a couple hundred, you can start a challenge, be it racing, demolition, road rules (outrunning/wrecking two or more pursuers), stunt runs or time trials. Each completed challenge is another step to upgrade your license – you start at D-class and work up to Elite, if I recall correctly, and you must complete more challenges each class to upgrade. Challenges reset with each upgrade, so you can take them again if you wish or take on new ones.
Some challenges, when complete, also unleash a new vehicle onto the open road! These will always be traveling near you much faster than normal traffic, so you can easily spot them. If you catch up to them and shut them down (give them a hard tap into the rails, say), they’ll be added to your Garage for selection later. Like all cars you suddenly come into, though, you’ll need to take it to a nearby service station for repair to properly christen and customize it, though.
One way in which vehicles are diversified in the game has to do with how Boost is applied to the vehicle: a Stunt vehicle gains boost power for doing dangerous things: driving against traffic, getting air, drifting. A Speed vehicle gains boost by going as fast as possible without it; you gain multipliers for sustaining the speed as long as possible without activating it. There’s also a Demolition-type that gains boost for smashing into other cars as much as possible.
With each vehicle in the game also comes a special Burning Route – an individual race designed to test that vehicle’s abilities. Use any method of boosting through these Burning Routes and you’ll unlock a new, special type of that vehicle in the Garage!
The most spectacular form of demolition in the game, though, is SHOWTIME! Each street in the game, along with its time trial, also has a SHOWTIME score! Select that and hold down both triggers and bumpers and BOOM! You’re tasked with crashing into as many vehicles as possible as your car rolls and spins through the air in slow motion, getting the highest score possible on each street. Take care not to slow down too much or go without touching another vehicle for too long, or the challenge is over
This game is super, super fun, holding a LOT of entertainment value, even though (to my knowledge) its multiplayer features (which were also many and amazing) were turned off long ago, and the biggest downloadable expansion to the game, Big Surf Island, was never ported to the PC. I highly recommend it if you want a really, really fun game that has aged so well, as well as one of the best racing games ever!

The package you get for 20 bucks is quite good. Doom 3, plus the extensions, companied by Ultimate Doom and Doom II gives really a lot of hours for your money. The multyplayer is dead but the singleplayer experience is all you need.
This game includes:
Doom 3 with some gameplay changes:
- More healthkits and ammo
- Flashlight has been removed as a seperate weapon and replaced with a shoulder mounted light
- Surround sound is now compatible with most soundcards rather than being exlusive to Creative EAX
- Ammo counter stays in the hud even for weapons that have their own ammo counter
- 16:9 screen ratio means zomed in view and removal of the ingame zoom
- Game is a lot brighter than the original Doom 3
Doom 3 Resurrection of Evil:
- Same changes as above
- Removal of arcade machines
Doom 3 Lost Levels:
- Cut down areas and levels from Doom 3
- Prototype area layouts (that actually made into Doom 3) have been put back into Lost Levels
- Last part of the last level is how Doom 3 should have been
Ultimate Doom:
- Medkit red cross has been changed to a pill with one half red and the other half white
- Nightmare is easier with normal speed imp fireballs and Pinky run speed
- The WAD file is compatible with Doom source ports, giving you limitless gameplay with mods
- Resolution is set higher, making targets distinguishable from far away but is locket to 30 frames
- I have the feeling that the game is easier than the original classic Doom
Doom 2 + No Rest for the Living:
- Same changes as Ultimate Doom
- No reference to Nazis and no Nazi soldiers
I pitty the fact that we are missing Final Doom and Master Levels for Doom. Overall the package is worth buying.

10/10, Sanctum 2 has been a fantastic experience the whole way through. An excellent blend of FPS and TD, and a personal favourite game of mine. There's a fair bit of criticism in that it's too different from the first Sanctum game, but I played this one first and love it while I enjoy the first Sanctum less, so it's probably a "which-I-played-first" bias in either case.
The gameplay is superb, the customization makes it even better, and the characters are all very interesting. Even as a TD-type game there's backstory for the game and its' characters, and pretty well done.
But the best part of the game in my opinion is the music. It fits it so perfectly, capturing the futuristicness of the game as well as the do-or-die atmosphere.
The DLC's are practically a must, as they add just as much or perhaps more than the vanilla game content, as well as expanding the story (which is pretty decent). I've played very little of the first Sanctum so I'm unsure how the story element was in that game, but in Sanctum 2 it's somewhat backburner, left in the form of comic-style loading screens giving you plot advancement, while still being interesting enough to leave you wanting to know what comes next.
Overall the game is fantastic, though be mindful that there's a significantly larger focus on FPS aspects than TD ones (though the towers are still of course vital). Also be prepared to branch out and try different builds and strategies, there's plenty to work with and the game keeps you on your toes.

I'm going to be a little brutal here. Yes, I know the game is EA. That does not mean I need to agree with EA in general or the fact that games can come out unfinished just because they are EA. They cost people money (I got this in a bundle not the free giveaway), therefore the product needs to offer an acceptable value for what we pay.
Now, here's my review:
The game tries to be similar to others on steam such as Spelunky. And that's great; if you're going to make a game, take inspirationg from the best in the genre. Aiming high is very commendable and totally fine.
But the game missed the mark with so many things. First of all, you have everything you will ever need right from the start like many varied weapons and infinite arrow. Secondly, non of the challenge you get from a game like Spelunky. you can easily take a number of hits and still be ok in Endorlight. And finally, non of the charm or character of a game that someone's worked on. There is simply nothing compelling about this product.
Before anyone plays the game, I highly recommend they remap their keyboard controls to something more practical, the default controls are very impractical. But default controls aside, the wall jumping mechanic in this game is somewhat halfassed, and gives you the impression that the only reason it exists is because the randomly generated levels can occasionally be impractical. "Instead of fixing the programming and making the levels manageable, we'll just allow the players to jump up walls to get out of the crap levels we generate. And therefore save ourselves some work." When you have wall jumps and no proper wall slides, or game mechanics that prop up and benefit from it, that's what I'm going to think.
Now people may get the impression I hate everything about this game, I do not, the look of the game is fine, some of the sprites are actually really nice. The attempt at making a Spelunky like game is something I find very welcome, I love Spelunky. But when the attempt is so bad, it's an insult to real games. So forgive me Spelunky, for mentioning you here. It's like saying my rusty trashbin looks exactly like the satelite NASA launched in June - the difference is that big. This game is broken in a lot of ways. It does not draw me in and make me feel like "I'm going to do this level this time". The controls are clunky and the jumping is iffy. I already have an axe, a whip and infinite arrows the moment I spawn, there's nothing I want to collect or find. And of course, because the game is EA, we have a lot of missing content, like the gems and gold we collect for no reason at all, we simply do not need them.
EDIT:In the comments below, it was brought to my attention that this game contains premade assets, which explains a lot.
Pros:
- An interesting game on paper, as an idea - not so much in practice
- looks ok, some sprites are nice though there's a lot of repetition in the level
Cons:
- Controls aren't great
- Responsiveness not great
- The wall jumps suck
- Not as challenging as it could be
- Missing content
3/10

It's a very immersive ride that I have taken from A to Z at least 4 times. If you want to forget the world and live through a demonic science fiction story, Doom 3 is the way to go.
The sounds require a bit of getting used to because they are equalized / dynamic compressed too extremely (though not as insanely as in Bioshock Infinite), but after a while this will feel alright.
People say that Doom 3 is visually too dark, but what they are missing is that this is a game for
gamers who want to go on an immersive ride instead of just having fun in the living room with friends. So, turn off the lights, use a big screen, tweak the FOV (The console allows to set anything you want.), and get lost for 12-18 hours in a dark science fiction tale that, while kind of routine once you know how to handle your weapons, will keep you on the edge throughout.
Some people don't like that it takes a while before the action starts. Those, too, are not
gamers. Drink up the mood! Role-play! Explore this science fiction reality while you're not yet under pressure and while things are still well lit.
Doom 3 uses real-time lighting throughout, and I believe it was even the first 3D 1st person campaign shooter that did this. While this has visual downsides (especially since the engine is old, so there is no hint of Global Illumination) compared to baked light-maps, it contributes immensely to the experience, and they show it off in quite a few places. Try to imagine what it's like to see this for the first time. Oooh! Aaah! Who wants to touch me.

I'm very surprised and pleased to see that this game is far better than what I expected. It is said that Alien Isolation is the best Alien game, and one of the best new gen games out there, but to be quite honest, there are a few quirks that make the game completely frustrating to the point of ruining the whole experience and not wanting to touch it again.
Now I find this little gem lost in the last pages of Steam, and to my surprise, I am enjoying it far more than Isolation, despite I'm not really into action shooters. It's not only the rich gameplay, but you also have all the superb graphics (for a PS3/XB360 game), but the sound, the weapons, everything that makes an 80's kid like me jump in joy while remembering the first Predator and also Aliens movies.
I don't care for multiplayer, and if you're like me, you won't be disappointed since the single player campaign has everything that made a game great in the PS2/PS3/XB/XB360 era.
Graphics: 10/10. When you see the requirements, you think it will look average, but you'l be surprised. Running full settings on my PC. Really good textures, solid 60+ frames, very nice light effects. Game is very well optimized. (again. Judging by the game's generation)
Sounds: 8/10. Sounds are great and faithful to both Predator and Alien movies, but the volume is a bit unbalanced. Weapons sound a bit low.
Gameplay: 9/10. Very easy to play, and although some keys are not what you're used to see in a shooter, it's nothing different than what you'd expect from a responsive, and well made game of this genre.
Campaign: 8.5/10. Okay. So I've only played 3 hours, but I know the game is short judging from the progress percentage. BUT! I see in the campaign menu that you can select story mode for Marines, Aliens and Predator! I have no idea how that will work, but I guess I'll see soon.
Overall, if you are not easily drawn to gimicky new gen stuff, and just want to have some fun with a genuinely very well made sci-fi-action-horror(ish)-FPS, you can't go wrong with this game.
My final note: 9/10. Much more enjoyable than Isolation, and that's from someone who loves horror games.

I have been on a small point-and-click binge lately, and this might be my favorite in the genre so far. This game suffers from some of the usual pitfalls, like the handful of puzzles that really don't make any damn sense.  There were also some imo subpar minigames thrown in that felt somewhat out of place, but they are only a few seconds long and completely skippable.  Not a big deal.  Some other folks watching me play said they found the minigames "charming" and I guess they kinda were, but meh.  YMMV.
Overall Fran Bow is a great experience that I'd recommend over pretty much any other point-and-click I have played to date.

If I was asked a couple years ago, sure, I would've reccomended this wholeheartedly. Unfortunately, the company appears to be succumbing to bad buisness practices. Originally, the store only had cosmetic items, buyable through a currency you gain by winning matches (and later, buying the steam version of the game). Then, they added bundles which require you to spend real money (No big deal, they were just reskins like everything else). After that, they went on to add "scrolls", an item you could get with the in-game currency that would increase your chances of becoming a certain class (This made the store no longer just for cosmetics and possibly disrupted some game balancing). It gets worse, as they recently changed the old currency to "premium currency", which you now have to pay for, and made a new, non-premium currency worth about 1/4th of the premium currency, and it can't be used to buy most items that premium currency can buy. The developers are also thinking about making some negative changes to a few of the classic classes to the game. The cherry on top of all of this? The moderation quality is terrible. Example: last week, I had played ToS, because despite all of the negatives, the game itself is seemingly unique (If you found an alternative, let me know) and it's fun to decieve people, plus I already paid for it when the game was better managed. I had reported a guy that  claimed that people who buy the game can't be banned, was "Gamethrowing" (Losing on purpose), and had 2 accounts playing at the same time, and had an innapropriate name, all of which are against the rules. I guess I accidentally proved him wrong, because I was the one who got banned for a week.
It's a shame that the game had to go from a game with high potential to a game where even those who are fans and those who are innocent get punished, and bad buisness practices run free. Speaking of which, I feel sorry for others who bought the steam version before now, as it seems they added new content and a bigger reward to it which old buyers such as myself have not recieved. If you want to try this game, I highly reccomend playing the free version, which has everything (except for the premium cosmetics and scrolls, which you have to buy anyway), and you can still play with FTP players.

Ah, it's a classic. Whatever platform you own this on, fun times are to be had.
You take control of one of four survivors of the Green Flu (Virus?), a nasty disease turning the population into flesh-eating horrors. The rest of the survivors are either A.I., or players (treat the A.I. nicely, and you shall be rewarded). You then proceed to embark on a journey from safehouse to safehoue, 'till the finale, where you must hold out for an amount of time before escape is available. In order to even make it to the finale, or move on at all, tight teamwork is needed. You can share items, heal others, and use z and x to say things such as Help and similar call-outs (after all this time, i still don't know what they're called. Voice commands? I don't know. Someone tell me.) to further help the team.
Now, about the zombies. They are fast. They come in large groups. They are smart. There are certain events which cause them to come in endless hordes, unless something is done that stops them from being attracted. Or the A.I. Director (the thing controlling all the zombies) can send a horde (this one is NOT endless) your way if you spend too much time in one place, or if it feels like it.
There are special infected (each special infected has their own music que, and there can be only around 3 in-game at a time) The Boomer spits bile at you, attratcing zombies. He explodes when shot, showering you in bile. He can also detonate at will, so if he's in your face, shove him away before shooting, or before he explodes.  The Smoker produces a long tounge that drags it's prey to it, where it then claws the living hell out of you. Shoot the tounge, or shoot it before then (it likes to stay far away form the group, so be careful). The Hunter can jump super long distances and great heights, screaming every time. He will pounce on you, clawing you until soemone gets him off, or kills him.   The Tank. The name speaks for itself. This thing is insanely strong, requiring the whole group to put it down. Each punch stuns you and sends you flying. Also, he can throw cars. Fun.    Finally, the Witch.  If you hear any crying women, turn your flashlights off and stay away. Sneak around her. You can shoot her, just expect her to make a beeline for whoever disturbed her, and proceed to down you in one hit. She also has very large health, and does the most damage in the game.
Well, that's all there is. It's a great game to play with friends, or alone. Multiplayer matches, or no. A must-have.

ICEY is a 2D character action game developed by a Chinese indie studio by the name of “Shanghai FantaBlade Network Technology Co., Ltd..” Despite releasing in mid-November, it seems to have gone completely under the radar, in general, mostly just receiving some critical praise and reviewing well on Steam, and that was it. For a studio’s first foray into gaming, which not only spent an absurd amount of time in development, but is also one of the first games to come from China, for these reasons we decided to take a look, and what we found was something special.
The story follows ICEY, who appears to be a cyborg, as she tears through progressively stronger generals until she can get a chance to challenge Judas, the antagonist. The story isn’t quite so simple as that however, the narrator is reminiscent of The Stanley Parable in that he will direct you to certain areas and tell you what to do, but can be ignored, leading to alternate endings and hidden goodies of all kinds, one of which even shows you what the game was like earlier in development, or a hidden platformer section with different mechanics compared to the base game.
For a first time through, the novelty is fantastic, and on return trips through the title, finding new ways to screw with the narrator is both fun, and can legitimately take some experimentation. The writing is fairly well done and provides some replay value in finding everything in the game, it’s handled surprisingly well for an indie studio working on a character action game, as many of the greats in this genre tend to go for more intense, upscaled scenarios. ICEY knows what it is and acts accordingly; it doesn’t try too hard to be something it isn’t.
While the story is fantastic thanks to the narrator, at the end of the day, it’s still a character action game, and while something like The Stanley Parable completely failed to be a fun game in its own right, ICEY succeeds with flying colors. The gameplay follows a fairly basic control layout, heavy and light attacks can be comboed together, as well as a dodge than can be timed to allow for a counter attack, or just used to fly around the battlefield and executions that return health and shield energy. It feels almost like a 2D Metal Gear Rising as tearing apart enemies with crazy combos then tearing them apart with executions that heal the player is a common occurrence, even on bosses, which thankfully become regular enemies later in the game. Enemies and secret areas also reward the player with money which can be spent on upgrades, which aren’t particularly interesting for the most part. Upgrading combos to deal more damage or increasing the health/shield bar isn’t exactly an engaging choice, but there are two special attacks that allow players to attack while invincible for short times but cost health to use. Unfortunately, the use of them is pretty questionable, and by sharing buttons with the shadow slash mechanic, accidentally draining one’s own health is too easy in the heat of combat.
ICEY feels like a genuinely fantastic and fun character action game, there was clearly a lot of thought put into how the character moves and acts for each individual combo, as each one has a legitimate use in and out of boss fights. It’s a shame then, that the enemy design can tank some encounters so hard. For the most part, the enemies work fine, and each serves to put some pressure on an encounter, especially when thrown in with bosses, but there’s one particular type of enemy that makes every single encounter they’re included in frustrating. Unlike many other character action games like Bayonetta or Metal Gear Rising, there’s no recovery time from taking hits in ICEY, meaning when enemies come in and attack with laser beams, the player can be juggled almost endlessly across the screen, being forced to take half or more of a health bar with no real options out of it.
While this can be avoided by dashing like crazy to avoid the lasers, the fact that laser enemies tend to come in groups, as well as one boss fight having a laser movement pattern that forces the player to get juggled to hell and back, means many encounters can force the player to lose over half of their health bar just from one bad dodge or movement. We’re all for having challenging gameplay in a character action title, hell games like Kingdom Hearts are at their best in critical mode, but this kind of difficulty isn’t how it should be handled. Being juggled by a laser appearing with little to no warning for half of a health bar is frustrating at best and downright unfair at worst. This does nothing to mention how some enemies that can grab and throw the player are also capable of juggling, albeit to a much less frustrating extent.
In terms of presentation, ICEY varies from looking fairly typical in non-combat scenes, as the environments aren’t particularly interesting, and while somewhat detailed, it does nothing to match the calibre of say Bastion or Transistor which also went for the same kind of background art. That said, enemy and boss designs are varied enough to keep things interesting, and the various particle and slash effects do help a lot in terms of adding to the gameplay. ICEY looks its best when in motion, fighting several enemies at once and dashing around the battlefield; it’s just a shame the art out in exploring the world doesn’t do much to match that same quality. It’s also worth mentioning the cyberpunk aesthetic in some areas does a good job adding to the game, and the final fight taking place out in the open room of well-detailed building deserves some brownie points, it does a good job of setting up a climactic encounter, even if the lasers have prevented us from passing it thus far.
In addition to all of this, we have to bring up how great the music is, being a somewhat small title, there’s not a lot of tracks to sift through, but we were hard-pressed to find a single bad one; every song does a good job setting the mood of the area, with the fighting music being enjoyable as well. It fits the cyberpunk aesthetic of the later areas and is great both in-game and on its own, which is laudable given the amount of games releasing lately with filler songs that do little to add to the game.
In terms of content, there’s a lot to enjoy here, especially with the narrator adding to new playthroughs, but that said, the game itself isn’t particularly replayable. Upgrades are basic, and if one runs the narrator dry to any degree, then there won’t be much novelty left for subsequent runs of the title, and while the combat is very enjoyable, it’s not something we see ourselves revisiting years from now when its contemporaries offer much more fleshed out gameplay. All that said, the game lasts long enough to be worth the money. Launching at a modest price point and lasting about 6-8 hours means getting value out of the game isn’t difficult, one run is more than enough to get all the enjoyment one would need to call it a worthwhile purchase. There’s enough variety of areas to keep the game from becoming stale, and the game does demand a certain level of skill that’s respectable, which can increase the playtime for those less inclined to play games similar to this.
ICEY is a flawed game, enemy designs can get frustrating, the environments aren’t particularly special and the gameplay is fairly basic as far as character action games go, but what it lacks in some areas, it more than makes up for with satisfying combat, great boss fights that can actually challenge the player, some unique mechanics that add extra layers of skill to the game for those that can use them, as well as having a great soundtrack layered on top of everything.

TLDR Overall a nice atmospheric story in a tight well-designed game.
Pros
+ Wonderful story that is player driven, accompanied by interesting characters and a decent plot.
+ Amazing soundtrack that establishes a great in-game atmosphere.
+ Gameplay that not only offers somewhat in-depth combat, but also allows for the story-telling to be told through the actions of the player, thanks to dynamic narration and excellent world interaction.
+ Wonderful hand-drawn watercolour art style. This game greatly benefits from good art direction.
Cons
- A bunch of filler that clutters up the game. This includes a number of boring wave modes, some weapon training modes, a score attack mode, and annoying pointless achievements. Can we please stop with all the filler? I just want to enjoy the story and finish the game. Maybe if you enjoy these sorts of things you could possibly consider this as a pro, but I personally do not.
- No real end game established. After you finish the game it loops back to the beginning so that you can finish all the filler and get all the unlocks and everything in a new game plus mode. The problem is that I'm never really at a point in-game where I feel like I have completed everything and I can just relax in the hub world. The game just keeps looping.
- The game was about four hours long for me, and I did take time to make sure that I collected all the secrets. While a four hour indie game isn't necessarily a bad thing, the developers definitely had the extra time to implement all the filler, as listed above. Maybe instead of the filler, they could have had a few more levels to help with the pacing of the story.

text:
A near perfect game.
Story:
The entire story comes from the narrator who has a personality of his own and is a central figure in the story. Without spoiling too much 'The Calamity" happens and almost everyone is dead. As you progress and meet 3 characters you learn more about the events leading up to The Calamity. You also learn more by entering the other survivor's dream worlds.
Gameplay:
I suppose that the best way to describe Bastion is a Hack and Slash with minor RPG elements. You can equip 2 weapons and a Secret Skill (requires a black tonic per use) from a pretty large arsenal that grows as you progress. The weapons include hammers, blades, cannons, guns, and more. You can mix and match to find your preference and upgrade their abilities by finding elements in the levels and blue crystals for cash. You can set your difficulty in the game with Idols. Each Idol you pray to will increase the exp rate in exchange for more difficult gameplay. EXP only upgrades the amount of special tonics (not black ones) that enhance certain abilities and your max health. It is certainly a challenge and makes the short levels a death walk. There are 14 levels and all of them take 10 - 20 minutes to complete if you get through it on the first go. With Idols of course it will take longer. Everything in the game is really balanced from the weaponry to secret skills, to special tonics. Only complaint is that in NG+ mode when you obtain a weapon in the level (even though you already have it. It takes the slot of another weapon you currently have.
Features
There is a New Game Plus mode which lets you keep everything from your previous game except the Bastion shards to build the Arsenal, Forge, Memorial, etc. Once you build it once in NG+ it will be fully upgraded though. I have not tried Score Attack Mode. There are gauntlet levels that you can access anytime through your fellow survivor dreams. Survive a wave of enemies basically. The Stranger (Narrator) one is the most annoying because he has 30 waves all because of the stupid alphabet. The music is very top notch and the narrator immerses you in the story and comments on your performance in the levels.
This is definitely a must buy if you like action games. It is very balanced, has a great story, has a gauntlet mode to test your metal, and is graphically beautiful.
Worth the money, enjoy the game even more on Steam

I'm always on the search for great under-rated games, and I am pleased to say this is one of them. I've only played about 6 hours so far, but they were 6 hours well spent in my own opinion. This game kept remiding me of Civilization, but that might just be because it's the only other strategy game I've played.
Winning is rewarding, especially after steamrolling over all the other clans and proclaiming dominance. The paths to victory are all very well done, I really have no complaiants. The clans themselves are all different enough and offer their own benefits to your playstyle. Combat is non-enaging, as to be expected in a strategy game(at least I think I've only played Civ 5), but I really didn't mind watching it most of the time. I do think that the combat and warband systems were fairly simple, troop paths and more troops would be recommended, but I didn't feel it lacked in any other aspects. If I'm being honest, if the systems were kept but more was added to them, I would be completely fine and would still enjoy the game.
The seasonal changes are alright, my problem just lies in the fact that only winter has any effect upon you clan and the territory in it. I did really like the random events that damage your clan like rat infestations or tremors, I just wish there were more of them. Speaking of the rats, silos should probably cover more of your food supply. It's kind of strange that I can generate 2000 food with 3 silos but can only store 900 of it.
The building systems were fine, but I feel that there should be a special type of clan member for building rather than just swapping out villagers, or maybe both. I also felt that there should be other means of revealing the map besides the scouts, maybe you can have your units reveal it as they march on or something.
I do have to appreciate that this game is completely bug-free from what I've experienced(something even some larger titles can't accomplish) and the AI was actually fairly decent. I say decent because it wasn't dumb, and I've only ever ecountered dumb AI in other games for some reason. I do have to question how the AIs somehow garnar more fame at much faster rates than me, but I can let that slide.
In summary, great strategy game. All it needs is some improvments in multiple aspects, maybe more complexity but really not all that necessary, and it would be even better.

TL;DR: A game that can't decide if its Frogger, or DDR, and ends up being a terrible version of both.
This will be a short one, mostly because the same is so insanely short I can't imagine why you would pay ten dollars for it, -even- if it was good.
Neon Drive looks cool, and it has good music. That is the entire summary of the positive parts of the game. The game basically is frogger, you move between four different lanes to avoid things that will kill you. On normal at least, you get two hits before you die, and checkpoints at predetermined parts of the level. Initially, this works out alright, but very quickly the design flaws and overall boneheaded decisions begin to show.
First of all, the angle is behind the car most of the time, so you can't see where you are going very easily. If this was just 'Press A when it says A' like a rhythm game (and the game feels like its trying to be one, as most of the time you're moving sorta-to-the-beat), then it wouldn't be too bad. Instead though, you have to dodge obstacles, and some obstacles have dead ends, like oldschool top down auto-scrolling games. You basically have to memorize the patterns for the first few stages. There are parts that change it up from just being behind the car, but these make the game even worse.
In the asteroids segment for example, you can't see most of the asteroids more than a second or two before they will hit, and so if you're completely out of place, you eat a hit. The spaceship chase sequence has the obstacles spawning behind others so that if you zigged when you should have zagged (and no indicator which you should have done), you eat a hit. By far the worst segment is the diving car chase. The segment before this was pretty bad, with a wash of cars and no easy indicator where you should be, but the diving segment is total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. When you are diving, the cars are moving right and left ahead of you...so you have zero indication what 'lane' the obstacle will be in before you get there. You will dodge right into a car when you were safe, and think you are safe and get nailed.
In addition to these issues, the car hitbox is wonky, and the slowdown effect after you get hit makes the mercy invincibility almost pointless, because it ♥♥♥♥s up your rythm.
Do not pay 10$ for pretty, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ frogger. Go play Frogger, or Spy Chase, or literally anything else. If you want the visuals and music, put on some vaporwave and watch a music video from the eighties or something.

At its core, Realm of the Mad God is a bullet hell game where you enter a fantasy world where pretty much everything has some sort of bullet type aspect weapon to use. Your basic swordsmen have short range attacks while your archers have longer range, but it is generally all firing bullets everywhere. It gets quite chaotic when many characters come into play - since this is a multiplayer game.
You can collect stuff in a run and save it for other runs - great if you want to save equipment for another character class to start next time, or if you buy extra hero slots, help build as you go with another character. Probably a good deal of this game involves saving for the next run or other heroes.
In many ways this is an extremely interesting game, since one wrong move means you may have to restart over from scratch. Of course, being free to play it has to make money from somewhere, and this comes from buying the aforementioned character slots, or unlocking new heroes, or buying equipment or items to go about your run.
I recommend trying it out since it is a free to play game.

Neon Drive is an aesthetically pleasing rhythm game where you drive a car through 7 total levels on 3 different difficulties (this is not including other modes). The game is extremely pleasing to watch, as the design work and colors are beautifully done, but some people have complaints about the need to memorize the levels to pass them, saying this isn't how a rhythm game should be done.
I disagree.
Although different, and more challenging than other rhythm games, this fact doesn't make Neon Drive a bad game, it just means you have to adapt to this game without assuming its like other games.
Overall, here's my opinion:
Pros:
Very well done soundtrack
Clean, retro/80s style graphics
License plate customization
Extra features on the levels, and on your vehicle! (you'll see what I mean when you play)
Fairly good response system (I played with a keyboard, so I can't say for controllers). The game answered my turns quickly.
Sexy main menu android ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)
The main con:
The game can get frustrating on difficulties above normal, as failures take time to start up the level again and if you screw up once you're back to a checkpoint/the start. This won't be terrible once you've played for a few hours, but for starters its a lot like Dark Souls. It'll have you hitting something in anger.
Overall, for anyone who enjoys aesthetically pleasing games or rhythm games $10 is a great price for this game. If it goes on sale even lower snag this ASAP. The soundtrack is also well worth it
Final score: 9.5/10

Gameplay mechanics are very flawed. When you're in a vehicle and try to reverse, the camera is totally broken. Shooting is ok.. cover is kinda awkward but the shooting sections are so unchallenging you don't even need it. Oh yeah, there's bullet time but that's a bit awkward and also unnecessary. The most ridiculous mechanic is being able to (only when you're told to as part of a mission), jump out of your own car straight into another car, while both are driving fast and in the same direction. A mechanic that would have been great in a game like Saints Row that completely repudiates any sense of realism. In Sleeping Dogs it not only doesn't fit, but somehow still manages to not even be that fun.
The city is well constructed and has lots of nice touches but I never really felt any desire to go sandboxing around.. it didn't seem that fun.
And the game seemed to get progressively more buggy and crash-happy towards the end.

After playing this game for almost 8 hours I have to say I didn't overly enjoy it.
To give some perspectives I typically play my games on the easiest difficulty setting because I'm more interested in the story than dying repeatedly, over and over again, on ungodly difficult battles. If you are hoping that my review is based upon a die-hard combat experience? Then this review is not for you, look elsewhere. And to note that the 'received this game for free' thing is because I received this as a gift from a friend, not from the developers, keep that in mind. Thanks.
Also to note that if you and your friends are NOT on the EXACT same progress in the single-player campaign then you CANNOT join each other's games; the host has to be further BEHIND or on the SAME stage as those whom want to join otherwise you can't join each other's games because the game will point-blank tell you you can't join because you're not on the same stage of the story as the host. This thoroughly prevents friends from joining you at all, and it stifles your ability to play this game together unless you want to go through the game solo or start over to get to the point where they are at.
Too many skills that are poorly arranged, they are in huge icons that are across a massive border that makes it very inconvenient for a new player to look over unless you want to spend at least 30-60 minutes looking over -each- skill. And like I said, there's simply TOO many of them! You have many skills across three different skill trees, unless you spend many, many hours theorycrafting builds, constantly resetting your own builds and so on, you won't find a build that lets you push through the game without constantly and consistently dying. Also to note, is that you will be ignoring a flat 40-60% of your entire available skills because they're either too ineffective or they just feel as if they're filler and not serious skills.
Which brings me to my next complaint of the game: The developers clearly don't understand how difficulty works. The 'casual' difficulty will still crush you mercilessly into the earth repeatedly unless you build a meta build, with meta gear, etc... Casual difficulty should make the combat effortless because people play that difficulty because they want to SEE the story, not get curb-stomped into the ground because of heavily overtuned enemies.
Do note that this game does not have any of the bugs that the first one had that made that game an utter hell.
Another thing that I personally feel makes this game less enjoyable is the very limited aspect of classes you can play as--you have the Hunter, whom is like the warrior/gunsman who uses magic, you have the Thaumaturge who is the focused spellcaster, and then you have the Arcane Mechanist or some such? Whom is literally just a guy using a large weapon looking like a gun that functions much like an engineer with magical-technological gear. To be honest, none of the classes except for the thaumaturge felt enjoyable to play as. Visually-speaking, the thaumaturge is the most fun one to play because of all of the spell effects.
I also did not expect this game to have utilized the same 'War Table' garbage that was evident in World of Wacraft: Warlords of Draenor/Legion, as well as the same system that was used in Mass Effect: Andromeda and Dragon Age: Inquisition. To summarize it for those who are not familiar with it, you send soldiers out onto missions with certain stats and counters to certain aspects in the missions. In the case of this game you have to talk to each of your captains and then assess which one is better fit for a mission in particular to increase your chances at victory in it. And once you send them out you have to wait in-game (ACTIVE in-game) minutes before it concludes. You can't alt-tab out to watch youtube until it finishes, because it PAUSES the timer until you're actually back in the game again which literally forces you to have to wait whilst playing the game before you can complete the missions. Though I've noticed that the timer continues regardless if you decide to quit the game until it ends.
Repeatedly I've died on Casual Difficulty playing as a Hunter with full points into Body, which is the stat for melee fighters. Both times I've literally been perma-caged into one spot and then nuked. At one point I got hit so hard on CASUAL difficulty with NEARLY ONE THOUSAND HEALTH in a SINGLE BLOW by ONE enemy. After this happened a second time I just hard-closed the game (Alt+F4 to those who don't know) because at that point I was kind of done with the bull****.
This game has a habit of forcing too many cutscenes, that stop you from actually playing. You could finish a quest, and as you're looking over the rewards--suddenly a cutscene happens where a thing is talking to you or other things happen, forcing you to have to abandon looking over what you got to deal with the new results of the cutscene. If you don't like excessive cutscenes interrupting your gameplay? Then this game isn't for you, likely.
For a game that claims itself to be a Diablo Clone Hack and Slash? It is not. It doesn't honestly know WHAT it is, it's a RPG/RTS, and it does both aspects really poorly, to be honest. This is nothing like Diablo or Diablo II.
I even went to look up builds SPECIFICALLY to help me survive in the single-player on CASUAL DIFFICULTY and I was STILL getting my butt kicked. I'm honestly not all that happy with this game or the first game, and I'd honestly say to others wanting to get it? Either get it during the Steam Summer Sale when it's super-cheap, or don't get it at all. Were it not for the overtuned mobs in the casual difficulty, I probably would have given this a recommend.

Do you like easy, walk in the park, casual sit back and relax games? Well then Doom isn't for you. But if you like lazer shooting, body blowing, gunslinging, rocket launching, goretastic slaughter of thousands of demons in an environment that will always keep you on the edge of your feet with your finger on the trigger... then yes. Doom is for you.
Anyways - my actual review.
So if you think that this edtion is not worth it for $15 more than the regular doom 3 game - you'd be mistaken. Doom 3 BFG's major differences over Doom 3 regular is as follows (excluding graphical remastering)
1) All Doom 3 Expansions (So you can play more Doom!)
2) Flashlight is no longer held as a weapon and can be toggled on and off with a key (So you can spend less time cowering in the dark and more time playing Doom!)
3) Inclusion of the original Doom 1 and 2 (So once you finish Doom 3 you will have more Doom!)
Seriously though, of all the classic FPS games Doom 1/2 would be my favorite. They are so fast paced, well ballanced and waaaaay ahead of their time. I love Half Life One, but Doom One blows it out of the water. Excelent metal music score to go along with the fast paced demon killing action as well. Honestly it's worth the extra $15 over Doom 3 just for Doom 1/2. A must buy.
P.S. I know that some people are afraid to play Doom 3 (which is in my opinion, the weakest of the Doom series) because it is full of jump scares and monster closets. When I first purchased and installed BSII:TSM it was the original 1997 version. By the time I got around to playing, it had been upgraded to the "remastered" 2010 edition. I don't know what the difference is but it would have been nice to be given the choice between the two rather than to force it on me. Apparently the update is aimed towards iOS and Android devices, not so great for PCs.
The difference between this and the first game in the series is fairly apparent. There are less engaging puzzles. It's more trial and error, typical point-and-click mechanics. The story is fairly bland but was interesting enough to keep me going.
Some parts are frustrating in a bad way. Having to complete things in a specific order to unlock a certain conversation option, when another method is clearly apparent yet unapproachable, is so very typical of many poorly designed adventure games of the '90s and BSII is no different.
There are many abrupt animation cues and continuity errors that make scene transitions jarring. The ending seemed rushed too; there was no closing dialogue, it just cuts to credits. Not to mention the credit title theme song repeats three times. There are also many grammatical errors and typos present in the subtitles. You will often hear a character say something completely different to what you are reading, not to mention some of the voice acting is terrible. Nico's character sounds completely different from the first game, I did not enjoy her performance at all.
BSII may have been an amazing game for its time, but it doesn't hold a flame to the likes of the Monkey Island series, and it doesn't particularly hold up to today's standards either, even with the recent remastered upgrade. There are still many issues plaguing the update that were meant to be fixed, including poor sound quality that continues to persist.
I can only recommend this game if you're a die hard fan of the genre.

If you are used to games like Civ, AoE, Rimworld, that kind of stuff, this game is a real letdown. It plays more like a board game than anything else. It is not a city builder nor a RTS game, it is more like a Colonists of Catan with RTS elements.
The map consists of tiles that you explore by having a scout sit at the edge of it untill the bar is filled. Each tile has the possibility to have rare or less rare resources on it, and sometimes there are some mobs to slay.
The amount of military units you will use at the peak of the game is about ~10 and that would be a 'large' army. There are no commands like Attack-Move, Stop, Hold Position, or Patrol so everything is done by the old fashioned RMB.
There are 3 types of military units, melee units, ranged units, and shield units. There is also a healer that takes literally a month to heal one guy. Theres the basic buildings, market, tower, lumber mill, etc, but your settlements feel like plastic, as in the
.
The gameplay is tedious and basic. It took a little from famous titles (Culture points from Civilization, the Tiles from Colonists of Catan, some misinterpreted Age of Empires elements) and doesn't know what it wants to be.
If you, like me, thought this was the next generation city building / RTS with Vikings,
. This is more like a family board game.

Bastion is a game that does just about everything different while keeping enough familiarity so that it doesn't feel alien and unusable. Narrative, combat mechanics, level exploration, weapon selection and upgrade system, level-up mechanics, art direction, currency / XP grinding and game difficulty... not a single one of these is really industry standard for an action/adventure. The designers of this game had a vision and were not satisfied with anything less than its full realization. The craftsmanship and lack of sloppiness/bugs in the game demonstrate to me that Supergiant Games did not get lucky; they did their homework and the legwork. Whether or not Bastion's genre / gameplay are up your alley, game developers should really look at Bastion as an example of what it means to make a new game.

Do you want a game that explores the devastation of a post-apocalyptic world and a boy's attempt to piece everything back together again? Do you want a story about redemption? Do you want a story that grips you, immerses you, strokes you tenderly at night while the soft glow of your computer screen beckons you to play just a little more? You want this game. You want the multitude of weapons you can command, that you can switch when you realize your strategy isn't working. You want the voice that narrates your actions, the voice of an old man who's seen too much and still tries anyway because of the actions of a boy who woke up alone. You want the soft, haunting melody, humming "I dig my hole you build a wall," and the foray into the characters' memories. You want the hope that people will continue on despite devastation. You want the hope that you can save other survivors.
You want to be immersed, to taste the ash and dust of the wasteland around you. One step after the other, the hammer heavy in your hand, your heart even heavier in your chest.
Buy this game. You will not be disappointed.

In an era where every most every AAA game has to be open world, Sleeping Dogs manages to stand out with a vibrant setting, compelling story, and varied gameplay. It's what the True Crime series always wanted to be, but never could. Storywise, if you like cop and crime dramas, particularly flicks like Internal Affairs and the Departed, this game draws heavily from that. Yes, all cop stories all boil down to some tired cliches, but SD manages to make it enjoyable with some surprisingly fleshed out characters.
Modern Hong Kong is lovingly crafted in Sleeping Dogs, and there's tons of stuff to do, both in and out of the main quest. Authentic Chinese dialog is interspersed with the English voiceovers, and the Asian characters don't sound like caricatures like some others games... (Deus Ex: HR).
But this is a game, and the gameplay is where it shines. There are a TON of different mission types, from car chases to gunfights to brawling. The hand-to-hand combat deserves some credit here, as it usually fun and engaging. It compares to the freeform fighting found in the Batman Arkham games, but does not have as many unique moves. Still, you can gradually learn new attacks and get a respectable arsenal. Many of the missions are action-packed, and allow you to hijack cars moving at high speeds or silently tail someone without tipping them off. My biggest complaint would be that there are too many missions that involve "chase this person" on foot or in a car.
This isn't a comprehensive or fleshed-out review in any case, but I highly recommend Sleeping Dogs. It's fun to play, and it looks and sounds fantastic. It's perhaps the best open world urban game I have played outside of the Grand Theft Auto series. Download the high-res texture pack!
Play this game if you enjoy: Grand Theft Auto, Yakuza, Crime Movies

Neon drive is a rithm game with neon style.
+ Very stylish graphics
+ Very smooth experience
+ Good music
+ Works on Arch Linux
- Takes too long to restart
- Some bugs (e.g., freezes after restart, infinite loop on menu)
- Short
Neon Drive is a rythm game where you control a car and must avoid obstacles. As the title of the game suggests the whole game has a very vibrant and colorful neon style. The music and graphics are very plesant and smooth while not distracting you from your main goal.
The controls are very simple, left and right and that's it. Most of the time you're driving iconic cars (e.g., DeLorean DMC-12, Lamborghini Countach) but when you're near the end of the level the car may transform into something else or the level will change orientation and mechanics to keep you interested.
The game itself is very simple but it's well designed for what it is. The game is silky smooth, the obstacles are easily discernable and the controls have very little input lag. It's a purely skill based game. The only issue is that the game is too small. You can easily finish the game in one day in normal mode. Even so the graphical style and music are worth IMO.
After beating the game I tried the Hard and Insane modes. Hard mode is a little bit faster than Normal and you lose once you hit instead of having another chance. Insane mode is even faster. Both can be beaten with patience but there are two annoyances. The first is that restarting takes too long when it should be instantaneous. The other is that sometimes the game freezes after restart and you must go through the ritual of pressing escape twice and wait 3 seconds. Small yet annoying issues.

Lovely to look at, and the music is fantastic. Moving with the music, in a rhythm game style also fun, but completing just the first level on normal was an exercise in frustration for me. Beyond the first level, the game feels like trying to play Through the Fire and Flames on Guitar Hero III, except if you make two mistakes, you lose.
In this game, you have to dodge obstacles in the road by weaving through four lanes, with a Guitar Hero look, but only using two buttons (left and right) to dodge them. The game is very demanding of players having quick reaction times and good timing in general. Players who get off on being super-dee-duper hardcore and telling less talented people to "git gud" will likely enjoy the game, but anyone not of that ilk might have a bad time.
You know what? This game is much, much, much harder than Dark Souls. I played DS on PS3 a few years ago and got to Plague Town before wimping out and quitting, and this game gut-punches you within the first few minutes, far harder than anything Dark Souls threw at me the entire time I played.
One might suggest playing the practice mode in Neon Drive, but one mistake sends you back to the start of the last set of dodges you need to get through. At times, it becomes more of an exercise of memorization of what path to take in a hurry than of actually reacting to the game "organically." The worst part about the practice mode, however, is that it distorts both the audio and video. Although both take on a more "retro" '80s look, which is cool, the music suffers greatly for it, becoming a bit muffled, and the music is by and large the best thing about the game. You can't lose in free play mode, but that's only unlocked
you beat the level, thus rendering free play mode useless to people who could genuinely benefit from being able to leisurely drive around and listen to the awesome music.
The music is so relaxing, but the gameplay is incredibly stressful. I'm sure there are folks out there with far,
better dexterity than I possess, who can complete the game without their lives being miserable, but this is one infuriating game and I do not possess the inherent reaction times necessary to continue.
If you don't play it, at least check out the soundtrack, though It's so good. <3

:: Welcome to another game of the "Aliens vs Predator" franchise ::
Let me answer the most popular questions for this game.

- Why would anyone play or purchase this game?
Owners of this game simply purchased this game for an addition to their "Aliens vs Predator" games on PC but with updated graphics, gore and playback value.

- Where is the fun in this game?
Unlike most FPS (First Person Shooter) games, there are three different species (Marine,  Alien, Predator) to choose and play the single-player campaign as. All individual specie campaigns have different goals and missions to complete, but throughout their campaign the main plot/story will be connected.  [ This game is not a continuance to the movies or comic books]

- Can you play this game online?
Yes, there are co-op, death and species matches with various maps to play with friends or others online.The popularity of playing this game online is very low due to not enough maps available or players joining games.

- What??? This game is not popular for online gaming? Why?
Although this game provided new updated graphical changes for the "Aliens vs Predator" game series, this game lacks in movement and control. To elaborate on this, the "Alien" specie is known for its agility to run and leap from walls, however this game provides a slower attack and jump speed than previous games. Similar problem is with the "Predator" specie controls and movement when switching weapons or visual displays while combating. ( As a "Marine," rapid fire from any weapon seems slow and cause less damage on enemies. Even head shots are ineffective at times during game play.)
- Now what?
Play and purchase this game if you are a fan of the Sci-Fi Horror genre, but don't forget to get your parent's permission first.

DOOM 3: BFG was something rather overlooked by many people in my eyes. Bethesda and id probably released this rather odd package to hype people up for the DOOM 4 (Yes I still call it DOOM 4, shut up).
While for XBOX360 the long load times made it suffer, it was a great package and PS3 players got to experience DOOM 3 on Playstation for the first time ever.
On PC this looked like a "Why?" sort of release and rightfully so. I will recommend this game VIVIDLY! Despite owners of all the previous DOOM's having no reason to buy this unless for achievements and bragging rights (and a very slightly sharper looking DOOM 3).
TL;DR will come at the end of the review.
The story: it's barebones. The writing is solid, though you'll face little of it since it's all logs (written AND audio) that you can easily skip/miss/don't care about.
"Don't care about?" - asks the reader.
Well... in case you've lived in a cave with no internet or a PC for the last 20 or so years... you know what DOOM is, you probably touched it at some point, and loved it if you're old school. Aaaaaand hated it if you're used to the modern gamer type.
DOOM II is nothing more than a DOOM with new levels and a new badass shotgun. This so called "Super Shotgun" would be kinda like the fat guy of weapons since it eats the ♥♥♥♥ out of those shells like a freshly broken up chick eats ice cream while watching Buffy The Vampire Slayer in a failed Nostalgia Night.
And then... DOOM 3...
Added 15% more story through text and audio logs that enrich the chaos in Mars. (Nothing more than to show Carmack can write in english and not just in coding language. He kind of excells at it. Too bad most of it gets bland after a while and barely classifies as story. I've seen better interactive collectibles.) Some dialogue, which DOOM and DOOM II lacked (and for their own good).
DOOM 3 suffered from this inclusion? No, not really.
It's a new inclusion to the DOOM franchise that adds to the experience and richness of what this franchise can bring and DOOM 3 is by far the better paced of all the DOOM's, the weapon introductions, the enemy presentations. All at the right moments.
+ DOOM
+ DOOM II and expansion +
+ DOOM 3 + Resurrection of Evil expansion +
(secret levels and 1 or 2 expansions were left out, and even critically acclaimed community mods)
+ DOOM 3's graphical improvements, while
, they look good enough and show how DOOM 3 still stands the test of time... though the faces are very ugly.
+ Controller Support (not that you should use it anyway)
+ Achievements (finally)
+ Great atmosphere, solid audio design.
+ [DOOM 3 COMPONENT]
It feels like a natural journey through the campaign and makes it far more enjoyable and interesting to visit all the locales.
+ [DOOM 3 COMPONENT] 3D Support.

It probably helped Windows OS be what it currently is because of the massive hype it raised. DOOM is an undenyable classic, not only because it managed to age well (unlike Wolfenstein 3D), but it raised a new genre in this industry. A classic is that: it changes but doesn't allow to be changed.

Summary: The game brings new classes and a bunch of new skills as well as one or two new things compared to the first, but outside that it is a recreation of the 1st game. There is neither much to the story or characters of this game. The audio and music is just as amazing as the first. There was one major bug and a couple minor ones. It was a fun ARPG to play, but it is so short and reliant on you replaying the story for more "content" that it slapped me with unexpected disappointment at the end. It is a game worthy of checking out if you played the first game. I would not recommend playing this game without playing the first game though. I also recommend getting it on sale as theres only about ~15 hours of true meat to the gameplay.
Content Quantity/Length:
Took me a little over 15 hours to complete a playthrough on Hard with a new character from level 1. This includes time spent planning skills, playing the optional tower defense minigames, and searching for secrets completionist style. The rest of the playtime comes from replaying the game Diablo style to level up to max (lvl 60), gaining "glory" after max lvl, grinding for perfect items etc. There are tons of ways to build your characters expecially with all the new stuff post lvl 30.
Gameplay Quality:
The game was relatively bug free. I only encountered 3 issues: Got stuck once (however its easily fixable by teleporting back to the lair), certain tooltips had code in their descriptions instead of actual descriptions especially in the tower defense minigames, runecrafting would cause a desktop crash which made the feature unusable. Movement in the game got frustrating especially as a melee hunter. Some enemies, especially large ones, had huge hitboxes that made it super easy to accidently click on them which meant your character with 10% HP would turn to attack instead of running. It killed me several times.
Story:
It picks up immediately after the end of the 1st game and presumably ends right before the beginning of the 3rd one. That means theres no easing you into the world nor a true ending. Thus I highly recommend playing the first one. I have heard bad things about the 3rd game being sloppy, so I likely wont finish the story of Van Helsing. Speaking of how the ending worked, the story was predictable from about 5-10 minutes in. The main antagonist had no "face" and was boring. Other characters suddenly appeared or disappeared without much story development. The ending was so quick and sudden that I had no idea it was the ending until the credits because it felt like standard dialogue. In summary, there was barely any substance to the story, it felt like a cash grab stretch of rushed story telling to connect the first and third games.
Audio
Voiceacting was mostly very well done. Prisoner 7(no spoilers, you meet him at the beginning of the game) was the only voice acting that I didnt like... sounded like a kid trying to speak in a demonic sounding voice. The music of the game was amazing and probably my favorite part. Overall not much else to say here.

This game is a really fun and simple to pick up game. (It's just like the card game Mafia if you have ever played that)
Basically the idea is at the beginning of each match everyone is assigned a role. The bad guys (Mafia, Serial Killer, etc.) all want to be the last alive, or kill everyone else. There is a day and night cycle and every night the SK and Mafia choose someone to kill, then during the day you have a minute or so to discuss with the other players who the bad guys are. I would definitely recommend picking it up seeing as it is only $5.

When I first played Binding of Isaac: Rebirth, I thought, "Hey, it's like Zelda dungeons only the hero is travelling deep into his own mom's uterus."
It's a lot more than that. Frustrating, challenging and deep with so much replay value that I can't believe I've spent about $20 total on it. It's a roguelike game that minimizes grinding (Greed mode notwithstanding) and rewards players that want to blend some strategic thought into their dungeon-crawler action.
Ultimately, you will learn that the value of items in this game is largely situational. Will you trade 2 keys for 5 bombs in hopes of finding a secret room? Sacrifice your last spirit heart for a chance at a Guppy item? Will you take Cursed Eye and Tiny Planet and hate yourself for the remainder of your run? It's all situational. You will develop principles of play and it will feel good when you make good decisions.
Recommended for players who don't mind dying. A lot.

Starbound was released to kickstarters about a month after I lost my Grandfather.
I did 3 things for 6 months after he died.  I took care of my kids the best I could, I cried when they went to bed, and I played Starbound.
The opening music still haunts me.  I still remember how unique and crazy this game was, and even though most of that eventually got removed, I can go back to old screenshots and invoke a sense of memory, of where I was emotionally while grieving when I took them.
Yeah, Starbound induced a few metric tons of negative energy in a lot of folk's lives.  Starbound is a "toxic" game by its own developer's description, because without the community, the people who loved it and wanted to see it succeed, there never would have been a place for any of the hate.
I used to do frequent "Starbound Adventures" series in the forums where I'd detail all the updates.  I actually enjoyed doing that in spite of how awful Chucklefish and the Starbound community were behaving toward each other.  I got super mad, then decided one day to just dive in and play.  It was fun.
Then nothing was updated for a long time, and as more nightly builds got pushed, I started seeing them remove content.  This is why I associate Starbound with Trees.
My biggest distraction from tragedy came in the form of Starbound's trees.  It became an obsession, something to do feverishly while taking breaks from the swollen eyes and snot.  I collected almost 600 unique tree seeds and made an entire planet from top to bottom a farm of them.  I'm not sure how many could actually be generated, but they were all different, and it felt like I was playing this epic-level Harvest Moon as I farmed trees and food.  I can never rate this game down because the collecting and planet-hopping was some of the biggest fun I'd ever had in a videogame, period.
Then they got rid of the trees.  The variety was slashed into fragments, and most of them became these dreadful brown/pastel mixes.  All of the color and imagination disappeaered.  They became background objects, the junk you ignore while you play any random SHMUP.  The farming sense faded instantly, and the wind was knocked out of me.  The one thing I was still enjoying in this game, gone.
I haven't played more than 10 minutes since the last time they made the experimental build a seperate library option.  I got on, made a character, warped around, I guess they decided the trees were "axed".  I don't know if it was a performance decision, but I can vouch that at the time I had my huge tree farm, I had zero lag with around 2000 trees on a single planet, around 500-600 variations among them, on an old 2012 system:
Radeon HD 6970 2GB graphics card
Intel Core i5-3570k
8 gigs of ram, no SSD.
144hz Asus 27" 1080p.
No lag ever, the game just ran beautifully, and it looked beautiful too.  Now its just drab and unappealing to me.  I'm trying to make sense of why all the color was taken out, all of that art, what a waste.

I like playing Street Fighter V and will play it a ton, but I I'd be joking if I supported the game and recommended it until the following are actually addressed.  If the following are things you can forgive then play the game.
- Input Lag: This is terrible in any video game let alone fighting games. Lower it. Especially in offline! I can understand if some input lag is needed for netplay, but why should that decision affect offline play? Players want a game where their reactions can be tested more than their ability to just simply guess. Input lag being 6.5 frames on average in this game is directly affecting the meta and no one is happy with it.
- Netcode: Capcom is releasing an update to the Capcom Fighter Network, but no where in their notes did they mention wanting to improve the netcode?? The netcode has very obvious flaws, such as 1 sided rollback where both players have different experiences and the game doesn't sync correctly. One player will have a smooth as butter match, the other is suffering unplayable conditions.
- Matchmaking - Connection Quality: The connection quality 'bars' are often not really telling anything. A 5 bar connection doesn't always mean a good experience. Why can't it differentiate better between connections or JUST SHOW THE PING?
- No Performance or Connection Quality testing or requirement for ranked mode.  If your opponent has a bad frame rate, the game will probably lag too when their computer falls behind during a Critical Art animation.  It's a bad experience for both players, lets just require frame rate tests or connection quality tests before allowing people to queue up in ranked!
I will say this, this is the only Street Fighter game I've liked and I believe this game gets too much slack for things that aren't really all that important in the game's whole lifespan. It's fun when it works right! The FGC wants this game to be better is all.
For Capcom to be selling this game as a competitive online and offline fighting game, they need to fix the above to match that vision.
Oh if you're not interested in fighting people online and only like offline, do not buy the game.  This Street Fighter is directed more towards Player VS Player experiences.  Which I enjoy!... but I want to be better...

A masterpiece game that definitely deserves 9/10
Basically the game is top-down adventure platformer with RPG mechanics, such as weapon upgrade system and "the distillery" as well as customizable difficulty elements through "idols". The game revolves around going through a pre-set story which you can go it through at your own pace. You play as a white haired unnamed boy who wakes up in the aftermath of a disaster, "the calamity". Eventually, the boy finds his way into a sanctuary, "the bastion" where he meets the person who narrates his adventures. However, the Bastion is not complete and that is where the boy steps in.
The story line is very touching and has some surprising twists and provides the player a satisfying amount of crumbles of information about the universe of the Bastion. Combined with great soundtracks to accompany the player makes Bastion a very memorable game.
The kid can be equipped with various weapons which he can customize to vanguish his many foes; Security systems gone haywire, wild beasts, scavengers and surviving "Ura" (people)
Gameplay wise Bastion is fairly well balanced and caters a proper difficulty for all kinds of players through it's "idol" system which truly starts to shine in the new game (plus).
The customization is simple but the combination of different weapon upgrades makes the player want to crave to try every loadout.
The hand drawn graphics are very impressive and clear. Nothing more to say about that.
The only complaint I have about this game is that it's control can occasionally feel a bit clunky. Particularly with walking, evasive rolling (which by the way is a bit too overpowered) and turret placement (Hint: The turrets are a reference to a hugely popular game. I'll let you to figure that out). And this all just made my thumb sore at the end of the day because you need to use 4 actions at the same time and many of them are dependent on your mouse movement so even with customizable options to set your own controls, I simply couldn't get perfect setup. That's why I had to deduct 1 point from this Bastion: A game that is a masterpiece aside from clunky controls and slight balance issues (Crits on a Kael hammer? HA)
Overall, highly recommended and you can probably pick this game at some point from the sales or Humble Bundle store with very cheap price

I don't even have words to describe the adventure this game provided me. To be honest, all I can say is that this game is amazing, but that's a pure understatement.
For a quick summary of Bastion, the plot follows the main character, known as "The Kid" as he wakes up after the calamity has taken place. The calamity is an event which reduced most people and the world to ash and rubble. He takes off towards the Bastion where he will go off to get cores to power up the Bastion so that he can fix the calamity.
The gameplay of the game is extremely engaging and keeps the players on their toes, even when playing the game on the easiest setting. You will find yourself constantly rolling and trying to avoid enemy attacks, and searching levels for health potions over and over again. The enemies do become harder, but thankfully not the point that I would call this  a Dark Souls game. [ THANK THE LORD!!! ]
The main point I love about Bastion is the story. It keeps the players interested and compels you to play more and more so you can find out what happens next or find out what happened before the game had begun. I will not say too much however, but the story truly is beautiful.
And I cannot leave out the next best thing, the music. I just don't know what to say about it. It is extremely fitting, and has a nice tune and beat to it, and always seems right for the situation you find yourself to be in, whether a fierce battle, or simply roaming around the Bastion and talking to people.
Overall, I would like to say that this game is great, but it's not. It's a bloody masterpiece and one that I must say, will outlive many. This is a MUST for gamers everywhere.
