Now that I've had a chance to play through all three campaigns, I can heartily recommend this game.
For starters, it looks gorgeous.  Visually it holds up very well considering how much graphics have advanced in just the pasts five years.  Sound effects are spot-on and the music is good too, although a bit repetitive, and there are moments when the ambient audio is a little too heavy-handed.
Gameplay is solid too.  The Marine plays exactly as you'd expect, not that that's a bad thing.  Also, easily the most terrifying campaign.  Even after the initial playthrough, the Xeno AI is good enough to constantly keep you on your toes.  The Predator layers on a lot of very cool mechanics that make you feel like the ultimate badass.  Both campaigns are very atmospheric and offer a couple really nice set-piece battles.
The Xeno campaign is perhaps the weakest.  Playing as one remains quite disorienting and the human AI is frightfully stupid; you can clear out a whole room by drawing Marines one at a time into the same dark corner.  Both the Xeno and its story move so fast that I often finished missions before even realizing it.  It picks up right at the end, no spoilers, but it's too little too late.
Once you gather all the collectibles in each campaign, there's no longer any real replayability, so how much you get out of this game will largely depend on whether you invest in the multiplayer community.  That's not really my scene, but I can easily see how playing as any of the three character types with friends would be a lot of fun.
For hardcore franchise fans, this will be a great treat.  For general FPS fans, there's a lot of variety here to keep you occupied for a while.  If you're at all curious, AvP is well worth picking up on sale.

I recently finished playing WATCH_DOGS and decided to pick this up on the summer sale. This game is the top dog of the pack.
Playing this game is like watching an action movie. It's not just endless waist-high-walls cover-based shooting. The game encourages you to make interesting maneuvers and most of the combat is actually hand-to-hand, with a wonderful system of combos, grapples, and counter-attacks.
Driving in this game is actually interesting given how different Hong Kong is compared to your standard big American city venue for these sorts of games. Little details like driving on the other side of the ride or the passenger seat being on the opposite side, to the cramped and sometimes confusing streets make it much more interesting getting around. Plus the licensed music in this game for the in-car radio is fantastic! I just about lost it when Dream Theater came on in the game.
The game does a good job of instilling constant fear that your role as undercover cop ascending the ranks of the Triads will be revealed. It's good the whole way, but the last few missions are absolutely gripping. I honestly grew to like several characters on both sides of the law, so when the♥♥♥♥♥♥starts to hit the fan it felt important.
The animations get a little screwy at times, but overall the game looks pretty good. Many games have more advanced graphical effects and better lighting, but the colorful and grimy Hong Kong setting is brimming with character.
It's a shame I passed this game up when it came out. I didn't think I'd want to play "another GTA-style game" at the time, but this game has style and character with the gameplay to back it up. I got this game for $5, but it's easily worth ten times more than that.

I bought this game mostly to try the original doom, but I thoroughly enjoyed the first two and am currently enjoying Doom 3.
The original Doom has a really good learning and difficulty curve, (Other than one episode, Thy Flesh Consumed. You have to scramble a bit at the start of that one.) as does Doom II. For example, enemies that are introduced as a mini boss are later used as regular uncommon enemies, such as the Baron of Hell. Another good example is bosses being later used as mini bosses once the player has learned how to beat them with only a little bit of difficulty. All in all, Doom and Doom II have aged REALLY well.
While I'm not finished Doom 3, it's an interesting take on the original Doom. It's less a hardcore non-linear shooter and more of a linear action horror. It has an attempt at a few jumpscares every now and then, but stays mostly action so far. Considering the age of the game, the visuals are mostly nice. Every now and then you get a close look at a low quality texture, but the guns, enemies, and lighting are all very good considering when the game was made, not that visuals are really all that big a deal. The difficulty progression is much slower in Doom 3 and it makes me kind of wish new enemies were introduced faster. If you're good at shooters/play a lot of shooters, veteran might be the difficulty you should try.
Doom and Doom II have very simple story telling methods. In Doom, you would get text at the end of an episode, and it sums up each episode in a very fitting tone. Doom II on the other hand, has the episode Hell On Earth which is really long compared to the episodes in Doom. Instead of just text at the end of the episode, theres text every few levels, after your character completes a big objective. Doom 3 on the other hand introduces many of the enemies with cutscenes, and has a story that is much more present during gameplay. The fact that the first two games lack this isn't exactly a bad thing though, because they were meant to be all action but with enough story for the game to make sense. They pulled it off excellently.
Doom and Doom II have great soundtracks, and I could listen to E1M1 and the track from Barrels o' fun (ahem Them Bones by Alice in Chains ahem) over and over. I haven't heard a lot of the music in Doom 3 yet but if any of it is anything like the title music, I'm excited to hear it. If you're a metal and/or grunge fan, check out some of the D1 and D2 soundtracks.
In conclusion, I feel this pack exceeds its price value.

Very enjoyable game.  Runs great on lower end specs, art and sound are perfect for a game like this.  Gameplay is confusing the first time you play, but after a few matches you figure it out real quick.  For $5, I've already gotten my moneys worth out of it and only had it for a day or two.
The game is equal parts deductive reasoning and crafting the perfect lie.  Figure out who's lying, who's acting suspicious, and who is connected to someone else's activities.  Then if you are playing an evil role, you need to have a story thought up in advance.  Something that's not easy to prove, but also not easy to disprove; just enough to make the majority doubt your guilt.  Very fun and easy to lose track of time while playing.
Now, the reason why there are so many negative reviews lately:  the game used to have a single currency, earned in game (Merit Points), spent on cosmetic skins.  Now there is also a premium currency (Town Points) that you must pay money for.  Some items in the shop can only be purchased with Town Points, while other items can be purchased with EITHER Town Points OR Merit Points.  However, the Merit Point cost is about 4x as much as the Town Point cost (1000 TP vs 4000 MP).
It does strike me as a bit of an odd choice on the dev's part, but considering it only affects the cosmetics of the game, I don't really see any reason to freak out about it and downvote the game because my townie can't look super mega awesome.  What a player looks like, or what house they live in, does not change what their role in the game is or their behavior.  Therefore, the gameplay is 100% unnaffected.
If you just want to play a fun game and don't care whether you look like a pilgrim or a roided out zombie santa, then for $5 you can't go wrong with this game.  You do start with a handful of skin options for your character and house, so it's not like you are completely locked into a specific one.  Plus the currency you start with is enough to buy at least 1 new character skin and 1 new house so, the choices do exist.

Creepy at first, we are presented with real life horror element such has♥♥♥♥♥♥and pedofila. Fran Bow does a great job in subtaly integrating these dark theme into its lore without overdoing it..
There was a time were artistic stop motion was a thing (wait you will get were i am going with this) were it was all about the craftsmanship and the facial expression coming to life frame by frame. Well Fran bow would have been an amazing stop motion movie. The character design are reminiscent of Tim burtons early work (Yes there was a time were my friend Burton was actually a good filmmaker) and the The creatures design are absolutely incredible. But i am happy that Fran bow is a game because it is reminding me of why i love the stop motion art in general.
Back to game at hand, i will say this if you are a fan of american mcgee Alice and you have been craving for a proper sequel and hate tim burton version of alice in wonderland. Then Fran bow should be the does of medication you have been craving for.
With that said there are it's fault some of the puzzle designed are weirdly designed. 95% percent can be solved if you pay attention to the level designed but i found my self looking at a guide for 2 of them that i won't detail them because i wouldn't want to reveal any spoiler. With that said that a problem with 90 % of the point and click genre in general so that not a big issue. Some of the mini game are fun but feel force and unnecessary, they do offer some interesting art style.
9.1/10 Verdict: Dark, Creepy and Underated. If you are a fan of point and click games Fran Bow is worth a full price Steam purchase.

This will not be a typical review. I will not cover the gameplay aspects as much as I should. But definitely read the whole thing, since the devs have done something awful to this game that you need to consider before buying this game. I have disliked this game, not for gameplay, but for the "customisation options". Please read before calling my review "Not helpful".
The gameplay is essentially Mafia. You get in a lobby with 15 people, and you all get a role assigned. The Town roles have to  execute all of the Mafia roles and most of the Neutral roles, the Mafia has to kill everyone and the Neutral have very specific objectives to win the game, and it's a lot of fun. I really like this game, for its gameplay. And if you like tabletop games like Werewolves and Mafia, you definitely need to play this game.
I have played this game since it was still a Kickstarter-project. I instantly fell in love with it, and before 1.0 launched I put at least 100 hours into it. The way customization worked before was that from each game you finished (so even if you died you had to stick around until the game was over) you got Town Points. The rate at which you gained these Town Points (or TP, as I will now call them) was: 5TP for a lost game, 10TP for a won game, and 25TP for each first win of the day. You also got TP for completing achievements (which are the game in the Steam version). A game lasts for about 20 minutes. If you take the win/lose rate to be 50/50, you'd get 7.5TP on average per game. So for every hour you played you would get around 22.5TP.
Now get this: each individual map/character/pet/etc. costs 1040TP. So you'd have to play for a loooong time to finally get ONE thing. It was grindy, but the gameplay definitely made up for it. But now that has changed. Patch 1.5.x completely changed the way customization worked. BlankMediaGames introduced so called "Merit Points" (or MP, as I will now call them). BMG introduced this as an alternative way to pay for options to customise your game. So instead of gaining TP at the end of each game, you'd get MP. TP became a premium currency which can only be obtained through micro-transactions.
MP is earned a lot quicker (I believe 40 per match, and 100 for the first win of the day), but the price of the customizations has been TRIPLED. And the best part is: not every character/house/map can be bought with these MP. Some are only unlockable by TP. So now you have to either grind an eternity or pay REAL MONEY to get what you want. This is so shady, and puts a stain on BMG's beautiful record.
Do I recommend this game for gameplay? A thousand times yes.
But this new way of customizing the game is stupid, and I hope they will roll back this new system.

Icey from beginning to end is an exemplary journey with a lively narrator and beautiful combat. ICEY is very reminiscent of the Stanley Parable, in which there is a narrator, who you are free to obey to disobey to your likening, At it's core, if you follow along and do not amble from the path that the narrator sets out for you, is a fun 2d hack and slash, with fast paced slashing and dodging, with no blocking however it has a system reminiscent of Metal Gear Rising Revengeance, in which you will be able to execute low health enemies and regain your health. How ever, if you choose to ignore the narrator, it opens up to a deep and very philosophical journey in which you much question your self and the theory of consciouness and self. While i will try to not spoil anything, I HIGHLY advise you play the game more than once, with the FIRST time you play it, following along with the narrator, and the next play throughs disobeying and choosing your own path. Fantablade being a chinese dev team, chose to narrate the game in chinese. It gives the game a very expressive narration due to the Chinese language being very vocal, which is very fitting with the actions you take. However with the recent announcement that they will have an english voice over, with acclaimed Stephanie Joosten as the voice actor, it will for sure gain more attention, and It will be nice to see the comparison between Chinese and English voice overs. The music as well, is very fitting to each part of the maps, for example, in the sewers, the music is very dark and brooding and feels very tepid. In the town or the city, it is very futuristic and gives a lighter and more dancing vibe. The artwork is beautifully crafted and the effects when ICEY fights are very beautiful and flashy, and gives the attacks a lot of weight. The game is quite short, with being able to complete the game once over in little over an hour to two hours. However, to full complete the game, you should play through it several times. It's also one of the few games that made me become enchanted by a character, much less a protaganist. I highly recommend playing this game, and i feel i will come back to it once the english voice over is here.

ICEY looks like a typical hack n slash on the surface. You might just be like I was when you saw this game. "Ah, well, guess this will keep me busy until the next Devil May Cry 5, or such and such a hack n slash because I love ma sexy stylish combos"...and then you avoided it for a bit...and then came back later when you saw a sale and you are wondering...hm, well, might as well get it but...should I? I'll just be hacking and slashing but...are the combo mechanics good? Can I do the Devil May Crys?
Well people. This is only ONE aspect of the game but not entirely the thing you actually should let concern you. The other aspect is what made me fall in love with the game for being so different than the usual hack n slash. Yes you can do the combos, yes you can do the jump cancels and dash cancels and parry timing issen counters...but how do we get to that point when we are making stylish combos....EXPERIMENTATION...right?.... RIGHT YOU ARE!
This game from the very get go, tests your ability to experiment. Not just in combo, no, mostly in doing things you'd never otherwise do in a game in general. There exist triple A games that tell you where to go, what to do...but in this game, you don't need to do just that. In fact, doing the opposite is quite rewarding. In other words, this game is pulling a Stanley Parable (remember that game?).
The game makes you fail over and over until you choose to allow for there to be story in your game (as if setting the game mode to easy) but this is a hoax! Yes, it may hurt your pride at first but...just believe in the game a bit. It wasn't trying to demasculate you and the such. It's merely a test of how willing you are to do something different...out of the ordinary. The narrator will tell you what to do...but you will be quite surprised when you try to do the opposite...of which I'm not spoiling. That's the whole purpose of the game after all. To play how you want. Play like a devil may cry pro, play like a one button masher, do what you are told, don't do what you are told. Though I will reccomended not doing what you are told...funny♥♥♥♥♥♥happens. SO BE EXPLORATIVE, BE EXPERIMENTAL, LOOK WHERE YOU NORMALLY WOULDN'T! You'll be surprised what you find and what this beautiful game has in store for you.
Have fun...and definitely buy this game. You don't need to be into hack n slashes to really enjoy this one at all. Let's just say, it's like Stanley Parable, but with more icing on top. You won't just be walking in this game. How I wish I bought this on its release day.

When I got this game, they had just announced it would be going into alpha soonish.  This was around October of 2013.  I have played this off and on for the last 2 and a half years.  Why off and on?  Simple, because early on, it was very easy to get to the endgame content due to the exceedingly high abundance of the resources more often than now.  In addition, with each new content update, I started anew to see how the flow of it had changed.  I was rarely disappointed.  Sure, there were times things felt broken or overly troublesome, but a fair amount of that was due to the code being very raw at the time.  Lag was a nigh constant since it was unoptimized.  But Chucklefish worked on it.  Refined it.  Improving on it.  Now, here we are, a couple of years past their original projected completion date, but this polish was highly needed.
The main draw of this game is it's Terraria-like gameplay mixed with Minecraft like generation of the universe.  Each world felt like it was a new map to experience, explore, and let's all be honest, exploit.  The traveling between systems feels kind of sluggish, yes, but it fits the theme of the game.  There is a fair bit of humor in the game, but some quips are only really 'understandable' by those who'd been playing.  Like the trick to killing Dreadwing originally - dig a hole, block it up to leave a single column to shoot out of, win face with a bow.
There are some downsides, no game is perfect.  As of my last playing, about 2 months ago, the gameplay bogged down quickly if you had a significant farm running, or a lot of lighting objects in operation.  This was the most annoying aspect in my personal opinion, as it meant you had to either spread your farms out over a large area, or have a beefy computer to handle hte processes running.  The resource hungry recipes in teh game also mean you will be spending a LOT of time hopping from one planet to the next at the right 'danger level' for the resources you need so that you can get that last bit of ore to make that last ingot to make that last peice of equipment you need to continue the quest chain can wear on you and drain some of the joy of exploration out of the game.
Simply put, by the end of this, the game is worth it.  By leaps and bounds (ha puns).  Is it for everyone?  Probably not.  But those who enjoy a Metrovania-style sandbox building game, they may find themselves looking up, seeing the stars, and wondering - What's around the next jump?

After adding the first Van Helsing to one of the most favorite games I've ever played, VH2 only polished and added to the enjoyment where the first one left off. I was still playing the first one up to the release of this game and continued playing it during this one. But VH2 not only left off where the last story ended, but improved on tons of things to make this game even more enjoyable than the first. So with this in mind, I wrote a review for people new to the series as well as one for people who have played the first game and are considering getting this one.
Newcomers to the Van Helsing trilogy-
Even if you haven't played the first one, it would still be enjoyable to start with VH2. The reason for this is much like any other game, such as Borderlands 2. Playing the first one AFTER the second one will give you more depth in the story as well as make you appreciate all the changes that were done in the second game. Even though I would recommend playing the first one first, I don't see any spoilers at all in VH2 to the storyline of VH1. There are even items/gear that is reverse compatible ;) which you will probably think is pretty keen of the developers. Yes, it plays like Diablo 3, but that is by all means not a bad thing. But that comparison is very similar to saying Battlefield plays like CoD or MoH. And what about the "Gears of War" and "God of War" comparisons in other games. Yah, it's kinda like that :/ All in all, if you get VH2, you will be getting a great funny and very enjoyable RPG which you can co op up to 4 players as well as PvP. When you play it, you'll know it's going to be a great game from the photobomb on the title screen hahaha.
Ones who've played the first Van Helsing-
It may look like the same game but many things have been polished to fit customer satisfaction. For instance there are still 6 pages of storage, but now most of the gear takes 2 blocks instead of 3, and the storage space has been significantly expanded. So now there is over double the storage space of the first game. Along with the max level reaching 60 instead of 30, there are doubled the skills to mess around with! So you have the option of lvl10ing the skills and tricks you have ported over OR taking them off and starting a whole new tree of new abilities. Or you can even mix it. Oh yeah, as I stated, you can export over your powered up character from the first game :) The Chimera is not as powerful as it looks but is still a great addition as well as a little storyline within the sp story. Also the 'sets' and 'epics' have 'ink infested' versions which are level 60s. So even though you may have a complete set with the level ranges at 33 38 and 45, you can still farm for the all level 60 versions of that same set :)))) OMG, and wait until you get your first 'godlike' item!!! Besides that they just expanded on everything that made the first game so fun to play like: glory, perks, weapons & gear, laughs, easter eggs, tower defense, etc. The story, I would like to compare to The Matrix Reloaded. Not the best story, but essential in the trilogy and to any fan of the first game. It was also fun to play through with more boss fights and loot drops. So basically, I would definitely recommend this game if you've played through the first one even just once.
The DLCs-
I've written separate reviews on each DLC.
Rating: 9/10

Well, i didn't expect much from this game as it was suggested by a doctor when i was in hospital... yeah strange i know - BOY WAS I WRONG
I was extremely suprised with the detail that went into the game's opening sequence, it immediately got me hooked. Despite the love of Hollywood to turn games into movies, there doesn't seem to be a need for a movie based on Left 4 Dead, as it's already been made several times over, from George A. Romero's 'Dawn of the Dead' to Danny Boyle's '28 Days Later'
I will speak on the single player as thats all i have played so far. In the game, you and three survivors must battle a zombie apocalypse with a simple goal; SURVIVE
Left 4 Dead is about the dreaded zombie apocalypse turning the vast majority of the population into a mindless, ravenous undead hordes.
A handful of humans remain immune to the zombie virus, and you play as a small group of them. There's Zoey, a young woman; Bill, the grizzled veteran; Louis, the middle-class office worker; and Francis, the biker. Armed with real and makeshift weapons, these survivors must battle their way to salvation. It's a simple plot that anyone can recognize, and Valve pulls it off with its trademark incredible attention to detail.
You battle through to a series of 'safe houses' that lead to a rescue point. The downside to single player is that the bots are passive; you always have to be in the lead, which is problematic when you're hurting.
Each scenario is presented like a movie, complete with poster If you survive, the "credits" display the statistics for the game, like who killed the most zombies, who inflicted the most headshots, who delivered the most friendly fire, and the like. By now i thought i'd seen it all but what really got me was at the end it says how many zombies were killed in the making of the film.
Dont let the 'zombies' lull you into a false sense of security - these are based on the 'fast zombies' (think 28 weeks later) - they dont dawdle - they sprint at you with inhuman speed, scale fences, and bust down doors to get at you. Horde zombies aren't smart, but they are dangerous in large numbers. The real danger comes in the form of some special zombies.
Boy you have to be aware of these... There's the hunter, which can leap across large distances to pin a survivor to the ground. (tricky little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to kill - think like a jack in a box with unlimited spring) Then there's the smoker, which has a frog-like tongue that can grab a survivor by the throat, and pull you into or up a building (always listen for the coughing). The boomer is a smelly corpulent zombie that vomits or explodes to spray survivors. Getting hit by the substance will not only temporarily blind survivors, but it drives the zombie horde into a feeding frenzy. (think like catnip for zombies) The tank is just that; built like a brick s*ithouse that can take an enormous amount of damage and dish out a fair amount. And finally, there's the witch, (NOT a old lady who eats little boys and girls); she's an enormously powerful zombie that can take down a survivor with a single swipe.
The game is paced almost perfectly so that you're always pushed to the edge. You'll run low on health. You'll run low on ammo or you'll run out entirely, requiring you to rely on pistols, which have unlimited ammo but aren't as effective as shotguns, assault rifles, and submachine guns. There are pipe bombs and Molotov bombs that you can scavenge, and you can turn propane tanks and gas canisters into weapons. The latter are particularly useful in the many "crescendo" elements in the game. These are points where you must initiate an action in order to open the way forward like having a van drive through a steel fence to open the route. The kicker is that the moment you initiate the action the zombie horde are going to come down on you like a tidal wave.
The good news is that you have time to prepare and place down gas and fuel canisters If a player falls victim to the zombie menace, you respawn at the last 'safe house' Supposedly as another survivor who has been found (though don't ask why the new survivor is exactly the same as the old survivor)
All in all - bloody brilliant Single Player - Multiplayer i have no experience of as yet

First off, the critisisms. 6/10. Barely passing but not terrible.
This game is Mortal Kombat in all it's gorey glory. Don't be fooled by the promises of a full story because that story is a series of pre-rendered (That are lower quality and resolution than the actual game) cut scenes following a story that holds up like wet tissue paper. Beyond the lack of substance in the story the fights in it consist of fighting 1, 2, and at one point 3 enemies with bosses splashed in because they don't want you getting bored. The first few fights with each new character, you go through most of the popular cast, you will spend getting beaten to a pulp until you learn each new characters move set. Once you get comfortable with that character you fight a boss and are immediatly put in the shoes of a new fighter. By the end of the game *spoiler* you have to fight Shao Kahn *spoiler end* who has unblockable attacks, armored animations, and who takes 40% damage on everything you do. Your best move, the x-ray animation, does 20% of his health at best.
In summary of the story, you get what you'd expect from a Mortal Kombat story. The worst parts are the terrible audio/visual effects in the cutscenes for the story and the final boss fight. You might be saying 'But the final boss fight is SUPPOSED to be hard!' and you'd be right. Hard is what it should be. Damn near unwinnable on Normal difficulty is a design flaw not a feature. The fights inbetween the start of the train wreck and the end are pretty easy. You'll find 1 or 2 super moves you like and spam them until your (quarter circle back) motion is flawless.
With all that said I still recommend this game because it IS Mortal Kombat. The Ladder is still alot of fun and if you beat it you get a nice little ending cutscene for that character.(sadly better than the whole story mode) The challenge tower will give you something new to do once you've beaten the Ladder on your favorite characters. Instead of the usual 'Female Ninja #1 and #2' style of female characters each one has it's own unique skillset that FEELS unique. The graphics in the fights look pretty great *story mode cutscenes not withstanding*. Most importantly the skill sets are all easy to learn but hard to master. You'll get the hang of your favorite character pretty fast and the more technical skills of each character will take you ages to land everytime. You know, like the old Arcade game we all loved? You're given a move list but it's not easy-mode.
Buy this game on sale and enjoy seeing your favorite character rend flesh from bone or turn your opponent into a baby. It's Mortal Kombat. If you're looking for a good story in your fighting game... try something else.

Buying this game and supporting it only tells Capcom that they can get away with making sub-par games and selling for a premium.  A seemingly growing trend in modern day game development. (probably something they are going to repeat with Marvel vs Capcom Infinite)
That being said, it's worth noting I was a huge player of Ultra Street Fighter 4, with almost 1000 hours clocked.  In USF4 it takes time to "git gud" and rightly so. I REALLY wanted to like SF5, however in SF5 the game is so heavily catered to the "new" player it feels as though you aren't doing anything meaningful to win a battle.
While the game shares some mechanics that are inspired by alpha, the crush counter system is a salt enducing cancer.  A system that encourages players to simply mash the heaviest attack in the hope that their opponent attempts to hit you. Combos are terribly easy and unrewarding, the netcode is broken at best and the game just falls flat on its face when it comes to having any depth.
There is no hype to be had here, maybe the occasional thrill but literally a barren desert of hype.
My advice to anyone reading would be to either invest in a different fighter, such as Killer Instinct, King of Fighters (if you have a console), Guilty Gear Xrd or even Tekken 7 when it hits in a few months.

There isn't really any way I could not recommend this. It's a labor of love that I'm sure destroyed its' creators lives in a variety of ways. I can't imagine the work involved, and they deserve much better than to be associated with the 'indie gaming' scene, which is a joke these days. Expecially since they still seem to respond in the forums. The story is excellent, the characters will live in my heart for many years, and the gameplay is varied and just challenging enough not to be boring.
And yet, I think that I personally don't like the things it ends up doing, at least when they're interpreted in a certain way. There's kind of a carefully studied binary ambiguity to the way the narrative is constructed, in which every interpretation you can make of a certain thing can be countermanded by an alternate, equally valid interpretation. I don't think this is a case of throwing random crypticisms at a board and pretending it means something a la Lost, but I do think it's something almost equally frustrating if not nearly as lazy; crafting the story in such a way that no, or very few, of the possible interpretations are definitively wrong. I would prefer more commitment in my storytelling, especially since I really want to know what actually happened to the characters I loved so much.
I would prefer the frame rate weren't locked and the game could use a few more animations that aren't represented by a mildly grotesque work of art, but much of this can be excused by the nature of the small team developing it. UIltimately highly recommended, but you might be a little frustrated if you like solid conclusions to narratives, or at least ones in which there is one interpetation of events. I waited for a sale, but there really isn't any reason to if you like classic adventure games at all.

Great game and lots of fun! It does have it's issues which I will list in a moment, but it is nothing to deter you from buying and playing it.
Pros:
1. Overall good game music

3. Screenshotting for steam is disabled while in game.
4. Shift+tab is disabled while in game so you cannot enter the steam overlay during gameplay to respond to PM's or whatever

Overall though, I still recommend this game to anyone who enjoys music based games and fighting games. STORY: You play as "the Kid" in the world of Cealondia which has been ravaged by the Calamity. You begin your journey escaping and later discover the Bastion. There you meet Rucks, our narrator and guide, who begins tasks you with collecting cores from various other locations to power the Bastion. Along the way you save Zulf, Zia, and other fauna from the world. Once all cores are collected an attack transpires that sends you on the quest to collect shards, and afterwards you are made to make 2 pivotal choices that affect your ending. The story is really interesting at first because the narration is done well enough to spark that interest, but since very little development happens outside of a few cut scenes and narrative tidbits, it can be quickly forgotten. In fact real attachment doesn't surface until the end of the story when you realize what the Bastion is capable of doing and how the Calamity started. Even when the attack happens the first time all you really feel is frustration because now you have to fix everything. The story is not interesting enough to demand finishing it.
DESIGN: The art style of the game is something special and won't really be forgotten easily. The game flows well and each level gets it's own distinctive feel and atmosphere. What really makes the design something special is that in each level as you move forward each block of land rises up to meet you. It does make the experience interesting, but may hamper exploration because it gives off the idea of linear design. The character models are very unique, but I find the enemy models too similar, especially when it comes down to the "monsters". The weapons all give vastly different fighting styles and there are so many that you may not play through each of them longer then their reveal level. Quite interesting level design that is fun to look at and even explore at times.
GAME PLAY: Bastion is an ARPG. You level up to acquire more buffs and with the "gems" you collect you buy more skills and buffs. You also have a small crafting system where you power up your weapons to do more effects or just more damage. As you level up the Bastion you gain side quests, challenges, and a shrine to increase the game difficulty for more rewards. Once you hop up in the Skyway there are two types of levels: challenge maps and story levels. In the challenge maps you are tasked with essentially mastering a weapon and the better you do the better the prize. A bit on the difficult side, but fun to do if you appreciate a well crafted challenge. The story levels maintain that artistic level, but they are all from point A to point B. Even when they change the item from cores to shards, they all play the same. The different play styles you can unlock with the weapons and skills is fun, along with the shrine buffs, but overall it is the same level over and over again. The game play is well crafted in that sense, but the sense of repetition and the length does set in.
SOUND: The music is superb and quite memorable because of the nice western style of it. The most memorable track is the fighting soundtrack because it inspires rapid movement since it is an ARPG. Apart from that one, each individual soundtrack is great for each level. The narrator does a great job in building the world and it's lore as well as making a few jokes here and there. Beautifully crafted and voiced, no complaints whatsoever.
FUN: The game initially is a lot of fun and breeds nothing, but excitement all through the first part. In the game with the help of design and narration, you build a relationship with yourself and "the kid." The proving grounds are also a fun way to catch a break from the story levels. However when the focus changes from cores to shards, the repetition begins to set in. While each level can be as fun, I found myself playing less and less frequently.
SUMMARY: The game is a great breath of fresh air in it's style and game play. Each aspect does work together in crafting a memorable experience. The sound, level and game play does carry well, but it is the repetition that holds it back from being an unbelievable experience.
VERDICT: Wait for a Sale

I highly recommend this game to fans of co-op games. Even though Left 4 Dead 2 is technically better, the original still manages to be a pretty awesome game in it's own terms.
The game is split up into a bunch of campaigns, each split into five chapters/levels (excluding two campaigns). The first four levels require a team of characters to progress to a safe house. Along the way, you encounter or are attacked/ambushed by hundreds of zombies, and while they are pretty to defeat, the sheer number of attacking enemies can be overwhelming. Teamwork is a key element when playing on normal difficulty or over. Adding to the enemies are a number of minibosses, which require different strategies to defeat. Some are pretty easy, while others keep you on your toes. The fifth and final level/chapter in the campaign is normally some kind of extraction from the area, which requires players to defend themsevles in a certain area for a set amount of time. It can get pretty intense.
There are four characters to choose from before the start of the campaigns. There's a computer guy, a biker, a war veteran, and a college girl. There's not much of a difference with who you choose, it's more of a personal preferance. But even so, there's quite a bit of dialouge for each character, some for scripted events in the campaigns, and a ton of comments/quotes for player use during gameplay. This is useful for players who don't have a microphone during multiplayer.
Speaking of multiplayer, there's an interesting versus mode, where some players play as the survivors, while the others take control of the game's minibosses. And not to mention a survival mode.
The graphics are pretty good. Even though this game is from 2009, it still holds up in today's standards. Lighting and flashlight mechanics are impressive. Textures are mostly high quality. Depending on your rig, the game maintains a good-maximum framerate, even when you have thirty zombies running around in your field of vision. I was surprised that the game ran so well, since I have a pretty bad graphics card for gaming. I managed to put almost all settings to max. On the negative side, I see black spots like a radius around fire ingame, although I'm sure it's just my graphics card (Intel 3000 integrated).
All in all, I think this a great game. I myself play mainly solo, but this is certainly best played coopertatively. Worth the money. 9/10.

Van Helsing has his work cut out for him. For all the monsters he's slain, the looming spectres of Diablo, Torchlight, and Path of Exile cast an imposing shadow over the rugged hero. To set itself apart, this modern dungeon crawler has to find a way to truly sink its claws into the player beyond the usual loot'n'grind. The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing II, the second part of a planned trilogy by Neocore Games, succeeds remarkably in carving out its own identity, but at the potentially steep price of polish and balance.
The visuals and soundwork of Van Helsing II are competent, with a few bright spots. The graphics are technically solid, with varied color palettes that provide atmosphere as Van Helsing explores underground caverns, snowy forests, and laboratories full of disgusting experiments. The voice acting is serviceable and the musical score is suitably sweeping and epic, with a few catchy songs, but nothing new for the genre.
A common criticism of dungeon crawlers is that they start off slowly, and Van Helsing II does everything in its power to defy that stereotype. Players of the first Van Helsing will be pleased to find that they can import their character into the sequel, with all of their skills and equipment intact. Newcomers are able to create a character of one of the three classes -- the iconic Hunter, the mage-like Thaumaturge, and the tech-oriented Arcane Mechanic -- that begins at level 30, giving them a set of gear and plenty of skillpoints to spend. Those who find the game's in-depth, granular skill system a little too daunting can start at level 1 without any major handicaps, giving them more time to learn the deep mechanics of the game.
These mechanics are much of what set Van Helsing II apart, but also where this ambitious title first stumbles. The game is unapologetically complex; each class has four primary stats and access to dozens of abilities, all of which can be upgraded up to ten times. There are plenty of ways to construct a character, but unfortunately, not all of them are viable. Many skills pale in comparison to others within the same tree, and it's easy to find yourself with a build that simply doesn't work. Luckily, a respecialization option is both cheap and accessible, making it easy enough to experiment until a satisfactory skillset is found.
There is a lot of content in Van Helsing II, and most of it is implemented well. The usual prerequisites for the genre are in place: a lengthy storyline with plenty of side quests, co-operative multiplayer modes for both the campaign and individual scenarios, and a 'Battle Royal' PvP offering for those wishing to test their mettle against other players. What sets Van Helsing II apart, however, is its dedication to making its single-player experience memorable to the player. Throughout the fifteen to twenty hour campaign, Van Helsing spends plenty of time fighting his way through hordes of enemies, but he also fortifies and defends his Secret Lair (yes, that's what it's called in the game).
The Lair -- the heart of the Resistance movement of which Van Helsing is a critical agent-- is unlocked early in the game, and houses merchants, alchemists, and enchanters capable of modifying and upgrading Van Helsing's equipment. It also grants access to a couple of additional minigames that add much-needed variety to the usual action-adventure fare, including tower defense-style sequences in which Van Helsing must prevent the antagonist's forces from discovering the Resistance's hideout, and a menu-driven command center where the player can build a small army and send them on missions that grant equipment and monetary rewards. Though fairly basic in design, both of these distractions are plenty of fun, and I often found myself teleporting back to base to play with them between campaign missions.
The combat itself doesn't introduce any shocking twists, but it stands proudly with the best in the genre. With eight of his abilities available on the skill bar at any given time, Van Helsing is never lacking for tools with which to fight, and a generous cooldown on potions and plenty of ways to restore health and mana keep things moving at a tight pace. Enemy variety is impressive, with three or four new kinds of foes introduced in each zone, and multiple difficulty levels allow players to suit the challenge to their preferences. The biggest problem that I found was that pure melee characters never really come into their own. Every class has ranged options (and, in fact, the Hunter is the only one that can melee at all), but for all the depth of the skill trees, there's no real way to avoid the punishment that comes from being surrounded by the game's dangerous enemies. It's certainly possible to succeed with a melee-oriented build, it just never reaches the destructive potential of the other choices.
It's a good thing, too, because the plot of the campaign doesn't stand too well on its own. The storyline is basic, but decent enough: after slaying the evil Professor Fulmigati in the first game, Van Helsing finds that the exiled General Harker has returned to take his place. Setting out on a mission to overthrow the new government, the monster hunter is joined once again by the ghost Katarina, who has to be one of the most obnoxious characters I've ever encountered in a videogame. A constant presence at Van Helsing's side, she's an endless font of overwrought sarcasm and grating negativity; in the first two hours of the game alone, she voices her distrust of a new character seven times. I counted. As if to make things worse, she and Van Helsing trade uninspired quips with depressing regularity; the tone of the story, which can get fairly dark at times, is completely offset by the constant, heavy-handed references to games, books, and movies the pair make. Occasionally, a gem of a line can inspire a smile, but for the most part, it's a distracting and desperate attempt at humor.
Further putting a dent in things are the technical issues. The game isn't particularly buggy, at least not in the conventional sense, but it found some creative ways to hamper my enjoyment. Load times are far too long for a game of this size, and even inexplicably happen just from alt-tabbing. The camera is solid enough during gameplay, but in cutscenes, it has a habit of taking nauseating jaunts for seemingly no reason. Oftentimes, a scene with two characters simply standing on either side of a table discussing tactics is lent a surreal air as the perspective randomly changes.
Despite these problems, it's hard not to recommend Van Helsing II. Most of the issues it has feel like the inevitable consequences of making an ambitious game on a small budget, and I have to applaud Neocore Games for packing so much content into their latest endeavor.

Pros:
::: Graphics are great, supporting D3D11 features, characters and environments really come to life...
::: Sound and foley is emersive
::: Story line is well written as well, involving a separate campaign storyline for each species including characters from the movies (Lance Henrikson's Weyland)
::: Multiplayer is fun and can be an exceptional experience depending upon which characters you play as
::: Multiplayer maps created from the movie locations, including the Nostromo, Fury 161 and Hadley's Hope (the colony on LV-426)
::: Separate mouse sensitivity for both the X and Y axis
::: Close combat system for those "close encounters"
::: Skirmish (both single and multiplayer) mode that pits a species against an onslaught of the Aliens which can be quite fun
::: The menus have a real Weyland-Yutani feel to them and are very well done
Cons:
::: Multiplayer can be a little bit unbalanced depending upon which species you play
::: Some of the situations in the marine campaign can be very challenging comparitively to the other species

Do I recommend this game to friends?
Short answer; yes. It's a very nice change of pace from what's out on the market right now.
Long answer; yes, but I feel that a lot of things could have been approached differently to provide a much better experience to the user.
I have a big problem with the way the driving mechanics work in this game. My average "clean drive" time ended up always being around 15 seconds because I would overestimate how my car drifts, or how the turning in my vehicle works. The camera was also VERY difficult to work with while driving.
The controls all together were very clunky. Right click is my action button? M to cycle through objectives instead of bringing up the map? The controls as a whole just felt very out-of-place. I was thinking console port, but that may not actually be the case.
The game actually ran very well, albeit with a few exceptions. I have an nVidia card in my system (as do a lot of you), but this game was optimized for AMD cards. With all graphical options turned up, I got 60 FPS in certain parts, but it mainly dropped to 20-30 FPS while driving during the day. There is a FIX for this, however; setting the "Enable Quality Anti-Aliasing" and "Screen Space Ambient Occlusion" options both to "Normal" in the Advanced Settings menu will GREATLY help out. Setting those options to "Normal" from their maximum settings took my card (GTX 770) from struggling to get 60 FPS and running up to 80 degrees Celcius, to maintaining 60 FPS at all times and barely cracking 55 degrees Celcius.
So if you have an nVidia card, heed this warning; KEEP "ENABLE QUALITY ANTI-ALIASING" AND "SCREEN SPACE AMBIENT OCCLUSION" TO NORMAL.
Fighting is a very fun part of the game, and collecting Sifu's statues is highly recommended. After you collect all 12 (technically 11, one is already there), you will be an unstoppable♥♥♥♥♥kicker on par with Jackie Chan or Bruce Lee.
Gunplay is not Sleeping Dogs's strong suit, as "guns are a rarity in Hong Kong" and the developers wanted to focus more on hand-to-hand combat. However, shootouts are intense, and you get to play around with some deadly tools of the trade at certain points in the game's storyline.
All in all, I did like the game. I would recommend this to friends who are looking for a good open world game with a rich environment to explore and a fun, action-filled fighting mechanic to put the hurting down on bad guys who need a good kick in the teeth. Story is not Sleeping Dogs's strong point, but there were moments where the game had me going, "Oh you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you're going to pay for that." or feeling sad for a character.
I would gladly give this game an 8 on a 10-point scale. The clunky-feeling controls, buggy-at-times cutscenes, and TERRIBLE (that's right, terrible) driving mechanics could make a case to bring that down to a 7, but if you can get past those problems, this is definitely an 8/10 game. If it's on sale, you're disrespecting yourself for not even considering picking it up.

This is a beautifully rendered game, with a good and growing cast of characters, the majority of which have interesting movesets. The action feels weighty, which is a good thing--attacks that hit sound and look important, and blocks sound like they have weight as well. The game gives a solidity to fighting that many other games in the genre lack. There are issues with character balance, but eventually they will be sorted out or the game will fail.
The offline modes are hugely lacking. Head-to-head is the only mode that is any good, and it loads remarkably slowly, even on a solid state drive. You can get around this if you do enough searching, but Capcom should have realized early on that people like to spend their time playing the game rather than watching a load screen that has been deliberately slowed down (See Update; this is no longer the case.) The AI is either incredibly weak or godlike, there is no in-between. This is most visible on Survival mode, where between one round and the next the computer will go from not blocking overheads to blocking EVERY mix-up.
The online mode is where I have the most complaint, which is too bad because that's also the mode that I (and I would guess many others) want to play most often.
Lag. Huge, unpredictable, awful amounts of lag. I play a lot of Dota2, and I experience game-affecting lag there about once every 50 games. Even in that situation there is the opportunity to pause and give the offender/server time to catch up. Here, though, there is no such opportunity--and unless it's hitting both players at once the player who is not affected is going to have a massive advantage. It's so bad and so frequent that when I win I don't even feel good about it because I don't know if my opponent was lagging out or not. When I lose due to lag I feel as though I've been robbed. Essentially, the lag makes it so that each game feels inconsequential and unfun.
Capcom has made a game that is not fun at this point unless you can play offline (most of my playtime is offline). Their bottom line should suffer. Do not purchase this game.
UPDATE: The patches applied in the spring of 2017 have improved my online experience significantly, though there are still many occasions where lag affects my play. On- and offIine load times have been improved significantly. I am upgrading my rating of this game to a CAUTIOUS buy. If you like 2D fighting games and good graphics (rather than anime), SFV is now where it's at.

Starbound is now out and I have completed the story so I can give a proper review of it. I will be covering what I consider to be the main aspects of the game.
Story-8/10
The story of the game is that a big monster blew up Earth and you escaped so you now have to find 6 artifacts that open the gate to the monster. (You find this out in the first hour.) The story has that Bethesda feel, where the game is like "oh no, this thing happened and you have to do something!," but you can just ignore it and do your own thing. The story is an interesting aspect, and actually takes you to the different planet types so you have time to upgrade your armor and weapons. I think that story isn't completely necessary, but it works well with the concepts already established.
Combat-9/10
The sword-and-gunplay is fun and focuses on dodging enemies. Your "Matter Manipulator," which is a building tool, can be useful for creating cover and such, but some enemies can go through walls. Each 2-handed weapon has a special ability, like grenade launchers and flashlights on guns or spin slashes and warp slashes on swords. There is a variety of weapons, allowing a ton of different playstyles. The bosses in the game are also very well designed and offer up a challenge when you first fight them. These bosses are located in developer-designed dungeons that have many secrets located in them. The combat never gets stale and fights are always interesting in one way or another.
Exploration-5/10
This aspect isn't the best part of the game. You usually see the same biomes and monsters over and over and while some monsters are randomly generated, by the end of the story you've seen all of the environments in the game already. It is fun at the start of the game, but it quickly gets stale and boring. Randomly generated dungeons are cool, but you often find the same style of dungeon as well.
Building-9/10
Building in the game is surprisingly deep and interesting. The colony system offers up an interesting thing to do after the story. The foreground and background building is similar to Terraria, but the game actually offers a good reason to build decorated houses so different tenants move in. This is one of my favorite parts of the game and I have spent hours searching for the right materials for my houses, which leads me to find new things in the game as well.
Soundtrack-10/10
The soundtrack in this game is beautiful and the main theme is one of the most memorable tracks that I have ever heard in games. I cannot stress enough that the soundtrack is worth buying and it adds a layer of charm to the game that I rarely see.
Overall-8/10
Starbound is not the best game ever made, but it definitely has a large amount of content that makes the game interesting for hours. It seems that this game was a board that ideas were thrown at, and some of those ideas stuck and mixed really well. The game also has a kind of charm to it that you don't see in AAA games. Starbound has been a great project to watch as it grew from alpha to beta, and finally to 1.0. Starbound has, in fact, left orbit and hopefully will go interstellar in further updates.

I bought this game on a whim back in early stages after a friend told me about it and it has been so much fun.
While the development process has been arguably slow, the developers have consistently improved the game with every big update. Every time another large update releases, it's like another new adventure almost worthy of another character. The full 1.0 version of the game releases in about a week from this post and it's
to keep me occupied.
The game may seem like a sci-fi terraria clone on the surface, but the game offers it's content differently. While Starbound is still essentially a sandbox game in terms of mechanics, updates have given the game more RPG-style gameplay elements such as hub worlds, side quests, and steady progression in the form of ship, tool, and augment upgrades.
The main quest missions are unlocked by creating gear out of higher tier materials, and main quests unlock higher tier crafting stations and planet types. In my opinion, this really weaves the whole sandbox-RPG thing together quite smoothly and forces players to participate in both genres, which is really important to note. The main missions are interesting, albeit unrelated dungeons that usually have some nice loot at the end.
The lore of the game is decently extensive, but it requires a bit of digging. The most interesting lore stories (lories?) are discovered by finding codices, which randomly spawn in containers and tell some pretty intriguing tales that usually follow specific characters.
The different races each have their own basic backstories and relations to one another as well as posessing an apparent style and demeanor for each:
By far the biggest problem with this game is performance. A lot of players, even on high-end PCs, will be experiencing highly fluctuating framerates depending on the environment in-game. While Starbound's community is welcoming, it's extremely difficult to find non-laggy servers to play on w/ friends. This makes LAN play the best multiplayer option, which is impractical, to say the least. This can drive some players away from this fantastic game, and I really hope the devs are working dilligently for a solution.

Before I get into the review, let me first make a brief statement: This game is short. Relatively speaking, of course.
As you can see, my playtime is only 4 hours and I was able to completely obtain every achievement and see the true ending in that time. While this may not be a long game, the story and gameplay are phenomenal. The action combat feels very satisfying; when you counter a projectile and dish out punishment or finish off a weakened enemy then use the generated crystals to perform a screen-wide blast attack you will feel like a real master. However, combat can quickly devolve into a dodge-fest and you will sometimes find yourself in a position where multiple things will attack you and it will be hard to escape. But, I guess this just adds to the combat.
The story itself is presented in a clever way as well. You have a Narrator, who guides you through the game. You can follow his arrows...or take your own path. Usually branching off into secret areas or interesting dialogue, even some of the game's endings.
However, some of these endings are key to understanding the true story of the game. They are presented as cryptic dialogue that is typed on a computer monitor. If you were to piece all of these text windows together you would get the real backstory of the game and it's world (thank you screenshot button).
All in all, a very fun and exciting experience for it's (moderately) cheap price AND a free soundtrack of the awesome music.
My Final Score: 4.8/5

So let me start this review off by saying that first and foremostly, I LOVE this game, and have been playing since beta.
It pains me to say that in it's current state i cannot reccomend starbound to new players.
While the game itself has a lot of thought put into it, and it's come very far since it's inception, right now it's a buggy mess. I've been replaying starbound's most recent patch, and it's apparent to me that none of the pressing issues from last patch have been addressed. myself and a large portion of the player base, including the people i play with, have incredible amounts of latency, even on singleplayer due to a handling issue with internal servers. The people i play with have a variety of different systems, some AMD, some intel, some low end, some high end. all have the same latency. This can range from irritating to unplayable at times. recently i've come across a debilitating  ( 2,000,000k!) memory leak when playing through the erchius horror mission that i've been able to replicate every subsequent run, provided i get hit by a SINGLE laser.  These are not new bugs. these are the same bugs that the starbound community have been talking about for at least a year now, and we haven't been formally adressed by chucklefish outside maybe one vague tweet or two.
overall, i think this game is a LOT of fun! when it works, it's breathtaking. i've been here from the start, and i hope to be here if these issues blow over, but for right now, i'm not going to play anymore, and i cannot, in good consience reccomend this game to anyone.

Another attempt as something cool, unique, and diverse, yet becomes a mess - I believe it was level 5 second half, where you're flying down through traffic. Here, you're expected to gauge the speed of the whole line of traffic you're moving into as well as the next. You're also expected to figure out which of the cars will actually get in your way. Yet another really cool concept that just becomes a memory game. To further their desire to make you replay ad nasuem to get more play time out of the game overall, there are sudden and surprising jumps in puzzles. What I mean by this is you're going through your block puzzle, reach a blinding white light and are immediately subjected to a new block where 3/4 are closed and only one path is open. Maybe this isn't what I thought I was getting into, but I don't love it. Overall I just feel "meh" about it. Bastion is a great game. I'll admit it's not for everyone. You'll either love it or you wont really feel too strongly about it.
But when you love it, the love is strong.
Bastion is a game with beautiful art, gameplay that is much deeper than it first appears to be, and the best narrator since morgan freeman. The narration is really the tipping point for most people. If you love the narration, you'll most likely love the game. but some people find the narration annoying (I really dont understand how) and if you dont like the narrator, I could see how the game would get old pretty fast. But honestly, the quality of his voice, and how well the reactionary narration is done, I dont see why you wouldnt love it.
The music is also incredible. Bastion has won a few awards for its soundtrack, and it really is spectacular. You will love Zia the moment you meet her.
The gameplay is also deep. At first it will seem like any other action rpg, but it's honestly one of the most deeply customizable games Ive played since Bravely Default. There are a total of 11 weapons that all have their own unique functions. The hammer is a powerful shortrange melee weapon, the bow is a powerful long range weapon with various added effects, the machete is a very fast melee weapon that doesnt do as much damage for more roa, etc. Everything has its unique strengths. You get to choose two, so you can really choose what style fits you best.
On top of that every weapon has 5 trade off style upgrades to apply at the forge, each one asking you to choose between something like extra damage or higher critical chance, or maybe add an AOE quality to your rifles bullets, inexchange for giving up its ability to pierce armor. So that give another huge level of depth to the combat. Even if two players both love using the breakers bow, for instance, one might love it for focusing on high damage and stunning enemies, while the other might equip it for fast draw and DOT. each weapon has multiple strateies depending on the player and no one will be the best for every situation. You get to experiment.
Then there's the spirits. These are just your run of the mill group of passive buffs you can choose from. but they add alot of depth because of how deep the weapon system is. For example, the leechade restores part of your health for every bit of damage you deal. This works incredibly well if you have DOT equipped to the bow, allowing you to run around sticking people with poison arrows that basically supply you with a steady stream of health.
To even FURTHER increase the customization is the idols. You invoke idols at the shrine which basically act as passive buffs for all enemies. One might make enemies move and attack alot faster, one makes enemies all drop grenades as they die, one makes enemies randomly turn intangible and invincible for a short period of time. With all ten idols activated, the game doesnt play around. Its seriously tough. But that difficulty is yours to set.
Bastion's story isnt anything super special, but i personally fell in love with it. Its one of those games where finishing it just makes you start new game plus as soon as you can.
Definitely worth a try, especially if its on sale.

The Alien campaign relies on stealth and deceit to overcome your enemies, you might get a little dizzy, because you get to move around freely on walls and ceilings.
The Predator campaign is a combination of the two, you use stealth a lot, but you can also shoot your enemies with your shoulder thingy, your spear or your flying disk thing.

I spent actual money to buy DLC for this game, that is how much I love it.
The story takes place in Hong Kong and it's your undercover cop who infiltrates a triad well known to him, and the love for his friends and his duty will be in conflict throughout the game. What elevates this story from the rest is the excellent voice acting and compelling characters that are both believeable and relateable.
The game is an open-world third-person action shooter. The combat is an improved version of the Batman: Arkham games formula, with the introduction of combos, melee weapons (like cleavers, batons and even fish!!), environmental executions and guns that, at first, feel kind of awkward, but I got used to them.
There is a lot of side activities in the world to complete: doing favors to increase fame, take part in illegal races, wipe out hidden triad gangs and sing karaoke.
The graphics are impressive, and the game really shines at night time. The city does feel alive, even though most of the pedestrians are walking or talking on a phone. The soundtrack is full of both chinese and english songs, with plenty of radio stations to choose from.
However, this game is far from perfect: the biggest complaint I have is that, when you have beaten all the story missions and favours and races, there is nothing to do. Trying to get involved in car chases with the police doesn't help since you will have upgrades that reduce heat faster than ever.
Overall, it's a fun game to spend time to, with a compelling story and many side activities, even though at the end there is nothing else to do.
SCORE: 89/100

Slave Zero is a great 3rd person action game, where you play as a giant mech with big guns and nonstop action!
The Good:
* This game has a great feeling of being a giant as you go through the streets murdering innocent people, crushing cars, and destroying buildings, in which you can pick up something's(mostly just cars, people, and metal rods from destroyed buildings) and throw them around.
* This game's combat is basically like all classic shooters back in the 90's, like Quake and Unreal Tournament. "Fast paced action shooting"
* The weapons in this game is somewhat good, they have a great kickass sound to them, especially the railgun, it feels so good and satisfying to here upon firing this weapon.
* There are great variety of enemies in different levels. There is some big enemies and small enemies, each that might do medium or heavy damage to you, depending on what weapon they have.
* The soundtrack is ok in my opinion, it's just basically futuristic music.
The Bad:
* The crosshair doesn't match up with your firing, it is slightly to the left of the crosshair and sense this is an old game it has to run through a program called nGlide. This program gives you more resolution options but no widescreen support. Normally the game is supposed to run in 640x480 resolution so the crosshair would match up with your firing, but this Steam Port forces the game to run in 1280x1024, which moves the crosshair slightly to the left. This may not be a big problem if this doesn't bother you, but it's just kinda annoying bug with in the game.
* The game's difficulty can be annoying at some parts. Were sometimes they would throw a ton of heavy damage enemies at you, which makes the game much harder in most levels. (This may not bother you so this one gets a past, "for now".)
* The game is basically unfinishable, where you encounter these enemies that are called Slave Units, which if you try to kill them the game would crash, you can just run pass them but at one point of the game you have to kill these two Slave Units that's at the end of a bridge in order to pass, but you can't because the game would crash every time you try to do so, which makes the game unfinishable. The Disc Version doesn't have this bug, but the Steam Port Version does for some reason, so get the disc lol! But now for some reason I did get pass this part and idk how I did it. so yey?
* Picking up objects is ok and all like what I said before, but this throwing objects feature isn't really a big part of the gameplay and later on in the game, this feature of throwing objects around is just there for show and slows down the pacing of the gameplay in my opinion. But you can use this in combat if you really want too.
* In conclusion of this review, Slave Zero is a great action game to play, if you can ignore most of the issues with this Steam Port, then you might have a good time playing this game. But if you can ever find the Disc Version of this game, then you can download this patch and would have a great time with this game.

: Before I start with my review, you need to know that my first (and favorite) Burnout game was BURNOUT LEGENDS (PSP). As such, my review is somewhat biased, so take it with a grain of salt. First and foremost, lots of DLC can't be accessed through normal means, pain in the a**. It prompts you to create an EA account too. For the gameplay it's "okay" at best. When you play Burnout Legends, it's HIGHSPEED, HIGH CARNAGE physics ALL THE TIME. I came to burnout for more unrealistic, over-the-top roadrage accidents-inducing madness. It's not there in Paradise. Plus in Legends you keep unlocking stuff every 2 gold medals (or something close) so there is always something to look up to. Here (paradise) it's extremely LONG AND TEDIOUS to unlock anything. Events are scattered on the map and you are forced to do the same over and over to "rank up" your liscense and get more cars (+/- 75 total). Oh btw, civilian's vehicules are 3x more tanky than yours, so don't even THINK of purposedly ramming into the crowd like a bloodthirsty psychopath, game punishes you for it. Your crashes and takedown would be a lot more satisfying if you could see your/their car flying at 3-4 times the power it currently is. Major let down. Also, no driver is in the car, none. If you crash while riding a bike, the game gets a quick black screen and respawn you on the middle of the road as if nothing happened. Very dissapointed as I expected a game with far more than this. Wish the speed would be higher than this too, felt underwhelming (I even used a save file to get every cars so that I could pick the fastest one after 1h of boring gameplay). There is no way I can recommend this game.

Ages ago when i first started playing this game (Before being available on steam) the game was being worked on with plenty of user based equipment and reccomendations, they added plenty of fun things and there was not so much of a paywall as there is now. These days i still think the game is fun, worth a go if its your first time trying it as it has plenty to do once you begin, but other than those first few days i would not reccomend this game.
Once you hit end-game tier, it becomes so repetitive and boring. You can still build stuff in club worlds but if you're not into that it just becomes one big grind. You can pay to get items faster or more desireable items which seems to be the only way to get them unless you spend an ungodly amount of time playing/have played since the very early days and have mad bank stashed. The devs of this game seem to have added a lot of unnecessary MMO features to the game which in my opinion takes away from the charm the game once had and adds a layer of difficulty, especially given there are little tutorials on how some of these features work (Good luck if you're returning to the game after a few months/years).
Levelling up many of the classes available is a breeze, does not take a lot of time and once thats finished you are not left with a lot more to do other than grind dungeons or materials. Sure there are daily log in rewards and everything is achieveable for free, but if you are looking for a bit of casual fun and dont have the time to spend playing i personally would give the game a miss overall.
Pro:
Charming graphics
Fun for the first few days (Especially if you are a new player)
Community does not seem to have died out, bound to be some people to play with
Unique MMO style game
Crafting and Building can be entertaining
Great for collectors (lots of things in the game to collect and add to your inventory of mounts/etc)
Interesting classes/items
Everything is available without paying, player trading etc.
Cons:
Depending on where you live, can be very laggy
Quickly run out of things to do, not a lot of variety in dungeons after a while
Repetitive
A paywall for good stuff does exist, and you can hit it very quickly. Can be very hard to get rare items otherwise
If you dont enjoy the building aspect, it becomes a large material grind/farm style game with not much else to it
Hard to re-learn many new features (Can be hard to learn as a beginner too, despite the basics)
If you dont want to spend money, everything that is free is quite hard to obtain/sometimes impossible.
Overall i would not reccomend the game unless you are looking for a quick new experience with a playerbase that has not died yet. I know that steam says i have not clocked much time, but i have played a lot and did not base this view off of nostalgia.

I never owned Dreamcast but if I had this game as a kid I would have loved it. Slave Zero is a fast-paced shooter with a lot of giant robots, awesome music, and big bosses.  The game itself is pretty simple but fun to play. Unfortunately, after battling game crashes and performance issues for about 90 minutes I am ready to give up on this port.
The game comes with a tool that can set almost any resolution if your computer can support it. It does make the game look a lot better. However, it seems like messing with resolution will potentially cause more crashes at least on my system.
For some reason, I get a lot of lag when there is too much on the screen but I am pretty sure it is not my computer . Restarting game tends to temporarily fix it so it must be a glitch. Some features like local multiplayer may need a workaround. I did not have a problem starting the game but apparently, it is a common issue depending on operating system.
Gameplay has a very arcade feel to it. This game does not mess around and throws you right into the none-stop action. Killing enemies and raining chaos feels very satisfying but I was a little disappointed by the lack of moves. You pretty much limited to flipping couple weapon and using rockets. You can also stamp but I never got anything accomplished with it. The character has a big arm with claws so it is kind of unfortunate that you do not get to melee as well.
There is no RPG element management and perhaps the game is better without it .
The uptempo music and cyberpunk settings give the game nice atmosphere. Although the voice acting is not great the plot motivates you to keep going and see how many overpowered robots you can trash.
I would give the game 7/10 but Steam port is less than serviceable. It depends on the system and how compatible your computer is with older games. Maybe it works better for some but not for me. I only wish I had the pleasure to play this game in a better state.

It looks like a racing game, and it definitely is, but exploration takes a solid front seat in this game. This is a third-person cyberpunk mecha action shooter. A love letter to video games, drenched in early/mid 90's anime, dystopian sci-fi, and Hong Kong cinema. Tight controls and exhaustive, yet refined shooting gameplay that will test your skills as a gamer. It's a straight-forward affair of action punctuated by intense boss battles that will leave you hungry for more. Seriously. Slave Zero was birthed from PC gaming's golden age when development was largely driven by passion instead of dollar signs. Infrogrames NA was a small, underpaid, and overworked team of veteran developers that clearly had a love for this type of schlocky science fiction. If you are willing to do a little bit of Googling to get the game up and runnning on a modern OS (there are many guides and resources to help you do this!), Slave Zero is an absolute treat of late 90's game design. Treat yourself!
Side note: I recommend skipping the widescreen patches and opting instead to play the game in its native 4:3 aspect ratio at an internal (defailt) resolution of 640x480 and let nGlide render it at 1080. The widescreen patches, though handy and well-crafted don't use the game's Steam-provided exe, thus you cannot track your game time but also there is something oddly satisfying experiencing the software rendered closer to its native state as the creator's intended.
