This is a wonderful game which unfortunately falls behind due several flaws inside and outside the game itself. The game suffers many technical issues going from not detecting controllers, slowdown issues which can glitch you out the map unless you restart the game (This is specially prevalent in the sewer levels), and freezing in the late stages. The full package makes it the usual port that came out and never got fixed except by fans.
If you can pass through all those problems, Slave Zero is a wonderful game that aged in a few departments. Is fast paced and with short yet several levels to beat. The controls are very simple regardless of playing with a controller or a keyboard, becoming casual friendly. And although graphically old since you're mostly seeing robots is barely an issue except of some cutscenes with humans. However, Slave Zero can become very stiff when comes to ammo, and for a very action packed game seems like shooting ememies punishes you in late game. You can end in several scenarios having a hard time against basic enemies or even bosses just for not having ammo enough of certain weapons, and with upgrades spending even more ammunition along your health not recovering after each stage it can become a big challenge even in the easiest mode for the wrong reasons.
In resume, Slave Zero has two big negatives: Buggy programming and obsolete ammo system. However, if you can find ways to solve its bugs while also become a master managing your weapons, it becomes a wonderful game. Otherwise, the first half of the game is still a fun time to give it a try.

Starbound is now out and I have completed the story so I can give a proper review of it. I will be covering what I consider to be the main aspects of the game.
Story-8/10
The story of the game is that a big monster blew up Earth and you escaped so you now have to find 6 artifacts that open the gate to the monster. (You find this out in the first hour.) The story has that Bethesda feel, where the game is like "oh no, this thing happened and you have to do something!," but you can just ignore it and do your own thing. The story is an interesting aspect, and actually takes you to the different planet types so you have time to upgrade your armor and weapons. I think that story isn't completely necessary, but it works well with the concepts already established.
Combat-9/10
The sword-and-gunplay is fun and focuses on dodging enemies. Your "Matter Manipulator," which is a building tool, can be useful for creating cover and such, but some enemies can go through walls. Each 2-handed weapon has a special ability, like grenade launchers and flashlights on guns or spin slashes and warp slashes on swords. There is a variety of weapons, allowing a ton of different playstyles. The bosses in the game are also very well designed and offer up a challenge when you first fight them. These bosses are located in developer-designed dungeons that have many secrets located in them. The combat never gets stale and fights are always interesting in one way or another.
Exploration-5/10
This aspect isn't the best part of the game. You usually see the same biomes and monsters over and over and while some monsters are randomly generated, by the end of the story you've seen all of the environments in the game already. It is fun at the start of the game, but it quickly gets stale and boring. Randomly generated dungeons are cool, but you often find the same style of dungeon as well.
Building-9/10
Building in the game is surprisingly deep and interesting. The colony system offers up an interesting thing to do after the story. The foreground and background building is similar to Terraria, but the game actually offers a good reason to build decorated houses so different tenants move in. This is one of my favorite parts of the game and I have spent hours searching for the right materials for my houses, which leads me to find new things in the game as well.
Soundtrack-10/10
The soundtrack in this game is beautiful and the main theme is one of the most memorable tracks that I have ever heard in games. I cannot stress enough that the soundtrack is worth buying and it adds a layer of charm to the game that I rarely see.
Overall-8/10
Starbound is not the best game ever made, but it definitely has a large amount of content that makes the game interesting for hours. It seems that this game was a board that ideas were thrown at, and some of those ideas stuck and mixed really well. The game also has a kind of charm to it that you don't see in AAA games. Starbound has been a great project to watch as it grew from alpha to beta, and finally to 1.0. Starbound has, in fact, left orbit and hopefully will go interstellar in further updates.
This game is still very fun and enchanting despite all the updates. Much rather play it on Xbox 360 without the updates but still a great experience. 9.5/10

I spent actual money to buy DLC for this game, that is how much I love it.
The story takes place in Hong Kong and it's your undercover cop who infiltrates a triad well known to him, and the love for his friends and his duty will be in conflict throughout the game. What elevates this story from the rest is the excellent voice acting and compelling characters that are both believeable and relateable.
The game is an open-world third-person action shooter. The combat is an improved version of the Batman: Arkham games formula, with the introduction of combos, melee weapons (like cleavers, batons and even fish!!), environmental executions and guns that, at first, feel kind of awkward, but I got used to them.
There is a lot of side activities in the world to complete: doing favors to increase fame, take part in illegal races, wipe out hidden triad gangs and sing karaoke.
The graphics are impressive, and the game really shines at night time. The city does feel alive, even though most of the pedestrians are walking or talking on a phone. The soundtrack is full of both chinese and english songs, with plenty of radio stations to choose from.
However, this game is far from perfect: the biggest complaint I have is that, when you have beaten all the story missions and favours and races, there is nothing to do. Trying to get involved in car chases with the police doesn't help since you will have upgrades that reduce heat faster than ever.
Overall, it's a fun game to spend time to, with a compelling story and many side activities, even though at the end there is nothing else to do.

Doom is upon us. And apparently it’s a good thing. I am yet to play it, but to keep in the mood I’ve decided to get a refresh on the previous game in the franchise, Doom 3. That, in turn, meant that the BFG edition is the way to go – I still have the original discs I’ve pre-ordered back in 2004, but I wanted to give the re-release a chance to prove to me that this is the definitive version of Doom 3 available. And here I am, writing this review after blazing through the entirety of the main campaign and both expansions on Veteran, with a generally positive opinion to give.
Right off the bat – Doom 3 is not exactly what most were expecting. It’s slower than the original two games, darker, focusing on few strong enemies rather than “horde” approach, and trying to introduce more storytelling and horror elements while keeping to what is essentially a classic, old-school FPS foundation. Not everyone liked it that way back during original release, and it is pretty much the same now, however to say that it is a bad game would be an injustice. Indeed, Doom 3 is very competent shooter with solid weapon designs and mechanics and decent enemy variation (if only their AI would be more competent…). I would not consider it overly challenging, at least on any difficulty setting lower than Nightmare – during my most recent playthrough I have died only two times in total, and I am not a very skilled FPS player.
Leaving the ports of Doom 1 and 2 included in this release aside for a moment, the newly added “Lost Mission” is certainly a high point of the package in my opinion. The short campaign is more combat-oriented than the main game’s single-player mode, and despite being very linear in nature provides good amounts of level variation and dials back on jumpscares and darkness. Conversely – “Resurrection of Evil”, the original add-on made by Nerve Software is the weakest of all the campaigns, trying on the story aspect a little bit too hard and sometimes feeling like it’s cobbled together from bits and pieces that didn’t make it into the final Doom 3 (funnily enough “Lost Mission” escapes that feeling despite actually being made from rejected level segments). Again, I can’t speak about multiplayer because I was never really interested in it, though the way I hear it it’s not very active, to say the least.
Visually – let’s be honest here – it really isn’t apparent that this game is almost 12 years old. Artwork still shines, with sharp textures and details accentuated by contrasting lighting, and shadow volumes produce an overall appearance that is very unique in the world of gaming to this day – I don’t think that up until idTech6 we had any other game engine that took an entirely dynamic approach to lighting. Character models are lacking up close, but aside from cutscenes you won’t get to look at them much from short distance. Sound design is solid, though most if not all samples are the same as in the original, thus retaining a somewhat lower than expected quality. I’ve not run into any bugs that would hinder my progress through the game, although once my controls have reset themselves to default with no apparent reason, and I encountered one enemy spawning waist-down in the floor in RoE, but that’s it.
I can’t say that BFG edition is “brighter” or “easier” than the original. I’ve seen reviews on Steam claiming that BFG “ruined the game” by making ammo more plentiful and lighting more intense, but can’t confirm that really. I have compared a few locations with the original running side-by-side and while lighting is a bit more contrasting in certain places, it’s nothing really all that apparent. And the armor-mounted flashlight is something the game needed from the get-go in my opinion. I also can’t say I’ve noticed there being more ammunition available throughout the games. Overall – if you’re someone who never played Doom 3, or played only the Xbox port for example, then BFG is a solid purchase in my eyes, especially on a sale. You get a solid shooter with quite a lot of character, and while some elements may not be so enjoyable (“Resurrection of Evil” in particular), overall the package holds up.
You also get ports of Ultimate Doom and Doom II with No Rest for the Living add-on – they are very ‘vanilla’, so to speak, but in and of themselves they are both fantastic games and an important piece of gaming history. It would be a shame not to at least get it on a sale.
(There are some screenshots on my profile of the game running unmodded – look at them if you want to have a general impression on the game looks.)

Having just recently taken a chance on this game despite some of the negativity, I am quite pleased.  I decided to give it a try as it has by far the largest active online population of any fighter on PC and on top of that has crossplatform with Playstation players.
I saw endless complaints of the game not having versus CPU or training modes, well it does now.  From my understanding the game was basically released as defacto early access and many of the early negative reviews stem from that.
Down to what matters - the game is fun.  The fighting feels more measured and less spastic than I remember SFIV being.  The V-moves are a nice addition and the charging of your V bar & EX bar all feel like they flow nicely with the gameplay and the moves.  The reversals are an interesting touch that remind me a bit of the combo breakers from Mortal Kombat.  All in all it feels like the skill floor is much lower than SFIV yet the ceiling is just as high.  Compared to SFIV the frame windows on moves are much more generous.  The end result is a more fun game where newbies can at least feel like they are doing something, but masters still reign.
The graphics are quite pleasing - things seem a bit more toned down and less over the top than SFIV as well.  Characters are more proportional feeling, animations seems to be a little more realistic and less cartoony, particle effects a bit less dramatic, the textures seem to be less high contrast and bright to give it a little less comic book feel.  This all may or may not be to your preferences.
The most important part of course is the online multiplayer.  After several hours of trying out casual matches I was satisfied with the system.  I played about 30 matches - only 2 had any lag and they were with people from another continent - and only 1 bad connection drop during handshake.  The rest of the matches played out as nicely as a local game.  I imagine I could tweak the settings to not have to deal with international players at the cost of potentially longer match wait times.  At default settings I was only waiting about 1-2 minutes on average for an opponent, not bad at all.  I noticed at least half of my opponents were Playstation players so the crossplatform gameplay is definitely helping out the population size.
So in the end I think it is a great fighting game.  I've been playing SF & other fighting games since the golden era of the arcades - now that they are pretty much extinct around me this is the next best thing.
EDIT 1 - So I've continued to play this game online for about a month now, matches are quick to find and only rarely laggy.  I still stand by my earlier assessment - this is a good fighting game for PC.

This is quite a nice game. It's terrible as a sequel to the original Doom games, but it -is- a good game! Please, let me explain. The original Doom and it's sequel, Doom II, are fast-paced shooters in which you strafe about wildly shooting at hordes of demons on a Mars base, with no real plot to speak of, and it's just raw FUN. Doom 3, on the other hand, really tries to...honestly, I'm not sure what the heck they were trying to do. Here's what we got, though: a shooter that cares more about jump scares and being dark; effectively a survival horror game in space with tons of health and ammo drops.
The game itself is good, despite being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ization of the original games' tone, because the shooting and some of the creepy tone work well enough to make for an exciting time. That said, the shadows really, really, really suck. They're graphically nice, but this game is DARK. On the bright side (see what I did there?), Doom 3 BFG Edition fixes one very big problem: the flashlight. In the original release of Doom 3, the flashlight is held in your hand like a gun...meaning for you to see well, you can't have a gun out. Guess what's in the dark? That's right, bunches of enemies. This is one of the biggest gripes people had with the game, myself included. People modded in a flashlight that worked while you had your gun out, and in Doom 3 BFG Edition, the developers have automatically made the flashlight/gun combo an automatic feature! The game is now eerily dark, but you do have a flashlight to make it "not suck" to use the technical jargon.
To quickly interject, the fact that Doom 3 BFG Edition includes Doom (1993) and Doom II is wonderful! I played through both and had a magnificent time. The games were just as good now as when I played them way back when, and I'm very rarely a nostalgia type of gamer. That said, people who didn't play them originally might not like them!
If you want a game that feels like the original two Doom games, Doom 3 is not it. Enemies are reskinned to the point that most of them look only barely like their original forms, with the exception of a few like the Revenant and Mancubus. Running/shooting is much slower-paced than the original games as well. If you go in wanting the "Doom" experience, you will not get it at all. However, this really was an enjoyable game for me. I definitely recommend it if you'd like a dark sci-fi/horror shooter and aren't expecting "Doom" from it.

It is hard for me to write about this game since I undoubtedly view it through nostalgia goggles, but I believe it still holds up quite well today. The game is very fun to play with great controls, a great variety of enemies, and beautifully designed futuristic areas.

I've noticed a lot of people comment on the story. The story is there purely for story's sake — it is the glue that ties all the missions together. Don't expect any intricate character development, or any sort of interaction among the characters whatsoever. Most of the exposition is presented at the very start of the game in the opening sequence and that's that. The hero of the game, Ch'an, doesn't communicate much with the rest of the cast - he merely executes Guardians' (the rebels) orders. This can be either good or bad depending on your preferences. If you're the kind of player that likes to assume the role of the protagonist - then this is the game for you - but on the other hand, it is hard to have some clear idea in terms of what Ch'an is like. The intro states that "Ch'an must permanently merge with the Slave," meaning he's doomed to stay inside the robot for all eternity Neon Genesis Evangelion style. It would be interesting to read about his backstory, but the game is so fast paced and focused on bringing down Sovkhan that there's never really any time to address that. It is only near the end of the game, during the final mission, when Sovkhan reveals (spoiler alert!) that he murdered Ch'an's father which possibly explains Ch'an's decision to permanently merge with the robot. Unfortunately, since the plot never really makes you feel invested in the characters, this grand revelation felt very underwhelming and anticlimatic. But you don't play Slave Zero for the story! It is the fast-paced action packed gameplay, one of a kind atmosphere, amazingly intricate boss fights, and great atmospheric music that makes the game what it is. All in all, It is a great cyberpunk adventure that is still very fun to play now.
Having said all that, I was quite disappointed by the Steam re-release. I must say I'm quite fortunate that I still own the original copy of the game because I've encountered a few issues with this version. First of all, a lot of functions don't work/are disabled for some reason. You can't turn on bump mapping, true color textures, the multiplayer doesn't work. I've also encountered numerous crashes throughout the game. I think Slave Zero deserved a much better treatment than this, but at least the game isn't completely forgotten and is actually available here. I'm still giving it a great score because I don't want to tarnish its image here, and because in spite of the butchered re-release — it's still a kickass 90s classic!

Even if you get the game running, you will still need to perform a few extra steps to get Direct3D support and Multiplayer up and running and you may become too exhausted to properly enjoy the game. In this case, I would Suggest one of two things:
1. If you want to skip the setup BS, and have a properly working version out of the box, Get the Version available on Good Old Games (GOG). Aside from the fact that it's DRM-free, It also comes installed prepped and ready for modern gaming action!
2. If you don't mind some DIY to get the game to work, wait for this game to go on sale (I got it for $1.94 CAD [75% off], but ultimatley returned it due to the effort required to get it running not being worth it).
Regardless of the way you get the game, you may just like the interesting mix of action, atmosphere, and fun that only a game from the late 90's can provide.

Overly simplistic QTE gameplay, 4 buttons, push the one that lights up, that's all the gameplay there is. The enviroment the gameplay is implemented in is what makes it interesting, because each succesful button hit equals to kicking a bad guy's♥♥♥♥♥in a cool way, or missing it causes them to hit you. The rythim changes based on the music playing, much like a Audiosurft of Guitar Hero titles work, and they have some really action pumping great stuff there to give your heart the bump-bump tempo while awesome (cartoonish) action is played on the screen.
However, being a low budget game, sadly it has some downsides. The campign is exactly the same levels twice from half of it, with the same music, just with a different character (=skin, nothing else), and I think I counted 2 max 3 bands playing all the music in the game, and that's a huge negative for a game that is based on music. The lacking variety of artists really makes the whole thing feel like you are listening to Blue Stahli's Kill Me Every Time, and then 20 times the slightly different remixes.
It's a pick it up once or twice and be done with it game, definitly worth picking up on a nice discount if you are looking for a relaxing yet at the same time adrenaline pumping simple game.
It's subpar compared to the other bigger titles that made this genre popular (Audisurf, whatever guitar controller game you can think of etc.), mostly due to the very-very low number of artists and tracks (24) that mostly all sound the same with one or two exceptionally good one. You can add your own songs however, but I got bored of it before I reached that point that I'd want to try. Doesn't means it's bad, it's just this long these type of games last for me.

Quick Summary – This is a direct continuation of the first game The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing (VH1), beginning immediately after the final boss battle of that game.  The gameplay is identical, and in fact you can import your VH1 character to play through the VH2 campaign. The same three character classes appear: Hunter, Thaumaturge, and Arcane Mechanic (the second 2 were DLC characters in VH1) and the character skills are basically the same up until around level 30. In VH2 there are more “end game” things to keep you playing after you’ve beaten the main story. If you enjoyed part 1 you should like part 2.
You play the title character Van Helsing, a monster hunter attempting to clear the cursed land of Borgova with your trusty (and sassy) ghost sidekick Lady Katarina. In the first game, you defeated an evil mad scientist and his clockwork monster army, but now a new hardass general has arrived to take up the evil reins. Once again, you and Katarina must work with the Borgova Resistance to destroy an army of abominations as well as face the various wild creatures of this tainted country.
The Van Helsing games are steampunk third person isometric hack / slash RPGs like the Diablo or Torchlight series, so if you’ve played one of those you should have a good idea what you’re in for (swords, sorcery, loot). Gameplay-wise your pal Katarina is like a mercenary in Diablo 2 or a pet in Torchlight. She has her own equipment/stats/skill trees though, so you’ll need to spend some time making sure her build is up to par. As you’d expect, there is an extensive randomized “loot” system where you can find magical/rare/epic equipment to outfit your hero (a lot of equipment is class specific but you can twink items between characters using a shared stash). If you search online you can hear rumors of “godlike” gear, though it’s so rare that 99% of players will probably never even see one.
In the first Van Helsing, the game was mostly over after you beat the last boss. The level cap was 30, and there wasn’t much to do after you finish except run “scenarios” which were hard bonus maps with upgraded loot. Bear in mind that in both Van Helsing games the main campaign maps are not randomized. Once you’ve played through the game you’ll know exactly where everything is. In VH2, there is a “veteran mode” which is a higher level playthrough of the same campaign (like True Vault Hunter in Borderlands, or Nightmare mode in Diablo) where the enemies are stronger and the loot is noticeably better. Additionally, the level cap is 60 and there are a bunch of new skills that weren’t in the first game. Oddly enough, you can adjust the game difficulty in veteran mode without penalty (higher level but easy mode!).
Pros:
+Nice graphics for an indie game. The story is decent (though it feels kind of short) and there are a huge number of pop culture references and pokes at other games. This is a logical continuation of the fun Van Helsing 1 game, leading directly to the third game and forming a cohesive storyline.
+There is a co-op multiplayer option though I wasn’t able to find anyone to play with immediately. Campaigns are always more fun when you go through them with a partner.
+If you liked the tower defense mission in the first game, there are a lot more in Van Helsing 2 though they’re basically optional quests. So if you hate Tower Defense just delegate the missions to your underlings.
Cons:
-My research shows a lot of complaints about the cooperative campaign “breaking” and stranding people’s characters unable to advance. I’ve experienced it once myself despite reports that the bug has been fixed. Multiplayer search is also pretty dead, you need to set up games with your friends and not rely on built in matchmaking. Alas a bunch of the Steam achievements are for multiplayer PVP 
-There is not all that much info online about this game. It’s hard to find comprehensive help on achievements / skill builds, probably due to the game’s indie nature. The game’s developer has basically moved on to Van Helsing 3 and won’t be doing much more for this game. You can play through the entire game and not understand a number of the “important” aspects. For example I didn’t even know what runecrafting / essences / trophies were or how they worked without researching online. They’re not even mentioned in the game’s tutorials.
-One thing to note if you’re importing a character from Van Helsing 1. Your Katarina will be significantly weaker than if you play through VH2 on normal and then switch to Veteran mode. This may be a bug, but it’s really annoying if you’re trying to build an “ultimate character.”
Overall I enjoyed this game, and if you liked Diablo, Torchlight, or Path of Exile you probably will too. Don’t expect it to be “better” than the first game though, it’s more like a second episode in the campaign. Going through single player takes about 12 hours to finish on normal mode, but if you don’t play through veteran mode (up to level 60), you’ll be missing out on literally half the skills/equipment.
10/10, would rebuild again.

I'm writing the Review at 120 hours logged.
After the playing the game for so long and completing it twice on the trot siding with 2 different endings, I feel i can write something accurate for someone to decide wether to buy this game or not.
Graphics,
Lets get this out of the way because the answer is obvious, the game is beautiful. From toxic radiated sunsets to high physcopathic full moons, there is always a point to just stop, look and spam that screenshot button. 9/10
Story Mode,
The story mode is a similar format to the previous Fallouts, but with a few more added choices. Your a father who has lost your son in the apocolyptic world. Yes, you are asked to save all of Boston in some fanatic stylish way, but you never lose sight of the goal, finding and saving your son. The voice over character you play as is great! But sometimes the speeches can drag on slightly, but no problems, there are sarcastic options for you move on quickly. So with lots of guns, explosions and a fantastic epic twist that i was not expecting 7/10.
Side questing,
No need to spend too much time on this. Plenty of side quests and lots to keep you busy, even from the start at level 1. Some of them can get a bit repetitive and boring, but others have fantastic characters and great humour. But what gives this such a good rating, is your followers have stories to tell and quests of there own to unlock extra perks. A simple but good 8/10.
Free-Roaming/Building Stuff
This is obviously the main part of the game, wandering off and doing random stuff. Like i said plenty of side quests and lots of stuff to modify such as guns, armour and power armour. Hell you can even dress up your dog! And the fun doesn't stop there, the Building Mode is one for the record. You can build all sorts of stuff! Here's a few i have done. Dog Mansion, Dance club, sniper towers, deathclaw arenas and torture sheds! The fun is endless! Just make sure you pick up all that junk. I suppose the only down side is once you have explored every single location (WHICH I STILL HAVE NOT DONE) the aim of the game could become slightly pointless, but by then you will be ready to start a new adventure and finish it all over again in a new unique way! 8/10
Conclusion,
Yes the game is buggy, yes it has annoying glitches and can crash a couple of times when you start a random war at Diamond City. But after 120 hours, i still feel like playing this game all over again just to see whatelse i can do to my characters outcome and what the game has to offer. A Solid overall  8/10 (No, New Vegas is not better.

The very first game I bought on Steam during a sale (I just dropped by randomly and decided it's too good to pass up, lol!), and I gotta say it's quite good - definitely a must-have if you like third person shooter / sandbox games.
Sleeping Dogs is quite similar in GTA with its freeroam and side tasks aside from the Main Story. The biggest difference however, you don't get to use firearms too often - instead, Martial Arts plays a major in this game. Wei Shen, your character, is so skillful that he can stand up against 10+ enemies with just his fist, and he is able to intercept any attacks as long as you time your QTE just right - nothing more satisfying than beating up tons of big guys and walk away unscathed! The game centers around Triad activities, so you still get to shoot bad guys every once in a while, especially during later missions.
One good thing about Sleeping Dogs, it's very easy to play. You get all kind of help text and instructions, and the Tutorial missions are easy to follow up. Even if you are new to TPS / Sandbox, you can master the control in no more than a few hours. The map is quite big with collectibles and side stuff you can complete during freeroam / after finishing the story, and bonuses are nice too (both for easing gameplay and/or improving Shen's abilities). Even at Medium setting (I have x86 system so it don't have 4 GB RAMs), the graphics still look good and smooth - most of the time I have stable 45 FPS, which is lowered down to 30 when too much stuff show up. This is where Sleeping Dogs is WAY better than Saint Row The Third.
However, there are still a few problems here and there - first, partial custom control is annoying. I mainly play on Arrow section, but for Sleeping Dogs I am forced to use WSAD because arrow keys and enter/backspace can't be reassigned - the devs are too lazy to make graphics for all keyboard layout so they just go cheap and force you to use their setting - not cool. Another thing, Sleeping Dogs is scripted to force you to play missions in a linear way - you can't bring weapons in because the story says so, and you can't keep weapons after the mission because the story says so. This makes me regret ever purchasing all those DLCs, only to find their perks CANNOT be used in the main story mission to make it more fun. Last but not least, some interaction are so fussy at time - walking up to a food vendor and press button only to find Wei does nothing yet they still talk like the deal is done, very funny.
But overall, Sleeping Dogs is a good game - Activision really did a stupid move by throwing it away, otherwise I believe it'd did its original job; rebooting True Crime series. That, for us, is also a good thing because now Sleeping Dogs has become its own series, with Triad War sequence announced already. I'll definitely give it a try once it hits Steam, assuming my PC can still handle it.

My opinion of this game changes based on the people I fight and I’m sure that's how it is for most people but they just don't know it...
Let me explain...
I’ve played fighting games my whole life, I played the first mortal kombats, MK9, SF Alpha series, SF 3rd Strike, USF4 and now I’m tackling Street fighter 5. Now I’m not about to claim to be the best player in the world because I know I’m nowhere close. But I do have a decent understanding of street fighter in general and how it relates to other fighters out there.
The game plays and looks absolutely beautiful. It's easy to learn and has a difficult learning curve, the supers are great and there's a great character roster with lots of different archetypes. However, that's where the problem lies.
Every character in the game has his strengths and weaknesses and now that the game has been out for a while players have learned their preferred characters strengths and exploited them. Unfortunately, the term "strengths" isn't things like damage output or how much life they have or their mobility. It's the game breaking cheese and tools that were implemented to help the new players out.
There are only a few characters that have this so called "strength"
Ryu: After Season 2, He was nerfed in my opinion but that doesn't excuse the fact that he's still a Shotokan character. Ryu is good at everything but excels at nothing. Players have seen this so they move on the other way to get wins: Throws... Capcom implemented some kind of system that allows players to constantly throw loop their opponents. All it takes is for them to corner their opponent, get a hard knockdown, mash out a couple of jabs and kicks and then throw again, unless your opponent sees it coming, you can get at least 3-4 throws in a row depending on the intelligence of your opponent. By that time, your opponent’s health just dropped about 50%
Ken: Probably my most hated character to play against. Ken’s heavy tatsu has been changed that it arcs and travels almost the entire screen, this allows an instant “get-in” and now has no need for “footsies.” That tatsu also beats out most normals, anti-airs, and special moves. Most kens will follow that up with an instant DP or…you guessed it, a throw loop…when he’s not spamming tatsus…Ken will probably do the same combo, ……………every time…………when he gets a chance its always: target combo -> DP or Tatsu. This simple combo does a surprisingly decent amount of damage and is very easy to set up. Ken also has a bigger potential for throw loops then Ryu does. Not to mention being another Shotokan character so anyone can pick him up day 1 and be an instant pro.
Chun Li: Am I about to get “poked” to death?? Chun Li, the queen of footsies. Chun Li’s standing Heavy punch reaches a long♥♥♥♥♥distance and does good damage. Ok then, doesn’t sound too bad, ill just jump over it right? Wrong…Chun Li’s Anti-Air AND amazing setup option is…wait for it…STANDING LIGHT KICK…and that is bulls h i t enough for anyone…
Cammy: Another victim of using the same combo over and over until they win: Crouching Medium punch -> Crouching Medium punch -> Spiral Arrow…until they win.
Bison: You would think that without Bison’s trademark Psycho Crusher, He wouldn’t be as bad a threat. And you’re right to a degree. Bison isn’t too bad until you get an opponent who overly relies on throws…because of how amazing his dash is. Bison’s dash is him warping in and out of space to get in close. If timed right, it can go through projectiles. When, he’s playing footsies out of nowhere he’ll disappear and reappear in front of you and grab your unprepared a$$...when he activates his V-Trigger. It’ll get even worse because now, his dash is faster, AND it can now teleport him BEHIND YOU. Making grabs that much easier. Also, the Devil’s Reverse, or for those who don’t play Bison…the “Goddamn Flying hand attack thing that keeps hitting me” is powered up as well. In V-trigger, Ex Devils Reverse will make bison disappear in the air for a solid half second and then he will reappear on whichever side your opponent decides. This means that blocking it is a complete 50/50 guessing game on which side to block.
Laura: You probably won’t be able to tell a pro Laura player from a blind guy feeling for his keys on his fight stick. Almost every normal that Laura has is safe on block or a frame trap. Mix that up with a command throw or two and you have yourself a win.
Balrog: Every time you face Balrog you’re going to be saying one of the following sentences every time
1.	Wait wasn’t I just winning that round??
2.	Holy Sh it look at that damage
3.	Damnit he has V-Trigger
4.	It took me 60 seconds to do all that damage to him and he just evened up the round in 5.
Balrogs damage output especially in v-trigger is something out of science fiction. He can link every special move together in an obscurely long combo that will in some cases do almost 65%-70% damage and your be there thinking WTF.
Guile: Spamming sonic booms until your opponent jumps. Then just do flash kick. Win. And for some reason, Guile players have this uncanny ability to hit a throw on you every time they go for one. I don’t know what it is but for some reason they always get it on you.
You get the idea. What makes this so irritating is that you would never see players using this kind of play when playing Ultra Street Fighter 4 would you? Throw loops, immense damage combos, Cheese. However, I have accepted the fact that this isn’t USF4 and I’m glad that it isn’t, if it was I wouldn’t buy it because I already own USF4 and I don’t want a clone of a game I already have.
This game does bring a few POSITIVES to the series that yours truly is happy to see:
Easier combos: 1 frame links in USF4 were ridiculous to execute especially in laggy online matches. SF5 widened that gap to 5 frame links.
New ranking system: I still don’t understand how the battle points and Player points in USF4 work. SF5 ranked system is easy to understand.
Easy troubleshooting: when watching your replays, it’s easy to see where you went wrong and what to fix in your own game play style. Learning matchups and taking advantage of it in an online match is very satisfying.
Overall: The game brings a lot to the table winning feels satisfying and it looks amazing. I would give this game a thumbs down if I had just gotten off a loss from a Ken or a Balrog and I would probably be complaining about NEEDED BALANCE PATCHES AND DEVS DON’T LISTEN and blah blah blah…but when I have a clear head and think about the experience as a whole that I have with the game, it’s definitely a positive one.

Street Fighter V is the latest installment in Crapcom's ever increasing attempt at running this franchise into the ground, made even more prevalent by the game's abysmal sales figures. Everything was wrong with this game from the word go. First off, you have no arcade mode. Yes, I'm not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you here folks, in a FIGHTING game you do not have one of the most basic and fundamental modes that should be put into any fighting game without even thinking twice. Next, you have the very ugly and unappealing cell shaded art style that makes half of the characters look like utter buffoons, especially Ken who looks as if he had cheese wiz sprayed on top of his skull. Then you have the omnipresent modern gaming feature that goes by the dreaded name Microtransactions. Now granted, you can unlock characters in this game by getting "fight money" but the game is so lacking in content that it would seem far too repetitive to even bother trying to get as much virtual currency to unlock said characters, not to mention all of the other superficial, empty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like alternative costumes that need to be purchased. Story mode? Don't even get me started. Charging full price for this game should be considered a crime against humanity. Not only does it not have an arcade mode, it's "story" is just a bunch of lazy, haphazard hand drawn cutscenes featuring no animation and each character is given about maybe 2 or 3 fights tops. I completed it in a single sitting. So, what else did this $60 game have to offer seeing as how two major elements of a fighting game lacked any content whatsoever? Online mode, of course. But oh wait, even THAT has issues as well. You spend more time battling the God awful server connections than actual opponents. I can't even count on both fingers and toes the amount of times the game disconnected me in the middle of the match, not to mention the completely obnoxious ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that infest this game's community to begin with. So what you are left with is a game that is completely and utterly empty and devoid of any real, substantive content, a bi-product of modern gaming that is slowly driving the industry further and further down the rabbit hole of million dollar budgets, no actual content, and pay to win mentalities. Fran Bow is one of the best horror games I've ever played. And it's a point & click game, no less!
Let's see...in this game you play as a young girl (Fran Bow); her parents have been brutaly murdered and she's in a mental hospital. From there, she escapes in the hope to find her cat and return home to her aunt. You do this in classic adventure style of clicking on everything in the hope to either get it into your inventory and/or finding combinations that progress the storyline. So far, things are standard. Pretty soon, however, you'll get a bottle with 'medicine' that lets you see a different other reality (a horrible overlay...kind of like in 'song of Saya'). As such, the levels play out in a Zelda-like combination of 2 different worlds that sort of interact with each other. It's really a stroke of genius here: it strongly highlights the setting (the other insane inhabitants are being plagued by strange shadows), it sets the character (which of what Fran sees is reality?) and allows for some decent puzzle aspects (some objects need to be picked up in the 'other' reality).
The quality of puzzles is pretty decent. Most of them make sense, used items don't linger in your inventory and chapters aren't too long, so the frustration levels don't get too high. That isn't to say the game is easy: you will get stuck at times. It's a part of these kind of games, so it's not like you can hold it against it.
But while the first 3-4 hours were absolutely wonderful, I have to say that I was more eager to find out about the story than to solve more puzzles. It has seven chapters (five, of which 2 are split into two), and I kind of feel that the main story drags on a bit too long. This may be just me, though.
Probably also worth mentioning is that there are a handful of mini-games within the game. While they break the otherwise rather monotone gameplay, they feel more like tech demo's than part of the experience (yes, you can make a block puzzle game with cogs in them. Congratulations...but why is it there in the first place?). Again: it's hard to complain about getting more game, but the game is certainly long enough without it.
Still...to get back to my opening: if you are into psychological horror (meaning: horror without jumpscares) and point & click games, you will like this game. It's a bit harder to recommend to someone who is just into one of these genres...you'll have to figure that out for yourself, I guess. For me, however, it's an easy thumbs up. :-)

Truly, a wonderful driving game for hardcore and casual gamers. With a plethora of things to do to keep playing, it doesn't try to overwhelm the player. By not constantly bugging the player to do the thing, it doesn't feel forced and more like a sandbox game than most other open-world games where the player can do whatever. Take Skyrim, for example. It constantly has reminders on the hud about the current objective. In Paradise, the only notifications on objective are during events. Even during events, the only thing the player is supposed to do is complete the objective. How the objective is completed is completely up to the player. The player can use any car in any event. n fortunately, some DLC is unavailable and the rest is confusing as to how to use it. Luckily, there is a mod to help! The Vanity Pack, which adds in Big Surf Island, the BSI vehicles, and the cop cars. It also adds in some non-DLC extras, such as car switching outside junkyards (which is a bit difficult to use. but can be used for more customization than the stock game), a speedometer, a rev counter, a more precise nitrous counter, custom vehicles, traffic vehicles, and the ability to use any car (as long as it's not being selected from the junkyerd). Fran Bow is a modern oldschool point and click adventure delving into the mind of a young, possibly disturbed, almost eleven year old girl. After a traumatic event she ends up in a mental ward from which she needs to escape. Because her cat and only friend in the world is calling her and a dark, ruthless shadow is haunting her. Things get macabre and imaginative very soon and reality splits up in layers (sort of) to.. well, to be able to proceed I guess. But I won't spoil anything about that. This is really a game you experience best for yourself, not reading any reviews before you start. Nevertheless, here are some global non-spoilerish pointers:
* Graphics are a bit low res, but well drawn. It still looked good fullscreen on my 27" monitor, although not that sharp. I  like the way spirits and creatures are depicted throughout the game and the backgrounds look colorful and imaginative.
* Characters in this game are interesting and have interesting, well thought out things to say. There's not a lot of choice in dialogue, but it's fun to hear what they have to say. While all sorts of gruesome scenes are on display Fran -almost- always keeps a certain whimsical approach to them. She's not scared easily and she's more curious than Mr Midnight or any other cat I know. This game will keep you up thinking and certainly has some cold surprises up its sleave, but it's also warmhearted and friendly at times.
* There isn't a lot going on in terms of music and sounds. There's no voice acting, but that's perfectly fine for a point and click adventure of this style imho. Most of the games impact is experienced through its graphics, the locations and its storyline.
* Most of the puzzles are easily solved, a couple of them take some more thinking. But there always are clues around, keep your eyes open and your short term memory functional. Click on everything and everyone. I enjoyed all of them, really.
All in all this game is highly recommendable. It's not a very long game but it's definitely one that will stick in your mind for a while. There are some achievements you probably won't find the first time around that might want to make you revisit the game at some time. Get it while it's on sale or for the full price. It's worth it!

Now that I've had a month or two away from this game, and having played the other game by Supergiant, Transistor, I think I am able to give this a proper review.
For those who love story that burrows deep into the gameplay, are able to sit on the edge of their seat and continue playing while the story unravels, and those who don't mind picking up story elements while fighting monsters, you'll absolutely LOVE Bastion. This is something that Supergiant does really well. They start you off with a minimal piece of story, enough to set you up as to generally where you are and what you're doing, and then you just PLAY. the rest of the bits? You figure them out along the way.
Bastion is a BEAUTIFUL pseudo-3D sort of beat-em-up, as there's a lot of button mashing (or mouse button mashing) involved in progressing through levels. However the way you decide to beat-em-up is totally up to you. Kid, the character you play as, will slowly unlock new weapons for you to try during levels to see if you like them. You get to take two weapons with you on your quest, usually one melee and one ranged. You also pick on ability tied to either of the weapons you chose. My personal preference is the Cael Hammer and Fang Repeater with Spiral Shot, or whatever that ability is called, but that's just my opinion. You can play through the game multiple times and try different weapon combinations.
There aren't many choices overall in the game, but there are two choices right at the end that are pretty big. One is a morality choice... if a person betrays you utterly and takes your ability to set the world right away, and you later find them dying in the middle of a courtyard, abandoned by his comrades, do you keep your amazing two-handed weapon and leave him to die or take him back with you to heal him? The other took me two hours to figure out. I wrote down the pros and cons of each, what we knew for sure and what the characters told us would happen but we couldn't be 100% sure about. I won't spoil that choice for you. Just know you'll probably be itching to play it again so you can see what happens with the other choice.
Bastion is an amazing game that I'd reccomend to almost anyone. If you play this, play the other Supergiant game, Transistor, afterward. It's great to see the similarities in how Supergiant designs games in such a beautiful way. The style is completely different too, with Bastion going down the Hi-Fantasy route whereas Transistor is more of a high-tech urban fantasy, more sci-fi. Definitely give this game a try!

It is always difficult to review a port which has a lot of chance to go awry during the course of its development. This new Mortal Kombat game enjoyed being one of those games that only got ported to PC years after its release. The advantage we'd relate to the passing of time would be a decent number of people willing to play the game. It has an assumption of having either a growing or just a steady community. Also, PC gamers are well aware of how low the chances are for a fighting game's release these days. And of course late release would make us believe the game is a decent, well-optimised port without any major glitches, issues.
So, before continuing reading my review I would like to say it straightforward: multiplayer with this game is just awful. I have been unable to find a host or host a game ever since I purchased it. In fact, a friend on Steam asked me to play together so that he could unlock a missing achievement. Neither hosting nor joining worked. I am amazed how bad a multiplayer code a game can have today!
Putting the horrendous multiplayer experience aside this game is very good! Although its story mode offers a store-telling which tries to tell you this is a sequel to previous Mortal Kombat games it is, essentially, a remake. Gameplay is similar to that of Street Fighter 4: no real 3D just 3D graphics. The game looks good, plays smoothly and offers a long single player experience.
Similarly to Street Fighter 4 the new MK offers ultra moves. Basically, a meter gets charged along the way and once it is fully charged we can unleash an X-ray move. This consists of a series of attacks and if the enemy is successfully hit each time the amount of damage they receive is just tremendous. As the game is very gory the X-ray utilises a lot of close-up shots focusing on the internal organs and bone structure of the enemy: we can see how these are crushed during the move.
The game's PC version (Komplete Edition) comes with some extra characters (such as Freddy from the Nightmare of the Elm Street horror franchise) that were only available via various DLCs on console. This is nice but expected 2 years after the console release date. The game has many unlockables, achievements and a Challenge Tower to further look for challenges in case you want to thrive.
Overall, this is  a good game and recommended but in case there are friends who only want to purchase it so that they can play with one another do bear in mind you'Ll have a tough time with multiplayer.

Cannot recommend to the masses out there, as this game caters almost 100% to a small niche of pro players and super tryhards. Everyone else is meant to just buy and watch the pros play or limit themselves to play with friends.
The game lacks a LOT of commodities for casual players that even SF4 and it's versions had, like arcade mode and more relaxed ways to play casually. The menu is a convulted mess with no visual appeal and no clear direction. You will wonder where to go most of the time. Plus updates are not handled by Steam but by the game itself. So you have to run the game to load an update that even disables your controls most of the time, requiring an atl+f4 to solve.
SFV wants to bombard you with pro play on every corner and it's main mode of play is pro ranked matching and international competitions. So non hard core players still interested in this game are better off just watching the professional league on Twich, unless they can do with half a game (which is way overpriced to what it offers) and being forever rank 876654th and without enough game money for even a single color swap. Same with story mode. Save your cash and just watch it on Youtube until Capcom decides to ask for a take down of those.
Visually, this game doesn't offer much of an upgrade to SF4, and anyway this kind of visual style doesn't really fit the classic Street Fighter feel (neither did SF4 but guess people are getting used to it). It's also rather demanding, putting yet another limitation onto most casual players out there who usually have less powerful computers. Sounds are music are the standard fare that were more or less impressive back in 2005.
Characters were also modified for the worst in my opinion, most of them with extremely ridiculous outfits (which anyway would take weeks for any casual to unlock). And some classics people were asking for are here but seriously impaired. Where the hell are Karin's counter moves and why all of her not removed interesting moves are gated behind a timer bar? All in all, the characters feel weaker than in past games, and some were given extremely unimaginative new specials and supers. As I said, some character specials are gated behind a timer bar called V trigger or whatever, basically gimping your character even further than ever before. In some cases, Like Karin as I said, all of her old SFA arsenal of rush attacks is gated behind this system, and her counters are completely gone. All of them.
My last complain has to do with the cosmetic side of things. You can grind in game money to unlock colors and outfits mostly through losing against the pros in ranked because of screw you. And since you will be earning little, the grind may be long. You can fork real cash for some stuff, but it's also over priced. And lastly, you will never get all outfits and variants  because Capcom decided to lock some to certain pro players, winners of events. So this game is also not for the completionist out there.
All in all, this game should be skipped if you are a casual fighting game fan. There's much better alternatives elsewhere. If you like 2D fighters with 3D visuals, get Ultimate Street Fighter 4 instead. If you want 2D, most Arc Sys games like Guilty gear and Blaz Blue offer a much better alternative and much more bang for your money.

Game Review:
Ah, yes Doom 3: BFG Edition a poor man's Doom game remastered. Kinda slow, kind boring. It also had reloading, it's basically anything the new (better) Doom is not.
Atmosphere:
At some points the darkness of the levels is somewhat creepy but at other times it's just too dark.
Music:
Other than the main theme it's very unmemorable, literally so unmemorable I might have to see if Doom 3 actually had more music.
Story:
It's at the same time basic and stupidly overdone. Mars blahblahblah, Demons blahblahblah. It's basic in Demons on Mars aspect, but everything feels unnecessary and weigh down the game as a result.
Weapons:
All the favorites like the Chainsaw, Shotgun, and The BFG 900 are here. Most of them play alright (The gun combat is a bit weak and slow like this whole game).
Graphics:
They're only alright as nothing looks absolutely fantastic in this game, other than the lighting effects. That makes sense as the engine this is on is made for lighting.
Overall:
Overall, despite my gripes I still have to recommend Doom 3 as it is good despite its problems. When you get to later in the game the FPS aspect picks up a little bit and the game gets better. The game wanted to have a good story like Half-Life (Also a better game) and play like a good FPS. It did nothing great and everything OK. You are going to want to get BFG Editon specifically, but get it on sale, or if you find it cheap.
Final Verdict:
Wait for a Sale.

Bought the game on release and played for nearly a year now (200+ hours, Gold rank). I was fine with lackluster single-player/offline content because I love fighting games and am happy with multiplayer.
After too many laggy matches, I've pretty much given up on the game because it's clear it's not improving. It takes a whole minute to find a match, only a third of those found matches actually connect, about a fifth of those never start, and half the started matches are unplayable because of lag. Sometimes it's apparent both players are lagging so we just sit around waiting for conditions to improve (rarely happens) and sometimes it's clearly asynchronous (esp. against PS4 players) because I have multiple-second input delay while they're just practicing combos on me. I just sit there waiting for the match to end because any attempt to play in the lag would just frustrate me. I live in an area with plenty of players, have good internet, and it boggles me when the online experience is this bad.
This was in December, when the game has been out for 10 months. It was in beta for almost half a year before that and yet the online experience has only gotten worse. I won't even get started on the single player content...
The mechanics are fun and I really hoped the game would be a success so it's honestly depressing that I can't recommend the game. The only reasons I can find to play this game again are if a friend came over, I found it at an arcade (no arcade version...), or I went to locals. I bought the game because they promised a good online experience though, so I feel misled as they clearly care more about the offline pro scene than the rest of their fan base.

Slave Zero is repetitive, but fun third person shooter with a lot of things to blow up. It have some flaws, but it doesn't overstay it's welcome.
It's 500 years in to the future. The game takes place in the capital of asian conglomerates – Megacity S1-9. The sovereign khan has taken it over with the help of giant biomechanical robots (or Slaves as they are called in the game). But not all hope is lost. An underground resistance known as The Guardians, stole one of those Slaves and now it's up to you the merge body and mind with him and save everyone, The story is paper thin. I wish for more detailed story, not just good vs evil, but this is what you get. This is a game focused entirely on action, not story and the action is good.
The released date is 1999, so of course the graphics are dated, but still it's nice too look at.
The gameplay is pretty straight forward. You are in control of giant mech that can stomp, throw cars or pieces of buildings or shoot his three weapons or weapon types to be precise – rockets, energy and balistic.  Through the whole game you will find upgrades for them. Some are hidden, but it's not necessery to search for them. Soon or later you will get them. All you need to do is run, gun, strafe and not get shot. All three weapon types are useful and their ammo runs fast, so you will be changing between them constantly. But don't worry, there is plenty health and ammo packs lying around. When enemy gets closer you can punch him to death. Also you can do this to buildings.
Level design is good. Most of the times you will be high in the sky, between bulding, killing innocent civilians from time to time, but there are also sewer, inside bases and so on. This is corridor shooter, so no exploration is required. Later levels can give you some headache. Seem like the city was build so high and you can fall to your doom. This is especially annoying, when some of the enemies can knock back you with a single shot and there is no way of defending againts that. I recommend saving often on those levels.
There is one impressive thing for a such an old game – level destruction. Bridges, buildings and so on. A lot of things in the envoirment can be demolish and with the combination of constantly attacking enemies, things can get hectic, but in a fun way.
Enemies are diverse. In the beginning helicopters, tanks and small mechs will attack you. Later you will face tougher with shields, armed with lazer that do tons of damage, flying robots, small annoying and fast, that attach to you and leach your life and so on.
I always look for a good boss battle. Here some are good, some are bad and some even annoying. Some are just not that fun, than others. A static giant mother ship pumping out mechs is not that interesting. But there some quite enjoyble to fight, like one that have really powerful weapons and you have constantly to go up, because there is rasing acid below you. It was quite tense battle. The final boss was disappointment to me. Just shoot, hide, get more ammo, rinse and repeat. The fight was not very creative. You have to hide from him because he do insane amount of damage.
Beside the bosses I have few other issies with the game. There is only three weapons. You can argue that, because with the upgrades the numbers is getting higher, but they are just that upgrades, not new weapons, although they fire differently. Let me have them all, it is action game, where you can blow stuff, you need more weapon variety. My next problem is the repetition. As much as I like the game, I can say that after the first hour you will see everything that the game offers, but still I find the gameplay enjoyable. It took me 5 h to beat it and as I said in the beginning it doesn't overstay it's welcome. Another small problem is that I took my a while to make the game run in 1080 p, but this maybe entirely my fault.
The sound design is great, especially the music. Fantastic fast techno tracks, fitting extremely well with the sci-fi setting and the action on screen. Sound fx are also great. Stomping and walking felt like i'm really in control of giant mech. And you can also distinct all weapons.
At the end of the day the question I have to answer is – does the game hold up? Yeah, to some degree. Graphics don't, but the gameplay is solid and controls are tight.  In the end I can say, I had fun playin the game. Non stop action, where you can blow a lot of things and you play as a giant mech. Whats not to like? I was impressed mostly with the level destruction. The game came out 16 years ago and I think it is an accomplishment. It have some problems, but nothing to make me quit. Slave Zero probably won't be stuck for a long in my mind. It doesn't have the nostalgia for me like Max Payne for example, but I still recommend it.

By some miracle, I've avoided most of the bugs people are complaining about.  I also don't care about multiplayer elements, so that's not a detraction either.
The story seems like a pretty good idea hastily thrown together.  Many plot elements have zero explanation, they simply "are".  There are loads of pop-culture references which border on fourth-wall breaking, and spice things up a little.  At many points there are FMV cutscenes between you and Katarina where you must make decisions on some things, such as doing something a certain way, removing armor from an altar, searching a body, etc.  These decisions never have a bearing on larger things, but it adds some appreciated variety.  The dialogue has hit or miss voice acting, but the game is definitely interesting enough.
I made four different characters and constantly ran into the same problem over and over again.  Everything chugs along peachy-keen until you get your face put in the dirt and you're f***** right in the a**.  This is not a particular boss fight (as far as I had gotten anyway), it's always some innocuous-seeming group of mobs - too many mobs - that do it.
The problem with this formula is that this is a completely linear ARPG.  There is no grinding for gear, or experience, or stats.  Reskilling is easy enough if you haven't spent too much money, but after awhile you get this creeping suspicion that the difficulty spikes are complete bull****, meant to breathe life into what is otherwise a tactically uninteresting game.
Other people complain about the tower-defense elements, or the commander aspect where you send subordinates on missions.  While these things don't bother me, I do ask - why?  The game has only one ending, and these things have no bearing, but these are far more involved than sidequests, so why are they there?
The skill trees are massive.  There are far too many abilities, and far too few points.  The progressive-skill design is complete nonsense.  Abilities not even remotely related to one another will be required to learn other abilities you may want.  It wouldn't be so bad to waste skill points like this, but like I said - no grinding.
My biggest gripe however is the GUI.  The game has controller support which in my opinion dumbs down the interface by sheer necessity, and in my opinion cripples the game.  You essentially have 6 hotkeys, and both mouse buttons.  The function keys can swap certain abilities on the mouse buttons, but even though skills might be able to be bound, depending on what type of skill it is it MAY NOT BE USABLE ON THAT PARTICULAR BUTTON.  This means that certain skills can only be left or right mouse-bound, even though the game says otherwise.  Any particular class has literally dozens of skills, but using any more than 8 is punishing because of the occasional need to kite.  It all feels much clunkier than it should have been.
So, essentially, the game would need massive retro-fitting to be a good LINEAR ARPG.  It simply breaks too many rules of good design with its self-imposed limitations to be enjoyable for very long, especially with the reality of games like Torchlight and Divinity: Original Sin. The latest (excepting recent exposition of 'MK X' of course) installment of the MK franchise is something of a reboot. Although Armageddon made a valiant attempt and I believe, successfully proved that there was still life in the MK universe, the finality of that game left the increasingly tedious development of the storyline without a credible future.
Without giving too many spoilers, MKKE tactfully (if unoriginally) preserves canonic prequel stories to a good extent and builds on the MK lore and setting whilst bringing the true essence of the gameplay back to its core.
Despite having full 3D Kombatant graphics, the game is mainly played as a 2D fighter, with the moves lists mostly simplified back to earlier titles. Although vombo (Kombo?) hits are recorded, each move is executed in turn, awaiting the full extent of the previous, making the fighting much less complex and tactical as tournament fans of the genre may prefer. However, this mechanical format encapsulates the more basic premise of the original game, rather than attempting to Kompete and Kopy other titles such as Streety Fighter and the Soul Caliber series. Although this may disappoint many fighting game enthusiasts, MKKE clearly shies away from earlier games which failed miserably in those areas.

A conservative approach to the complexity of the fighting lends itself to a lot more focus on quality of the product and the aspects of the franchise that originally kept it set aapart from its rivals. The gore, the characters and the fatalities are at the forefront of the experience and through retelling the stories of the first MK titles, one gets a feeling of what MK I, II and III really could have been had the technology been available - albeit this also brings with it the typical reliancve on spamming uppercuts and sweeps or certain special moves that plagued the arcade originals.
Doing away with obscure mini games such as the racing and puzzles, MKKE keeps the alternate modes rooted firmly in the core engine of the fighting, although multiplayer and tag-team possibilities increase the fun dramatically for up to four players. The storyline mode, too, has diverted away from past attempts at a poor RPG whilst giving the actual arcade experience a narrative which ties in with the overall storyline - keeping the storyline mode closer to the arcade mode and involving each of the characters in a number of bouts along the way although with more than a hint of homage to the cliché(but allegedly fan favourite) Scorpion/Sub Zero and f course, gratuitously borderline soft-porn attire and poses of the females.
The downsides are esentially related, that of slow gameplay (a little irrelevant aside from aesthetics, due to the practically turn-based nature of the kombat) and multiplayer issues. Online multiplayer is never well catered for in this genre, and without the slow tick rate, then the multiplayer experience would essentially be down to a battle of latency.
Overall, if you loved MK I and II - this game should fill a void and provide a few hours of simple, overly rithless bloodthirsty fun. However, if you want a more challenging, tournament beat-em-up and are used to the strategies of Street Fighter etc. you may find it lacking.

What's worse than a game with nice environments that nonetheless strings you along on a completely linear journey with an annoying companion? A game that pretends to offer you choices for exploration, but then puts you in time out and complains at you for minutes on end whining that "I worked really hard on this game! Do you not like it? Come on, man, making a game is hard."
I wanted to like this game. Cool looking protagonist and some meta humor are things I can usually get behind pretty easily, but I HAAAAATE this narrator. At first he seemed like he was going to be a pretty enjoyable part of the game; go off the beaten path marked by the arrows and you get rewarded with funny dialogue. Do you know the game's advanced movement mechanics? Watch in enjoyment as the narrator is baffled by the fact that you got over the ravine without extending the bridge. This is great!...Then I ignored one of the arrows, went into a part of the game that "wasn't completed yet," and was forced to listen to the narrator go into depth about previous iterations of the game and all the life-destroying effort he put into it while I'm literally locked in an inescapable room with a giant TV displaying the protagonist wielding a sword that had ranged capabilities instead of the piece of junk I was stuck with...Why are you showing me a game I would rather be playing while refusing to even let me play the game you want me to complete so badly?
Okay, so if you go off the beaten path, there is a chance you will get rewarded with a pittance of money, a meta line of sarcasm from the narrator, or being locked into a whiney narration sequence that literally makes you unable to play the game for a while (oh wait, did I say "rewarded"? Oops). One of them even has you start playing a different game and then I get kicked out of that game right when I had accepted my fate and started enjoying it a bit. Even when you *DO* follow the narrator's instructions and keep going down the main path, his constant lines of "Icey knows that she will be completely lost without the arrows" becomes infuriating to no end. I'm already following the path! Stop trying to get me to enjoy myself by actually exploring your game when you're just going to punish me for doing so by making me backtrack at best or locking me in a cage at worst! This game gives you a dash ability that easily and entertainingly produces sustained flight and you are forced into sewers and being punished for exploring.
The combat is...decent, but while there are some cool moves in the arsenal, the weakest enemies are way too easy to stunlock and the slightly harder ones can hardly be stunned at all and will just attack you before you can finish a single combo. Oh sure, there's an indicator that they are about to counter-attack, but Icey's attacks produce so much visual shine that you can't even see what you are hitting. And if you get stuck on something and want to grind up a bit...good luck. Everything in this game drops miniscule amounts of money compared to what upgrades cost and there's only like 10 short levels in this entire thing.
I got some serious catharsis from a couple of sequences near the end of the game where you get the options of going against the narrators commands through pure inaction. His anger became fuel for my patience as I finally got the chance to put him through what he did to me all those times I was locked in a room. However, those sweet, sweet moments of revenge were not worth having to put up with him in the first place. Let me explore and if I don't like what I find, let me go back to the main game on my own schedule. I would not recommend this game.
(Oh right, the game has an interesting aesthetic choice of this game is being run as some sort of test program and lots of menu options have file extensions and other things like that which lead to interesting meta moments when the "experiment" crashed and such, but small pros like that fail to outweigh the cons)

Sleeping Dogs' opening scenes do their best to sell us on the kinetic possibilities of the game's setting- a claustrophobic, richly detailed world in which the player can bust through restaurants and apartments, launch themselves from rooftops and through glass ceilings or onto double-decker buses, scramble up walls etc, essentially creating over and over again his or her own frantic Jackie Chan-esque action fantasy.
When completing tasks, Sleeping Dogs does a wonderful job continuing to deliver these fantasies. What happens when one ventures from the beaten path, however, sadly exposes these immersive fantasies as pre-determined bs, and the needlessly 'open' environment as underthought and underdeveloped. You see, each one of these spontaneous seeming parkour escapes is scripted. Try to climb a wall elsewhere in the city and the avatar stands there looking confused as to what he's doing there and what the player could possibly want him to do. Outside of areas with their playable scenes fixed (rooftops, alleyways, etc), Sleeping Dogs' world is all blandly painted hallways. Where other open world games actually encourage exploration (GTA) or at the very least offer the same service regardless of where the player chooses to take his/her fun (Just Cause 2), Sleeping Dogs loses interest in you when you attempt to find your own meaning in its world. While presenting itself as an open world, the game's openness only stretches as far as allowing the player the ability to walk between its small number of amusement rides (on the rails, its thrills scripted, predetermined).
Provided you stick to the path provided, Sleeping Dogs is actually a thoroughly entertaining action game. If you seek adventure and free-roaming chaos however, its non-scripted world is roughly as tedious as Arkham City albeit with better combat, less grappling hooks, and impossibly slippery cars.

It's hard to know what to think with SFV. By itself, SFV is a great fighting game with a good roster of characters, great visuals, and a good competitive scene. On the flipside, the mechanics are very dumbed down compared to SFIV and the roster is lacking many major characters from previous games (like Sagat and Blanka), while in terms of features the game has been sorely lacking since release. The fact that we had to wait so long to get a story mode was a slap in the face, and the lack of an arcade mode seems like some kind of sick joke.
On top of this, it seems like Capcom hasn't learned from their previous games and still continues their greedy, money grubbing practices by releasing a half finished game and releasing a ton of extra skins for real money that are unavailable with in-game currency and overpriced with real currency. It's a common theme with capcom, but I had hoped with the introduction of fight money that they would have stopped.
The online play is also pretty fun, but it lags quite a bit. It's often hard to find matches where people aren't lagging all over the place, which is very frustrating and makes it a lot less fun than it could be.
By itself, SFV is a good fighting game and I recommend it if you like street fighter. However, if you have to choose between this or a game like Guilty Gear or BlazBlue, I'd say go with the latter.

Probably the most metal point&click adventure that has ever or will ever be made... And it's about a little girl trying to find her lost kitty.
Fran Bow is pretty typical in regards to point&click mechanics - find the things, rub the things on other things, solve the puzzle, move on. It does have one unique mechanic in the form of pills or a remote that allow you to switch between different versions of the world in order to otain new items and solve puzzles. The puzzle design is well done with most of the puzzles being pretty straight-forward but there are a few stumpers here, too.
The aesthetics are the highligh of the game, however. The dialog is always just a little off, a little weird in a good way, and the artsyle is a bit... surreal... Everything about the game just has a unique tone and it all fits together nicely. The story and lore are all pretty interesting, too. Obviously calling it a story of a girl finding her cat is an over-simplification. There are a lot of layers to this story that begin with a young girl who ends up in a classic, twisted, labotomy-performing style insane asylum after her parants were mysteriously killed.
Overall, a fantastic game that's probably 10 hours long and well worth the purchase for P&C fans. Must-buy!

TL;DR at the bottom
Wow. Coming from a guy who spent a lot of time playing Left 4 Dead 2, I can personally say this game is actually really awesome. Some people simply don't play this game, because everything that's in this game is in Left 4 Dead 2. Which is true to a degree, however there are some differences. First of all, there are only Left 4 Dead campaigns (which is obviously expected). Second of all, There are no melee weapons either. Third of all, the community is almost dead.
Ok so why the hell would I recommend this game? Well, it feels like a better game. Let me explain. Valve wanted to create an amazing 4 player co-op zombie survival game and they did! It was pretty damn scary, it had great characters, the tone of the game was really dark, and it was a ton of fun! On top of that you could actually see your own legs! Left 4 Dead 2 just feels like an upgrade of the game by adding new campaigns, characters, and melee weapons. Left 4 Dead never got the attention it deserved (in my opinion) because Valve decided to release L4D2 way earlier than it was supposed to be released.
hat I'm trying to say is, Left 4 Dead feels more like a classic Valve game and feels like a simple game compared to Left 4 Dead 2. Left 4 Dead 2 is a great game, but Left 4 Dead is simply a classic.
TL;DR
Left 4 Dead is a great FPS game created by Valve that's taken place in the Zombie apocalypse. It's an amazing 4 player co-op game that anyone can enjoy! If you're still not satisfied of what this game has to offer, go buy L4D2.
Overall rating 9/10
